Let  
\[
\eta_\beta(x)=x^T\beta,\qquad \pi_\beta(x)=\frac{e^{x^T\beta}}{1+e^{x^T\beta}},\qquad 
q_\beta(x)=1-\pi_\beta(x),\qquad s_\beta(x)=\{\pi_\beta(x)q_\beta(x)\}^{1/2}.
\]
Write \(\pi^*(x)=\pi_{\beta^*}(x)\), \(q^*(x)=q_{\beta^*}(x)\), \(s^*(x)=s_{\beta^*}(x)\).

---

## (i) Loss function whose minimizer solves the estimating equation

Since
\[
\frac{\pi_\beta(x)}{q_\beta(x)}=e^{x^T\beta},
\]
we have, for \(Y\in\{0,1\}\),
\[
\frac{Y-\pi_\beta(X)}{\{\pi_\beta(X)q_\beta(X)\}^{1/2}}
=
Y e^{-X^T\beta/2}-(1-Y)e^{X^T\beta/2}.
\]
Therefore define the empirical loss
\[
\boxed{
\kappa_n(\beta)
=
\frac{2}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n
\left[
Y_i e^{-X_i^T\beta/2}+(1-Y_i)e^{X_i^T\beta/2}
\right].
}
\]
Equivalently, with \(\widetilde Y_i=2Y_i-1\in\{-1,1\}\),
\[
\kappa_n(\beta)=\frac{2}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n \exp\left(-\frac{\widetilde Y_i X_i^T\beta}{2}\right),
\]
the exponential loss.

Differentiating,
\[
\nabla_\beta \kappa_n(\beta)
=
\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n
\left[
-Y_i e^{-X_i^T\beta/2}+(1-Y_i)e^{X_i^T\beta/2}
\right]X_i
=
-\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n
\frac{Y_i-\pi_\beta(X_i)}{s_\beta(X_i)}X_i.
\]
Thus the estimating equation is precisely \(\nabla_\beta\kappa_n(\beta)=0\).

Also,
\[
\nabla_\beta^2\kappa_n(\beta)
=
\frac{1}{2n}\sum_{i=1}^n
\left[
Y_i e^{-X_i^T\beta/2}+(1-Y_i)e^{X_i^T\beta/2}
\right]X_iX_i^T
\succeq 0.
\]
Hence \(\kappa_n\) is convex, so any solution of the estimating equation is a global minimizer. If the Hessian is positive definite, the minimizer is unique.

---

## (ii) Consistency of \(\widetilde\beta\)

Assume the following regularity conditions.

1. \(\beta^*\) is identifiable:
   \[
   E(XX^T)\quad\text{is positive definite}.
   \]
2. A local uniform law of large numbers holds for \(\kappa_n\) in a neighborhood of \(\beta^*\). A sufficient condition is that for some \(r>0\),
   \[
   E\left[\|X\|^2 e^{r\|X\|/2}\right]<\infty.
   \]
3. \(\widetilde\beta\) is a finite global minimizer of \(\kappa_n\), equivalently a finite solution of the estimating equation from part (i).

Let
\[
\ell_\beta(X,Y)
=
2\left[
Y e^{-X^T\beta/2}+(1-Y)e^{X^T\beta/2}
\right],
\]
so that \(\kappa_n(\beta)=P_n\ell_\beta\), and define the population loss
\[
K(\beta)=E\ell_\beta(X,Y).
\]

Conditional on \(X\),
\[
E\{\ell_\beta(X,Y)\mid X\}
=
2\left[
\pi^*(X)e^{-X^T\beta/2}+q^*(X)e^{X^T\beta/2}
\right].
\]
Writing \(\delta=\beta-\beta^*\), one checks that
\[
E\{\ell_\beta(X,Y)\mid X\}
=
4s^*(X)\cosh\left(\frac{X^T\delta}{2}\right).
\]
Therefore
\[
K(\beta)-K(\beta^*)
=
4E\left[
s^*(X)\left\{
\cosh\left(\frac{X^T(\beta-\beta^*)}{2}\right)-1
\right\}
\right]\ge 0.
\]
Equality holds iff \(X^T(\beta-\beta^*)=0\) a.s. Since \(E(XX^T)\) is positive definite, this implies \(\beta=\beta^*\). Thus \(\beta^*\) is the unique minimizer of \(K\).

Now fix \(0<\varepsilon<r\). Since \(K\) is continuous and has a unique minimizer at \(\beta^*\),
\[
a_\varepsilon
:=
\inf_{\|\beta-\beta^*\|=\varepsilon}
\{K(\beta)-K(\beta^*)\}
>0.
\]
If \(\|\widetilde\beta-\beta^*\|>\varepsilon\), let
\[
\bar\beta
=
\beta^*
+
\varepsilon
\frac{\widetilde\beta-\beta^*}{\|\widetilde\beta-\beta^*\|}.
\]
By convexity of \(\kappa_n\) and since \(\widetilde\beta\) minimizes \(\kappa_n\),
\[
\kappa_n(\bar\beta)\le \kappa_n(\beta^*).
\]
Hence
\[
a_\varepsilon
\le
K(\bar\beta)-K(\beta^*)
\le
2\sup_{\|\beta-\beta^*\|\le \varepsilon}
|\kappa_n(\beta)-K(\beta)|.
\]
By the local uniform law of large numbers, the right-hand side is \(o_p(1)\). Therefore
\[
P(\|\widetilde\beta-\beta^*\|>\varepsilon)\to 0.
\]
Thus
\[
\boxed{\widetilde\beta\xrightarrow{p}\beta^*.}
\]

---

## (iii) Asymptotic normality of \(\widetilde\beta\)

Define the estimating function
\[
\psi(Z;\beta)
=
\frac{Y-\pi_\beta(X)}{s_\beta(X)}X,
\qquad Z=(X,Y).
\]
Using the representation above,
\[
\psi(Z;\beta)
=
\left[
Y e^{-X^T\beta/2}-(1-Y)e^{X^T\beta/2}
\right]X.
\]
The estimating equation is
\[
P_n\psi(\cdot;\widetilde\beta)=0.
\]

\[

=

\[
\boxed{

\right].

\]

the exponential loss.

\[
\nabla_\beta \kappa_n(\beta)
=
\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n
\left[
-Y_i e^{-X_i^T\beta/2}+(1-Y_i)e^{X_i^T\beta/2}
\right]X_i
=
-\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n
\frac{Y_i-\pi_\beta(X_i)}{s_\beta(X_i)}X_i.
\]

\[
\nabla_\beta^2\kappa_n(\beta)
=

\left[
Y_i e^{-X_i^T\beta/2}+(1-Y_i)e^{X_i^T\beta/2}
\right]X_iX_i^T

\]

Let

\[
\eta_\beta(X)=X^T\beta,\qquad 
\pi_\beta(X)=\frac{e^{X^T\beta}}{1+e^{X^T\beta}},\qquad 
s_\beta(X)=\{\pi_\beta(X)(1-\pi_\beta(X))\}^{1/2}.
\]

Also write \(\pi^*=\pi_{\beta^*}(X)\), \(s^*=s_{\beta^*}(X)\).

Useful identities are

\[
\frac{\pi_\beta(X)}{s_\beta(X)}=e^{X^T\beta/2},
\qquad 
\frac{1-\pi_\beta(X)}{s_\beta(X)}=e^{-X^T\beta/2}.
\]

---

## (i) Loss function whose minimizer is \(\tilde\beta\)

Define the empirical loss

\[
\kappa_n(\beta)
=
\frac{2}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n
\exp\left\{\frac{1-2Y_i}{2}X_i^T\beta\right\}.
\]

Equivalently,

\[
\kappa_n(\beta)
=
\frac{2}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n
\left[
Y_i e^{-X_i^T\beta/2}
+
(1-Y_i)e^{X_i^T\beta/2}
\right].
\]

Then

\[
\nabla_\beta \kappa_n(\beta)
=
\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n
\left[
(1-Y_i)e^{X_i^T\beta/2}
-
Y_i e^{-X_i^T\beta/2}
\right]X_i.
\]

Using the identities above,

\[
(1-Y_i)e^{X_i^T\beta/2}
-
Y_i e^{-X_i^T\beta/2}
=
-\frac{Y_i-\pi_\beta(X_i)}{s_\beta(X_i)}.
\]

Hence

\[
\nabla_\beta \kappa_n(\beta)
=
-\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n
\frac{Y_i-\pi_\beta(X_i)}{s_\beta(X_i)}X_i.
\]

Thus the estimating equation defining \(\tilde\beta\) is precisely \(\nabla_\beta \kappa_n(\beta)=0\).

Moreover,

\[
\nabla_\beta^2\kappa_n(\beta)
=
\frac1{2n}\sum_{i=1}^n
\exp\left\{\frac{1-2Y_i}{2}X_i^T\beta\right\}

\succeq 0,
\]

so \(\kappa_n\) is convex. Therefore any solution of the estimating equation is a global minimizer of \(\kappa_n\). Hence

\[
\boxed{
\tilde\beta=\arg\min_\beta \kappa_n(\beta)
}
\]

whenever the estimating equation has a solution.

---

I impose the following standard regularity assumptions.

1. \(p\) is fixed and \(\beta^*\) is an interior point of the parameter space.
2. Identifiability: for every \(a\neq 0\),

\[
P(a^TX\neq 0)>0.
\]

A sufficient condition is \(E[XX^T]\) positive definite.

\[
E\left[\sup_{\beta\in C}
\exp\left\{\frac12 |X^T\beta|\right\}\right]<\infty.
\]

\[
K(\beta)=E\{\kappa_n(\beta)\}
=
E\left[
2Y e^{-X^T\beta/2}
+
2(1-Y)e^{X^T\beta/2}
\right].
\]

\[

=
E\left[
2\pi^* e^{-X^T\beta/2}
+
2(1-\pi^*)e^{X^T\beta/2}
\right].
\]

Let \(\delta=\beta-\beta^*\). Since \(X^T\beta=X^T\beta^*+X^T\delta\),

\[
\pi^* e^{-X^T\beta^*/2}
=
(1-\pi^*)e^{X^T\beta^*/2}
=
s^*.
\]

\[
K(\beta)
=
4E\left[
s^* \cosh\left(\frac{X^T(\beta-\beta^*)}{2}\right)
\right].

\[
K(\beta^*)=4E[s^*],

and hence

\[
K(\beta)-K(\beta^*)
=
4E\left[
s^*

\cosh\left(\frac{X^T(\beta-\beta^*)}{2}\right)-1
\right\}
\right]\ge 0.

\[

\[
\sup_{\beta\in C}|\kappa_n(\beta)-K(\beta)|\xrightarrow{p}0

\[

=
\frac{\pi_\beta(X)-Y}{s_\beta(X)}X,

\[

\[

\[

\[

\[

\[

\[

\[
v^T(V_{\beta^*}-U_{\beta^*})v

\[
T=a^TX

\[

\[

\qquad
E[ZZ^T]=J.
\]

\[
\inf_b E[(T-b^TZ)^2]\ge 0.

\[

response.text:
Let \(X_1=x,\ X_2=y\). Since
\[
\bar X=\frac{X_1+X_2}{2},
\]
we have
\[
T=\max\left\{X_1,\frac{X_1+X_2}{2}\right\}
=
\begin{cases}
X_1, & X_1\ge X_2,\\[2mm]
\dfrac{X_1+X_2}{2}, & X_1<X_2.
\end{cases}
\]

---

## (a) CDF of \(T\)

For \(0\le t\le 1\),
\[
\{T\le t\}
=
\left\{X_1\le t,\ \frac{X_1+X_2}{2}\le t\right\}
=
\{x\le t,\ x+y\le 2t\}.
\]

Thus \(F_T(t)\) is the area in the unit square satisfying those inequalities.

For \(0\le t\le \frac12\),
\[
F_T(t)=\int_0^t (2t-x)\,dx
=2t^2-\frac{t^2}{2}
=\frac32 t^2.
\]

For \(\frac12<t\le 1\), the line \(x+y=2t\) exceeds \(1\) for \(x\le 2t-1\), so
\[
F_T(t)
=
\int_0^{2t-1}1\,dx+\int_{2t-1}^t (2t-x)\,dx.
\]
Hence
\[
F_T(t)
=
(2t-1)+\frac{1-t^2}{2}
=
2t-\frac12-\frac{t^2}{2}.
\]

Therefore
\[
\boxed{
F_T(t)=
\begin{cases}
0, & t<0,\\[1mm]
\dfrac32 t^2, & 0\le t\le \dfrac12,\\[2mm]
2t-\dfrac12-\dfrac{t^2}{2}, & \dfrac12<t\le 1,\\[2mm]
1, & t\ge 1.
\end{cases}}
\]

The corresponding density is
\[
f_T(t)=
\begin{cases}
3t, & 0<t<\frac12,\\[1mm]
2-t, & \frac12<t<1.
\end{cases}
\]

---

## (b) \(\mathbb E[T]\)

Using the density,
\[
\mathbb E[T]
=
\int_0^{1/2} t(3t)\,dt+\int_{1/2}^1 t(2-t)\,dt.
\]
Compute:
\[
\int_0^{1/2}3t^2\,dt=\frac18,
\]
and
\[
\int_{1/2}^1(2t-t^2)\,dt
=
\left[t^2-\frac{t^3}{3}\right]_{1/2}^1
=
\frac{11}{24}.
\]
Therefore
\[
\boxed{\mathbb E[T]=\frac18+\frac{11}{24}=\frac{7}{12}.}
\]

---

## Conditional law of \(X_1\mid T=t\)

This will be used for parts (c) and (d).

Let
\[
A=\{X_1\ge X_2\},\qquad B=\{X_1<X_2\}.
\]

On \(A\), \(T=X_1\). Thus for fixed \(T=t\), this contributes the vertical segment \(x=t,\ 0\le y\le t\), having weight proportional to \(t\).

On \(B\), \(T=(X_1+X_2)/2\). For fixed \(T=t\), we have
\[
x+y=2t,\qquad x<y,
\]
so
\[
x\in [a(t),t],
\qquad 
a(t)=\max\{0,2t-1\}.
\]
The change of variables \((x,y)\mapsto (x,t)\), with \(y=2t-x\), has Jacobian \(2\). Hence the continuous contribution has density proportional to \(2\,dx\) on \([a(t),t]\).

Thus a regular conditional distribution is
\[
\mathbb P(X_1\in du\mid T=t)
=
\frac{t}{f_T(t)}\delta_t(du)
+
\frac{2}{f_T(t)}\mathbf 1_{\{a(t)\le u\le t\}}\,du,
\]
where
\[
f_T(t)=t+2(t-a(t)).
\]

Equivalently:

- If \(0<t\le \frac12\), then \(a(t)=0\), \(f_T(t)=3t\). So
  \[
  X_1\mid T=t
  \sim
  \frac13\delta_t+\frac23\operatorname{Unif}[0,t].
  \]

- If \(\frac12<t\le 1\), then \(a(t)=2t-1\), \(f_T(t)=2-t\). So
  \[
  X_1\mid T=t
  \sim
  \frac{t}{2-t}\delta_t
  +
  \frac{2(1-t)}{2-t}\operatorname{Unif}[2t-1,t].
  \]

At \(t=0\), we take the natural continuous extension, giving \(X_1=0\).

---

## (c) \(\mathbb E[X_1\mid T=t]\)

### Case 1: \(0\le t\le \frac12\)

Here
\[
X_1\mid T=t\sim \frac13\delta_t+\frac23\operatorname{Unif}[0,t].
\]
Therefore
\[
\mathbb E[X_1\mid T=t]
=
\frac13 t+\frac23\cdot \frac t2
=
\frac{2t}{3}.
\]

### Case 2: \(\frac12<t\le 1\)

Here
\[
X_1\mid T=t
\sim
\frac{t}{2-t}\delta_t
+
\frac{2(1-t)}{2-t}\operatorname{Unif}[2t-1,t].
\]
The mean of \(\operatorname{Unif}[2t-1,t]\) is
\[
\frac{(2t-1)+t}{2}=\frac{3t-1}{2}.
\]
Thus
\[
\mathbb E[X_1\mid T=t]
=
\frac{t}{2-t}t
+
\frac{2(1-t)}{2-t}\cdot \frac{3t-1}{2}.
\]
Simplifying,
\[
\mathbb E[X_1\mid T=t]
=
\frac{t^2+(1-t)(3t-1)}{2-t}
=
\frac{-2t^2+4t-1}{2-t}.
\]

Therefore
\[
\boxed{
\mathbb E[X_1\mid T=t]
=
\begin{cases}
\dfrac{2t}{3}, & 0\le t\le \dfrac12,\\[2mm]
\dfrac{-2t^2+4t-1}{2-t}, & \dfrac12<t\le 1.
\end{cases}}
\]

The two formulas agree at \(t=\frac12\).

---

## (d) \(\operatorname{Var}(X_1\mid T=t)\)

### Case 1: \(0\le t\le \frac12\)

Again,
\[

Let \(X_1=x,\ X_2=y\). Since
\[
\bar X=\frac{X_1+X_2}{2},
\]
we have
\[
T=\max\left\{X_1,\frac{X_1+X_2}{2}\right\}
=
\begin{cases}
X_1, & X_1\ge X_2,\\[2mm]
\dfrac{X_1+X_2}{2}, & X_1<X_2.
\end{cases}
\]

---

## (a) CDF of \(T\)

For \(0\le t\le 1\),
\[
\{T\le t\}
=
\left\{X_1\le t,\ \frac{X_1+X_2}{2}\le t\right\}
=
\{x\le t,\ x+y\le 2t\}.
\]

Thus \(F_T(t)\) is the area in the unit square satisfying those inequalities.

For \(0\le t\le \frac12\),
\[
F_T(t)=\int_0^t (2t-x)\,dx
=2t^2-\frac{t^2}{2}
=\frac32 t^2.
\]

For \(\frac12<t\le 1\), the line \(x+y=2t\) exceeds \(1\) for \(x\le 2t-1\), so
\[
F_T(t)
=
\int_0^{2t-1}1\,dx+\int_{2t-1}^t (2t-x)\,dx.
\]
Hence
\[
F_T(t)
=
(2t-1)+\frac{1-t^2}{2}
=
2t-\frac12-\frac{t^2}{2}.
\]

Therefore
\[
\boxed{
F_T(t)=
\begin{cases}
0, & t<0,\\[1mm]
\dfrac32 t^2, & 0\le t\le \dfrac12,\\[2mm]
2t-\dfrac12-\dfrac{t^2}{2}, & \dfrac12<t\le 1,\\[2mm]
1, & t\ge 1.
\end{cases}}
\]

The corresponding density is
\[
f_T(t)=
\begin{cases}
3t, & 0<t<\frac12,\\[1mm]
2-t, & \frac12<t<1.
\end{cases}
\]

---

## (b) \(\mathbb E[T]\)

Using the density,
\[
\mathbb E[T]
=
\int_0^{1/2} t(3t)\,dt+\int_{1/2}^1 t(2-t)\,dt.
\]
Compute:
\[
\int_0^{1/2}3t^2\,dt=\frac18,
\]
and
\[
\int_{1/2}^1(2t-t^2)\,dt
=
\left[t^2-\frac{t^3}{3}\right]_{1/2}^1
=
\frac{11}{24}.
\]
Therefore
\[
\boxed{\mathbb E[T]=\frac18+\frac{11}{24}=\frac{7}{12}.}
\]

---

## Conditional law of \(X_1\mid T=t\)

This will be used for parts (c) and (d).

Let
\[
A=\{X_1\ge X_2\},\qquad B=\{X_1<X_2\}.
\]

On \(A\), \(T=X_1\). Thus for fixed \(T=t\), this contributes the vertical segment \(x=t,\ 0\le y\le t\), having weight proportional to \(t\).

On \(B\), \(T=(X_1+X_2)/2\). For fixed \(T=t\), we have
\[
x+y=2t,\qquad x<y,
\]
so
\[
x\in [a(t),t],
\qquad 
a(t)=\max\{0,2t-1\}.
\]
The change of variables \((x,y)\mapsto (x,t)\), with \(y=2t-x\), has Jacobian \(2\). Hence the continuous contribution has density proportional to \(2\,dx\) on \([a(t),t]\).

Thus a regular conditional distribution is
\[
\mathbb P(X_1\in du\mid T=t)
=
\frac{t}{f_T(t)}\delta_t(du)
+
\frac{2}{f_T(t)}\mathbf 1_{\{a(t)\le u\le t\}}\,du,
\]
where
\[
f_T(t)=t+2(t-a(t)).
\]

Equivalently:

- If \(0<t\le \frac12\), then \(a(t)=0\), \(f_T(t)=3t\). So
  \[
  X_1\mid T=t
  \sim
  \frac13\delta_t+\frac23\operatorname{Unif}[0,t].
  \]

- If \(\frac12<t\le 1\), then \(a(t)=2t-1\), \(f_T(t)=2-t\). So
  \[
  X_1\mid T=t
  \sim
  \frac{t}{2-t}\delta_t
  +
  \frac{2(1-t)}{2-t}\operatorname{Unif}[2t-1,t].
  \]

At \(t=0\), we take the natural continuous extension, giving \(X_1=0\).

---

## (c) \(\mathbb E[X_1\mid T=t]\)

### Case 1: \(0\le t\le \frac12\)

Here
\[
X_1\mid T=t\sim \frac13\delta_t+\frac23\operatorname{Unif}[0,t].
\]
Therefore
\[
\mathbb E[X_1\mid T=t]
=
\frac13 t+\frac23\cdot \frac t2
=
\frac{2t}{3}.
\]

### Case 2: \(\frac12<t\le 1\)

Here
\[
X_1\mid T=t
\sim
\frac{t}{2-t}\delta_t
+
\frac{2(1-t)}{2-t}\operatorname{Unif}[2t-1,t].
\]
The mean of \(\operatorname{Unif}[2t-1,t]\) is
\[
\frac{(2t-1)+t}{2}=\frac{3t-1}{2}.
\]
Thus
\[
\mathbb E[X_1\mid T=t]
=
\frac{t}{2-t}t
+
\frac{2(1-t)}{2-t}\cdot \frac{3t-1}{2}.
\]
Simplifying,
\[
\mathbb E[X_1\mid T=t]
=
\frac{t^2+(1-t)(3t-1)}{2-t}
=
\frac{-2t^2+4t-1}{2-t}.
\]

Therefore
\[
\boxed{
\mathbb E[X_1\mid T=t]
=
\begin{cases}
\dfrac{2t}{3}, & 0\le t\le \dfrac12,\\[2mm]
\dfrac{-2t^2+4t-1}{2-t}, & \dfrac12<t\le 1.
\end{cases}}
\]

The two formulas agree at \(t=\frac12\).

---

## (d) \(\operatorname{Var}(X_1\mid T=t)\)

### Case 1: \(0\le t\le \frac12\)

Again,
\[
X_1\mid T=t\sim \frac13\delta_t+\frac23\operatorname{Unif}[0,t].
\]

\[
\operatorname{Var}(X_1\mid T=t)
=
\frac23\cdot \frac{t^2}{12}
+
\frac13\frac23\left(t-\frac t2\right)^2.
\]
Thus
\[
\operatorname{Var}(X_1\mid T=t)
=
\frac{t^2}{18}+\frac{t^2}{18}
=
\frac{t^2}{9}.
\]

### Case 2: \(\frac12<t\le 1\)

Now
\[
X_1\mid T=t
\sim
\frac{t}{2-t}\delta_t
+
\frac{2(1-t)}{2-t}\operatorname{Unif}[2t-1,t].
\]
The uniform component has length
\[
t-(2t-1)=1-t,
\]
so its variance is
\[
\frac{(1-t)^2}{12}.
\]
Its mean is
\[
\frac{3t-1}{2}.
\]
The difference between the atom location \(t\) and the uniform mean is
\[
t-\frac{3t-1}{2}=\frac{1-t}{2}.
\]
Hence
\[
\operatorname{Var}(X_1\mid T=t)
=
\frac{2(1-t)}{2-t}\cdot \frac{(1-t)^2}{12}
+
\frac{t}{2-t}\frac{2(1-t)}{2-t}\left(\frac{1-t}{2}\right)^2.
\]
Simplifying,
\[
\operatorname{Var}(X_1\mid T=t)
=
\frac{(1-t)^3}{6(2-t)}
+
\frac{t(1-t)^3}{2(2-t)^2}.
\]
Putting over a common denominator,
\[
\operatorname{Var}(X_1\mid T=t)
=
\frac{(1-t)^3(1+t)}{3(2-t)^2}.
\]

Therefore
\[
\boxed{
\operatorname{Var}(X_1\mid T=t)
=
\begin{cases}
\dfrac{t^2}{9}, & 0\le t\le \dfrac12,\\[2mm]
\dfrac{(1-t)^3(1+t)}{3(2-t)^2}, & \dfrac12<t\le 1.
\end{cases}}
\]

Again, the two formulas agree at \(t=\frac12\), and at \(t=1\) the variance is \(0\), as expected.

response.text:
Let \(X=X_1\) and \(Y=X_2\). Then \(X,Y\) are independent Uniform\([0,1]\), and

\[
\bar X=\frac{X+Y}{2},\qquad T=\max\left\{X,\frac{X+Y}{2}\right\}.
\]

Observe that

\[
X\ge \frac{X+Y}{2}\iff X\ge Y.
\]

Hence

\[
T=
\begin{cases}
X, & Y\le X,\\[3pt]
\dfrac{X+Y}{2}, & Y>X.
\end{cases}
\]

---

## (a) CDF of \(T\)

For \(0\le t\le 1\),

\[
\{T\le t\}
=
\left\{X\le t,\ \frac{X+Y}{2}\le t\right\}
=
\{X\le t,\ X+Y\le 2t\}.
\]

Thus \(F_T(t)\) is the area in the unit square satisfying those inequalities.

For \(0\le t\le \frac12\),

\[
F_T(t)=\int_0^t (2t-x)\,dx
=2t^2-\frac{t^2}{2}
=\frac32 t^2.
\]

For \(\frac12\le t\le 1\), split according to whether \(2t-x\ge 1\):

\[
F_T(t)
=
\int_0^{2t-1}1\,dx+\int_{2t-1}^t (2t-x)\,dx.
\]

Therefore

\[
F_T(t)
=
(2t-1)+\left[2tx-\frac{x^2}{2}\right]_{2t-1}^t
=
2t-\frac12-\frac{t^2}{2}.
\]

Hence

\[
\boxed{
F_T(t)=
\begin{cases}
0, & t<0,\\[4pt]
\dfrac32 t^2, & 0\le t\le \dfrac12,\\[8pt]
2t-\dfrac12-\dfrac{t^2}{2}, & \dfrac12\le t\le 1,\\[8pt]
1, & t\ge 1.
\end{cases}}
\]

Thus the density is

\[
f_T(t)=
\begin{cases}
3t, & 0<t<\dfrac12,\\[4pt]
2-t, & \dfrac12<t<1.
\end{cases}
\]

---

## (b) \(\mathbb E[T]\)

Using the density,

\[
\mathbb E[T]
=
\int_0^{1/2} t(3t)\,dt+\int_{1/2}^1 t(2-t)\,dt.
\]

Compute:

\[
\int_0^{1/2}3t^2\,dt
=
\left[t^3\right]_0^{1/2}
=
\frac18,
\]

and

\[
\int_{1/2}^1 (2t-t^2)\,dt
=
\left[t^2-\frac{t^3}{3}\right]_{1/2}^1
=
\frac23-\left(\frac14-\frac1{24}\right)
=
\frac{11}{24}.
\]

Therefore

\[
\boxed{\mathbb E[T]=\frac18+\frac{11}{24}=\frac{7}{12}.}
\]

---

## Conditional distribution of \(X_1\) given \(T=t\)

We need this for parts (c) and (d). Let \(g\) be bounded and measurable. Then

\[
\mathbb E[g(X)h(T)]
=
\int_0^1\int_0^1 g(x)h(T(x,y))\,dy\,dx.
\]

Split into the regions \(y\le x\) and \(y>x\):

\[
\mathbb E[g(X)h(T)]
=
\int_0^1\int_0^x g(x)h(x)\,dy\,dx
+
\int_0^1\int_x^1 g(x)h\left(\frac{x+y}{2}\right)\,dy\,dx.
\]

The first term is

\[
\int_0^1 xg(x)h(x)\,dx.
\]

In the second term, set

\[
t=\frac{x+y}{2},\qquad dy=2\,dt.
\]

Then \(y>x\) corresponds to \(t>x\), and \(y\le 1\) corresponds to \(t\le \frac{x+1}{2}\). Thus

\[
\int_0^1\int_x^1 g(x)h\left(\frac{x+y}{2}\right)\,dy\,dx
=
\int_0^1\int_x^{(x+1)/2}2g(x)h(t)\,dt\,dx.
\]

Switching the order of integration, the range for \(x\) at fixed \(t\) is

\[
\max(0,2t-1)\le x\le t.
\]

Let

\[
a(t)=\max(0,2t-1).
\]

Then

\[
\mathbb E[g(X)h(T)]
=
\int_0^1 h(t)\left[tg(t)+2\int_{a(t)}^t g(x)\,dx\right]dt.
\]

Taking \(g\equiv 1\) gives

\[
f_T(t)=t+2(t-a(t)).
\]

Therefore, for \(0<t<1\),

\[
\mathbb E[g(X_1)\mid T=t]
=
\frac{tg(t)+2\int_{a(t)}^t g(x)\,dx}{t+2(t-a(t))}.
\]

Equivalently, conditionally on \(T=t\), \(X_1\) has an atom at \(x=t\) of weight \(t/f_T(t)\), plus a continuous component with density \(2/f_T(t)\) on \([a(t),t]\).

---

## (c) \(\mathbb E[X_1\mid T=t]\)

Take \(g(x)=x\). Then

\[
\mathbb E[X_1\mid T=t]
=
\frac{t^2+2\int_{a(t)}^t x\,dx}{t+2(t-a(t))}
=
\frac{t^2+t^2-a(t)^2}{t+2(t-a(t))}.
\]

So

\[
\mathbb E[X_1\mid T=t]
=
\frac{2t^2-a(t)^2}{t+2(t-a(t))}.
\]

If \(0\le t\le \frac12\), then \(a(t)=0\), so

\[
\mathbb E[X_1\mid T=t]
=
\frac{2t^2}{3t}
=
\frac{2t}{3}.
\]

If \(\frac12\le t\le 1\), then \(a(t)=2t-1\), so

\[
\mathbb E[X_1\mid T=t]
=
\frac{2t^2-(2t-1)^2}{2-t}
=
\frac{-2t^2+4t-1}{2-t}.
\]

Thus, using the continuous endpoint version,

\[
\boxed{
\mathbb E[X_1\mid T=t]
=
\begin{cases}
\dfrac{2t}{3}, & 0\le t\le \dfrac12,\\[8pt]
\dfrac{-2t^2+4t-1}{2-t}, & \dfrac12\le t\le 1.
\end{cases}}
\]

---

## (d) \(\operatorname{Var}(X_1\mid T=t)\)

First compute the conditional second moment. Taking \(g(x)=x^2\),

\[
\mathbb E[X_1^2\mid T=t]
=
\frac{t^3+2\int_{a(t)}^t x^2\,dx}{t+2(t-a(t))}.
\]

Since

\[
2\int_{a(t)}^t x^2\,dx
=
\frac23\left(t^3-a(t)^3\right),
\]

we get

\[
\mathbb E[X_1^2\mid T=t]
=
\frac{\frac53 t^3-\frac23 a(t)^3}{t+2(t-a(t))}.
\]

### Case 1: \(0\le t\le \frac12\)

Here \(a(t)=0\) and \(f_T(t)=3t\). Hence

\[
\mathbb E[X_1^2\mid T=t]
=
\frac{\frac53 t^3}{3t}
=
\frac59 t^2.
\]

Since

\[
\mathbb E[X_1\mid T=t]=\frac{2t}{3},
\]

we obtain

\[
\operatorname{Var}(X_1\mid T=t)
=
\frac59 t^2-\frac49 t^2
=
\frac19 t^2.
\]

### Case 2: \(\frac12\le t\le 1\)

Here \(a(t)=2t-1\) and \(f_T(t)=2-t\). Thus

\[
\mathbb E[X_1^2\mid T=t]
=
\frac{\frac53 t^3-\frac23(2t-1)^3}{2-t}.
\]

Expanding,

\[
\mathbb E[X_1^2\mid T=t]
=
\frac{-11t^3+24t^2-12t+2}{3(2-t)}.
\]

Also,

\[
\mathbb E[X_1\mid T=t]
=
\frac{-2t^2+4t-1}{2-t}.
\]

Therefore

\[
\operatorname{Var}(X_1\mid T=t)
=
\frac{-11t^3+24t^2-12t+2}{3(2-t)}
-
\left(\frac{-2t^2+4t-1}{2-t}\right)^2.
\]

Simplifying gives

\[
\operatorname{Var}(X_1\mid T=t)
=
\frac{(1-t)^3(1+t)}{3(2-t)^2}.
\]

Hence

\[
\boxed{
\operatorname{Var}(X_1\mid T=t)
=
\begin{cases}
\dfrac{t^2}{9}, & 0\le t\le \dfrac12,\\[10pt]
\dfrac{(1-t)^3(1+t)}{3(2-t)^2}, & \dfrac12\le t\le 1.
\end{cases}}
\]

The two formulas agree at \(t=\frac12\), and the endpoint values are understood by continuous extension.

Let \(X=X_1\) and \(Y=X_2\). Then \(X,Y\) are independent Uniform\([0,1]\), and

\[
\bar X=\frac{X+Y}{2},\qquad T=\max\left\{X,\frac{X+Y}{2}\right\}.
\]

Observe that

\[
X\ge \frac{X+Y}{2}\iff X\ge Y.
\]

Hence

\[
T=
\begin{cases}
X, & Y\le X,\\[3pt]
\dfrac{X+Y}{2}, & Y>X.
\end{cases}
\]

---

## (a) CDF of \(T\)

For \(0\le t\le 1\),

\[
\{T\le t\}
=
\left\{X\le t,\ \frac{X+Y}{2}\le t\right\}
=
\{X\le t,\ X+Y\le 2t\}.
\]

Thus \(F_T(t)\) is the area in the unit square satisfying those inequalities.

For \(0\le t\le \frac12\),

\[
F_T(t)=\int_0^t (2t-x)\,dx
=2t^2-\frac{t^2}{2}
=\frac32 t^2.
\]

For \(\frac12\le t\le 1\), split according to whether \(2t-x\ge 1\):

\[
F_T(t)
=
\int_0^{2t-1}1\,dx+\int_{2t-1}^t (2t-x)\,dx.
\]

Therefore

\[
F_T(t)
=
(2t-1)+\left[2tx-\frac{x^2}{2}\right]_{2t-1}^t
=
2t-\frac12-\frac{t^2}{2}.
\]

Hence

\[
\boxed{
F_T(t)=
\begin{cases}
0, & t<0,\\[4pt]
\dfrac32 t^2, & 0\le t\le \dfrac12,\\[8pt]
2t-\dfrac12-\dfrac{t^2}{2}, & \dfrac12\le t\le 1,\\[8pt]
1, & t\ge 1.
\end{cases}}
\]

Thus the density is

\[
f_T(t)=
\begin{cases}
3t, & 0<t<\dfrac12,\\[4pt]
2-t, & \dfrac12<t<1.
\end{cases}
\]

---

## (b) \(\mathbb E[T]\)

Using the density,

\[
\mathbb E[T]
=
\int_0^{1/2} t(3t)\,dt+\int_{1/2}^1 t(2-t)\,dt.
\]

Compute:

\[
\int_0^{1/2}3t^2\,dt
=
\left[t^3\right]_0^{1/2}
=
\frac18,
\]

and

\[
\int_{1/2}^1 (2t-t^2)\,dt
=
\left[t^2-\frac{t^3}{3}\right]_{1/2}^1
=
\frac23-\left(\frac14-\frac1{24}\right)
=
\frac{11}{24}.
\]

Therefore

\[
\boxed{\mathbb E[T]=\frac18+\frac{11}{24}=\frac{7}{12}.}
\]

---

## Conditional distribution of \(X_1\) given \(T=t\)

We need this for parts (c) and (d). Let \(g\) be bounded and measurable. Then

\[
\mathbb E[g(X)h(T)]
=
\int_0^1\int_0^1 g(x)h(T(x,y))\,dy\,dx.
\]

Split into the regions \(y\le x\) and \(y>x\):

\[
\mathbb E[g(X)h(T)]
=
\int_0^1\int_0^x g(x)h(x)\,dy\,dx
+
\int_0^1\int_x^1 g(x)h\left(\frac{x+y}{2}\right)\,dy\,dx.
\]

The first term is

\[
\int_0^1 xg(x)h(x)\,dx.
\]

In the second term, set

\[
t=\frac{x+y}{2},\qquad dy=2\,dt.
\]

Then \(y>x\) corresponds to \(t>x\), and \(y\le 1\) corresponds to \(t\le \frac{x+1}{2}\). Thus

\[
\int_0^1\int_x^1 g(x)h\left(\frac{x+y}{2}\right)\,dy\,dx
=
\int_0^1\int_x^{(x+1)/2}2g(x)h(t)\,dt\,dx.
\]

Switching the order of integration, the range for \(x\) at fixed \(t\) is

\[
\max(0,2t-1)\le x\le t.
\]

Let

\[
a(t)=\max(0,2t-1).
\]

Then

\[
\mathbb E[g(X)h(T)]
=
\int_0^1 h(t)\left[tg(t)+2\int_{a(t)}^t g(x)\,dx\right]dt.
\]

Taking \(g\equiv 1\) gives

\[
f_T(t)=t+2(t-a(t)).
\]

Therefore, for \(0<t<1\),

\[
\mathbb E[g(X_1)\mid T=t]
=
\frac{tg(t)+2\int_{a(t)}^t g(x)\,dx}{t+2(t-a(t))}.
\]

Equivalently, conditionally on \(T=t\), \(X_1\) has an atom at \(x=t\) of weight \(t/f_T(t)\), plus a continuous component with density \(2/f_T(t)\) on \([a(t),t]\).

---

## (c) \(\mathbb E[X_1\mid T=t]\)

Take \(g(x)=x\). Then

\[
\mathbb E[X_1\mid T=t]
=
\frac{t^2+2\int_{a(t)}^t x\,dx}{t+2(t-a(t))}
=
\frac{t^2+t^2-a(t)^2}{t+2(t-a(t))}.
\]

So

\[
\mathbb E[X_1\mid T=t]
=
\frac{2t^2-a(t)^2}{t+2(t-a(t))}.
\]

If \(0\le t\le \frac12\), then \(a(t)=0\), so

\[
\mathbb E[X_1\mid T=t]
=
\frac{2t^2}{3t}
=
\frac{2t}{3}.
\]

If \(\frac12\le t\le 1\), then \(a(t)=2t-1\), so

\[
\mathbb E[X_1\mid T=t]
=
\frac{2t^2-(2t-1)^2}{2-t}
=
\frac{-2t^2+4t-1}{2-t}.
\]

Thus, using the continuous endpoint version,

\[
\boxed{
\mathbb E[X_1\mid T=t]
=
\begin{cases}
\dfrac{2t}{3}, & 0\le t\le \dfrac12,\\[8pt]
\dfrac{-2t^2+4t-1}{2-t}, & \dfrac12\le t\le 1.
\end{cases}}
\]

---

## (d) \(\operatorname{Var}(X_1\mid T=t)\)

First compute the conditional second moment. Taking \(g(x)=x^2\),

\[
\mathbb E[X_1^2\mid T=t]
=
\frac{t^3+2\int_{a(t)}^t x^2\,dx}{t+2(t-a(t))}.
\]

Since

\[
2\int_{a(t)}^t x^2\,dx
=
\frac23\left(t^3-a(t)^3\right),
\]

we get

\[
\mathbb E[X_1^2\mid T=t]
=
\frac{\frac53 t^3-\frac23 a(t)^3}{t+2(t-a(t))}.
\]

### Case 1: \(0\le t\le \frac12\)

Here \(a(t)=0\) and \(f_T(t)=3t\). Hence

\[
\mathbb E[X_1^2\mid T=t]
=
\frac{\frac53 t^3}{3t}
=
\frac59 t^2.
\]

Since

\[
\mathbb E[X_1\mid T=t]=\frac{2t}{3},
\]

we obtain

\[
\operatorname{Var}(X_1\mid T=t)
=
\frac59 t^2-\frac49 t^2
=
\frac19 t^2.
\]

### Case 2: \(\frac12\le t\le 1\)

Here \(a(t)=2t-1\) and \(f_T(t)=2-t\). Thus

\[
\mathbb E[X_1^2\mid T=t]
=
\frac{\frac53 t^3-\frac23(2t-1)^3}{2-t}.
\]

Expanding,

\[
\mathbb E[X_1^2\mid T=t]
=
\frac{-11t^3+24t^2-12t+2}{3(2-t)}.
\]

Also,

\[
\mathbb E[X_1\mid T=t]
=
\frac{-2t^2+4t-1}{2-t}.
\]

Therefore

\[
\operatorname{Var}(X_1\mid T=t)
=
\frac{-11t^3+24t^2-12t+2}{3(2-t)}
-
\left(\frac{-2t^2+4t-1}{2-t}\right)^2.
\]

Simplifying gives

\[
\operatorname{Var}(X_1\mid T=t)
=
\frac{(1-t)^3(1+t)}{3(2-t)^2}.
\]

Hence

\[
\boxed{
\operatorname{Var}(X_1\mid T=t)
=
\begin{cases}
\dfrac{t^2}{9}, & 0\le t\le \dfrac12,\\[10pt]
\dfrac{(1-t)^3(1+t)}{3(2-t)^2}, & \dfrac12\le t\le 1.
\end{cases}}
\]

The two formulas agree at \(t=\frac12\), and the endpoint values are understood by continuous extension.

\int_B \left[x\mathbf 1_C(x)+2\int_x^{(x+1)/2}\mathbf 1_C(t)\,dt\right]dx.
\]

Switching the order of integration, let

\[
a(t)=\max\{0,2t-1\}.
\]

Then

\[
\mathbb P(X\in B,T\in C)
=
\int_C \left[t\mathbf 1_B(t)+2\int_{a(t)}^t \mathbf 1_B(x)\,dx\right]dt.
\]

Thus a regular conditional distribution of \(X_1\) given \(T=t\) is

\[
\mathbb P(X_1\in dx\mid T=t)
=
\frac{t\,\delta_t(dx)+2\mathbf 1_{[a(t),t]}(x)\,dx}{t+2(t-a(t))}.
\]

Therefore, for bounded measurable \(g\),

\[
\mathbb E[g(X_1)\mid T=t]
=
\frac{t g(t)+2\int_{a(t)}^t g(x)\,dx}{t+2(t-a(t))}.
\]

Taking \(g(x)=x\),

\[
\mathbb E[X_1\mid T=t]
=
\frac{t^2+2\int_{a(t)}^t x\,dx}{t+2(t-a(t))}
=
\frac{2t^2-a(t)^2}{3t-2a(t)}.
\]

Hence

\[
\boxed{
\mathbb E[X_1\mid T=t]
=
\begin{cases}
\dfrac{2t}{3}, & 0\le t\le \dfrac12,\\[10pt]
\dfrac{-2t^2+4t-1}{2-t}, & \dfrac12\le t\le 1.
\end{cases}}
\]

At \(t=1/2\), both formulas give \(1/3\).

---

## (d) \(\operatorname{Var}(X_1\mid T=t)\)

Using the same conditional distribution,

\[
\mathbb E[X_1^2\mid T=t]
=
\frac{t^3+2\int_{a(t)}^t x^2\,dx}{t+2(t-a(t))}
=
\frac{t^3+\frac23(t^3-a(t)^3)}{3t-2a(t)}.
\]

Thus

\[
\mathbb E[X_1^2\mid T=t]
=
\frac{\frac53 t^3-\frac23 a(t)^3}{3t-2a(t)}.
\]

### Case 1: \(0\le t\le 1/2\)

Then \(a(t)=0\), so

\[
\mathbb E[X_1^2\mid T=t]
=
\frac{\frac53 t^3}{3t}
=
\frac59 t^2.
\]

Since

\[
\mathbb E[X_1\mid T=t]=\frac{2t}{3},
\]

we get

\[
\operatorname{Var}(X_1\mid T=t)
=
\frac59 t^2-\frac49 t^2
=
\frac19 t^2.
\]

### Case 2: \(1/2\le t\le 1\)

Then \(a(t)=2t-1\). After simplification,

\[
\operatorname{Var}(X_1\mid T=t)
=
\frac{(1-t)^3(1+t)}{3(2-t)^2}.
\]

Therefore

\[
\boxed{
\operatorname{Var}(X_1\mid T=t)
=
\begin{cases}
\dfrac{t^2}{9}, & 0\le t\le \dfrac12,\\[10pt]
\dfrac{(1-t)^3(1+t)}{3(2-t)^2}, & \dfrac12\le t\le 1.
\end{cases}}
\]

## Part 0

Take \(\mathcal X=\{0,1\}\). Let \(Z\in\{0,1\}\) with

\[
\mathbb P(Z=0)=\mathbb P(Z=1)=\frac12,
\]

and define

\[
f(x,z)=x\oplus z,
\]

where \(\oplus\) denotes addition modulo \(2\). Thus \(z=0\) gives the identity map and \(z=1\) gives the transposition \(0\leftrightarrow 1\).

The transition matrix is

\[
P=\begin{pmatrix}
1/2 & 1/2\\
1/2 & 1/2
\end{pmatrix},
\]

which is irreducible and aperiodic.

However, in the grand coupling, starting from \(0\) and \(1\),

\[
X_t^0 \oplus X_t^1 = 1
\]

for every \(t\). Thus the two trajectories never meet, so

\[
\mathbb P(\tau_c=+\infty)=1.
\]

Therefore Assumption (C) fails.

---

## Part I

Let \(\mathcal X=\{0,1,2\}\), let \(Z\in\{-1,+1\}\) with

\[
\mathbb P(Z=1)=\mathbb P(Z=-1)=\frac12,
\]

and define

\[
f(i,z)=\max(0,\min(i+z,2)).
\]

Thus \(Z=+1\) pushes the chain one step to the right, with reflection at \(2\), and \(Z=-1\) pushes the chain one step to the left, with reflection at \(0\).

The transition matrix is

\[
P=
\begin{pmatrix}
1/2 & 1/2 & 0\\
1/2 & 0 & 1/2\\
0 & 1/2 & 1/2
\end{pmatrix}.
\]

This chain is irreducible, and since \(P(0,0)>0\) and \(P(2,2)>0\), it is aperiodic.

The matrix \(P\) is doubly stochastic, so the stationary distribution is

\[
\pi=\left(\frac13,\frac13,\frac13\right).
\]

Now consider the grand coupling. Let \(U=f(\cdot,+1)\) and \(D=f(\cdot,-1)\). Starting from all three states, after one step the images are either

\[
U(\{0,1,2\})=\{1,2\}
\]

or

\[
D(\{0,1,2\})=\{0,1\}.
\]

Coalescence occurs exactly when two consecutive increments are equal. Indeed,

\[
U\circ U
\]

maps every state to \(2\), while

\[
D\circ D
\]

maps every state to \(0\). If the signs alternate, coalescence does not occur.

Since an i.i.d. sequence of \(\pm1\) signs almost surely contains two consecutive equal signs, Assumption (C) holds.

At the first coalescence time \(\tau_c\), the common value is either \(0\) or \(2\), never \(1\). Hence

\[
\mathbb P(X_{\tau_c}^{x_0}=1)=0,
\]

whereas

\[
\pi(1)=\frac13.
\]

Thus \(X_{\tau_c}^{x_0}\) is not distributed according to \(\pi\).

---

# Part II

Recall that

\[
f_t(x)=f(x,Z_t),
\]

and for \(s<t\),

\[
F_s^t=f_{t-1}\circ f_{t-2}\circ \cdots \circ f_s.
\]

---

## (2)

Fix \(t>0\). The random maps

\[
(f_{-t},f_{-t+1},\dots,f_{-1})
\]

and

\[
(f_1,f_2,\dots,f_t)
\]

have the same joint distribution, because the \(Z_i\)'s are i.i.d.

Therefore the composed random maps

\[
F_{-t}^0=f_{-1}\circ\cdots\circ f_{-t}
\]

and

\[
F_1^{t+1}=f_t\circ\cdots\circ f_1
\]

have the same distribution as random functions \(\mathcal X\to\mathcal X\). Hence, for any \(x_0,y\in\mathcal X\),

\[
\mathbb P(F_{-t}^0(x_0)=y)
=
\mathbb P(F_1^{t+1}(x_0)=y),
\]

and also

\[
\mathbb P(\forall x\in\mathcal X,\ F_{-t}^0(x)=y)
=
\mathbb P(\forall x\in\mathcal X,\ F_1^{t+1}(x)=y).
\]

---

## (3)

Define

\[
M=\min\{t>0:F_{-t}^0\text{ is constant}\}.
\]

We prove that \(M<\infty\) a.s. under Assumption (C).

For \(n\ge1\),

\[
\{M\le n\}
=
\{F_{-n}^0\text{ is constant}\}.
\]

Indeed, if \(F_{-m}^0\) is constant for some \(m\le n\), then

\[
F_{-n}^0
=
F_{-m}^0\circ F_{-n}^{-m}
\]

is also constant.

Similarly, in the forward grand coupling,

\[
X_n^x=F_1^{n+1}(x).
\]

Therefore

\[
\{\tau_c\le n\}
=
\{F_1^{n+1}\text{ is constant}\}.
\]

Using part (2), summing over the possible constant values \(y\in\mathcal X\),

\[
\mathbb P(F_{-n}^0\text{ is constant})
=
\mathbb P(F_1^{n+1}\text{ is constant}).
\]

Hence

\[
\mathbb P(M\le n)=\mathbb P(\tau_c\le n).
\]

By Assumption (C),

\[
\mathbb P(\tau_c<\infty)=1,
\]

so

\[
\lim_{n\to\infty}\mathbb P(\tau_c\le n)=1.
\]

Therefore

\[
\lim_{n\to\infty}\mathbb P(M\le n)=1,
\]

which proves

\[
\mathbb P(M<\infty)=1.
\]

---

## (4)

We prove that for any \(x,y\in\mathcal X\) and any integer \(k\ge0\),

\[
\mathbb P\left(F_{-M}^0(x)=F_{-k-M}^0(y)\right)=1.
\]

Work pathwise on the event \(\{M<\infty\}\), which has probability \(1\) by part (3). Let \(M=m\). By definition, \(F_{-m}^0\) is constant. Let its common value be \(c\). Then

\[
F_{-m}^0(x)=c
\]

for every \(x\in\mathcal X\).

For \(k\ge1\),

\[
F_{-m-k}^0
=
F_{-m}^0\circ F_{-m-k}^{-m}.
\]

Since \(F_{-m}^0\) is constant with value \(c\), the whole composition is also constant with value \(c\). Thus

\[
F_{-m-k}^0(y)=c=F_{-m}^0(x).
\]

The case \(k=0\) is immediate. Therefore

\[
\mathbb P\left(F_{-M}^0(x)=F_{-k-M}^0(y)\right)=1.
\]

---

## (5)

We prove that for every \(x_0\in\mathcal X\),

\[
F_{-M}^0(x_0)\sim \pi.
\]

Let

\[
Y=F_{-M}^0(x_0).
\]

Also define, for deterministic \(n\ge1\),

\[
Y_n=F_{-n}^0(x_0).
\]

By part (4), once \(n\ge M\),

\[
Y_n=Y.
\]

Thus

\[
Y_n\to Y \qquad \text{a.s.}
\]

Now consider \(f_0(x)=f(x,Z_0)\). Since \(Y\) depends only on

\[
Z_{-1},Z_{-2},\dots,
\]

it is independent of \(Z_0\).

For each \(n\),

\[
f_0(Y_n)
=
f_0\circ f_{-1}\circ \cdots \circ f_{-n}(x_0)
=
F_{-n}^{1}(x_0).
\]

The composition \(F_{-n}^{1}\) uses the maps

\[
f_{-n},f_{-n+1},\dots,f_{0}.
\]

These have the same joint distribution as

\[
f_{-n-1},f_{-n},\dots,f_{-1}.
\]

Therefore

\[
F_{-n}^{1}(x_0)\stackrel d=F_{-n-1}^{0}(x_0)=Y_{n+1}.
\]

Hence

\[
f_0(Y_n)\stackrel d=Y_{n+1}.
\]

Let \(h:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R\) be bounded. Since \(Y_n\to Y\) a.s. and \(\mathcal X\) is finite,

\[
h(f_0(Y_n))\to h(f_0(Y))
\]

a.s., and

\[
h(Y_{n+1})\to h(Y)
\]

a.s. Therefore, by dominated convergence,

\[
\mathbb E[h(f_0(Y))]
=
\lim_{n\to\infty}\mathbb E[h(f_0(Y_n))]
=
\lim_{n\to\infty}\mathbb E[h(Y_{n+1})]
=
\mathbb E[h(Y)].
\]

Thus

\[
f(Y,Z_0)\stackrel d=Y.
\]

Since \(Y\) is independent of \(Z_0\), let \(\mu\) be the law of \(Y\). Then for every \(y\in\mathcal X\),

\[
\mu(y)
=
\mathbb P(Y=y)
=
\mathbb P(f(Y,Z_0)=y)
=
\sum_{x\in\mathcal X}\mu(x)\mathbb P(f(x,Z_0)=y).
\]

But

\[
\mathbb P(f(x,Z_0)=y)=P(x,y),
\]

so

\[
\mu(y)=\sum_x \mu(x)P(x,y).
\]

Thus

\[
\mu P=\mu.
\]

So \(\mu\) is a stationary distribution. Since the finite irreducible Markov chain has a unique stationary distribution, namely \(\pi\), we conclude

\[
\mu=\pi.
\]

Therefore

\[
F_{-M}^0(x_0)\sim \pi.
\]

---

## (6)

The algorithm is the standard coupling-from-the-past algorithm.

Initialize \(t=0\) and let \(\Phi\) be the identity map on \(\mathcal X\). Repeat:

1. Set \(t\leftarrow t+1\).
2. Generate a fresh \(Z_{-t}\).
3. Update

   \[
   \Phi \leftarrow \Phi\circ f(\cdot,Z_{-t}).
   \]

   After this update,

   \[
   \Phi=F_{-t}^0.
   \]

4. If \(\Phi\) is constant, output \(\Phi(x_0)\) and stop.

By part (3), the stopping time is \(M<\infty\) a.s. By part (5), the output

\[
F_{-M}^0(x_0)
\]

has distribution \(\pi\).

---

# Part III

We again consider

\[
\mathcal X=\{0,1,2\},
\]

with

\[
f(i,z)=\max(0,\min(i+z,2)),
\]

and

\[
\mathbb P(Z=1)=\mathbb P(Z=-1)=\frac12.
\]

Let \(U=f(\cdot,+1)\) and \(D=f(\cdot,-1)\).

The transition matrix is

\[
P=
\begin{pmatrix}
1/2 & 1/2 & 0\\
1/2 & 0 & 1/2\\
0 & 1/2 & 1/2
\end{pmatrix}.
\]

Solving \(\pi P=\pi\), we get

\[
\pi_0=\pi_1=\pi_2,
\]

so

\[
\pi=\left(\frac13,\frac13,\frac13\right).
\]

Now analyze Algorithm 2.

At \(t=1\), neither \(U\) nor \(D\) is constant, so the algorithm cannot stop.

At \(t=2\), the possible sign words are

\[
UU,\ UD,\ DU,\ DD.
\]

The compositions \(UU\) and \(DD\) are constant, while \(UD\) and \(DU\) are not. Moreover,

\[
UU \text{ outputs }2,
\qquad
DD \text{ outputs }0.
\]

Thus at \(t=2\), the algorithm stops with probability \(1/2\), but never outputs \(1\).

If the algorithm reaches \(t=3\), it discards the previous variables and generates a fresh block of length \(3\). The length-three sign words are

\[
UUU,\ UUD,\ UDU,\ UDD,\ DUU,\ DUD,\ DDU,\ DDD.
\]

The alternating words \(UDU\) and \(DUD\) are not constant. Among the remaining six words, the output is \(1\) only for

\[
UUD \quad \text{and} \quad DDU.
\]

Hence, for a fresh length-three block,

\[
\mathbb P(\text{constant and output }1)=\frac{2}{8}=\frac14,
\]

and

\[
\mathbb P(\text{not constant})=\frac{2}{8}=\frac14.
\]

Therefore

\[
\mathbb P(\text{Algorithm 2 outputs }1)
\le
\mathbb P(\text{output }1\text{ at }t=3)
+
\mathbb P(\text{algorithm reaches }t=4).
\]

The probability of reaching \(t=3\) is \(1/2\), because the \(t=2\) block must fail. Hence

\[
\mathbb P(\text{output }1\text{ at }t=3)
=
\frac12\cdot \frac14
=
\frac18.
\]

Similarly,

\[
\mathbb P(\text{algorithm reaches }t=4)
=
\frac12\cdot \frac14
=
\frac18.
\]

Thus

\[
\mathbb P(\text{Algorithm 2 outputs }1)
\le
\frac18+\frac18
=
\frac14.
\]

But

\[
\pi(1)=\frac13.
\]

Since

\[
\frac14<\frac13,
\]

Algorithm 2 does not output a random variable with distribution \(\pi\).

## (2)

Fix \(t>0\). The random maps

\[
(f_{-t},f_{-t+1},\dots,f_{-1})
\]

and

\[
(f_1,f_2,\dots,f_t)
\]

have the same joint distribution, because the \(Z_i\)'s are i.i.d.

Therefore the composed random maps

\[
F_{-t}^0=f_{-1}\circ\cdots\circ f_{-t}
\]

and

\[
F_1^{t+1}=f_t\circ\cdots\circ f_1
\]

have the same distribution as random functions \(\mathcal X\to\mathcal X\). Hence, for any \(x_0,y\in\mathcal X\),

\[
\mathbb P(F_{-t}^0(x_0)=y)
=
\mathbb P(F_1^{t+1}(x_0)=y),
\]

and also

\[
\mathbb P(\forall x\in\mathcal X,\ F_{-t}^0(x)=y)
=
\mathbb P(\forall x\in\mathcal X,\ F_1^{t+1}(x)=y).
\]

---

## (3)

Define

\[
M=\min\{t>0:F_{-t}^0\text{ is constant}\}.
\]

We prove that \(M<\infty\) a.s. under Assumption (C).

For \(n\ge1\),

\[
\{M\le n\}
=
\{F_{-n}^0\text{ is constant}\}.
\]

Indeed, if \(F_{-m}^0\) is constant for some \(m\le n\), then

\[
F_{-n}^0
=
F_{-m}^0\circ F_{-n}^{-m}
\]

is also constant.

Similarly, in the forward grand coupling,

\[
X_n^x=F_1^{n+1}(x).
\]

Therefore

\[
\{\tau_c\le n\}
=
\{F_1^{n+1}\text{ is constant}\}.
\]

Using part (2), summing over the possible constant values \(y\in\mathcal X\),

\[
\mathbb P(F_{-n}^0\text{ is constant})
=
\mathbb P(F_1^{n+1}\text{ is constant}).
\]

Hence

\[
\mathbb P(M\le n)=\mathbb P(\tau_c\le n).
\]

By Assumption (C),

\[
\mathbb P(\tau_c<\infty)=1,
\]

so

\[
\lim_{n\to\infty}\mathbb P(\tau_c\le n)=1.
\]

Therefore

\[
\lim_{n\to\infty}\mathbb P(M\le n)=1,
\]

which proves

\[
\mathbb P(M<\infty)=1.
\]

---

## (4)

We prove that for any \(x,y\in\mathcal X\) and any integer \(k\ge0\),

\[
\mathbb P\left(F_{-M}^0(x)=F_{-k-M}^0(y)\right)=1.
\]

Work pathwise on the event \(\{M<\infty\}\), which has probability \(1\) by part (3). Let \(M=m\). By definition, \(F_{-m}^0\) is constant. Let its common value be \(c\). Then

\[
F_{-m}^0(x)=c
\]

for every \(x\in\mathcal X\).

For \(k\ge1\),

\[
F_{-m-k}^0
=
F_{-m}^0\circ F_{-m-k}^{-m}.
\]

Since \(F_{-m}^0\) is constant with value \(c\), the whole composition is also constant with value \(c\). Thus

\[
F_{-m-k}^0(y)=c=F_{-m}^0(x).
\]

The case \(k=0\) is immediate. Therefore

\[
\mathbb P\left(F_{-M}^0(x)=F_{-k-M}^0(y)\right)=1.
\]

---

## (5)

We prove that for every \(x_0\in\mathcal X\),

\[
F_{-M}^0(x_0)\sim \pi.
\]

Let

\[
Y=F_{-M}^0(x_0).
\]

Also define, for deterministic \(n\ge1\),

\[
Y_n=F_{-n}^0(x_0).
\]

By part (4), once \(n\ge M\),

\[
Y_n=Y.
\]

Thus

\[
Y_n\to Y \qquad \text{a.s.}
\]

Now consider \(f_0(x)=f(x,Z_0)\). Since \(Y\) depends only on

\[
Z_{-1},Z_{-2},\dots,
\]

it is independent of \(Z_0\).

For each \(n\),

\[
f_0(Y_n)
=
f_0\circ f_{-1}\circ \cdots \circ f_{-n}(x_0)
=
F_{-n}^{1}(x_0).
\]

The composition \(F_{-n}^{1}\) uses the maps

\[
f_{-n},f_{-n+1},\dots,f_{0}.
\]

These have the same joint distribution as

\[
f_{-n-1},f_{-n},\dots,f_{-1}.
\]

Therefore

\[
F_{-n}^{1}(x_0)\stackrel d=F_{-n-1}^{0}(x_0)=Y_{n+1}.
\]

Hence

\[
f_0(Y_n)\stackrel d=Y_{n+1}.
\]

Let \(h:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R\) be bounded. Since \(Y_n\to Y\) a.s. and \(\mathcal X\) is finite,

\[
h(f_0(Y_n))\to h(f_0(Y))
\]

a.s., and

\[
h(Y_{n+1})\to h(Y)
\]

a.s. Therefore, by dominated convergence,

\[
\mathbb E[h(f_0(Y))]
=
\lim_{n\to\infty}\mathbb E[h(f_0(Y_n))]
=
\lim_{n\to\infty}\mathbb E[h(Y_{n+1})]
=
\mathbb E[h(Y)].
\]

Thus

\[
f(Y,Z_0)\stackrel d=Y.
\]

Since \(Y\) is independent of \(Z_0\), let \(\mu\) be the law of \(Y\). Then for every \(y\in\mathcal X\),

\[
\mu(y)
=
\mathbb P(Y=y)
=
\mathbb P(f(Y,Z_0)=y)
=
\sum_{x\in\mathcal X}\mu(x)\mathbb P(f(x,Z_0)=y).
\]

But

\[
\mathbb P(f(x,Z_0)=y)=P(x,y),
\]

so

\[
\mu(y)=\sum_x \mu(x)P(x,y).
\]

Thus

\[
\mu P=\mu.
\]

So \(\mu\) is a stationary distribution. Since the finite irreducible Markov chain has a unique stationary distribution, namely \(\pi\), we conclude

\[
\mu=\pi.
\]

Therefore

\[
F_{-M}^0(x_0)\sim \pi.
\]

---

## (6)

The algorithm is the standard coupling-from-the-past algorithm.

Initialize \(t=0\) and let \(\Phi\) be the identity map on \(\mathcal X\). Repeat:

1. Set \(t\leftarrow t+1\).
2. Generate a fresh \(Z_{-t}\).
3. Update

   \[
   \Phi \leftarrow \Phi\circ f(\cdot,Z_{-t}).
   \]

   After this update,

   \[
   \Phi=F_{-t}^0.
   \]

4. If \(\Phi\) is constant, output \(\Phi(x_0)\) and stop.

By part (3), the stopping time is \(M<\infty\) a.s. By part (5), the output

\[
F_{-M}^0(x_0)
\]

has distribution \(\pi\).

---

# Part III

We again consider

\[
\mathcal X=\{0,1,2\},
\]

with

\[
f(i,z)=\max(0,\min(i+z,2)),
\]

and

\[
\mathbb P(Z=1)=\mathbb P(Z=-1)=\frac12.
\]

Let \(U=f(\cdot,+1)\) and \(D=f(\cdot,-1)\).

The transition matrix is

\[
P=
\begin{pmatrix}
1/2 & 1/2 & 0\\
1/2 & 0 & 1/2\\
0 & 1/2 & 1/2
\end{pmatrix}.
\]

Solving \(\pi P=\pi\), we get

\[
\pi_0=\pi_1=\pi_2,
\]

so

\[
\pi=\left(\frac13,\frac13,\frac13\right).
\]

Now analyze Algorithm 2.

At \(t=1\), neither \(U\) nor \(D\) is constant, so the algorithm cannot stop.

At \(t=2\), the possible sign words are

\[
UU,\ UD,\ DU,\ DD.
\]

The compositions \(UU\) and \(DD\) are constant, while \(UD\) and \(DU\) are not. Moreover,

\[
UU \text{ outputs }2,
\qquad
DD \text{ outputs }0.
\]

Thus at \(t=2\), the algorithm stops with probability \(1/2\), but never outputs \(1\).

If the algorithm reaches \(t=3\), it discards the previous variables and generates a fresh block of length \(3\). The length-three sign words are

\[
UUU,\ UUD,\ UDU,\ UDD,\ DUU,\ DUD,\ DDU,\ DDD.
\]

The alternating words \(UDU\) and \(DUD\) are not constant. Among the remaining six words, the output is \(1\) only for

\[
UUD \quad \text{and} \quad DDU.
\]

Hence, for a fresh length-three block,

\[
\mathbb P(\text{constant and output }1)=\frac{2}{8}=\frac14,
\]

and

\[
\mathbb P(\text{not constant})=\frac{2}{8}=\frac14.
\]

Therefore

\[
\mathbb P(\text{Algorithm 2 outputs }1)
\le
\mathbb P(\text{output }1\text{ at }t=3)
+
\mathbb P(\text{algorithm reaches }t=4).
\]

The probability of reaching \(t=3\) is \(1/2\), because the \(t=2\) block must fail. Hence

\[
\mathbb P(\text{output }1\text{ at }t=3)
=
\frac12\cdot \frac14
=
\frac18.
\]

Similarly,

\[
\mathbb P(\text{algorithm reaches }t=4)
=
\frac12\cdot \frac14
=
\frac18.
\]

Thus

\[
\mathbb P(\text{Algorithm 2 outputs }1)
\le
\frac18+\frac18
=
\frac14.
\]

But

\[
\pi(1)=\frac13.
\]

Since

\[
\frac14<\frac13,
\]

Algorithm 2 does not output a random variable with distribution \(\pi\).

## Part 0

Take \(\mathcal X=\{0,1\}\). Let \(Z\sim \mathrm{Bernoulli}(1/2)\), and define

\[
f(x,z)=x\oplus z,
\]

where \(\oplus\) denotes addition mod \(2\). Thus \(z=0\) gives the identity map and \(z=1\) gives the flip map.

Then

\[
P(x,y)=\mathbb P(f(x,Z)=y)=\frac12,\qquad x,y\in\{0,1\}.
\]

So

\[
P=\begin{pmatrix}
1/2&1/2\\
1/2&1/2
\end{pmatrix},
\]

which is irreducible and aperiodic. However, each random map \(f(\cdot,Z_t)\) is a bijection of \(\{0,1\}\), hence every composition is also a bijection and therefore never constant. Thus the two coupled chains never coalesce:

\[
\mathbb P(\tau_c=+\infty)=1.
\]

So Assumption (C) need not hold for an arbitrary random mapping representation.

---

## Part I

Let \(\mathcal X=\{0,1,2\}\). Let \(Z\in\{c,r\}\) with

\[
\mathbb P(Z=c)=\mathbb P(Z=r)=\frac12.
\]

Define

\[
f(x,c)=0,\qquad f(x,r)=x+1 \pmod 3.
\]

Thus \(c\) is the constant map to \(0\), while \(r\) is the cyclic permutation \(0\to1\to2\to0\).

The transition matrix is

\[
P=
\begin{pmatrix}
1/2&1/2&0\\
1/2&0&1/2\\
1&0&0
\end{pmatrix}.
\]

This chain is irreducible, since \(0\to1\to2\to0\) is possible, and aperiodic since \(P(0,0)>0\).

Before the first occurrence of \(c\), the maps are only cyclic permutations, so the grand coupling has not coalesced. At the first time \(c\) occurs, every state is sent to \(0\). Hence

\[
\tau_c=\min\{t\ge1:Z_t=c\},
\]

and for every \(x_0\in\mathcal X\),

\[
X^{x_0}_{\tau_c}=0 \qquad \text{a.s.}
\]

But the stationary distribution is not \(\delta_0\). Solving \(\pi P=\pi\), we get

\[
\pi_1=\frac12\pi_0,\qquad \pi_2=\frac12\pi_1=\frac14\pi_0,
\]

so

\[
\pi_0+\pi_1+\pi_2=\pi_0\left(1+\frac12+\frac14\right)=1,
\]

and therefore

\[
\pi=\left(\frac47,\frac27,\frac17\right).
\]

Thus \(X^{x_0}_{\tau_c}\sim \delta_0\neq \pi\).

---

## Part II

Write \(f_t(x)=f(x,Z_t)\). We use the convention \(F^s_s=\mathrm{id}\).

### (2)

For fixed \(t>0\),

\[
F^0_{-t}=f_{-1}\circ f_{-2}\circ\cdots\circ f_{-t},
\]

while

\[
F^{t+1}_1=f_t\circ f_{t-1}\circ\cdots\circ f_1.
\]

The random maps \(f_s\) are i.i.d., so the ordered \(t\)-tuple

\[
(f_{-t},f_{-t+1},\dots,f_{-1})
\]

has the same distribution as

\[
(f_1,f_2,\dots,f_t).
\]

Therefore the random functions \(F^0_{-t}\) and \(F^{t+1}_1\) have the same law. Hence for any \(x_0,y\in\mathcal X\),

\[
\mathbb P(F^0_{-t}(x_0)=y)
=
\mathbb P(F^{t+1}_1(x_0)=y).
\]

Similarly, since the full random functions have the same law,

\[
\mathbb P(\forall x\in\mathcal X,\ F^0_{-t}(x)=y)
=
\mathbb P(\forall x\in\mathcal X,\ F^{t+1}_1(x)=y).
\]

---

### (3)

Recall

\[
M=\min\{t>0:F^0_{-t}\text{ is constant}\}.
\]

For \(t\ge1\),

\[
\{M\le t\}=\{F^0_{-t}\text{ is constant}\}.
\]

Indeed, if \(F^0_{-m}\) is constant for some \(m\le t\), then

\[
F^0_{-t}=F^0_{-m}\circ F^{-m}_{-t}
\]

is also constant.

Similarly, for the forward grand coupling,

\[
\{\tau_c\le t\}=\{F^{t+1}_1\text{ is constant}\}.
\]

By part (2), the random functions \(F^0_{-t}\) and \(F^{t+1}_1\) have the same distribution, so

\[
\mathbb P(M>t)
=
\mathbb P(F^0_{-t}\text{ is not constant})
=
\mathbb P(F^{t+1}_1\text{ is not constant})
=
\mathbb P(\tau_c>t).
\]

Under Assumption (C), \(\tau_c<\infty\) a.s., so

\[
\mathbb P(\tau_c>t)\to0.
\]

Therefore

\[
\mathbb P(M=\infty)=\lim_{t\to\infty}\mathbb P(M>t)=0.
\]

Thus \(M<\infty\) a.s.

---

### (4)

Fix \(x,y\in\mathcal X\) and \(k\ge0\). On the event \(\{M=m\}\), the map \(F^0_{-m}\) is constant. Hence

\[
F^0_{-m}(x)=F^0_{-m}(u)
\]

for every \(u\in\mathcal X\).

But

\[
F^0_{-k-m}
=
F^0_{-m}\circ F^{-m}_{-k-m}.
\]

Therefore

\[
F^0_{-k-m}(y)
=
F^0_{-m}\bigl(F^{-m}_{-k-m}(y)\bigr)
=
F^0_{-m}(x).
\]

Since \(M<\infty\) a.s., we conclude

\[
\mathbb P\bigl(F^0_{-M}(x)=F^0_{-k-M}(y)\bigr)=1.
\]

---

Define for each \(n\in\mathbb Z\)

\[
M_n=\min\{t>0:F^n_{n-t}\text{ is constant}\},
\]

and

\[
Y_n=F^n_{n-M_n}(x_0).
\]

\[
Y_0=F^0_{-M}(x_0)

has the same distribution as \(Y_1\).

We now prove a pathwise relation. Since \(F^0_{-M_0}\) is constant,

\[
F^1_{-M_0}=f_0\circ F^0_{-M_0}

is also constant. Hence

\[
M_1\le M_0+1.
\]

Thus \(1-M_1\ge -M_0\). Since \(F^1_{1-M_1}\) is constant,

\[
F^1_{-M_0}(x_0)
=
F^1_{1-M_1}\bigl(F^{1-M_1}_{-M_0}(x_0)\bigr)
=
F^1_{1-M_1}(x_0)
=
Y_1.
\]

But

\[
F^1_{-M_0}(x_0)
=
f_0(F^0_{-M_0}(x_0))
=
f(Y_0,Z_0).
\]

Therefore

\[
f(Y_0,Z_0)=Y_1 \qquad \text{a.s.}
\]

Since \(Y_1\stackrel d=Y_0\), we have

\[
f(Y_0,Z_0)\stackrel d=Y_0.
\]

Also, \(Y_0\) is measurable with respect to \(\sigma(Z_{-1},Z_{-2},\dots)\), so \(Y_0\) is independent of \(Z_0\).

Let \(\mu\) be the law of \(Y_0\). Then for every \(y\in\mathcal X\),

\[
\mu(y)
=
\mathbb P(Y_0=y)
=
\mathbb P(f(Y_0,Z_0)=y).
\]

Using independence of \(Y_0\) and \(Z_0\),

\[
\mathbb P(f(Y_0,Z_0)=y)
=
\sum_{x\in\mathcal X}\mu(x)\mathbb P(f(x,Z_0)=y)
=
\sum_{x\in\mathcal X}\mu(x)P(x,y).
\]

Thus

\[
\mu=\mu P.
\]

So \(\mu\) is a stationary distribution for \(P\). Since \(P\) is irreducible on the finite set \(\mathcal X\), the stationary distribution is unique. Therefore

\[
\mu=\pi.
\]

Hence

\[
F^0_{-M}(x_0)\sim \pi.
\]

---

### (6)

The algorithm is the usual coupling-from-the-past algorithm.

Initialize \(t=0\) and \(G=\mathrm{id}_{\mathcal X}\). Then repeat:

1. Set \(t\leftarrow t+1\).
2. Generate a fresh \(Z_{-t}\).
3. Let \(g_t(x)=f(x,Z_{-t})\).
4. Update

   \[
   G\leftarrow G\circ g_t.
   \]

   After this update,

   \[
   G=F^0_{-t}.
   \]

5. If \(G\) is constant, output \(G(x_0)\) and stop.

By part (3), this algorithm stops a.s. at time \(M\), and by part (5), the output

\[
G(x_0)=F^0_{-M}(x_0)
\]

has distribution \(\pi\).

---

## Part III

### (7)

Here \(\mathcal X=\{0,1,2\}\) and

\[
f(i,z)=\max(0,\min(i+z,2)),

Thus for \(t\ge2\),

\[

=

=
1-2^{1-t}.
\]

=

=
\sum_{r=2}^t 2^{1-r}K_{t-r}.
\]

\[
q_t
=

\[
q_t=
\frac{p_t}{3}
-
\frac{2^{1-t}}{3}\sum_{n=0}^{t-2}(-1)^n.

\[

\begin{cases}

p_t/3-2^{1-t}/3, & t\text{ even}.
\end{cases}

\[

\[
\mathbb P(\text{output}=1)
=
\sum_{t\ge1}

\[
\prod_{t=1}^n(1-p_t)
=
\prod_{t=2}^n 2^{1-t}
\to0.

\[
\sum_{t\ge1}
\left(\prod_{s<t}(1-p_s)\right)p_t
=

\]

\[
\mathbb P(\text{output}=1)
<
\frac13
\sum_{t\ge1}

## Part 0

Take \(\mathcal X=\{0,1\}\). Let \(Z\sim \mathrm{Bernoulli}(1/2)\), and define

\[
f(x,z)=x\oplus z,
\]

where \(\oplus\) denotes addition mod \(2\). Thus \(z=0\) gives the identity map and \(z=1\) gives the flip map.

Then

\[
P(x,y)=\mathbb P(f(x,Z)=y)=\frac12,\qquad x,y\in\{0,1\}.
\]

So

\[
P=\begin{pmatrix}
1/2&1/2\\
1/2&1/2
\end{pmatrix},
\]

which is irreducible and aperiodic. However, each random map \(f(\cdot,Z_t)\) is a bijection of \(\{0,1\}\), hence every composition is also a bijection and therefore never constant. Thus the two coupled chains never coalesce:

\[
\mathbb P(\tau_c=+\infty)=1.
\]

So Assumption (C) need not hold for an arbitrary random mapping representation.

---

## Part I

Let \(\mathcal X=\{0,1,2\}\). Let \(Z\in\{c,r\}\) with

\[
\mathbb P(Z=c)=\mathbb P(Z=r)=\frac12.
\]

Define

\[
f(x,c)=0,\qquad f(x,r)=x+1 \pmod 3.
\]

Thus \(c\) is the constant map to \(0\), while \(r\) is the cyclic permutation \(0\to1\to2\to0\).

The transition matrix is

\[
P=
\begin{pmatrix}
1/2&1/2&0\\
1/2&0&1/2\\
1&0&0
\end{pmatrix}.
\]

This chain is irreducible, since \(0\to1\to2\to0\) is possible, and aperiodic since \(P(0,0)>0\).

Before the first occurrence of \(c\), the maps are only cyclic permutations, so the grand coupling has not coalesced. At the first time \(c\) occurs, every state is sent to \(0\). Hence

\[
\tau_c=\min\{t\ge1:Z_t=c\},
\]

and for every \(x_0\in\mathcal X\),

\[
X^{x_0}_{\tau_c}=0 \qquad \text{a.s.}
\]

But the stationary distribution is not \(\delta_0\). Solving \(\pi P=\pi\), we get

\[
\pi_1=\frac12\pi_0,\qquad \pi_2=\frac12\pi_1=\frac14\pi_0,
\]

so

\[
\pi_0+\pi_1+\pi_2=\pi_0\left(1+\frac12+\frac14\right)=1,
\]

and therefore

\[
\pi=\left(\frac47,\frac27,\frac17\right).
\]

Thus \(X^{x_0}_{\tau_c}\sim \delta_0\neq \pi\).

---

## Part II

Write \(f_t(x)=f(x,Z_t)\). We use the convention \(F^s_s=\mathrm{id}\).

### (2)

For fixed \(t>0\),

\[
F^0_{-t}=f_{-1}\circ f_{-2}\circ\cdots\circ f_{-t},
\]

while

\[
F^{t+1}_1=f_t\circ f_{t-1}\circ\cdots\circ f_1.
\]

The random maps \(f_s\) are i.i.d., so the ordered \(t\)-tuple

\[
(f_{-t},f_{-t+1},\dots,f_{-1})
\]

has the same distribution as

\[
(f_1,f_2,\dots,f_t).
\]

Therefore the random functions \(F^0_{-t}\) and \(F^{t+1}_1\) have the same law. Hence for any \(x_0,y\in\mathcal X\),

\[
\mathbb P(F^0_{-t}(x_0)=y)
=
\mathbb P(F^{t+1}_1(x_0)=y).
\]

Similarly, since the full random functions have the same law,

\[
\mathbb P(\forall x\in\mathcal X,\ F^0_{-t}(x)=y)
=
\mathbb P(\forall x\in\mathcal X,\ F^{t+1}_1(x)=y).
\]

---

### (3)

Recall

\[
M=\min\{t>0:F^0_{-t}\text{ is constant}\}.
\]

For \(t\ge1\),

\[
\{M\le t\}=\{F^0_{-t}\text{ is constant}\}.
\]

Indeed, if \(F^0_{-m}\) is constant for some \(m\le t\), then

\[
F^0_{-t}=F^0_{-m}\circ F^{-m}_{-t}
\]

is also constant.

Similarly, for the forward grand coupling,

\[
\{\tau_c\le t\}=\{F^{t+1}_1\text{ is constant}\}.
\]

By part (2), the random functions \(F^0_{-t}\) and \(F^{t+1}_1\) have the same distribution, so

\[
\mathbb P(M>t)
=
\mathbb P(F^0_{-t}\text{ is not constant})
=
\mathbb P(F^{t+1}_1\text{ is not constant})
=
\mathbb P(\tau_c>t).
\]

Under Assumption (C), \(\tau_c<\infty\) a.s., so

\[
\mathbb P(\tau_c>t)\to0.
\]

Therefore

\[
\mathbb P(M=\infty)=\lim_{t\to\infty}\mathbb P(M>t)=0.
\]

Thus \(M<\infty\) a.s.

---

### (4)

Fix \(x,y\in\mathcal X\) and \(k\ge0\). On the event \(\{M=m\}\), the map \(F^0_{-m}\) is constant. Hence

\[
F^0_{-m}(x)=F^0_{-m}(u)
\]

for every \(u\in\mathcal X\).

But

\[
F^0_{-k-m}
=
F^0_{-m}\circ F^{-m}_{-k-m}.
\]

Therefore

\[
F^0_{-k-m}(y)
=
F^0_{-m}\bigl(F^{-m}_{-k-m}(y)\bigr)
=
F^0_{-m}(x).
\]

Since \(M<\infty\) a.s., we conclude

\[
\mathbb P\bigl(F^0_{-M}(x)=F^0_{-k-M}(y)\bigr)=1.
\]

---

### (5)

Define for each \(n\in\mathbb Z\)

\[
M_n=\min\{t>0:F^n_{n-t}\text{ is constant}\},
\]

and

\[
Y_n=F^n_{n-M_n}(x_0).
\]

By stationarity of the two-sided i.i.d. sequence \((Z_t)_{t\in\mathbb Z}\), the random variables \(Y_n\) all have the same distribution. In particular,

\[
Y_0=F^0_{-M}(x_0)
\]

has the same distribution as \(Y_1\).

We now prove a pathwise relation. Since \(F^0_{-M_0}\) is constant,

\[
F^1_{-M_0}=f_0\circ F^0_{-M_0}
\]

is also constant. Hence

\[
M_1\le M_0+1.
\]

Thus \(1-M_1\ge -M_0\). Since \(F^1_{1-M_1}\) is constant,

\[
F^1_{-M_0}(x_0)
=
F^1_{1-M_1}\bigl(F^{1-M_1}_{-M_0}(x_0)\bigr)
=
F^1_{1-M_1}(x_0)
=
Y_1.
\]

But

\[
F^1_{-M_0}(x_0)
=
f_0(F^0_{-M_0}(x_0))
=
f(Y_0,Z_0).
\]

Therefore

\[
f(Y_0,Z_0)=Y_1 \qquad \text{a.s.}
\]

Since \(Y_1\stackrel d=Y_0\), we have

\[
f(Y_0,Z_0)\stackrel d=Y_0.
\]

Also, \(Y_0\) is measurable with respect to \(\sigma(Z_{-1},Z_{-2},\dots)\), so \(Y_0\) is independent of \(Z_0\).

Let \(\mu\) be the law of \(Y_0\). Then for every \(y\in\mathcal X\),

\[
\mu(y)
=
\mathbb P(Y_0=y)
=
\mathbb P(f(Y_0,Z_0)=y).
\]

Using independence of \(Y_0\) and \(Z_0\),

\[
\mathbb P(f(Y_0,Z_0)=y)
=
\sum_{x\in\mathcal X}\mu(x)\mathbb P(f(x,Z_0)=y)
=
\sum_{x\in\mathcal X}\mu(x)P(x,y).
\]

Thus

\[
\mu=\mu P.
\]

So \(\mu\) is a stationary distribution for \(P\). Since \(P\) is irreducible on the finite set \(\mathcal X\), the stationary distribution is unique. Therefore

\[
\mu=\pi.
\]

Hence

\[
F^0_{-M}(x_0)\sim \pi.
\]

---

### (6)

The algorithm is the usual coupling-from-the-past algorithm.

Initialize \(t=0\) and \(G=\mathrm{id}_{\mathcal X}\). Then repeat:

1. Set \(t\leftarrow t+1\).
2. Generate a fresh \(Z_{-t}\).
3. Let \(g_t(x)=f(x,Z_{-t})\).
4. Update

   \[
   G\leftarrow G\circ g_t.
   \]

   After this update,

   \[
   G=F^0_{-t}.
   \]

5. If \(G\) is constant, output \(G(x_0)\) and stop.

By part (3), this algorithm stops a.s. at time \(M\), and by part (5), the output

\[
G(x_0)=F^0_{-M}(x_0)
\]

has distribution \(\pi\).

---

## Part III

### (7)

Here \(\mathcal X=\{0,1,2\}\) and

\[
f(i,z)=\max(0,\min(i+z,2)),
\]

with

\[
\mathbb P(Z=1)=\mathbb P(Z=-1)=\frac12.
\]

Thus the transition matrix is

\[
P=
\begin{pmatrix}
1/2&1/2&0\\
1/2&0&1/2\\
0&1/2&1/2
\end{pmatrix}.
\]

This matrix is doubly stochastic, so the stationary distribution is uniform:

\[
\pi=\left(\frac13,\frac13,\frac13\right).
\]

We now show that Algorithm 2 does not output this distribution.

Let \(U\) denote the map corresponding to \(Z=1\), and \(D\) the map corresponding to \(Z=-1\). Then

\[
U(0)=1,\quad U(1)=2,\quad U(2)=2,
\]

and

\[
D(0)=0,\quad D(1)=0,\quad D(2)=1.
\]

Observe that

\[
U\circ U
\]

is the constant map to \(2\), and

\[

\]

\[

=
1-\frac{2}{2^t}
=
1-2^{1-t}.
\]

Also \(p_1=0\).

Let \(q_t\) be the probability that an independently generated block of length \(t\) is constant and its constant value is \(1\).

Suppose the first repeated adjacent symbol occurs at position \(r\), where \(2\le r\le t\). For a fixed sign, the probability of this event is \(2^{-r}\). The remaining \(t-r\) steps evolve as the original reflected random walk.

Let

\[

\]

\[

\]

Diagonalizing \(P\), or solving the recurrence directly, gives

\[
K_n=\frac13\left(1-\left(-\frac12\right)^n\right).
\]

Therefore, for \(t\ge2\),

\[
q_t
=
\sum_{r=2}^t 2^{-r}\left(K_{t-r}+K_{t-r}\right)
=
\sum_{r=2}^t 2^{1-r}K_{t-r}.
\]

Substituting the formula for \(K_n\),

\[
q_t
=
\frac13\sum_{r=2}^t 2^{1-r}
-
\frac13\sum_{r=2}^t 2^{1-r}\left(-\frac12\right)^{t-r}.
\]

The first sum is \(p_t\). For the second sum, set \(n=t-r\). Then

\[
\sum_{r=2}^t 2^{1-r}\left(-\frac12\right)^{t-r}
=
2^{1-t}\sum_{n=0}^{t-2}(-1)^n.
\]

\[
q_t=
\frac{p_t}{3}
-
\frac{2^{1-t}}{3}\sum_{n=0}^{t-2}(-1)^n.
\]

Hence

\[
q_t=
\begin{cases}
p_t/3, & t\text{ odd},\\[4pt]

=
\prod_{t=2}^n 2^{1-t}
\to0.

=
1.

\[

\frac13

1/2&1/2\\
1/2&1/2
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
This chain is irreducible and aperiodic.

1/4&3/4&0\\
1/4&1/4&1/2\\
3/4&1/4&0
\end{pmatrix}.

\mathbb P(f(\widehat X,Z)=y).
\]
By independence,
\[
\mathbb P(f(\widehat X,Z)=y)
=
\sum_{x\in\mathcal X}\mu(x)\mathbb P(f(x,Z)=y)
=
\sum_{x\in\mathcal X}\mu(x)P(x,y).
\]
Thus \(\mu P=\mu\). Since \(P\) is irreducible on a finite state space, the stationary distribution is unique. Therefore \(\mu=\pi\).

Now define, for \(r\in\mathbb Z\),
\[
M_r=\min\{m>0:F_{r-m}^r\text{ is constant}\},
\]
and
\[
Y_r=F_{r-M_r}^r(x_0).
\]
Thus \(M_0=M\) and
\[
Y_0=F_{-M}^0(x_0).
\]

By stationarity of the i.i.d. sequence \((Z_t)\),
\[
Y_1\stackrel d=Y_0.
\]

Also, \(Y_0\) depends only on \(Z_{-1},Z_{-2},\dots\), so \(Y_0\) is independent of \(Z_0\).

We now show that
\[
f(Y_0,Z_0)=Y_1
\]
a.s.

Indeed,
\[
f(Y_0,Z_0)
=
f_0(F_{-M_0}^0(x_0))
=
F_{-M_0}^1(x_0).
\]
Since \(F_{-M_0}^0\) is constant, the map \(F_{-M_0}^1=f_0\circ F_{-M_0}^0\) is also constant. Therefore
\[
M_1\le M_0+1.
\]
Thus \(-M_0\le 1-M_1\), and
\[
F_{-M_0}^1
=
F_{1-M_1}^1\circ F_{-M_0}^{1-M_1}.
\]
But \(F_{1-M_1}^1\) is constant, so the common value of \(F_{-M_0}^1\) is the same as the common value of \(F_{1-M_1}^1\). Hence
\[
F_{-M_0}^1(x_0)=F_{1-M_1}^1(x_0)=Y_1.
\]
Therefore
\[
f(Y_0,Z_0)=Y_1\stackrel d=Y_0.
\]

Since \(Y_0\) is independent of \(Z_0\), the lemma applies. Hence
\[
Y_0=F_{-M}^0(x_0)\sim\pi.
\]

---

## (6)

The algorithm is the standard coupling-from-the-past algorithm.

Start with \(G_0=\mathrm{id}\). For \(t=1,2,3,\dots\):

1. Generate \(Z_{-t}\).
2. Let \(f_{-t}(x)=f(x,Z_{-t})\).
3. Update
   \[
   G_t=G_{t-1}\circ f_{-t}.
   \]
   Then \(G_t=F_{-t}^0\).
4. Check whether \(G_t\) is constant on \(\mathcal X\).
5. If \(G_t\) is constant, output \(G_t(x_0)\) and stop.

By part (3), the stopping time is \(M<\infty\) a.s. By part (5), the output
\[
G_M(x_0)=F_{-M}^0(x_0)
\]
has distribution \(\pi\).

---

# Part III

We now consider \(\mathcal X=\{0,1,2\}\) and
\[
f(i,z)=\max(0,\min(i+z,2)),
\]
with
\[
\mathbb P(Z=1)=\mathbb P(Z=-1)=1/2.
\]

Let \(U\) denote the map corresponding to \(Z=1\), and \(D\) the map corresponding to \(Z=-1\).

The transition matrix is
\[
P=
\begin{pmatrix}
1/2&1/2&0\\
1/2&0&1/2\\
0&1/2&1/2
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
This matrix is doubly stochastic, so the uniform distribution is stationary. Therefore
\[
\pi=\left(\frac13,\frac13,\frac13\right).
\]

We show Algorithm 2 does not output \(\pi\).

A block of length \(1\) is never constant, because neither \(U\) nor \(D\) is constant.

For a block of length \(2\):

- \(UU\) maps every state to \(2\),
- \(DD\) maps every state to \(0\),
- \(UD\) and \(DU\) are not constant.

Thus Algorithm 2 stops at \(t=2\) with probability \(1/2\), and if it stops then the output is either \(0\) or \(2\), never \(1\). Therefore the probability of reaching \(t=3\) is \(1/2\).

Now consider a fresh block of length \(3\). The output is \(1\) exactly for the two words
\[
UU D,\qquad DD U.
\]
Each has probability \(1/8\), so
\[
\mathbb P(F_{-3}^0\text{ is constant to }1)=\frac{2}{8}=\frac14.
\]
Hence the total probability that Algorithm 2 outputs \(1\) at iteration \(t=3\) is
\[
\frac12\cdot\frac14=\frac18.
\]

The probability of reaching iteration \(t=4\) is the probability of failing at \(t=2\) and failing at \(t=3\). The length \(3\) block fails only for the alternating words \(UDU\) and \(DUD\), so that failure probability is \(1/4\). Therefore
\[
\mathbb P(\text{reach }t=4)
=
\frac12\cdot\frac14
=
\frac18.
\]

Even if every later output were equal to \(1\), we would have
\[
\mathbb P(\text{Algorithm 2 outputs }1)
\le
\frac18+\frac18
=
\frac14.
\]
But under \(\pi\),
\[
\pi(1)=\frac13.
\]
Since
\[
\frac14<\frac13,
\]
Algorithm 2 cannot output a random variable with distribution \(\pi\).

## (1) Boxplots, skewness, and interpretation of the original ANOVA p-value

I use Tukey hinges for the quartiles, so for \(n=5\) the ordered observations are

\[
(\min,\ Q_1,\ \text{median},\ Q_3,\ \max).
\]

The ordered data and five-number summaries are:

| School | Ordered salaries | Min | \(Q_1\) | Median | \(Q_3\) | Max | IQR |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| RU | \(31,56,78,143,210\) | 31 | 56 | 78 | 143 | 210 | 87 |
| PS | \(26,30,37,54,70\) | 26 | 30 | 37 | 54 | 70 | 24 |
| UC | \(21,22,24,36,65\) | 21 | 22 | 24 | 36 | 65 | 14 |

Thus the boxplots would have boxes from \(Q_1\) to \(Q_3\), median lines at the medians above, and whiskers to the listed minima and maxima.

### Interpretation of the original ANOVA p-value \(p=0.06\)

The original one-way ANOVA is testing

\[
H_0:\mu_{\text{RU}}=\mu_{\text{PS}}=\mu_{\text{UC}}
\]

against the alternative that at least one mean differs.

A p-value of \(0.06\) is borderline: at the \(5\%\) level we would not reject \(H_0\), but at the \(10\%\) level we would reject.

The boxplots explain why the result is borderline. RU appears shifted upward relative to PS and UC: its median is 78, while PS and UC have medians 37 and 24. In fact, the RU lower quartile 56 is slightly above the PS upper quartile 54 and well above the UC upper quartile 36. However, RU also has much larger spread, with IQR 87 compared with 24 and 14 for PS and UC. That large within-group variation weakens the ANOVA evidence.

### Skewness and ANOVA assumptions

All three samples are right-skewed:

- RU has a long upper tail: \(78\) to \(210\) is much longer than \(31\) to \(78\).
- PS also has a longer upper tail, especially because of 70.
- UC is strongly right-skewed because of the large value 65. Using the \(1.5\text{ IQR}\) rule, UC has upper fence \(36+1.5(14)=57\), so 65 would be flagged as an upper outlier.

The classical one-way ANOVA F-test assumes:

1. independent samples,
2. approximately normal errors within each group,
3. equal within-group variances.

The boxplots suggest that assumptions 2 and 3 are questionable: the groups are right-skewed, and the spread increases strongly with the level. The balanced design \(n=5\) per group gives the F-test some robustness to unequal variances, but with such small and skewed samples the original p-value should be interpreted cautiously.

---

## (2) Spread-vs-level plot and optimal power transformation

For a spread-vs-level plot, use the median as the group level and the IQR as the group spread.

| School | Median \(m_i\) | IQR \(s_i\) | \(\log m_i\) | \(\log s_i\) |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| RU | 78 | 87 | 4.3567 | 4.4659 |
| PS | 37 | 24 | 3.6109 | 3.1781 |
| UC | 24 | 14 | 3.1781 | 2.6391 |

Fit the regression line

\[
\log(s_i)=a+b\log(m_i).
\]

Using the three points gives

\[
b
=
\frac{\sum_i(\log m_i-\overline{\log m})(\log s_i-\overline{\log s})}
{\sum_i(\log m_i-\overline{\log m})^2}
\approx 1.569.
\]

For a power transformation \(g(y)=y^\lambda\), the transformed spread is approximately

\[
s_i^* \approx |g'(m_i)|s_i
= |\lambda|m_i^{\lambda-1}s_i.
\]

If \(s_i\propto m_i^b\), then

\[
s_i^* \propto m_i^{b+\lambda-1}.
\]

To stabilize spread, set the exponent equal to zero:

\[
b+\lambda-1=0.
\]

Hence

\[
\lambda=1-b\approx 1-1.569=-0.569.
\]

So the optimal power transformation is approximately

\[
Y^\lambda = Y^{-0.57}.
\]

A convenient nearby ladder-of-powers choice is

\[
Y^{-1/2}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{Y}}.
\]

Equivalently, to preserve ordering, one may use the Box-Cox form

\[
g(Y)=\frac{Y^{-1/2}-1}{-1/2}=2(1-Y^{-1/2}),
\]

which is an affine transformation of \(Y^{-1/2}\), so it gives the same ANOVA F-statistic.

---

## (3) ANOVA after transformation

Using the convenient transformation

\[
Z=Y^{-1/2},
\]

the transformed group means are approximately

\[
\bar Z_{\text{RU}}=0.1158,\qquad
\bar Z_{\text{PS}}=0.1597,\qquad
\bar Z_{\text{UC}}=0.1852.
\]

The one-way ANOVA table for \(Z=Y^{-1/2}\) is:

| Source | df | SS | MS | F |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| School | 2 | 0.01233 | 0.00617 | 4.12 |
| Error | 12 | 0.01798 | 0.00150 |  |
| Total | 14 | 0.03031 |  |  |

Thus

\[
F=\frac{0.00617}{0.00150}\approx 4.12.
\]

With \(2\) and \(12\) degrees of freedom,

\[
p=P(F_{2,12}\ge 4.12)\approx 0.044.
\]

So after the variance-stabilizing transformation, the ANOVA becomes significant at the \(5\%\) level. The transformation reduces the strong spread-versus-level pattern seen in the original salaries, making the ANOVA assumptions more plausible. Using the exact power \(\lambda\approx -0.57\) gives essentially the same conclusion, with \(F\approx 4.1\) and \(p\approx 0.044\).

|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| RU | \(31,56,78,143,210\) | 31 | 56 | 78 | 143 | 210 | 87 |
| PS | \(26,30,37,54,70\) | 26 | 30 | 37 | 54 | 70 | 24 |

The original one-way ANOVA is testing

\[
H_0:\mu_{\text{RU}}=\mu_{\text{PS}}=\mu_{\text{UC}}

against the alternative that at least one mean differs.

- RU has a long upper tail: \(78\) to \(210\) is much longer than \(31\) to \(78\).

2. approximately normal errors within each group,

\[
b
=
\frac{\sum_i(\log m_i-\overline{\log m})(\log s_i-\overline{\log s})}

\]

\[

\[

\]

## (1) Boxplots and interpretation of the given ANOVA p-value

First sort each sample:

- RU: \(31,56,78,143,210\)
- PS: \(26,30,37,54,70\)
- UC: \(21,22,24,36,65\)

Using the usual Tukey/R boxplot hinges for \(n=5\), the five-number summaries are:

\[
\begin{array}{c|ccccc|c}
\text{School} & \min & Q_1 & \text{Median} & Q_3 & \max & \text{IQR}\\
\hline
\text{RU} & 31 & 56 & 78 & 143 & 210 & 87\\
\text{PS} & 26 & 30 & 37 & 54 & 70 & 24\\
\text{UC} & 21 & 22 & 24 & 36 & 65 & 14
\end{array}
\]

So the boxplots would show:

- RU has the largest median and by far the largest spread.
- PS and UC are much closer to each other, with substantial overlap.
- All three groups have long upper tails relative to their lower tails, especially UC because of the observation 65.

The given ANOVA p-value is approximately \(0.06\). Thus the classical one-way ANOVA gives marginal evidence against equality of the three school means: not significant at the \(5\%\) level, but significant at the \(10\%\) level. Visually, this is consistent with the boxplots: RU appears higher, but the RU sample also has very large variability, and the samples are tiny.

The one-way ANOVA \(F\)-test assumes independent observations and approximately normal errors with common variance:

\[
Y_{ij}=\mu_i+\varepsilon_{ij}, \qquad \varepsilon_{ij}\overset{iid}{\sim}N(0,\sigma^2).
\]

The boxplots suggest these assumptions are questionable:

- The samples are right-skewed.
- The group spreads are very unequal: RU is much more variable than PS and UC.
- With only \(n=5\) per group, normality is hard to justify.

So the original ANOVA p-value should be interpreted cautiously.

---

## (2) Spread-vs-level plot and optimal power transformation

For a spread-vs-level plot, use the group median as the level and the IQR as the spread.

\[
\begin{array}{c|cc}
\text{School} & \text{Median} & \text{IQR}\\
\hline
\text{RU} & 78 & 87\\
\text{PS} & 37 & 24\\
\text{UC} & 24 & 14
\end{array}
\]

Plot

\[
\log(\text{IQR}) \quad \text{versus} \quad \log(\text{Median}).
\]

The three log-points are approximately

\[
\begin{array}{c|cc}
\text{School} & \log(\text{Median}) & \log(\text{IQR})\\
\hline
\text{RU} & 4.357 & 4.466\\
\text{PS} & 3.611 & 3.178\\
\text{UC} & 3.178 & 2.639
\end{array}
\]

Fitting a line

\[
\log(\text{IQR}) = a + b\log(\text{Median})
\]

gives approximately

\[
b \approx 1.57.
\]

By the Tukey spread-vs-level rule, the variance-stabilizing power is

\[
\lambda = 1-b \approx 1-1.57 = -0.57.
\]

Thus the optimal power transformation is approximately

\[
y \mapsto y^{-0.57}.
\]

A convenient nearby ladder-of-powers choice is

\[
y \mapsto y^{-1/2},
\]

or, to preserve the order of the original observations,

\[
y \mapsto 2\left(1-y^{-1/2}\right),
\]

which is an affine transformation of \(y^{-1/2}\) and therefore gives the same ANOVA \(F\)-statistic.

---

## (3) ANOVA after transformation

Using the estimated transformation \(z=y^{-0.57}\), the transformed group means are approximately

\[
\begin{array}{c|c}
\text{School} & \bar z_i\\
\hline
\text{RU} & 0.0864\\
\text{PS} & 0.1239\\
\text{UC} & 0.1468
\end{array}
\]

The one-way ANOVA table on the transformed scale is approximately

\[
\begin{array}{c|cccc}
\text{Source} & df & SS & MS & F\\
\hline
\text{School} & 2 & 0.00928 & 0.00464 & 4.09\\
\text{Error} & 12 & 0.01361 & 0.00113 & \\
\hline
\text{Total} & 14 & 0.02289 & &
\end{array}
\]

Thus

\[
F \approx 4.09, \qquad df=(2,12).
\]

For \(F_{2,12}\),

\[
p \approx 0.044.
\]

So after the variance-stabilizing transformation, the school effect is significant at the \(5\%\) level. The evidence of differences among schools is driven mainly by RU being higher than PS and UC, while PS and UC remain relatively close.

## (1) Boxplots and interpretation of the given ANOVA p-value

First sort each sample:

- RU: \(31,56,78,143,210\)
- PS: \(26,30,37,54,70\)
- UC: \(21,22,24,36,65\)

Using the usual Tukey/R boxplot hinges for \(n=5\), the five-number summaries are:

\[
\begin{array}{c|ccccc|c}
\text{School} & \min & Q_1 & \text{Median} & Q_3 & \max & \text{IQR}\\
\hline
\text{RU} & 31 & 56 & 78 & 143 & 210 & 87\\
\text{PS} & 26 & 30 & 37 & 54 & 70 & 24\\
\text{UC} & 21 & 22 & 24 & 36 & 65 & 14
\end{array}
\]

So the boxplots would show:

- RU has the largest median and by far the largest spread.
- PS and UC are much closer to each other, with substantial overlap.
- All three groups have long upper tails relative to their lower tails, especially UC because of the observation 65.

The given ANOVA p-value is approximately \(0.06\). Thus the classical one-way ANOVA gives marginal evidence against equality of the three school means: not significant at the \(5\%\) level, but significant at the \(10\%\) level. Visually, this is consistent with the boxplots: RU appears higher, but the RU sample also has very large variability, and the samples are tiny.

The one-way ANOVA \(F\)-test assumes independent observations and approximately normal errors with common variance:

\[
Y_{ij}=\mu_i+\varepsilon_{ij}, \qquad \varepsilon_{ij}\overset{iid}{\sim}N(0,\sigma^2).
\]

The boxplots suggest these assumptions are questionable:

- The samples are right-skewed.
- The group spreads are very unequal: RU is much more variable than PS and UC.
- With only \(n=5\) per group, normality is hard to justify.

So the original ANOVA p-value should be interpreted cautiously.

---

## (2) Spread-vs-level plot and optimal power transformation

For a spread-vs-level plot, use the group median as the level and the IQR as the spread.

\[
\begin{array}{c|cc}
\text{School} & \text{Median} & \text{IQR}\\
\hline
\text{RU} & 78 & 87\\
\text{PS} & 37 & 24\\
\text{UC} & 24 & 14
\end{array}
\]

Plot

\[
\log(\text{IQR}) \quad \text{versus} \quad \log(\text{Median}).
\]

The three log-points are approximately

\[
\begin{array}{c|cc}
\text{School} & \log(\text{Median}) & \log(\text{IQR})\\
\hline
\text{RU} & 4.357 & 4.466\\
\text{PS} & 3.611 & 3.178\\
\text{UC} & 3.178 & 2.639
\end{array}
\]

Fitting a line

\[
\log(\text{IQR}) = a + b\log(\text{Median})
\]

gives approximately

\[
b \approx 1.57.
\]

By the Tukey spread-vs-level rule, the variance-stabilizing power is

\[
\lambda = 1-b \approx 1-1.57 = -0.57.
\]

Thus the optimal power transformation is approximately

\[
y \mapsto y^{-0.57}.
\]

A convenient nearby ladder-of-powers choice is

\[
y \mapsto y^{-1/2},
\]

or, to preserve the order of the original observations,

\[
y \mapsto 2\left(1-y^{-1/2}\right),
\]

which is an affine transformation of \(y^{-1/2}\) and therefore gives the same ANOVA \(F\)-statistic.

---

Using the estimated transformation \(z=y^{-0.57}\), the transformed group means are approximately

\[
\begin{array}{c|c}
\text{School} & \bar z_i\\
\hline
\text{RU} & 0.0864\\
\text{PS} & 0.1239\\
\text{UC} & 0.1468
\end{array}
\]

\[
\begin{array}{c|cccc}
\text{Source} & df & SS & MS & F\\
\hline

\text{Error} & 12 & 0.01361 & 0.00113 & \\
\hline
\text{Total} & 14 & 0.02289 & &
\end{array}
\]

Thus

\[
F \approx 4.09, \qquad df=(2,12).
\]

For \(F_{2,12}\),

\[
p \approx 0.044.
\]

So after the variance-stabilizing transformation, the school effect is significant at the \(5\%\) level. The evidence of differences among schools is driven mainly by RU being higher than PS and UC, while PS and UC remain relatively close.

Let \(x_{(1)}\le \cdots \le x_{(5)}\). I use the usual Tukey/R boxplot quartiles for \(n=5\), i.e.  
\[
Q_1=x_{(2)},\qquad \text{median}=x_{(3)},\qquad Q_3=x_{(4)}.
\]

## (1) Boxplots, skewness, and ANOVA assumptions

Sorted samples:

- RU: \(31,56,78,143,210\)
- PS: \(26,30,37,54,70\)
- UC: \(21,22,24,36,65\)

Thus the five-number summaries are:

| School | Min | \(Q_1\) | Median | \(Q_3\) | Max | IQR |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| RU | 31 | 56 | 78 | 143 | 210 | 87 |
| PS | 26 | 30 | 37 | 54 | 70 | 24 |
| UC | 21 | 22 | 24 | 36 | 65 | 14 |

Text version of the boxplots:

\[
\begin{array}{rcl}
\text{RU} &:& 31 \;-\; [56 \mid 78 \mid 143]\;-\;210,\\
\text{PS} &:& 26 \;-\; [30 \mid 37 \mid 54]\;-\;70,\\
\text{UC} &:& 21 \;-\; [22 \mid 24 \mid 36]\;-\;65.
\end{array}
\]

The boxplots show that RU tends to have higher salaries: its median \(78\) is above every PS and UC observation. PS and UC overlap substantially.

However, RU also has much larger spread. The IQRs are \(87,24,14\), and the sample standard deviations are approximately

\[
s_{\text{RU}}=72.6,\qquad s_{\text{PS}}=18.3,\qquad s_{\text{UC}}=18.6.
\]

All three samples are right-skewed, especially RU and UC, with long upper tails/high observations.

The original ANOVA \(F\)-test p-value is \(0.06\). At the \(5\%\) level this is not formally significant, but it is borderline. The boxplots explain this: RU appears higher, but the very large within-RU variability and right-skewness inflate the error variance.

The usual one-way ANOVA assumptions are:

\[
Y_{ij}=\mu_i+\varepsilon_{ij},\qquad \varepsilon_{ij}\stackrel{\text{iid}}{\sim}N(0,\sigma^2).
\]

The boxplots suggest violations of both approximate normality and equal variance. Independence cannot be checked from the boxplots, but assuming independent alumni samples, the main concern is the strong skewness and nonconstant spread.

---

## (2) Spread-versus-level plot and optimal power transformation

For each school, take

\[
\text{level}=\text{median},\qquad \text{spread}=Q_3-Q_1.
\]

Thus:

| School | Median \(m\) | IQR \(s\) | \(\log m\) | \(\log s\) |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| RU | 78 | 87 | 4.357 | 4.466 |
| PS | 37 | 24 | 3.611 | 3.178 |
| UC | 24 | 14 | 3.178 | 2.639 |

Fit the spread-versus-level line

\[
\log(\text{spread}) = a+b\log(\text{level}).
\]

The least-squares slope is

\[
\hat b
=
\frac{\sum_i (\log m_i-\overline{\log m})(\log s_i-\overline{\log s})}
{\sum_i(\log m_i-\overline{\log m})^2}
\approx 1.57.
\]

For a power transformation \(Y^\lambda\), the variance-stabilizing rule from the spread-versus-level plot is

\[
\lambda = 1-\hat b.
\]

Therefore

\[
\hat\lambda \approx 1-1.57=-0.57.
\]

So the optimal power is approximately \(-0.57\), which on the usual ladder of powers is rounded to

\[
\boxed{\lambda=-\frac12}.
\]

Thus a reciprocal square-root transformation is suggested. In Box-Cox form,

\[
Y^{(-1/2)}
=
\frac{Y^{-1/2}-1}{-1/2}
=
2(1-Y^{-1/2}),
\]

which is monotone increasing in \(Y\). For the ANOVA \(F\)-statistic, using \(Y^{-1/2}\) or \(2(1-Y^{-1/2})\) gives the same \(F\), since they differ by a linear transformation.

---

## (3) ANOVA after transformation

Use

\[
Z=Y^{-1/2}.
\]

The transformed group means are approximately

\[
\bar Z_{\text{RU}}=0.1158,\qquad
\bar Z_{\text{PS}}=0.1597,\qquad
\bar Z_{\text{UC}}=0.1852.
\]

The ANOVA table for \(Z\) is:

| Source | df | SS | MS | \(F\) |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| School | 2 | 0.012334 | 0.006167 | 4.116 |
| Error | 12 | 0.017981 | 0.001498 | |
| Total | 14 | 0.030315 | | |

Thus

\[
F=\frac{0.006167}{0.001498}\approx 4.12.
\]

With \(2\) and \(12\) degrees of freedom,

\[
p=P(F_{2,12}\ge 4.12)\approx 0.044.
\]

So after the reciprocal square-root transformation, the ANOVA gives

\[
\boxed{F\approx 4.12,\qquad p\approx 0.044.}
\]

At the \(5\%\) level, we would reject equality of the transformed mean salaries. The evidence for a school effect is stronger after stabilizing the spread, and the conclusion is mainly driven by RU being higher than PS and UC on the original salary scale.

\[

Sorted samples:

- RU: \(31,56,78,143,210\)
- PS: \(26,30,37,54,70\)
- UC: \(21,22,24,36,65\)

Thus the five-number summaries are:

| School | Min | \(Q_1\) | Median | \(Q_3\) | Max | IQR |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| RU | 31 | 56 | 78 | 143 | 210 | 87 |
| PS | 26 | 30 | 37 | 54 | 70 | 24 |
| UC | 21 | 22 | 24 | 36 | 65 | 14 |

Text version of the boxplots:

\[
\begin{array}{rcl}
\text{RU} &:& 31 \;-\; [56 \mid 78 \mid 143]\;-\;210,\\
\text{PS} &:& 26 \;-\; [30 \mid 37 \mid 54]\;-\;70,\\
\text{UC} &:& 21 \;-\; [22 \mid 24 \mid 36]\;-\;65.
\end{array}
\]

The boxplots show that RU tends to have higher salaries: its median \(78\) is above every PS and UC observation. PS and UC overlap substantially.

However, RU also has much larger spread. The IQRs are \(87,24,14\), and the sample standard deviations are approximately

\[
s_{\text{RU}}=72.6,\qquad s_{\text{PS}}=18.3,\qquad s_{\text{UC}}=18.6.
\]

All three samples are right-skewed, especially RU and UC, with long upper tails/high observations.

The original ANOVA \(F\)-test p-value is \(0.06\). At the \(5\%\) level this is not formally significant, but it is borderline. The boxplots explain this: RU appears higher, but the very large within-RU variability and right-skewness inflate the error variance.

The usual one-way ANOVA assumptions are:

\[
Y_{ij}=\mu_i+\varepsilon_{ij},\qquad \varepsilon_{ij}\stackrel{\text{iid}}{\sim}N(0,\sigma^2).
\]

The boxplots suggest violations of both approximate normality and equal variance. Independence cannot be checked from the boxplots, but assuming independent alumni samples, the main concern is the strong skewness and nonconstant spread.

---

## (2) Spread-versus-level plot and optimal power transformation

For each school, take

\[
\text{level}=\text{median},\qquad \text{spread}=Q_3-Q_1.
\]

Thus:

| School | Median \(m\) | IQR \(s\) | \(\log m\) | \(\log s\) |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| RU | 78 | 87 | 4.357 | 4.466 |
| PS | 37 | 24 | 3.611 | 3.178 |
| UC | 24 | 14 | 3.178 | 2.639 |

Fit the spread-versus-level line

\[
\log(\text{spread}) = a+b\log(\text{level}).
\]

The least-squares slope is

\[
\hat b
=
\frac{\sum_i (\log m_i-\overline{\log m})(\log s_i-\overline{\log s})}
{\sum_i(\log m_i-\overline{\log m})^2}
\approx 1.57.
\]

For a power transformation \(Y^\lambda\), the variance-stabilizing rule from the spread-versus-level plot is

\[
\lambda = 1-\hat b.
\]

Therefore

\[
\hat\lambda \approx 1-1.57=-0.57.
\]

So the optimal power is approximately \(-0.57\), which on the usual ladder of powers is rounded to

\[
\boxed{\lambda=-\frac12}.
\]

Thus a reciprocal square-root transformation is suggested. In Box-Cox form,

\[
Y^{(-1/2)}
=
\frac{Y^{-1/2}-1}{-1/2}
=
2(1-Y^{-1/2}),
\]

which is monotone increasing in \(Y\). For the ANOVA \(F\)-statistic, using \(Y^{-1/2}\) or \(2(1-Y^{-1/2})\) gives the same \(F\), since they differ by a linear transformation.

\[

The transformed group means are approximately

\[
\bar Z_{\text{RU}}=0.1158,\qquad
\bar Z_{\text{PS}}=0.1597,\qquad
\bar Z_{\text{UC}}=0.1852.

|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| School | 2 | 0.012334 | 0.006167 | 4.116 |
| Error | 12 | 0.017981 | 0.001498 | |
| Total | 14 | 0.030315 | | |

\[

\[

\[
\boxed{F\approx 4.12,\qquad p\approx 0.044.}

\[

Thus Piscataway’s estimated mean July temperature is

\[
\boxed{82.71^\circ\text{F},\quad SE=1.63^\circ\text{F}}
\]

## (B) 95% prediction interval for next year’s New Brunswick temperature

Assuming the New Brunswick yearly observations are approximately normal and independent, a 95% prediction interval for a future observation \(X_{\text{new}}\) is

\[
\bar X \pm t_{0.975,6}s_X\sqrt{1+\frac1n}.
\]

Here

\[
t_{0.975,6}=2.447,\qquad s_X=4.082,\qquad n=7.

\[

\]

\boxed{(73.3,\ 94.7)^\circ\text{F}}
