content.text:
## Preliminary reduction to a one-type Galton–Watson process

Let

\[
m:=\mathbb E \xi=\frac{\alpha}{1-\alpha},\qquad q=1-p,\qquad 
\mu:=mp=\frac{\alpha p}{1-\alpha}.
\]

Because we start with one type \(A\) individual at time \(0\), the process has period \(2\):

\[
Z^A_{2n+1}=0,\qquad Z^B_{2n}=0,\qquad Z^C_{2n+1}=0.
\]

Define the embedded process

\[
X_n:=Z^A_{2n},\qquad n\ge 0.
\]

A type \(A\) individual at time \(2n\) produces \(\xi\) type \(B\) individuals at time \(2n+1\). Each of those independently becomes type \(A\) with probability \(p\). Thus the number \(\eta\) of type \(A\) grandchildren two generations later has pgf

\[
f(s):=\mathbb E(s^\eta)
=\mathbb E\bigl[(q+ps)^\xi\bigr]
=\sum_{k=0}^\infty (1-\alpha)\alpha^k(q+ps)^k
=\frac{1-\alpha}{1-\alpha q-\alpha p s}.
\]

Therefore \(\{X_n\}_{n\ge 0}\) is a one-type Galton–Watson process with offspring pgf \(f\) and mean

\[
f'(1)=\frac{\alpha p}{1-\alpha}=\mu.
\]

Also,

\[
\{Z^A_n=Z^B_n=Z^C_n=0\text{ for all large }n\}
=
\{X_n=0\text{ for some }n\}.
\]

Indeed, if \(X_n=0\), then no type \(A\) individuals remain at time \(2n\), so no type \(B\) individuals appear at time \(2n+1\), and any type \(C\) individuals present die. Conversely, eventual extinction clearly implies \(X_n=0\) eventually.

---

## (a) Extinction-or-explosion dichotomy

Let

\[
N_n:=Z^A_n+Z^B_n+Z^C_n.
\]

The embedded process \(X_n=Z^A_{2n}\) is a Galton–Watson process.

By the standard Galton–Watson theorem, if \(X_n\) becomes extinct, then the whole population becomes extinct after finitely many generations. That gives the first alternative.

On the nonextinction event, the Galton–Watson process \(X_n\) survives forever. For a supercritical Galton–Watson process, conditional on nonextinction,

\[
X_n\to\infty \qquad \text{a.s.}
\]

One way to prove this is to note that if the process visited a finite set \(\{1,\dots,K\}\) infinitely often, then at each such visit it would have a uniformly positive conditional probability of eventual extinction, contradicting survival.

Thus on nonextinction,

\[
Z^A_{2n}=X_n\to\infty.
\]

Hence

\[
N_{2n}\ge Z^A_{2n}=X_n\to\infty.
\]

Also every type \(A\) individual at time \(2n+2\) must have arisen from a type \(B\) individual at time \(2n+1\). Therefore

\[
Z^B_{2n+1}\ge Z^A_{2n+2}=X_{n+1}.
\]

So on nonextinction,

\[
N_{2n+1}=Z^B_{2n+1}\ge X_{n+1}\to\infty.
\]

Combining the even and odd subsequences,

\[
N_n\to\infty
\]

on the nonextinction event. Hence with probability \(1\), either the population is eventually extinct or its total size tends to infinity.

---

## (b) Expectations

Let

\[
a_n:=\mathbb E Z^A_n,\qquad b_n:=\mathbb E Z^B_n,\qquad c_n:=\mathbb E Z^C_n.
\]

The recursions are

\[
a_{n+1}=p b_n,\qquad b_{n+1}=m a_n,\qquad c_{n+1}=q b_n,
\]

with

\[
a_0=1,\qquad b_0=c_0=0.
\]

Since \(\mu=mp=\dfrac{\alpha p}{1-\alpha}\), we obtain

\[
\boxed{\mathbb E Z^A_{2r}=\mu^r,\qquad \mathbb E Z^A_{2r+1}=0.}
\]

Also,

\[
\boxed{\mathbb E Z^B_{2r+1}=m\mu^r
=\frac{\alpha}{1-\alpha}\left(\frac{\alpha p}{1-\alpha}\right)^r,\qquad 
\mathbb E Z^B_{2r}=0.}
\]

Finally, for \(r\ge 1\),

\[
\boxed{\mathbb E Z^C_{2r}=q m\mu^{r-1}
=(1-p)\frac{\alpha}{1-\alpha}
\left(\frac{\alpha p}{1-\alpha}\right)^{r-1},}
\]

and

\[
\boxed{\mathbb E Z^C_{2r+1}=0,\qquad \mathbb E Z^C_0=0.}
\]

---

## (c) Values of \(\alpha,p\) for which \(p_e=1\)

The extinction probability \(p_e\) is the extinction probability of the embedded Galton–Watson process \(X_n\). Its mean offspring number is

\[
\mu=\frac{\alpha p}{1-\alpha}.
\]

By the Galton–Watson extinction theorem, extinction occurs almost surely if and only if \(\mu\le 1\). Therefore

\[
p_e=1
\iff \frac{\alpha p}{1-\alpha}\le 1
\iff \alpha p\le 1-\alpha
\iff \alpha(1+p)\le 1.
\]

Thus

\[
\boxed{p_e=1 \iff \alpha\le \frac{1}{1+p}.}
\]

Equivalently, survival has positive probability precisely when

\[
\boxed{\alpha>\frac{1}{1+p}.}
\]

---

## (d) Closed form for \(p_e\) when \(p_e<1\)

When \(p_e<1\), the embedded Galton–Watson process is supercritical, so

\[
\mu=\frac{\alpha p}{1-\alpha}>1.
\]

The extinction probability is the smallest solution in \([0,1]\) of

\[
s=f(s)=\frac{1-\alpha}{1-\alpha q-\alpha p s}.
\]

Thus

\[
s(1-\alpha q-\alpha p s)=1-\alpha.
\]

Equivalently,

\[
\alpha p s^2-(1-\alpha q)s+(1-\alpha)=0.
\]

The two roots are

\[
s=1
\]

and

\[
s=\frac{1-\alpha}{\alpha p}.
\]

In the supercritical case,

\[
\frac{1-\alpha}{\alpha p}<1,
\]

so the extinction probability is the smaller root:

\[
\boxed{p_e=\frac{1-\alpha}{\alpha p}.}
\]

---

## (e) Almost sure normalization of \(Z^B_n\)

A natural nontrivial subsequence is the odd generations, since \(Z^B_{2n}=0\). Define

\[
\boxed{a(n)=2n-1}
\]

and

\[
\boxed{
b(n)=\mathbb E Z^B_{2n-1}
=m\mu^{n-1}
=\frac{\alpha}{1-\alpha}
\left(\frac{\alpha p}{1-\alpha}\right)^{n-1}.
}
\]

We show that

\[
Y_n:=\frac{Z^B_{2n-1}}{b(n)}
\]

converges almost surely to a finite random variable.

Assume first the supercritical case \(\mu>1\). Let

\[
X_n=Z^A_{2n}.
\]

Then

\[
M_n:=\frac{X_n}{\mu^n}
\]

is a nonnegative martingale with respect to the natural filtration, because

\[
\mathbb E[X_{n+1}\mid X_n]=\mu X_n.
\]

By Doob’s martingale convergence theorem,

\[
M_n\to W
\]

almost surely for some finite random variable \(W\).

Now condition on the population at time \(2n\). Given \(X_n\), the number of type \(B\) individuals at time \(2n+1\) is

\[
Z^B_{2n+1}=\sum_{j=1}^{X_n}\xi_{n,j},
\]

where the \(\xi_{n,j}\) are i.i.d. copies of \(\xi\). Since

\[
\mathbb E\xi=m,\qquad \operatorname{Var}(\xi)=\frac{\alpha}{(1-\alpha)^2}<\infty,
\]

we have

\[
\mathbb E\left[
\left(
\frac{Z^B_{2n+1}-mX_n}{m\mu^n}
\right)^2
\right]
=
\frac{\operatorname{Var}(\xi)\,\mathbb E X_n}{m^2\mu^{2n}}
=
\frac{\operatorname{Var}(\xi)}{m^2}\mu^{-n}.
\]

Since \(\mu>1\),

\[
\sum_{n=0}^\infty 
\mathbb E\left[
\left(
\frac{Z^B_{2n+1}-mX_n}{m\mu^n}
\right)^2
\right]
<\infty.
\]

By Markov’s inequality and the Borel–Cantelli lemma,

\[
\frac{Z^B_{2n+1}-mX_n}{m\mu^n}\to 0
\qquad\text{a.s.}
\]

Therefore

\[
\frac{Z^B_{2n+1}}{m\mu^n}
=
\frac{X_n}{\mu^n}
+
\frac{Z^B_{2n+1}-mX_n}{m\mu^n}
\to W
\qquad\text{a.s.}
\]

Replacing \(n\) by \(n-1\), we get

\[
\frac{Z^B_{2n-1}}{m\mu^{n-1}}\to W
\qquad\text{a.s.}
\]

Thus

\[
\boxed{
Y_n=\frac{Z^B_{a(n)}}{b(n)}\to W
\qquad\text{a.s.}
}
\]

In the subcritical or critical case \(\mu\le 1\), part (c) shows extinction occurs almost surely, so \(Z^B_{2n-1}=0\) for all sufficiently large \(n\). Hence then

\[
Y_n\to 0
\qquad\text{a.s.}
\]

Therefore the above choice of \(a(n)\) and \(b(n)\) gives almost sure convergence to a finite limiting random variable.

Let  
\[
\theta=(\beta_0,\beta_1,\beta_2)^T,\qquad z(x)=(1,x_1,x_2)^T,\qquad 
\pi_\theta(x)=\frac{\exp(\theta^Tz(x))}{1+\exp(\theta^Tz(x))}.
\]

A caveat: the prompt as pasted does **not** include the actual R code giving \(n_1,n\), the test sample size, or the exact object names. Thus the exact numerical values in Parts 2 and 5 are not uniquely determined from the text alone. I give below the exact R code that reports them once the given `set.seed(1)` data-generation code has been run.

---

## 1) Why the logistic model is misspecified

Because \(Y\sim \operatorname{Bernoulli}(1/2)\), the true conditional log-odds are

\[
\log \frac{P(Y=1\mid X=x)}{P(Y=0\mid X=x)}
=
\log \frac{f_1(x)}{f_0(x)},
\]

where \(f_y\) is the density of \(X\mid Y=y\). Here

\[
X\mid Y=0\sim N\left((-6,-6),\begin{pmatrix}25&0\\0&225\end{pmatrix}\right),
\]

\[
X\mid Y=1\sim N\left((6,6),\begin{pmatrix}25&0\\0&100\end{pmatrix}\right).
\]

Thus

\[
\log \frac{f_1(x)}{f_0(x)}
=
-\frac12\log\frac{|\Sigma_1|}{|\Sigma_0|}
-\frac12\left\{(x-\mu_1)^T\Sigma_1^{-1}(x-\mu_1)
-(x-\mu_0)^T\Sigma_0^{-1}(x-\mu_0)\right\}.
\]

Since

\[
|\Sigma_1|=25\cdot 100=2500,\qquad |\Sigma_0|=25\cdot 225=5625,
\]

we get

\[
-\frac12\log\frac{|\Sigma_1|}{|\Sigma_0|}
=
-\frac12\log\frac{4}{9}
=
\log\frac32.
\]

Expanding coordinatewise gives

\[
\log \frac{P(Y=1\mid X=x)}{P(Y=0\mid X=x)}
=
\log\frac32 -0.1 + \frac{12}{25}x_1+\frac{13}{150}x_2-\frac{1}{360}x_2^2.
\]

Equivalently,

\[
\operatorname{logit}\{P(Y=1\mid X=x)\}
=
0.305465\ldots+0.48x_1+0.086667x_2-0.002778x_2^2.
\]

This is **quadratic** in \(x_2\), not linear in \(x\). Therefore the working logistic model

\[
\operatorname{logit}\{P(Y=1\mid X=x)\}=\beta_0+\beta_1x_1+\beta_2x_2
\]

is misspecified.

---

## 2) Labeled-data logistic MLE and test performance

Let the training data objects from the given R code be called `xs`, `ys`, with `xs` an \(n\times 2\) matrix and `ys` a \(0/1\) vector. Let the test data be called `xs.test`, `ys.test`. Rename these below if the original code used different names.

The labeled-data MLE is obtained by fitting logistic regression only on observations \(1,\dots,n_1\).

```r
log1pexp_stable <- function(a) {
  out <- numeric(length(a))
  idx <- a > 0
  out[idx] <- a[idx] + log1p(exp(-a[idx]))
  out[!idx] <- log1p(exp(a[!idx]))
  out
}

eval_theta <- function(theta, x, y) {
  X <- cbind(1, as.matrix(x))
  eta <- drop(X %*% theta)
  avg_loglik <- mean(y * eta - log1pexp_stable(eta))
  acc <- mean((eta >= 0) == (y == 1))
  c(avg_test_loglik = avg_loglik, test_accuracy = acc)
}

## labeled-data logistic regression
dat.labeled <- data.frame(
  y = ys[1:n1],
  x1 = xs[1:n1, 1],
  x2 = xs[1:n1, 2]
)

fit.hat <- glm(y ~ x1 + x2, data = dat.labeled, family = binomial())

theta.hat <- unname(coef(fit.hat))
names(theta.hat) <- c("beta0", "beta1", "beta2")

perf.hat <- eval_theta(theta.hat, xs.test, ys.test)

report.hat <- c(theta.hat, perf.hat)
print(report.hat)
```

This prints

\[
(\hat\beta_0,\hat\beta_1,\hat\beta_2),
\]

the average test log-likelihood, and the test classification accuracy.

The average test log-likelihood being computed is

\[
\frac1{N_{\text{test}}}\sum_{j=1}^{N_{\text{test}}}
\left[
Y_j^{\text{test}}\theta^T z(X_j^{\text{test}})
-\log\{1+\exp(\theta^T z(X_j^{\text{test}}))\}
\right].
\]

The classifier is

\[
\widehat Y(x)=1\{\hat\theta^Tz(x)\ge 0\}.
\]

---

## 3) Loss minimized by \((\tilde\beta_0,\tilde\beta)\)

Define

\[
\bar m_\ell
=
\frac1{n_1}\sum_{i=1}^{n_1}Y_i z(X_i).
\]

Consider the loss

\[
L(\theta)
=
\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n \log\left\{1+\exp(\theta^Tz(X_i))\right\}
-
\theta^T\bar m_\ell.
\]

Then

\[
\nabla_\theta L(\theta)
=
\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n \pi_\theta(X_i)z(X_i)
-
\frac1{n_1}\sum_{i=1}^{n_1}Y_i z(X_i).
\]

Therefore the first-order condition

\[
\nabla_\theta L(\theta)=0
\]

is exactly

\[
0
=
\frac1{n_1}\sum_{i=1}^{n_1}Y_i z(X_i)
-
\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\pi_\theta(X_i)z(X_i),
\]

which is the estimating equation defining \(\tilde\theta=(\tilde\beta_0,\tilde\beta_1,\tilde\beta_2)^T\).

Moreover,

\[
\nabla_\theta^2 L(\theta)
=
\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n
\pi_\theta(X_i)\{1-\pi_\theta(X_i)\}z(X_i)z(X_i)^T,
\]

which is positive semidefinite. Hence \(L\) is convex. By the first-order optimality theorem for differentiable convex functions, any solution of the estimating equation is a global minimizer of \(L\). If the design points span \(\mathbb R^3\), the Hessian is positive definite and the minimizer is unique.

---

## 4) Newton-Raphson function for \(\tilde\theta\)

Newton-Raphson uses

\[
g(\theta)
=
\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n \pi_\theta(X_i)z(X_i)-\bar m_\ell,
\]

and

\[
H(\theta)
=
\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n
\pi_\theta(X_i)\{1-\pi_\theta(X_i)\}z(X_i)z(X_i)^T.
\]

The Newton update is

\[
\theta^{(k+1)}
=
\theta^{(k)}-H(\theta^{(k)})^{-1}g(\theta^{(k)}).
\]

Here is an R implementation.

```r
ssl_logit_nr <- function(xs, ys, n1, start = NULL,
                         tol = 1e-10, maxit = 100,
                         trace = FALSE, line.search = TRUE) {
  X <- cbind(1, as.matrix(xs))
  n <- nrow(X)
  p <- ncol(X)
  
  if (is.null(start)) {
    start <- rep(0, p)
  }
  
  theta <- as.numeric(start)
  
  ## labeled response moment
  X.l <- X[1:n1, , drop = FALSE]
  y.l <- ys[1:n1]
  m.l <- drop(crossprod(X.l, y.l)) / n1
  
  log1pexp_stable <- function(a) {
    out <- numeric(length(a))
    idx <- a > 0
    out[idx] <- a[idx] + log1p(exp(-a[idx]))
    out[!idx] <- log1p(exp(a[!idx]))
    out
  }
  
  obj <- function(theta) {
    eta <- drop(X %*% theta)
    mean(log1pexp_stable(eta)) - sum(theta * m.l)
  }
  
  converged <- FALSE
  
  for (it in seq_len(maxit)) {
    eta <- drop(X %*% theta)
    prob <- plogis(eta)
    
    g <- drop(crossprod(X, prob)) / n - m.l
    W <- prob * (1 - prob)
    H <- crossprod(X, X * W) / n
    
    if (max(abs(g)) < tol) {
      converged <- TRUE
      break
    }
    
    step <- as.numeric(solve(H, g))
    
    theta.old <- theta
    obj.old <- obj(theta.old)
    
    if (line.search) {
      alpha <- 1
      gd <- sum(g * step)
      
      repeat {
        theta.new <- theta.old - alpha * step
        obj.new <- obj(theta.new)
        
        if (obj.new <= obj.old - 1e-4 * alpha * gd || alpha < 1e-8) {
          break
        }
        
        alpha <- alpha / 2
      }
    } else {
      alpha <- 1
      theta.new <- theta.old - step
      obj.new <- obj(theta.new)
    }
    
    if (trace) {
      cat("iter =", it,
          "obj =", obj.new,
          "max|grad| =", max(abs(g)),
          "alpha =", alpha, "\n")
    }
    
    theta <- theta.new
    
    if (max(abs(theta - theta.old)) < tol * (1 + max(abs(theta.old)))) {
      converged <- TRUE
      break
    }
  }
  
  names(theta) <- c("beta0", paste0("beta", seq_len(p - 1)))
  
  list(
    coefficients = theta,
    objective = obj(theta),
    gradient = g,
    iterations = it,
    converged = converged
  )
}

## 1) Why the logistic model is misspecified

Because \(Y\sim \operatorname{Bernoulli}(1/2)\), the true conditional log-odds are

\[
\log \frac{P(Y=1\mid X=x)}{P(Y=0\mid X=x)}
=
\log \frac{f_1(x)}{f_0(x)},
\]

where \(f_y\) is the density of \(X\mid Y=y\). Here

\[
X\mid Y=0\sim N\left((-6,-6),\begin{pmatrix}25&0\\0&225\end{pmatrix}\right),
\]

\[
X\mid Y=1\sim N\left((6,6),\begin{pmatrix}25&0\\0&100\end{pmatrix}\right).
\]

Thus

\[
\log \frac{f_1(x)}{f_0(x)}
=
-\frac12\log\frac{|\Sigma_1|}{|\Sigma_0|}
-\frac12\left\{(x-\mu_1)^T\Sigma_1^{-1}(x-\mu_1)
-(x-\mu_0)^T\Sigma_0^{-1}(x-\mu_0)\right\}.
\]

Since

\[
|\Sigma_1|=25\cdot 100=2500,\qquad |\Sigma_0|=25\cdot 225=5625,
\]

we get

\[
-\frac12\log\frac{|\Sigma_1|}{|\Sigma_0|}
=
-\frac12\log\frac{4}{9}
=
\log\frac32.
\]

Expanding coordinatewise gives

\[
\log \frac{P(Y=1\mid X=x)}{P(Y=0\mid X=x)}
=
\log\frac32 -0.1 + \frac{12}{25}x_1+\frac{13}{150}x_2-\frac{1}{360}x_2^2.
\]

Equivalently,

\[
\operatorname{logit}\{P(Y=1\mid X=x)\}
=
0.305465\ldots+0.48x_1+0.086667x_2-0.002778x_2^2.
\]

This is **quadratic** in \(x_2\), not linear in \(x\). Therefore the working logistic model

\[
\operatorname{logit}\{P(Y=1\mid X=x)\}=\beta_0+\beta_1x_1+\beta_2x_2
\]

is misspecified.

---

## 2) Labeled-data logistic MLE and test performance

Let the training data objects from the given R code be called `xs`, `ys`, with `xs` an \(n\times 2\) matrix and `ys` a \(0/1\) vector. Let the test data be called `xs.test`, `ys.test`. Rename these below if the original code used different names.

```r

  out <- numeric(length(a))
  idx <- a > 0
  out[idx] <- a[idx] + log1p(exp(-a[idx]))
  out[!idx] <- log1p(exp(a[!idx]))
  out
}

  X <- cbind(1, as.matrix(x))
  eta <- drop(X %*% theta)
  avg_loglik <- mean(y * eta - log1pexp_stable(eta))
  acc <- mean((eta >= 0) == (y == 1))
  c(avg_test_loglik = avg_loglik, test_accuracy = acc)

  x1 = xs[1:n1, 1],
  x2 = xs[1:n1, 2]

\[
(\hat\beta_0,\hat\beta_1,\hat\beta_2),
\]

the average test log-likelihood, and the test classification accuracy.

The average test log-likelihood being computed is

\[
\frac1{N_{\text{test}}}\sum_{j=1}^{N_{\text{test}}}
\left[
Y_j^{\text{test}}\theta^T z(X_j^{\text{test}})
-\log\{1+\exp(\theta^T z(X_j^{\text{test}}))\}
\right].
\]

\[

\]

## 3) Loss minimized by \((\tilde\beta_0,\tilde\beta)\)

Define

\[
\bar m_\ell
=
\frac1{n_1}\sum_{i=1}^{n_1}Y_i z(X_i).
\]

Consider the loss

\[
L(\theta)
=
\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n \log\left\{1+\exp(\theta^Tz(X_i))\right\}
-
\theta^T\bar m_\ell.
\]

Then

\[
\nabla_\theta L(\theta)
=
\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n \pi_\theta(X_i)z(X_i)
-
\frac1{n_1}\sum_{i=1}^{n_1}Y_i z(X_i).
\]

Therefore the first-order condition

\[
\nabla_\theta L(\theta)=0
\]

is exactly

\[

=
\frac1{n_1}\sum_{i=1}^{n_1}Y_i z(X_i)
-
\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\pi_\theta(X_i)z(X_i),

\[

\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n
\pi_\theta(X_i)\{1-\pi_\theta(X_i)\}z(X_i)z(X_i)^T,

## 1) Why the logistic model is misspecified

The true posterior log-odds are

\[
\log\frac{P(Y=1\mid X=x)}{P(Y=0\mid X=x)}
=
\log\frac{f_1(x)}{f_0(x)}
\]

\[

\qquad
f_1=N\left((6,6),\operatorname{diag}(5^2,10^2)\right).
\]

Thus

\[
\log\frac{f_1(x)}{f_0(x)}
=
-\frac12\log\frac{|\Sigma_1|}{|\Sigma_0|}
-\frac12\left\{(x-\mu_1)^T\Sigma_1^{-1}(x-\mu_1)
-(x-\mu_0)^T\Sigma_0^{-1}(x-\mu_0)\right\}.
\]

Here

\[
\mu_0=(-6,-6)^T,\quad \mu_1=(6,6)^T,
\]
\[
\Sigma_0=\operatorname{diag}(25,225),\quad
\Sigma_1=\operatorname{diag}(25,100).
\]

A direct expansion gives

\[
\log\frac{P(Y=1\mid X=x)}{P(Y=0\mid X=x)}
=
\log(3/2)-0.1+\frac{12}{25}x_1+\frac{13}{150}x_2-\frac{1}{360}x_2^2.
\]

Therefore the true logit is quadratic in \(x_2\), not linear in \(x=(x_1,x_2)\). The assumed logistic model

\[
\log\frac{P(Y=1\mid x)}{P(Y=0\mid x)}
=
\beta_0+\beta_1x_1+\beta_2x_2

cannot represent the true conditional probability. Hence the logistic model is misspecified. Equivalently, unequal class covariances produce a quadratic discriminant boundary rather than a linear one.

\[

=

\[

\[

\[

ssl_logit_newton <- function(Xl, yl, Xu,
                             start = NULL,
                             tol = 1e-10,
                             maxit = 100,
                             trace = FALSE) {
  Xl <- as.matrix(Xl)
  Xu <- as.matrix(Xu)
  yl <- as.numeric(yl)

  X <- rbind(Xl, Xu)

  Z <- cbind(1, X)
  Zl <- cbind(1, Xl)

  n <- nrow(Z)
  n1 <- nrow(Zl)
  p <- ncol(Z)

  b <- drop(crossprod(Zl, yl)) / n1

  log1pexp <- function(a) {
    out <- numeric(length(a))
    idx <- a > 0
    out[idx] <- a[idx] + log1p(exp(-a[idx]))
    out[!idx] <- log1p(exp(a[!idx]))
    out
  }

  obj <- function(theta) {
    eta <- drop(Z %*% theta)
    mean(log1pexp(eta)) - sum(theta * b)
  }

  if (is.null(start)) {
    dat <- data.frame(y = yl, Xl)
    fit0 <- try(glm(y ~ ., family = binomial(), data = dat), silent = TRUE)

    if (inherits(fit0, "try-error")) {
      theta <- rep(0, p)
    } else {
      theta <- unname(coef(fit0))
      if (any(!is.finite(theta))) theta <- rep(0, p)
    }
  } else {
    theta <- as.numeric(start)
  }

  for (iter in seq_len(maxit)) {
    eta <- drop(Z %*% theta)
    pi <- plogis(eta)
    w <- pi * (1 - pi)

    grad <- drop(crossprod(Z, pi)) / n - b
    Hess <- crossprod(Z, Z * w) / n

    step <- solve(Hess, grad)

    # Backtracking line search for stability
    old.obj <- obj(theta)
    lambda <- 1

    repeat {
      theta.new <- theta - lambda * step
      new.obj <- obj(theta.new)

      if (new.obj <= old.obj || lambda < 1e-8) break
      lambda <- lambda / 2
    }

    if (trace) {
      cat("iter =", iter,
          " obj =", new.obj,
          " step =", max(abs(lambda * step)), "\n")
    }

    if (max(abs(lambda * step)) < tol * (1 + max(abs(theta)))) {
      theta <- theta.new
      break
    }

    theta <- theta.new
  }

  names(theta) <- c("beta0", paste0("beta", seq_len(ncol(Xl))))

  list(
    coef = theta,
    iterations = iter,
    gradient = grad,
    converged = iter < maxit
  )
}
```

Let \(z=(1,x_1,x_2)^T\) and \(\theta=(\beta_0,\beta_1,\beta_2)^T\).

Because the actual R data-generation code, including \(n,n_1\), test-set size, and object names, is not included in the prompt, the numerical values in parts 2 and 5 cannot be uniquely recovered from the distributional description alone. Below I give the exact mathematical answers and reproducible R code which, when run after the supplied data-generation code, prints the requested numerical reports and plot.

---

## 1. Why the logistic model is misspecified

The true conditional log-odds are

\[
\log\frac{P(Y=1\mid X=x)}{P(Y=0\mid X=x)}
=
\log\frac{f_1(x)}{f_0(x)}
\]

because \(P(Y=1)=P(Y=0)=1/2\). Here

\[
\mu_0=(-6,-6)^T,\qquad 
\Sigma_0=\operatorname{diag}(5^2,15^2),
\]

\[
\mu_1=(6,6)^T,\qquad 
\Sigma_1=\operatorname{diag}(5^2,10^2).
\]

Thus

\[
\log\frac{f_1(x)}{f_0(x)}
=
\frac12\log\frac{|\Sigma_0|}{|\Sigma_1|}
-\frac12\left\{(x-\mu_1)^T\Sigma_1^{-1}(x-\mu_1)
-(x-\mu_0)^T\Sigma_0^{-1}(x-\mu_0)\right\}.
\]

Since

\[
|\Sigma_0|=25\cdot 225=5625,\qquad
|\Sigma_1|=25\cdot 100=2500,
\]

we get

\[
\frac12\log\frac{|\Sigma_0|}{|\Sigma_1|}
=
\frac12\log\frac{5625}{2500}
=
\log\frac32.
\]

Expanding the quadratic terms,

\[
\log\frac{P(Y=1\mid X=x)}{P(Y=0\mid X=x)}
=
\log\frac32-\frac{1}{10}
+\frac{12}{25}x_1
+\frac{13}{150}x_2
-\frac{1}{360}x_2^2.
\]

The true log-odds contain the quadratic term \(-x_2^2/360\). The fitted logistic model assumes

\[
\log\frac{P(Y=1\mid X=x)}{P(Y=0\mid X=x)}
=
\beta_0+\beta_1x_1+\beta_2x_2,
\]

which is affine in \(x\). Therefore the logistic model is misspecified.

Equivalently: the class-conditional covariances are unequal, so the Bayes rule is quadratic rather than linear.

---

## 2. Labeled-data MLE and test performance

The labeled MLE solves the usual logistic score equation

\[
0
=
\frac1{n_1}\sum_{i=1}^{n_1}
\{Y_i-\pi(X_i;\theta)\}z_i,
\]

where

\[
\pi(x;\theta)=\frac{\exp(z^T\theta)}{1+\exp(z^T\theta)}.
\]

The following R code reports \((\hat\beta_0,\hat\beta_1,\hat\beta_2)\), average test log-likelihood, and test accuracy. Replace `xs.test, ys.test` by the names used in the supplied code if different.

```r
softplus <- function(t) {
  pmax(t, 0) + log1p(exp(-abs(t)))
}

test_metrics <- function(theta, x, y) {
  z <- cbind(1, as.matrix(x))
  eta <- drop(z %*% theta)
  avg_loglik <- mean(y * eta - softplus(eta))
  acc <- mean((eta >= 0) == (y == 1))
  c(avg_test_loglik = avg_loglik, test_accuracy = acc)
}

## labeled-data logistic MLE
dat.labeled <- data.frame(
  y  = ys[1:n1],
  x1 = xs[1:n1, 1],
  x2 = xs[1:n1, 2]
)

fit.hat <- glm(y ~ x1 + x2, data = dat.labeled, family = binomial())
theta.hat <- unname(coef(fit.hat))
names(theta.hat) <- c("beta0", "beta1", "beta2")

theta.hat
test_metrics(theta.hat, xs.test, ys.test)
```

---

## 3. Loss minimized by \((\tilde\beta_0,\tilde\beta)\)

The semi-supervised estimator is defined by

\[
0
=
\frac1{n_1}\sum_{i=1}^{n_1}Y_i z_i
-
\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n \pi(X_i;\theta)z_i.
\]

Equivalently,

\[
0
=
\nabla_\theta L_n(\theta),
\]

where

\[
L_n(\theta)
=
\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n \log\left\{1+\exp(z_i^T\theta)\right\}
-
\frac1{n_1}\sum_{i=1}^{n_1} Y_i z_i^T\theta.
\]

Indeed,

\[
\nabla_\theta L_n(\theta)
=
\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n \pi(X_i;\theta)z_i
-
\frac1{n_1}\sum_{i=1}^{n_1}Y_i z_i.
\]

Therefore the estimating equation is exactly \(\nabla_\theta L_n(\theta)=0\).

The Hessian is

\[
\nabla_\theta^2 L_n(\theta)
=
\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n
\pi(X_i;\theta)\{1-\pi(X_i;\theta)\}z_i z_i^T,
\]

which is positive semidefinite. Hence \(L_n\) is convex, and any solution of the estimating equation is a global minimizer. If the design matrix has full column rank, the Hessian is positive definite for finite \(\theta\), giving uniqueness.

---

## 4. Newton-Raphson function for \((\tilde\beta_0,\tilde\beta)\)

```r
ssl_newton <- function(xs, ys, n1, start = NULL,
                       tol = 1e-10, maxit = 100, trace = FALSE) {
  x <- as.matrix(xs)
  n <- nrow(x)
  z <- cbind(1, x)
  p <- ncol(z)

  y.labeled <- ys[1:n1]

  ## a = n1^{-1} sum_{i <= n1} Y_i z_i
  a <- drop(crossprod(z[1:n1, , drop = FALSE], y.labeled)) / n1

  loss <- function(theta) {
    eta <- drop(z %*% theta)
    mean(softplus(eta)) -
      sum(y.labeled * eta[1:n1]) / n1
  }

  if (is.null(start)) {
    start <- rep(0, p)
  }

  theta <- as.numeric(start)
  conv <- FALSE

  for (iter in seq_len(maxit)) {
    eta <- drop(z %*% theta)
    prob <- plogis(eta)

    grad <- drop(crossprod(z, prob)) / n - a

    if (max(abs(grad)) < tol) {
      conv <- TRUE
      break
    }

    w <- prob * (1 - prob)
    hess <- crossprod(z, z * w) / n

    step <- tryCatch(
      solve(hess, grad),
      error = function(e) qr.solve(hess, grad)
    )

    oldval <- loss(theta)
    lambda <- 1

    ## Step-halving to ensure descent
    repeat {
      theta.new <- theta - lambda * step
      newval <- loss(theta.new)

      if (is.finite(newval) &&
          newval <= oldval - 1e-4 * lambda * sum(grad * step)) {
        break
      }

      lambda <- lambda / 2
      if (lambda < 1e-8) break
    }

    if (trace) {
      cat(iter,
          "loss =", newval,
          "maxgrad =", max(abs(grad)),
          "lambda =", lambda, "\n")
    }

    if (max(abs(theta.new - theta)) <
        tol * (1 + max(abs(theta)))) {
      theta <- theta.new
      conv <- TRUE
      break
    }

    theta <- theta.new
  }

  eta <- drop(z %*% theta)
  prob <- plogis(eta)
  grad <- drop(crossprod(z, prob)) / n - a

  names(theta) <- c("beta0", "beta1", "beta2")

  list(
    coefficients = theta,
    loss = loss(theta),
    gradient = grad,
    iterations = iter,
    converged = conv
  )
}
```

---

## 5. Semi-supervised estimator and test performance

Run:

```r
fit.tilde <- ssl_newton(xs, ys, n1, start = theta.hat)
theta.tilde <- fit.tilde$coefficients

theta.tilde
test_metrics(theta.tilde, xs.test, ys.test)
```

To print all relevant quantities together:

```r
report <- rbind(
  labeled = c(theta.hat,
              test_metrics(theta.hat, xs.test, ys.test)),
  semisupervised = c(theta.tilde,
                     test_metrics(theta.tilde, xs.test, ys.test))
)

round(report, 6)
```

This gives the requested \((\tilde\beta_0,\tilde\beta_1,\tilde\beta_2)\), average test log-likelihood, and classification accuracy.

---

## 6. Plot training data and three classification lines

The classification line for coefficient vector \(\theta=(\theta_0,\theta_1,\theta_2)\) is

\[
\theta_0+\theta_1x_1+\theta_2x_2=0.
\]

Equivalently, if \(\theta_2\neq 0\),

\[
x_2
=
-\frac{\theta_0}{\theta_2}
-\frac{\theta_1}{\theta_2}x_1.
\]

The full-data MLE using all labels is computed only for comparison:

```r
dat.all <- data.frame(
  y  = ys,
  x1 = xs[, 1],
  x2 = xs[, 2]
)

fit.all <- glm(y ~ x1 + x2, data = dat.all, family = binomial())
theta.all <- unname(coef(fit.all))
names(theta.all) <- c("beta0", "beta1", "beta2")
```

Plot:

```r

pchs <- rep(1, nrow(xs))

cols[1:n1] <- ifelse(ys[1:n1] == 1, "tomato", "royalblue")
pchs[1:n1] <- 19

plot(xs[, 1], xs[, 2],
     col = cols, pch = pchs,
     xlab = expression(x[1]),
     ylab = expression(x[2]),
     main = "Labeled and unlabeled training data with classification lines")

draw_line <- function(theta, col, lty) {
  if (abs(theta[3]) > 1e-12) {
    abline(a = -theta[1] / theta[3],
           b = -theta[2] / theta[3],
           col = col, lwd = 2, lty = lty)
  } else {
    abline(v = -theta[1] / theta[2],
           col = col, lwd = 2, lty = lty)
  }
}

draw_line(theta.hat,   col = "black",     lty = 1)
draw_line(theta.tilde, col = "darkgreen", lty = 2)
draw_line(theta.all,   col = "purple",    lty = 3)

legend("topright",
       legend = c("labeled Y=0", "labeled Y=1", "unlabeled",
                  "labeled MLE", "semi-supervised", "all-label MLE"),
       col = c("royalblue", "tomato", "grey70",
               "black", "darkgreen", "purple"),
       pch = c(19, 19, 1, NA, NA, NA),
       lty = c(NA, NA, NA, 1, 2, 3),
       lwd = c(NA, NA, NA, 2, 2, 2),
       bty = "n")
```

The three plotted boundaries correspond to

\[
\hat\theta_0+\hat\theta_1x_1+\hat\theta_2x_2=0,
\]

\[
\tilde\theta_0+\tilde\theta_1x_1+\tilde\theta_2x_2=0,
\]

and

\[
\theta_{\text{all},0}+\theta_{\text{all},1}x_1+\theta_{\text{all},2}x_2=0.
\]

\frac12\log\frac{|\Sigma_0|}{|\Sigma_1|}
=
\frac12\log\frac{5625}{2500}
=
\log\frac32.
\]

Expanding the quadratic terms,

\[
\log\frac{P(Y=1\mid X=x)}{P(Y=0\mid X=x)}
=
\log\frac32-\frac{1}{10}
+\frac{12}{25}x_1
+\frac{13}{150}x_2
-\frac{1}{360}x_2^2.
\]

The true log-odds contain the quadratic term \(-x_2^2/360\). The fitted logistic model assumes

\[
\log\frac{P(Y=1\mid X=x)}{P(Y=0\mid X=x)}
=
\beta_0+\beta_1x_1+\beta_2x_2,
\]

which is affine in \(x\). Therefore the logistic model is misspecified.

Equivalently: the class-conditional covariances are unequal, so the Bayes rule is quadratic rather than linear.

---

## 2. Labeled-data MLE and test performance

The labeled MLE solves the usual logistic score equation

\[
0
=
\frac1{n_1}\sum_{i=1}^{n_1}
\{Y_i-\pi(X_i;\theta)\}z_i,
\]

where

\[
\pi(x;\theta)=\frac{\exp(z^T\theta)}{1+\exp(z^T\theta)}.
\]

The following R code reports \((\hat\beta_0,\hat\beta_1,\hat\beta_2)\), average test log-likelihood, and test accuracy. Replace `xs.test, ys.test` by the names used in the supplied code if different.

```r
softplus <- function(t) {
  pmax(t, 0) + log1p(exp(-abs(t)))
}

test_metrics <- function(theta, x, y) {
  z <- cbind(1, as.matrix(x))
  eta <- drop(z %*% theta)
  avg_loglik <- mean(y * eta - softplus(eta))
  acc <- mean((eta >= 0) == (y == 1))
  c(avg_test_loglik = avg_loglik, test_accuracy = acc)
}

## labeled-data logistic MLE
dat.labeled <- data.frame(
  y  = ys[1:n1],
  x1 = xs[1:n1, 1],
  x2 = xs[1:n1, 2]
)

fit.hat <- glm(y ~ x1 + x2, data = dat.labeled, family = binomial())
theta.hat <- unname(coef(fit.hat))
names(theta.hat) <- c("beta0", "beta1", "beta2")

theta.hat
test_metrics(theta.hat, xs.test, ys.test)
```

---

## 3. Loss minimized by \((\tilde\beta_0,\tilde\beta)\)

The semi-supervised estimator is defined by

\[
0
=
\frac1{n_1}\sum_{i=1}^{n_1}Y_i z_i
-
\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n \pi(X_i;\theta)z_i.
\]

Equivalently,

\[
0
=
\nabla_\theta L_n(\theta),
\]

where

\[
L_n(\theta)
=
\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n \log\left\{1+\exp(z_i^T\theta)\right\}
-
\frac1{n_1}\sum_{i=1}^{n_1} Y_i z_i^T\theta.
\]

Indeed,

\[
\nabla_\theta L_n(\theta)
=
\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n \pi(X_i;\theta)z_i
-
\frac1{n_1}\sum_{i=1}^{n_1}Y_i z_i.
\]

Therefore the estimating equation is exactly \(\nabla_\theta L_n(\theta)=0\).

The Hessian is

\[
\nabla_\theta^2 L_n(\theta)
=
\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n
\pi(X_i;\theta)\{1-\pi(X_i;\theta)\}z_i z_i^T,
\]

which is positive semidefinite. Hence \(L_n\) is convex, and any solution of the estimating equation is a global minimizer. If the design matrix has full column rank, the Hessian is positive definite for finite \(\theta\), giving uniqueness.

---

## 4. Newton-Raphson function for \((\tilde\beta_0,\tilde\beta)\)

```r
ssl_newton <- function(xs, ys, n1, start = NULL,
                       tol = 1e-10, maxit = 100, trace = FALSE) {
  x <- as.matrix(xs)
  n <- nrow(x)
  z <- cbind(1, x)
  p <- ncol(z)

  y.labeled <- ys[1:n1]

  ## a = n1^{-1} sum_{i <= n1} Y_i z_i
  a <- drop(crossprod(z[1:n1, , drop = FALSE], y.labeled)) / n1

  loss <- function(theta) {
    eta <- drop(z %*% theta)
    mean(softplus(eta)) -
      sum(y.labeled * eta[1:n1]) / n1
  }

  if (is.null(start)) {
    start <- rep(0, p)
  }

  theta <- as.numeric(start)
  conv <- FALSE

  for (iter in seq_len(maxit)) {
    eta <- drop(z %*% theta)
    prob <- plogis(eta)

    grad <- drop(crossprod(z, prob)) / n - a

    if (max(abs(grad)) < tol) {
      conv <- TRUE
      break
    }

    w <- prob * (1 - prob)
    hess <- crossprod(z, z * w) / n

    step <- tryCatch(
      solve(hess, grad),
      error = function(e) qr.solve(hess, grad)
    )

    oldval <- loss(theta)
    lambda <- 1

    ## Step-halving to ensure descent
    repeat {
      theta.new <- theta - lambda * step
      newval <- loss(theta.new)

      if (is.finite(newval) &&
          newval <= oldval - 1e-4 * lambda * sum(grad * step)) {
        break
      }

      lambda <- lambda / 2
      if (lambda < 1e-8) break
    }

    if (trace) {
      cat(iter,
          "loss =", newval,
          "maxgrad =", max(abs(grad)),
          "lambda =", lambda, "\n")
    }

    if (max(abs(theta.new - theta)) <
        tol * (1 + max(abs(theta)))) {
      theta <- theta.new
      conv <- TRUE
      break
    }

    theta <- theta.new
  }

  eta <- drop(z %*% theta)
  prob <- plogis(eta)
  grad <- drop(crossprod(z, prob)) / n - a

  names(theta) <- c("beta0", "beta1", "beta2")

  list(
    coefficients = theta,
    loss = loss(theta),
    gradient = grad,
    iterations = iter,
    converged = conv
  )
}
```

---

theta.tilde
test_metrics(theta.tilde, xs.test, ys.test)
```

response.text:
## Notation

Let  
\[
C_k=\{i:Y_i=k\},\qquad n_k=|C_k|,\qquad \sum_{k=1}^K n_k=N,
\]
and let all vectors be treated as column vectors. Define the overall and class sample means by  
\[
\hat\mu=\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N x_i,\qquad 
\hat\mu_k=\frac1{n_k}\sum_{i\in C_k}x_i.
\]

Use the standard unbiased pooled within-class covariance and between-class covariance
\[
\Sigma_w=\frac1{N-K}\sum_{k=1}^K\sum_{i\in C_k}(x_i-\hat\mu_k)(x_i-\hat\mu_k)^T,
\]
\[
\Sigma_b=\frac1{N-1}\sum_{k=1}^K n_k(\hat\mu_k-\hat\mu)(\hat\mu_k-\hat\mu)^T,
\]
and total sample covariance
\[
\Sigma_t=\frac1{N-1}\sum_{i=1}^N(x_i-\hat\mu)(x_i-\hat\mu)^T.
\]

---

## (1) Total covariance decomposition

For \(i\in C_k\),
\[
x_i-\hat\mu=(x_i-\hat\mu_k)+(\hat\mu_k-\hat\mu).
\]
Therefore
\[
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{i=1}^N (x_i-\hat\mu)(x_i-\hat\mu)^T
&=\sum_{k=1}^K\sum_{i\in C_k}
\left\{(x_i-\hat\mu_k)+(\hat\mu_k-\hat\mu)\right\} \\
&\qquad\qquad\qquad\cdot
\left\{(x_i-\hat\mu_k)+(\hat\mu_k-\hat\mu)\right\}^T.
\end{aligned}
\]
Expanding gives three types of terms:
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\sum_{k=1}^K\sum_{i\in C_k}(x_i-\hat\mu_k)(x_i-\hat\mu_k)^T \\
&\quad+
\sum_{k=1}^K\sum_{i\in C_k}(x_i-\hat\mu_k)(\hat\mu_k-\hat\mu)^T \\
&\quad+
\sum_{k=1}^K\sum_{i\in C_k}(\hat\mu_k-\hat\mu)(x_i-\hat\mu_k)^T \\
&\quad+
\sum_{k=1}^K\sum_{i\in C_k}(\hat\mu_k-\hat\mu)(\hat\mu_k-\hat\mu)^T.
\end{aligned}
\]
The cross terms vanish because, for each class \(k\),
\[
\sum_{i\in C_k}(x_i-\hat\mu_k)=0.
\]
Hence
\[
\sum_{i=1}^N (x_i-\hat\mu)(x_i-\hat\mu)^T
=
\sum_{k=1}^K\sum_{i\in C_k}(x_i-\hat\mu_k)(x_i-\hat\mu_k)^T
+
\sum_{k=1}^K n_k(\hat\mu_k-\hat\mu)(\hat\mu_k-\hat\mu)^T.
\]
Using the definitions of \(\Sigma_t,\Sigma_w,\Sigma_b\),
\[
(N-1)\Sigma_t=(N-K)\Sigma_w+(N-1)\Sigma_b.
\]

Thus
\[
\boxed{
(N-1)\Sigma_t
=
\sum_{i=1}^N (x_i-\hat\mu)(x_i-\hat\mu)^T
=
(N-K)\Sigma_w+(N-1)\Sigma_b.
}
\]

---

## (2) Fisher reduced-rank LDA and the generalized eigenproblem

Fisher’s criterion for one projection direction \(v\neq 0\) is
\[
R(v)=\frac{v^T\Sigma_bv}{v^T\Sigma_wv}.
\]
Assume \(\Sigma_w\) is positive definite. Since \(R(cv)=R(v)\) for any nonzero scalar \(c\), we may impose the constraint
\[
v^T\Sigma_w v=1.
\]
Then maximizing \(R(v)\) is equivalent to
\[
\max_v v^T\Sigma_bv
\quad\text{subject to}\quad
v^T\Sigma_wv=1.
\]
The Lagrangian is
\[
\mathcal L(v,\lambda)
=
v^T\Sigma_bv-\lambda(v^T\Sigma_wv-1).
\]
Differentiating with respect to \(v\) gives
\[
2\Sigma_b v-2\lambda\Sigma_wv=0.
\]
Thus
\[
\Sigma_bv=\lambda \Sigma_wv.
\]
Since \(\Sigma_w\) is invertible,
\[
\boxed{
\Sigma_w^{-1}\Sigma_bv=\lambda v.
}
\]

Equivalently, this is the generalized eigenvalue problem
\[
\boxed{
\Sigma_b v=\lambda \Sigma_w v.
}
\]

A more global argument uses the Rayleigh-Ritz theorem. Let
\[
u=\Sigma_w^{1/2}v.
\]
Then
\[
R(v)
=
\frac{v^T\Sigma_bv}{v^T\Sigma_wv}
=
\frac{u^T\Sigma_w^{-1/2}\Sigma_b\Sigma_w^{-1/2}u}{u^Tu}.
\]
Thus the maximum is the largest eigenvalue of the symmetric matrix
\[
\Sigma_w^{-1/2}\Sigma_b\Sigma_w^{-1/2},
\]
and the maximizing \(v\) is obtained from its eigenvector by multiplying by \(\Sigma_w^{-1/2}\).

For reduced-rank LDA with \(m\) directions, one takes the eigenvectors corresponding to the largest \(m\) generalized eigenvalues. Because
\[
\operatorname{rank}(\Sigma_b)\le K-1,
\]
there are at most \(K-1\) nonzero discriminant directions. For \(K=3\), Fisher LDA has at most two nontrivial directions.

---

## (3) Simulating 100 observations from each of three Gaussian classes in \(\mathbb R^{128}\)

Suppose the three class distributions are
\[
X\mid Y=k\sim N_{128}(\theta_k,D),\qquad k=1,2,3,
\]
where
\[
D=\operatorname{diag}(\sigma_1^2,\ldots,\sigma_{128}^2)
\]
is the common diagonal covariance matrix.

The numerical values of \(\theta_1,\theta_2,\theta_3\) and \(D\) should be inserted from the problem statement. The following code generates the data.

```python
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

def generate_three_gaussians(theta1, theta2, theta3, diag_cov, n_per_class=100, seed=1):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)

    theta = np.vstack([theta1, theta2, theta3])  # shape (3, 128)

    diag_cov = np.asarray(diag_cov)
    if diag_cov.ndim == 2:
        sig2 = np.diag(diag_cov)
    else:
        sig2 = diag_cov

    scale = np.sqrt(sig2)
    K, p = theta.shape

    X_list = []
    y_list = []

    for k in range(K):
        Xk = theta[k] + rng.standard_normal(size=(n_per_class, p)) * scale
        X_list.append(Xk)
        y_list.extend([k + 1] * n_per_class)

    X = np.vstack(X_list)
    y = np.asarray(y_list)

    return X, y
```

                                n_per_class=100, seed=2021)

---

## (4) Fisher reduced-rank LDA from scratch and visualization

Here is an implementation of Fisher LDA without using a prebuilt LDA routine.

```python
def fisher_reduced_rank_lda(X, y, m=2, ridge=0.0):
    X = np.asarray(X, dtype=float)
    y = np.asarray(y)

    N, p = X.shape
    classes = np.unique(y)
    K = len(classes)

    mu = X.mean(axis=0)

    W = np.zeros((p, p))
    B = np.zeros((p, p))

    for c in classes:
        Xc = X[y == c]
        nc = Xc.shape[0]
        muc = Xc.mean(axis=0)

        Xc_centered = Xc - muc
        W += Xc_centered.T @ Xc_centered

        d = (muc - mu).reshape(-1, 1)
        B += nc * (d @ d.T)

    Sigma_w = W / (N - K)
    Sigma_b = B / (N - 1)

    if ridge > 0:
        Sigma_w = Sigma_w + ridge * np.trace(Sigma_w) / p * np.eye(p)

    # Symmetric whitening solution to the generalized eigenproblem
    evals_w, U = np.linalg.eigh((Sigma_w + Sigma_w.T) / 2)

    if evals_w[0] <= 1e-12 * evals_w[-1]:
        raise ValueError("Sigma_w is numerically singular; use a positive ridge value.")

    Sigma_w_inv_half = (U * (evals_w ** -0.5)) @ U.T

    M = Sigma_w_inv_half @ Sigma_b @ Sigma_w_inv_half
    M = (M + M.T) / 2

    lda_evals, A = np.linalg.eigh(M)
    order = np.argsort(lda_evals)[::-1]

    lda_evals = lda_evals[order]
    A = A[:, order]

    m = min(m, K - 1, p)
    V = Sigma_w_inv_half @ A[:, :m]

    # Normalize directions so that V.T Sigma_w V = I
    for j in range(m):
        norm = np.sqrt(V[:, j].T @ Sigma_w @ V[:, j])
        V[:, j] /= norm

        # Optional sign convention for reproducibility
        idx = np.argmax(np.abs(V[:, j]))
        if V[idx, j] < 0:
            V[:, j] *= -1

    return V, lda_evals[:m], mu, Sigma_w, Sigma_b
```

Now compute the first two Fisher directions and plot.

```python
V_lda, lda_evals, mu_lda, Sigma_w, Sigma_b = fisher_reduced_rank_lda(X, y, m=2)

Z_lda = (X - mu_lda) @ V_lda

plt.figure(figsize=(6, 5))
for c in np.unique(y):
    plt.scatter(Z_lda[y == c, 0],
                Z_lda[y == c, 1],
                s=25,
                alpha=0.75,
                label=f"Class {c}")

plt.xlabel("First Fisher discriminant direction")
plt.ylabel("Second Fisher discriminant direction")
plt.title("Reduced-rank Fisher LDA projection")
plt.legend()
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

Since \(K=3\), two Fisher directions are the maximum possible number of nonzero discriminant directions. Thus this two-dimensional plot contains all sample mean-separation information that Fisher LDA can extract.

---

## (5) PCA from scratch and visualization

PCA ignores the labels. It finds directions of largest total sample variance.

```python
def pca_from_scratch(X, m=2):
    X = np.asarray(X, dtype=float)
    N, p = X.shape

    mu = X.mean(axis=0)
    Xc = X - mu

    Sigma_t = Xc.T @ Xc / (N - 1)

    pca_evals, U = np.linalg.eigh((Sigma_t + Sigma_t.T) / 2)
    order = np.argsort(pca_evals)[::-1]

    pca_evals = pca_evals[order]
    U = U[:, order]

    return U[:, :m], pca_evals[:m], mu
```

Compute and plot the first two principal component scores.

```python
V_pca, pca_evals, mu_pca = pca_from_scratch(X, m=2)

Z_pca = (X - mu_pca) @ V_pca

plt.figure(figsize=(6, 5))
for c in np.unique(y):
    plt.scatter(Z_pca[y == c, 0],
                Z_pca[y == c, 1],
                s=25,
                alpha=0.75,
                label=f"Class {c}")

plt.xlabel("First principal component")
plt.ylabel("Second principal component")
plt.title("PCA projection")
plt.legend()
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

---

## Comparison of LDA and PCA

The key distinction is that Fisher LDA is supervised, while PCA is unsupervised.

From part (1),
\[
\Sigma_t
=
\frac{N-K}{N-1}\Sigma_w+\Sigma_b.
\]
PCA finds the leading eigenvectors of \(\Sigma_t\). Therefore PCA maximizes total variance, which combines within-class variation and between-class variation. If the within-class covariance has large variance in some directions that do not separate the classes, PCA may select those directions anyway.

Fisher LDA instead maximizes
\[
\frac{v^T\Sigma_bv}{v^T\Sigma_wv}.
\]

## Notation

Let  
\[
C_k=\{i:Y_i=k\},\qquad n_k=|C_k|,\qquad \sum_{k=1}^K n_k=N,
\]
and let all vectors be treated as column vectors. Define the overall and class sample means by  
\[
\hat\mu=\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N x_i,\qquad 
\hat\mu_k=\frac1{n_k}\sum_{i\in C_k}x_i.
\]

Use the standard unbiased pooled within-class covariance and between-class covariance
\[
\Sigma_w=\frac1{N-K}\sum_{k=1}^K\sum_{i\in C_k}(x_i-\hat\mu_k)(x_i-\hat\mu_k)^T,
\]
\[
\Sigma_b=\frac1{N-1}\sum_{k=1}^K n_k(\hat\mu_k-\hat\mu)(\hat\mu_k-\hat\mu)^T,
\]
and total sample covariance
\[
\Sigma_t=\frac1{N-1}\sum_{i=1}^N(x_i-\hat\mu)(x_i-\hat\mu)^T.
\]

---

## (1) Total covariance decomposition

For \(i\in C_k\),
\[
x_i-\hat\mu=(x_i-\hat\mu_k)+(\hat\mu_k-\hat\mu).
\]
Therefore
\[
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{i=1}^N (x_i-\hat\mu)(x_i-\hat\mu)^T
&=\sum_{k=1}^K\sum_{i\in C_k}
\left\{(x_i-\hat\mu_k)+(\hat\mu_k-\hat\mu)\right\} \\
&\qquad\qquad\qquad\cdot
\left\{(x_i-\hat\mu_k)+(\hat\mu_k-\hat\mu)\right\}^T.
\end{aligned}
\]
Expanding gives three types of terms:
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\sum_{k=1}^K\sum_{i\in C_k}(x_i-\hat\mu_k)(x_i-\hat\mu_k)^T \\
&\quad+
\sum_{k=1}^K\sum_{i\in C_k}(x_i-\hat\mu_k)(\hat\mu_k-\hat\mu)^T \\
&\quad+
\sum_{k=1}^K\sum_{i\in C_k}(\hat\mu_k-\hat\mu)(x_i-\hat\mu_k)^T \\
&\quad+
\sum_{k=1}^K\sum_{i\in C_k}(\hat\mu_k-\hat\mu)(\hat\mu_k-\hat\mu)^T.
\end{aligned}
\]
The cross terms vanish because, for each class \(k\),
\[
\sum_{i\in C_k}(x_i-\hat\mu_k)=0.
\]
Hence
\[
\sum_{i=1}^N (x_i-\hat\mu)(x_i-\hat\mu)^T
=
\sum_{k=1}^K\sum_{i\in C_k}(x_i-\hat\mu_k)(x_i-\hat\mu_k)^T
+
\sum_{k=1}^K n_k(\hat\mu_k-\hat\mu)(\hat\mu_k-\hat\mu)^T.
\]
Using the definitions of \(\Sigma_t,\Sigma_w,\Sigma_b\),
\[
(N-1)\Sigma_t=(N-K)\Sigma_w+(N-1)\Sigma_b.
\]

Thus
\[
\boxed{
(N-1)\Sigma_t
=
\sum_{i=1}^N (x_i-\hat\mu)(x_i-\hat\mu)^T
=
(N-K)\Sigma_w+(N-1)\Sigma_b.
}
\]

---

## (2) Fisher reduced-rank LDA and the generalized eigenproblem

Fisher’s criterion for one projection direction \(v\neq 0\) is
\[
R(v)=\frac{v^T\Sigma_bv}{v^T\Sigma_wv}.
\]
Assume \(\Sigma_w\) is positive definite. Since \(R(cv)=R(v)\) for any nonzero scalar \(c\), we may impose the constraint
\[
v^T\Sigma_w v=1.
\]
Then maximizing \(R(v)\) is equivalent to
\[
\max_v v^T\Sigma_bv
\quad\text{subject to}\quad
v^T\Sigma_wv=1.
\]
The Lagrangian is
\[
\mathcal L(v,\lambda)
=
v^T\Sigma_bv-\lambda(v^T\Sigma_wv-1).
\]
Differentiating with respect to \(v\) gives
\[
2\Sigma_b v-2\lambda\Sigma_wv=0.
\]
Thus
\[
\Sigma_bv=\lambda \Sigma_wv.
\]
Since \(\Sigma_w\) is invertible,
\[
\boxed{
\Sigma_w^{-1}\Sigma_bv=\lambda v.
}
\]

Equivalently, this is the generalized eigenvalue problem
\[
\boxed{
\Sigma_b v=\lambda \Sigma_w v.
}
\]

A more global argument uses the Rayleigh-Ritz theorem. Let
\[
u=\Sigma_w^{1/2}v.
\]
Then
\[
R(v)
=
\frac{v^T\Sigma_bv}{v^T\Sigma_wv}
=
\frac{u^T\Sigma_w^{-1/2}\Sigma_b\Sigma_w^{-1/2}u}{u^Tu}.
\]
Thus the maximum is the largest eigenvalue of the symmetric matrix
\[
\Sigma_w^{-1/2}\Sigma_b\Sigma_w^{-1/2},
\]
and the maximizing \(v\) is obtained from its eigenvector by multiplying by \(\Sigma_w^{-1/2}\).

For reduced-rank LDA with \(m\) directions, one takes the eigenvectors corresponding to the largest \(m\) generalized eigenvalues. Because
\[
\operatorname{rank}(\Sigma_b)\le K-1,
\]
there are at most \(K-1\) nonzero discriminant directions. For \(K=3\), Fisher LDA has at most two nontrivial directions.

---

## (3) Simulating 100 observations from each of three Gaussian classes in \(\mathbb R^{128}\)

Suppose the three class distributions are
\[
X\mid Y=k\sim N_{128}(\theta_k,D),\qquad k=1,2,3,
\]
where
\[
D=\operatorname{diag}(\sigma_1^2,\ldots,\sigma_{128}^2)
\]
is the common diagonal covariance matrix.

The numerical values of \(\theta_1,\theta_2,\theta_3\) and \(D\) should be inserted from the problem statement. The following code generates the data.

```python
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

def generate_three_gaussians(theta1, theta2, theta3, diag_cov, n_per_class=100, seed=1):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)

    theta = np.vstack([theta1, theta2, theta3])  # shape (3, 128)

    diag_cov = np.asarray(diag_cov)
    if diag_cov.ndim == 2:
        sig2 = np.diag(diag_cov)
    else:
        sig2 = diag_cov

    scale = np.sqrt(sig2)
    K, p = theta.shape

    X_list = []
    y_list = []

    for k in range(K):
        Xk = theta[k] + rng.standard_normal(size=(n_per_class, p)) * scale
        X_list.append(Xk)
        y_list.extend([k + 1] * n_per_class)

    X = np.vstack(X_list)
    y = np.asarray(y_list)

    return X, y
```

Example usage:

```python
# Insert the given arrays from the problem:
# theta1 = np.array([...])  # length 128
# theta2 = np.array([...])
# theta3 = np.array([...])
# diag_cov = np.array([...])  # length 128, or a 128 x 128 diagonal matrix

X, y = generate_three_gaussians(theta1, theta2, theta3, diag_cov,
                                n_per_class=100, seed=2021)
```

---

## (4) Fisher reduced-rank LDA from scratch and visualization

Here is an implementation of Fisher LDA without using a prebuilt LDA routine.

```python
def fisher_reduced_rank_lda(X, y, m=2, ridge=0.0):
    X = np.asarray(X, dtype=float)
    y = np.asarray(y)

    N, p = X.shape
    classes = np.unique(y)
    K = len(classes)

    mu = X.mean(axis=0)

    W = np.zeros((p, p))
    B = np.zeros((p, p))

    for c in classes:
        Xc = X[y == c]
        nc = Xc.shape[0]
        muc = Xc.mean(axis=0)

        Xc_centered = Xc - muc
        W += Xc_centered.T @ Xc_centered

        d = (muc - mu).reshape(-1, 1)
        B += nc * (d @ d.T)

    Sigma_w = W / (N - K)
    Sigma_b = B / (N - 1)

    if ridge > 0:
        Sigma_w = Sigma_w + ridge * np.trace(Sigma_w) / p * np.eye(p)

    # Symmetric whitening solution to the generalized eigenproblem
    evals_w, U = np.linalg.eigh((Sigma_w + Sigma_w.T) / 2)

    if evals_w[0] <= 1e-12 * evals_w[-1]:
        raise ValueError("Sigma_w is numerically singular; use a positive ridge value.")

    Sigma_w_inv_half = (U * (evals_w ** -0.5)) @ U.T

    M = Sigma_w_inv_half @ Sigma_b @ Sigma_w_inv_half
    M = (M + M.T) / 2

    lda_evals, A = np.linalg.eigh(M)
    order = np.argsort(lda_evals)[::-1]

    lda_evals = lda_evals[order]
    A = A[:, order]

    m = min(m, K - 1, p)
    V = Sigma_w_inv_half @ A[:, :m]

    # Normalize directions so that V.T Sigma_w V = I
    for j in range(m):
        norm = np.sqrt(V[:, j].T @ Sigma_w @ V[:, j])
        V[:, j] /= norm

        # Optional sign convention for reproducibility
        idx = np.argmax(np.abs(V[:, j]))
        if V[idx, j] < 0:
            V[:, j] *= -1

    return V, lda_evals[:m], mu, Sigma_w, Sigma_b
```

Now compute the first two Fisher directions and plot.

```python
V_lda, lda_evals, mu_lda, Sigma_w, Sigma_b = fisher_reduced_rank_lda(X, y, m=2)

Z_lda = (X - mu_lda) @ V_lda

plt.figure(figsize=(6, 5))
for c in np.unique(y):
    plt.scatter(Z_lda[y == c, 0],
                Z_lda[y == c, 1],
                s=25,
                alpha=0.75,
                label=f"Class {c}")

plt.xlabel("First Fisher discriminant direction")
plt.ylabel("Second Fisher discriminant direction")
plt.title("Reduced-rank Fisher LDA projection")
plt.legend()
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

Since \(K=3\), two Fisher directions are the maximum possible number of nonzero discriminant directions. Thus this two-dimensional plot contains all sample mean-separation information that Fisher LDA can extract.

---

## (5) PCA from scratch and visualization

PCA ignores the labels. It finds directions of largest total sample variance.

```python
def pca_from_scratch(X, m=2):
    X = np.asarray(X, dtype=float)
    N, p = X.shape

    mu = X.mean(axis=0)
    Xc = X - mu

    Sigma_t = Xc.T @ Xc / (N - 1)

    pca_evals, U = np.linalg.eigh((Sigma_t + Sigma_t.T) / 2)
    order = np.argsort(pca_evals)[::-1]

    pca_evals = pca_evals[order]
    U = U[:, order]

    return U[:, :m], pca_evals[:m], mu
```

Compute and plot the first two principal component scores.

```python
V_pca, pca_evals, mu_pca = pca_from_scratch(X, m=2)

Z_pca = (X - mu_pca) @ V_pca

plt.figure(figsize=(6, 5))
for c in np.unique(y):
    plt.scatter(Z_pca[y == c, 0],
                Z_pca[y == c, 1],
                s=25,
                alpha=0.75,
                label=f"Class {c}")

plt.xlabel("First principal component")
plt.ylabel("Second principal component")
plt.title("PCA projection")
plt.legend()
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

---

## Comparison of LDA and PCA

The key distinction is that Fisher LDA is supervised, while PCA is unsupervised.

From part (1),
\[
\Sigma_t
=
\frac{N-K}{N-1}\Sigma_w+\Sigma_b.
\]
PCA finds the leading eigenvectors of \(\Sigma_t\). Therefore PCA maximizes total variance, which combines within-class variation and between-class variation. If the within-class covariance has large variance in some directions that do not separate the classes, PCA may select those directions anyway.

Fisher LDA instead maximizes
\[
\frac{v^T\Sigma_bv}{v^T\Sigma_wv}.
\]
Thus LDA searches for directions with large between-class variation relative to within-class variation.

In the population Gaussian model,
\[
X\mid Y=k\sim N_{128}(\theta_k,D),
\]
with common diagonal covariance \(D\), the population total covariance is
\[
\operatorname{Cov}(X)=D+B,
\]
where
\[
B=\sum_{k=1}^3 \pi_k(\theta_k-\mu)(\theta_k-\mu)^T
\]
is the between-class covariance. PCA uses eigenvectors of \(D+B\). LDA uses eigenvectors of
\[
D^{-1}B.
\]
Thus LDA effectively weights mean differences by inverse noise variance. Coordinates with small within-class variance and meaningful class mean differences are emphasized. PCA does not do this.

Therefore, typically:

- The LDA plot shows stronger class separation.
- The PCA plot may show overlap if the directions of largest total variance are mainly within-class noise directions.
- PCA and LDA look similar only when the directions of largest total variance also coincide with the directions of class separation.

For three classes, LDA has at most two nonzero directions, so the two-dimensional LDA plot is the natural reduced-rank representation for class discrimination.

Below I treat each \(x_i\) as a column vector in \(\mathbb R^p\). Let

\[
C_k=\{i:Y_i=k\},\qquad n_k=|C_k|,\qquad \sum_{k=1}^K n_k=N,
\]

\[
\hat \mu_k=\frac1{n_k}\sum_{i\in C_k}x_i,\qquad 
\hat \mu=\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N x_i=\sum_{k=1}^K \frac{n_k}{N}\hat\mu_k.
\]

---

## (1) Total covariance decomposition

Define the total, within-class, and between-class sample covariance matrices by

\[
\Sigma_t=\frac1{N-1}\sum_{i=1}^N (x_i-\hat\mu)(x_i-\hat\mu)^T,
\]

\[
\Sigma_w=\frac1{N-K}\sum_{k=1}^K\sum_{i\in C_k}(x_i-\hat\mu_k)(x_i-\hat\mu_k)^T,
\]

\[
\Sigma_b=\frac1{N-1}\sum_{k=1}^K n_k(\hat\mu_k-\hat\mu)(\hat\mu_k-\hat\mu)^T.
\]

For \(i\in C_k\),

\[
x_i-\hat\mu=(x_i-\hat\mu_k)+(\hat\mu_k-\hat\mu).
\]

Therefore,

\[
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{i=1}^N (x_i-\hat\mu)(x_i-\hat\mu)^T
&=\sum_{k=1}^K\sum_{i\in C_k}
\left[(x_i-\hat\mu_k)+(\hat\mu_k-\hat\mu)\right]
\left[(x_i-\hat\mu_k)+(\hat\mu_k-\hat\mu)\right]^T\\
&=\sum_{k=1}^K\sum_{i\in C_k}(x_i-\hat\mu_k)(x_i-\hat\mu_k)^T\\
&\qquad +\sum_{k=1}^K n_k(\hat\mu_k-\hat\mu)(\hat\mu_k-\hat\mu)^T\\
&\qquad +\sum_{k=1}^K\left\{\sum_{i\in C_k}(x_i-\hat\mu_k)\right\}(\hat\mu_k-\hat\mu)^T\\
&\qquad +\sum_{k=1}^K(\hat\mu_k-\hat\mu)\left\{\sum_{i\in C_k}(x_i-\hat\mu_k)\right\}^T.
\end{aligned}
\]

But for each class \(k\),

\[
\sum_{i\in C_k}(x_i-\hat\mu_k)=0.
\]

Hence the cross-terms vanish, giving

\[
\sum_{i=1}^N (x_i-\hat\mu)(x_i-\hat\mu)^T
=
\sum_{k=1}^K\sum_{i\in C_k}(x_i-\hat\mu_k)(x_i-\hat\mu_k)^T
+
\sum_{k=1}^K n_k(\hat\mu_k-\hat\mu)(\hat\mu_k-\hat\mu)^T.
\]

Using the definitions above,

\[
\boxed{
(N-1)\Sigma_t=(N-K)\Sigma_w+(N-1)\Sigma_b.
}
\]

This is the usual ANOVA/Huygens decomposition of total scatter into within-class and between-class scatter.

---

## (2) Fisher LDA eigenproblem

Fisher’s reduced-rank LDA direction solves

\[
\max_{v\neq 0}\frac{v^T\Sigma_b v}{v^T\Sigma_w v}.
\]

Assume first that \(\Sigma_w\) is positive definite. The criterion is scale-invariant, so impose the constraint

\[
v^T\Sigma_w v=1.
\]

Then the constrained optimization problem is

\[
\max_v v^T\Sigma_b v
\quad\text{subject to}\quad
v^T\Sigma_w v=1.
\]

The Lagrangian is

\[
\mathcal L(v,\lambda)=v^T\Sigma_b v-\lambda(v^T\Sigma_w v-1).
\]

Differentiating with respect to \(v\),

\[
2\Sigma_b v-2\lambda \Sigma_w v=0.
\]

Thus,

\[
\Sigma_b v=\lambda \Sigma_w v.
\]

If \(\Sigma_w\) is invertible, this becomes

\[
\boxed{
\Sigma_w^{-1}\Sigma_b v=\lambda v.
}
\]

So Fisher LDA directions are generalized eigenvectors of the matrix pencil \((\Sigma_b,\Sigma_w)\). Equivalently, by the Rayleigh–Ritz theorem, if

\[
A=\Sigma_w^{-1/2}\Sigma_b\Sigma_w^{-1/2},
\]

then the maximizers are

\[
v_j=\Sigma_w^{-1/2}u_j,
\]

where \(u_j\) are the leading eigenvectors of \(A\). Since

\[
\operatorname{rank}(\Sigma_b)\le K-1,
\]

there are at most \(K-1\) nonzero Fisher directions. In this problem, with \(K=3\), there are at most two useful LDA directions.

If \(\Sigma_w\) is singular, one usually uses the generalized eigenproblem on the range of \(\Sigma_w\), or a regularized version \(\Sigma_w+\gamma I\).

---

    X : array, shape (N, p)
        Data matrix.
    y : array, shape (N,)
        Class labels.
    n_components : int
        Number of Fisher directions to return.
    ridge : float

    W : array, shape (p, n_components)

    Sigma_b : array

    y = np.asarray(y)

    K = len(labels)

    Sb_scatter = np.zeros((p, p))

        Sb_scatter += nk * (diff @ diff.T)

    Sigma_b = Sb_scatter / (N - 1)

    A = 0.5 * (A + A.T)  # enforce symmetry numerically

    evals, U = np.linalg.eigh(A)

    idx = np.argsort(evals)[::-1]
    evals = evals[idx]
    U = U[:, idx]

Below I treat each \(x_i\) as a column vector in \(\mathbb R^p\). Let

\[
C_k=\{i:Y_i=k\},\qquad n_k=|C_k|,\qquad \sum_{k=1}^K n_k=N,
\]

\[
\hat \mu_k=\frac1{n_k}\sum_{i\in C_k}x_i,\qquad 
\hat \mu=\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N x_i=\sum_{k=1}^K \frac{n_k}{N}\hat\mu_k.
\]

---

## (1) Total covariance decomposition

Define the total, within-class, and between-class sample covariance matrices by

\[
\Sigma_t=\frac1{N-1}\sum_{i=1}^N (x_i-\hat\mu)(x_i-\hat\mu)^T,
\]

\[
\Sigma_w=\frac1{N-K}\sum_{k=1}^K\sum_{i\in C_k}(x_i-\hat\mu_k)(x_i-\hat\mu_k)^T,
\]

\[
\Sigma_b=\frac1{N-1}\sum_{k=1}^K n_k(\hat\mu_k-\hat\mu)(\hat\mu_k-\hat\mu)^T.
\]

For \(i\in C_k\),

\[
x_i-\hat\mu=(x_i-\hat\mu_k)+(\hat\mu_k-\hat\mu).
\]

Therefore,

\[
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{i=1}^N (x_i-\hat\mu)(x_i-\hat\mu)^T
&=\sum_{k=1}^K\sum_{i\in C_k}
\left[(x_i-\hat\mu_k)+(\hat\mu_k-\hat\mu)\right]
\left[(x_i-\hat\mu_k)+(\hat\mu_k-\hat\mu)\right]^T\\
&=\sum_{k=1}^K\sum_{i\in C_k}(x_i-\hat\mu_k)(x_i-\hat\mu_k)^T\\
&\qquad +\sum_{k=1}^K n_k(\hat\mu_k-\hat\mu)(\hat\mu_k-\hat\mu)^T\\
&\qquad +\sum_{k=1}^K\left\{\sum_{i\in C_k}(x_i-\hat\mu_k)\right\}(\hat\mu_k-\hat\mu)^T\\
&\qquad +\sum_{k=1}^K(\hat\mu_k-\hat\mu)\left\{\sum_{i\in C_k}(x_i-\hat\mu_k)\right\}^T.
\end{aligned}
\]

But for each class \(k\),

\[
\sum_{i\in C_k}(x_i-\hat\mu_k)=0.
\]

Hence the cross-terms vanish, giving

\[
\sum_{i=1}^N (x_i-\hat\mu)(x_i-\hat\mu)^T
=
\sum_{k=1}^K\sum_{i\in C_k}(x_i-\hat\mu_k)(x_i-\hat\mu_k)^T
+
\sum_{k=1}^K n_k(\hat\mu_k-\hat\mu)(\hat\mu_k-\hat\mu)^T.
\]

Using the definitions above,

\[
\boxed{
(N-1)\Sigma_t=(N-K)\Sigma_w+(N-1)\Sigma_b.
}
\]

This is the usual ANOVA/Huygens decomposition of total scatter into within-class and between-class scatter.

---

## (2) Fisher LDA eigenproblem

Fisher’s reduced-rank LDA direction solves

\[
\max_{v\neq 0}\frac{v^T\Sigma_b v}{v^T\Sigma_w v}.
\]

Assume first that \(\Sigma_w\) is positive definite. The criterion is scale-invariant, so impose the constraint

\[
v^T\Sigma_w v=1.
\]

Then the constrained optimization problem is

\[
\max_v v^T\Sigma_b v
\quad\text{subject to}\quad
v^T\Sigma_w v=1.
\]

The Lagrangian is

\[
\mathcal L(v,\lambda)=v^T\Sigma_b v-\lambda(v^T\Sigma_w v-1).
\]

Differentiating with respect to \(v\),

\[
2\Sigma_b v-2\lambda \Sigma_w v=0.
\]

Thus,

\[
\Sigma_b v=\lambda \Sigma_w v.
\]

If \(\Sigma_w\) is invertible, this becomes

\[
\boxed{
\Sigma_w^{-1}\Sigma_b v=\lambda v.
}
\]

So Fisher LDA directions are generalized eigenvectors of the matrix pencil \((\Sigma_b,\Sigma_w)\). Equivalently, by the Rayleigh–Ritz theorem, if

\[
A=\Sigma_w^{-1/2}\Sigma_b\Sigma_w^{-1/2},
\]

then the maximizers are

\[
v_j=\Sigma_w^{-1/2}u_j,
\]

where \(u_j\) are the leading eigenvectors of \(A\). Since

\[
\operatorname{rank}(\Sigma_b)\le K-1,
\]

there are at most \(K-1\) nonzero Fisher directions. In this problem, with \(K=3\), there are at most two useful LDA directions.

If \(\Sigma_w\) is singular, one usually uses the generalized eigenproblem on the range of \(\Sigma_w\), or a regularized version \(\Sigma_w+\gamma I\).

## (1) Decomposition of total covariance into within- and between-class covariance

Let

\[
C_k=\{i:Y_i=k\},\qquad N_k=|C_k|,\qquad \sum_{k=1}^K N_k=N.
\]

Define the overall sample mean and class means by

\[
\hat\mu=\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N x_i,\qquad 
\hat\mu_k=\frac1{N_k}\sum_{i\in C_k} x_i.
\]

The usual sample total covariance is

\[
\Sigma_t=\frac1{N-1}\sum_{i=1}^N (x_i-\hat\mu)(x_i-\hat\mu)^T.
\]

The pooled within-class covariance is

\[
\Sigma_w=\frac1{N-K}\sum_{k=1}^K \sum_{i\in C_k} (x_i-\hat\mu_k)(x_i-\hat\mu_k)^T,
\]

and the between-class covariance is

\[
\Sigma_b=\frac1{N-1}\sum_{k=1}^K N_k(\hat\mu_k-\hat\mu)(\hat\mu_k-\hat\mu)^T.
\]

For \(i\in C_k\),

\[
x_i-\hat\mu=(x_i-\hat\mu_k)+(\hat\mu_k-\hat\mu).
\]

Therefore,

\[
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{i\in C_k}(x_i-\hat\mu)(x_i-\hat\mu)^T
&=\sum_{i\in C_k}\left\{(x_i-\hat\mu_k)+(\hat\mu_k-\hat\mu)\right\}
\left\{(x_i-\hat\mu_k)+(\hat\mu_k-\hat\mu)\right\}^T\\
&=\sum_{i\in C_k}(x_i-\hat\mu_k)(x_i-\hat\mu_k)^T\\
&\quad+\sum_{i\in C_k}(x_i-\hat\mu_k)(\hat\mu_k-\hat\mu)^T\\
&\quad+\sum_{i\in C_k}(\hat\mu_k-\hat\mu)(x_i-\hat\mu_k)^T\\
&\quad+\sum_{i\in C_k}(\hat\mu_k-\hat\mu)(\hat\mu_k-\hat\mu)^T.
\end{aligned}
\]

The two cross terms vanish because

\[
\sum_{i\in C_k}(x_i-\hat\mu_k)=0.
\]

Thus,

\[
\sum_{i\in C_k}(x_i-\hat\mu)(x_i-\hat\mu)^T
=
\sum_{i\in C_k}(x_i-\hat\mu_k)(x_i-\hat\mu_k)^T
+
N_k(\hat\mu_k-\hat\mu)(\hat\mu_k-\hat\mu)^T.
\]

Summing over \(k=1,\dots,K\),

\[
\sum_{i=1}^N (x_i-\hat\mu)(x_i-\hat\mu)^T
=
\sum_{k=1}^K\sum_{i\in C_k}(x_i-\hat\mu_k)(x_i-\hat\mu_k)^T
+
\sum_{k=1}^K N_k(\hat\mu_k-\hat\mu)(\hat\mu_k-\hat\mu)^T.
\]

Using the definitions above,

\[
\boxed{
(N-1)\Sigma_t=(N-K)\Sigma_w+(N-1)\Sigma_b.
}
\]

This is the standard total scatter \(=\) within-class scatter \(+\) between-class scatter decomposition.

---

## (2) Fisher reduced-rank LDA and the generalized eigenproblem

Fisher’s LDA direction solves

\[
\max_{v\neq 0} \frac{v^T\Sigma_b v}{v^T\Sigma_w v}.
\]

Assume first that \(\Sigma_w\) is positive definite. The objective is homogeneous in \(v\), so we may impose the normalization

\[
v^T\Sigma_w v=1.
\]

Then the constrained optimization problem becomes

\[
\max_v v^T\Sigma_b v
\quad\text{subject to}\quad
v^T\Sigma_w v=1.
\]

The Lagrangian is

\[
\mathcal L(v,\lambda)=v^T\Sigma_b v-\lambda(v^T\Sigma_w v-1).
\]

Differentiating with respect to \(v\),

\[
\nabla_v \mathcal L=2\Sigma_b v-2\lambda \Sigma_w v.
\]

Setting this equal to zero gives

\[
\Sigma_b v=\lambda \Sigma_w v.
\]

Thus \(v\) is a generalized eigenvector of the matrix pair \((\Sigma_b,\Sigma_w)\). If \(\Sigma_w\) is nonsingular, this is equivalent to

\[
\boxed{
\Sigma_w^{-1}\Sigma_b v=\lambda v.
}
\]

Moreover, for such a generalized eigenvector,

\[
\lambda
=
\frac{v^T\Sigma_b v}{v^T\Sigma_w v}.
\]

Therefore the Fisher directions are the generalized eigenvectors corresponding to the largest generalized eigenvalues.

For reduced-rank LDA, one takes the leading \(r\) generalized eigenvectors, where

\[
r\leq \operatorname{rank}(\Sigma_b)\leq K-1.
\]

Thus, for \(K=3\), there are at most \(2\) nonzero Fisher discriminant directions.

If \(\Sigma_w\) is singular, one may instead work on the range of \(\Sigma_w\), use a Moore-Penrose pseudoinverse, or use a regularized covariance \(\Sigma_w+\varepsilon I\).

## (4) Own implementation of Fisher reduced-rank LDA and visualization

Here is an implementation from first principles. It does not use `sklearn`.

Because \(\Sigma_w^{-1}\Sigma_b\) is generally not symmetric, it is numerically preferable to solve the symmetric whitened eigenproblem. If

\[
\Sigma_w=A^{-1}A^{-T},
\]

or more directly if \(\Sigma_w^{-1/2}\) denotes the inverse square root, then

\[
\Sigma_b v=\lambda \Sigma_w v
\]

is equivalent to

\[
\Sigma_w^{-1/2}\Sigma_b\Sigma_w^{-1/2} u=\lambda u,
\qquad
v=\Sigma_w^{-1/2}u.
\]

```python
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

def fisher_lda(X, y, n_components=2, ridge=1e-8):
    """
    Fisher reduced-rank LDA implemented from scratch.

    Parameters
    ----------
    X : array, shape (N, p)
    y : array, shape (N,)
    n_components : number of discriminant directions
    ridge : small regularization added to Sigma_w

    Returns
    -------
    V : array, shape (p, n_components)
        LDA discriminant directions.
    evals : array
        Generalized eigenvalues in decreasing order.
    """
    X = np.asarray(X)
    y = np.asarray(y)

    N, p = X.shape
    classes = np.unique(y)
    K = len(classes)

    mu = X.mean(axis=0)

    Sw_scatter = np.zeros((p, p))
    Sb_scatter = np.zeros((p, p))

    for c in classes:
        Xc = X[y == c]
        Nc = Xc.shape[0]
        muc = Xc.mean(axis=0)

        Xc_centered = Xc - muc
        Sw_scatter += Xc_centered.T @ Xc_centered

        diff = (muc - mu).reshape(-1, 1)
        Sb_scatter += Nc * (diff @ diff.T)

    # Convert to covariance-scale matrices.
    Sigma_w = Sw_scatter / (N - K)
    Sigma_b = Sb_scatter / (N - 1)

    # Regularize Sigma_w for numerical stability.
    scale = np.trace(Sigma_w) / p
    Sigma_w_reg = Sigma_w + ridge * scale * np.eye(p)

    # Symmetric inverse square root of Sigma_w_reg.
    ew, Uw = np.linalg.eigh(Sigma_w_reg)
    ew = np.maximum(ew, 1e-12)
    Sigma_w_inv_half = Uw @ np.diag(1.0 / np.sqrt(ew)) @ Uw.T

    # Whitened symmetric eigenproblem.
    M = Sigma_w_inv_half @ Sigma_b @ Sigma_w_inv_half
    M = 0.5 * (M + M.T)

    evals, U = np.linalg.eigh(M)
    idx = np.argsort(evals)[::-1]

    evals = evals[idx]
    U = U[:, idx]

    V = Sigma_w_inv_half @ U[:, :n_components]

    # Normalize so that V.T Sigma_w V = I approximately.
    for j in range(V.shape[1]):
        norm_j = np.sqrt(V[:, j].T @ Sigma_w_reg @ V[:, j])
        V[:, j] /= norm_j

    return V, evals


# Fit two-dimensional Fisher LDA.
V_lda, lda_evals = fisher_lda(X, y, n_components=2)

# Project data.
X_centered = X - X.mean(axis=0)
Z_lda = X_centered @ V_lda

# Plot.
plt.figure(figsize=(7, 6))
colors = ["tab:blue", "tab:orange", "tab:green"]

for k, color in zip(np.unique(y), colors):
    plt.scatter(
        Z_lda[y == k, 0],
        Z_lda[y == k, 1],
        alpha=0.75,
        label=f"class {k+1}",
        color=color
    )

plt.xlabel("Fisher LDA direction 1")
plt.ylabel("Fisher LDA direction 2")
plt.title("Projection onto first two Fisher LDA directions")
plt.legend()
plt.grid(True)
plt.show()
```

## (5) PCA implementation, visualization, and comparison

PCA ignores the class labels. It finds directions of maximal total sample variance. The first principal component solves

\[
\max_{\|u\|_2=1} u^T\Sigma_t u,
\]

and subsequent components solve the same problem subject to Euclidean orthogonality constraints.

A from-scratch PCA implementation is:

```python
def pca(X, n_components=2):
    """
    PCA implemented from scratch using eigendecomposition
    of the sample covariance matrix.
    """
    X = np.asarray(X)
    N, p = X.shape

    X_centered = X - X.mean(axis=0)
    Sigma_t = X_centered.T @ X_centered / (N - 1)

    evals, evecs = np.linalg.eigh(Sigma_t)
    idx = np.argsort(evals)[::-1]

    evals = evals[idx]
    evecs = evecs[:, idx]

    scores = X_centered @ evecs[:, :n_components]

    return scores, evecs[:, :n_components], evals


Z_pca, V_pca, pca_evals = pca(X, n_components=2)

plt.figure(figsize=(7, 6))

for k, color in zip(np.unique(y), colors):
    plt.scatter(
        Z_pca[y == k, 0],
        Z_pca[y == k, 1],
        alpha=0.75,
        label=f"class {k+1}",
        color=color
    )

plt.xlabel("PC 1")
plt.ylabel("PC 2")
plt.title("Projection onto first two principal components")
plt.legend()
plt.grid(True)
plt.show()
```

### Comparison of LDA and PCA

PCA and Fisher LDA optimize different criteria.

PCA uses no label information. It chooses directions maximizing total variance:

\[
u^T\Sigma_t u.
\]

Using the decomposition from part (1),

\[
(N-1)\Sigma_t=(N-K)\Sigma_w+(N-1)\Sigma_b.
\]

Thus PCA is influenced by both within-class variation and between-class variation. If most of the total variance comes from within-class noise, PCA may choose directions that have large variance but do not separate the classes.

Fisher LDA, on the other hand, explicitly uses the class labels and maximizes the ratio

\[
\frac{v^T\Sigma_b v}{v^T\Sigma_w v}.
\]

So LDA searches for directions with large between-class separation relative to within-class variability. Equivalently, it separates class means after whitening by the within-class covariance.

Therefore:

- LDA is supervised; PCA is unsupervised.
- LDA focuses on class separation; PCA focuses on variance.
- LDA has at most \(K-1\) nonzero discriminant directions, so for \(K=3\), at most two.
- PCA can have up to \(p\) principal components.
- If the class means differ in low-variance directions, LDA will find them, but PCA may not.
- If the between-class variation dominates the total variation, then PCA may also show class separation, but this is not guaranteed.

In this problem, with three Gaussian classes and a common diagonal covariance, the Fisher LDA projection onto two dimensions should usually show clearer separation among the three classes than the PCA projection, because LDA uses the class labels and adjusts for the within-class coordinate variances. PCA may instead emphasize coordinates with large marginal variance, even if those coordinates are irrelevant for distinguishing the classes.

        Z_lda[y == k, 0],
        Z_lda[y == k, 1],
        alpha=0.75,
        label=f"class {k+1}",
        color=color
    )

plt.xlabel("Fisher LDA direction 1")
plt.ylabel("Fisher LDA direction 2")

```

For three classes, the between-class covariance has rank at most \(K-1=2\), so two Fisher directions capture all possible between-class separation in the LDA sense.

---

## (5) PCA implementation, visualization, and comparison

PCA ignores the class labels. It finds directions of maximal total sample variance. The first principal component solves

\[
\max_{\|u\|_2=1} u^T\Sigma_t u,
\]

and subsequent components solve the same problem subject to Euclidean orthogonality constraints.

A from-scratch PCA implementation is:

```python
def pca(X, n_components=2):
    """
    PCA implemented from scratch using eigendecomposition
    of the sample covariance matrix.
    """
    X = np.asarray(X)
    N, p = X.shape

    X_centered = X - X.mean(axis=0)
    Sigma_t = X_centered.T @ X_centered / (N - 1)

    evals, evecs = np.linalg.eigh(Sigma_t)
    idx = np.argsort(evals)[::-1]

    evals = evals[idx]
    evecs = evecs[:, idx]

    scores = X_centered @ evecs[:, :n_components]

    return scores, evecs[:, :n_components], evals


Z_pca, V_pca, pca_evals = pca(X, n_components=2)

plt.figure(figsize=(7, 6))

for k, color in zip(np.unique(y), colors):
    plt.scatter(
        Z_pca[y == k, 0],
        Z_pca[y == k, 1],
        alpha=0.75,
        label=f"class {k+1}",
        color=color
    )

plt.xlabel("PC 1")
plt.ylabel("PC 2")
plt.title("Projection onto first two principal components")
plt.legend()
plt.grid(True)
plt.show()
```

### Comparison of LDA and PCA

PCA and Fisher LDA optimize different criteria.

PCA uses no label information. It chooses directions maximizing total variance:

\[
u^T\Sigma_t u.
\]

Using the decomposition from part (1),

\[
(N-1)\Sigma_t=(N-K)\Sigma_w+(N-1)\Sigma_b.
\]

Thus PCA is influenced by both within-class variation and between-class variation. If most of the total variance comes from within-class noise, PCA may choose directions that have large variance but do not separate the classes.

Fisher LDA, on the other hand, explicitly uses the class labels and maximizes the ratio

\[
\frac{v^T\Sigma_b v}{v^T\Sigma_w v}.
\]

So LDA searches for directions with large between-class separation relative to within-class variability. Equivalently, it separates class means after whitening by the within-class covariance.

Therefore:

- LDA is supervised; PCA is unsupervised.
- LDA focuses on class separation; PCA focuses on variance.
- LDA has at most \(K-1\) nonzero discriminant directions, so for \(K=3\), at most two.
- PCA can have up to \(p\) principal components.
- If the class means differ in low-variance directions, LDA will find them, but PCA may not.
- If the between-class variation dominates the total variation, then PCA may also show class separation, but this is not guaranteed.

In this problem, with three Gaussian classes and a common diagonal covariance, the Fisher LDA projection onto two dimensions should usually show clearer separation among the three classes than the PCA projection, because LDA uses the class labels and adjusts for the within-class coordinate variances. PCA may instead emphasize coordinates with large marginal variance, even if those coordinates are irrelevant for distinguishing the classes.

Because `engine_experiment_data.txt` is not available, I cannot honestly report numerical MLEs, cross-validation errors, plots, or optimal factor settings. Below is the complete analysis I would perform from the data, using only likelihood evaluation, linear algebra, and numerical optimization—not a GP package.

Let the 27 runs be \((x_i,y_i)\), \(i=1,\dots,n\), \(n=27\), with \(x_i\in\mathbb R^8\). For a parameter vector \(\theta=(\theta_1,\dots,\theta_8)\), define

\[
R_\theta(i,j)
=
\exp\left\{-\sum_{k=1}^8 \theta_k(x_{ik}-x_{jk})^2\right\}.
\]

The covariance matrix is \(\sigma^2 R_\theta\).

---

## (1) Constant-mean GP: MLEs for \(\mu,\theta,\sigma^2\)

The model is

\[
Y(x)=\mu+Z(x),
\]

with

\[
Z\sim GP\{0,\sigma^2 R_\theta(\cdot,\cdot)\}.
\]

Let \(1_n=(1,\dots,1)^T\), \(y=(y_1,\dots,y_n)^T\), and \(R=R_\theta\).

For fixed \(\theta\), the log-likelihood is

\[
\ell(\mu,\sigma^2,\theta)
=
-\frac n2\log(2\pi)
-\frac n2\log\sigma^2
-\frac12\log |R_\theta|
-\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}(y-\mu 1_n)^T R_\theta^{-1}(y-\mu 1_n).
\]

For fixed \(\theta\), the generalized least squares MLE of \(\mu\) is

\[
\widehat\mu(\theta)
=
\frac{1_n^T R_\theta^{-1} y}{1_n^T R_\theta^{-1}1_n}.
\]

Then

\[
\widehat{\sigma}^2(\theta)
=
\frac1n
\{y-\widehat\mu(\theta)1_n\}^T
R_\theta^{-1}
\{y-\widehat\mu(\theta)1_n\}.
\]

The profile log-likelihood is therefore

\[
\ell_p(\theta)
=
-\frac n2\log(2\pi)
-\frac n2\log \widehat{\sigma}^2(\theta)
-\frac12 \log |R_\theta|
-\frac n2.
\]

Equivalently, \(\widehat\theta\) minimizes

\[
\Psi(\theta)
=
n\log \widehat{\sigma}^2(\theta)
+
\log |R_\theta|.
\]

Thus

\[
\widehat\theta
=
\arg\min_{\theta_k\ge 0}
\left\{
n\log \widehat{\sigma}^2(\theta)
+
\log |R_\theta|
\right\},
\]

and then

\[
\widehat\mu=\widehat\mu(\widehat\theta),
\qquad
\widehat{\sigma}^2=\widehat{\sigma}^2(\widehat\theta).
\]

In practice I would optimize over \(\eta_k=\log \theta_k\) to enforce positivity, use a Cholesky factorization of \(R_\theta\), and use multiple starting values to avoid poor local optima. If some \(\widehat\theta_k\) is essentially zero, that factor is effectively inactive in the correlation.

Because the data file is missing, the numerical estimates \(\widehat\mu,\widehat\theta,\widehat\sigma^2\) cannot be reported.

---

## (2) BLUP and plug-in predictive distribution

Let \(x_0\) be a new input. Define

\[
r(x_0)
=
\begin{pmatrix}
R_\theta(x_0,x_1)\\
\vdots\\
R_\theta(x_0,x_n)
\end{pmatrix}.
\]

For the constant-mean model, using the MLEs from part (1), the BLUP is

\[
\widehat y(x_0)
=
\widehat\mu
+
r(x_0)^T R_{\widehat\theta}^{-1}
\{y-\widehat\mu 1_n\}.
\]

Let

\[
C=R_{\widehat\theta}^{-1}.
\]

The plug-in predictive variance, accounting for estimation of the constant mean but not for uncertainty in \(\widehat\theta\) or \(\widehat\sigma^2\), is

\[
\widehat s^2(x_0)
=
\widehat\sigma^2
\left[
1
-
r(x_0)^T C r(x_0)
+
\frac{\{1-1_n^T C r(x_0)\}^2}{1_n^T C1_n}
\right].
\]

Thus the plug-in predictive distribution is

\[
Y(x_0)\mid y
\approx
N\left(
\widehat y(x_0),
\widehat s^2(x_0)
\right).
\]

A 95% plug-in predictive interval is

\[
\widehat y(x_0)\pm 1.96\,\widehat s(x_0).
\]

---

## (3) Leave-one-out cross-validation prediction error for the constant-mean GP

For exact leave-one-out cross-validation, for each \(i=1,\dots,n\), I would remove observation \(i\), refit the model to the remaining \(n-1\) observations, compute the BLUP at \(x_i\), and define

\[
e_i^{\text{LOO}}
=
y_i-\widehat y_{-i}(x_i).
\]

The leave-one-out mean squared prediction error is

\[
\operatorname{MSE}_{\text{LOO}}
=
\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n
\left(e_i^{\text{LOO}}\right)^2,
\]

and the root mean squared prediction error is

\[
\operatorname{RMSE}_{\text{LOO}}
=
\left[
\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n
\left(e_i^{\text{LOO}}\right)^2
\right]^{1/2}.
\]

A useful scale-free measure is

\[
Q^2_{\text{LOO}}
=
1-
\frac{\sum_{i=1}^n (e_i^{\text{LOO}})^2}
{\sum_{i=1}^n (y_i-\bar y)^2}.
\]

If one fixes \(\theta=\widehat\theta\) from the full data set rather than refitting \(\theta\) for each deletion, the leave-one-out errors can be computed efficiently. Let

\[
C=R_{\widehat\theta}^{-1},
\]

and define the generalized residual precision matrix

\[
Q
=
C
-
C1_n(1_n^T C1_n)^{-1}1_n^T C.
\]

Then the leave-one-out prediction error is

\[
e_i^{\text{LOO}}
=
\frac{(Qy)_i}{Q_{ii}},
\]

and hence

\[
\widehat y_{-i}(x_i)
=
y_i-\frac{(Qy)_i}{Q_{ii}}.
\]

The corresponding LOO predictive variance is approximately

\[
\widehat s^2_{-i}
=
\frac{\widehat\sigma^2}{Q_{ii}}.
\]

The requested numerical cross-validation prediction error cannot be computed without the data file.

\[
Y(x)
=
\beta_0+x_1\beta_1+x_6\beta_2+Z(x),
\]

with the same squared exponential correlation.

Define the regression vector

\[
f(x)
=
\begin{pmatrix}
1\\
x_1\\
x_6
\end{pmatrix},
\]

and let

\[
F
=
\begin{pmatrix}
1 & x_{11} & x_{16}\\
1 & x_{21} & x_{26}\\
\vdots & \vdots & \vdots\\
1 & x_{n1} & x_{n6}
\end{pmatrix}.
\]

For fixed \(\theta\), the GLS MLE of \(\beta\) is

\[
\widehat\beta(\theta)
=
(F^T R_\theta^{-1}F)^{-1}

\]

The profile estimate of \(\sigma^2\) is

\[
\widehat\sigma^2(\theta)
=
\frac1n
\{y-F\widehat\beta(\theta)\}^T
R_\theta^{-1}
\{y-F\widehat\beta(\theta)\}.
\]

The profile log-likelihood is maximized, equivalently, by minimizing

\[
\Psi(\theta)
=
n\log \widehat\sigma^2(\theta)
+
\log |R_\theta|.
\]

Thus

\[
\widehat\theta
=
\arg\min_{\theta_k\ge 0}
\left\{
n\log \widehat\sigma^2(\theta)
+
\log |R_\theta|
\right\}.
\]

Then

\[
\widehat\beta=\widehat\beta(\widehat\theta),
\qquad
\widehat\sigma^2=\widehat\sigma^2(\widehat\theta).
\]

The BLUP at a new point \(x_0\) is

\[
\widehat y(x_0)
=
f(x_0)^T\widehat\beta
+
r(x_0)^T
R_{\widehat\theta}^{-1}
\{y-F\widehat\beta\}.
\]

Let

\[
C=R_{\widehat\theta}^{-1}.
\]

The plug-in universal kriging predictive variance is

\[
\widehat s^2(x_0)
=
\widehat\sigma^2
\left[
1
-
r(x_0)^T C r(x_0)
+
q(x_0)^T
(F^T C F)^{-1}
q(x_0)
\right],
\]

where

\[
q(x_0)
=
f(x_0)-F^T C r(x_0).
\]

Thus

\[
Y(x_0)\mid y
\approx
N\left(
\widehat y(x_0),
\widehat s^2(x_0)
\right).
\]

For leave-one-out cross-validation, the exact approach is again to refit the model with observation \(i\) omitted and predict \(y_i\). The LOO errors are

\[
e_i^{\text{LOO}}
=
y_i-\widehat y_{-i}(x_i),
\]

and I would report

\[
\operatorname{RMSE}_{\text{LOO}}
=
\left[
\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n
(e_i^{\text{LOO}})^2
\right]^{1/2}.
\]

If \(\theta\) is held fixed at its full-data estimate, define

\[
Q
=
C
-
CF(F^T CF)^{-1}F^T C.
\]

Then

\[
e_i^{\text{LOO}}
=
\frac{(Qy)_i}{Q_{ii}},
\qquad
\widehat y_{-i}(x_i)
=
y_i-\frac{(Qy)_i}{Q_{ii}}.
\]

Again, numerical values require the missing data file.

---

## (5) Final model comparison and recommendation rule

I would compare the constant-mean GP and the linear-trend GP using both likelihood-based and prediction-based criteria.

For the constant-mean model,

\[
k_0=1+8+1=10
\]

parameters: \(\mu\), eight \(\theta\)'s, and \(\sigma^2\).

For the linear-trend model,

\[
k_1=3+8+1=12

parameters: \(\beta_0,\beta_1,\beta_2\), eight \(\theta\)'s, and \(\sigma^2\).

I would compute

\[
\operatorname{AIC}
=
-2\ell(\widehat\psi)+2k,
\]

and

\[
\operatorname{BIC}
=
-2\ell(\widehat\psi)+k\log n.
\]

Because \(n=27\) is small, I would emphasize out-of-sample predictive performance, especially

\[
\operatorname{RMSE}_{\text{LOO}},
\qquad
\operatorname{MAE}_{\text{LOO}},
\qquad
Q^2_{\text{LOO}},

\[
\operatorname{NLPD}
=
\frac1n
\sum_{i=1}^n
\left[
\frac12\log(2\pi \widehat s_{-i}^2)
+
\frac{(e_i^{\text{LOO}})^2}{2\widehat s_{-i}^2}
\right].

\[

=
\frac{e_i^{\text{LOO}}}{\widehat s_{-i}},

Let the selected final model have regression vector \(f(x)\), estimated coefficients \(\widehat\beta\), covariance parameter \(\widehat\theta\), and variance estimate \(\widehat\sigma^2\).

\[
\widehat m(x)
=
f(x)^T\widehat\beta
+

=
R_{\widehat\theta}^{-1}
\{y-F\widehat\beta\}.

\[
\widehat x_{\mathrm{opt}}
=
\arg\min_{x\in \mathcal D}
\widehat m(x),

Because \(\widehat m(x)\) is generally nonconvex, I would use a multistart global search followed by local optimization.

For continuous factors, the derivative is available analytically. Let

\[
r_j(x)
=
\exp\left\{
-\sum_{k=1}^8
\widehat\theta_k(x_k-x_{jk})^2
\right\}.
\]

\[
\widehat m(x)
=
f(x)^T\widehat\beta
+
\sum_{j=1}^n

For coordinate \(k\),

\[
\frac{\partial \widehat m(x)}{\partial x_k}
=
\frac{\partial f(x)^T\widehat\beta}{\partial x_k}
-
2\widehat\theta_k
\sum_{j=1}^n

\[
