Let \(1_n=(1,\dots,1)^T\), \(y=(y_1,\dots,y_n)^T\), and \(R=R_\theta\).

For fixed \(\theta\), the log-likelihood is

\[
\ell(\mu,\sigma^2,\theta)
=
-\frac n2\log(2\pi)
-\frac n2\log\sigma^2
-\frac12\log |R_\theta|
-\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}(y-\mu 1_n)^T R_\theta^{-1}(y-\mu 1_n).
\]

For fixed \(\theta\), the generalized least squares MLE of \(\mu\) is

\[
\widehat\mu(\theta)
=
\frac{1_n^T R_\theta^{-1} y}{1_n^T R_\theta^{-1}1_n}.
\]

Then

\[
\widehat{\sigma}^2(\theta)
=
\frac1n
\{y-\widehat\mu(\theta)1_n\}^T
R_\theta^{-1}
\{y-\widehat\mu(\theta)1_n\}.
\]

The profile log-likelihood is therefore

\[
\ell_p(\theta)
=
-\frac n2\log(2\pi)
-\frac n2\log \widehat{\sigma}^2(\theta)
-\frac12 \log |R_\theta|
-\frac n2.
\]

Equivalently, \(\widehat\theta\) minimizes

\[
\Psi(\theta)
=
n\log \widehat{\sigma}^2(\theta)
+
\log |R_\theta|.
\]

Thus

\[
\widehat\theta
=
\arg\min_{\theta_k\ge 0}
\left\{
n\log \widehat{\sigma}^2(\theta)
+
\log |R_\theta|
\right\},
\]

and then

\[
\widehat\mu=\widehat\mu(\widehat\theta),
\qquad
\widehat{\sigma}^2=\widehat{\sigma}^2(\widehat\theta).
\]

In practice I would optimize over \(\eta_k=\log \theta_k\) to enforce positivity, use a Cholesky factorization of \(R_\theta\), and use multiple starting values to avoid poor local optima. If some \(\widehat\theta_k\) is essentially zero, that factor is effectively inactive in the correlation.

Because the data file is missing, the numerical estimates \(\widehat\mu,\widehat\theta,\widehat\sigma^2\) cannot be reported.

---

## (2) BLUP and plug-in predictive distribution

Let \(x_0\) be a new input. Define

\[
r(x_0)
=
\begin{pmatrix}
R_\theta(x_0,x_1)\\
\vdots\\
R_\theta(x_0,x_n)
\end{pmatrix}.
\]

For the constant-mean model, using the MLEs from part (1), the BLUP is

\[
\widehat y(x_0)
=
\widehat\mu
+
r(x_0)^T R_{\widehat\theta}^{-1}
\{y-\widehat\mu 1_n\}.
\]

Let

\[
C=R_{\widehat\theta}^{-1}.
\]

The plug-in predictive variance, accounting for estimation of the constant mean but not for uncertainty in \(\widehat\theta\) or \(\widehat\sigma^2\), is

\[
\widehat s^2(x_0)
=
\widehat\sigma^2
\left[
1
-
r(x_0)^T C r(x_0)
+
\frac{\{1-1_n^T C r(x_0)\}^2}{1_n^T C1_n}
\right].
\]

Thus the plug-in predictive distribution is

\[
Y(x_0)\mid y
\approx
N\left(
\widehat y(x_0),
\widehat s^2(x_0)
\right).
\]

A 95% plug-in predictive interval is

\[
\widehat y(x_0)\pm 1.96\,\widehat s(x_0).
\]

---

## (3) Leave-one-out cross-validation prediction error for the constant-mean GP

For exact leave-one-out cross-validation, for each \(i=1,\dots,n\), I would remove observation \(i\), refit the model to the remaining \(n-1\) observations, compute the BLUP at \(x_i\), and define

\[
e_i^{\text{LOO}}
=
y_i-\widehat y_{-i}(x_i).
\]

The leave-one-out mean squared prediction error is

\[
\operatorname{MSE}_{\text{LOO}}
=
\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n
\left(e_i^{\text{LOO}}\right)^2,
\]

and the root mean squared prediction error is

\[
\operatorname{RMSE}_{\text{LOO}}
=
\left[
\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n
\left(e_i^{\text{LOO}}\right)^2
\right]^{1/2}.
\]

A useful scale-free measure is

\[
Q^2_{\text{LOO}}
=
1-
\frac{\sum_{i=1}^n (e_i^{\text{LOO}})^2}
{\sum_{i=1}^n (y_i-\bar y)^2}.
\]

If one fixes \(\theta=\widehat\theta\) from the full data set rather than refitting \(\theta\) for each deletion, the leave-one-out errors can be computed efficiently. Let

\[
C=R_{\widehat\theta}^{-1},
\]

and define the generalized residual precision matrix

\[
Q
=
C
-
C1_n(1_n^T C1_n)^{-1}1_n^T C.
\]

Then the leave-one-out prediction error is

\[
e_i^{\text{LOO}}
=
\frac{(Qy)_i}{Q_{ii}},
\]

and hence

\[
\widehat y_{-i}(x_i)
=
y_i-\frac{(Qy)_i}{Q_{ii}}.
\]

The corresponding LOO predictive variance is approximately

\[
\widehat s^2_{-i}
=
\frac{\widehat\sigma^2}{Q_{ii}}.
\]

The requested numerical cross-validation prediction error cannot be computed without the data file.

---

## (4) Linear trend GP using \(x_1\) and \(x_6\)

Now use the model

\[
Y(x)
=
\beta_0+x_1\beta_1+x_6\beta_2+Z(x),
\]

with the same squared exponential correlation.

Define the regression vector

\[
f(x)
=
\begin{pmatrix}
1\\
x_1\\
x_6
\end{pmatrix},
\]

and let

\[
F
=
\begin{pmatrix}
1 & x_{11} & x_{16}\\
1 & x_{21} & x_{26}\\
\vdots & \vdots & \vdots\\
1 & x_{n1} & x_{n6}
\end{pmatrix}.
\]

For fixed \(\theta\), the GLS MLE of \(\beta\) is

\[
\widehat\beta(\theta)
=
(F^T R_\theta^{-1}F)^{-1}
F^T R_\theta^{-1}y.
\]

The profile estimate of \(\sigma^2\) is

\[
\widehat\sigma^2(\theta)
=
\frac1n
\{y-F\widehat\beta(\theta)\}^T
R_\theta^{-1}
\{y-F\widehat\beta(\theta)\}.
\]

The profile log-likelihood is maximized, equivalently, by minimizing

\[
\Psi(\theta)
=
n\log \widehat\sigma^2(\theta)
+
\log |R_\theta|.
\]

Thus

\[
\widehat\theta
=
\arg\min_{\theta_k\ge 0}
\left\{
n\log \widehat\sigma^2(\theta)
+
\log |R_\theta|
\right\}.
\]

Then

\[
\widehat\beta=\widehat\beta(\widehat\theta),
\qquad
\widehat\sigma^2=\widehat\sigma^2(\widehat\theta).
\]

The BLUP at a new point \(x_0\) is

\[
\widehat y(x_0)
=
f(x_0)^T\widehat\beta
+
r(x_0)^T
R_{\widehat\theta}^{-1}
\{y-F\widehat\beta\}.
\]

Let

\[
C=R_{\widehat\theta}^{-1}.
\]

The plug-in universal kriging predictive variance is

\[
\widehat s^2(x_0)
=
\widehat\sigma^2
\left[
1
-
r(x_0)^T C r(x_0)
+
q(x_0)^T
(F^T C F)^{-1}
q(x_0)
\right],
\]

where

\[
q(x_0)
=
f(x_0)-F^T C r(x_0).
\]

Thus

\[
Y(x_0)\mid y
\approx
N\left(
\widehat y(x_0),
\widehat s^2(x_0)
\right).
\]

For leave-one-out cross-validation, the exact approach is again to refit the model with observation \(i\) omitted and predict \(y_i\). The LOO errors are

\[
e_i^{\text{LOO}}
=
y_i-\widehat y_{-i}(x_i),
\]

and I would report

\[
\operatorname{RMSE}_{\text{LOO}}
=
\left[
\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n
(e_i^{\text{LOO}})^2
\right]^{1/2}.
\]

If \(\theta\) is held fixed at its full-data estimate, define

\[
Q
=
C
-
CF(F^T CF)^{-1}F^T C.
\]

Then

\[
e_i^{\text{LOO}}
=
\frac{(Qy)_i}{Q_{ii}},
\qquad
\widehat y_{-i}(x_i)
=
y_i-\frac{(Qy)_i}{Q_{ii}}.
\]

Again, numerical values require the missing data file.

---

## (5) Final model comparison and recommendation rule

I would compare the constant-mean GP and the linear-trend GP using both likelihood-based and prediction-based criteria.

For the constant-mean model,

\[
k_0=1+8+1=10
\]

parameters: \(\mu\), eight \(\theta\)'s, and \(\sigma^2\).

For the linear-trend model,

\[
k_1=3+8+1=12
\]

parameters: \(\beta_0,\beta_1,\beta_2\), eight \(\theta\)'s, and \(\sigma^2\).

I would compute

\[
\operatorname{AIC}
=
-2\ell(\widehat\psi)+2k,
\]

and

\[
\operatorname{BIC}
=
-2\ell(\widehat\psi)+k\log n.
\]

Because \(n=27\) is small, I would emphasize out-of-sample predictive performance, especially

\[
\operatorname{RMSE}_{\text{LOO}},
\qquad
\operatorname{MAE}_{\text{LOO}},
\qquad
Q^2_{\text{LOO}},
\]

and, if predictive variances are used,

\[
\operatorname{NLPD}
=
\frac1n
\sum_{i=1}^n
\left[
\frac12\log(2\pi \widehat s_{-i}^2)
+
\frac{(e_i^{\text{LOO}})^2}{2\widehat s_{-i}^2}
\right].
\]

A good probabilistic predictor should also have approximately calibrated standardized LOO errors,

\[
z_i
=
\frac{e_i^{\text{LOO}}}{\widehat s_{-i}},
\]

with empirical variance near one and no obvious trend against fitted values.

My model-selection rule would be:

- choose the linear-trend GP if it gives materially smaller LOO RMSE/MAE, larger \(Q^2_{\text{LOO}}\), smaller NLPD, and acceptable AIC/BIC;
- otherwise choose the simpler constant-mean GP.

Without the data, the final model cannot be selected numerically.

---

## (6) BLUP as a function of \(x_1\) with 95% predictive bands

Let the selected final model have regression vector \(f(x)\), estimated coefficients \(\widehat\beta\), covariance parameter \(\widehat\theta\), and variance estimate \(\widehat\sigma^2\).

To plot the fitted response as a function of \(x_1\), one must hold the other factors fixed. I would typically choose either

1. their nominal center values, or  
2. the estimated optimal values from part (7).

Let

\[
x(t)
=
(t,c_2,c_3,\dots,c_8),
\]

where \(t\) varies over the experimental range of \(x_1\) and \((c_2,\dots,c_8)\) are fixed.

For each grid value \(t\), compute

\[
\widehat m(t)
=
\widehat y\{x(t)\},
\]

and

\[
\widehat s^2(t)
=
\widehat s^2\{x(t)\}.
\]

Then plot

\[
t\mapsto \widehat m(t),
\]

with 95% plug-in predictive bands

\[
\widehat m(t)\pm 1.96\,\widehat s(t).
\]

The plot cannot be produced numerically without the data.

---

## (7) Optimization of the eight factor settings

For the final fitted model, the predicted mean response has the form

\[
\widehat m(x)
=
f(x)^T\widehat\beta
+
r(x)^T\widehat\alpha,
\]

where

\[
\widehat\alpha
=
R_{\widehat\theta}^{-1}
\{y-F\widehat\beta\}.
\]

The goal is to solve

\[
\widehat x_{\mathrm{opt}}
=
\arg\min_{x\in \mathcal D}
\widehat m(x),
\]

where \(\mathcal D\) is the feasible region for the eight factors, usually the product of their experimental ranges.

Because \(\widehat m(x)\) is generally nonconvex, I would use a multistart global search followed by local optimization.

For continuous factors, the derivative is available analytically. Let

\[
r_j(x)
=
\exp\left\{
-\sum_{k=1}^8
\widehat\theta_k(x_k-x_{jk})^2
\right\}.
\]

Then

\[
\widehat m(x)
=
f(x)^T\widehat\beta
+
\sum_{j=1}^n
\widehat\alpha_j r_j(x).
\]

For coordinate \(k\),

\[
\frac{\partial \widehat m(x)}{\partial x_k}
=
\frac{\partial f(x)^T\widehat\beta}{\partial x_k}
-
2\widehat\theta_k
\sum_{j=1}^n
\widehat\alpha_j
r_j(x)(x_k-x_{jk}).
\]

For the linear-trend model,

\[
\frac{\partial f(x)^T\widehat\beta}{\partial x_k}
=
\begin{cases}
\widehat\beta_1, & k=1,\\
\widehat\beta_2, & k=6,\\
0, & \text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
\]

The algorithm would be:

1. Scale all factors to their coded experimental ranges.
2. Generate many starting points in \(\mathcal D\), for example by Latin hypercube or Sobol sampling.
3. Evaluate \(\widehat m(x)\) at all starting points.
4. Keep the best several candidates.
5. From each candidate, run a bounded gradient-based optimizer such as L-BFGS-B using the gradient above.
6. Compare all local minima and choose the one with the smallest predicted gap lift.
7. Report \(\widehat x_{\mathrm{opt}}\), \(\widehat m(\widehat x_{\mathrm{opt}})\), and the predictive standard error \(\widehat s(\widehat x_{\mathrm{opt}})\).

If some factors are genuinely discrete rather than continuous, I would enumerate their possible levels and run the continuous optimization conditionally on each discrete combination.

The numerical optimum cannot be reported without the missing experiment file.

Because `engine_experiment_data.txt` is not available, numerical MLEs, CV errors, plots, and optimal settings cannot be honestly reported. I would not fabricate them. Below is the complete analysis I would carry out from the 27 observations once the data file is available, using only linear algebra and numerical optimization, not a GP package.

Let the data be  
\[
\mathcal D=\{(x_i,y_i):i=1,\dots,n\},\qquad n=27,\quad x_i\in\mathbb R^8,
\]
and define, for \(\theta=(\theta_1,\dots,\theta_8)^\top\),
\[
R_\theta(i,j)=\exp\left\{-\sum_{k=1}^8\theta_k(x_{ik}-x_{jk})^2\right\}.
\]
The covariance matrix of \(Y=(Y(x_1),\dots,Y(x_n))^\top\) is \(\sigma^2R_\theta\). In computation I would work with coded/scaled factor levels and use Cholesky decompositions of \(R_\theta\), adding only a tiny numerical jitter if needed for stability.

---

## (1) MLEs for the constant-mean GP model

The model is

\[
Y(x)=\mu+Z(x),
\]
with
\[
\operatorname{Cov}\{Z(x),Z(x')\}=\sigma^2\exp\left\{-\sum_{k=1}^8\theta_k(x_k-x_k')^2\right\}.
\]

Let \(1_n\) denote the \(n\)-vector of ones. The log-likelihood is

\[
\ell(\mu,\sigma^2,\theta)
=
-\frac n2\log(2\pi)
-\frac n2\log\sigma^2
-\frac12\log |R_\theta|
-\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}(y-\mu 1_n)^\top R_\theta^{-1}(y-\mu 1_n).
\]

For fixed \(\theta\), the generalized least-squares MLE of \(\mu\) is

\[
\widehat\mu(\theta)
=
\frac{1_n^\top R_\theta^{-1}y}{1_n^\top R_\theta^{-1}1_n}.
\]

Define the generalized residual sum of squares

\[
S(\theta)
=
\{y-\widehat\mu(\theta)1_n\}^\top R_\theta^{-1}
\{y-\widehat\mu(\theta)1_n\}.
\]

For fixed \(\theta\), the MLE of \(\sigma^2\) is

\[
\widehat{\sigma}^2(\theta)=\frac{S(\theta)}{n}.
\]

Therefore the profile log-likelihood is, up to an additive constant,

\[
\ell_p(\theta)
=
-\frac12\left[
\log |R_\theta|
+n\log\left\{\frac{S(\theta)}{n}\right\}
\right].
\]

Equivalently, the MLE of \(\theta\) is

\[
\widehat\theta
=
\arg\min_{\theta_k\ge 0}
\left[
\log |R_\theta|
+n\log\left\{\frac{S(\theta)}{n}\right\}
\right].
\]

Once \(\widehat\theta\) is found,

\[
\widehat\mu=\widehat\mu(\widehat\theta),
\qquad
\widehat\sigma^2=\widehat\sigma^2(\widehat\theta).
\]

A useful expression for numerical optimization is the profile score. Let

\[
\alpha=R_\theta^{-1}\{y-\widehat\mu(\theta)1_n\}.
\]

Then

\[
\frac{\partial R_\theta(i,j)}{\partial \theta_k}
=
-(x_{ik}-x_{jk})^2 R_\theta(i,j),
\]

and

\[
\frac{\partial}{\partial \theta_k}
\left[
\log |R_\theta|+n\log\{S(\theta)/n\}
\right]
=
\operatorname{tr}\left(R_\theta^{-1}\frac{\partial R_\theta}{\partial \theta_k}\right)
-
\frac{n}{S(\theta)}
\alpha^\top
\frac{\partial R_\theta}{\partial \theta_k}
\alpha.
\]

In practice I would optimize over \(\eta_k=\log\theta_k\) using a multistart quasi-Newton method such as L-BFGS-B, evaluating determinants and solves by Cholesky factorization.

Because the dataset is unavailable, the numerical values

\[
\widehat\mu,\quad
\widehat\sigma^2,\quad
\widehat\theta_1,\dots,\widehat\theta_8
\]

cannot be reported.

---

## (2) BLUP and plug-in predictive distribution for the constant-mean model

For a new input \(x_0\), define the correlation vector

\[
r(x_0)
=
\begin{pmatrix}
\phi(x_0-x_1;\widehat\theta)\\
\vdots\\
\phi(x_0-x_n;\widehat\theta)
\end{pmatrix}.
\]

The ordinary kriging BLUP is

\[
\widehat y(x_0)
=
\widehat\mu
+
r(x_0)^\top R_{\widehat\theta}^{-1}
\{y-\widehat\mu 1_n\}.
\]

The plug-in predictive variance, accounting for estimation of the constant mean but treating \(\widehat\theta\) and \(\widehat\sigma^2\) as fixed, is

\[
\widehat v(x_0)
=
\widehat\sigma^2
\left[
1
-
r(x_0)^\top R_{\widehat\theta}^{-1}r(x_0)
+
\frac{
\left\{
1-1_n^\top R_{\widehat\theta}^{-1}r(x_0)
\right\}^2
}{
1_n^\top R_{\widehat\theta}^{-1}1_n
}
\right].
\]

Thus the plug-in predictive distribution is

\[
Y(x_0)\mid y
\approx
N\left(
\widehat y(x_0),\widehat v(x_0)
\right).
\]

A pointwise 95% predictive interval is

\[
\widehat y(x_0)\pm 1.96\sqrt{\widehat v(x_0)}.
\]

---

## (3) Leave-one-out cross-validation prediction error for the constant-mean BLUP

For honest leave-one-out cross-validation, for each \(i=1,\dots,n\) I would:

1. Delete observation \(i\).
2. Refit the GP model on the remaining \(n-1\) observations, including re-estimation of \(\theta,\mu,\sigma^2\).
3. Predict \(y_i\) using the fitted BLUP.
4. Compute the residual
   \[
   e_i^{\text{LOO}}=y_i-\widehat y_{-i}(x_i).
   \]

The main prediction error summaries would be

\[
\operatorname{PRESS}
=
\sum_{i=1}^n
\left(e_i^{\text{LOO}}\right)^2,
\]

\[
\operatorname{RMSE}_{\text{LOO}}
=
\left[
\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n
\left(e_i^{\text{LOO}}\right)^2
\right]^{1/2},
\]

\[
\operatorname{MAE}_{\text{LOO}}
=
\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n
|e_i^{\text{LOO}}|.
\]

If I keep \(\widehat\theta\) fixed rather than re-estimating it in every fold, the LOO residuals can be obtained algebraically. Let

\[
F=1_n,
\]

and define

\[
M
=
R_{\widehat\theta}^{-1}
-
R_{\widehat\theta}^{-1}F
\left(F^\top R_{\widehat\theta}^{-1}F\right)^{-1}
F^\top R_{\widehat\theta}^{-1}.
\]

Then

\[
e_i^{\text{LOO}}
=
\frac{(My)_i}{M_{ii}},
\]

and

\[
\widehat y_{-i}(x_i)
=
y_i-\frac{(My)_i}{M_{ii}}.
\]

The corresponding LOO predictive variance is approximately

\[
\widehat v_i^{\text{LOO}}
=
\frac{\widehat\sigma^2}{M_{ii}}.
\]

One can also compute standardized LOO residuals

\[
z_i
=
\frac{e_i^{\text{LOO}}}{\sqrt{\widehat v_i^{\text{LOO}}}}
=
\frac{(My)_i}{\sqrt{\widehat\sigma^2 M_{ii}}}.
\]

The numerical CV error cannot be reported without the data.

---

## (4) GP with linear mean in \(x_1\) and \(x_6\)

Now the model is

\[
Y(x)=\beta_0+x_1\beta_1+x_6\beta_2+Z(x).
\]

Let

\[
f(x)=
\begin{pmatrix}
1\\
x_1\\
x_6
\end{pmatrix},
\]

and let \(F\) be the \(n\times 3\) design matrix whose \(i\)th row is

\[
f(x_i)^\top=(1,x_{i1},x_{i6}).
\]

The log-likelihood is

\[
\ell(\beta,\sigma^2,\theta)
=
-\frac n2\log(2\pi)
-\frac n2\log\sigma^2
-\frac12\log |R_\theta|
-\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}

=

\left[

-

+

-

\pm

Because `engine_experiment_data.txt` is not available, numerical MLEs, CV errors, plots, and optimal settings cannot be honestly reported. I would not fabricate them. Below is the complete analysis I would carry out from the 27 observations once the data file is available, using only linear algebra and numerical optimization, not a GP package.

Let the data be  
\[
\mathcal D=\{(x_i,y_i):i=1,\dots,n\},\qquad n=27,\quad x_i\in\mathbb R^8,
\]
and define, for \(\theta=(\theta_1,\dots,\theta_8)^\top\),
\[
R_\theta(i,j)=\exp\left\{-\sum_{k=1}^8\theta_k(x_{ik}-x_{jk})^2\right\}.
\]
The covariance matrix of \(Y=(Y(x_1),\dots,Y(x_n))^\top\) is \(\sigma^2R_\theta\). In computation I would work with coded/scaled factor levels and use Cholesky decompositions of \(R_\theta\), adding only a tiny numerical jitter if needed for stability.

---

## (1) MLEs for the constant-mean GP model

The model is

\[
Y(x)=\mu+Z(x),
\]
with
\[
\operatorname{Cov}\{Z(x),Z(x')\}=\sigma^2\exp\left\{-\sum_{k=1}^8\theta_k(x_k-x_k')^2\right\}.
\]

Let \(1_n\) denote the \(n\)-vector of ones. The log-likelihood is

\[
\ell(\mu,\sigma^2,\theta)
=
-\frac n2\log(2\pi)
-\frac n2\log\sigma^2
-\frac12\log |R_\theta|
-\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}(y-\mu 1_n)^\top R_\theta^{-1}(y-\mu 1_n).
\]

For fixed \(\theta\), the generalized least-squares MLE of \(\mu\) is

\[
\widehat\mu(\theta)
=
\frac{1_n^\top R_\theta^{-1}y}{1_n^\top R_\theta^{-1}1_n}.
\]

Define the generalized residual sum of squares

\[
S(\theta)
=
\{y-\widehat\mu(\theta)1_n\}^\top R_\theta^{-1}
\{y-\widehat\mu(\theta)1_n\}.
\]

For fixed \(\theta\), the MLE of \(\sigma^2\) is

\[
\widehat{\sigma}^2(\theta)=\frac{S(\theta)}{n}.
\]

Therefore the profile log-likelihood is, up to an additive constant,

\[
\ell_p(\theta)
=
-\frac12\left[
\log |R_\theta|
+n\log\left\{\frac{S(\theta)}{n}\right\}
\right].
\]

Equivalently, the MLE of \(\theta\) is

\[
\widehat\theta
=
\arg\min_{\theta_k\ge 0}
\left[
\log |R_\theta|
+n\log\left\{\frac{S(\theta)}{n}\right\}
\right].
\]

Once \(\widehat\theta\) is found,

\[
\widehat\mu=\widehat\mu(\widehat\theta),
\qquad
\widehat\sigma^2=\widehat\sigma^2(\widehat\theta).
\]

A useful expression for numerical optimization is the profile score. Let

\[
\alpha=R_\theta^{-1}\{y-\widehat\mu(\theta)1_n\}.
\]

Then

\[
\frac{\partial R_\theta(i,j)}{\partial \theta_k}
=
-(x_{ik}-x_{jk})^2 R_\theta(i,j),
\]

and

\[
\frac{\partial}{\partial \theta_k}
\left[
\log |R_\theta|+n\log\{S(\theta)/n\}
\right]
=
\operatorname{tr}\left(R_\theta^{-1}\frac{\partial R_\theta}{\partial \theta_k}\right)
-
\frac{n}{S(\theta)}
\alpha^\top
\frac{\partial R_\theta}{\partial \theta_k}
\alpha.
\]

In practice I would optimize over \(\eta_k=\log\theta_k\) using a multistart quasi-Newton method such as L-BFGS-B, evaluating determinants and solves by Cholesky factorization.

Because the dataset is unavailable, the numerical values

\[
\widehat\mu,\quad
\widehat\sigma^2,\quad
\widehat\theta_1,\dots,\widehat\theta_8
\]

cannot be reported.

---

## (2) BLUP and plug-in predictive distribution for the constant-mean model

For a new input \(x_0\), define the correlation vector

\[
r(x_0)
=
\begin{pmatrix}
\phi(x_0-x_1;\widehat\theta)\\
\vdots\\
\phi(x_0-x_n;\widehat\theta)
\end{pmatrix}.
\]

The ordinary kriging BLUP is

\[
\widehat y(x_0)
=
\widehat\mu
+
r(x_0)^\top R_{\widehat\theta}^{-1}
\{y-\widehat\mu 1_n\}.
\]

The plug-in predictive variance, accounting for estimation of the constant mean but treating \(\widehat\theta\) and \(\widehat\sigma^2\) as fixed, is

\[
\widehat v(x_0)
=
\widehat\sigma^2
\left[
1
-
r(x_0)^\top R_{\widehat\theta}^{-1}r(x_0)
+
\frac{
\left\{
1-1_n^\top R_{\widehat\theta}^{-1}r(x_0)
\right\}^2
}{
1_n^\top R_{\widehat\theta}^{-1}1_n
}
\right].
\]

Thus the plug-in predictive distribution is

\[
Y(x_0)\mid y
\approx
N\left(
\widehat y(x_0),\widehat v(x_0)
\right).
\]

A pointwise 95% predictive interval is

\[
\widehat y(x_0)\pm 1.96\sqrt{\widehat v(x_0)}.
\]

---

## (3) Leave-one-out cross-validation prediction error for the constant-mean BLUP

For honest leave-one-out cross-validation, for each \(i=1,\dots,n\) I would:

1. Delete observation \(i\).
2. Refit the GP model on the remaining \(n-1\) observations, including re-estimation of \(\theta,\mu,\sigma^2\).
3. Predict \(y_i\) using the fitted BLUP.
4. Compute the residual
   \[
   e_i^{\text{LOO}}=y_i-\widehat y_{-i}(x_i).
   \]

The main prediction error summaries would be

\[
\operatorname{PRESS}
=
\sum_{i=1}^n
\left(e_i^{\text{LOO}}\right)^2,
\]

\[
\operatorname{RMSE}_{\text{LOO}}
=
\left[
\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n
\left(e_i^{\text{LOO}}\right)^2
\right]^{1/2},
\]

\[
\operatorname{MAE}_{\text{LOO}}
=
\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n
|e_i^{\text{LOO}}|.
\]

\[

\[

=

\]

Then

\[

=
\frac{(My)_i}{M_{ii}},

\[

=
y_i-\frac{(My)_i}{M_{ii}}.
\]

The corresponding LOO predictive variance is approximately

\[
\widehat v_i^{\text{LOO}}
=
\frac{\widehat\sigma^2}{M_{ii}}.
\]

\[
z_i
=
\frac{e_i^{\text{LOO}}}{\sqrt{\widehat v_i^{\text{LOO}}}}

The numerical CV error cannot be reported without the data.

Because `engine_experiment_data.txt` is not available, I cannot give defensible numerical estimates, CV errors, plots, or optimal factor settings. Below is the complete analysis I would carry out from the data, using only linear algebra and numerical optimization, not GP packages.

Let the 27 runs be  
\[
x^{(j)}=(x^{(j)}_1,\ldots,x^{(j)}_8)^T,\qquad j=1,\ldots,n,\quad n=27,
\]
and let \(y=(y_1,\ldots,y_n)^T\). For a given \(\theta=(\theta_1,\ldots,\theta_8)^T\), define the \(n\times n\) correlation matrix
\[
R_\theta(j,k)
=
\exp\left\{
-\sum_{\ell=1}^8 \theta_\ell\left(x^{(j)}_\ell-x^{(k)}_\ell\right)^2
\right\}.
\]
Then
\[
y\sim N(F\beta,\sigma^2 R_\theta),
\]
where \(F\) is the mean-model design matrix.

In practice I would code or standardize the eight factors before fitting, e.g. to \([0,1]\) or \([-1,1]\), because the numerical scale of the \(\theta_\ell\)’s depends directly on the scale of the inputs.

---

## (1) Constant-mean GP model

The model is
\[
Y(x)=\mu+Z(x),
\]
with
\[
\operatorname{Cov}\{Z(x),Z(x')\}
=
\sigma^2
\exp\left\{
-\sum_{\ell=1}^8 \theta_\ell (x_\ell-x'_\ell)^2
\right\}.
\]

Here
\[
F=\mathbf 1_n,\qquad \beta=\mu.
\]

The log-likelihood is
\[
\ell(\mu,\sigma^2,\theta)
=
-\frac n2\log(2\pi)
-\frac n2\log\sigma^2
-\frac12\log|R_\theta|
-\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}(y-\mu\mathbf 1)^T R_\theta^{-1}(y-\mu\mathbf 1).
\]

For fixed \(\theta\), the MLE of \(\mu\) is the generalized least-squares estimator
\[
\widehat\mu(\theta)
=
\frac{\mathbf 1^T R_\theta^{-1}y}
{\mathbf 1^T R_\theta^{-1}\mathbf 1}.
\]

Define the generalized residual sum of squares
\[
S(\theta)
=
\left(y-\widehat\mu(\theta)\mathbf 1\right)^T
R_\theta^{-1}
\left(y-\widehat\mu(\theta)\mathbf 1\right).
\]

Then the MLE of \(\sigma^2\), for fixed \(\theta\), is
\[
\widehat{\sigma}^2(\theta)=\frac{S(\theta)}{n}.
\]

The concentrated log-likelihood is therefore, up to an additive constant,
\[
\ell_c(\theta)
=
-\frac n2\log \widehat{\sigma}^2(\theta)
-\frac12\log |R_\theta|.
\]

Equivalently, the MLE of \(\theta\) solves
\[
\widehat\theta
=
\arg\min_{\theta\in [0,\infty)^8}
\left\{
n\log \widehat{\sigma}^2(\theta)
+
\log |R_\theta|
\right\}.
\]

Numerically, I would optimize over \(\eta_\ell=\log\theta_\ell\) to enforce \(\theta_\ell>0\), using Cholesky decompositions of \(R_\theta\) to compute \(R_\theta^{-1}y\), \(R_\theta^{-1}\mathbf 1\), and \(\log|R_\theta|\).

The final estimates would be
\[
\widehat\theta=\widehat\theta_{\mathrm{MLE}},
\]
\[
\widehat\mu=\widehat\mu(\widehat\theta),
\]
\[
\widehat{\sigma}^2
=
\widehat{\sigma}^2(\widehat\theta).
\]

Because the data file is missing, the numerical values of  
\[
\widehat\mu,\qquad \widehat\theta_1,\ldots,\widehat\theta_8,\qquad \widehat{\sigma}^2
\]
cannot be reported.

---

## (2) BLUP and plug-in predictive distribution

For a new input \(x_0\), define
\[
r_0
=
\begin{pmatrix}
\phi(x_0-x^{(1)};\widehat\theta)\\
\vdots\\
\phi(x_0-x^{(n)};\widehat\theta)
\end{pmatrix}
\]
with
\[
\phi(x_0-x^{(j)};\widehat\theta)
=
\exp\left\{
-\sum_{\ell=1}^8 \widehat\theta_\ell
(x_{0\ell}-x^{(j)}_\ell)^2
\right\}.
\]

For the constant-mean model, the BLUP, also called the ordinary kriging predictor, is
\[
\widehat y(x_0)
=
\widehat\mu
+
r_0^T R_{\widehat\theta}^{-1}
\left(y-\widehat\mu \mathbf 1\right).
\]

The plug-in predictive variance is
\[
\widehat s^2(x_0)
=
\widehat{\sigma}^2
\left[
1
-
r_0^T R_{\widehat\theta}^{-1}r_0
+
\frac{
\left(1-\mathbf 1^T R_{\widehat\theta}^{-1}r_0\right)^2
}{
\mathbf 1^T R_{\widehat\theta}^{-1}\mathbf 1
}
\right].
\]

Thus the plug-in predictive distribution is
\[
Y(x_0)\mid y
\approx
N\left(
\widehat y(x_0),
\widehat s^2(x_0)
\right).
\]

This predictive distribution treats \(\widehat\theta,\widehat\mu,\widehat{\sigma}^2\) as fixed and does not account for uncertainty in estimating them.

---

## (3) Leave-one-out cross-validation error for the constant-mean BLUP

For exact leave-one-out cross-validation, for each \(i=1,\ldots,n\):

1. Remove observation \(i\).
2. Refit the GP model to the remaining \(n-1=26\) observations.
3. Predict \(y_i\) at \(x^{(i)}\) using the BLUP based on the training data.
4. Compute the prediction error
   \[
   e_i = y_i-\widehat y_{(-i)}(x^{(i)}).
   \]

The leave-one-out mean squared prediction error is
\[
\operatorname{CV\text{-}MSE}
=
\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n e_i^2,
\]
and the leave-one-out root mean squared prediction error is
\[
\operatorname{CV\text{-}RMSE}
=
\left(
\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n e_i^2
\right)^{1/2}.
\]

A useful computational shortcut, if \(\widehat\theta\) is held fixed at its full-data value, is as follows. Define
\[
H
=
R_{\widehat\theta}^{-1}
-
R_{\widehat\theta}^{-1}\mathbf 1
\left(
\mathbf 1^T R_{\widehat\theta}^{-1}\mathbf 1
\right)^{-1}
\mathbf 1^T R_{\widehat\theta}^{-1}.
\]
Then
\[
a=Hy.
\]
The leave-one-out prediction error with \(\widehat\theta\) fixed is
\[
e_i^{\mathrm{LOO}}
=
\frac{a_i}{H_{ii}},
\]
and the corresponding leave-one-out predictor is
\[
\widehat y_{(-i)}(x^{(i)})
=
y_i-\frac{a_i}{H_{ii}}.
\]

The numerical value of \(\operatorname{CV\text{-}RMSE}\) cannot be reported without the data.

---

## (4) Linear-mean GP model with \(x_1\) and \(x_6\)

Now the model is
\[
Y(x)
=
\beta_0+x_1\beta_1+x_6\beta_2+Z(x).
\]

Define
\[
f(x)=
\begin{pmatrix}
1\\
x_1\\
x_6
\end{pmatrix}.
\]

The design matrix is
\[
F=
\begin{pmatrix}
1 & x^{(1)}_1 & x^{(1)}_6\\
\vdots & \vdots & \vdots\\
1 & x^{(n)}_1 & x^{(n)}_6
\end{pmatrix}.
\]

For fixed \(\theta\), the generalized least-squares estimator is
\[
\widehat\beta(\theta)
=
\left(F^T R_\theta^{-1}F\right)^{-1}
F^T R_\theta^{-1}y.
\]

The residual sum of squares is
\[
S(\theta)
=
\left(y-F\widehat\beta(\theta)\right)^T
R_\theta^{-1}
\left(y-F\widehat\beta(\theta)\right).
\]

The MLE of \(\sigma^2\), for fixed \(\theta\), is
\[
\widehat{\sigma}^2(\theta)=\frac{S(\theta)}{n}.
\]

The concentrated likelihood is maximized by
\[
\widehat\theta
=
\arg\min_{\theta\in[0,\infty)^8}
\left\{
n\log\widehat{\sigma}^2(\theta)+\log|R_\theta|
\right\}.
\]

Then
\[
\widehat\beta=\widehat\beta(\widehat\theta),
\qquad
\widehat{\sigma}^2=\widehat{\sigma}^2(\widehat\theta).
\]

For prediction at \(x_0\), let
\[
f_0=f(x_0)=
\begin{pmatrix}
1\\
x_{01}\\
x_{06}
\end{pmatrix}.
\]

Let
\[
r_0=
\begin{pmatrix}
\phi(x_0-x^{(1)};\widehat\theta)\\
\vdots\\
\phi(x_0-x^{(n)};\widehat\theta)
\end{pmatrix}.
\]

The universal kriging BLUP is
\[
\widehat y(x_0)
=
f_0^T\widehat\beta
+
r_0^T R_{\widehat\theta}^{-1}
\left(y-F\widehat\beta\right).
\]

The plug-in predictive variance is
\[
\widehat s^2(x_0)
=
\widehat{\sigma}^2
\left[
1
-
r_0^T R_{\widehat\theta}^{-1}r_0
+
\left(
f_0-F^T R_{\widehat\theta}^{-1}r_0
\right)^T
\left(
F^T R_{\widehat\theta}^{-1}F
\right)^{-1}
\left(
f_0-F^T R_{\widehat\theta}^{-1}r_0
\right)
\right].
\]

Thus
\[
Y(x_0)\mid y
\approx
N\left(
\widehat y(x_0),
\widehat s^2(x_0)
\right).
\]

For leave-one-out CV, the exact procedure is the same as before: for each deleted observation, refit the full linear-mean GP to the remaining 26 observations and predict the deleted response.

If \(\widehat\theta\) is held fixed, the fast leave-one-out formula becomes
\[
H
=
R_{\widehat\theta}^{-1}
-
R_{\widehat\theta}^{-1}F
\left(
F^T R_{\widehat\theta}^{-1}F
\right)^{-1}
F^T R_{\widehat\theta}^{-1},
\]
\[
a=Hy,
\]
\[
e_i^{\mathrm{LOO}}
=
\frac{a_i}{H_{ii}},
\]
and
\[
\operatorname{CV\text{-}RMSE}
=
\left(
\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n
\left(\frac{a_i}{H_{ii}}\right)^2
\right)^{1/2}.
\]

Again, the numerical CV error cannot be computed without the data.

---

## (5) Final model choice

I would compare the constant-mean model and the linear-mean model using both likelihood-based and predictive measures.

For model \(m\), define
\[
k_m = \text{number of estimated parameters}.
\]

For the constant-mean GP,
\[
k_1 = 1+8+1=10,
\]
corresponding to \(\mu\), eight \(\theta_\ell\)’s, and \(\sigma^2\).

For the linear-mean GP,
\[
k_2 = 3+8+1=12,
\]
corresponding to \(\beta_0,\beta_1,\beta_2\), eight \(\theta_\ell\)’s, and \(\sigma^2\).

I would compute:

\[
\operatorname{AIC}
=
-2\ell(\widehat\beta,\widehat\sigma^2,\widehat\theta)
+
2k,
\]

\[
\operatorname{BIC}
=
-2\ell(\widehat\beta,\widehat\sigma^2,\widehat\theta)
+
k\log n,
\]

and, because \(n=27\) is small relative to the number of parameters, also

\[
\operatorname{AICc}
=
\operatorname{AIC}
+
\frac{2k(k+1)}{n-k-1}.
\]

More importantly, I would compare predictive performance using leave-one-out quantities:

\[
\operatorname{CV\text{-}RMSE}
=
\left(
\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n e_i^2
\right)^{1/2},
\]

\[
\operatorname{CV\text{-}MAE}
=
\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n |e_i|,
\]

and the leave-one-out negative log predictive density,

\[
\operatorname{NLPD}
=
\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n
\left[
\frac12\log(2\pi \widehat s_{(-i)}^2)
+
\frac{e_i^2}{2\widehat s_{(-i)}^2}
\right].
\]

A natural summary table would be:

\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c|c}
\text{Model} & \log L & \text{AICc} & \text{BIC} & \text{LOO RMSE} & \text{LOO NLPD}\\
\hline
\mu+Z(x) & \cdots & \cdots & \cdots & \cdots & \cdots\\
\beta_0+x_1\beta_1+x_6\beta_2+Z(x) & \cdots & \cdots & \cdots & \cdots & \cdots
\end{array}
\]

The final model would be chosen as follows:

- If the linear-mean model has meaningfully lower LOO RMSE and LOO NLPD, and is not strongly penalized by AICc/BIC, I would choose the linear-mean model.
- If the two models have essentially equal predictive performance, I would choose the simpler constant-mean GP.
- I would also check standardized LOO residuals,
  \[
  z_i=\frac{e_i}{\widehat s_{(-i)}},
  \]
  to see whether they are roughly centered at zero with unit scale.

Because the dataset is unavailable, I cannot honestly declare one of the two models to be the empirical winner.

---

## (6) BLUP as a function of \(x_1\) with 95% predictive bands

A plot of the BLUP as a function of \(x_1\) is not uniquely defined unless the other seven factors are fixed. I would choose a reference setting
\[
x^\dagger_{-1}
=
(x_2^\dagger,\ldots,x_8^\dagger),
\]
for example the design center, nominal engineering settings, or the estimated optimum for the other seven factors.

For a grid
\[
t_1,\ldots,t_G
\]
over the experimental range of \(x_1\), define
\[
x(t_g)
=
(t_g,x_2^\dagger,\ldots,x_8^\dagger).
\]

For each grid point, compute
\[
\widehat m(t_g)
=
\widehat y\{x(t_g)\},
\]
and
\[
\widehat s(t_g)
=
\widehat s\{x(t_g)\}.
\]

The pointwise 95% plug-in predictive bands are
\[
\widehat m(t_g)
\pm
1.96\,\widehat s(t_g).
\]

Thus the plot consists of:

- the curve \(t\mapsto \widehat m(t)\);
- the lower band
  \[
  \widehat m(t)-1.96\,\widehat s(t);
  \]
- the upper band
  \[
  \widehat m(t)+1.96\,\widehat s(t).
  \]

These are pointwise predictive bands and do not account for uncertainty in \(\widehat\theta\).

---

## (7) Optimization of the eight factor settings

The objective is to minimize the fitted posterior mean or BLUP over the feasible factor region \(\mathcal X\):

\[
\widehat x_{\mathrm{opt}}
=
\arg\min_{x\in\mathcal X}
\widehat y(x).
\]

For the final fitted GP model, write
\[
\widehat y(x)
=
f(x)^T\widehat\beta
+
r(x)^T R_{\widehat\theta}^{-1}
\left(y-F\widehat\beta\right).
\]

Let
\[
\alpha
=
R_{\widehat\theta}^{-1}
\left(y-F\widehat\beta\right).
\]

Then
\[
\widehat y(x)
=
f(x)^T\widehat\beta
+
\sum_{j=1}^n \alpha_j r_j(x),
\]
where
\[
r_j(x)
=
\exp\left\{
-\sum_{\ell=1}^8
\widehat\theta_\ell
(x_\ell-x_\ell^{(j)})^2
\right\}.
\]

The gradient is available analytically. For coordinate \(\ell\),

\[
\frac{\partial \widehat y(x)}{\partial x_\ell}
=
\frac{\partial f(x)^T}{\partial x_\ell}\widehat\beta
+
\sum_{j=1}^n
\alpha_j r_j(x)
\left[
-2\widehat\theta_\ell
(x_\ell-x_\ell^{(j)})
\right].
\]

For the constant-mean model,
\[
\frac{\partial f(x)^T}{\partial x_\ell}\widehat\beta=0.
\]

For the linear-mean model,
\[
f(x)^T\widehat\beta
=
\widehat\beta_0+x_1\widehat\beta_1+x_6\widehat\beta_2,
\]
so
\[
\frac{\partial f(x)^T}{\partial x_\ell}\widehat\beta
=
\begin{cases}
\widehat\beta_1, & \ell=1,\\
\widehat\beta_2, & \ell=6,\\
0, & \text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
\]

Because the BLUP surface is nonlinear and may have multiple local minima, I would use a global-search plus local-refinement algorithm:

1. Define the feasible region
   \[
   \mathcal X
   =
   \prod_{\ell=1}^8 [L_\ell,U_\ell],
   \]
   using the experimental factor limits.

2. Generate a large space-filling sample in \(\mathcal X\), for example by a Latin hypercube design.

3. Evaluate \(\widehat y(x)\) at all candidate points.

4. Select the best \(M\) points as starting values.

5. From each starting value, run a bound-constrained quasi-Newton optimizer such as L-BFGS-B, using the analytic gradient above.

6. Compare all local optima and take the one with the smallest predicted gap lift.

7. Report
   \[
   \widehat x_{\mathrm{opt}}
   =
   (\widehat x_1,\ldots,\widehat x_8),
   \]
   together with
   \[
   \widehat y(\widehat x_{\mathrm{opt}})
   \]
   and the predictive standard deviation
   \[
   \widehat s(\widehat x_{\mathrm{opt}}).
   \]

If some factors are discrete or categorical, I would enumerate their admissible settings and perform the continuous optimization conditionally on each discrete combination.

Because the data file is missing, the numerical optimal settings cannot be computed.

Y(x)=\mu+Z(x),
\]
with
\[
\operatorname{Cov}\{Z(x),Z(x')\}
=
\sigma^2
\exp\left\{
-\sum_{\ell=1}^8 \theta_\ell (x_\ell-x'_\ell)^2
\right\}.
\]

Here
\[
F=\mathbf 1_n,\qquad \beta=\mu.
\]

The log-likelihood is
\[
\ell(\mu,\sigma^2,\theta)
=
-\frac n2\log(2\pi)
-\frac n2\log\sigma^2
-\frac12\log|R_\theta|
-\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}(y-\mu\mathbf 1)^T R_\theta^{-1}(y-\mu\mathbf 1).
\]

For fixed \(\theta\), the MLE of \(\mu\) is the generalized least-squares estimator
\[
\widehat\mu(\theta)
=
\frac{\mathbf 1^T R_\theta^{-1}y}
{\mathbf 1^T R_\theta^{-1}\mathbf 1}.
\]

Define the generalized residual sum of squares
\[
S(\theta)
=
\left(y-\widehat\mu(\theta)\mathbf 1\right)^T
R_\theta^{-1}
\left(y-\widehat\mu(\theta)\mathbf 1\right).
\]

Then the MLE of \(\sigma^2\), for fixed \(\theta\), is
\[
\widehat{\sigma}^2(\theta)=\frac{S(\theta)}{n}.
\]

The concentrated log-likelihood is therefore, up to an additive constant,
\[
\ell_c(\theta)
=
-\frac n2\log \widehat{\sigma}^2(\theta)
-\frac12\log |R_\theta|.
\]

Equivalently, the MLE of \(\theta\) solves
\[
\widehat\theta
=
\arg\min_{\theta\in [0,\infty)^8}
\left\{
n\log \widehat{\sigma}^2(\theta)
+
\log |R_\theta|
\right\}.
\]

Numerically, I would optimize over \(\eta_\ell=\log\theta_\ell\) to enforce \(\theta_\ell>0\), using Cholesky decompositions of \(R_\theta\) to compute \(R_\theta^{-1}y\), \(R_\theta^{-1}\mathbf 1\), and \(\log|R_\theta|\).

The final estimates would be
\[
\widehat\theta=\widehat\theta_{\mathrm{MLE}},
\]
\[
\widehat\mu=\widehat\mu(\widehat\theta),
\]
\[
\widehat{\sigma}^2
=
\widehat{\sigma}^2(\widehat\theta).
\]

Because the data file is missing, the numerical values of  
\[
\widehat\mu,\qquad \widehat\theta_1,\ldots,\widehat\theta_8,\qquad \widehat{\sigma}^2
\]
cannot be reported.

---

## (2) BLUP and plug-in predictive distribution

For a new input \(x_0\), define
\[
r_0
=
\begin{pmatrix}
\phi(x_0-x^{(1)};\widehat\theta)\\
\vdots\\
\phi(x_0-x^{(n)};\widehat\theta)
\end{pmatrix}
\]
with
\[
\phi(x_0-x^{(j)};\widehat\theta)
=
\exp\left\{
-\sum_{\ell=1}^8 \widehat\theta_\ell
(x_{0\ell}-x^{(j)}_\ell)^2
\right\}.
\]

For the constant-mean model, the BLUP, also called the ordinary kriging predictor, is
\[
\widehat y(x_0)
=
\widehat\mu
+
r_0^T R_{\widehat\theta}^{-1}
\left(y-\widehat\mu \mathbf 1\right).
\]

The plug-in predictive variance is
\[
\widehat s^2(x_0)
=
\widehat{\sigma}^2
\left[
1
-
r_0^T R_{\widehat\theta}^{-1}r_0
+
\frac{
\left(1-\mathbf 1^T R_{\widehat\theta}^{-1}r_0\right)^2
}{
\mathbf 1^T R_{\widehat\theta}^{-1}\mathbf 1
}
\right].
\]

Thus the plug-in predictive distribution is
\[
Y(x_0)\mid y
\approx
N\left(
\widehat y(x_0),
\widehat s^2(x_0)
\right).
\]

This predictive distribution treats \(\widehat\theta,\widehat\mu,\widehat{\sigma}^2\) as fixed and does not account for uncertainty in estimating them.

---

## (3) Leave-one-out cross-validation error for the constant-mean BLUP

For exact leave-one-out cross-validation, for each \(i=1,\ldots,n\):

1. Remove observation \(i\).
2. Refit the GP model to the remaining \(n-1=26\) observations.
3. Predict \(y_i\) at \(x^{(i)}\) using the BLUP based on the training data.
4. Compute the prediction error
   \[
   e_i = y_i-\widehat y_{(-i)}(x^{(i)}).
   \]

The leave-one-out mean squared prediction error is
\[
\operatorname{CV\text{-}MSE}
=
\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n e_i^2,
\]
and the leave-one-out root mean squared prediction error is
\[
\operatorname{CV\text{-}RMSE}
=
\left(
\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n e_i^2
\right)^{1/2}.
\]

A useful computational shortcut, if \(\widehat\theta\) is held fixed at its full-data value, is as follows. Define
\[
H
=
R_{\widehat\theta}^{-1}
-
R_{\widehat\theta}^{-1}\mathbf 1
\left(
\mathbf 1^T R_{\widehat\theta}^{-1}\mathbf 1
\right)^{-1}
\mathbf 1^T R_{\widehat\theta}^{-1}.
\]
Then
\[
a=Hy.
\]
The leave-one-out prediction error with \(\widehat\theta\) fixed is
\[
e_i^{\mathrm{LOO}}
=
\frac{a_i}{H_{ii}},
\]
and the corresponding leave-one-out predictor is
\[
\widehat y_{(-i)}(x^{(i)})
=
y_i-\frac{a_i}{H_{ii}}.
\]

The numerical value of \(\operatorname{CV\text{-}RMSE}\) cannot be reported without the data.

---

## (4) Linear-mean GP model with \(x_1\) and \(x_6\)

Now the model is
\[
Y(x)
=
\beta_0+x_1\beta_1+x_6\beta_2+Z(x).
\]

Define
\[
f(x)=
\begin{pmatrix}
1\\
x_1\\
x_6
\end{pmatrix}.
\]

The design matrix is
\[
F=
\begin{pmatrix}
1 & x^{(1)}_1 & x^{(1)}_6\\
\vdots & \vdots & \vdots\\
1 & x^{(n)}_1 & x^{(n)}_6
\end{pmatrix}.
\]

For fixed \(\theta\), the generalized least-squares estimator is
\[
\widehat\beta(\theta)
=
\left(F^T R_\theta^{-1}F\right)^{-1}
F^T R_\theta^{-1}y.
\]

The residual sum of squares is
\[
S(\theta)
=
\left(y-F\widehat\beta(\theta)\right)^T
R_\theta^{-1}
\left(y-F\widehat\beta(\theta)\right).
\]

The MLE of \(\sigma^2\), for fixed \(\theta\), is
\[
\widehat{\sigma}^2(\theta)=\frac{S(\theta)}{n}.
\]

The concentrated likelihood is maximized by
\[
\widehat\theta
=
\arg\min_{\theta\in[0,\infty)^8}
\left\{
n\log\widehat{\sigma}^2(\theta)+\log|R_\theta|
\right\}.
\]

Then
\[
\widehat\beta=\widehat\beta(\widehat\theta),
\qquad
\widehat{\sigma}^2=\widehat{\sigma}^2(\widehat\theta).
\]

For prediction at \(x_0\), let
\[
f_0=f(x_0)=
\begin{pmatrix}
1\\
x_{01}\\
x_{06}
\end{pmatrix}.
\]

Let
\[
r_0=
\begin{pmatrix}
\phi(x_0-x^{(1)};\widehat\theta)\\
\vdots\\
\phi(x_0-x^{(n)};\widehat\theta)
\end{pmatrix}.
\]

The universal kriging BLUP is
\[
\widehat y(x_0)
=
f_0^T\widehat\beta
+
r_0^T R_{\widehat\theta}^{-1}
\left(y-F\widehat\beta\right).
\]

The plug-in predictive variance is
\[
\widehat s^2(x_0)
=
\widehat{\sigma}^2
\left[
1
-
r_0^T R_{\widehat\theta}^{-1}r_0
+
\left(
f_0-F^T R_{\widehat\theta}^{-1}r_0
\right)^T
\left(
F^T R_{\widehat\theta}^{-1}F
\right)^{-1}
\left(
f_0-F^T R_{\widehat\theta}^{-1}r_0
\right)
\right].
\]

Thus
\[
Y(x_0)\mid y
\approx
N\left(
\widehat y(x_0),
\widehat s^2(x_0)
\right).
\]

For leave-one-out CV, the exact procedure is the same as before: for each deleted observation, refit the full linear-mean GP to the remaining 26 observations and predict the deleted response.

If \(\widehat\theta\) is held fixed, the fast leave-one-out formula becomes
\[
H
=
R_{\widehat\theta}^{-1}
-
R_{\widehat\theta}^{-1}F
\left(
F^T R_{\widehat\theta}^{-1}F
\right)^{-1}
F^T R_{\widehat\theta}^{-1},
\]
\[
a=Hy,
\]
\[
e_i^{\mathrm{LOO}}
=
\frac{a_i}{H_{ii}},
\]
and
\[
\operatorname{CV\text{-}RMSE}
=
\left(
\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n
\left(\frac{a_i}{H_{ii}}\right)^2
\right)^{1/2}.
\]

Again, the numerical CV error cannot be computed without the data.

---

## (5) Final model choice

I would compare the constant-mean model and the linear-mean model using both likelihood-based and predictive measures.

For model \(m\), define
\[
k_m = \text{number of estimated parameters}.
\]

For the constant-mean GP,
\[
k_1 = 1+8+1=10,
\]
corresponding to \(\mu\), eight \(\theta_\ell\)’s, and \(\sigma^2\).

For the linear-mean GP,
\[
k_2 = 3+8+1=12,
\]
corresponding to \(\beta_0,\beta_1,\beta_2\), eight \(\theta_\ell\)’s, and \(\sigma^2\).

I would compute:

\[
\operatorname{AIC}
=
-2\ell(\widehat\beta,\widehat\sigma^2,\widehat\theta)
+
2k,
\]

\[
\operatorname{BIC}
=
-2\ell(\widehat\beta,\widehat\sigma^2,\widehat\theta)
+
k\log n,
\]

and, because \(n=27\) is small relative to the number of parameters, also

\[
\operatorname{AICc}
=
\operatorname{AIC}
+
\frac{2k(k+1)}{n-k-1}.
\]

More importantly, I would compare predictive performance using leave-one-out quantities:

\[
\operatorname{CV\text{-}RMSE}
=
\left(
\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n e_i^2
\right)^{1/2},
\]

\[
\operatorname{CV\text{-}MAE}
=
\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n |e_i|,
\]

and the leave-one-out negative log predictive density,

\[
\operatorname{NLPD}
=
\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n
\left[
\frac12\log(2\pi \widehat s_{(-i)}^2)
+
\frac{e_i^2}{2\widehat s_{(-i)}^2}
\right].
\]

A natural summary table would be:

\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c|c}
\text{Model} & \log L & \text{AICc} & \text{BIC} & \text{LOO RMSE} & \text{LOO NLPD}\\
\hline
\mu+Z(x) & \cdots & \cdots & \cdots & \cdots & \cdots\\
\beta_0+x_1\beta_1+x_6\beta_2+Z(x) & \cdots & \cdots & \cdots & \cdots & \cdots
\end{array}
\]

The final model would be chosen as follows:

- If the linear-mean model has meaningfully lower LOO RMSE and LOO NLPD, and is not strongly penalized by AICc/BIC, I would choose the linear-mean model.
- If the two models have essentially equal predictive performance, I would choose the simpler constant-mean GP.
- I would also check standardized LOO residuals,
  \[
  z_i=\frac{e_i}{\widehat s_{(-i)}},

Because the dataset is unavailable, I cannot honestly declare one of the two models to be the empirical winner.

## (6) BLUP as a function of \(x_1\) with 95% predictive bands

A plot of the BLUP as a function of \(x_1\) is not uniquely defined unless the other seven factors are fixed. I would choose a reference setting
\[
x^\dagger_{-1}
=
(x_2^\dagger,\ldots,x_8^\dagger),
\]

For a grid
\[

\]
over the experimental range of \(x_1\), define
\[
x(t_g)
=
(t_g,x_2^\dagger,\ldots,x_8^\dagger).
\]

For each grid point, compute
\[
\widehat m(t_g)
=
\widehat y\{x(t_g)\},
\]
and
\[
\widehat s(t_g)
=
\widehat s\{x(t_g)\}.
\]

The pointwise 95% plug-in predictive bands are
\[
\widehat m(t_g)
\pm
1.96\,\widehat s(t_g).
\]

Thus the plot consists of:

- the curve \(t\mapsto \widehat m(t)\);
- the lower band
  \[
  \widehat m(t)-1.96\,\widehat s(t);
  \]
- the upper band
  \[
  \widehat m(t)+1.96\,\widehat s(t).
  \]

These are pointwise predictive bands and do not account for uncertainty in \(\widehat\theta\).

The objective is to minimize the fitted posterior mean or BLUP over the feasible factor region \(\mathcal X\):

\[
\widehat x_{\mathrm{opt}}
=
\arg\min_{x\in\mathcal X}
\widehat y(x).
\]

For the final fitted GP model, write

=
f(x)^T\widehat\beta
+

\]

Let
\[

=
R_{\widehat\theta}^{-1}
\left(y-F\widehat\beta\right).
\]

Then
\[

=

+

where

\widehat\theta_\ell

\right\}.
\]

The gradient is available analytically. For coordinate \(\ell\),

\[
\frac{\partial \widehat y(x)}{\partial x_\ell}
=
\frac{\partial f(x)^T}{\partial x_\ell}\widehat\beta
+
\sum_{j=1}^n
\alpha_j r_j(x)
\left[
-2\widehat\theta_\ell
(x_\ell-x_\ell^{(j)})
\right].
\]

For the constant-mean model,
\[
\frac{\partial f(x)^T}{\partial x_\ell}\widehat\beta=0.
\]

For the linear-mean model,
\[
f(x)^T\widehat\beta
=
\widehat\beta_0+x_1\widehat\beta_1+x_6\widehat\beta_2,

\[
\frac{\partial f(x)^T}{\partial x_\ell}\widehat\beta
=
\begin{cases}
\widehat\beta_1, & \ell=1,\\
\widehat\beta_2, & \ell=6,\\
0, & \text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}

7. Report
   \[
   \widehat x_{\mathrm{opt}}

## Part I

### I(1)(a) Definition of contiguity

For probability measures \(P_n,Q_n\) on \((\Omega_n,\mathcal A_n)\), we say

\[
P_n \triangleleft Q_n
\]

if for every sequence of events \(A_n\in \mathcal A_n\),

\[
Q_n(A_n)\to 0 \implies P_n(A_n)\to 0.
\]

Equivalently, events that are asymptotically negligible under \(Q_n\) are also asymptotically negligible under \(P_n\).

---

### I(1)(b) Bounded \(\chi^2\)-divergence implies contiguity

Let

\[
L_n=\frac{dP_n}{dQ_n}.
\]

Since \(\chi^2(P_n\|Q_n)<\infty\), we have \(P_n\ll Q_n\). For any event \(A_n\),

\[
P_n(A_n)=\int_{A_n} L_n\,dQ_n.
\]

Write

\[
P_n(A_n)
=
Q_n(A_n)+\int_{A_n}(L_n-1)\,dQ_n.
\]

By Cauchy–Schwarz,

\[
\left|\int_{A_n}(L_n-1)\,dQ_n\right|
\le
\left(\int (L_n-1)^2\,dQ_n\right)^{1/2}
Q_n(A_n)^{1/2}.
\]

Thus

\[
P_n(A_n)
\le
Q_n(A_n)+\chi^2(P_n\|Q_n)^{1/2}Q_n(A_n)^{1/2}.
\]

If \(\sup_n \chi^2(P_n\|Q_n)<\infty\) and \(Q_n(A_n)\to 0\), then the right-hand side tends to \(0\). Hence

\[
P_n(A_n)\to 0.
\]

Therefore

\[
P_n\triangleleft Q_n.
\]

---

## I(2)(a) Definition of LAN

Consider the i.i.d. experiment

\[
\mathcal E_n=\{P_\theta^{\otimes n}:\theta\in\Theta\},
\]

where \(\Theta\subset \mathbb R^k\) is open.

The model is **locally asymptotically normal**, LAN, at \(\theta\in\Theta\) if there exist random vectors \(\Delta_{n,\theta}\in\mathbb R^k\) and a symmetric nonnegative definite matrix \(I_\theta\) such that, under \(P_\theta^{\otimes n}\),

\[
\Delta_{n,\theta}\Rightarrow N_k(0,I_\theta),
\]

and for every bounded sequence \(h_n\in\mathbb R^k\) with \(\theta+h_n/\sqrt n\in\Theta\),

\[
\log\frac{dP_{\theta+h_n/\sqrt n}^{\otimes n}}{dP_\theta^{\otimes n}}
=
h_n^\top \Delta_{n,\theta}
-\frac12 h_n^\top I_\theta h_n
+o_{P_\theta}(1).
\]

The matrix \(I_\theta\) is the Fisher information matrix, and \(\Delta_{n,\theta}\) is called the central sequence.

---

## I(2)(b) Verification of LAN under smoothness assumptions

Assume the model is dominated by a \(\sigma\)-finite measure \(\mu\), with densities

\[
p_\theta=\frac{dP_\theta}{d\mu}.
\]

Let

\[
\ell_\theta(x)=\log p_\theta(x)
\]

be the log-density. Assume that in a neighborhood of a fixed \(\theta\),

1. \(p_\eta(x)>0\) for \(\mu\)-a.e. \(x\),
2. \(\eta\mapsto \ell_\eta(x)\) is twice continuously differentiable for \(\mu\)-a.e. \(x\),
3. differentiation under the integral sign is valid,
4. the score
   \[
   s_\theta(x)=\nabla_\theta \ell_\theta(x)
   \]
   satisfies
   \[
   E_\theta \|s_\theta(X)\|^2<\infty,
   \]
5. the Hessian
   \[
   H_\theta(x)=\nabla_\theta^2 \ell_\theta(x)
   \]
   satisfies a local dominated-continuity condition ensuring
   \[
   E_\theta\left[
   \sup_{\|\eta-\theta\|\le r}\|H_\eta(X)-H_\theta(X)\|
   \right]\to 0
   \qquad r\downarrow 0.
   \]

Then

\[
E_\theta s_\theta(X)=0.
\]

Indeed,

\[
E_\theta s_\theta(X)
=
\int \nabla_\theta \log p_\theta(x)\,p_\theta(x)\,d\mu(x)
=
\int \nabla_\theta p_\theta(x)\,d\mu(x)
=
\nabla_\theta 1
=
0.
\]

Also,

\[
I_\theta
=
E_\theta[s_\theta(X)s_\theta(X)^\top]
\]

is the Fisher information matrix. Differentiating \(\int p_\theta\,d\mu=1\) twice gives

\[
E_\theta H_\theta(X)
=
-I_\theta.
\]

Now let \(X_1,\dots,X_n\overset{iid}{\sim}P_\theta\). Define

\[
\Delta_{n,\theta}
=
\frac1{\sqrt n}\sum_{i=1}^n s_\theta(X_i).
\]

By the multivariate central limit theorem,

\[
\Delta_{n,\theta}\Rightarrow N_k(0,I_\theta).
\]

For fixed bounded \(h_n\), Taylor expand:

\[
\ell_{\theta+h_n/\sqrt n}(X_i)-\ell_\theta(X_i)
=
\frac1{\sqrt n}h_n^\top s_\theta(X_i)
+
\frac1{2n}h_n^\top H_\theta(X_i)h_n
+
r_{n,i}.
\]

Summing over \(i\),

\[
\log\frac{dP_{\theta+h_n/\sqrt n}^{\otimes n}}{dP_\theta^{\otimes n}}
=
h_n^\top \Delta_{n,\theta}
+
\frac12 h_n^\top
\left(
\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n H_\theta(X_i)
\right)
h_n
+
\sum_{i=1}^n r_{n,i}.
\]

By the law of large numbers,

\[
\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n H_\theta(X_i)
\to
E_\theta H_\theta(X)
=
-I_\theta
\]

in probability. The local continuity assumption on the Hessian gives

\[
\sum_{i=1}^n r_{n,i}=o_{P_\theta}(1).
\]

Therefore

\[
\log\frac{dP_{\theta+h_n/\sqrt n}^{\otimes n}}{dP_\theta^{\otimes n}}
=
h_n^\top \Delta_{n,\theta}
-\frac12 h_n^\top I_\theta h_n
+o_{P_\theta}(1).
\]

Thus the model is LAN at \(\theta\).

---

## I(3)(a) Neyman–Pearson lemma

# Part II

Let

\[

\qquad
Q_n=Q^{\otimes n},
\]

\[

\[

\qquad

Then

\[

\to

\]

=

=

\[

\[
E_{P_n}\Psi_n
=

\]

Thus for all sufficiently large \(n\),

\[
E_{P_n}\Psi_n\le \alpha.
\]

\[

=
Q_n\left(\log L_n\ge n(D-\varepsilon)\right).
\]

\[

Therefore

\[

=

=

\le
e^{-n(D-\varepsilon)}.
\]

\[
\beta_n(\alpha)
\le
e^{-n(D-\varepsilon)}.
\]

Thus

\[

\ge
D-\varepsilon.
\]

\[

\[

\le

\[

\[

\]

\[

\ge

\left[

-
P_n\left(\frac1n\log L_n>D+\varepsilon\right)

\le

\le

\[

## Part I

### I(1)(a) Definition of contiguity

For probability measures \(P_n,Q_n\) on \((\Omega_n,\mathcal A_n)\), we say

\[
P_n \triangleleft Q_n
\]

if for every sequence of events \(A_n\in \mathcal A_n\),

\[
Q_n(A_n)\to 0 \implies P_n(A_n)\to 0.
\]

Equivalently, events that are asymptotically negligible under \(Q_n\) are also asymptotically negligible under \(P_n\).

---

### I(1)(b) Bounded \(\chi^2\)-divergence implies contiguity

Let

\[
L_n=\frac{dP_n}{dQ_n}.
\]

Since \(\chi^2(P_n\|Q_n)<\infty\), we have \(P_n\ll Q_n\). For any event \(A_n\),

\[
P_n(A_n)=\int_{A_n} L_n\,dQ_n.
\]

Write

\[
P_n(A_n)
=
Q_n(A_n)+\int_{A_n}(L_n-1)\,dQ_n.
\]

By Cauchy–Schwarz,

\[
\left|\int_{A_n}(L_n-1)\,dQ_n\right|
\le
\left(\int (L_n-1)^2\,dQ_n\right)^{1/2}
Q_n(A_n)^{1/2}.
\]

Thus

\[
P_n(A_n)
\le
Q_n(A_n)+\chi^2(P_n\|Q_n)^{1/2}Q_n(A_n)^{1/2}.
\]

If \(\sup_n \chi^2(P_n\|Q_n)<\infty\) and \(Q_n(A_n)\to 0\), then the right-hand side tends to \(0\). Hence

\[
P_n(A_n)\to 0.
\]

Therefore

\[
P_n\triangleleft Q_n.
\]

---

## I(2)(a) Definition of LAN

Consider the i.i.d. experiment

\[
\mathcal E_n=\{P_\theta^{\otimes n}:\theta\in\Theta\},
\]

where \(\Theta\subset \mathbb R^k\) is open.

The model is **locally asymptotically normal**, LAN, at \(\theta\in\Theta\) if there exist random vectors \(\Delta_{n,\theta}\in\mathbb R^k\) and a symmetric nonnegative definite matrix \(I_\theta\) such that, under \(P_\theta^{\otimes n}\),

\[
\Delta_{n,\theta}\Rightarrow N_k(0,I_\theta),
\]

and for every bounded sequence \(h_n\in\mathbb R^k\) with \(\theta+h_n/\sqrt n\in\Theta\),

\[
\log\frac{dP_{\theta+h_n/\sqrt n}^{\otimes n}}{dP_\theta^{\otimes n}}
=
h_n^\top \Delta_{n,\theta}
-\frac12 h_n^\top I_\theta h_n
+o_{P_\theta}(1).
\]

The matrix \(I_\theta\) is the Fisher information matrix, and \(\Delta_{n,\theta}\) is called the central sequence.

---

## I(2)(b) Verification of LAN under smoothness assumptions

Assume the model is dominated by a \(\sigma\)-finite measure \(\mu\), with densities

\[
p_\theta=\frac{dP_\theta}{d\mu}.
\]

Let

\[
\ell_\theta(x)=\log p_\theta(x)
\]

be the log-density. Assume that in a neighborhood of a fixed \(\theta\),

1. \(p_\eta(x)>0\) for \(\mu\)-a.e. \(x\),
2. \(\eta\mapsto \ell_\eta(x)\) is twice continuously differentiable for \(\mu\)-a.e. \(x\),
3. differentiation under the integral sign is valid,
4. the score
   \[
   s_\theta(x)=\nabla_\theta \ell_\theta(x)
   \]
   satisfies
   \[
   E_\theta \|s_\theta(X)\|^2<\infty,
   \]
5. the Hessian
   \[
   H_\theta(x)=\nabla_\theta^2 \ell_\theta(x)
   \]
   satisfies a local dominated-continuity condition ensuring
   \[
   E_\theta\left[
   \sup_{\|\eta-\theta\|\le r}\|H_\eta(X)-H_\theta(X)\|
   \right]\to 0
   \qquad r\downarrow 0.
   \]

Then

\[
E_\theta s_\theta(X)=0.
\]

Indeed,

\[
E_\theta s_\theta(X)
=
\int \nabla_\theta \log p_\theta(x)\,p_\theta(x)\,d\mu(x)
=
\int \nabla_\theta p_\theta(x)\,d\mu(x)
=
\nabla_\theta 1
=
0.
\]

Also,

\[
I_\theta
=
E_\theta[s_\theta(X)s_\theta(X)^\top]
\]

is the Fisher information matrix. Differentiating \(\int p_\theta\,d\mu=1\) twice gives

\[
E_\theta H_\theta(X)
=
-I_\theta.
\]

Now let \(X_1,\dots,X_n\overset{iid}{\sim}P_\theta\). Define

\[
\Delta_{n,\theta}
=
\frac1{\sqrt n}\sum_{i=1}^n s_\theta(X_i).
\]

By the multivariate central limit theorem,

\[
\Delta_{n,\theta}\Rightarrow N_k(0,I_\theta).
\]

For fixed bounded \(h_n\), Taylor expand:

\[
\ell_{\theta+h_n/\sqrt n}(X_i)-\ell_\theta(X_i)
=
\frac1{\sqrt n}h_n^\top s_\theta(X_i)
+
\frac1{2n}h_n^\top H_\theta(X_i)h_n
+
r_{n,i}.
\]

Summing over \(i\),

\[
\log\frac{dP_{\theta+h_n/\sqrt n}^{\otimes n}}{dP_\theta^{\otimes n}}
=
h_n^\top \Delta_{n,\theta}
+
\frac12 h_n^\top
\left(
\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n H_\theta(X_i)
\right)
h_n
+
\sum_{i=1}^n r_{n,i}.
\]

By the law of large numbers,

\[
\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n H_\theta(X_i)
\to
E_\theta H_\theta(X)
=
-I_\theta
\]

in probability. The local continuity assumption on the Hessian gives

\[
\sum_{i=1}^n r_{n,i}=o_{P_\theta}(1).
\]

Therefore

\[
\log\frac{dP_{\theta+h_n/\sqrt n}^{\otimes n}}{dP_\theta^{\otimes n}}
=
h_n^\top \Delta_{n,\theta}
-\frac12 h_n^\top I_\theta h_n
+o_{P_\theta}(1).
\]

Thus the model is LAN at \(\theta\).

\]

\ge

\[
-\frac1n\log \beta_n(\alpha)
\le
D+\varepsilon
-\frac1n\log\left(\frac{1-\alpha}{2}\right).

\[
R_\alpha
\le
D+\varepsilon.
\]

\[
\boxed{
R_\alpha\le D_{KL}(P\|Q).
}
\]

\[
\boxed{
R_\alpha
=
D_{KL}(P\|Q)
}
\]

## Part I

### (1)(a) Definition of contiguity

Let \(P_n,Q_n\) be probability measures on \((\Omega_n,\mathcal A_n)\). We say

\[
P_n \triangleleft Q_n
\]

that is, \(\{P_n\}\) is contiguous with respect to \(\{Q_n\}\), if for every sequence of events \(A_n\in \mathcal A_n\),

\[
Q_n(A_n)\to 0 \implies P_n(A_n)\to 0.
\]

Equivalently, any event sequence that is asymptotically negligible under \(Q_n\) is also asymptotically negligible under \(P_n\).

---

### (1)(b) Bounded \(\chi^2\)-divergence implies contiguity

Assume

\[
\sup_n \chi^2(P_n\|Q_n)<\infty.
\]

Let

\[
L_n=\frac{dP_n}{dQ_n}.
\]

For any \(A_n\in \mathcal A_n\),

\[
P_n(A_n)=\int_{A_n} L_n\,dQ_n
=Q_n(A_n)+\int_{A_n}(L_n-1)\,dQ_n.
\]

By Cauchy-Schwarz,

\[
\left|\int_{A_n}(L_n-1)\,dQ_n\right|
\le \left(\int (L_n-1)^2\,dQ_n\right)^{1/2} Q_n(A_n)^{1/2}.
\]

Thus

\[
P_n(A_n)
\le Q_n(A_n)+\chi^2(P_n\|Q_n)^{1/2}Q_n(A_n)^{1/2}.
\]

If \(Q_n(A_n)\to 0\), and \(\sup_n\chi^2(P_n\|Q_n)<\infty\), then the right-hand side tends to \(0\). Hence

\[
P_n(A_n)\to 0.
\]

Therefore

\[
P_n\triangleleft Q_n.
\]

---

## (2)(a) Definition of LAN

For an i.i.d. parametric model \((P_\theta:\theta\in\Theta)\), write

\[
P_{\theta}^{(n)}=P_\theta^{\otimes n}.
\]

The model is called locally asymptotically normal, LAN, at \(\theta\in\Theta\), if there exist random vectors \(\Delta_{n,\theta}\in\mathbb R^k\) and a symmetric nonnegative definite matrix \(I_\theta\), usually the Fisher information matrix, such that under \(P_\theta^{(n)}\),

\[
\Delta_{n,\theta}\Rightarrow N(0,I_\theta),
\]

and for every fixed \(h\in\mathbb R^k\) such that \(\theta+h/\sqrt n\in\Theta\) for large \(n\),

\[
\log\frac{dP_{\theta+h/\sqrt n}^{(n)}}{dP_\theta^{(n)}}
=
h^\top \Delta_{n,\theta}
-\frac12 h^\top I_\theta h
+o_{P_\theta}(1).
\]

A stronger common formulation requires the remainder to be uniform over \(h\) in compact subsets of \(\mathbb R^k\).

---

### (2)(b) Verification under smoothness assumptions

Assume the model is dominated by a \(\sigma\)-finite measure \(\mu\), with densities \(p_\theta=dP_\theta/d\mu\). Let

\[
\ell_\theta(x)=\log p_\theta(x)
\]

be the log-density. Suppose that in a neighborhood \(U\) of \(\theta\):

1. \(p_\eta(x)>0\) for \(\eta\in U\), for \(\mu\)-a.e. \(x\);
2. \(\ell_\eta(x)\) is twice continuously differentiable in \(\eta\);
3. the score vector

   \[
   s_\theta(x)=\nabla_\theta \ell_\theta(x)
   \]

   satisfies

   \[
   \mathbb E_\theta \|s_\theta(X)\|^2<\infty;
   \]

4. the Hessian

   \[
   H_\eta(x)=\nabla_\theta^2 \ell_\eta(x)
   \]

   satisfies a local domination condition, for example,

   \[
   \sup_{\eta\in U}\|H_\eta(x)\|\le G(x),
   \qquad \mathbb E_\theta G(X)<\infty;
   \]

5. differentiation under the integral sign is valid, so that

   \[
   \mathbb E_\theta s_\theta(X)=0,
   \qquad 
   \mathbb E_\theta H_\theta(X)=-I_\theta,
   \]

   where

   \[
   I_\theta=\mathbb E_\theta[s_\theta(X)s_\theta(X)^\top].
   \]

Let \(X_1,\dots,X_n\overset{iid}{\sim}P_\theta\). Define the central sequence

\[
\Delta_{n,\theta}
=
\frac1{\sqrt n}\sum_{i=1}^n s_\theta(X_i).
\]

By the multivariate central limit theorem,

\[
\Delta_{n,\theta}\Rightarrow N(0,I_\theta).
\]

Now consider the log-likelihood ratio:

\[
\Lambda_n(h)
=
\log\frac{dP_{\theta+h/\sqrt n}^{(n)}}{dP_\theta^{(n)}}
=
\sum_{i=1}^n
\left[
\ell_{\theta+h/\sqrt n}(X_i)-\ell_\theta(X_i)
\right].
\]

Using Taylor expansion with integral remainder,

\[
\ell_{\theta+h/\sqrt n}(X_i)-\ell_\theta(X_i)
=
\frac1{\sqrt n}h^\top s_\theta(X_i)
+
\frac1n\int_0^1(1-t)
h^\top H_{\theta+t h/\sqrt n}(X_i)h\,dt.
\]

Summing over \(i\),

\[
\Lambda_n(h)
=
h^\top \Delta_{n,\theta}
+
\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n
\int_0^1(1-t)
h^\top H_{\theta+t h/\sqrt n}(X_i)h\,dt.
\]

By the law of large numbers and the domination condition,

\[
\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n
\int_0^1(1-t)
h^\top H_{\theta+t h/\sqrt n}(X_i)h\,dt
\to
\frac12 h^\top \mathbb E_\theta[H_\theta(X)]h
\]

in \(P_\theta\)-probability. Since

\[
\mathbb E_\theta[H_\theta(X)]=-I_\theta,
\]

we get

\[
\Lambda_n(h)
=
h^\top \Delta_{n,\theta}
-\frac12 h^\top I_\theta h
+o_{P_\theta}(1).
\]

Thus the model is LAN at \(\theta\).

---

## (3)(a) Neyman-Pearson lemma

Let \(P_0,P_1\) be two probability measures with densities \(p_0,p_1\) with respect to a common dominating measure. Consider testing

\[
H_0:P=P_0
\qquad\text{vs.}\qquad
H_1:P=P_1.
\]

Among all tests \(\varphi\) satisfying the level constraint

\[
\mathbb E_{P_0}\varphi\le \alpha,
\]

the most powerful test rejects \(H_0\) for large likelihood ratio

\[
\frac{p_1}{p_0}.
\]

More precisely, there exist \(c\ge 0\) and \(\gamma\in[0,1]\) such that

\[
\varphi^*
=
\mathbf 1\left\{\frac{p_1}{p_0}>c\right\}
+
\gamma \mathbf 1\left\{\frac{p_1}{p_0}=c\right\}
\]

has size \(\alpha\), and for every other test \(\varphi\) with \(\mathbb E_{P_0}\varphi\le\alpha\),

\[
\mathbb E_{P_1}\varphi
\le
\mathbb E_{P_1}\varphi^*.
\]

---

### (3)(b) Minimum sum of type I and type II errors in Gaussian location model

We observe

\[
X\sim N(\theta,I_p).
\]

We test

\[
H_0:\theta=\theta_0
\qquad\text{vs.}\qquad
H_1:\theta=\theta_1.
\]

Let

\[
P_0=N(\theta_0,I_p),
\qquad
P_1=N(\theta_1,I_p).
\]

Let \(\varphi(X)=1\) denote rejection of \(H_0\). The type I and type II errors are

\[
\alpha=P_0(\varphi=1),
\qquad
\beta=P_1(\varphi=0).
\]

We want to minimize

\[
\alpha+\beta.
\]

Equivalently,

\[
\alpha+\beta
=
P_0(\varphi=1)+P_1(\varphi=0)
=
1-\left(P_1(\varphi=1)-P_0(\varphi=1)\right).
\]

Thus minimizing \(\alpha+\beta\) is equivalent to maximizing

\[
P_1(\varphi=1)-P_0(\varphi=1).
\]

By the Neyman-Pearson lemma, the optimal test rejects \(H_0\) when

\[
\frac{dP_1}{dP_0}(X)>1.
\]

For Gaussian location models with common covariance \(I_p\),

\[
\log\frac{dP_1}{dP_0}(X)
=
(\theta_1-\theta_0)^\top X
-\frac12\left(\|\theta_1\|^2-\|\theta_0\|^2\right).
\]

Let

\[
v=\theta_1-\theta_0,
\qquad
\delta=\|v\|.
\]

The likelihood-ratio test rejects \(H_0\) when

\[
v^\top X
>
\frac12 v^\top(\theta_0+\theta_1).
\]

Under \(H_0\),

\[
v^\top X\sim N(v^\top\theta_0,\delta^2),
\]

and the rejection threshold is

\[
v^\top\theta_0+\frac{\delta^2}{2}.
\]

Hence

\[
\alpha
=
P_0\left(v^\top X>v^\top\theta_0+\frac{\delta^2}{2}\right)
=
1-\Phi\left(\frac{\delta}{2}\right)
=
\Phi\left(-\frac{\delta}{2}\right).
\]

Similarly, under \(H_1\),

\[
v^\top X\sim N(v^\top\theta_1,\delta^2),
\]

and the type II error is

\[
\beta
=
P_1\left(v^\top X\le v^\top\theta_0+\frac{\delta^2}{2}\right)
=
\Phi\left(-\frac{\delta}{2}\right).
\]

Therefore the minimum possible sum is

\[
\boxed{
\inf_\varphi(\alpha+\beta)
=
2\Phi\left(-\frac{\|\theta_1-\theta_0\|}{2}\right)
}.
\]

Equivalently,

\[
\inf_\varphi(\alpha+\beta)
=
1-\operatorname{TV}(P_0,P_1).
\]

---

# Part II

Let

\[
P_n=P^{\otimes n},
\qquad
Q_n=Q^{\otimes n}.
\]

Write

\[
Z=\frac{dP}{dQ},
\qquad
L_n=\frac{dP_n}{dQ_n}=\prod_{i=1}^n Z(X_i).
\]

Since \(D_{KL}(P\|Q)<\infty\), we have \(P\ll Q\), and

\[
D_{KL}(P\|Q)
=
\mathbb E_P\log Z.
\]

Let

\[
D=D_{KL}(P\|Q).
\]

For a test \(\Psi:\mathcal X^n\to\{0,1\}\), define the acceptance region of \(P\) by

\[
A_\Psi=\{\Psi=0\}.
\]

The constraint

\[
\mathbb E_{P_n}\Psi\le \alpha
\]

is equivalent to

\[
P_n(A_\Psi)\ge 1-\alpha.
\]

The quantity being minimized is

\[
\mathbb E_{Q_n}(1-\Psi)=Q_n(A_\Psi).
\]

Thus

\[
\inf_{\Psi:\mathbb E_{P_n}\Psi\le \alpha}
\mathbb E_{Q_n}(1-\Psi)
=
\inf_{A:\,P_n(A)\ge 1-\alpha} Q_n(A).
\]

---

## (1) Show \(R_\alpha\ge D_{KL}(P\|Q)\)

Fix \(\varepsilon>0\). Define the likelihood-ratio acceptance region

\[
A_{n,\varepsilon}
=
\left\{
\log L_n
\ge n(D-\varepsilon)
\right\}.
\]

Equivalently,

\[
A_{n,\varepsilon}
=
\left\{
\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n \log Z(X_i)
\ge D-\varepsilon
\right\}.
\]

Under \(P_n\), the variables \(\log Z(X_i)\) are i.i.d. with mean \(D\). By the strong law of large numbers,

\[
\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n \log Z(X_i)
\to D
\qquad P_n\text{-a.s.}
\]

Therefore

\[
P_n(A_{n,\varepsilon})\to 1.
\]

Since \(\alpha\in(0,1)\), for all sufficiently large \(n\),

\[
P_n(A_{n,\varepsilon})\ge 1-\alpha.
\]

Thus the test

\[
\Psi_{n,\varepsilon}=\mathbf 1_{A_{n,\varepsilon}^c}
\]

is feasible for all large \(n\).

Now bound its type II error under \(Q_n\). On \(A_{n,\varepsilon}\),

\[
L_n\ge e^{n(D-\varepsilon)}.
\]

Hence

\[
1_{A_{n,\varepsilon}}
\le
e^{-n(D-\varepsilon)} L_n 1_{A_{n,\varepsilon}}.
\]

Integrating with respect to \(Q_n\),

\[
Q_n(A_{n,\varepsilon})
\le
e^{-n(D-\varepsilon)}
\int L_n\,dQ_n
=
e^{-n(D-\varepsilon)}.
\]

Therefore, for all large \(n\),

\[
\inf_{\Psi:\mathbb E_{P_n}\Psi\le \alpha}
\mathbb E_{Q_n}(1-\Psi)
\le
e^{-n(D-\varepsilon)}.
\]

Taking logarithms,

\[
-\frac1n
\log
\inf_{\Psi:\mathbb E_{P_n}\Psi\le \alpha}
\mathbb E_{Q_n}(1-\Psi)
\ge
D-\varepsilon.
\]

Thus

\[
R_\alpha\ge D-\varepsilon.
\]

Since \(\varepsilon>0\) is arbitrary,

\[
\boxed{
R_\alpha\ge D_{KL}(P\|Q)
}.
\]

This is the achievability half of Chernoff-Stein and uses likelihood-ratio tests, which are the Neyman-Pearson optimal form for simple hypotheses.

---

## (2) Prove the inequality

We prove that for every event \(A\) and every \(x>0\),

\[
P(A)-xQ(A)
\le
P\left(\log\frac{dP}{dQ}>\log x\right).
\]

Let

\[
Z=\frac{dP}{dQ}.
\]

Then

\[
P(A)-xQ(A)
=
\int_A Z\,dQ-x\int_A dQ
=
\int_A (Z-x)\,dQ.
\]

Split according to \(\{Z>x\}\) and \(\{Z\le x\}\):

\[
\int_A(Z-x)\,dQ
=
\int_{A\cap\{Z>x\}}(Z-x)\,dQ
+
\int_{A\cap\{Z\le x\}}(Z-x)\,dQ.
\]

The second integral is nonpositive, so

\[
P(A)-xQ(A)
\le
\int_{A\cap\{Z>x\}}(Z-x)\,dQ.
\]

Since \(Z-x\le Z\),

\[
\int_{A\cap\{Z>x\}}(Z-x)\,dQ
\le
\int_{\{Z>x\}} Z\,dQ
=
P(Z>x).
\]

Finally,

\[
\{Z>x\}
=
\left\{
\log Z>\log x
\right\}.
\]

Therefore

\[
\boxed{
P(A)-xQ(A)
\le
P\left(\log\frac{dP}{dQ}>\log x\right)
}.
\]

---

## (3) Prove \(R_\alpha\le D_{KL}(P\|Q)\)

We now apply the inequality from part (2) to the product measures \(P_n,Q_n\).

Let

\[
L_n=\frac{dP_n}{dQ_n}.
\]

For any feasible test \(\Psi\), define

\[
A=\{\Psi=0\}.
\]

Then

\[
P_n(A)\ge 1-\alpha.
\]

By part (2), for any \(x>0\),

\[
P_n(A)-xQ_n(A)
\le
P_n(\log L_n>\log x).
\]

Choose

\[
x=e^{n(D+\varepsilon)}
\]

for some fixed \(\varepsilon>0\). Then

\[
P_n(A)-e^{n(D+\varepsilon)}Q_n(A)
\le
P_n(\log L_n>n(D+\varepsilon)).
\]

Rearranging,

\[
Q_n(A)
\ge
e^{-n(D+\varepsilon)}
\left[
P_n(A)
-
P_n(\log L_n>n(D+\varepsilon))
\right].
\]

Since \(P_n(A)\ge 1-\alpha\),

\[
Q_n(A)
\ge
e^{-n(D+\varepsilon)}
\left[
1-\alpha
-
P_n(\log L_n>n(D+\varepsilon))
\right].
\]

Now under \(P_n\),

\[
\frac1n\log L_n
=
\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n \log Z(X_i)
\to D
\]

almost surely, by the strong law of large numbers. Hence

\[
P_n(\log L_n>n(D+\varepsilon))\to 0.
\]

Therefore, for all sufficiently large \(n\),

\[
P_n(\log L_n>n(D+\varepsilon))
\le
\frac{1-\alpha}{2}.
\]

Thus every feasible test satisfies

\[
Q_n(A)
\ge
\frac{1-\alpha}{2}e^{-n(D+\varepsilon)}.
\]

Consequently,

\[
\inf_{\Psi:\mathbb E_{P_n}\Psi\le\alpha}
\mathbb E_{Q_n}(1-\Psi)
\ge
\frac{1-\alpha}{2}e^{-n(D+\varepsilon)}.
\]

Taking logarithms,

\[
-\frac1n
\log
\inf_{\Psi:\mathbb E_{P_n}\Psi\le\alpha}
\mathbb E_{Q_n}(1-\Psi)
\le
D+\varepsilon
-\frac1n\log\left(\frac{1-\alpha}{2}\right).
\]

Taking \(\liminf\) gives

\[
R_\alpha\le D+\varepsilon.
\]

Since \(\varepsilon>0\) is arbitrary,

\[
\boxed{
R_\alpha\le D_{KL}(P\|Q)
}.
\]

Combining with part (1),

\[
\boxed{
R_\alpha=D_{KL}(P\|Q)
}.
\]

This is the Chernoff-Stein lemma.

\Delta_{n,\theta}
=
\frac1{\sqrt n}\sum_{i=1}^n s_\theta(X_i).
\]

By the multivariate central limit theorem,

\[
\Delta_{n,\theta}\Rightarrow N(0,I_\theta).
\]

Now consider the log-likelihood ratio:

\[
\Lambda_n(h)
=
\log\frac{dP_{\theta+h/\sqrt n}^{(n)}}{dP_\theta^{(n)}}
=
\sum_{i=1}^n
\left[
\ell_{\theta+h/\sqrt n}(X_i)-\ell_\theta(X_i)
\right].
\]

Using Taylor expansion with integral remainder,

\[
\ell_{\theta+h/\sqrt n}(X_i)-\ell_\theta(X_i)
=
\frac1{\sqrt n}h^\top s_\theta(X_i)
+
\frac1n\int_0^1(1-t)
h^\top H_{\theta+t h/\sqrt n}(X_i)h\,dt.
\]

Summing over \(i\),

\[
\Lambda_n(h)
=
h^\top \Delta_{n,\theta}
+
\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n
\int_0^1(1-t)
h^\top H_{\theta+t h/\sqrt n}(X_i)h\,dt.
\]

By the law of large numbers and the domination condition,

\[
\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n
\int_0^1(1-t)
h^\top H_{\theta+t h/\sqrt n}(X_i)h\,dt
\to
\frac12 h^\top \mathbb E_\theta[H_\theta(X)]h
\]

in \(P_\theta\)-probability. Since

\[
\mathbb E_\theta[H_\theta(X)]=-I_\theta,
\]

we get

\[
\Lambda_n(h)
=
h^\top \Delta_{n,\theta}
-\frac12 h^\top I_\theta h
+o_{P_\theta}(1).
\]

Thus the model is LAN at \(\theta\).

---

## (3)(a) Neyman-Pearson lemma

Let \(P_0,P_1\) be two probability measures with densities \(p_0,p_1\) with respect to a common dominating measure. Consider testing

\[
H_0:P=P_0
\qquad\text{vs.}\qquad
H_1:P=P_1.
\]

Among all tests \(\varphi\) satisfying the level constraint

\[
\mathbb E_{P_0}\varphi\le \alpha,
\]

the most powerful test rejects \(H_0\) for large likelihood ratio

\[
\frac{p_1}{p_0}.
\]

More precisely, there exist \(c\ge 0\) and \(\gamma\in[0,1]\) such that

\[
\varphi^*
=
\mathbf 1\left\{\frac{p_1}{p_0}>c\right\}
+
\gamma \mathbf 1\left\{\frac{p_1}{p_0}=c\right\}
\]

has size \(\alpha\), and for every other test \(\varphi\) with \(\mathbb E_{P_0}\varphi\le\alpha\),

\[
\mathbb E_{P_1}\varphi
\le
\mathbb E_{P_1}\varphi^*.
\]

---

### (3)(b) Minimum sum of type I and type II errors in Gaussian location model

We observe

\[
X\sim N(\theta,I_p).
\]

We test

\[
H_0:\theta=\theta_0
\qquad\text{vs.}\qquad
H_1:\theta=\theta_1.
\]

Let

\[
P_0=N(\theta_0,I_p),
\qquad
P_1=N(\theta_1,I_p).
\]

Let \(\varphi(X)=1\) denote rejection of \(H_0\). The type I and type II errors are

\[
\alpha=P_0(\varphi=1),
\qquad
\beta=P_1(\varphi=0).
\]

We want to minimize

\[
\alpha+\beta.
\]

Equivalently,

\[
\alpha+\beta
=
P_0(\varphi=1)+P_1(\varphi=0)
=
1-\left(P_1(\varphi=1)-P_0(\varphi=1)\right).
\]

Thus minimizing \(\alpha+\beta\) is equivalent to maximizing

\[
P_1(\varphi=1)-P_0(\varphi=1).
\]

By the Neyman-Pearson lemma, the optimal test rejects \(H_0\) when

\[
\frac{dP_1}{dP_0}(X)>1.
\]

For Gaussian location models with common covariance \(I_p\),

\[
\log\frac{dP_1}{dP_0}(X)
=
(\theta_1-\theta_0)^\top X
-\frac12\left(\|\theta_1\|^2-\|\theta_0\|^2\right).
\]

Let

\[
v=\theta_1-\theta_0,
\qquad
\delta=\|v\|.
\]

The likelihood-ratio test rejects \(H_0\) when

\[
v^\top X
>
\frac12 v^\top(\theta_0+\theta_1).
\]

Under \(H_0\),

\[
v^\top X\sim N(v^\top\theta_0,\delta^2),
\]

and the rejection threshold is

\[
v^\top\theta_0+\frac{\delta^2}{2}.
\]

Hence

\[
\alpha
=
P_0\left(v^\top X>v^\top\theta_0+\frac{\delta^2}{2}\right)
=
1-\Phi\left(\frac{\delta}{2}\right)
=
\Phi\left(-\frac{\delta}{2}\right).
\]

Similarly, under \(H_1\),

\[
v^\top X\sim N(v^\top\theta_1,\delta^2),
\]

and the type II error is

\[
\beta
=
P_1\left(v^\top X\le v^\top\theta_0+\frac{\delta^2}{2}\right)
=
\Phi\left(-\frac{\delta}{2}\right).
\]

Therefore the minimum possible sum is

\[
\boxed{
\inf_\varphi(\alpha+\beta)
=
2\Phi\left(-\frac{\|\theta_1-\theta_0\|}{2}\right)
}.
\]

Equivalently,

\[
\inf_\varphi(\alpha+\beta)
=
1-\operatorname{TV}(P_0,P_1).
\]

---

# Part II

Let

\[
P_n=P^{\otimes n},
\qquad
Q_n=Q^{\otimes n}.
\]

Write

\[
Z=\frac{dP}{dQ},
\qquad
L_n=\frac{dP_n}{dQ_n}=\prod_{i=1}^n Z(X_i).
\]

Since \(D_{KL}(P\|Q)<\infty\), we have \(P\ll Q\), and

\[
D_{KL}(P\|Q)
=
\mathbb E_P\log Z.
\]

Let

\[
D=D_{KL}(P\|Q).
\]

For a test \(\Psi:\mathcal X^n\to\{0,1\}\), define the acceptance region of \(P\) by

\[
A_\Psi=\{\Psi=0\}.
\]

The constraint

\[
\mathbb E_{P_n}\Psi\le \alpha
\]

is equivalent to

\[
P_n(A_\Psi)\ge 1-\alpha.
\]

The quantity being minimized is

\[
\mathbb E_{Q_n}(1-\Psi)=Q_n(A_\Psi).
\]

Thus

\[
\inf_{\Psi:\mathbb E_{P_n}\Psi\le \alpha}
\mathbb E_{Q_n}(1-\Psi)
=
\inf_{A:\,P_n(A)\ge 1-\alpha} Q_n(A).
\]

---

## (1) Show \(R_\alpha\ge D_{KL}(P\|Q)\)

Fix \(\varepsilon>0\). Define the likelihood-ratio acceptance region

\[
A_{n,\varepsilon}
=
\left\{
\log L_n
\ge n(D-\varepsilon)
\right\}.
\]

Equivalently,

\[
A_{n,\varepsilon}
=
\left\{
\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n \log Z(X_i)
\ge D-\varepsilon
\right\}.
\]

Under \(P_n\), the variables \(\log Z(X_i)\) are i.i.d. with mean \(D\). By the strong law of large numbers,

\[
\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n \log Z(X_i)
\to D
\qquad P_n\text{-a.s.}
\]

Therefore

\[
P_n(A_{n,\varepsilon})\to 1.
\]

Since \(\alpha\in(0,1)\), for all sufficiently large \(n\),

\[
P_n(A_{n,\varepsilon})\ge 1-\alpha.
\]

Thus the test

\[
\Psi_{n,\varepsilon}=\mathbf 1_{A_{n,\varepsilon}^c}
\]

is feasible for all large \(n\).

Now bound its type II error under \(Q_n\). On \(A_{n,\varepsilon}\),

\[
L_n\ge e^{n(D-\varepsilon)}.
\]

Hence

\[
1_{A_{n,\varepsilon}}
\le
e^{-n(D-\varepsilon)} L_n 1_{A_{n,\varepsilon}}.
\]

Integrating with respect to \(Q_n\),

\[
Q_n(A_{n,\varepsilon})
\le
e^{-n(D-\varepsilon)}
\int L_n\,dQ_n
=
e^{-n(D-\varepsilon)}.
\]

Therefore, for all large \(n\),

\[
\inf_{\Psi:\mathbb E_{P_n}\Psi\le \alpha}
\mathbb E_{Q_n}(1-\Psi)
\le
e^{-n(D-\varepsilon)}.
\]

Taking logarithms,

\[
-\frac1n
\log
\inf_{\Psi:\mathbb E_{P_n}\Psi\le \alpha}
\mathbb E_{Q_n}(1-\Psi)
\ge
D-\varepsilon.
\]

Thus

\[
R_\alpha\ge D-\varepsilon.
\]

Since \(\varepsilon>0\) is arbitrary,

\[
\boxed{
R_\alpha\ge D_{KL}(P\|Q)
}.
\]

This is the achievability half of Chernoff-Stein and uses likelihood-ratio tests, which are the Neyman-Pearson optimal form for simple hypotheses.

---

## (2) Prove the inequality

We prove that for every event \(A\) and every \(x>0\),

\[
P(A)-xQ(A)
\le
P\left(\log\frac{dP}{dQ}>\log x\right).
\]

Let

\[
Z=\frac{dP}{dQ}.
\]

Then

\[
P(A)-xQ(A)
=
\int_A Z\,dQ-x\int_A dQ
=
\int_A (Z-x)\,dQ.
\]

Split according to \(\{Z>x\}\) and \(\{Z\le x\}\):

\[
\int_A(Z-x)\,dQ
=
\int_{A\cap\{Z>x\}}(Z-x)\,dQ
+
\int_{A\cap\{Z\le x\}}(Z-x)\,dQ.
\]

The second integral is nonpositive, so

\[
P(A)-xQ(A)
\le
\int_{A\cap\{Z>x\}}(Z-x)\,dQ.
\]

Since \(Z-x\le Z\),

\[
\int_{A\cap\{Z>x\}}(Z-x)\,dQ
\le
\int_{\{Z>x\}} Z\,dQ
=
P(Z>x).
\]

Finally,

\[
\{Z>x\}
=
\left\{
\log Z>\log x
\right\}.
\]

Therefore

\[
\boxed{
P(A)-xQ(A)
\le
P\left(\log\frac{dP}{dQ}>\log x\right)
}.
\]

---

## (3) Prove \(R_\alpha\le D_{KL}(P\|Q)\)

We now apply the inequality from part (2) to the product measures \(P_n,Q_n\).

Let

\[
L_n=\frac{dP_n}{dQ_n}.
\]

For any feasible test \(\Psi\), define

\[
A=\{\Psi=0\}.
\]

Then

\[
P_n(A)\ge 1-\alpha.
\]

By part (2), for any \(x>0\),

\[
P_n(A)-xQ_n(A)
\le
P_n(\log L_n>\log x).
\]

Choose

\[
x=e^{n(D+\varepsilon)}
\]

for some fixed \(\varepsilon>0\). Then

\[
P_n(A)-e^{n(D+\varepsilon)}Q_n(A)
\le
P_n(\log L_n>n(D+\varepsilon)).
\]

Rearranging,

\[
Q_n(A)
\ge
e^{-n(D+\varepsilon)}
\left[
P_n(A)
-
P_n(\log L_n>n(D+\varepsilon))
\right].
\]

Since \(P_n(A)\ge 1-\alpha\),

\[
Q_n(A)
\ge
e^{-n(D+\varepsilon)}
\left[
1-\alpha
-
P_n(\log L_n>n(D+\varepsilon))
\right].
\]

Now under \(P_n\),

\[
\frac1n\log L_n
=
\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n \log Z(X_i)
\to D
\]

almost surely, by the strong law of large numbers. Hence

\[
P_n(\log L_n>n(D+\varepsilon))\to 0.
\]

Therefore, for all sufficiently large \(n\),

\[
P_n(\log L_n>n(D+\varepsilon))
\le
\frac{1-\alpha}{2}.
\]

Thus every feasible test satisfies

\[
Q_n(A)
\ge
\frac{1-\alpha}{2}e^{-n(D+\varepsilon)}.
\]

Consequently,

\[
\inf_{\Psi:\mathbb E_{P_n}\Psi\le\alpha}
\mathbb E_{Q_n}(1-\Psi)
\ge
\frac{1-\alpha}{2}e^{-n(D+\varepsilon)}.
\]

Taking logarithms,

\[
-\frac1n
\log
\inf_{\Psi:\mathbb E_{P_n}\Psi\le\alpha}
\mathbb E_{Q_n}(1-\Psi)
\le
D+\varepsilon
-\frac1n\log\left(\frac{1-\alpha}{2}\right).
\]

Taking \(\liminf\) gives

\[
R_\alpha\le D+\varepsilon.
\]

Since \(\varepsilon>0\) is arbitrary,

\[
\boxed{
R_\alpha\le D_{KL}(P\|Q)
}.
\]

Combining with part (1),

\[
\boxed{
R_\alpha=D_{KL}(P\|Q)
}.
\]

This is the Chernoff-Stein lemma.
