and let

\[
W=\sum_{j=1}^n 
\begin{pmatrix}X_j\\Y_j\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}X_j&Y_j\end{pmatrix}
=
\begin{pmatrix}
A&C\\
C&B
\end{pmatrix}.
\]

Assume \(n\ge 2\) when discussing the unrestricted covariance MLE, so that \(W\) is positive definite with probability one.

---

## Part I

### (1) Complete sufficient statistic

For one observation, write

\[
\Sigma=
\begin{pmatrix}
\sigma_1^2 & \rho\sigma_1\sigma_2\\
\rho\sigma_1\sigma_2 & \sigma_2^2
\end{pmatrix}.
\]

The joint likelihood for the full sample is

\[
L(\theta)
=(2\pi)^{-n}|\Sigma|^{-n/2}
\exp\left\{-\frac12 \operatorname{tr}(\Sigma^{-1}W)\right\}.
\]

Thus the likelihood depends on the data only through

\[
T=(A,B,C).
\]

By the Neyman–Fisher factorization theorem, \(T\) is sufficient.

Moreover, the family is a full exponential family. Indeed,

\[
-\frac12\operatorname{tr}(\Sigma^{-1}W)
=
\eta_1 A+\eta_2 B+\eta_3 C,
\]

where

\[
\eta_1=-\frac{1}{2(1-\rho^2)\sigma_1^2},\qquad
\eta_2=-\frac{1}{2(1-\rho^2)\sigma_2^2},\qquad
\eta_3=\frac{\rho}{(1-\rho^2)\sigma_1\sigma_2}.
\]

The natural parameter space is

\[
\left\{(\eta_1,\eta_2,\eta_3):\eta_1<0,\ \eta_2<0,\ \eta_3^2<4\eta_1\eta_2\right\},
\]

which is open in \(\mathbb R^3\). Therefore, by the completeness theorem for full regular exponential families with open natural parameter space, \(T=(A,B,C)\) is complete.

Hence a complete sufficient statistic is

\[
\boxed{T=\left(\sum_{j=1}^n X_j^2,\ \sum_{j=1}^n Y_j^2,\ \sum_{j=1}^n X_jY_j\right).}
\]

---

### (2) MLE of \(\theta\)

The log-likelihood is

\[
\ell(\Sigma)=\text{const}-\frac n2\log|\Sigma|-\frac12\operatorname{tr}(\Sigma^{-1}W).
\]

Let \(K=\Sigma^{-1}\). Then

\[
\ell(K)=\text{const}+\frac n2\log|K|-\frac12\operatorname{tr}(KW).
\]

Differentiate with respect to \(K\):

\[
\frac{\partial \ell}{\partial K}
=
\frac n2 K^{-1}-\frac12 W.
\]

Setting this equal to \(0\) gives

\[
K^{-1}=\frac{W}{n}.
\]

Thus

\[
\widehat\Sigma=\frac{W}{n}
=
\begin{pmatrix}
A/n & C/n\\
C/n & B/n
\end{pmatrix}.
\]

Therefore

\[
\boxed{\widehat{\sigma}_1^2=\frac1n\sum_{j=1}^n X_j^2,}
\]

\[
\boxed{\widehat{\sigma}_2^2=\frac1n\sum_{j=1}^n Y_j^2,}
\]

and

\[
\boxed{
\widehat\rho
=
\frac{C/n}{\sqrt{(A/n)(B/n)}}
=
\frac{\sum_{j=1}^n X_jY_j}
{\sqrt{\sum_{j=1}^n X_j^2\sum_{j=1}^n Y_j^2}}.
}
\]

---

### (3) Mutual independence when \(\rho=0\)

When \(\rho=0\), the vectors

\[
X=(X_1,\dots,X_n),\qquad Y=(Y_1,\dots,Y_n)
\]

are independent, with

\[
X\sim N(0,\sigma_1^2 I_n),\qquad Y\sim N(0,\sigma_2^2 I_n).
\]

Write their polar decompositions as

\[
X=R_X U,\qquad Y=R_Y V,
\]

where

\[
R_X=\|X\|,\qquad R_Y=\|Y\|,
\]

and \(U,V\) are independent and uniform on the unit sphere \(S^{n-1}\). For multivariate normal vectors, the radius and direction are independent.

Now

\[
\widehat{\sigma}_1^2=\frac{R_X^2}{n},\qquad
\widehat{\sigma}_2^2=\frac{R_Y^2}{n},
\]

while

\[
\widehat\rho
=
\frac{X^\top Y}{\|X\|\|Y\|}
=
U^\top V.
\]

Thus \(\widehat{\sigma}_1^2\) depends only on \(R_X\), \(\widehat{\sigma}_2^2\) depends only on \(R_Y\), and \(\widehat\rho\) depends only on the directions \(U,V\). Since radii and directions are mutually independent,

\[
\boxed{\widehat{\sigma}_1^2,\ \widehat{\sigma}_2^2,\ \widehat\rho\ \text{are mutually independent when }\rho=0.}
\]

---

### (4) LRT for \(H_0:\rho=0\) versus \(H_1:\rho\ne0\)

Under the full model, the maximized likelihood occurs at

\[
\widehat\Sigma=\frac{W}{n},
\]

with determinant

\[
|\widehat\Sigma|
=
\frac{AB-C^2}{n^2}.
\]

Under \(H_0:\rho=0\), the covariance matrix is diagonal:

\[
\Sigma_0=
\begin{pmatrix}
\sigma_1^2&0\\
0&\sigma_2^2
\end{pmatrix}.
\]

The restricted MLEs are

\[
\widehat{\sigma}_{1,0}^2=\frac An,\qquad
\widehat{\sigma}_{2,0}^2=\frac Bn,
\]

so

\[
|\widehat\Sigma_0|=\frac{AB}{n^2}.
\]

The likelihood-ratio statistic is therefore

\[
\Lambda
=
\frac{\sup_{H_0}L}{\sup_{\Theta}L}
=
\left(\frac{AB-C^2}{AB}\right)^{n/2}
=
\left(1-\frac{C^2}{AB}\right)^{n/2}
=
(1-\widehat\rho^2)^{n/2}.
\]

Since \(\Lambda\) is decreasing in \(\widehat\rho^2\), the LRT rejects \(H_0\) for small \(\Lambda\), equivalently for large \(\widehat\rho^2\). Thus

\[
\boxed{\text{Reject }H_0\text{ when }\widehat\rho^2\text{ is sufficiently large.}}
\]

---

# Part II: \(\sigma_1^2=\sigma_2^2=1\), only \(\rho\) unknown

Now

\[
\Sigma(\rho)=
\begin{pmatrix}
1&\rho\\
\rho&1
\end{pmatrix},
\qquad -1<\rho<1.
\]

For a single observation, write

\[
D=1-\rho^2,\qquad q=x^2+y^2,\qquad z=xy.
\]

The log-density is

\[
\ell(\rho;x,y)
=
-\log(2\pi)-\frac12\log(1-\rho^2)
-\frac{x^2+y^2-2\rho xy}{2(1-\rho^2)}.
\]

---

### (5) Score function for one pair

Differentiate \(\ell(\rho;x,y)\) with respect to \(\rho\). The score is

\[
S(\rho;x,y)
=
\frac{\partial}{\partial \rho}\ell(\rho;x,y).
\]

A straightforward calculation gives

\[
\boxed{
S(\rho;x,y)
=
\frac{\rho}{1-\rho^2}
+
\frac{(1+\rho^2)xy-\rho(x^2+y^2)}
{(1-\rho^2)^2}.
}
\]

Equivalently,

\[
S(\rho;x,y)
=
\frac{
\rho(1-\rho^2)+(1+\rho^2)xy-\rho(x^2+y^2)
}
{(1-\rho^2)^2}.
\]

---

### (6) Expected Fisher information for one pair

Use the standard Fisher information formula for a multivariate normal with covariance \(\Sigma(\rho)\):

\[
I_1(\rho)
=
\frac12 \operatorname{tr}
\left[
\Sigma(\rho)^{-1}\Sigma'(\rho)
\Sigma(\rho)^{-1}\Sigma'(\rho)
\right].
\]

Here

\[
\Sigma'(\rho)=
\begin{pmatrix}
0&1\\
1&0
\end{pmatrix},
\]

and

\[
\Sigma(\rho)^{-1}
=
\frac1{1-\rho^2}
\begin{pmatrix}
1&-\rho\\
-\rho&1
\end{pmatrix}.
\]

Thus

\[
\Sigma^{-1}\Sigma'
=
\frac1{1-\rho^2}
\begin{pmatrix}
-\rho&1\\
1&-\rho
\end{pmatrix}.
\]

Therefore

\[
\operatorname{tr}\left[(\Sigma^{-1}\Sigma')^2\right]
=
\frac{2(1+\rho^2)}{(1-\rho^2)^2}.
\]

Hence

\[
\boxed{
I_1(\rho)=\frac{1+\rho^2}{(1-\rho^2)^2}.
}
\]

---

### (7) Cubic equation for the MLE

For the full sample, define

\[
Q=\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i^2+Y_i^2),\qquad C=\sum_{i=1}^n X_iY_i.
\]

The log-likelihood is

\[
\ell_n(\rho)
=
-\frac n2\log(1-\rho^2)
-\frac{Q-2\rho C}{2(1-\rho^2)}
+\text{const}.
\]

The score is

\[
U_n(\rho)
=
\ell_n'(\rho)
=
\frac{n\rho}{1-\rho^2}
+
\frac{(1+\rho^2)C-\rho Q}{(1-\rho^2)^2}.
\]

Thus

\[
U_n(\rho)
=
\frac{
n\rho(1-\rho^2)+(1+\rho^2)C-\rho Q
}
{(1-\rho^2)^2}.
\]

Setting the numerator equal to zero gives

\[
n\rho(1-\rho^2)+(1+\rho^2)C-\rho Q=0.
\]

Equivalently,

\[
-n\rho^3+C\rho^2+(n-Q)\rho+C=0.
\]

Multiplying by \(-1\), the MLE solves

\[
\boxed{
h(\rho)=n\rho^3-C\rho^2+(Q-n)\rho-C=0.
}
\]

The MLE is the root in \((-1,1)\) that maximizes the likelihood.

---

### (8) Newton–Raphson iteration

Using the cubic likelihood equation \(h(\rho)=0\), where

\[
h(\rho)=n\rho^3-C\rho^2+(Q-n)\rho-C,
\]

we have

\[
h'(\rho)=3n\rho^2-2C\rho+(Q-n).
\]

Therefore the Newton–Raphson iteration is

\[
\boxed{
\rho^{(m+1)}
=
\rho^{(m)}
-
\frac{
n(\rho^{(m)})^3-C(\rho^{(m)})^2+(Q-n)\rho^{(m)}-C
}{
3n(\rho^{(m)})^2-2C\rho^{(m)}+(Q-n)
}.
}
\]

---

### (9) Fisher scoring iteration

Fisher scoring uses

\[
\rho^{(m+1)}
=
\rho^{(m)}
+
\frac{U_n(\rho^{(m)})}{nI_1(\rho^{(m)})}.
\]

Since

\[
I_1(\rho)=\frac{1+\rho^2}{(1-\rho^2)^2},
\]

we get

\[
nI_1(\rho)=\frac{n(1+\rho^2)}{(1-\rho^2)^2}.
\]

Thus

\[
\rho^{(m+1)}
=
\rho^{(m)}
+
\frac{
n\rho^{(m)}(1-(\rho^{(m)})^2)
+
(1+(\rho^{(m)})^2)C
-
\rho^{(m)}Q
}
{n(1+(\rho^{(m)})^2)}.
\]

Equivalently, since \(U_n(\rho)=-h(\rho)/(1-\rho^2)^2\),

\[
\boxed{
\rho^{(m+1)}
=
\rho^{(m)}
-
\frac{h(\rho^{(m)})}
{n(1+(\rho^{(m)})^2)}.
}
\]

---

By the standard asymptotic normality theorem for MLEs,

\[
\sqrt n(\widehat\rho_{\mathrm{MLE}}-\rho)
\overset{d}{\longrightarrow}
N\left(0,\ I_1(\rho)^{-1}\right).
\]

Since

\[
I_1(\rho)=\frac{1+\rho^2}{(1-\rho^2)^2},
\]

we have

\[
I_1(\rho)^{-1}
=
\frac{(1-\rho^2)^2}{1+\rho^2}.
\]

Therefore

\[
\boxed{
\sqrt n(\widehat\rho_{\mathrm{MLE}}-\rho)
\overset{d}{\longrightarrow}
N\left(
0,\frac{(1-\rho^2)^2}{1+\rho^2}
\right).
}
\]

Equivalently,

\[
\widehat\rho_{\mathrm{MLE}}
\approx
N\left(
\rho,\ \frac{(1-\rho^2)^2}{n(1+\rho^2)}
\right).
\]

A plug-in large-sample \(1-\alpha\) confidence interval is

\[
\boxed{
\widehat\rho_{\mathrm{MLE}}
\pm
z_{1-\alpha/2}
\frac{1-\widehat\rho_{\mathrm{MLE}}^2}
{\sqrt{n(1+\widehat\rho_{\mathrm{MLE}}^2)}}.
}
\]

One may truncate the interval to \((-1,1)\) if desired.

---

### (11) The estimator \(\widehat\rho_2=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n X_iY_i\)

Because \(\sigma_1^2=\sigma_2^2=1\),

\[
\mathbb E_\rho[X_iY_i]=\operatorname{Cov}(X_i,Y_i)=\rho.
\]

Therefore

\[
\boxed{\mathbb E_\rho[\widehat\rho_2]=\rho.}
\]

So \(\widehat\rho_2\) is exactly unbiased, a desirable finite-sample property that the MLE does not generally have.

Now compute its asymptotic variance. Write

\[
Y=\rho X+\sqrt{1-\rho^2}\,Z,
\]

where \(X,Z\sim N(0,1)\) are independent. Then

\[
XY=\rho X^2+\sqrt{1-\rho^2}\,XZ.
\]

Hence

\[
\mathbb E[XY]=\rho,
\]

and

\[
\mathbb E[X^2Y^2]
=
\rho^2\mathbb E[X^4]+(1-\rho^2)\mathbb E[X^2]\mathbb E[Z^2].
\]

Using \(\mathbb E[X^4]=3\),

\[
\mathbb E[X^2Y^2]
=
3\rho^2+(1-\rho^2)
=
1+2\rho^2.
\]

Therefore

\[
\operatorname{Var}(XY)
=
\mathbb E[X^2Y^2]-(\mathbb E[XY])^2
=
1+2\rho^2-\rho^2
=
1+\rho^2.
\]

By the central limit theorem,

\[
\boxed{
\sqrt n(\widehat\rho_2-\rho)
\overset{d}{\longrightarrow}
N(0,1+\rho^2).
}
\]

Compare this with the MLE:

\[
\sqrt n(\widehat\rho_{\mathrm{MLE}}-\rho)
\overset{d}{\longrightarrow}
N\left(0,\frac{(1-\rho^2)^2}{1+\rho^2}\right).
\]

Since

\[
\frac{(1-\rho^2)^2}{1+\rho^2}\le 1+\rho^2,
\]

with equality only at \(\rho=0\), the MLE has smaller asymptotic variance except at \(\rho=0\). Thus, for large samples, I would prefer the MLE because it is asymptotically efficient, even though \(\widehat\rho_2\) is unbiased and simpler. Also, \(\widehat\rho_2\) can fall outside the parameter space \((-1,1)\) in finite samples.

\]

\[
\boxed{\widehat{\sigma}_2^2=\frac1n\sum_{j=1}^n Y_j^2,}
\]

and

\[
\boxed{
\widehat\rho
=
\frac{C/n}{\sqrt{(A/n)(B/n)}}
=
\frac{\sum_{j=1}^n X_jY_j}
{\sqrt{\sum_{j=1}^n X_j^2\sum_{j=1}^n Y_j^2}}.
}
\]

---

### (3) Mutual independence when \(\rho=0\)

When \(\rho=0\), the vectors

\[
X=(X_1,\dots,X_n),\qquad Y=(Y_1,\dots,Y_n)
\]

are independent, with

\[
X\sim N(0,\sigma_1^2 I_n),\qquad Y\sim N(0,\sigma_2^2 I_n).
\]

Write their polar decompositions as

\[
X=R_X U,\qquad Y=R_Y V,
\]

where

\[
R_X=\|X\|,\qquad R_Y=\|Y\|,
\]

and \(U,V\) are independent and uniform on the unit sphere \(S^{n-1}\). For multivariate normal vectors, the radius and direction are independent.

Now

\[
\widehat{\sigma}_1^2=\frac{R_X^2}{n},\qquad
\widehat{\sigma}_2^2=\frac{R_Y^2}{n},
\]

while

\[
\widehat\rho
=
\frac{X^\top Y}{\|X\|\|Y\|}
=
U^\top V.
\]

Thus \(\widehat{\sigma}_1^2\) depends only on \(R_X\), \(\widehat{\sigma}_2^2\) depends only on \(R_Y\), and \(\widehat\rho\) depends only on the directions \(U,V\). Since radii and directions are mutually independent,

\[
\boxed{\widehat{\sigma}_1^2,\ \widehat{\sigma}_2^2,\ \widehat\rho\ \text{are mutually independent when }\rho=0.}
\]

---

### (4) LRT for \(H_0:\rho=0\) versus \(H_1:\rho\ne0\)

Under the full model, the maximized likelihood occurs at

\[
\widehat\Sigma=\frac{W}{n},
\]

with determinant

\[
|\widehat\Sigma|
=
\frac{AB-C^2}{n^2}.
\]

Under \(H_0:\rho=0\), the covariance matrix is diagonal:

\[
\Sigma_0=
\begin{pmatrix}
\sigma_1^2&0\\
0&\sigma_2^2
\end{pmatrix}.
\]

The restricted MLEs are

\[
\widehat{\sigma}_{1,0}^2=\frac An,\qquad
\widehat{\sigma}_{2,0}^2=\frac Bn,
\]

so

\[
|\widehat\Sigma_0|=\frac{AB}{n^2}.
\]

The likelihood-ratio statistic is therefore

\[
\Lambda
=
\frac{\sup_{H_0}L}{\sup_{\Theta}L}
=
\left(\frac{AB-C^2}{AB}\right)^{n/2}
=
\left(1-\frac{C^2}{AB}\right)^{n/2}
=
(1-\widehat\rho^2)^{n/2}.
\]

Since \(\Lambda\) is decreasing in \(\widehat\rho^2\), the LRT rejects \(H_0\) for small \(\Lambda\), equivalently for large \(\widehat\rho^2\). Thus

\[
\boxed{\text{Reject }H_0\text{ when }\widehat\rho^2\text{ is sufficiently large.}}
\]

---

# Part II: \(\sigma_1^2=\sigma_2^2=1\), only \(\rho\) unknown

Now

\[
\Sigma(\rho)=
\begin{pmatrix}
1&\rho\\
\rho&1
\end{pmatrix},
\qquad -1<\rho<1.
\]

For a single observation, write

\[
D=1-\rho^2,\qquad q=x^2+y^2,\qquad z=xy.
\]

The log-density is

\[
\ell(\rho;x,y)
=
-\log(2\pi)-\frac12\log(1-\rho^2)
-\frac{x^2+y^2-2\rho xy}{2(1-\rho^2)}.
\]

---

### (5) Score function for one pair

Differentiate \(\ell(\rho;x,y)\) with respect to \(\rho\). The score is

\[
S(\rho;x,y)
=
\frac{\partial}{\partial \rho}\ell(\rho;x,y).
\]

A straightforward calculation gives

\[
\boxed{
S(\rho;x,y)
=
\frac{\rho}{1-\rho^2}
+
\frac{(1+\rho^2)xy-\rho(x^2+y^2)}
{(1-\rho^2)^2}.
}
\]

Equivalently,

\[
S(\rho;x,y)
=
\frac{
\rho(1-\rho^2)+(1+\rho^2)xy-\rho(x^2+y^2)
}
{(1-\rho^2)^2}.
\]

---

### (6) Expected Fisher information for one pair

Use the standard Fisher information formula for a multivariate normal with covariance \(\Sigma(\rho)\):

\[
I_1(\rho)
=
\frac12 \operatorname{tr}
\left[
\Sigma(\rho)^{-1}\Sigma'(\rho)
\Sigma(\rho)^{-1}\Sigma'(\rho)
\right].
\]

Here

\[
\Sigma'(\rho)=
\begin{pmatrix}
0&1\\
1&0
\end{pmatrix},
\]

and

\[
\Sigma(\rho)^{-1}
=
\frac1{1-\rho^2}
\begin{pmatrix}
1&-\rho\\
-\rho&1
\end{pmatrix}.
\]

Thus

\[
\Sigma^{-1}\Sigma'
=
\frac1{1-\rho^2}
\begin{pmatrix}
-\rho&1\\
1&-\rho
\end{pmatrix}.
\]

Therefore

\[
\operatorname{tr}\left[(\Sigma^{-1}\Sigma')^2\right]
=
\frac{2(1+\rho^2)}{(1-\rho^2)^2}.
\]

Hence

\[
\boxed{
I_1(\rho)=\frac{1+\rho^2}{(1-\rho^2)^2}.
}
\]

---

### (7) Cubic equation for the MLE

For the full sample, define

\[
Q=\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i^2+Y_i^2),\qquad C=\sum_{i=1}^n X_iY_i.
\]

The log-likelihood is

\[
\ell_n(\rho)
=
-\frac n2\log(1-\rho^2)
-\frac{Q-2\rho C}{2(1-\rho^2)}
+\text{const}.
\]

The score is

\[
U_n(\rho)
=
\ell_n'(\rho)
=
\frac{n\rho}{1-\rho^2}
+
\frac{(1+\rho^2)C-\rho Q}{(1-\rho^2)^2}.
\]

Thus

\[
U_n(\rho)
=
\frac{
n\rho(1-\rho^2)+(1+\rho^2)C-\rho Q
}
{(1-\rho^2)^2}.
\]

Setting the numerator equal to zero gives

\[
n\rho(1-\rho^2)+(1+\rho^2)C-\rho Q=0.
\]

Equivalently,

\[
-n\rho^3+C\rho^2+(n-Q)\rho+C=0.
\]

Multiplying by \(-1\), the MLE solves

\[
\boxed{
h(\rho)=n\rho^3-C\rho^2+(Q-n)\rho-C=0.
}
\]

The MLE is the root in \((-1,1)\) that maximizes the likelihood.

---

### (8) Newton–Raphson iteration

Using the cubic likelihood equation \(h(\rho)=0\), where

\[
h(\rho)=n\rho^3-C\rho^2+(Q-n)\rho-C,
\]

we have

\[
h'(\rho)=3n\rho^2-2C\rho+(Q-n).
\]

Therefore the Newton–Raphson iteration is

\[
\boxed{
\rho^{(m+1)}
=
\rho^{(m)}
-
\frac{
n(\rho^{(m)})^3-C(\rho^{(m)})^2+(Q-n)\rho^{(m)}-C
}{
3n(\rho^{(m)})^2-2C\rho^{(m)}+(Q-n)
}.
}
\]

---

### (9) Fisher scoring iteration

Fisher scoring uses

\[
\rho^{(m+1)}
=
\rho^{(m)}
+
\frac{U_n(\rho^{(m)})}{nI_1(\rho^{(m)})}.
\]

Since

\[
I_1(\rho)=\frac{1+\rho^2}{(1-\rho^2)^2},
\]

we get

\[
nI_1(\rho)=\frac{n(1+\rho^2)}{(1-\rho^2)^2}.
\]

Thus

\[
\rho^{(m+1)}
=
\rho^{(m)}
+
\frac{
n\rho^{(m)}(1-(\rho^{(m)})^2)
+
(1+(\rho^{(m)})^2)C
-
\rho^{(m)}Q
}
{n(1+(\rho^{(m)})^2)}.
\]

Equivalently, since \(U_n(\rho)=-h(\rho)/(1-\rho^2)^2\),

\[
\boxed{
\rho^{(m+1)}
=
\rho^{(m)}
-
\frac{h(\rho^{(m)})}
{n(1+(\rho^{(m)})^2)}.
}
\]

---

### (10) Asymptotic distribution and large-sample CI for \(\rho\)

By the standard asymptotic normality theorem for MLEs,

\[
\sqrt n(\widehat\rho_{\mathrm{MLE}}-\rho)
\overset{d}{\longrightarrow}
N\left(0,\ I_1(\rho)^{-1}\right).
\]

Since

\[
I_1(\rho)=\frac{1+\rho^2}{(1-\rho^2)^2},
\]

we have

\[
I_1(\rho)^{-1}
=
\frac{(1-\rho^2)^2}{1+\rho^2}.
\]

Therefore

\[
\boxed{
\sqrt n(\widehat\rho_{\mathrm{MLE}}-\rho)
\overset{d}{\longrightarrow}
N\left(
0,\frac{(1-\rho^2)^2}{1+\rho^2}
\right).
}
\]

Equivalently,

\[
\widehat\rho_{\mathrm{MLE}}
\approx
N\left(
\rho,\ \frac{(1-\rho^2)^2}{n(1+\rho^2)}
\right).
\]

A plug-in large-sample \(1-\alpha\) confidence interval is

\[
\boxed{
\widehat\rho_{\mathrm{MLE}}
\pm
z_{1-\alpha/2}
\frac{1-\widehat\rho_{\mathrm{MLE}}^2}
{\sqrt{n(1+\widehat\rho_{\mathrm{MLE}}^2)}}.
}
\]

One may truncate the interval to \((-1,1)\) if desired.

---

### (11) The estimator \(\widehat\rho_2=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n X_iY_i\)

Because \(\sigma_1^2=\sigma_2^2=1\),

\[
\mathbb E_\rho[X_iY_i]=\operatorname{Cov}(X_i,Y_i)=\rho.
\]

Therefore

\[
\boxed{\mathbb E_\rho[\widehat\rho_2]=\rho.}
\]

So \(\widehat\rho_2\) is exactly unbiased, a desirable finite-sample property that the MLE does not generally have.

Now compute its asymptotic variance. Write

\[
Y=\rho X+\sqrt{1-\rho^2}\,Z,
\]

where \(X,Z\sim N(0,1)\) are independent. Then

\[
XY=\rho X^2+\sqrt{1-\rho^2}\,XZ.
\]

Hence

\[
\mathbb E[XY]=\rho,
\]

and

\[
\mathbb E[X^2Y^2]
=
\rho^2\mathbb E[X^4]+(1-\rho^2)\mathbb E[X^2]\mathbb E[Z^2].
\]

Using \(\mathbb E[X^4]=3\),

\[
\mathbb E[X^2Y^2]
=
3\rho^2+(1-\rho^2)
=
1+2\rho^2.
\]

Therefore

\[
\operatorname{Var}(XY)
=
\mathbb E[X^2Y^2]-(\mathbb E[XY])^2
=
1+2\rho^2-\rho^2
=
1+\rho^2.
\]

By the central limit theorem,

\[
\boxed{
\sqrt n(\widehat\rho_2-\rho)
\overset{d}{\longrightarrow}
N(0,1+\rho^2).
}
\]

Compare this with the MLE:

\[
\sqrt n(\widehat\rho_{\mathrm{MLE}}-\rho)
\overset{d}{\longrightarrow}
N\left(0,\frac{(1-\rho^2)^2}{1+\rho^2}\right).
\]

Since

\[
\frac{(1-\rho^2)^2}{1+\rho^2}\le 1+\rho^2,
\]

with equality only at \(\rho=0\), the MLE has smaller asymptotic variance except at \(\rho=0\). Thus, for large samples, I would prefer the MLE because it is asymptotically efficient, even though \(\widehat\rho_2\) is unbiased and simpler. Also, \(\widehat\rho_2\) can fall outside the parameter space \((-1,1)\) in finite samples.

response.text:
Assume, as is standard/necessary here, that \(\mathbb E\varepsilon=0\). Let

\[
S:=S_{\beta^*}=\{j:\beta^*_j\neq 0\},\qquad s:=|S|,\qquad \Delta:=\hat\beta-\beta^*,
\]

and write \(\|A\|_{\max}=\max_{j,k}|A_{jk}|\).

---

## (i)

Since \(y_0=x_0^T\beta^*+\varepsilon_0\),

\[
y_0-x_0^T\hat\beta
=\varepsilon_0-x_0^T(\hat\beta-\beta^*)
=\varepsilon_0-x_0^T\Delta .
\]

Conditional on the training data, \(\Delta\) is fixed, and \((x_0,\varepsilon_0)\) is independent of the training data. Hence

\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb E_{\rm out}\{(y_0-x_0^T\hat\beta)^2\}
&=\mathbb E_{\rm out}\{(\varepsilon_0-x_0^T\Delta)^2\}\\
&=\mathbb E\varepsilon_0^2+\mathbb E_{\rm out}\{(x_0^T\Delta)^2\}
-2\mathbb E_{\rm out}\{\varepsilon_0 x_0^T\Delta\}.
\end{aligned}
\]

Because \(\varepsilon_0\) is independent of \(x_0\), \(\mathbb E\varepsilon_0=0\), and \(\Delta\) is fixed conditionally on the training data,

\[
\mathbb E_{\rm out}\{\varepsilon_0 x_0^T\Delta\}
=(\mathbb E\varepsilon_0)\,\mathbb E(x_0^T\Delta)=0.
\]

Also,

\[
\mathbb E_{\rm out}\{(y_0-x_0^T\beta^*)^2\}
=\mathbb E\varepsilon_0^2.
\]

Therefore

\[
\boxed{
\mathbb E_{\rm out}\{(y_0-x_0^T\hat\beta)^2\}
=
\mathbb E_{\rm out}\{(y_0-x_0^T\beta^*)^2\}
+
\mathbb E_{\rm out}\{(x_0^T(\hat\beta-\beta^*))^2\}.
}
\]

Equivalently,

\[
\mathbb E_{\rm out}\{(x_0^T\Delta)^2\}=\Delta^T\Sigma\Delta.
\]

---

## (ii)

For fixed \(j,k\),

\[
\tilde\Sigma_{jk}-\Sigma_{jk}
=
\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n \left(x_{ij}x_{ik}-\mathbb E[x_jx_k]\right).
\]

Since \(|x_i|\le B_0\) a.s., each coordinate satisfies \(|x_{ij}|\le B_0\), hence

\[
|x_{ij}x_{ik}|\le B_0^2.
\]

By Hoeffding’s inequality, for every \(t>0\),

\[
\mathbb P\left(\left|\tilde\Sigma_{jk}-\Sigma_{jk}\right|\ge t\right)
\le
2\exp\left(-\frac{nt^2}{2B_0^4}\right).
\]

Taking a union bound over \(p^2\) pairs \((j,k)\),

\[
\mathbb P\left(\|\tilde\Sigma-\Sigma\|_{\max}\ge t\right)
\le
2p^2\exp\left(-\frac{nt^2}{2B_0^4}\right).
\]

Let \(t=B_1\lambda_0\), where \(\lambda_0=\sqrt{\log(p/\delta)/n}\). Choose for example

\[
B_1=2B_0^2.
\]

Then

\[
\frac{nB_1^2\lambda_0^2}{2B_0^4}
=
2\log(p/\delta),
\]

so

\[
\mathbb P\left(\|\tilde\Sigma-\Sigma\|_{\max}\ge B_1\lambda_0\right)
\le
2p^2 e^{-2\log(p/\delta)}
=
2\delta^2.
\]

For \(\delta\le 1\), this is at most \(2\delta\). Thus with \(k_1=2\),

\[
\boxed{
\mathbb P(\Omega_1)\ge 1-k_1\delta,
\qquad
\Omega_1:=\left\{\|\tilde\Sigma-\Sigma\|_{\max}\le B_1\lambda_0\right\}.
}
\]

---

## (iii)

Fix \(\xi_0>1\). Assume \(\eta_0\) is sufficiently small, specifically

\[
B_1(1+\xi_0)^2\eta_0\le \frac{(\nu_0^*)^2}{2}.
\]

Then set

\[
\nu_0^2:=\frac{(\nu_0^*)^2}{2}.
\]

Let \(b\in\mathbb R^p\) satisfy the cone condition

\[
\sum_{j\notin S}|b_j|
\le
\xi_0\sum_{j\in S}|b_j|.
\]

Write \(\|b_S\|_1=\sum_{j\in S}|b_j|\). On \(\Omega_1\),

\[
\begin{aligned}
b^T\tilde\Sigma b
&=b^T\Sigma b+b^T(\tilde\Sigma-\Sigma)b\\
&\ge b^T\Sigma b-\|\tilde\Sigma-\Sigma\|_{\max}\|b\|_1^2\\
&\ge b^T\Sigma b-B_1\lambda_0\|b\|_1^2.
\end{aligned}
\]

By the cone condition,

\[
\|b\|_1
=
\|b_S\|_1+\|b_{S^c}\|_1
\le
(1+\xi_0)\|b_S\|_1.
\]

By (A3),

\[
b^T\Sigma b\ge (\nu_0^*)^2\|b\|_2^2
\ge
(\nu_0^*)^2\|b_S\|_2^2
\ge
\frac{(\nu_0^*)^2}{s}\|b_S\|_1^2.
\]

Therefore

\[
\begin{aligned}
b^T\tilde\Sigma b
&\ge
\frac{(\nu_0^*)^2}{s}\|b_S\|_1^2
-
B_1\lambda_0(1+\xi_0)^2\|b_S\|_1^2\\
&=
\frac{1}{s}
\left[
(\nu_0^*)^2
-
B_1s\lambda_0(1+\xi_0)^2
\right]
\|b_S\|_1^2.
\end{aligned}
\]

Using (A4), \(s\lambda_0\le \eta_0\), hence

\[
b^T\tilde\Sigma b
\ge
\frac{1}{s}
\left[
(\nu_0^*)^2
-
B_1(1+\xi_0)^2\eta_0
\right]\|b_S\|_1^2
\ge
\frac{\nu_0^2}{s}\|b_S\|_1^2.
\]

Thus

\[
\boxed{
\nu_0^2\left(\sum_{j\in S}|b_j|\right)^2
\le
s\, b^T\tilde\Sigma b.
}
\]

This is the desired compatibility/restricted-eigenvalue condition for \(\tilde\Sigma\).

---

## (iv)

Define the empirical score vector

\[
G_n:=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n x_i\varepsilon_i
=
\frac1n X^T\varepsilon.
\]

Let \(c>0\) be the universal constant in the standard concentration inequality for sums of independent sub-Gaussian random variables. Conditional on the design \(x_1,\dots,x_n\), for each coordinate \(j\),

\[
(G_n)_j=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n x_{ij}\varepsilon_i.
\]

Since \(|x_{ij}|\le B_0\), the conditional sub-Gaussian variance proxy is bounded by \(C\sigma^2 B_0^2/n\). Therefore there exists a constant \(B_2=B_2(\sigma,B_0)\) such that

\[
\mathbb P\left(\left|(G_n)_j\right|\ge B_2\lambda_0\mid x_1,\dots,x_n\right)
\le
2\exp\{-2\log(p/\delta)\}.
\]

Equivalently,

\[
\mathbb P\left(\left|(G_n)_j\right|\ge B_2\lambda_0\right)
\le
2\left(\frac{\delta}{p}\right)^2.
\]

By the union bound over \(j=1,\dots,p\),

\[
\mathbb P\left(\|G_n\|_\infty\ge B_2\lambda_0\right)
\le
2p\left(\frac{\delta}{p}\right)^2
=
\frac{2\delta^2}{p}
\le
2\delta.
\]

Define

\[
\boxed{
\Omega_2:=
\left\{
\left\|
\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n x_i\varepsilon_i
\right\|_\infty
\le
B_2\lambda_0
\right\}.
}
\]

Then

\[
\boxed{
\mathbb P(\Omega_2)\ge 1-k_2\delta
}
\]

with \(k_2=2\).

Now choose

\[
\boxed{
\lambda
=
\frac{\xi_0+1}{\xi_0-1}\,B_2\lambda_0.
}
\]

On \(\Omega_2\),

\[
\|G_n\|_\infty\le B_2\lambda_0
=
\frac{\xi_0-1}{\xi_0+1}\lambda.
\]

Using the standard Lasso basic inequality and the compatibility condition from part (iii), one obtains on \(\Omega_1\cap\Omega_2\)

\[
\boxed{
\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n \left(x_i^T(\hat\beta-\beta^*)\right)^2
\le
M_0 s\lambda_0^2,
}
\]

and

\[
\boxed{
\|\hat\beta-\beta^*\|_1
\le
M_0 s\lambda_0.
}
\]

Here \(M_0\) depends only on \(B_0,\sigma,\xi_0,\nu_0\), not on \(n,p,s\).

For completeness, the basic argument is as follows. Let \(Q:=\Delta^T\tilde\Sigma\Delta=n^{-1}\sum_i(x_i^T\Delta)^2\). The Lasso basic inequality gives

\[
\frac12 Q
\le
G_n^T\Delta+\lambda(\|\beta^*\|_1-\|\beta^*+\Delta\|_1).
\]

On \(\Omega_2\),

\[
G_n^T\Delta\le \|G_n\|_\infty\|\Delta\|_1.
\]

Also,

\[
\|\beta^*\|_1-\|\beta^*+\Delta\|_1
\le
\|\Delta_S\|_1-\|\Delta_{S^c}\|_1.

\[
y_0-x_0^T\hat\beta

=\varepsilon_0-x_0^T\Delta .

\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb E_{\rm out}\{(y_0-x_0^T\hat\beta)^2\}
&=\mathbb E_{\rm out}\{(\varepsilon_0-x_0^T\Delta)^2\}\\
&=\mathbb E\varepsilon_0^2+\mathbb E_{\rm out}\{(x_0^T\Delta)^2\}
-2\mathbb E_{\rm out}\{\varepsilon_0 x_0^T\Delta\}.
\end{aligned}
\]

\[
\mathbb E_{\rm out}\{\varepsilon_0 x_0^T\Delta\}
=(\mathbb E\varepsilon_0)\,\mathbb E(x_0^T\Delta)=0.
\]

Also,

\[
\mathbb E_{\rm out}\{(y_0-x_0^T\beta^*)^2\}
=\mathbb E\varepsilon_0^2.
\]

Therefore

\[
\boxed{
\mathbb E_{\rm out}\{(y_0-x_0^T\hat\beta)^2\}
=
\mathbb E_{\rm out}\{(y_0-x_0^T\beta^*)^2\}
+
\mathbb E_{\rm out}\{(x_0^T(\hat\beta-\beta^*))^2\}.
}
\]

Equivalently,

\[
\mathbb E_{\rm out}\{(x_0^T\Delta)^2\}=\Delta^T\Sigma\Delta.
\]

---

For fixed \(j,k\),

\[
\tilde\Sigma_{jk}-\Sigma_{jk}
=
\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n \left(x_{ij}x_{ik}-\mathbb E[x_jx_k]\right).

|x_{ij}x_{ik}|\le B_0^2.

\[
\mathbb P\left(\left|\tilde\Sigma_{jk}-\Sigma_{jk}\right|\ge t\right)
\le
2\exp\left(-\frac{nt^2}{2B_0^4}\right).
\]

\[
\mathbb P\left(\|\tilde\Sigma-\Sigma\|_{\max}\ge t\right)
\le
2p^2\exp\left(-\frac{nt^2}{2B_0^4}\right).

\[
\frac{nB_1^2\lambda_0^2}{2B_0^4}

2\log(p/\delta),

\[
\mathbb P\left(\|\tilde\Sigma-\Sigma\|_{\max}\ge B_1\lambda_0\right)

2p^2 e^{-2\log(p/\delta)}

2\delta^2.

\[
\boxed{
\mathbb P(\Omega_1)\ge 1-k_1\delta,

\Omega_1:=\left\{\|\tilde\Sigma-\Sigma\|_{\max}\le B_1\lambda_0\right\}.

\|b_S\|_1+\|b_{S^c}\|_1

\le
2\left(\frac{\delta}{p}\right)^2.
\]

By the union bound over \(j=1,\dots,p\),

\[
\mathbb P\left(\|G_n\|_\infty\ge B_2\lambda_0\right)
\le
2p\left(\frac{\delta}{p}\right)^2
=
\frac{2\delta^2}{p}
\le
2\delta.

Define

\[

\Omega_2:=
\left\{
\left\|
\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n x_i\varepsilon_i
\right\|_\infty
\le
B_2\lambda_0

with \(k_2=2\).

\lambda

\le

\[
\nu_0^2\|\Delta_S\|_1^2\le sQ.
\]

\[
Q
\le
\frac{4s(\lambda+\|G_n\|_\infty)^2}{\nu_0^2}
\lesssim s\lambda_0^2,
\]

and similarly,

\[
\|\Delta\|_1
\le
(1+\xi_0)\|\Delta_S\|_1
\lesssim s\lambda_0.
\]

---

By part (i),

\[
\mathbb E_{\rm out}\{(y_0-x_0^T\hat\beta)^2\}
=
\mathbb E_{\rm out}\{(y_0-x_0^T\beta^*)^2\}
+
\Delta^T\Sigma\Delta.

\Delta^T\Sigma\Delta

\Delta^T\tilde\Sigma\Delta+\Delta^T(\Sigma-\tilde\Sigma)\Delta\\
&\le
\Delta^T\tilde\Sigma\Delta
+
\|\Sigma-\tilde\Sigma\|_{\max}\|\Delta\|_1^2\\
&\le
\Delta^T\tilde\Sigma\Delta
+
B_1\lambda_0\|\Delta\|_1^2.
\end{aligned}

\[

=
\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n (x_i^T\Delta)^2
\le
M_0s\lambda_0^2,
\]

and

\[
\|\Delta\|_1\le M_0s\lambda_0.
\]

Therefore

\[
\begin{aligned}
\Delta^T\Sigma\Delta
&\le
M_0s\lambda_0^2
+
B_1\lambda_0(M_0s\lambda_0)^2\\
&=
M_0s\lambda_0^2
+
B_1M_0^2s^2\lambda_0^3\\
&=
\left(M_0+B_1M_0^2s\lambda_0\right)s\lambda_0^2.
\end{aligned}

\[
\Delta^T\Sigma\Delta
\le
\left(M_0+B_1M_0^2\eta_0\right)s\lambda_0^2.

M_1:=M_0+B_1M_0^2\eta_0.

\boxed{
\mathbb E_{\rm out}\{(y_0-x_0^T\hat\beta)^2\}
\le
\mathbb E_{\rm out}\{(y_0-x_0^T\beta^*)^2\}
+
M_1 |S_{\beta^*}|\lambda_0^2.
}
\]

\[
\mathbb P(\Omega_1\cap\Omega_2)
\ge

Condition on the training data, so \(\hat\beta\) and hence \(h=\hat\beta-\beta^*\) are fixed. For an independent test point,
\[
y_0=x_0^T\beta^*+\varepsilon_0.
\]
Thus
\[
y_0-x_0^T\hat\beta
=\varepsilon_0-x_0^T(\hat\beta-\beta^*)
=\varepsilon_0-x_0^Th.
\]
Therefore
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb E_{\rm out}\{(y_0-x_0^T\hat\beta)^2\}
&=\mathbb E_{\rm out}\{(\varepsilon_0-x_0^Th)^2\}\\
&=\mathbb E(\varepsilon_0^2)
-2\,\mathbb E(\varepsilon_0 x_0^Th)
+\mathbb E\{(x_0^Th)^2\}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Since \(\varepsilon_0\) is independent of \(x_0\) and \(\mathbb E\varepsilon_0=0\),
\[
\mathbb E(\varepsilon_0 x_0^Th)=\mathbb E\varepsilon_0\cdot \mathbb E(x_0^Th)=0.
\]

\[
y_0-x_0^T\beta^*=\varepsilon_0.

\[
\boxed{
\mathbb E_{\rm out}\{(y_0-x_0^T\hat\beta)^2\}
=
\mathbb E_{\rm out}\{(y_0-x_0^T\beta^*)^2\}
+
\mathbb E_{\rm out}\{(x_0^T(\hat\beta-\beta^*))^2\}.
}
\]

Equivalently, the excess out-of-sample prediction error is
\[
\mathbb E_{\rm out}\{(x_0^Th)^2\}=h^T\Sigma h.

\[
\|\widetilde\Sigma-\Sigma\|_{\max}

\qquad

\[

|x_{ij}x_{ik}|\le B_0^2.

\[
\mathbb P\left(

2\exp\left(-\frac{nt^2}{2B_0^4}\right).

2p^2\exp\left(-\frac{nt^2}{2B_0^4}\right).

2p^2

Assume, as is standard for the linear model here, that \(\mathbb E\varepsilon=0\). Otherwise part (i) is not true in general.

\[
S:=S_{\beta^*}:=\{j:\beta_j^*\neq 0\},\qquad s:=|S|,
\]
and write
\[
d:=\hat\beta-\beta^*,\qquad 
\tilde \Sigma:=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n x_i x_i^T,\qquad 
z:=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n x_i\varepsilon_i.
\]

---

## (i) Bias-variance/excess-risk decomposition

\[
y_0=x_0^T\beta^*+\varepsilon_0,
\]

\[
y_0-x_0^T\hat\beta
=
\varepsilon_0-x_0^T(\hat\beta-\beta^*).
\]

\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb E_{\rm out}\{(y_0-x_0^T\hat\beta)^2\}
&=
\mathbb E_{\rm out}\left[\left\{\varepsilon_0-x_0^T(\hat\beta-\beta^*)\right\}^2\right]\\
&=
\mathbb E_{\rm out}(\varepsilon_0^2)
+
\mathbb E_{\rm out}\{(x_0^T(\hat\beta-\beta^*))^2\}\\
&\qquad
-2\mathbb E_{\rm out}\{\varepsilon_0 x_0^T(\hat\beta-\beta^*)\}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Because \(\varepsilon_0\) is independent of \(x_0\) and has mean zero,
\[
\mathbb E_{\rm out}\{\varepsilon_0 x_0^T(\hat\beta-\beta^*)\}
=
\mathbb E(\varepsilon_0)\,\mathbb E_{\rm out}\{x_0^T(\hat\beta-\beta^*)\}=0.
\]
Also
\[
\mathbb E_{\rm out}(\varepsilon_0^2)
=
\mathbb E_{\rm out}\{(y_0-x_0^T\beta^*)^2\}.
\]
Therefore
\[
\boxed{
\mathbb E_{\rm out}\{(y_0-x_0^T\hat\beta)^2\}
=
\mathbb E_{\rm out}\{(y_0-x_0^T\beta^*)^2\}
+
\mathbb E_{\rm out}\{(x_0^T(\hat\beta-\beta^*))^2\}.
}
\]

---

## (ii) Entrywise concentration of \(\tilde\Sigma\)

\[
\tilde \Sigma_{jk}-\Sigma_{jk}
=
\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\left(x_{ij}x_{ik}-\mathbb E[x_jx_k]\right).

\[
\mathbb P\left(\left|\tilde \Sigma_{jk}-\Sigma_{jk}\right|\ge t\right)
\le

\]

\[
\mathbb P\left(\|\tilde \Sigma-\Sigma\|_{\max}\ge t\right)
\le

\[
\lambda_0=\sqrt{\frac{\log(p/\delta)}{n}}

\[

## (iii) Transfer of compatibility from \(\Sigma\) to \(\tilde\Sigma\)

+

\le
(\lambda+\|z\|_\infty)\|d_S\|_1.
\]

\[

=
\xi_0\|d_S\|_1.

\[

\le

\le

\le
M_0 s\lambda_0^2

\[
\boxed{
\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n (x_i^T(\hat\beta-\beta^*))^2

M_0 s\lambda_0^2,
}
\]

\[
\boxed{
\|\hat\beta-\beta^*\|_1
\le
M_0 s\lambda_0.
}
\]

\[

\]

\[
\begin{aligned}

&=
d^T\tilde\Sigma d+d^T(\Sigma-\tilde\Sigma)d\\
&\le

&\le
d^T\tilde\Sigma d+B_1\lambda_0\|d\|_1^2.
\end{aligned}
\]

\[
d^T\tilde\Sigma d\le M_0 s\lambda_0^2,
\]
and
\[
\|d\|_1\le M_0 s\lambda_0.
\]
Hence
\[
\begin{aligned}
d^T\Sigma d
&\le
M_0s\lambda_0^2
+
B_1\lambda_0(M_0s\lambda_0)^2\\
&=
M_0s\lambda_0^2
+
B_1M_0^2s^2\lambda_0^3\\
&=
\left(M_0+B_1M_0^2s\lambda_0\right)s\lambda_0^2.
\end{aligned}
\]

\[
d^T\Sigma d
\le
\left(M_0+B_1M_0^2\eta_0\right)s\lambda_0^2.
\]
Define
\[
M_1:=M_0+B_1M_0^2\eta_0.
\]
Therefore, on \(\Omega_1\cap\Omega_2\),
\[
\boxed{
\mathbb E_{\rm out}\{(y_0-x_0^T\hat\beta)^2\}
\le
\mathbb E_{\rm out}\{(y_0-x_0^T\beta^*)^2\}
+
M_1 |S_{\beta^*}|\lambda_0^2.
}
\]

Moreover,
\[
\mathbb P(\Omega_1\cap\Omega_2)
\ge
1-(k_1+k_2)\delta.
\]

Let an ordering be represented by a permutation \(\sigma=(\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_n)\), where  
\[
\sigma_1 \prec \sigma_2 \prec \cdots \prec \sigma_n .
\]
Since the \(Y_i\)'s have continuous densities, ties have probability \(0\).

A basic fact we will use repeatedly is the **exponential race formula**: if \(Y_i\sim \mathrm{Exp}(\lambda_i)\) independently, then for any permutation \(\sigma\),
\[
\mathbb P(\sigma_1\prec_Y \cdots \prec_Y \sigma_n)
=
\prod_{k=1}^n
\frac{\lambda_{\sigma_k}}{\sum_{\ell=k}^n \lambda_{\sigma_\ell}}.
\]
Here \(\lambda_i=i\).

---

## (i)

We need
\[
\mathbb P(i\prec_Y j \text{ for all } j\neq i)
=
\mathbb P(Y_i=\min_{1\le r\le n}Y_r).
\]
For independent exponentials, the probability that \(Y_i\) is the minimum is proportional to its rate:
\[
\mathbb P(Y_i=\min_r Y_r)
=
\frac{i}{\sum_{r=1}^n r}
=
\frac{i}{n(n+1)/2}.
\]
Therefore
\[
\boxed{
\mathbb P(i\prec_Y j \ \forall j\neq i)=\frac{2i}{n(n+1)}.
}
\]

---

## (ii)

The usual ordering \(1\prec_Y 2\prec_Y \cdots \prec_Y n\) has probability
\[
Q_n
=
\prod_{k=1}^n
\frac{k}{\sum_{r=k}^n r}.
\]
Now
\[
\sum_{r=k}^n r
=
\frac{(n+k)(n-k+1)}{2}.
\]
Hence
\[
Q_n
=
\prod_{k=1}^n
\frac{2k}{(n+k)(n-k+1)}.
\]
Thus
\[
Q_n
=
\frac{2^n n!}{\prod_{k=1}^n (n+k)\prod_{k=1}^n(n-k+1)}.
\]
But
\[
\prod_{k=1}^n(n+k)=\frac{(2n)!}{n!},
\qquad
\prod_{k=1}^n(n-k+1)=n!,
\]
so the denominator is \((2n)!\). Therefore
\[
\boxed{
Q_n=\mathbb P(1\prec_Y 2\prec_Y \cdots \prec_Y n)
=
\frac{2^n n!}{(2n)!}.
}
\]

---

## (iii)

The reverse ordering is
\[
n\prec_Y n-1\prec_Y \cdots \prec_Y 1.
\]
Using the exponential race formula,
\[
P_n
=
\prod_{m=1}^n
\frac{m}{\sum_{r=1}^m r}
=
\prod_{m=1}^n
\frac{m}{m(m+1)/2}
=
\prod_{m=1}^n
\frac{2}{m+1}.
\]
Therefore
\[
\boxed{
P_n=\mathbb P(n\prec_Y n-1\prec_Y \cdots \prec_Y 1)
=
\frac{2^n}{(n+1)!}.
}
\]

---

## (iv)

From (ii) and (iii),
\[
\frac{P_n}{Q_n}
=
\frac{2^n/(n+1)!}{2^n n!/(2n)!}
=
\frac{(2n)!}{n!(n+1)!}.
\]
Thus
\[
\frac{P_n}{Q_n}
=
\frac{1}{n+1}\binom{2n}{n},
\]
the \(n\)-th Catalan number.

By Stirling’s approximation,
\[
\binom{2n}{n}
\sim
\frac{4^n}{\sqrt{\pi n}},
\]
so
\[
\frac{P_n}{Q_n}
\sim
\frac{4^n}{\sqrt{\pi}n^{3/2}}.
\]
Therefore
\[
\left(\frac{P_n}{Q_n}\right)^{1/n}
=
4\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{\pi}n^{3/2}}\right)^{1/n}(1+o(1))^{1/n}.
\]
Since
\[
\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{\pi}n^{3/2}}\right)^{1/n}\to 1,
\]
we get
\[
\boxed{
\left(\frac{P_n}{Q_n}\right)^{1/n}\sim 4.
}
\]

---

## (v)

Let \(\rho_{n,m}\) denote the restriction map from orderings of \(\{1,\dots,n\}\) to orderings of \(\{1,\dots,m\}\), obtained by deleting the labels \(m+1,\dots,n\).

Because \(Y'_i=Y_i\) for \(1\le i\le m\), for any \(i,j\le m\),
\[
i\prec_{Y'} j
\iff
Y_i<Y_j
\iff
i\prec_Y j.
\]
Thus, pathwise,
\[
\prec_{Y'}=\rho_{n,m}(\prec_Y).
\]
Consequently, for any ordering \(\pi\) of \(\{1,\dots,m\}\),
\[
\boxed{
\mathbb P(\prec_{Y'}=\pi)
=
\mathbb P(\rho_{n,m}(\prec_Y)=\pi)
=
\sum_{\sigma:\rho_{n,m}(\sigma)=\pi}
\mathbb P(\prec_Y=\sigma).
}
\]

Equivalently, if \(\pi=(\pi_1,\dots,\pi_m)\), then
\[
\boxed{
\mathbb P(\prec_{Y'}=\pi)
=
\prod_{k=1}^m
\frac{\pi_k}{\sum_{\ell=k}^m \pi_\ell}.
}
\]

For the recursive \(Z\)-construction, the normalizing constant is
\[
\sum_{j=0}^{i-1}(i-j)=\frac{i(i+1)}2,
\]
so
\[
\boxed{
\mathbb P(Z_i=j)=\frac{2(i-j)}{i(i+1)},
\qquad j=0,\dots,i-1.
}
\]
The construction is projectively consistent: deleting labels \(m+1,\dots,n\) from the ordering \(\prec_{Z(n)}\) gives exactly \(\prec_{Z(m)}\). Therefore the infinite ordering \(\prec_{Z(\infty)}\) is well-defined.

---

## (vi)

Interpret “highest-ranked” as the maximal element of the ordering, i.e. the last element when the order is written as
\[
\sigma_1\prec \sigma_2\prec\cdots\prec\sigma_n.
\]

Let \(E_i\) be the event that, when \(i\) is inserted into the ordering of \(\{1,\dots,i-1\}\), it is inserted into the last position. This occurs exactly when
\[
Z_i=i-1.
\]
Therefore
\[
\mathbb P(E_i)
=
\mathbb P(Z_i=i-1)
=
\frac{2(i-(i-1))}{i(i+1)}
=
\frac{2}{i(i+1)}.
\]
Hence
\[
\sum_{i=2}^\infty \mathbb P(E_i)
=
\sum_{i=2}^\infty \frac{2}{i(i+1)}
<\infty.
\]
By the **Borel–Cantelli lemma**, with probability \(1\), only finitely many of the events \(E_i\) occur.

If \(E_i\) does not occur, then inserting \(i\) does not change the current last element of the ordering. Therefore the highest-ranked element \(M_n\) changes only on the events \(E_i\). Since only finitely many such events occur almost surely, the sequence \((M_n)\) is eventually constant almost surely.

Thus the limit exists and is finite with probability \(1\):
\[
\boxed{
M_\infty=\lim_{n\to\infty}M_n
\text{ exists and is finite a.s.}
}
\]

A convention note: if “highest-ranked” were instead interpreted as the first position in the displayed order, then the relevant probabilities would be \(\mathbb P(Z_i=0)=2/(i+1)\), whose sum diverges, and the asserted conclusion would fail.

\[
\pi_1 \prec \pi_2 \prec \cdots \prec \pi_n .
\]
Here \(Y_i\sim \mathrm{Exp}(i)\), independently.

A basic fact we will use repeatedly is the exponential race formula: if \(Y_i\sim \mathrm{Exp}(\lambda_i)\) independently, then for any permutation \(\pi\) of \([n]\),
\[
\mathbb P(Y_{\pi_1}<Y_{\pi_2}<\cdots<Y_{\pi_n})
=
\prod_{r=1}^n \frac{\lambda_{\pi_r}}{\sum_{s=r}^n \lambda_{\pi_s}}.
\]
This follows from the fact that the minimum is attained at \(i\) with probability \(\lambda_i/\sum_j\lambda_j\), and then the memoryless property allows iteration.

Here \(\lambda_i=i\).

---

## (i)

We want
\[
\mathbb P(i\prec_Y j \text{ for all } j\neq i)
=
\mathbb P(Y_i=\min_{1\le k\le n}Y_k).
\]
By the exponential race formula,
\[
\mathbb P(Y_i=\min_k Y_k)
=
\frac{i}{\sum_{k=1}^n k}
=
\frac{i}{n(n+1)/2}.
\]
Therefore
\[
\boxed{
\mathbb P(i\prec_Y j \text{ for all } j\neq i)
=
\frac{2i}{n(n+1)}.
}
\]

---

## (ii)

The usual ordering \(1\prec_Y 2\prec_Y \cdots \prec_Y n\) corresponds to the permutation \((1,2,\dots,n)\). Hence
\[
Q_n
=
\mathbb P(Y_1<Y_2<\cdots<Y_n)
=
\prod_{k=1}^n \frac{k}{\sum_{\ell=k}^n \ell}.
\]
Now
\[
\sum_{\ell=k}^n \ell
=
\frac{(n+k)(n-k+1)}{2}.
\]
Thus
\[
Q_n
=
\prod_{k=1}^n \frac{2k}{(n+k)(n-k+1)}.
\]
Therefore
\[
Q_n
=
\frac{2^n n!}{\left(\prod_{k=1}^n(n+k)\right)\left(\prod_{k=1}^n(n-k+1)\right)}.
\]
But
\[
\prod_{k=1}^n(n+k)=\frac{(2n)!}{n!},
\qquad
\prod_{k=1}^n(n-k+1)=n!.
\]
So the denominator is \((2n)!\), and therefore
\[
\boxed{
Q_n
=
\frac{2^n n!}{(2n)!}.
}
\]

---

The reverse ordering is
\[
n\prec_Y n-1\prec_Y \cdots \prec_Y 1.
\]
At the first step we must choose \(n\) from \(\{1,\dots,n\}\), then \(n-1\) from \(\{1,\dots,n-1\}\), and so on. Therefore
\[
P_n
=
\prod_{k=1}^n \frac{k}{\sum_{\ell=1}^k \ell}
=
\prod_{k=1}^n \frac{k}{k(k+1)/2}.
\]
Thus
\[
P_n
=
\prod_{k=1}^n \frac{2}{k+1}
=
\frac{2^n}{(n+1)!}.
\]
Hence
\[
\boxed{
P_n
=
\frac{2^n}{(n+1)!}.
}
\]

---

\[
\frac{P_n}{Q_n}
=
\frac{2^n/(n+1)!}{2^n n!/(2n)!}
=
\frac{(2n)!}{n!(n+1)!}.
\]

\[
\frac{P_n}{Q_n}
=
\frac{1}{n+1}\binom{2n}{n},
\]
the \(n\)-th Catalan number.

By Stirling’s approximation,
\[
n!\sim \sqrt{2\pi n}\left(\frac ne\right)^n,
\]
so
\[
\binom{2n}{n}
\sim
\frac{4^n}{\sqrt{\pi n}}.
\]
Therefore
\[
\frac{P_n}{Q_n}
=
\frac{1}{n+1}\binom{2n}{n}
\sim
\frac{4^n}{\sqrt{\pi}n^{3/2}}.
\]
Taking \(n\)-th roots,
\[
\left(\frac{P_n}{Q_n}\right)^{1/n}
\sim
4\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{\pi}n^{3/2}}\right)^{1/n}.
\]
Since
\[
\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{\pi}n^{3/2}}\right)^{1/n}\to 1,
\]
we obtain
\[
\boxed{
\left(\frac{P_n}{Q_n}\right)^{1/n}\sim 4.
}
\]

---

## (v)

Let \(R_{n,m}\) be the restriction map from orderings of \([n]\) to orderings of \([m]\), obtained by deleting the labels \(m+1,\dots,n\).

\[

\[
\boxed{
\mathbb P(\prec_{Y'}=\sigma)

\sum_{\pi:\,R_{n,m}(\pi)=\sigma}

}

If \(\sigma=(\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_m)\), then explicitly,
\[
\mathbb P(\prec_{Y'}=\sigma)
=
\prod_{r=1}^m

\[

\qquad j=0,\dots,i-1.
\]

At step \(i\), the new element \(i\) is inserted into position \(Z_i+1\). It becomes the highest-ranked element exactly when it is inserted in the last position, namely when
\[

\]
Therefore
\[
\mathbb P(Z_i=i-1)
=
\frac{2}{i(i+1)}.
\]

\[

\]

\[
\sum_{i=1}^\infty \mathbb P(A_i)
=
\sum_{i=1}^\infty \frac{2}{i(i+1)}
<\infty.
\]
By the first Borel–Cantelli lemma,
\[
\mathbb P(A_i \text{ infinitely often})=0.
\]
Hence, with probability \(1\), only finitely many inserted elements ever become the highest-ranked element.

\[
M_\infty=\lim_{n\to\infty}M_n

exists and is finite almost surely.

Hence
\[
\boxed{
\mathbb P(M_\infty<\infty)=1.
}
\]

\[

\[
\mathbb P(i\prec_Y j\ \forall j\neq i)
=
\frac{i}{\sum_{k=1}^n k}
=
\frac{i}{n(n+1)/2}.

\[

\[

=

\[
\sum_{\ell=k}^n \ell
=
\frac{(n+k)(n-k+1)}{2}.

\[
Q_n
=
\prod_{k=1}^n
\frac{2k}{(n+k)(n-k+1)}.

\[

=
\frac{2^n n!}{\left(\prod_{k=1}^n (n+k)\right)\left(\prod_{k=1}^n(n-k+1)\right)}.

\[
\prod_{k=1}^n(n+k)=\frac{(2n)!}{n!},

\prod_{k=1}^n(n-k+1)=n!,

For the insertion process, first normalize the law of \(Z_i\). Since
\[

\[

\[
\mathbb P(A_i)
=
\mathbb P(Z_i=i-1)
=

\[

=

\[
M_\infty=\lim_{n\to\infty}M_n
\]
exists almost surely and is finite almost surely.

Therefore
\[
\boxed{\mathbb P(M_\infty<\infty)=1.}
\]

Let $n$ be a positive integer. Consider a simple random walk on $\mathbb{Z}^2$ starting at $(n, 0)$. Let

\[
X_k:=S_{k,x},\qquad Y_k:=S_{k,y}.
\]

The horizontal increments are

\[
\xi_k:=X_k-X_{k-1},
\]

where

\[
P(\xi_k=1)=\frac14,\qquad P(\xi_k=-1)=\frac14,\qquad P(\xi_k=0)=\frac12.
\]

They are i.i.d., with

\[
\mathbb E[\xi_k]=0,\qquad \operatorname{Var}(\xi_k)=\mathbb E[\xi_k^2]=\frac12.
\]

Also

\[
X_k=n+\sum_{j=1}^k \xi_j.
\]

---

## Part A

Yes, \(\{S_{k,x}\}_{k\ge 0}=\{X_k\}_{k\ge 0}\) is a Markov chain.

Its state space is \(\mathbb Z\), with initial state \(X_0=n\), and transition probabilities

\[
p(i,j)=P(X_{k+1}=j\mid X_k=i)
=
\begin{cases}
\frac14, & j=i+1,\\[2mm]
\frac14, & j=i-1,\\[2mm]
\frac12, & j=i,\\[2mm]
0, & \text{otherwise.}
\end{cases}
\]

The holding probability \(1/2\) comes from the up/down moves, which do not change the \(x\)-coordinate.

It is also a martingale. Indeed, with respect to the natural filtration \(\mathcal F_k=\sigma(S_0,\dots,S_k)\),

\[
\mathbb E[X_{k+1}\mid \mathcal F_k]
=
X_k+\mathbb E[\xi_{k+1}]
=
X_k.
\]

Thus \(\{X_k\}\) is a martingale.

---

## Part B

Let

\[
T_{0,x}:=\inf\{k\ge 0:X_k=0\}.
\]

We first compute the probability of ever hitting \(0\).

For an integer \(a>n\), define

\[
T_a:=\inf\{k\ge 0:X_k=a\},
\qquad
\tau_a:=T_{0,x}\wedge T_a.
\]

The stopped process \(X_{k\wedge \tau_a}\) is bounded between \(0\) and \(a\). Since \(X_k\) is a martingale, optional stopping gives

\[
\mathbb E[X_{\tau_a}]=X_0=n.
\]

But

\[
X_{\tau_a}
=
\begin{cases}
0, & T_{0,x}<T_a,\\
a, & T_a<T_{0,x}.
\end{cases}
\]

Therefore

\[
n=\mathbb E[X_{\tau_a}]
=
a\,P(T_a<T_{0,x}),
\]

so

\[
P(T_a<T_{0,x})=\frac{n}{a}.
\]

Hence

\[
P(T_{0,x}<T_a)=1-\frac{n}{a}.
\]

Since \(\{T_{0,x}<T_a\}\subseteq \{T_{0,x}<\infty\}\), we have

\[
P(T_{0,x}<\infty)\ge 1-\frac{n}{a}.
\]

Letting \(a\to\infty\),

\[
P(T_{0,x}<\infty)=1.
\]

Thus

\[
\boxed{P(T_{0,x}=\infty)=0.}
\]

Now we show that the expectation is infinite.

Suppose for contradiction that

\[
\mathbb E[T_{0,x}]<\infty.
\]

For each \(m\), the stopping time \(T_{0,x}\wedge m\) is bounded, so optional stopping for the martingale \(X_k\) gives

\[
\mathbb E[X_{T_{0,x}\wedge m}]=X_0=n.
\]

But \(T_{0,x}<\infty\) a.s., and

\[
X_{T_{0,x}}=0.
\]

Moreover, since the horizontal step size is at most \(1\),

\[
|X_{T_{0,x}\wedge m}|\le n+T_{0,x}.
\]

Under the assumed integrability of \(T_{0,x}\), the right-hand side is integrable. Therefore by dominated convergence,

\[
\mathbb E[X_{T_{0,x}\wedge m}]
\to
\mathbb E[X_{T_{0,x}}]
=
0.
\]

This contradicts the fact that \(\mathbb E[X_{T_{0,x}\wedge m}]=n\) for every \(m\).

Hence

\[
\boxed{\mathbb E[T_{0,x}]=\infty.}
\]

---

## Part C

Let

\[
m_n:=\lfloor n^{1.5}\rfloor=\lfloor n^{3/2}\rfloor,
\]

and write

\[
H_k:=X_k-n=\sum_{j=1}^k \xi_j.
\]

Then

\[
\mathbb E[H_k]=0,
\qquad
\operatorname{Var}(H_k)=\frac{k}{2}.
\]

---

### Part C(i)

We want to prove

\[
P_{1,n}:=P(D_{m_n}\ge n/2)\to 1.
\]

The complementary event is

\[
\{D_{m_n}<n/2\}.
\]

If \(D_{m_n}<n/2\), then in particular

\[
|X_{m_n}|<n/2.
\]

\[

Yes, \(\{S_{k,x}\}_{k\ge 0}=\{X_k\}_{k\ge 0}\) is a time-homogeneous Markov chain on state space \(\mathbb Z\), started at \(X_0=n\), with transition probabilities
\[
p(i,j)=P(X_{k+1}=j\mid X_k=i)
=
\begin{cases}
\frac14,& j=i+1,\\[2mm]
\frac14,& j=i-1,\\[2mm]
\frac12,& j=i,\\[2mm]
0,&\text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
\]
So \(X_k\) is a lazy simple symmetric random walk on \(\mathbb Z\).

It is also a martingale. Indeed, with respect to either its own natural filtration or the full filtration of the two-dimensional walk,
\[
\mathbb E[X_{k+1}\mid \mathcal F_k]
=
\mathbb E[X_k+\xi_{k+1}\mid \mathcal F_k]
=
X_k+\mathbb E[\xi_{k+1}]
=
X_k.
\]

Therefore \(\{S_{k,x}\}\) is a martingale.

---

Let
\[
T_a^X:=\inf\{k\ge 0:X_k=a\}.
\]
The problem’s \(T_{0,x}\) is \(T_0^X\).

\[
\tau_N:=T_0^X\wedge T_N^X.
\]

Let
\[
h_i=P_i(T_N^X<T_0^X),\qquad i=0,1,\dots,N.
\]
Then \(h_0=0\), \(h_N=1\), and for \(1\le i\le N-1\),
\[
h_i=\frac14 h_{i-1}+\frac12 h_i+\frac14 h_{i+1}.
\]
Equivalently,
\[
h_{i+1}-2h_i+h_{i-1}=0.
\]
Thus \(h_i\) is linear in \(i\), and using the boundary values,
\[
h_i=\frac{i}{N}.
\]
Therefore
\[
P_n(T_N^X<T_0^X)=\frac nN.

\[
\mathbb E_n[T_0^X]\ge \mathbb E_n[\tau_N]=2n(N-n).

\[
\mathbb E[T_{0,x}]=\infty.

Thus
\[
\boxed{P[T_{0,x}=\infty]=0,\qquad \mathbb E[T_{0,x}]=\infty.}

Let
\[
m_n:=\lfloor n^{1.5}\rfloor.

\[

Write
\[

\[

so
\[

Therefore by Chebyshev’s inequality,
\[
P(D_{m_n}<n/2)

\[

=

\le \frac{2n^{3/2}}{n^2}
=

\[

\[

\[

\[

\[

\[

F_{0.95;9,9}\approx 3.18.

Equivalently, the rejection region using the larger variance in the numerator is

F_{\text{obs}}>3.18.

\boxed{(0.050,\;0.254)}.

\[

\[
\widehat{\operatorname{SE}}\{\hat\mu(1.2)\}
=

=
\sqrt{1.548964}
\approx 1.245.
\]

\[
3.76\pm t_{0.975,58}(1.245)

\approx 3.76\pm 2.49.

So

\boxed{(1.27,\;6.25)}.

\[

=

\approx 1.546.

\[
3.76\pm t_{0.975,58}(1.546)
=

Hence

\boxed{(0.67,\;6.85)}.

\widehat{\operatorname{SE}}\{\hat\mu(4.3)\}

$Y_1, \dots, Y_n$ i.i.d. with density $f_\theta(y) = \frac1\theta r y^{r-1} e^{-y^r/\theta}$, $y>0$, where $r>0$ is known. (1) Find the MLE of $\theta$. (2) Find its limiting distribution as $n \to \infty$.

response.text:
Let

\[
S=\sum_{i=1}^n Y_i^r.
\]

Since \(r>0\) is known, the likelihood as a function of \(\theta>0\) is

\[
L(\theta)
=\prod_{i=1}^n \frac1\theta rY_i^{r-1}e^{-Y_i^r/\theta}
= r^n\prod_{i=1}^n Y_i^{r-1}\theta^{-n}\exp\left(-\frac{S}{\theta}\right).
\]

Thus the log-likelihood is

\[
\ell(\theta)
= C - n\log\theta-\frac{S}{\theta},
\]

where \(C\) does not depend on \(\theta\).

Differentiate:

\[
\ell'(\theta)
= -\frac{n}{\theta}+\frac{S}{\theta^2}.
\]

Setting \(\ell'(\theta)=0\) gives

\[
-\frac{n}{\theta}+\frac{S}{\theta^2}=0
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\widehat\theta=\frac{S}{n}
=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n Y_i^r.
\]

Also,

\[
\ell''(\theta)
=\frac{n}{\theta^2}-\frac{2S}{\theta^3},
\]

and at \(\widehat\theta=S/n\),

\[
\ell''(\widehat\theta)
= -\frac{n^3}{S^2}<0.
\]

Moreover, \(\ell(\theta)\to-\infty\) as \(\theta\downarrow 0\) and as \(\theta\to\infty\), so this critical point is the global maximum.

Therefore,

\[
\boxed{\widehat\theta_{\text{MLE}}=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n Y_i^r.}
\]

For the limiting distribution, define

\[
X_i=Y_i^r.
\]

Then for \(x>0\),

\[
\mathbb P(X_i\le x)
=\mathbb P(Y_i\le x^{1/r})
=1-e^{-x/\theta},
\]

so

\[
X_i\sim \operatorname{Exp}\left(\text{mean } \theta\right).
\]

Hence

\[
\mathbb E[X_i]=\theta,\qquad \operatorname{Var}(X_i)=\theta^2.
\]

Since

\[
\widehat\theta=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n X_i,
\]

the central limit theorem gives

\[
\sqrt n(\widehat\theta-\theta)
\overset{d}{\longrightarrow}
N(0,\theta^2).
\]

Equivalently,

\[
\boxed{\frac{\sqrt n}{\theta}(\widehat\theta-\theta)
\overset{d}{\longrightarrow}N(0,1).}
\]

Thus the MLE is asymptotically normal:

\[
\boxed{\widehat\theta \approx N\left(\theta,\frac{\theta^2}{n}\right)}
\]

for large \(n\).

\]

\[
\ell(\theta)=-n\log\theta-\frac{1}{\theta}\sum_{i=1}^n y_i^r.

\ell''(\widehat\theta)
=-\frac{n}{\widehat\theta^2}<0,

Since \(X_i=Y_i^r\sim \operatorname{Exp}(\text{mean }\theta)\),

\[

The empirical frequency table is missing from the prompt, so the numerical Pearson statistic, p-value, observed \(\bar X\), and \(z\)-value cannot be uniquely computed from the information given.

What can be computed from the null model is as follows.

Under uniformity,

\[
X\sim \operatorname{Hypergeometric}(N=49,K=25,n=6),
\]

so

\[
P(X=x)=\frac{\binom{25}{x}\binom{24}{6-x}}{\binom{49}{6}},
\qquad x=0,\dots,6.
\]

The null probabilities are approximately

\[
\begin{array}{c|ccccccc}
x & 0 & 1 & 2 & 3 & 4 & 5 & 6\\
\hline
P(X=x) & 0.00963 & 0.07599 & 0.22796 & 0.33293 & 0.24967 & 0.09119 & 0.01266
\end{array}
\]

For 100 trials the expected counts are

\[
100p_x \approx
(0.963,\ 7.599,\ 22.796,\ 33.293,\ 24.967,\ 9.119,\ 1.266).
\]

If the observed counts are \(O_0,\dots,O_6\), then the Pearson statistic is

\[
\chi^2
=
\sum_{x=0}^6
\frac{(O_x-100p_x)^2}{100p_x}.
\]

Because the expected counts for \(x=0\) and \(x=6\) are below 5, one should usually combine tail categories, for example using cells

\[
\{0,1\},\quad \{2\},\quad \{3\},\quad \{4\},\quad \{5,6\}.
\]

Then

\[
\chi^2_{\text{grouped}}
=
\frac{(O_0+O_1-8.562)^2}{8.562}
+
\frac{(O_2-22.796)^2}{22.796}
+
\frac{(O_3-33.293)^2}{33.293}
+
\frac{(O_4-24.967)^2}{24.967}
+
\frac{(O_5+O_6-10.385)^2}{10.385}.
\]

With no parameters estimated, the grouped Pearson test has

\[
df = 5-1 = 4,
\]

so the p-value is

\[
p=\Pr\{\chi^2_4 \ge \chi^2_{\text{grouped}}\}.
\]

For the sample mean,

\[
\bar X = \frac{1}{100}\sum_{x=0}^6 xO_x.
\]

Under the null,

\[
E(X)=6\frac{25}{49}=\frac{150}{49}\approx 3.061,
\]

and

\[
\operatorname{Var}(X)
=
6\frac{25}{49}\frac{24}{49}\frac{43}{48}
=
\frac{3225}{2401}.
\]

Thus

\[
\operatorname{SD}(\bar X)
=
\sqrt{\frac{3225}{2401\cdot 100}}
\approx 0.116.
\]

So the \(z\)-statistic is

\[
z
=
\frac{\bar X-3.06}{0.116}.
\]

Conclusion depends on the observed counts. If the Pearson p-value or the \(z\)-test p-value is small, say below \(0.05\), we reject uniformity. If not, we do not have strong evidence against uniformity. But statistical testing cannot prove the gadget is uniform; it can only assess whether the data provide significant evidence against uniformity.

Please provide the empirical frequency table, and I can compute the exact statistic, p-value, \(\bar X\), and \(z\)-value.

## (1) Least-squares estimates and fitted line

For simple linear regression with an intercept,

\[
\hat\beta_1=\frac{\sum_{i=1}^n (x_i-\bar x)(y_i-\bar y)}
{\sum_{i=1}^n (x_i-\bar x)^2},
\qquad
\hat\beta_0=\bar y-\hat\beta_1\bar x.
\]

Here

\[
\bar x=\frac{-5-3+0+2+1}{5}=-1,
\qquad
\bar y=\frac{-2+1+4+6+3}{5}=\frac{12}{5}=2.4.
\]

Compute

\[
S_{xx}=\sum (x_i-\bar x)^2=34,
\]

and

\[
S_{xy}=\sum (x_i-\bar x)(y_i-\bar y)=34.
\]

Thus

\[
\hat\beta_1=\frac{S_{xy}}{S_{xx}}=\frac{34}{34}=1,
\]

and

\[
\hat\beta_0=\bar y-\hat\beta_1\bar x=2.4-1(-1)=3.4.
\]

So the fitted regression line is

\[
\boxed{\hat y = 3.4+x.}
\]

The scatterplot consists of the points

\[
(-5,-2),\;(-3,1),\;(0,4),\;(2,6),\;(1,3),
\]

with fitted line \(\hat y=x+3.4\).

A schematic plot is:

    +--------------------------------

```

## (2) Fitted values \(\hat y_i\)

Using

\[
\hat y_i=3.4+x_i,
\]

we get:

\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c|c}
i & x_i & y_i & \hat y_i \\ \hline
1 & -5 & -2 & -1.6 \\
2 & -3 & 1 & 0.4 \\
3 & 0 & 4 & 3.4 \\
4 & 2 & 6 & 5.4 \\
5 & 1 & 3 & 4.4
\end{array}
\]

So

\[
\boxed{\hat y=(-1.6,\;0.4,\;3.4,\;5.4,\;4.4).}
\]

---

## (3) Residuals and residual plot

The residuals are

\[
e_i=y_i-\hat y_i.
\]

Thus:

\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c}
i & x_i & y_i & \hat y_i & e_i \\ \hline
1 & -5 & -2 & -1.6 & -0.4 \\
2 & -3 & 1 & 0.4 & 0.6 \\
3 & 0 & 4 & 3.4 & 0.6 \\
4 & 2 & 6 & 5.4 & 0.6 \\
5 & 1 & 3 & 4.4 & -1.4
\end{array}
\]

So

\[
\boxed{e=(-0.4,\;0.6,\;0.6,\;0.6,\;-1.4).}
\]

Residual plot points \((x_i,e_i)\) are

\[
(-5,-0.4),\;(-3,0.6),\;(0,0.6),\;(2,0.6),\;(1,-1.4).
\]

A schematic residual plot is:

```

 0.0 |--------------------------------
-0.5 | ●
-1.0 |
-1.5 |                       ●
     +--------------------------------
       -5     -3      0      1      2
                         x
```

---

## (4) Compute \(R^2\)

We use

\[
R^2=1-\frac{\text{SSE}}{\text{SST}},
\]

where

\[
\text{SSE}=\sum e_i^2.
\]

Compute

\[
\text{SSE}=(-0.4)^2+(0.6)^2+(0.6)^2+(0.6)^2+(-1.4)^2.
\]

So

\[
\text{SSE}=0.16+0.36+0.36+0.36+1.96=3.2.
\]

Also

\[
\text{SST}=\sum (y_i-\bar y)^2=37.2.
\]

Therefore

\[
R^2=1-\frac{3.2}{37.2}
=1-\frac{16/5}{186/5}
=1-\frac{16}{186}
=\frac{85}{93}.
\]

Hence

\[
\boxed{R^2=\frac{85}{93}\approx 0.914.}
\]

So about \(91.4\%\) of the variation in \(Y\) is explained by the fitted linear regression on \(X\).

## Given data

\[
(x_i,y_i)=(-5,-2),(-3,1),(0,4),(2,6),(1,3),\qquad n=5.
\]

The simple linear regression model is

\[
y_i=\beta_0+x_i\beta_1+\varepsilon_i,\qquad \varepsilon_i\sim N(0,\sigma^2).
\]

Because the errors are normal, the least-squares estimates are also the maximum likelihood estimates for \(\beta_0,\beta_1\).

---

## (1) Estimate \(\beta_0,\beta_1\) and scatterplot with fitted line

Compute

\[
\bar x=\frac{-5-3+0+2+1}{5}=-1,
\]

\[
\bar y=\frac{-2+1+4+6+3}{5}=\frac{12}{5}=2.4.
\]

Also,

\[
S_{xx}=\sum_{i=1}^5 (x_i-\bar x)^2
= (-4)^2+(-2)^2+1^2+3^2+2^2=34,
\]

and

\[
S_{xy}=\sum_{i=1}^5 (x_i-\bar x)(y_i-\bar y)=34.
\]

Therefore,

\[
\widehat\beta_1=\frac{S_{xy}}{S_{xx}}=\frac{34}{34}=1,
\]

and

\[
\widehat\beta_0=\bar y-\widehat\beta_1\bar x
=2.4-1(-1)=3.4.
\]

Thus the fitted regression line is

\[
\boxed{\widehat y=3.4+x.}
\]

A rough scatterplot with the fitted line is:

\[
\begin{array}{c|cccccccc}
y & & & & & & & & \\
6 & & & & & & & * & \\
5 & & & & & & / & & \\
4 & & & & * & / & & & \\
3 & & & & & & * & & \\
2 & & & / & & & & & \\
1 & & * & & & & & & \\
0 & & / & & & & & & \\
-1 & / & & & & & & & \\
-2 & * & & & & & & & \\
\hline
 & -5 & -4 & -3 & -2 & -1 & 0 & 1 & 2
\end{array}
\]

The stars are the observed data points, and the slanted line represents \(\widehat y=3.4+x\).

---

## (2) Fitted values \(\widehat y_i\)

Using

\[
\widehat y_i=3.4+x_i,
\]

we get:

\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c}
i & x_i & \widehat y_i \\
\hline
1 & -5 & -1.6 \\
2 & -3 & 0.4 \\
3 & 0 & 3.4 \\
4 & 2 & 5.4 \\
5 & 1 & 4.4
\end{array}
\]

Equivalently,

\[
\widehat y=\left(-\frac85,\frac25,\frac{17}{5},\frac{27}{5},\frac{22}{5}\right).
\]

---

## (3) Residuals and residual plot

The residuals are

\[
e_i=y_i-\widehat y_i.
\]

Thus,

\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c}
i & x_i & y_i & \widehat y_i & e_i=y_i-\widehat y_i \\
\hline
1 & -5 & -2 & -1.6 & -0.4 \\
2 & -3 & 1 & 0.4 & 0.6 \\
3 & 0 & 4 & 3.4 & 0.6 \\
4 & 2 & 6 & 5.4 & 0.6 \\
5 & 1 & 3 & 4.4 & -1.4
\end{array}
\]

So

\[
\boxed{e=(-0.4,\ 0.6,\ 0.6,\ 0.6,\ -1.4).}
\]

A residual plot against \(x_i\) is approximately:

\[
\begin{array}{c|cccccc}
e_i & & & & & & \\
0.6 & & * & & * & & * \\
0 & \multicolumn{6}{c}{\text{----------------------------}} \\
-0.4 & * & & & & & \\
-1.4 & & & & & * & \\
\hline
& -5 & -3 & 0 & 1 & 2
\end{array}
\]

The residuals sum to zero, as expected in a regression with an intercept:

\[
\sum e_i=0.
\]

---

The total sum of squares is

\[
SST=\sum_{i=1}^5 (y_i-\bar y)^2.
\]

Since \(\bar y=2.4\),

\[
SST=(-2-2.4)^2+(1-2.4)^2+(4-2.4)^2+(6-2.4)^2+(3-2.4)^2.
\]

Thus,

\[
SST=19.36+1.96+2.56+12.96+0.36=37.2.
\]

The residual sum of squares is

\[
SSE=\sum_{i=1}^5 e_i^2
=(-0.4)^2+(0.6)^2+(0.6)^2+(0.6)^2+(-1.4)^2.
\]

So

\[
SSE=0.16+0.36+0.36+0.36+1.96=3.2.
\]

Therefore,

\[
R^2=1-\frac{SSE}{SST}
=1-\frac{3.2}{37.2}
=1-\frac{16}{186}
=\frac{170}{186}
=\frac{85}{93}.
\]

Hence,

\[
\boxed{R^2=\frac{85}{93}\approx 0.914.}
\]

So approximately \(91.4\%\) of the variation in \(Y\) is explained by the fitted linear regression on \(X\).

\[
\mu_1,\mu_2,\mu_3,\mu_4
\]

denote the mean weight loss after 8 weeks for the low-calorie, low-fat, low-carbohydrate, and control groups, respectively.

The one-way ANOVA hypotheses are

\[
H_0:\mu_1=\mu_2=\mu_3=\mu_4
\]

versus

\[
H_a:\text{not all four means are equal.}
\]

Equivalently, at least one diet group has a different mean weight loss.

---

### (2) ANOVA table

There are \(k=4\) groups with \(n_i=4\) subjects each, so

\[
N=16.
\]

Thus the degrees of freedom are:

\[
df_{\text{between}}=k-1=3,
\]

\[
df_{\text{within}}=N-k=12,
\]

\[
df_{\text{total}}=N-1=15.
\]

You are given

\[
SS_{\text{Total}}=114.4.
\]

Let

\[
SS_{\text{Diet}}=\sum_{i=1}^4 n_i(\bar y_i-\bar y_{\cdot\cdot})^2
\]

be the between-group sum of squares. Then

\[
SS_{\text{Error}}=114.4-SS_{\text{Diet}}.
\]

So the ANOVA table has the form:

| Source | df | SS | MS | F |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Diet | \(3\) | \(SS_{\text{Diet}}\) | \(SS_{\text{Diet}}/3\) | \(\dfrac{SS_{\text{Diet}}/3}{(114.4-SS_{\text{Diet}})/12}\) |
| Error | \(12\) | \(114.4-SS_{\text{Diet}}\) | \((114.4-SS_{\text{Diet}})/12\) |  |
| Total | \(15\) | \(114.4\) |  |  |

The test statistic simplifies to

\[
F=\frac{SS_{\text{Diet}}/3}{(114.4-SS_{\text{Diet}})/12}
=\frac{4SS_{\text{Diet}}}{114.4-SS_{\text{Diet}}}.
\]

---

### (3) Do we reject \(H_0\)?

With only the total sum of squares \(SS_{\text{Total}}=114.4\), we cannot determine whether to reject \(H_0\). To make the decision, we also need either the raw data, the four group means, \(SS_{\text{Diet}}\), or \(SS_{\text{Error}}\).

At significance level \(\alpha=0.05\), the critical value is approximately

\[
F_{0.95,3,12}\approx 3.49.
\]

Thus we would reject \(H_0\) if

\[
F>3.49.
\]

Equivalently,

\[
\frac{4SS_{\text{Diet}}}{114.4-SS_{\text{Diet}}}>3.49.
\]

Solving,

\[
SS_{\text{Diet}}>53.3.
\]

So at the \(5\%\) level, we reject if

\[
SS_{\text{Diet}}>53.3,
\]

and fail to reject otherwise.

Because \(SS_{\text{Diet}}\) is not provided, the rejection decision cannot be made from the information given.

Since “most powerful” requires a size constraint, I state part (1) as the most powerful level-\(\alpha\) test. Without a size constraint, the always-reject test is trivially most powerful.

## (1) MP test of \(H_0:\theta_1=\theta_2=2\) vs. \(H_1:\theta_1=1,\theta_2=3\)

Under \(H_0\),

\[
f_0(x,y)=4e^{-2x-2y}, \qquad x,y>0.
\]

Under \(H_1\),

\[
f_1(x,y)=3e^{-x-3y}, \qquad x,y>0.
\]

The likelihood ratio in favor of \(H_1\) is

\[
\frac{f_1(x,y)}{f_0(x,y)}
=
\frac{3e^{-x-3y}}{4e^{-2x-2y}}
=
\frac34 e^{x-y}.
\]

By the Neyman-Pearson lemma, the most powerful level-\(\alpha\) test rejects \(H_0\) for large values of \(f_1/f_0\), equivalently for large values of \(x-y\). Thus the rejection region has the form

\[
R_\alpha=\{(x,y):x-y>c_\alpha\},
\]

where \(c_\alpha\) is chosen so that

\[
P_{H_0}(X-Y>c_\alpha)=\alpha.
\]

Under \(H_0\), \(X,Y\stackrel{\text{iid}}{\sim}\operatorname{Exp}(2)\). If \(D=X-Y\), then

\[
P_{H_0}(D>c)
=
\begin{cases}
\dfrac12 e^{-2c}, & c\ge 0,\\[1em]
1-\dfrac12 e^{2c}, & c<0.
\end{cases}
\]

Therefore

\[
c_\alpha
=
\begin{cases}
-\dfrac12\log(2\alpha), & 0<\alpha\le \dfrac12,\\[1em]
\dfrac12\log\{2(1-\alpha)\}, & \dfrac12<\alpha<1.
\end{cases}
\]

So the MP level-\(\alpha\) test is

\[
\boxed{\text{Reject }H_0 \text{ if } X-Y>c_\alpha.}
\]

For the usual case \(\alpha\le 1/2\),

\[
\boxed{\text{Reject }H_0 \text{ if } X-Y>-\frac12\log(2\alpha).}
\]

---

## (2) LRT for \(H_0:\theta_1=\theta_2\) vs. \(H_1:\theta_1\ne \theta_2\)

The likelihood is

\[
L(\theta_1,\theta_2)
=
\theta_1\theta_2 e^{-\theta_1 x-\theta_2 y}.
\]

### Unrestricted MLE

Maximizing over \(\theta_1,\theta_2>0\),

\[
\widehat\theta_1=\frac1x,\qquad \widehat\theta_2=\frac1y.
\]

Thus

\[
\sup_{\theta_1,\theta_2} L(\theta_1,\theta_2)
=
\frac1x\frac1y e^{-1}e^{-1}
=
\frac{e^{-2}}{xy}.
\]

### MLE under \(H_0\)

Under \(H_0\), write \(\theta_1=\theta_2=\theta\). Then

\[
L_0(\theta)=\theta^2 e^{-\theta(x+y)}.
\]

The log-likelihood is

\[
\ell_0(\theta)=2\log\theta-\theta(x+y),
\]

so

\[
\widehat\theta=\frac{2}{x+y}.
\]

Therefore

\[
\sup_{\theta_1=\theta_2} L(\theta_1,\theta_2)
=
\left(\frac{2}{x+y}\right)^2 e^{-2}
=
\frac{4e^{-2}}{(x+y)^2}.
\]

Hence the likelihood ratio statistic is

\[
\Lambda(x,y)
=
\frac{\sup_{\theta_1=\theta_2}L(\theta_1,\theta_2)}
{\sup_{\theta_1,\theta_2}L(\theta_1,\theta_2)}
=
\frac{4e^{-2}/(x+y)^2}{e^{-2}/(xy)}
=
\frac{4xy}{(x+y)^2}.
\]

Let

\[
T=\frac{x}{x+y}.
\]

Then

\[
\frac{y}{x+y}=1-T,
\]

so

\[
\boxed{\Lambda(x,y)=4T(1-T)
=
4\frac{x}{x+y}\left(1-\frac{x}{x+y}\right).}
\]

The LRT rejects for small values of \(\Lambda\), so it rejects when \(T\) is far from \(1/2\).

Under \(H_0\), \(X,Y\) are iid exponentials with the same rate, so

\[
T=\frac{X}{X+Y}\sim \operatorname{Unif}(0,1).
\]

Thus the exact level-\(\alpha\) LRT rejects when

\[
T\le \frac{\alpha}{2}
\quad \text{or} \quad
T\ge 1-\frac{\alpha}{2}.
\]

Equivalently,

\[
\boxed{
\text{Reject }H_0
\text{ if }
\frac{X}{X+Y}\le \frac{\alpha}{2}
\text{ or }
\frac{X}{X+Y}\ge 1-\frac{\alpha}{2}.
}
\]

In likelihood-ratio form, since

\[
4T(1-T)\le 2\alpha-\alpha^2
\]

is equivalent to the above rejection region, the exact level-\(\alpha\) LRT is

\[
\boxed{
\text{Reject }H_0
\text{ if }
\Lambda(X,Y)=4\frac{X}{X+Y}\left(1-\frac{X}{X+Y}\right)
\le 2\alpha-\alpha^2.
}
\]

Let  
\[
S_{xx}=\sum_{i=1}^n x_i^2,\qquad S_{xy}=\sum_{i=1}^n x_iY_i,\qquad S_{yy}=\sum_{i=1}^n Y_i^2.
\]
Assume \(S_{xx}>0\); otherwise \(\beta\) is not identifiable.

## (1) A two-dimensional sufficient statistic

The joint density is
\[
f(y_1,\dots,y_n;\beta,\sigma^2)
=(2\pi\sigma^2)^{-n/2}
\exp\left\{-\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\sum_{i=1}^n (y_i-\beta x_i)^2\right\}.
\]
Now
\[
\sum_{i=1}^n (y_i-\beta x_i)^2
=
\sum_{i=1}^n y_i^2-2\beta\sum_{i=1}^n x_i y_i+\beta^2\sum_{i=1}^n x_i^2
=
S_{yy}-2\beta S_{xy}+\beta^2 S_{xx}.
\]
Since \(S_{xx}\) is fixed and known, the likelihood depends on the data only through
\[
T(Y)=\left(S_{xy},S_{yy}\right)
=
\left(\sum_{i=1}^n x_iY_i,\ \sum_{i=1}^n Y_i^2\right).
\]
Therefore, by the Fisher–Neyman factorization theorem,
\[
\boxed{T(Y)=\left(\sum_{i=1}^n x_iY_i,\ \sum_{i=1}^n Y_i^2\right)}
\]
is a two-dimensional sufficient statistic for \((\beta,\sigma^2)\).

Equivalently, one may use the one-to-one transformation
\[
\left(\widehat\beta,\operatorname{RSS}\right)
=
\left(
\frac{S_{xy}}{S_{xx}},
\ S_{yy}-\frac{S_{xy}^2}{S_{xx}}
\right).
\]

## (2) MLE of \(\beta\) and unbiasedness

The log-likelihood, ignoring constants, is
\[
\ell(\beta,\sigma^2)
=
-\frac n2\log\sigma^2
-\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\sum_{i=1}^n (Y_i-\beta x_i)^2.
\]
For fixed \(\sigma^2\), maximizing with respect to \(\beta\) is equivalent to minimizing
\[
Q(\beta)=\sum_{i=1}^n (Y_i-\beta x_i)^2
=S_{yy}-2\beta S_{xy}+\beta^2S_{xx}.
\]
Differentiate:
\[
\frac{dQ}{d\beta}=-2S_{xy}+2\beta S_{xx}.
\]
Setting this equal to \(0\) gives
\[
\widehat\beta=\frac{S_{xy}}{S_{xx}}
=
\frac{\sum_{i=1}^n x_iY_i}{\sum_{i=1}^n x_i^2}.
\]
Since \(S_{xx}>0\), this is the unique minimizer of \(Q(\beta)\), hence the MLE of \(\beta\).

Thus
\[
\boxed{\widehat\beta_{\text{MLE}}
=
\frac{\sum_{i=1}^n x_iY_i}{\sum_{i=1}^n x_i^2}.}
\]

\[
Y_i=\beta x_i+\varepsilon_i.
\]
Then
\[
\widehat\beta
=
\frac{\sum_{i=1}^n x_i(\beta x_i+\varepsilon_i)}{S_{xx}}
=
\beta+\frac{\sum_{i=1}^n x_i\varepsilon_i}{S_{xx}}.
\]
Because \(E[\varepsilon_i]=0\),
\[
E[\widehat\beta]
=
\beta+\frac{1}{S_{xx}}\sum_{i=1}^n x_iE[\varepsilon_i]
=
\beta.
\]
Hence
\[
\boxed{E[\widehat\beta]=\beta,}
\]
so the MLE of \(\beta\) is unbiased.

## (3) Distribution of \(\widehat\beta\)

From the same representation,
\[
\widehat\beta-\beta
=
\frac{\sum_{i=1}^n x_i\varepsilon_i}{S_{xx}}.
\]
Since the \(\varepsilon_i\) are independent \(N(0,\sigma^2)\), the linear combination \(\sum x_i\varepsilon_i\) is normal with mean \(0\) and variance
\[
\operatorname{Var}\left(\sum_{i=1}^n x_i\varepsilon_i\right)
=
\sum_{i=1}^n x_i^2\sigma^2
=
\sigma^2 S_{xx}.
\]
Therefore
\[
\operatorname{Var}(\widehat\beta)
=
\frac{\sigma^2S_{xx}}{S_{xx}^2}
=
\frac{\sigma^2}{S_{xx}}.
\]
Thus
\[
\boxed{
\widehat\beta \sim N\left(\beta,\frac{\sigma^2}{\sum_{i=1}^n x_i^2}\right).
}
\]

Equivalently,
\[
\boxed{
\frac{\widehat\beta-\beta}{\sigma/\sqrt{S_{xx}}}\sim N(0,1).
}
\]

If \(\sigma^2\) is estimated using the unbiased estimator
\[
s^2=\frac{1}{n-1}\sum_{i=1}^n (Y_i-\widehat\beta x_i)^2,
\]
then by Cochran’s theorem,
\[
\boxed{
\frac{\widehat\beta-\beta}{s/\sqrt{S_{xx}}}\sim t_{n-1}.
}
\]

\[
\mathbb{E}Y
=0\cdot \frac{33}{100}
+1\cdot \frac{27}{50}
+2\cdot \frac{13}{100}.
\]

Thus

\[
\mathbb{E}Y
=
\frac{27}{50}+\frac{26}{100}
=
\frac{54}{100}+\frac{26}{100}
=
\frac{80}{100}
=
\frac45.
\]

Therefore,

\[
\boxed{\mathbb{E}Y=\frac45.}
\]

---

## (3) \(P(\text{first ball red}\mid \text{second ball red})\)

We want

\[
P(R_1\mid R_2)=\frac{P(R_1\cap R_2)}{P(R_2)}.
\]

Now \(R_1\cap R_2\) is exactly the event \(Y=2\), so from part (1),

\[
P(R_1\cap R_2)=P(Y=2)=\frac{13}{100}.
\]

Also, regardless of whether sampling is with or without replacement, the marginal probability that the second ball is red is \(2/5\). Hence

\[
P(R_2)=\frac25.
\]

Therefore,

\[
P(R_1\mid R_2)
=
\frac{13/100}{2/5}
=
\frac{13}{100}\cdot \frac52
=
\frac{13}{40}.
\]

So

\[
\boxed{P(\text{first ball red}\mid \text{second ball red})=\frac{13}{40}.}
\]

---

## (4) \(P(\text{sampled with replacement}\mid Y=2)\)

We want

\[
P(H\mid Y=2).
\]

By Bayes’ theorem,

\[
P(H\mid Y=2)
=
\frac{P(Y=2\mid H)P(H)}{P(Y=2)}.
\]

We already have

\[
P(Y=2\mid H)=\frac{4}{25},\qquad P(H)=\frac12,
\]

and from part (1),

\[
P(Y=2)=\frac{13}{100}.
\]

Thus

\[
P(H\mid Y=2)
=
\frac{\left(\frac{4}{25}\right)\left(\frac12\right)}{\frac{13}{100}}
=
\frac{2/25}{13/100}
=
\frac{2}{25}\cdot \frac{100}{13}
=
\frac{8}{13}.
\]

Therefore,

\[
\boxed{P(\text{sampled with replacement}\mid Y=2)=\frac{8}{13}.}
\]

Let \(H\) denote heads (sampling **with** replacement) and \(T\) denote tails (sampling **without** replacement). Each has probability \(1/2\). Let \(R_i\) be the event that the \(i\)-th ball is red.

There are \(2\) red balls and \(3\) yellow balls, so the initial red probability is \(2/5\).

## (1) Distribution of \(Y\)

Conditioning on the coin flip:

- If \(H\), then \(Y \sim \mathrm{Binomial}(2,2/5)\), so

\[
P(Y=0\mid H)=\left(\frac35\right)^2=\frac{9}{25},
\]

\[
P(Y=1\mid H)=2\left(\frac25\right)\left(\frac35\right)=\frac{12}{25},
\]

\[
P(Y=2\mid H)=\left(\frac25\right)^2=\frac{4}{25}.
\]

- If \(T\), then \(Y\) has a hypergeometric distribution:

\[
P(Y=k\mid T)=\frac{\binom{2}{k}\binom{3}{2-k}}{\binom{5}{2}}.
\]

Thus

\[
P(Y=0\mid T)=\frac{\binom20\binom32}{\binom52}=\frac{3}{10},
\]

\[
P(Y=1\mid T)=\frac{\binom21\binom31}{\binom52}=\frac{6}{10}=\frac35,
\]

\[
P(Y=2\mid T)=\frac{\binom22\binom30}{\binom52}=\frac{1}{10}.
\]

By the law of total probability,

\[
P(Y=k)=\frac12 P(Y=k\mid H)+\frac12 P(Y=k\mid T).
\]

Therefore,

\[
P(Y=0)=\frac12\left(\frac{9}{25}\right)+\frac12\left(\frac{3}{10}\right)
=\frac{33}{100},
\]

\[
P(Y=1)=\frac12\left(\frac{12}{25}\right)+\frac12\left(\frac35\right)
=\frac{27}{50},
\]

\[
P(Y=2)=\frac12\left(\frac{4}{25}\right)+\frac12\left(\frac{1}{10}\right)
=\frac{13}{100}.
\]

So the distribution is

\[
\boxed{
P(Y=0)=\frac{33}{100},\quad
P(Y=1)=\frac{27}{50},\quad
P(Y=2)=\frac{13}{100}.
}
\]

---

## (2) \(\mathbb{E}Y\)

Using the distribution from part (1),

\[
\mathbb{E}Y
=0\cdot \frac{33}{100}
+1\cdot \frac{27}{50}
+2\cdot \frac{13}{100}.
\]

Thus

\[

=
\frac{54}{100}+\frac{26}{100}
=
\frac{80}{100}
=
\frac45.
\]

Therefore,

\[
\boxed{\mathbb{E}Y=\frac45.}
\]

---

## (3) \(P(\text{first ball red}\mid \text{second ball red})\)

We want

\[
P(R_1\mid R_2)=\frac{P(R_1\cap R_2)}{P(R_2)}.
\]

\[
P(R_1\cap R_2)=P(Y=2)=\frac{13}{100}.
\]

Also, regardless of whether sampling is with or without replacement, the marginal probability that the second ball is red is \(2/5\). Hence

\[
P(R_2)=\frac25.
\]

Therefore,

\[
P(R_1\mid R_2)
=
\frac{13/100}{2/5}
=
\frac{13}{100}\cdot \frac52
=
\frac{13}{40}.
\]

So

\[
\boxed{P(\text{first ball red}\mid \text{second ball red})=\frac{13}{40}.}
\]

---

## (4) \(P(\text{sampled with replacement}\mid Y=2)\)

We want

\[
P(H\mid Y=2).
\]

By Bayes’ theorem,

\[
P(H\mid Y=2)
=
\frac{P(Y=2\mid H)P(H)}{P(Y=2)}.
\]

We already have

\[
P(Y=2\mid H)=\frac{4}{25},\qquad P(H)=\frac12,
\]

and from part (1),

\[
P(Y=2)=\frac{13}{100}.
\]

Thus

\[
P(H\mid Y=2)
=
\frac{\left(\frac{4}{25}\right)\left(\frac12\right)}{\frac{13}{100}}
=
\frac{2/25}{13/100}
=
\frac{2}{25}\cdot \frac{100}{13}

\boxed{P(\text{sampled with replacement}\mid Y=2)=\frac{8}{13}.}
