Let \(\Phi\) denote the standard normal cdf and \(z_\gamma=\Phi^{-1}(\gamma)\).

## 1. Most powerful level-\(\alpha\) test for \(H_0:\theta=\theta_0\) vs. \(H_1:\theta=\theta_1\)

Put
\[
\mu_i=X\theta_i,\qquad i=0,1,
\]
and
\[
\Delta=\mu_1-\mu_0=X(\theta_1-\theta_0),\qquad d=\|\Delta\|_2.
\]

Under \(H_i\),
\[
Y\sim N(\mu_i,I_n).
\]

If \(d>0\), the log-likelihood ratio is
\[
\log \frac{dP_1}{dP_0}(Y)
=\Delta^\top Y-\frac12\left(\|\mu_1\|^2-\|\mu_0\|^2\right).
\]
Equivalently,
\[
\log \frac{dP_1}{dP_0}(Y)
=\Delta^\top(Y-\mu_0)-\frac12 d^2.
\]
Thus the likelihood ratio is an increasing function of
\[
T=\frac{\Delta^\top(Y-\mu_0)}{d}.
\]
Under \(H_0\),
\[
T\sim N(0,1),
\]
while under \(H_1\),
\[
T\sim N(d,1).
\]

By the Neyman-Pearson lemma, the most powerful level-\(\alpha\) test rejects \(H_0\) when
\[
T>z_{1-\alpha}.
\]
It has exact level \(\alpha\), and its power is
\[
P_{\theta_1}(T>z_{1-\alpha})
=
1-\Phi(z_{1-\alpha}-d)
=
\Phi(d-z_{1-\alpha}).
\]

Therefore the maximal power is
\[
\boxed{\Phi\!\left(\|X(\theta_1-\theta_0)\|_2-z_{1-\alpha}\right)}.
\]

If \(d=0\), then \(P_{\theta_0}=P_{\theta_1}\), so no test can have power exceeding its size. The maximal power is then \(\alpha\), which is also given by the same formula since \(\Phi(-z_{1-\alpha})=\alpha\).

---

## 2(a). Bernstein-von Mises theorem for the posterior

Let the true parameter be some fixed \(\theta^\star\in\mathbb R^p\). Assume throughout that
\[
\frac{X^\top X}{n}\to \Sigma
\]
with \(\Sigma\) positive definite. If \(\Sigma\) were singular, a full \(p\)-dimensional \(\sqrt n\)-Bernstein-von Mises theorem would generally fail in nonidentifiable directions.

Let
\[
S_n=X^\top X,\qquad A=\Lambda^{-1}.
\]
Since \(\Lambda\) is nonsingular and is a covariance matrix, \(A\) is positive definite.

The likelihood is
\[
p(Y\mid \theta)\propto \exp\left\{-\frac12\|Y-X\theta\|^2\right\},
\]
and the prior is
\[
\pi(\theta)\propto \exp\left\{-\frac12\theta^\top A\theta\right\}.
\]
Thus the posterior density satisfies
\[
\pi(\theta\mid Y)
\propto
\exp\left\{
-\frac12\left(\|Y-X\theta\|^2+\theta^\top A\theta\right)
\right\}.
\]
Expanding and completing the square,
\[
\|Y-X\theta\|^2+\theta^\top A\theta
=
\theta^\top(S_n+A)\theta-2\theta^\top X^\top Y+\text{constant}.
\]
Therefore
\[
\theta\mid Y \sim N(m_n,V_n),
\]
where
\[
V_n=(S_n+A)^{-1},
\qquad
m_n=(S_n+A)^{-1}X^\top Y.
\]

Because \(S_n/n\to \Sigma\succ 0\), \(S_n\) is invertible for all large \(n\). Define the least-squares estimator
\[
\widehat\theta_n=S_n^{-1}X^\top Y.
\]
Then
\[
m_n=(S_n+A)^{-1}S_n\widehat\theta_n.
\]
Hence
\[
m_n-\widehat\theta_n
=
\left((S_n+A)^{-1}S_n-I_p\right)\widehat\theta_n
=
-(S_n+A)^{-1}A\widehat\theta_n.
\]

Under the true parameter \(\theta^\star\),
\[
Y=X\theta^\star+\varepsilon,
\]
so
\[
\widehat\theta_n-\theta^\star
=
S_n^{-1}X^\top\varepsilon.
\]
Conditionally on \(X\),
\[
\widehat\theta_n-\theta^\star\sim N(0,S_n^{-1}).
\]
Since
\[
S_n^{-1}
=
\frac1n\left(\frac{S_n}{n}\right)^{-1}
=
O(n^{-1}),
\]
we have
\[
\widehat\theta_n=\theta^\star+O_P(n^{-1/2}),
\]
and in particular \(\widehat\theta_n=O_P(1)\).

Now consider the posterior distribution of
\[
Z_n=\sqrt n(\theta-\widehat\theta_n).
\]
Since \(\theta\mid Y\sim N(m_n,V_n)\),
\[
Z_n\mid Y \sim N(a_n,B_n),
\]
where
\[
a_n=\sqrt n(m_n-\widehat\theta_n),
\qquad
B_n=nV_n.
\]

First,
\[
B_n=n(S_n+A)^{-1}
=
\left(\frac{S_n}{n}+\frac{A}{n}\right)^{-1}.
\]
Because \(S_n/n\to \Sigma\) and \(A/n\to 0\),
\[
B_n\to \Sigma^{-1}.
\]

Second,
\[
a_n
=
-\sqrt n(S_n+A)^{-1}A\widehat\theta_n.
\]
Since \(S_n/n\to\Sigma\succ0\), there exists \(c>0\) such that for large \(n\),
\[
\lambda_{\min}(S_n)\ge cn.
\]
Thus
\[
\|(S_n+A)^{-1}\|=O(n^{-1}).
\]
Therefore
\[
\|a_n\|
\le
\sqrt n\,\|(S_n+A)^{-1}\|\,\|A\|\,\|\widehat\theta_n\|
=
O_P(n^{-1/2})
\to 0.
\]

Hence
\[
a_n\to 0,
\qquad
B_n\to \Sigma^{-1}.
\]

To conclude convergence in total variation, use the KL divergence formula for multivariate Gaussians. If \(C=\Sigma^{-1}\), then
\[
D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\left(N(a_n,B_n)\,\|\,N(0,C)\right)
=
\frac12\left[
\operatorname{tr}(C^{-1}B_n)
+a_n^\top C^{-1}a_n
-p
+\log\frac{\det C}{\det B_n}
\right].
\]
Since \(a_n\to0\) and \(B_n\to C\), the right-hand side tends to \(0\). By Pinsker's inequality,
\[
\left\|N(a_n,B_n)-N(0,\Sigma^{-1})\right\|_{\mathrm{TV}}
\to 0.
\]

Thus
\[
\boxed{
\left\|
\Pi\!\left(\sqrt n(\theta-\widehat\theta_n)\in\cdot\mid Y\right)
-
N(0,\Sigma^{-1})
\right\|_{\mathrm{TV}}
\to 0
}
\]
in \(P_{\theta^\star}\)-probability.

Equivalently,
\[
\boxed{
\left\|
\Pi\!\left(\sqrt n(\theta-\theta^\star)\in\cdot\mid Y\right)
-
N\!\left(\sqrt n(\widehat\theta_n-\theta^\star),\Sigma^{-1}\right)
\right\|_{\mathrm{TV}}
\to 0.
}
\]

Also,
\[
\sqrt n(\widehat\theta_n-\theta^\star)\mid X
\sim N\left(0,\left(\frac{X^\top X}{n}\right)^{-1}\right)
\Rightarrow N(0,\Sigma^{-1}).
\]
This is the Bernstein-von Mises theorem in this model.

---

## 2(b). Limit of the posterior mean as \(\lambda\to\infty\) for \(\Lambda=\lambda I_p\)

If \(\Lambda=\lambda I_p\), then
\[
\Lambda^{-1}=\lambda^{-1}I_p.
\]
Therefore the posterior covariance and mean are
\[
V_\lambda=(X^\top X+\lambda^{-1}I_p)^{-1},
\]
and
\[
m_\lambda
=
(X^\top X+\lambda^{-1}I_p)^{-1}X^\top Y.
\]
This is the ridge regression estimator with ridge penalty \(\lambda^{-1}\).

If \(X\) has full column rank, then \(X^\top X\) is invertible, and as \(\lambda\to\infty\),
\[
X^\top X+\lambda^{-1}I_p\to X^\top X.
\]
Therefore
\[
\boxed{
m_\lambda\to (X^\top X)^{-1}X^\top Y.
}
\]

So the posterior mean converges to the ordinary least-squares estimator.

Let \(\Phi\) denote the standard normal cdf and \(z_\gamma=\Phi^{-1}(\gamma)\).

## 1. Most powerful level-\(\alpha\) test for \(H_0:\theta=\theta_0\) vs. \(H_1:\theta=\theta_1\)

Put
\[
\mu_i=X\theta_i,\qquad i=0,1,
\]
and
\[
\Delta=\mu_1-\mu_0=X(\theta_1-\theta_0),\qquad d=\|\Delta\|_2.
\]

Under \(H_i\),
\[
Y\sim N(\mu_i,I_n).
\]

If \(d>0\), the log-likelihood ratio is
\[
\log \frac{dP_1}{dP_0}(Y)
=\Delta^\top Y-\frac12\left(\|\mu_1\|^2-\|\mu_0\|^2\right).
\]
Equivalently,
\[
\log \frac{dP_1}{dP_0}(Y)
=\Delta^\top(Y-\mu_0)-\frac12 d^2.
\]
Thus the likelihood ratio is an increasing function of
\[
T=\frac{\Delta^\top(Y-\mu_0)}{d}.
\]
Under \(H_0\),
\[
T\sim N(0,1),
\]
while under \(H_1\),
\[
T\sim N(d,1).
\]

By the Neyman-Pearson lemma, the most powerful level-\(\alpha\) test rejects \(H_0\) when
\[
T>z_{1-\alpha}.
\]
It has exact level \(\alpha\), and its power is
\[
P_{\theta_1}(T>z_{1-\alpha})
=
1-\Phi(z_{1-\alpha}-d)
=
\Phi(d-z_{1-\alpha}).
\]

Therefore the maximal power is
\[
\boxed{\Phi\!\left(\|X(\theta_1-\theta_0)\|_2-z_{1-\alpha}\right)}.
\]

If \(d=0\), then \(P_{\theta_0}=P_{\theta_1}\), so no test can have power exceeding its size. The maximal power is then \(\alpha\), which is also given by the same formula since \(\Phi(-z_{1-\alpha})=\alpha\).

---

## 2(a). Bernstein-von Mises theorem for the posterior

Let the true parameter be some fixed \(\theta^\star\in\mathbb R^p\). Assume throughout that
\[
\frac{X^\top X}{n}\to \Sigma
\]
with \(\Sigma\) positive definite. If \(\Sigma\) were singular, a full \(p\)-dimensional \(\sqrt n\)-Bernstein-von Mises theorem would generally fail in nonidentifiable directions.

Let
\[
S_n=X^\top X,\qquad A=\Lambda^{-1}.
\]
Since \(\Lambda\) is nonsingular and is a covariance matrix, \(A\) is positive definite.

The likelihood is
\[
p(Y\mid \theta)\propto \exp\left\{-\frac12\|Y-X\theta\|^2\right\},
\]
and the prior is
\[
\pi(\theta)\propto \exp\left\{-\frac12\theta^\top A\theta\right\}.
\]
Thus the posterior density satisfies
\[
\pi(\theta\mid Y)
\propto
\exp\left\{
-\frac12\left(\|Y-X\theta\|^2+\theta^\top A\theta\right)
\right\}.
\]
Expanding and completing the square,
\[
\|Y-X\theta\|^2+\theta^\top A\theta
=
\theta^\top(S_n+A)\theta-2\theta^\top X^\top Y+\text{constant}.
\]
Therefore
\[
\theta\mid Y \sim N(m_n,V_n),
\]
where
\[
V_n=(S_n+A)^{-1},
\qquad
m_n=(S_n+A)^{-1}X^\top Y.
\]

Because \(S_n/n\to \Sigma\succ 0\), \(S_n\) is invertible for all large \(n\). Define the least-squares estimator
\[
\widehat\theta_n=S_n^{-1}X^\top Y.
\]
Then
\[
m_n=(S_n+A)^{-1}S_n\widehat\theta_n.
\]
Hence
\[
m_n-\widehat\theta_n
=
\left((S_n+A)^{-1}S_n-I_p\right)\widehat\theta_n
=
-(S_n+A)^{-1}A\widehat\theta_n.
\]

Under the true parameter \(\theta^\star\),
\[
Y=X\theta^\star+\varepsilon,
\]
so
\[
\widehat\theta_n-\theta^\star
=
S_n^{-1}X^\top\varepsilon.
\]
Conditionally on \(X\),
\[
\widehat\theta_n-\theta^\star\sim N(0,S_n^{-1}).
\]
Since
\[
S_n^{-1}
=
\frac1n\left(\frac{S_n}{n}\right)^{-1}
=
O(n^{-1}),
\]
we have
\[
\widehat\theta_n=\theta^\star+O_P(n^{-1/2}),
\]
and in particular \(\widehat\theta_n=O_P(1)\).

Now consider the posterior distribution of
\[
Z_n=\sqrt n(\theta-\widehat\theta_n).
\]
Since \(\theta\mid Y\sim N(m_n,V_n)\),
\[
Z_n\mid Y \sim N(a_n,B_n),
\]
where
\[
a_n=\sqrt n(m_n-\widehat\theta_n),
\qquad
B_n=nV_n.
\]

First,
\[
B_n=n(S_n+A)^{-1}
=
\left(\frac{S_n}{n}+\frac{A}{n}\right)^{-1}.
\]
Because \(S_n/n\to \Sigma\) and \(A/n\to 0\),
\[
B_n\to \Sigma^{-1}.
\]

Second,
\[
a_n
=
-\sqrt n(S_n+A)^{-1}A\widehat\theta_n.
\]
Since \(S_n/n\to\Sigma\succ0\), there exists \(c>0\) such that for large \(n\),
\[
\lambda_{\min}(S_n)\ge cn.
\]
Thus
\[
\|(S_n+A)^{-1}\|=O(n^{-1}).
\]
Therefore
\[
\|a_n\|
\le
\sqrt n\,\|(S_n+A)^{-1}\|\,\|A\|\,\|\widehat\theta_n\|
=
O_P(n^{-1/2})
\to 0.
\]

Hence
\[
a_n\to 0,
\qquad
B_n\to \Sigma^{-1}.
\]

To conclude convergence in total variation, use the KL divergence formula for multivariate Gaussians. If \(C=\Sigma^{-1}\), then
\[
D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\left(N(a_n,B_n)\,\|\,N(0,C)\right)
=
\frac12\left[
\operatorname{tr}(C^{-1}B_n)
+a_n^\top C^{-1}a_n
-p
+\log\frac{\det C}{\det B_n}
\right].
\]
Since \(a_n\to0\) and \(B_n\to C\), the right-hand side tends to \(0\). By Pinsker's inequality,
\[
\left\|N(a_n,B_n)-N(0,\Sigma^{-1})\right\|_{\mathrm{TV}}
\to 0.
\]

Thus
\[
\boxed{
\left\|
\Pi\!\left(\sqrt n(\theta-\widehat\theta_n)\in\cdot\mid Y\right)
-
N(0,\Sigma^{-1})
\right\|_{\mathrm{TV}}
\to 0
}
\]
in \(P_{\theta^\star}\)-probability.

Equivalently,
\[
\boxed{
\left\|
\Pi\!\left(\sqrt n(\theta-\theta^\star)\in\cdot\mid Y\right)
-
N\!\left(\sqrt n(\widehat\theta_n-\theta^\star),\Sigma^{-1}\right)
\right\|_{\mathrm{TV}}
\to 0.
}
\]

Also,
\[
\sqrt n(\widehat\theta_n-\theta^\star)\mid X
\sim N\left(0,\left(\frac{X^\top X}{n}\right)^{-1}\right)
\Rightarrow N(0,\Sigma^{-1}).
\]
This is the Bernstein-von Mises theorem in this model.

---

## 2(b). Limit of the posterior mean as \(\lambda\to\infty\) for \(\Lambda=\lambda I_p\)

If \(\Lambda=\lambda I_p\), then
\[
\Lambda^{-1}=\lambda^{-1}I_p.
\]
Therefore the posterior covariance and mean are
\[
V_\lambda=(X^\top X+\lambda^{-1}I_p)^{-1},
\]
and
\[
m_\lambda
=
(X^\top X+\lambda^{-1}I_p)^{-1}X^\top Y.
\]
This is the ridge regression estimator with ridge penalty \(\lambda^{-1}\).

If \(X\) has full column rank, then \(X^\top X\) is invertible, and as \(\lambda\to\infty\),
\[
X^\top X+\lambda^{-1}I_p\to X^\top X.
\]
Therefore
\[
\boxed{
m_\lambda\to (X^\top X)^{-1}X^\top Y.
}
\]

So the posterior mean converges to the ordinary least-squares estimator.

response.text:
Let \(P_n f=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n f(x_i,y_i)\), \(\bar x=P_nx\), \(\bar y=P_ny\). Define the population least-squares/control-variate coefficient

\[
\beta^*:=\arg\min_\beta \mathbb E\{y-\alpha^*-x^T\beta\}^2
=\Sigma^{-1}\mathbb E\{x(y-\alpha^*)\},
\]

when \(\Sigma=\mathbb E(xx^T)\) is nonsingular, and define

\[
\varphi(x,y):=y-\alpha^*-x^T\beta^*.
\]

Then \(\mathbb E\varphi=0\) and \(\mathbb E(x\varphi)=0\).

---

## (i) Least-squares intercept

The objective is

\[
Q_n(\alpha,\beta)=\frac1{2n}\sum_{i=1}^n (y_i-\alpha-x_i^T\beta)^2 .
\]

For any minimizer \((\hat\alpha,\hat\beta)\), the first-order condition with respect to the unpenalized intercept \(\alpha\) is

\[
0=\frac{\partial Q_n}{\partial \alpha}(\hat\alpha,\hat\beta)
=-\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n (y_i-\hat\alpha-x_i^T\hat\beta).
\]

Therefore

\[
\hat\alpha
=\bar y-\bar x^T\hat\beta .
\]

---

## (ii) Fixed \(p\): asymptotic normality of \(\hat\alpha\)

Assume \(p\) is fixed, \(\Sigma=\mathbb E(xx^T)\) is nonsingular, and the relevant second moments are finite.

By part (i),

\[
\hat\alpha-\alpha^*
=
\bar y-\alpha^*-\bar x^T\hat\beta .
\]

Add and subtract \(\bar x^T\beta^*\):

\[
\hat\alpha-\alpha^*
=
P_n(y-\alpha^*-x^T\beta^*)-\bar x^T(\hat\beta-\beta^*).
\]

Thus

\[
\sqrt n(\hat\alpha-\alpha^*)
=
\frac1{\sqrt n}\sum_{i=1}^n \varphi(x_i,y_i)
-\sqrt n\,\bar x^T(\hat\beta-\beta^*).
\]

For fixed \(p\), standard least-squares consistency gives

\[
\hat\beta\overset{p}\to \beta^*,
\]

and since \(\mathbb E x=0\),

\[
\bar x=O_p(n^{-1/2}).
\]

Hence

\[
\sqrt n\,\bar x^T(\hat\beta-\beta^*)
=
O_p(1)o_p(1)
=o_p(1).
\]

By the classical central limit theorem,

\[
\frac1{\sqrt n}\sum_{i=1}^n \varphi(x_i,y_i)
\overset{d}\longrightarrow N(0,V),
\]

where

\[
V=\mathbb E\{\varphi^2(x,y)\}
=
\mathbb E\{y-\alpha^*-x^T\beta^*\}^2.
\]

Therefore

\[
\boxed{
\sqrt n(\hat\alpha-\alpha^*)\overset{d}\longrightarrow N(0,V)
}
\]

with influence function

\[
\boxed{
\varphi(x,y)=y-\alpha^*-x^T\beta^*.
}
\]

---

## (iii) Lasso intercept

The Lasso objective is

\[
L_n(\alpha,\beta)
=
\frac1{2n}\sum_{i=1}^n (y_i-\alpha-x_i^T\beta)^2
+\lambda\|\beta\|_1.
\]

The penalty does not involve \(\alpha\). Therefore, for any minimizer \((\tilde\alpha,\tilde\beta)\), the first-order condition with respect to \(\alpha\) is

\[
0
=
-\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n (y_i-\tilde\alpha-x_i^T\tilde\beta).
\]

Hence

\[
\boxed{
\tilde\alpha=\bar y-\bar x^T\tilde\beta .
}
\]

Equivalently, after profiling out the intercept, \(\tilde\beta\) minimizes the centered Lasso problem

\[
\tilde\beta
\in
\arg\min_\beta
\left\{
\frac1{2n}\sum_{i=1}^n
\left[(y_i-\bar y)-(x_i-\bar x)^T\beta\right]^2
+\lambda\|\beta\|_1
\right\}.
\]

---

## (iv) Conditions for standard Lasso bounds

Let

\[
\varepsilon_i
=
y_i-\alpha^*-x_i^T\beta^*
=
\varphi(x_i,y_i),
\qquad
S:=S_{\beta^*}:=\{j:\beta_j^*\neq 0\},
\qquad
s:=|S|.
\]

The standard Lasso bounds are of the form

\[
\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n
\left\{(x_i-\bar x)^T(\tilde\beta-\beta^*)\right\}^2
=
O_p(s\lambda_0^2),
\]

and

\[
\|\tilde\beta-\beta^*\|_1
=
O_p(s\lambda_0),
\]

with

\[
\lambda_0=\sqrt{\frac{\log(1+p)}{n}}.
\]

A weak and standard set of sufficient technical conditions is the following.

1. **Sparsity.**  
   \(\beta^*\) is sparse with support size \(s=|S_{\beta^*}|\), and typically

   \[
   s\frac{\log(1+p)}{n}\to 0.
   \]

2. **Score concentration.**  
   The empirical score satisfies

   \[
   \left\|
   \frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n
   (x_i-\bar x)(\varepsilon_i-\bar\varepsilon)
   \right\|_\infty
   =
   O_p\left(\sqrt{\frac{\log(1+p)}{n}}\right).
   \]

   This holds, for example, if \(|x^{(j)}|\le B_0\) a.s. and the residual \(\varepsilon\) is uniformly bounded or sub-Gaussian, together with \(\mathbb E(x\varepsilon)=0\).

3. **Restricted eigenvalue / compatibility condition.**  
   There exists \(\kappa>0\) such that with probability tending to one, for every \(h\in\mathbb R^p\) satisfying a cone condition

   \[
   \|h_{S^c}\|_1\le c\|h_S\|_1,
   \]

   one has

   \[
   \frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\{(x_i-\bar x)^Th\}^2
   \ge
   \kappa^2 \|h_S\|_2^2,
   \]

   or equivalently the compatibility version

   \[
   \frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\{(x_i-\bar x)^Th\}^2
   \ge
   \frac{\kappa^2}{s}\|h_S\|_1^2.
   \]

Under these conditions and with \(\lambda\asymp \lambda_0\), standard Lasso theory yields

\[
\boxed{
\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n
\left\{(x_i-\bar x)^T(\tilde\beta-\beta^*)\right\}^2
=
O_p\left(s\frac{\log(1+p)}{n}\right)
}
\]

and

\[
\boxed{
\|\tilde\beta-\beta^*\|_1
=
O_p\left(s\sqrt{\frac{\log(1+p)}{n}}\right).
}
\]

---

## (v) High-probability event and basic inequality

Assume additionally that the residual is bounded:

\[
|\varepsilon|=|y-\alpha^*-x^T\beta^*|\le B_\varepsilon
\qquad\text{a.s.}
\]

Let

\[
\lambda_{0,\delta}
=
C_0
\sqrt{\frac{\log((1+p)/\delta)}{n}}.
\]

One may take

\[
\boxed{
C_0=4B_0B_\varepsilon .
}
\]

Define the event

\[
\Omega_0
=
\left\{
\left\|
\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n
(x_i-\bar x)(\varepsilon_i-\bar\varepsilon)
\right\|_\infty
\le
\lambda_{0,\delta}
\right\}.
\]

Using Hoeffding’s inequality and a union bound, under \(|x^{(j)}|\le B_0\) and \(|\varepsilon|\le B_\varepsilon\),

\[
\mathbb P(\Omega_0)\ge 1-2\delta.
\]

Let

\[
h:=\tilde\beta-\beta^*.
\]

Because \(\tilde\beta\) minimizes the centered Lasso criterion,

\[
\frac1{2n}\sum_{i=1}^n
\left[(\varepsilon_i-\bar\varepsilon)-(x_i-\bar x)^Th\right]^2
+\lambda\|\beta^*+h\|_1
\le
\frac1{2n}\sum_{i=1}^n
(\varepsilon_i-\bar\varepsilon)^2
+\lambda\|\beta^*\|_1.
\]

Expanding gives

\[
\frac1{2n}\sum_{i=1}^n
\{(x_i-\bar x)^Th\}^2
+\lambda\|\beta^*+h\|_1
\le
\left[
\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n
(x_i-\bar x)(\varepsilon_i-\bar\varepsilon)
\right]^T h
+\lambda\|\beta^*\|_1.
\]

On \(\Omega_0\),

\[
\left|
\left[
\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n
(x_i-\bar x)(\varepsilon_i-\bar\varepsilon)
\right]^T h
\right|
\le
\lambda_{0,\delta}\|h\|_1.
\]

Thus, with \(\lambda=A_0\lambda_{0,\delta}\), \(A_0>1\),

\[
\boxed{
\frac1{2n}\sum_{i=1}^n
\{(x_i-\bar x)^T(\tilde\beta-\beta^*)\}^2
+\lambda\|\tilde\beta\|_1
\le
\lambda_{0,\delta}\|\tilde\beta-\beta^*\|_1
+\lambda\|\beta^*\|_1.
}
\]

Equivalently, writing \(S=S_{\beta^*}\),

\[
\boxed{
\frac1{2n}\sum_{i=1}^n
\{(x_i-\bar x)^Th\}^2
+(\lambda-\lambda_{0,\delta})\|h_{S^c}\|_1
\le
(\lambda+\lambda_{0,\delta})\|h_S\|_1.
}
\]

Since \(\lambda=A_0\lambda_{0,\delta}\), this becomes

\[
\boxed{
\frac1{2n}\sum_{i=1}^n
\{(x_i-\bar x)^Th\}^2
+(A_0-1)\lambda_{0,\delta}\|h_{S^c}\|_1
\le
(A_0+1)\lambda_{0,\delta}\|h_S\|_1.
}
\]

In particular,

\[
\|h_{S^c}\|_1
\le
\frac{A_0+1}{A_0-1}\|h_S\|_1.
\]

---

## (vi) Asymptotic normality of \(\tilde\alpha\)

By part (iii),

\[
\tilde\alpha-\alpha^*
=
\bar y-\alpha^*-\bar x^T\tilde\beta.
\]

Add and subtract \(\bar x^T\beta^*\):

\[
\tilde\alpha-\alpha^*
=
P_n(y-\alpha^*-x^T\beta^*)
-\bar x^T(\tilde\beta-\beta^*).
\]

Thus

\[
\sqrt n(\tilde\alpha-\alpha^*)
=
\frac1{\sqrt n}\sum_{i=1}^n \varepsilon_i
-
\sqrt n\,\bar x^T(\tilde\beta-\beta^*).
\]

The first term satisfies, by the classical central limit theorem,

\[
\frac1{\sqrt n}\sum_{i=1}^n \varepsilon_i
\overset{d}\longrightarrow N(0,V),
\]

where

\[
V=\mathbb E(\varepsilon^2)
=
\mathbb E\{y-\alpha^*-x^T\beta^*\}^2.
\]

It remains to show that the second term is \(o_p(1)\). By Hölder’s inequality,

\[
\left|
\sqrt n\,\bar x^T(\tilde\beta-\beta^*)
\right|
\le
\sqrt n\,\|\bar x\|_\infty
\|\tilde\beta-\beta^*\|_1.
\]

Since \(|x^{(j)}|\le B_0\) a.s. and \(\mathbb E x^{(j)}=0\), Hoeffding’s inequality and a union bound give

\|\bar x\|_\infty

Let \(P_n f=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n f(x_i,y_i)\), \(\bar x=P_nx\), \(\bar y=P_ny\). Define the population least-squares/control-variate coefficient

\[
\beta^*:=\arg\min_\beta \mathbb E\{y-\alpha^*-x^T\beta\}^2
=\Sigma^{-1}\mathbb E\{x(y-\alpha^*)\},
\]

when \(\Sigma=\mathbb E(xx^T)\) is nonsingular, and define

\[
\varphi(x,y):=y-\alpha^*-x^T\beta^*.
\]

Then \(\mathbb E\varphi=0\) and \(\mathbb E(x\varphi)=0\).

---

## (i) Least-squares intercept

The objective is

\[
Q_n(\alpha,\beta)=\frac1{2n}\sum_{i=1}^n (y_i-\alpha-x_i^T\beta)^2 .
\]

For any minimizer \((\hat\alpha,\hat\beta)\), the first-order condition with respect to the unpenalized intercept \(\alpha\) is

\[
0=\frac{\partial Q_n}{\partial \alpha}(\hat\alpha,\hat\beta)
=-\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n (y_i-\hat\alpha-x_i^T\hat\beta).
\]

Therefore

\[
\hat\alpha
=\bar y-\bar x^T\hat\beta .
\]

---

## (ii) Fixed \(p\): asymptotic normality of \(\hat\alpha\)

Assume \(p\) is fixed, \(\Sigma=\mathbb E(xx^T)\) is nonsingular, and the relevant second moments are finite.

By part (i),

\[
\hat\alpha-\alpha^*
=
\bar y-\alpha^*-\bar x^T\hat\beta .
\]

Add and subtract \(\bar x^T\beta^*\):

\[
\hat\alpha-\alpha^*
=
P_n(y-\alpha^*-x^T\beta^*)-\bar x^T(\hat\beta-\beta^*).
\]

Thus

\[
\sqrt n(\hat\alpha-\alpha^*)
=
\frac1{\sqrt n}\sum_{i=1}^n \varphi(x_i,y_i)
-\sqrt n\,\bar x^T(\hat\beta-\beta^*).
\]

For fixed \(p\), standard least-squares consistency gives

\[
\hat\beta\overset{p}\to \beta^*,
\]

and since \(\mathbb E x=0\),

\[
\bar x=O_p(n^{-1/2}).
\]

Hence

\[
\sqrt n\,\bar x^T(\hat\beta-\beta^*)
=
O_p(1)o_p(1)
=o_p(1).
\]

By the classical central limit theorem,

\[
\frac1{\sqrt n}\sum_{i=1}^n \varphi(x_i,y_i)
\overset{d}\longrightarrow N(0,V),
\]

where

\[
V=\mathbb E\{\varphi^2(x,y)\}
=
\mathbb E\{y-\alpha^*-x^T\beta^*\}^2.
\]

Therefore

\[
\boxed{
\sqrt n(\hat\alpha-\alpha^*)\overset{d}\longrightarrow N(0,V)
}
\]

with influence function

\[
\boxed{
\varphi(x,y)=y-\alpha^*-x^T\beta^*.
}
\]

---

## (iii) Lasso intercept

The Lasso objective is

\[
L_n(\alpha,\beta)
=
\frac1{2n}\sum_{i=1}^n (y_i-\alpha-x_i^T\beta)^2
+\lambda\|\beta\|_1.
\]

The penalty does not involve \(\alpha\). Therefore, for any minimizer \((\tilde\alpha,\tilde\beta)\), the first-order condition with respect to \(\alpha\) is

\[
0
=
-\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n (y_i-\tilde\alpha-x_i^T\tilde\beta).
\]

Hence

\[
\boxed{
\tilde\alpha=\bar y-\bar x^T\tilde\beta .
}
\]

Equivalently, after profiling out the intercept, \(\tilde\beta\) minimizes the centered Lasso problem

\[
\tilde\beta
\in
\arg\min_\beta
\left\{
\frac1{2n}\sum_{i=1}^n
\left[(y_i-\bar y)-(x_i-\bar x)^T\beta\right]^2
+\lambda\|\beta\|_1
\right\}.
\]

---

## (iv) Conditions for standard Lasso bounds

Let

\[
\varepsilon_i
=
y_i-\alpha^*-x_i^T\beta^*
=
\varphi(x_i,y_i),
\qquad
S:=S_{\beta^*}:=\{j:\beta_j^*\neq 0\},
\qquad
s:=|S|.
\]

The standard Lasso bounds are of the form

\[
\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n
\left\{(x_i-\bar x)^T(\tilde\beta-\beta^*)\right\}^2
=
O_p(s\lambda_0^2),
\]

and

\[
\|\tilde\beta-\beta^*\|_1
=
O_p(s\lambda_0),
\]

with

\[
\lambda_0=\sqrt{\frac{\log(1+p)}{n}}.
\]

A weak and standard set of sufficient technical conditions is the following.

1. **Sparsity.**  
   \(\beta^*\) is sparse with support size \(s=|S_{\beta^*}|\), and typically

   \[
   s\frac{\log(1+p)}{n}\to 0.
   \]

2. **Score concentration.**  
   The empirical score satisfies

   \[
   \left\|
   \frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n
   (x_i-\bar x)(\varepsilon_i-\bar\varepsilon)
   \right\|_\infty
   =
   O_p\left(\sqrt{\frac{\log(1+p)}{n}}\right).
   \]

   This holds, for example, if \(|x^{(j)}|\le B_0\) a.s. and the residual \(\varepsilon\) is uniformly bounded or sub-Gaussian, together with \(\mathbb E(x\varepsilon)=0\).

3. **Restricted eigenvalue / compatibility condition.**  
   There exists \(\kappa>0\) such that with probability tending to one, for every \(h\in\mathbb R^p\) satisfying a cone condition

   \[
   \|h_{S^c}\|_1\le c\|h_S\|_1,
   \]

   one has

   \[
   \frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\{(x_i-\bar x)^Th\}^2
   \ge
   \kappa^2 \|h_S\|_2^2,
   \]

   or equivalently the compatibility version

   \[
   \frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\{(x_i-\bar x)^Th\}^2
   \ge
   \frac{\kappa^2}{s}\|h_S\|_1^2.
   \]

Under these conditions and with \(\lambda\asymp \lambda_0\), standard Lasso theory yields

\[
\boxed{
\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n
\left\{(x_i-\bar x)^T(\tilde\beta-\beta^*)\right\}^2
=
O_p\left(s\frac{\log(1+p)}{n}\right)
}
\]

and

\[
\boxed{
\|\tilde\beta-\beta^*\|_1
=
O_p\left(s\sqrt{\frac{\log(1+p)}{n}}\right).
}
\]

---

## (v) High-probability event and basic inequality

Assume additionally that the residual is bounded:

\[
|\varepsilon|=|y-\alpha^*-x^T\beta^*|\le B_\varepsilon
\qquad\text{a.s.}
\]

Let

\[
\lambda_{0,\delta}
=
C_0
\sqrt{\frac{\log((1+p)/\delta)}{n}}.
\]

One may take

\[
\boxed{
C_0=4B_0B_\varepsilon .
}
\]

Define the event

\[
\Omega_0
=
\left\{
\left\|
\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n
(x_i-\bar x)(\varepsilon_i-\bar\varepsilon)
\right\|_\infty
\le
\lambda_{0,\delta}
\right\}.
\]

Using Hoeffding’s inequality and a union bound, under \(|x^{(j)}|\le B_0\) and \(|\varepsilon|\le B_\varepsilon\),

\[
\mathbb P(\Omega_0)\ge 1-2\delta.
\]

Let

\[
h:=\tilde\beta-\beta^*.
\]

Because \(\tilde\beta\) minimizes the centered Lasso criterion,

\[
\frac1{2n}\sum_{i=1}^n
\left[(\varepsilon_i-\bar\varepsilon)-(x_i-\bar x)^Th\right]^2
+\lambda\|\beta^*+h\|_1
\le
\frac1{2n}\sum_{i=1}^n
(\varepsilon_i-\bar\varepsilon)^2
+\lambda\|\beta^*\|_1.
\]

Expanding gives

\[
\frac1{2n}\sum_{i=1}^n
\{(x_i-\bar x)^Th\}^2
+\lambda\|\beta^*+h\|_1
\le
\left[
\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n
(x_i-\bar x)(\varepsilon_i-\bar\varepsilon)
\right]^T h
+\lambda\|\beta^*\|_1.
\]

On \(\Omega_0\),

\[
\left|
\left[
\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n
(x_i-\bar x)(\varepsilon_i-\bar\varepsilon)
\right]^T h
\right|
\le
\lambda_{0,\delta}\|h\|_1.
\]

Thus, with \(\lambda=A_0\lambda_{0,\delta}\), \(A_0>1\),

\[
\boxed{
\frac1{2n}\sum_{i=1}^n
\{(x_i-\bar x)^T(\tilde\beta-\beta^*)\}^2
+\lambda\|\tilde\beta\|_1
\le
\lambda_{0,\delta}\|\tilde\beta-\beta^*\|_1
+\lambda\|\beta^*\|_1.
}
\]

Equivalently, writing \(S=S_{\beta^*}\),

\[
\boxed{
\frac1{2n}\sum_{i=1}^n
\{(x_i-\bar x)^Th\}^2
+(\lambda-\lambda_{0,\delta})\|h_{S^c}\|_1
\le
(\lambda+\lambda_{0,\delta})\|h_S\|_1.
}
\]

Since \(\lambda=A_0\lambda_{0,\delta}\), this becomes

\[
\boxed{
\frac1{2n}\sum_{i=1}^n
\{(x_i-\bar x)^Th\}^2
+(A_0-1)\lambda_{0,\delta}\|h_{S^c}\|_1
\le
(A_0+1)\lambda_{0,\delta}\|h_S\|_1.
}
\]

In particular,

\[
\|h_{S^c}\|_1
\le
\frac{A_0+1}{A_0-1}\|h_S\|_1.
\]

---

## (vi) Asymptotic normality of \(\tilde\alpha\)

By part (iii),

\[
\tilde\alpha-\alpha^*
=
\bar y-\alpha^*-\bar x^T\tilde\beta.
\]

Add and subtract \(\bar x^T\beta^*\):

\[
\tilde\alpha-\alpha^*
=
P_n(y-\alpha^*-x^T\beta^*)
-\bar x^T(\tilde\beta-\beta^*).
\]

Thus

\[
\sqrt n(\tilde\alpha-\alpha^*)
=
\frac1{\sqrt n}\sum_{i=1}^n \varepsilon_i
-
\sqrt n\,\bar x^T(\tilde\beta-\beta^*).
\]

The first term satisfies, by the classical central limit theorem,

\[
\frac1{\sqrt n}\sum_{i=1}^n \varepsilon_i
\overset{d}\longrightarrow N(0,V),
\]

where

\[
V=\mathbb E(\varepsilon^2)
=
\mathbb E\{y-\alpha^*-x^T\beta^*\}^2.
\]

It remains to show that the second term is \(o_p(1)\). By Hölder’s inequality,

\[
\left|
\sqrt n\,\bar x^T(\tilde\beta-\beta^*)
\right|
\le
\sqrt n\,\|\bar x\|_\infty
\|\tilde\beta-\beta^*\|_1.
\]

Since \(|x^{(j)}|\le B_0\) a.s. and \(\mathbb E x^{(j)}=0\), Hoeffding’s inequality and a union bound give

\[
\|\bar x\|_\infty
=
O_p\left(\sqrt{\frac{\log(1+p)}{n}}\right).
\]

By the assumed Lasso \(\ell_1\)-bound,

\[
\|\tilde\beta-\beta^*\|_1
=
O_p\left(
s\sqrt{\frac{\log(1+p)}{n}}
\right),
\qquad s=|S_{\beta^*}|.
\]

Therefore

\[
\left|
\sqrt n\,\bar x^T(\tilde\beta-\beta^*)
\right|
=
O_p\left(
\sqrt n
\sqrt{\frac{\log(1+p)}{n}}
s\sqrt{\frac{\log(1+p)}{n}}
\right)
=
O_p\left(
\frac{s\log(1+p)}{\sqrt n}
\right).
\]

Under the condition

\[
(1+s)\log(1+p)=o(n^{1/2}),
\]

we have

\[
\frac{s\log(1+p)}{\sqrt n}\to 0,
\]

and hence

\[
\sqrt n\,\bar x^T(\tilde\beta-\beta^*)
=o_p(1).
\]

Thus, by Slutsky’s theorem,

\[
\boxed{
\sqrt n(\tilde\alpha-\alpha^*)
\overset{d}\longrightarrow N(0,V),
}
\]

with the same variance as in part (ii),

\[
\boxed{
V=\mathbb E\{y-\alpha^*-x^T\beta^*\}^2.
}
\]

\[
\beta^*=\Sigma^{-1}\mathbb E\{x(y-\alpha^*)\}.
\]

\[

\]

\[

\[

=-\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n (y_i-\hat\alpha-x_i^\top\hat\beta).
\]
Hence
\[
\hat\alpha=\bar y-\bar x^\top\hat\beta,
\]
where
\[
\bar y=\frac1n\sum_i y_i,\qquad \bar x=\frac1n\sum_i x_i.
\]

\[
\hat\alpha-\alpha^*
=\bar y-\alpha^*-\bar x^\top\hat\beta.

\[

=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n (y_i-\alpha^*-x_i^\top\beta^*)
-\bar x^\top(\hat\beta-\beta^*).
\]
Thus
\[
\sqrt n(\hat\alpha-\alpha^*)
=
\frac1{\sqrt n}\sum_{i=1}^n \{y_i-\alpha^*-x_i^\top\beta^*\}
-\sqrt n\,\bar x^\top(\hat\beta-\beta^*).
\]

\[
\hat\beta\to_p \beta^*.
\]

\[
\sqrt n\,\bar x=O_p(1).
\]
Therefore
\[
\sqrt n\,\bar x^\top(\hat\beta-\beta^*)=o_p(1).
\]

\[
\sqrt n(\hat\alpha-\alpha^*)
=
\frac1{\sqrt n}\sum_{i=1}^n \varphi(x_i,y_i)+o_p(1),

\[
\boxed{\varphi(x,y)=y-\alpha^*-x^\top\beta^*.}

\[
\sqrt n(\hat\alpha-\alpha^*)\xrightarrow{d}N(0,V),

where
\[
\boxed{V=\mathbb E\{\varphi^2(x,y)\}
=\mathbb E\{y-\alpha^*-x^\top\beta^*\}^2.}
\]

The Lasso criterion is
\[

=

Therefore
\[

[2023 summer phd probability — problem 1]

Part I, Exercise 1. Let $(X_n)_{n\ge1}$ be a sequence of random variables.
Prove the equivalence: $X_n \xrightarrow{P} 0 \iff \mathbb{E}[\min(1, |X_n|)] \to 0$.

response.text:
Let

\[
Y_n:=\min(1,|X_n|).
\]

Then \(0\le Y_n\le 1\), so \(\mathbb E[Y_n]\) is always well-defined.

We prove both directions.

---

## \((\Rightarrow)\) Suppose \(X_n \xrightarrow{P}0\)

By definition, for every \(\varepsilon>0\),

\[
\mathbb P(|X_n|>\varepsilon)\to 0.
\]

Fix \(0<\varepsilon<1\). We split according to whether \(|X_n|\le \varepsilon\) or \(|X_n|>\varepsilon\). Since \(\min(1,|X_n|)\le \varepsilon\) on \(\{|X_n|\le \varepsilon\}\), and \(\min(1,|X_n|)\le 1\) always, we have

\[
\min(1,|X_n|)
\le \varepsilon + \mathbf 1_{\{|X_n|>\varepsilon\}}.
\]

Taking expectations,

\[
\mathbb E[\min(1,|X_n|)]
\le \varepsilon + \mathbb P(|X_n|>\varepsilon).
\]

Letting \(n\to\infty\), using convergence in probability,

\[
\limsup_{n\to\infty}\mathbb E[\min(1,|X_n|)]
\le \varepsilon.
\]

Since this holds for every \(0<\varepsilon<1\), letting \(\varepsilon\downarrow 0\) gives

\[
\mathbb E[\min(1,|X_n|)]\to 0.
\]

---

## \((\Leftarrow)\) Suppose \(\mathbb E[\min(1,|X_n|)]\to 0\)

We must show that for every \(\varepsilon>0\),

\[
\mathbb P(|X_n|>\varepsilon)\to 0.
\]

On the event \(\{|X_n|>\varepsilon\}\), we have

\[
\min(1,|X_n|)\ge \min(1,\varepsilon).
\]

Therefore,

\[
\min(1,\varepsilon)\mathbf 1_{\{|X_n|>\varepsilon\}}
\le \min(1,|X_n|).
\]

Taking expectations gives

\[
\min(1,\varepsilon)\mathbb P(|X_n|>\varepsilon)
\le \mathbb E[\min(1,|X_n|)].
\]

Since \(\min(1,\varepsilon)>0\), we obtain

\[
\mathbb P(|X_n|>\varepsilon)
\le
\frac{\mathbb E[\min(1,|X_n|)]}{\min(1,\varepsilon)}

\]

we get

=
\int_A 2 f(v)p(v)\,dv.

---

### (1) Prove \(\bar d(t)\le 2d(t)\)

For any \(x,y\in \mathcal X\), by the triangle inequality for total variation distance,

\[
\|P^t(x,\cdot)-P^t(y,\cdot)\|_{TV}
\le 
\|P^t(x,\cdot)-\pi\|_{TV}
+
\|\pi-P^t(y,\cdot)\|_{TV}.
\]

Each term is at most \(d(t)\), so

\[
\|P^t(x,\cdot)-P^t(y,\cdot)\|_{TV}\le 2d(t).
\]

Taking the maximum over \(x,y\) gives

\[
\bar d(t)\le 2d(t).
\]

---

### (2) Prove \(d(t)\le \bar d(t)\)

Since \(\pi\) is stationary, \(\pi P^t=\pi\). Thus

\[
\pi(\cdot)=\sum_{y\in\mathcal X}\pi(y)P^t(y,\cdot).
\]

Fix \(x\in\mathcal X\). Then

\[
P^t(x,\cdot)-\pi
=
\sum_{y\in\mathcal X}\pi(y)\bigl(P^t(x,\cdot)-P^t(y,\cdot)\bigr).
\]

Using convexity of the total variation norm,

\[
\|P^t(x,\cdot)-\pi\|_{TV}
\le
\sum_{y\in\mathcal X}\pi(y)
\|P^t(x,\cdot)-P^t(y,\cdot)\|_{TV}.
\]

Each term is at most \(\bar d(t)\), so

\[
\|P^t(x,\cdot)-\pi\|_{TV}\le \bar d(t).
\]

Taking the maximum over \(x\) gives

\[
d(t)\le \bar d(t).
\]

---

### (3) Prove \(d(t+1)\le d(t)\)

For any probability measures \(\mu,\nu\) and any Markov kernel \(P\),

\[
\|\mu P-\nu P\|_{TV}\le \|\mu-\nu\|_{TV}.
\]

Indeed,

\[
\begin{aligned}
\|\mu P-\nu P\|_{TV}
&=
\frac12\sum_y \left|\sum_x(\mu(x)-\nu(x))P(x,y)\right| \\
&\le
\frac12\sum_y\sum_x|\mu(x)-\nu(x)|P(x,y) \\
&=
\frac12\sum_x|\mu(x)-\nu(x)|\sum_yP(x,y) \\
&=
\|\mu-\nu\|_{TV}.
\end{aligned}
\]

Now use \(\pi P=\pi\). For any \(x\),

\[
\begin{aligned}
\|P^{t+1}(x,\cdot)-\pi\|_{TV}
&=
\|P^t(x,\cdot)P-\pi P\|_{TV}\\
&\le
\|P^t(x,\cdot)-\pi\|_{TV}.
\end{aligned}
\]

Taking the maximum over \(x\),

\[
d(t+1)\le d(t).
\]

\[
\begin{aligned}

&=

&\le
\bar d(t)\|P^s(x,\cdot)-P^s(y,\cdot)\|_{TV}.
\end{aligned}
\]

Taking the maximum over \(x,y\),

\[
\bar d(s+t)\le \bar d(s)\bar d(t).
\]

Now let \(m=t_{\mathrm{mix}}\). By definition,

\[
d(m)\le \frac14.

\[
\bar d(m)\le 2d(m)\le \frac12.

Using submultiplicativity repeatedly,

\[
\bar d(km)\le \bar d(m)^k\le \left(\frac12\right)^k.
\]

By part (2),

\[
d(km)\le \bar d(km).
\]

Therefore

\[
d(k\,t_{\mathrm{mix}})\le 2^{-k}.

---

Since \(Z\sim \mathrm{Unif}\{1,\dots,T\}\) is independent of the chain,

\[

&=

\[
\|\nu_x-\pi\|_{TV}
\le
\frac1{7m}\sum_{t=1}^{7m}
\|P^t(x,\cdot)-\pi\|_{TV}
\le
\frac1{7m}\sum_{t=1}^{7m} d(t).

\[

Since \(d(t)\le 1\) always, the first block contributes at most \(m\).

\[

For block \(j\ge 2\), i.e. \(t\in\{jm+1,\dots,(j+1)m\}\), monotonicity gives

\[
d(t)\le d(jm).
\]

By part (4),

\[
d(jm)\le 2^{-j}.

Hence

\[

\[

\le

=

Therefore

\[
\|\nu_x-\pi\|_{TV}
\le
\frac1{7m}\cdot \frac{7m}{4}
=
\frac14.
\]

Since the bound is uniform in \(x\),

\[
\boxed{\max_x \|\nu_x-\pi\|_{TV}\le \frac14.}
\]

=\frac{60.6}{3.1524}

## (5) If ANOVA rejects, how to find which means differ?

Use a multiple-comparisons procedure controlling the familywise error rate, such as:

- Tukey’s HSD,
- Bonferroni pairwise comparisons,
- Scheffé’s method,

\[
|\bar Y_{\cdot j\cdot}-\bar Y_{\cdot j'\cdot}|

\[
an=2(3)=6

observations, Tukey’s cutoff is

\[
q_{0.90;4,16}\sqrt{\frac{MS_E}{6}}.

\[

The same is done for the four-bedroom variable and the style variable.

For house \(i\), let \(C(i)\) be its assigned cluster.

The within-cluster average dissimilarity is

\[
a(i)
=
\frac{1}{|C(i)|-1}
\sum_{\substack{j\in C(i)\\j\ne i}} d(i,j).

Since there are only two clusters, the between-cluster average dissimilarity is simply

\[
b(i)
=
\frac{1}{|C'|}

where \(C'\) is the other cluster.

\[
s(i)
=
\frac{b(i)-a(i)}{\max\{a(i),b(i)\}}.

The silhouette plot would display the seven \(s(i)\) values as horizontal bars, grouped by cluster and usually sorted from largest to smallest within each cluster.

[2024 fall ms math-stat — problem 2]

Single observation $Y$ with density $f(y\mid\theta) = (\theta+1)y^\theta$, $0<y<1$. Test $H_0: \theta = 0$ vs $H_a: \theta > 0$ at level $\alpha$. (1) Show a UMP test exists, find it, and give its exact form in terms of $\alpha$. (2) Give its power function in terms of $\alpha$.

response.text:
Let \(0<\alpha<1\). The density is

\[
f(y\mid \theta)=(\theta+1)y^\theta,\qquad 0<y<1,
\]

with \(\theta>-1\). We test

\[
H_0:\theta=0 \qquad \text{vs.}\qquad H_a:\theta>0.
\]

Under \(H_0\), \(Y\sim \operatorname{Unif}(0,1)\).

---

## (1) UMP level \(\alpha\) test

For fixed \(\theta>0\), the likelihood ratio of \(\theta\) versus \(0\) is

\[
\frac{f(y\mid \theta)}{f(y\mid 0)}
=
(\theta+1)y^\theta.
\]

Since \(\theta>0\), this is an increasing function of \(y\) on \((0,1)\). Therefore, by the Neyman–Pearson lemma, the most powerful level \(\alpha\) test of

\[
H_0:\theta=0
\]

against the simple alternative

\[
H_1:\theta=\theta_1>0
\]

rejects for large values of \(Y\).

Because the rejection region has the same form for every \(\theta_1>0\), namely

\[
Y>c,
\]

the same test is most powerful against every simple alternative \(\theta_1>0\). Hence it is UMP for testing \(H_0:\theta=0\) against \(H_a:\theta>0\).

Under \(H_0\), \(Y\sim \operatorname{Unif}(0,1)\), so choose \(c\) such that

\[
P_0(Y>c)=\alpha.
\]

Since \(P_0(Y>c)=1-c\), we get

\[
c=1-\alpha.
\]

Thus the UMP level \(\alpha\) test is

\[
\varphi_\alpha(Y)
=
\begin{cases}
1, & Y>1-\alpha,\\
0, & Y\le 1-\alpha.
\end{cases}
\]

Equivalently, reject \(H_0\) iff

\[
Y>1-\alpha.
\]

Because the distribution is continuous, no randomization is needed. Its size is exactly

\[
P_0(Y>1-\alpha)=\alpha.
\]

---

## (2) Power function

For general \(\theta>-1\), the CDF of \(Y\) is

\[
F_\theta(y)
=
\int_0^y (\theta+1)t^\theta\,dt
=
y^{\theta+1}, \qquad 0<y<1.
\]

Therefore the power function of the test is

\[
\pi(\theta)
=
P_\theta(Y>1-\alpha).
\]

Using the CDF,

\[
\pi(\theta)
=
1-F_\theta(1-\alpha)
=
1-(1-\alpha)^{\theta+1}.
\]

In particular, under \(H_0\),

\[
\pi(0)=1-(1-\alpha)=\alpha,
\]

so the test has exact level \(\alpha\).

Thus the power function is

\[
\boxed{\pi(\theta)=1-(1-\alpha)^{\theta+1}}, \qquad \theta>-1,
\]

and on the alternative \(\theta>0\),

\[
\boxed{\pi(\theta)=1-(1-\alpha)^{\theta+1}>\alpha.}
\]

$Y_1, Y_2$ have joint density $f(y_1,y_2\mid\theta) = \frac{8}{\theta^4}y_1 y_2$ for $0 \le y_2 \le y_1 \le \theta$. (1) Is $Y_2$ a sufficient statistic for $\theta$? (prove). (2) Find the MLE of $\theta$. (3) Is the MLE unbiased?

response.text:
**Given joint density**
\[
f(y_1,y_2\mid \theta)=\frac{8}{\theta^4}y_1y_2,\qquad 0\le y_2\le y_1\le \theta.
\]

Equivalently,
\[
f(y_1,y_2\mid \theta)=\frac{8}{\theta^4}y_1y_2\,\mathbf 1\{0\le y_2\le y_1\le \theta\}.
\]

---

## (1) Is \(Y_2\) sufficient for \(\theta\)?

No, \(Y_2\) is **not** sufficient for \(\theta\).

One way to prove this is by examining the conditional distribution of \(Y_1\) given \(Y_2\). If \(Y_2\) were sufficient for \(\theta\), then the conditional distribution of the full data \((Y_1,Y_2)\) given \(Y_2\) would not depend on \(\theta\).

First find the marginal density of \(Y_2\):

\[
f_{Y_2}(y_2\mid \theta)
= \int_{y_2}^{\theta} \frac{8}{\theta^4}y_1y_2\,dy_1,
\qquad 0\le y_2\le \theta.
\]

Thus

\[
f_{Y_2}(y_2\mid \theta)
= \frac{8y_2}{\theta^4}\int_{y_2}^{\theta} y_1\,dy_1
= \frac{8y_2}{\theta^4}\cdot \frac{\theta^2-y_2^2}{2}
= \frac{4y_2(\theta^2-y_2^2)}{\theta^4}.
\]

Therefore, for \(y_2\le y_1\le \theta\),

\[
f_{Y_1\mid Y_2}(y_1\mid y_2,\theta)
=
\frac{f(y_1,y_2\mid \theta)}{f_{Y_2}(y_2\mid \theta)}.
\]

So

\[
f_{Y_1\mid Y_2}(y_1\mid y_2,\theta)
=
\frac{\frac{8}{\theta^4}y_1y_2}{\frac{4y_2(\theta^2-y_2^2)}{\theta^4}}
=
\frac{2y_1}{\theta^2-y_2^2},
\qquad y_2\le y_1\le \theta.
\]

This conditional density depends on \(\theta\), both through the denominator and through the support \(y_1\le \theta\). Hence the conditional distribution of \(Y_1\) given \(Y_2\) depends on \(\theta\).

Therefore, by the conditional distribution characterization of sufficiency, \(Y_2\) is **not sufficient** for \(\theta\).

---

## (2) Find the MLE of \(\theta\)

The likelihood is

\[
L(\theta;y_1,y_2)
=
\frac{8}{\theta^4}y_1y_2\mathbf 1\{0\le y_2\le y_1\le \theta\}.
\]

For observed \(0<y_2\le y_1\), the likelihood as a function of \(\theta\) is

\[
L(\theta)
=
\frac{8y_1y_2}{\theta^4},\qquad \theta\ge y_1.
\]

Since \(\theta^{-4}\) is strictly decreasing in \(\theta\), the likelihood is maximized by taking the smallest allowable value of \(\theta\), namely

\[
\widehat\theta_{\text{MLE}}=Y_1.
\]

So the MLE is

\[
\boxed{\widehat\theta=Y_1.}
\]

---

## (3) Is the MLE unbiased?

The MLE is \(\widehat\theta=Y_1\). We compute \(E_\theta[Y_1]\).

First find the marginal density of \(Y_1\):

\[
f_{Y_1}(y_1\mid \theta)
=
\int_0^{y_1}\frac{8}{\theta^4}y_1y_2\,dy_2,
\qquad 0\le y_1\le \theta.
\]

Thus

\[
f_{Y_1}(y_1\mid \theta)
=
\frac{8y_1}{\theta^4}\int_0^{y_1}y_2\,dy_2
=
\frac{8y_1}{\theta^4}\cdot \frac{y_1^2}{2}
=
\frac{4y_1^3}{\theta^4}.
\]

Then

\[
E_\theta[Y_1]
=
\int_0^\theta y_1\frac{4y_1^3}{\theta^4}\,dy_1
=
\frac{4}{\theta^4}\int_0^\theta y_1^4\,dy_1
=
\frac{4}{\theta^4}\cdot \frac{\theta^5}{5}
=
\frac{4\theta}{5}.
\]

Therefore,

\[
E_\theta[\widehat\theta]
=
E_\theta[Y_1]
=
\frac{4\theta}{5}
\neq \theta.
\]

So the MLE is biased downward, with bias

\[
\operatorname{Bias}_\theta(\widehat\theta)
=
\frac{4\theta}{5}-\theta
=
-\frac{\theta}{5}.
\]

Hence the MLE is **not unbiased**.

\[
\boxed{\widehat\theta=Y_1 \text{ is biased, with } E_\theta[\widehat\theta]=\frac{4\theta}{5}.}
\]

Let the parameter space be \(\Theta=(0,\infty)\). Write the joint density as

\[
f_\theta(y_1,y_2)=\frac{8}{\theta^4}y_1y_2\,\mathbf 1\{0\le y_2\le y_1\le \theta\}.
\]

## (1) Is \(Y_2\) sufficient for \(\theta\)?

No.

To prove this rigorously, compute the conditional distribution of \(Y_1\) given \(Y_2\). First, the marginal density of \(Y_2\) is

\[
f_{Y_2}(t\mid \theta)
= \int_t^\theta \frac{8}{\theta^4} y_1 t\,dy_1
= \frac{4t}{\theta^4}(\theta^2-t^2),
\qquad 0<t<\theta.
\]

Hence, for \(0<t<\theta\),

\[
f_{Y_1\mid Y_2}(x\mid t;\theta)
=
\frac{f_\theta(x,t)}{f_{Y_2}(t\mid\theta)}
=
\frac{\frac{8}{\theta^4}xt}{\frac{4t}{\theta^4}(\theta^2-t^2)}
=
\frac{2x}{\theta^2-t^2},
\qquad t\le x\le \theta.
\]

This conditional density depends on \(\theta\), both through the denominator and through its support.

For example, for \(0<t<2\),

\[
P_\theta(Y_1\le 2\mid Y_2=t)
=
\frac{\int_t^2 2x\,dx}{\theta^2-t^2}
=
\frac{4-t^2}{\theta^2-t^2}.
\]

Taking \(\theta=3\) and \(\theta=4\), this gives

\[
P_3(Y_1\le 2\mid Y_2=t)
=
\frac{4-t^2}{9-t^2},
\]

whereas

\[
P_4(Y_1\le 2\mid Y_2=t)
=
\frac{4-t^2}{16-t^2}.
\]

These differ on a set of positive probability. Therefore the conditional distribution of the full data given \(Y_2\) depends on \(\theta\). By the conditional-distribution criterion for sufficiency, \(Y_2\) is not sufficient for \(\theta\).

\[
\boxed{Y_2 \text{ is not sufficient for } \theta.}
\]

---

## (2) Find the MLE of \(\theta\)

For an observed pair \((y_1,y_2)\) with \(0\le y_2\le y_1\), the likelihood is

\[
L(\theta;y_1,y_2)
=
\frac{8}{\theta^4}y_1y_2\,\mathbf 1\{\theta\ge y_1\}.
\]

For \(\theta\ge y_1\),

\[
L(\theta;y_1,y_2)\propto \theta^{-4},
\]

which is strictly decreasing in \(\theta\). Thus the likelihood is maximized by taking the smallest allowable value of \(\theta\), namely

\[
\widehat\theta_{\text{MLE}}=y_1.
\]

Therefore,

\[
\boxed{\widehat\theta_{\text{MLE}}=Y_1.}
\]

---

## (3) Is the MLE unbiased?

We need compute \(E_\theta[Y_1]\). The marginal density of \(Y_1\) is

\[
f_{Y_1}(x\mid\theta)
=
\int_0^x \frac{8}{\theta^4}xy_2\,dy_2
=
\frac{8x}{\theta^4}\cdot \frac{x^2}{2}
=
\frac{4x^3}{\theta^4},
\qquad 0<x<\theta.
\]

Thus

\[
E_\theta[Y_1]
=
\int_0^\theta x\frac{4x^3}{\theta^4}\,dx
=
\frac{4}{\theta^4}\int_0^\theta x^4\,dx
=
\frac{4}{\theta^4}\cdot \frac{\theta^5}{5}
=
\frac{4\theta}{5}.
\]

Since

\[
E_\theta[\widehat\theta_{\text{MLE}}]
=
E_\theta[Y_1]
=
\frac{4\theta}{5}
\neq \theta,
\]

the MLE is biased downward. Its bias is

\[
\operatorname{Bias}_\theta(Y_1)
=
\frac{4\theta}{5}-\theta
=
-\frac{\theta}{5}.
\]

Therefore,

\[
\boxed{\widehat\theta_{\text{MLE}}=Y_1 \text{ is not unbiased.}}
\]

[2024 fall ms math-stat — problem 3]

$Y_1, Y_2$ have joint density $f(y_1,y_2\mid\theta) = \frac{8}{\theta^4}y_1 y_2$ for $0 \le y_2 \le y_1 \le \theta$. (1) Is $Y_2$ a sufficient statistic for $\theta$? (prove). (2) Find the MLE of $\theta$. (3) Is the MLE unbiased?

response.text:
**(1) Is \(Y_2\) sufficient for \(\theta\)?**

No.

By the Neyman–Fisher factorization theorem, \(Y_2\) would be sufficient for \(\theta\) only if the joint density could be written as

\[
f(y_1,y_2\mid \theta)=g_\theta(y_2)h(y_1,y_2),
\]

where all dependence on \(\theta\) is through \(y_2\).

But the joint density is

\[
f(y_1,y_2\mid \theta)=\frac{8}{\theta^4}y_1y_2 \mathbf 1\{0\le y_2\le y_1\le \theta\}.
\]

The support condition contains the restriction \(y_1\le \theta\), which depends on \(y_1\), not only on \(y_2\). Thus the likelihood depends on \(\theta\) through \(Y_1\), so \(Y_2\) cannot be sufficient.

Equivalently, compute the conditional distribution of \(Y_1\) given \(Y_2=y_2\). First,

\[
f_{Y_2}(y_2\mid \theta)
=
\int_{y_2}^{\theta} \frac{8}{\theta^4}y_1y_2\,dy_1
=
\frac{8y_2}{\theta^4}\cdot \frac{\theta^2-y_2^2}{2}
=
\frac{4y_2(\theta^2-y_2^2)}{\theta^4},
\]

for \(0\le y_2\le \theta\). Hence

\[
f_{Y_1\mid Y_2}(y_1\mid y_2,\theta)
=
\frac{f(y_1,y_2\mid \theta)}{f_{Y_2}(y_2\mid \theta)}
=
\frac{\frac{8}{\theta^4}y_1y_2}{\frac{4y_2(\theta^2-y_2^2)}{\theta^4}}
=
\frac{2y_1}{\theta^2-y_2^2},
\]

for

\[
y_2\le y_1\le \theta.
\]

This conditional distribution depends on \(\theta\). Therefore \(Y_2\) is not sufficient for \(\theta\).

\[
\boxed{Y_2 \text{ is not sufficient for } \theta.}
\]

---

**(2) Find the MLE of \(\theta\).**

For observed \((y_1,y_2)\), the likelihood is

\[
L(\theta;y_1,y_2)
=
\frac{8}{\theta^4}y_1y_2 \mathbf 1\{\theta\ge y_1\}.
\]

For fixed data with \(y_1y_2>0\), this is proportional to

\[
\theta^{-4}\mathbf 1\{\theta\ge y_1\}.
\]

Since \(\theta^{-4}\) is strictly decreasing in \(\theta\), the likelihood is maximized by taking the smallest permissible \(\theta\), namely

\[
\widehat{\theta}_{\text{MLE}}=y_1.
\]

Thus

\[
\boxed{\widehat{\theta}_{\text{MLE}}=Y_1.}
\]

---

**(3) Is the MLE unbiased?**

Since the MLE is \(\widehat{\theta}=Y_1\), we compute \(E_\theta[Y_1]\).

The marginal density of \(Y_1\) is

\[
f_{Y_1}(y_1\mid \theta)
=
\int_0^{y_1} \frac{8}{\theta^4}y_1y_2\,dy_2
=
\frac{8y_1}{\theta^4}\cdot \frac{y_1^2}{2}
=
\frac{4y_1^3}{\theta^4},
\]

for \(0\le y_1\le \theta\). Therefore

\[
E_\theta[Y_1]
=
\int_0^\theta y_1 \frac{4y_1^3}{\theta^4}\,dy_1
=
\frac{4}{\theta^4}\int_0^\theta y_1^4\,dy_1
=
\frac{4}{\theta^4}\cdot \frac{\theta^5}{5}
=
\frac{4}{5}\theta.
\]

Thus

\[
E_\theta[\widehat{\theta}_{\text{MLE}}]
=
\frac{4}{5}\theta \neq \theta.
\]

So the MLE is biased downward. Its bias is

\[
\operatorname{Bias}_\theta(\widehat{\theta})
=
E_\theta[\widehat{\theta}]-\theta
=
\frac{4}{5}\theta-\theta
=
-\frac{1}{5}\theta.
\]

Therefore,

\[
\boxed{\widehat{\theta}_{\text{MLE}}=Y_1 \text{ is biased, with bias } -\frac{\theta}{5}.}
\]

[2024 fall ms probability — problem 1]

$X$ has pmf $P(X=x) = c(2x+1)$ for $x = 0,1,2$. (1) Find $c$. (2) Compute $P(X=2)$. (3) $\mathbb{E}[X]$. (4) $\operatorname{Var}(X)$. (5) For 10 i.i.d. copies, find the distribution of the maximum. (6) Compute $P(\min(X_1,\dots,X_{10}) > 0)$.

response.thinking:
**Addressing rigorous calculations**

I need to create a thorough and straightforward answer that tackles all parts. First, I should discuss the distribution and possibly include the probability mass function (pmf) and cumulative distribution function (cdf). I'll determine the pmf with weights and calculate the expected values, variance, and other statistical measures. Then, I’ll compute the cumulative distribution function for independent variables, defining probabilities for specific intervals. Finally, I need to emphasize independence in these calculations and provide clear labels throughout.
response.text:
Let

\[
P(X=x)=c(2x+1), \qquad x=0,1,2.
\]

The unnormalized weights are

\[
2(0)+1=1,\qquad 2(1)+1=3,\qquad 2(2)+1=5.
\]

So the probabilities are proportional to \(1,3,5\).

---

### (1) Find \(c\)

Since probabilities must sum to 1,

\[
\sum_{x=0}^2 c(2x+1)=1.
\]

Thus

\[
c(1+3+5)=1,
\]

so

\[
9c=1.
\]

Therefore,

\[
\boxed{c=\frac{1}{9}}.
\]

---

### (2) Compute \(P(X=2)\)

\[
P(X=2)=c(2(2)+1)=\frac{1}{9}\cdot 5.
\]

Hence

\[
\boxed{P(X=2)=\frac{5}{9}}.
\]

---

### (3) Compute \(\mathbb{E}[X]\)

The pmf is

\[
P(X=0)=\frac{1}{9},\qquad P(X=1)=\frac{3}{9},\qquad P(X=2)=\frac{5}{9}.
\]

Therefore,

\[
\mathbb{E}[X]
=0\cdot \frac{1}{9}+1\cdot \frac{3}{9}+2\cdot \frac{5}{9}.
\]

So

\[
\mathbb{E}[X]=\frac{3}{9}+\frac{10}{9}
=\frac{13}{9}.
\]

Thus

\[
\boxed{\mathbb{E}[X]=\frac{13}{9}}.
\]

---

### (4) Compute \(\operatorname{Var}(X)\)

We use

\[
\operatorname{Var}(X)=\mathbb{E}[X^2]-\left(\mathbb{E}[X]\right)^2.
\]

First compute

\[
\mathbb{E}[X^2]
=0^2\cdot \frac{1}{9}+1^2\cdot \frac{3}{9}+2^2\cdot \frac{5}{9}.
\]

Thus

\[
\mathbb{E}[X^2]
=\frac{3}{9}+\frac{20}{9}
=\frac{23}{9}.
\]

Since \(\mathbb{E}[X]=13/9\),

\[
\operatorname{Var}(X)
=\frac{23}{9}-\left(\frac{13}{9}\right)^2.
\]

Putting over a common denominator,

\[
\operatorname{Var}(X)
=\frac{207}{81}-\frac{169}{81}
=\frac{38}{81}.
\]

Therefore,

\[
\boxed{\operatorname{Var}(X)=\frac{38}{81}}.
\]

---

### (5) For 10 i.i.d. copies, find the distribution of the maximum

Let

\[
M=\max(X_1,\dots,X_{10}),
\]

where \(X_1,\dots,X_{10}\) are i.i.d. copies of \(X\).

First compute the cdf of \(X\):

\[
P(X\le 0)=\frac{1}{9},
\]

\[
P(X\le 1)=\frac{1}{9}+\frac{3}{9}=\frac{4}{9},
\]

\[
P(X\le 2)=1.
\]

Using independence,

\[
P(M\le m)=P(X_1\le m,\dots,X_{10}\le m)
=\left(P(X\le m)\right)^{10}.
\]

Thus the cdf of \(M\) is

\[
P(M\le m)=
\begin{cases}
0, & m<0,\\[4pt]
\left(\frac{1}{9}\right)^{10}, & 0\le m<1,\\[4pt]
\left(\frac{4}{9}\right)^{10}, & 1\le m<2,\\[4pt]
1, & m\ge 2.
\end{cases}
\]

Equivalently, the pmf of \(M\) is

\[
P(M=0)=\left(\frac{1}{9}\right)^{10},
\]

\[
P(M=1)=\left(\frac{4}{9}\right)^{10}-\left(\frac{1}{9}\right)^{10},
\]

and

\[
P(M=2)=1-\left(\frac{4}{9}\right)^{10}.
\]

So

\[
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
P(M=0)&=\left(\frac{1}{9}\right)^{10},\\
P(M=1)&=\left(\frac{4}{9}\right)^{10}-\left(\frac{1}{9}\right)^{10},\\
P(M=2)&=1-\left(\frac{4}{9}\right)^{10}.
\end{aligned}
}
\]

---

### (6) Compute \(P(\min(X_1,\dots,X_{10})>0)\)

Let

\[
Y=\min(X_1,\dots,X_{10}).
\]

The event \(\{Y>0\}\) means all ten variables are positive:

\[
\min(X_1,\dots,X_{10})>0
\iff X_1>0,\dots,X_{10}>0.
\]

Now

\[
P(X>0)=P(X=1)+P(X=2)=\frac{3}{9}+\frac{5}{9}=\frac{8}{9}.
\]

By independence,

\[
P(\min(X_1,\dots,X_{10})>0)
=\left(P(X>0)\right)^{10}
=\left(\frac{8}{9}\right)^{10}.
\]

Therefore,

\[
\boxed{P(\min(X_1,\dots,X_{10})>0)=\left(\frac{8}{9}\right)^{10}}.
\]

Use a **paired \(t\)-test**, because baseline and final measurements are taken on the same patients.

Define the paired reductions

\[
D_i = B_i - F_i,
\]

so that \(D_i>0\) means cholesterol decreased. Assume

\[
D_1,\dots,D_{10} \overset{iid}{\sim} N(\mu_D,\sigma_D^2).
\]

\[
H_0:\mu_D \le 0
\]

\[
H_1:\mu_D > 0.
\]

\[
T=\frac{\bar D}{s_D/\sqrt{10}},

\[
\bar D = \frac1{10}\sum_{i=1}^{10} D_i,
\qquad
s_D^2 = \frac1{9}\sum_{i=1}^{10}(D_i-\bar D)^2.
\]

\[
T \sim t_9.
\]

At significance level \(\alpha=0.05\), reject \(H_0\) if

\[
T > t_{0.95,9} \approx 1.833.

\[

1500 insects in six dose groups of 250; $X_j$ = log-dose, $Y_j$ = number dead. Logistic regression with MLEs $\hat\beta_0 = -2.64$, $\hat\beta_1 = 0.67$. (1) State the fitted response function. (2) Estimated probability of death at $X = 3.5$. (3) Estimated median lethal dose (50% mortality).

response.thinking:
**Calculating logistic regression stats**

I need to solve a logistic regression exam question focused on a grouped binomial problem using maximum likelihood estimates. 

First, I’ll state the fitted response function. Then, at X=3.5, I’ll compute eta and convert that into a probability, which comes out to about 0.427. 

Next, for the median lethal dose (LD50), I find it occurs at a log-dose of about 3.94, which translates to an actual dose of approximately 51.4 using the natural logarithm. It's crucial to keep in mind the log-dose scales during these calculations.
**Clarifying logistic regression terms**

I need to find out whether "log" refers to the natural logarithm. If it's log10 for the dose, then the LD50 would equal 10 raised to the power of 3.94. 

For rigor, the data is grouped with n_j=250. The deaths, Y_j, follow a binomial distribution with parameters 250 and p_j, where the logit(p_j) is represented as beta0 + beta1 X_j. 

I also should clarify that the fitted response function, possibly denoted as \hat\pi(x), represents the estimated mean deaths, and I’ll calculate the expected number of dead, which would be 250 times \hat pi for the group.
response.text:
**Model:** For dose group \(j\), assume

\[
Y_j \sim \operatorname{Binomial}(250,\pi_j),
\qquad 
\log\left(\frac{\pi_j}{1-\pi_j}\right)=\beta_0+\beta_1 X_j,
\]

where \(X_j=\log(\text{dose})\).

Given

\[
\hat\beta_0=-2.64,\qquad \hat\beta_1=0.67.
\]

---

### (1) Fitted response function

The fitted probability of death at log-dose \(X=x\) is

\[
\hat\pi(x)
=
\frac{\exp(\hat\beta_0+\hat\beta_1 x)}
{1+\exp(\hat\beta_0+\hat\beta_1 x)}.
\]

Thus

\[
\boxed{
\hat\pi(x)
=
\frac{\exp(-2.64+0.67x)}
{1+\exp(-2.64+0.67x)}
}
\]

Equivalently,

\[
\boxed{
\log\left(\frac{\hat\pi(x)}{1-\hat\pi(x)}\right)
=
-2.64+0.67x
}
\]

---

### (2) Estimated probability of death at \(X=3.5\)

Compute the fitted linear predictor:

\[
\hat\eta
=
-2.64+0.67(3.5)
=
-2.64+2.345
=
-0.295.
\]

Therefore

\[
\hat\pi(3.5)
=
\frac{e^{-0.295}}{1+e^{-0.295}}
=
\frac{1}{1+e^{0.295}}.
\]

Numerically,

\[
\hat\pi(3.5)\approx 0.427.
\]

So the estimated probability of death is

\[
\boxed{\hat\pi(3.5)\approx 0.427}
\]

or about \(42.7\%\).

---

### (3) Estimated median lethal dose

The median lethal dose corresponds to \(50\%\) mortality, so set

\[
\hat\pi(x)=0.5.
\]

For a logistic model, \(\hat\pi(x)=0.5\) implies the logit is zero:

\[
-2.64+0.67x=0.
\]

Solving,

\[
x=\frac{2.64}{0.67}\approx 3.94.
\]

Thus the estimated median lethal log-dose is

\[
\boxed{\widehat{X}_{50}\approx 3.94.}
\]

Since \(X=\log(\text{dose})\), the median lethal dose on the original dose scale is

\[
\boxed{\widehat{\mathrm{LD}}_{50}=\exp(3.94)\approx 51.4}
\]

assuming the log is natural.

\]

versus

\[

\]

Assume \(m_1\) is the full model

\[
Y=\text{kid's IQ},\qquad X_1=\text{mom's IQ},\qquad X_2=\text{mom's age},
\]

\[
m_1:\quad Y_i=\beta_0+\beta_1X_{1i}+\beta_2X_{2i}+\varepsilon_i.
\]

### (1) Sample size

Residual df for \(m_1\) is \(431\). Since the model has 3 parameters \((\beta_0,\beta_1,\beta_2)\),

\[
n-3=431 \implies n=434.
\]

\[
\boxed{n=434}
\]

---

### (2) Fitted model \(m_1\)

\[
\boxed{\widehat{Y}=17.596+0.604X_1+0.388X_2}
\]

That is,

\[
\widehat{\text{kid IQ}}
=
17.596+0.604(\text{mom IQ})+0.388(\text{mom age}).
\]

---

### (3) LS estimate of \(\beta_1\) and interpretation

\[
\boxed{\hat\beta_1=0.604}
\]

Interpretation: holding mother’s age fixed, a 1-point increase in mother’s IQ is associated with an estimated increase of about \(0.604\) points in the child’s IQ.

---

### (4) Test \(H_0:\beta_1=0\) at 5%

Test statistic:

\[
t=\frac{\hat\beta_1-0}{SE(\hat\beta_1)}
=
\frac{0.604}{0.0587}
\approx 10.29.
\]

Degrees of freedom: \(431\).

At level \(\alpha=0.05\), the critical value is approximately

\[
t_{0.975,431}\approx 1.96.
\]

Since

\[
|10.29|>1.96,
\]

we reject \(H_0\).

Equivalently, the p-value is extremely small, \(p<2.2\times 10^{-16}\).

\[
\boxed{\text{Reject }H_0. \text{ Mom's IQ is a significant predictor of kid's IQ controlling for mom's age.}}
\]

---

### (5) Overall \(F\)-statistic for \(m_1\)

The overall model test is

\[
H_0:\beta_1=\beta_2=0
\]

versus

\[
H_1:\text{at least one of }\beta_1,\beta_2\neq 0.
\]

Using

\[
F=\frac{R^2/p}{(1-R^2)/(n-p-1)},
\]

where \(p=2\) predictors, \(R^2=0.2036\), and \(n-p-1=431\),

\[
F
=
\frac{0.2036/2}{(1-0.2036)/431}
=
\frac{0.1018}{0.7964/431}
\approx 55.1.
\]

So

\[
\boxed{F\approx 55.1 \text{ on }(2,431)\text{ df}}
\]

with p-value essentially \(<2.2\times 10^{-16}\).

---

### (6) \(t\)-statistic for testing \(\beta_2=0\)

\[
t=\frac{\hat\beta_2}{SE(\hat\beta_2)}
=
\frac{0.388}{0.326}
\approx 1.19.
\]

\[
\boxed{t\approx 1.19}
\]

with \(431\) degrees of freedom. The corresponding two-sided p-value is about \(0.235\).

---

### (7) Hypotheses for the nested `anova(m2,m1)` test

Assuming \(m_2\) is the reduced model with mother’s IQ only,

\[
m_2:\quad Y_i=\beta_0+\beta_1X_{1i}+\varepsilon_i,
\]

and \(m_1\) is the full model with both \(X_1\) and \(X_2\), the nested ANOVA tests whether adding mother’s age significantly improves the model.

Thus

\[
H_0:\beta_2=0
\]

versus

\[
H_1:\beta_2\neq 0.
\]

Equivalently,

\[
H_0:\text{mom's age adds no explanatory power after controlling for mom's IQ}
\]

versus

\[
H_1:\text{mom's age adds explanatory power after controlling for mom's IQ}.
\]

---

### (8) Blanked ANOVA quantities and conclusion

For the nested comparison, the extra-sum-of-squares \(F\)-test has

\[
F=t_{\beta_2}^2\approx (1.19)^2\approx 1.42.
\]

The numerator df is the number of added predictors:

\[
df_1=1,
\]

and the denominator df is the residual df of the full model:

\[
df_2=431.
\]

So the p-value is

\[
p=P(F_{1,431}\ge 1.42)\approx 0.235.
\]

Using the given residual standard error,

\[
MSE=(18.26)^2\approx 333.43,
\]

\[
RSS_{\text{full}}=431(333.43)\approx 143707.
\]

The extra sum of squares is approximately

\[
SS_{\text{added}}=F\cdot MSE\approx 1.42(333.43)\approx 472.
\]

So

\[
RSS_{\text{reduced}}\approx 143707+472=144179.
\]

Thus the nested ANOVA table entries are approximately

\[
\begin{array}{c|ccccc}
\text{Model} & \text{Res.Df} & RSS & Df & F & p\text{-value}\\
\hline
m_2 & 432 & 144179 &  &  &  \\
m_1 & 431 & 143707 & 1 & 1.42 & 0.235
\end{array}
\]

\[
p\approx 0.235>0.05,
\]

so we fail to reject \(H_0\). There is not significant evidence at the 5% level that mother’s age improves prediction of kid’s IQ after accounting for mother’s IQ.

[2024 spring ms math-stat — problem 1]

Density $f(X) = (\lambda/2)e^{-\lambda|X-a|}$, $\lambda > 0$. Observations: $-7,-5,-3,1,2,6,10$. (1) For fixed $\lambda$, find the MLE of $a$. (2) Find the MLE of $\lambda$ at that $a$. (3) In a new world with $a = 2$ known but only censored data (of 20 obs, 5 are $> 15$ and 15 are $\le 15$), find the MLE of $\lambda$.

response.text:
For the Laplace density

\[
f(x\mid a,\lambda)=\frac{\lambda}{2}e^{-\lambda |x-a|},\qquad \lambda>0,
\]

with observations

\[
-7,-5,-3,1,2,6,10,
\]

the likelihood is

\[
L(a,\lambda)=\prod_{i=1}^7 \frac{\lambda}{2}e^{-\lambda |x_i-a|}
=\left(\frac{\lambda}{2}\right)^7
\exp\left\{-\lambda\sum_{i=1}^7 |x_i-a|\right\}.
\]

The log-likelihood is

\[
\ell(a,\lambda)=7\log \lambda-7\log 2-\lambda\sum_{i=1}^7 |x_i-a|.
\]

---

## (1) MLE of \(a\) for fixed \(\lambda\)

For fixed \(\lambda>0\), maximizing \(\ell(a,\lambda)\) over \(a\) is equivalent to minimizing

\[
\sum_{i=1}^7 |x_i-a|.
\]

A standard result is that any median minimizes the sum of absolute deviations. Since the data are already ordered,

\[
-7< -5< -3<1<2<6<10,
\]

and there are \(7\) observations, the unique sample median is the fourth observation:

\[
\hat a=1.
\]

Thus,

\[
\boxed{\hat a=1.}
\]

---

## (2) MLE of \(\lambda\) at \(\hat a=1\)

At \(a=1\),

\[
\sum_{i=1}^7 |x_i-1|
=|-7-1|+|-5-1|+|-3-1|+|1-1|+|2-1|+|6-1|+|10-1|.
\]

So

\[
\sum_{i=1}^7 |x_i-1|
=8+6+4+0+1+5+9=33.
\]

Therefore the log-likelihood as a function of \(\lambda\) is

\[
\ell(1,\lambda)=7\log\lambda-7\log 2-33\lambda.
\]

Differentiate:

\[
\frac{d}{d\lambda}\ell(1,\lambda)=\frac{7}{\lambda}-33.
\]

Set equal to zero:

\[
\frac{7}{\lambda}-33=0,
\]

so

\[
\hat\lambda=\frac{7}{33}.
\]

The second derivative is

\[
\frac{d^2}{d\lambda^2}\ell(1,\lambda)=-\frac{7}{\lambda^2}<0,
\]

so this is indeed the maximizer.

Thus,

\[
\boxed{\hat\lambda=\frac{7}{33}.}
\]

---

## (3) Censored data with \(a=2\) known

Now \(a=2\) is known. We observe only that out of \(20\) observations,

\[
5>15,\qquad 15\le 15.
\]

For \(X\sim \text{Laplace}(a=2,\lambda)\),

\[
P(X>15)=\int_{15}^{\infty}\frac{\lambda}{2}e^{-\lambda(x-2)}\,dx,
\]

since \(15>2\). Thus

\[
P(X>15)=\frac{1}{2}e^{-13\lambda}.
\]

Let

\[
p(\lambda)=P(X>15)=\frac12 e^{-13\lambda}.
\]

The censored-data likelihood is binomial:

\[
L(\lambda)\propto \left[p(\lambda)\right]^5\left[1-p(\lambda)\right]^{15}.
\]

That is,

\[
L(\lambda)\propto
\left(\frac12 e^{-13\lambda}\right)^5
\left(1-\frac12 e^{-13\lambda}\right)^{15}.
\]

The binomial likelihood is maximized when

\[
p(\lambda)=\frac{5}{20}=\frac14.
\]

So we solve

\[
\frac12 e^{-13\lambda}=\frac14.
\]

Hence

\[
e^{-13\lambda}=\frac12,
\]

and therefore

\[
-13\lambda=-\log 2.
\]

Thus

\[
\boxed{\hat\lambda=\frac{\log 2}{13}.}
\]

Final answers:

\[
\boxed{\hat a=1,}
\]

\[
\boxed{\hat\lambda=\frac{7}{33}\text{ for the uncensored sample,}}
\]

and for the censored sample with \(a=2\),

\[
\boxed{\hat\lambda=\frac{\log 2}{13}.}
\]

\[
-7,-5,-3,1,2,6,10.
\]

\[
f(x\mid a,\lambda)=\frac{\lambda}{2}e^{-\lambda |x-a|},\qquad \lambda>0.
\]

The likelihood is

\[
L(a,\lambda)
=\prod_{i=1}^n \frac{\lambda}{2}e^{-\lambda |x_i-a|}
=\left(\frac{\lambda}{2}\right)^n
\exp\left\{-\lambda \sum_{i=1}^n |x_i-a|\right\}.
\]

Here \(n=7\).

---

## (1) MLE of \(a\) for fixed \(\lambda\)

For fixed \(\lambda\), maximizing the likelihood is equivalent to minimizing

\[
\sum_{i=1}^7 |x_i-a|.
\]

It is a standard result that the minimizer of the sum of absolute deviations is any sample median. Since \(n=7\) is odd, the sample median is unique.

The ordered observations are

\[
-7,-5,-3,1,2,6,10.
\]

The fourth observation is \(1\), so

\[
\widehat a = 1.
\]

Thus, for fixed \(\lambda\),

\[
\boxed{\widehat a = 1.}
\]

---

## (2) MLE of \(\lambda\) at that value of \(a\)

At \(\widehat a=1\), compute

\[
\sum_{i=1}^7 |x_i-\widehat a|
=
|-7-1|+|-5-1|+|-3-1|+|1-1|+|2-1|+|6-1|+|10-1|.
\]

Thus

\[
\sum_{i=1}^7 |x_i-1|
=
8+6+4+0+1+5+9
=33.
\]

The likelihood as a function of \(\lambda\) is

\[
L(\lambda)
=
\left(\frac{\lambda}{2}\right)^7 e^{-33\lambda}.
\]

The log-likelihood is

\[
\ell(\lambda)=7\log \lambda -7\log 2 -33\lambda.
\]

Differentiate:

\[
\ell'(\lambda)=\frac{7}{\lambda}-33.
\]

Set equal to zero:

\[
\frac{7}{\lambda}-33=0
\]

so

\[
\widehat\lambda=\frac{7}{33}.
\]

Also,

\[
\ell''(\lambda)=-\frac{7}{\lambda^2}<0,
\]

so this is indeed a maximum.

Therefore,

\[
\boxed{\widehat \lambda=\frac{7}{33}.}
\]

=\frac12 e^{-13\lambda}.
\]

\[
p(\lambda)=P(X>15)=\frac12 e^{-13\lambda}.
\]

\[
L(\lambda)
=
[p(\lambda)]^5[1-p(\lambda)]^{15}.
\]

This is a binomial likelihood with observed proportion

\[
\widehat p=\frac{5}{20}=\frac14.
\]

Since

\[
p(\lambda)=\frac12 e^{-13\lambda},

\[

\[

\[

\[

Let \(\theta>0\). The density is

\[
f(x\mid \theta)=\frac{2x}{\theta^2},\qquad 0<x<\theta.
\]

For \(k>-2\),

\[
\mathbb E_\theta[X^k]
=\int_0^\theta x^k \frac{2x}{\theta^2}\,dx
=\frac{2}{\theta^2}\frac{\theta^{k+2}}{k+2}
=\frac{2\theta^k}{k+2}.
\]

## (1) \(\mathbb E_\theta X\) and \(\operatorname{Var}_\theta X\)

Using the moment formula,

\[
\mathbb E_\theta X=\frac{2\theta}{3}.
\]

Also,

\[
\mathbb E_\theta X^2=\frac{2\theta^2}{4}=\frac{\theta^2}{2}.
\]

Therefore,

\[
\operatorname{Var}_\theta(X)
=\mathbb E_\theta X^2-(\mathbb E_\theta X)^2
=\frac{\theta^2}{2}-\left(\frac{2\theta}{3}\right)^2
=\frac{\theta^2}{2}-\frac{4\theta^2}{9}
=\frac{\theta^2}{18}.
\]

So

\[
\boxed{\mathbb E_\theta X=\frac{2\theta}{3}},\qquad
\boxed{\operatorname{Var}_\theta(X)=\frac{\theta^2}{18}}.
\]

---

## (2) Minimize MSE among estimators \(\delta_c(X)=cX\)

We estimate \(\theta\) under squared-error loss. The risk/MSE is

\[
R(\theta,\delta_c)
=\mathbb E_\theta[(cX-\theta)^2].
\]

Compute:

\[
\mathbb E_\theta[(cX-\theta)^2]
=c^2\mathbb E_\theta X^2-2c\theta \mathbb E_\theta X+\theta^2.
\]

Using the moments above,

\[
R(\theta,\delta_c)
=c^2\frac{\theta^2}{2}
-2c\theta\frac{2\theta}{3}
+\theta^2.
\]

Thus

\[
R(\theta,\delta_c)
=\theta^2\left(\frac{c^2}{2}-\frac{4c}{3}+1\right).
\]

Since \(\theta^2>0\), minimize

\[
\frac{c^2}{2}-\frac{4c}{3}+1.
\]

Differentiate with respect to \(c\):

\[
\frac{d}{dc}\left(\frac{c^2}{2}-\frac{4c}{3}+1\right)
=c-\frac{4}{3}.
\]

Setting equal to zero gives

\[
c=\frac{4}{3}.
\]

The second derivative is \(1>0\), so this is the minimizer. Therefore the best estimator in this class is

\[
\boxed{\delta_{4/3}(X)=\frac{4}{3}X}.
\]

Its minimum MSE is

\[
R(\theta,\delta_{4/3})
=\theta^2\left(\frac{1}{9}\right)
=\frac{\theta^2}{9}.
\]

---

## (3) Is \(\delta_{4/3}(X)=\frac43X\) unbiased for \(\theta\)?

We compute

\[
\mathbb E_\theta\left[\frac43 X\right]
=\frac43 \mathbb E_\theta X
=\frac43\cdot \frac{2\theta}{3}
=\frac{8\theta}{9}.
\]

Since

\[
\frac{8\theta}{9}\neq \theta
\]

for \(\theta\neq 0\), the estimator is not unbiased for \(\theta\).

Thus

\[
\boxed{\frac43X \text{ is biased for } \theta.}
\]

Its bias is

\[
\operatorname{Bias}_\theta\left(\frac43X\right)
=\frac{8\theta}{9}-\theta
=-\frac{\theta}{9}.
\]

---

## (4) Find an unbiased estimator of \(\theta(1-\theta)\)

We want a function \(g(X)\) such that

\[
\mathbb E_\theta[g(X)]=\theta(1-\theta)=\theta-\theta^2.
\]

Using the moments from part (1), try an estimator of the form

\[
g(X)=aX+bX^2.
\]

Then

\[
\mathbb E_\theta[g(X)]
=a\mathbb E_\theta X+b\mathbb E_\theta X^2
=a\frac{2\theta}{3}+b\frac{\theta^2}{2}.
\]

We need

\[
a\frac{2\theta}{3}+b\frac{\theta^2}{2}
=\theta-\theta^2.
\]

Matching coefficients of \(\theta\) and \(\theta^2\),

\[
\frac{2a}{3}=1,
\qquad
\frac{b}{2}=-1.
\]

Hence

\[
a=\frac32,
\qquad
b=-2.
\]

Therefore an unbiased estimator is

\[
\boxed{g(X)=\frac32 X-2X^2}.
\]

Indeed,

\[
\mathbb E_\theta\left[\frac32 X-2X^2\right]
=\frac32\cdot \frac{2\theta}{3}
-2\cdot \frac{\theta^2}{2}
=\theta-\theta^2
=\theta(1-\theta).
\]

So

\[
\boxed{\frac32X-2X^2 \text{ is unbiased for } \theta(1-\theta).}
\]

[2024 spring ms probability — problem 3]

Generate $X$ from $f(x) = 2x$ ($0<x<1$) if $Y=1$, or $g(x) = 3x^2$ if $Y=0$, where $P(Y=1) = 1/2$. (1) Find the cdf of $X$. (2) Find $P(Y=1 \mid X \le 1/2)$. (3) Find $\operatorname{Cov}(X, Y)$.

response.text:
Let  
\[
P(Y=1)=P(Y=0)=\frac12,
\]
with conditional densities
\[
f_{X\mid Y=1}(x)=2x,\qquad 0<x<1,
\]
and
\[
f_{X\mid Y=0}(x)=3x^2,\qquad 0<x<1.
\]

### (1) CDF of \(X\)

First compute the conditional CDFs:

\[
F_{X\mid Y=1}(x)=
\begin{cases}
0, & x\le 0,\\
x^2, & 0<x<1,\\
1, & x\ge 1,
\end{cases}
\]

and

\[
F_{X\mid Y=0}(x)=
\begin{cases}
0, & x\le 0,\\
x^3, & 0<x<1,\\
1, & x\ge 1.
\end{cases}
\]

By the law of total probability,

\[
F_X(x)=P(X\le x)=\frac12 F_{X\mid Y=1}(x)+\frac12 F_{X\mid Y=0}(x).
\]

Therefore,

\[
F_X(x)=
\begin{cases}
0, & x\le 0,\\[4pt]
\dfrac12 x^2+\dfrac12 x^3, & 0<x<1,\\[6pt]
1, & x\ge 1.
\end{cases}
\]

---

### (2) Find \(P(Y=1\mid X\le 1/2)\)

Using Bayes’ rule,

\[
P(Y=1\mid X\le 1/2)
=
\frac{P(X\le 1/2\mid Y=1)P(Y=1)}
{P(X\le 1/2)}.
\]

Now,

\[
P(X\le 1/2\mid Y=1)=\left(\frac12\right)^2=\frac14,
\]

and

\[
P(X\le 1/2\mid Y=0)=\left(\frac12\right)^3=\frac18.
\]

Thus,

\[
P(X\le 1/2)
=
\frac12\cdot \frac14+\frac12\cdot \frac18
=
\frac18+\frac1{16}
=
\frac3{16}.
\]

Also,

\[
P(X\le 1/2,Y=1)=\frac12\cdot \frac14=\frac18.
\]

Hence,

\[
P(Y=1\mid X\le 1/2)
=
\frac{1/8}{3/16}
=
\frac23.
\]

So,

\[
\boxed{P(Y=1\mid X\le 1/2)=\frac23.}
\]

---

### (3) Find \(\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)\)

We use

\[
\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)=E[XY]-E[X]E[Y].
\]

Since \(Y\in\{0,1\}\),

\[
E[Y]=P(Y=1)=\frac12.
\]

Also,

\[
E[XY]=E[X\mathbf 1_{\{Y=1\}}]
=
P(Y=1)E[X\mid Y=1].
\]

Now

\[
E[X\mid Y=1]=\int_0^1 x(2x)\,dx
=
2\int_0^1 x^2\,dx
=
\frac23.
\]

Therefore,

\[
E[XY]=\frac12\cdot \frac23=\frac13.
\]

Next,

\[
E[X]
=
\frac12 E[X\mid Y=1]+\frac12 E[X\mid Y=0].
\]

We already have

\[
E[X\mid Y=1]=\frac23.
\]

Also,

\[
E[X\mid Y=0]
=
\int_0^1 x(3x^2)\,dx
=
3\int_0^1 x^3\,dx
=
\frac34.
\]

Thus,

\[
E[X]
=
\frac12\cdot \frac23+\frac12\cdot \frac34
=
\frac13+\frac38
=
\frac{17}{24}.
\]

Therefore,

\[
\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)
=
\frac13-\frac{17}{24}\cdot \frac12
=
\frac13-\frac{17}{48}
=
\frac{16}{48}-\frac{17}{48}
=
-\frac1{48}.
\]

Hence,

\[
\boxed{\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)=-\frac1{48}.}
\]

response.text:
## 1) Stationary/KKT condition

Let \(\widehat\Sigma=X^TX/n\), \(\xi=\xi^*\), and

\[
Q(u)=\frac12 u^T\widehat\Sigma u-u^T\xi+\lambda\|u\|_1 .
\]

Since \(Q\) is convex, \(\widehat u_\lambda\) is optimal iff

\[
0\in \widehat\Sigma \widehat u_\lambda-\xi+\lambda \partial \|\widehat u_\lambda\|_1 .
\]

Equivalently, there exists \(z\in\mathbb R^p\) such that

\[
\widehat\Sigma \widehat u_\lambda-\xi+\lambda z=0,
\]

where

\[
z_j=
\begin{cases}
\operatorname{sign}(\widehat u_{\lambda,j}), & \widehat u_{\lambda,j}\neq 0,\\
\in [-1,1], & \widehat u_{\lambda,j}=0.
\end{cases}
\]

Componentwise, the KKT conditions are

\[
(\widehat\Sigma \widehat u_\lambda-\xi)_j
=
-\lambda \operatorname{sign}(\widehat u_{\lambda,j})
\quad\text{if }\widehat u_{\lambda,j}\neq 0,
\]

and

\[
|(\widehat\Sigma \widehat u_\lambda-\xi)_j|\le \lambda
\quad\text{if }\widehat u_{\lambda,j}=0.
\]

---

## 2) Coordinate descent update

Fix all coordinates except the \(j\)-th. Write the current iterate as \(u^0\). Define

\[
a_j=\widehat\Sigma_{jj},
\]

and

\[
b_j=\xi_j-\sum_{k\neq j}\widehat\Sigma_{jk}u_k^0.
\]

As a function of \(v=u_j\), the objective becomes, up to constants independent of \(v\),

\[
q_j(v)=\frac12 a_jv^2-b_jv+\lambda |v|.
\]

Thus the coordinate update solves

\[
u_j^{\text{new}}
=
\arg\min_v\left\{\frac12 a_jv^2-b_jv+\lambda |v|\right\}.
\]

Using the soft-thresholding operator

\[
S(x,t)=\operatorname{sign}(x)(|x|-t)_+,
\]

the update is

\[
\boxed{
u_j^{\text{new}}
=
\frac{S(b_j,\lambda)}{a_j}
}
\]

or equivalently,

\[
\boxed{
u_j^{\text{new}}
=
S\left(
u_j^0-\frac{(\widehat\Sigma u^0-\xi)_j}{\widehat\Sigma_{jj}},
\frac{\lambda}{\widehat\Sigma_{jj}}
\right).
}
\]

A full coordinate descent iteration consists of cycling through \(j=1,\dots,p\).

---

## 3) Proximal gradient update

Split

\[
Q(u)=f(u)+\lambda \|u\|_1,
\]

where

\[
f(u)=\frac12 u^T\widehat\Sigma u-u^T\xi.
\]

Then

\[
\nabla f(u)=\widehat\Sigma u-\xi.
\]

Given current iterate \(u^0\) and step size \(\tau>0\), the proximal gradient update is

\[
u^{\text{new}}
=
\operatorname{prox}_{\tau\lambda\|\cdot\|_1}
\left(
u^0-\tau(\widehat\Sigma u^0-\xi)
\right).
\]

Because the proximal operator of the \(\ell_1\)-norm is soft-thresholding,

\[
\boxed{
u^{\text{new}}
=
S\left(
u^0-\tau(\widehat\Sigma u^0-\xi),
\tau\lambda
\right),
}
\]

componentwise,

\[
\boxed{
u_j^{\text{new}}
=
S\left(
u_j^0-\tau(\widehat\Sigma u^0-\xi)_j,
\tau\lambda
\right).
}
\]

For guaranteed monotone convergence, it is standard to take \(\tau\le 1/L\), where

\[
L=\lambda_{\max}(\widehat\Sigma).
\]

---

## 4) Coordinate descent implementation in R

The prompt as provided here refers to “the given R code” for generating the data and \(\xi^*\), but that code is not included in the message. Therefore the numerical iteration count and final vector cannot be uniquely reproduced here. The following code implements the required coordinate descent algorithm and will produce the requested numerical output when run with the supplied data-generating code.

The tuning parameter is

\[
\lambda=1.2\sqrt{\frac{\log p}{n}}
=
1.2\sqrt{\frac{\log 600}{600}}
\approx 0.123906.
\]

```r
soft <- function(x, t) {
  sign(x) * pmax(abs(x) - t, 0)
}

kkt_violation <- function(u, Shat, xi, lambda, zero.tol = 1e-8) {
  r <- as.vector(Shat %*% u - xi)

  nz <- abs(u) > zero.tol
  viol <- numeric(length(u))

  viol[nz] <- abs(r[nz] + lambda * sign(u[nz]))
  viol[!nz] <- pmax(abs(r[!nz]) - lambda, 0)

  list(
    max_violation = max(viol),
    active_size = sum(nz),
    worst_coordinate = which.max(viol),
    residual = r,
    component_violation = viol
  )
}

cd_lasso_precision <- function(Shat, xi, lambda,
                               tol = 1e-5,
                               maxit = 100000,
                               track = c(2, 4, 6, 8, 10)) {
  p <- length(xi)

  u <- numeric(p)
  grad <- -xi          # grad = Shat %*% u - xi, initially u = 0
  d <- diag(Shat)

  if (any(d <= 0)) stop("Some diagonal entries of Shat are nonpositive.")

  path <- matrix(NA_real_, nrow = maxit + 1, ncol = length(track))
  colnames(path) <- paste0("j=", track)
  path[1, ] <- u[track]

  l1.change <- Inf

  for (iter in seq_len(maxit)) {
    u.old.sweep <- u

    for (j in seq_len(p)) {
      old <- u[j]

      # b_j = xi_j - sum_{k != j} Shat[j,k] u_k
      # using grad_j = Shat[j,] u - xi_j
      z <- d[j] * old - grad[j]

      new <- soft(z, lambda) / d[j]

      if (new != old) {
        delta <- new - old
        u[j] <- new
        grad <- grad + delta * Shat[, j]
      }
    }

    l1.change <- sum(abs(u - u.old.sweep))
    path[iter + 1, ] <- u[track]

    if (l1.change < tol) break
  }

  path <- path[seq_len(iter + 1), , drop = FALSE]

  list(
    u = u,
    iter = iter,
    l1.change = l1.change,
    path = path,
    kkt = kkt_violation(u, Shat, xi, lambda)
  )
}
```

## 5) Proximal gradient implementation in R

```r
pg_lasso_precision <- function(Shat, xi, lambda, tau,
                               tol = 1e-5,
                               maxit = 1000000,
                               track = c(2, 4, 6, 8, 10)) {
  p <- length(xi)

  u <- numeric(p)

  path <- matrix(NA_real_, nrow = maxit + 1, ncol = length(track))
  colnames(path) <- paste0("j=", track)
  path[1, ] <- u[track]

  l1.change <- Inf

  for (iter in seq_len(maxit)) {
    u.old <- u

    grad <- as.vector(Shat %*% u - xi)

    u <- soft(u - tau * grad, tau * lambda)

    l1.change <- sum(abs(u - u.old))
    path[iter + 1, ] <- u[track]

    if (l1.change < tol) break
  }

  path <- path[seq_len(iter + 1), , drop = FALSE]

  list(
    u = u,
    iter = iter,
    l1.change = l1.change,
    path = path,
    tau = tau,
    kkt = kkt_violation(u, Shat, xi, lambda)
  )
}
```

Run proximal gradient for the requested step sizes.

    xi = xi,
    lambda = lambda,
    tau = tau,
    tol = 1e-5,
    track = c(2, 4, 6, 8, 10)
  )

  cat("Iterations:", fit$iter, "\n")
  cat("Final l1 change:", fit$l1.change, "\n")
  cat("First 10 components:\n")

  cat("KKT max violation:", fit$kkt$max_violation, "\n")
  cat("Active set size:", fit$kkt$active_size, "\n")
  cat("Worst KKT coordinate:", fit$kkt$worst_coordinate, "\n")
}
```

  fit <- fits_pg[[a]]

  matplot(
    0:fit$iter,

## 1) Stationary/KKT condition

Let \(\widehat\Sigma=X^TX/n\), \(\xi=\xi^*\), and

\[
Q(u)=\frac12 u^T\widehat\Sigma u-u^T\xi+\lambda\|u\|_1 .
\]

Since \(Q\) is convex, \(\widehat u_\lambda\) is optimal iff

\[
0\in \widehat\Sigma \widehat u_\lambda-\xi+\lambda \partial \|\widehat u_\lambda\|_1 .
\]

Equivalently, there exists \(z\in\mathbb R^p\) such that

\[
\widehat\Sigma \widehat u_\lambda-\xi+\lambda z=0,
\]

where

\[
z_j=
\begin{cases}
\operatorname{sign}(\widehat u_{\lambda,j}), & \widehat u_{\lambda,j}\neq 0,\\
\in [-1,1], & \widehat u_{\lambda,j}=0.
\end{cases}
\]

Componentwise, the KKT conditions are

\[
(\widehat\Sigma \widehat u_\lambda-\xi)_j
=
-\lambda \operatorname{sign}(\widehat u_{\lambda,j})
\quad\text{if }\widehat u_{\lambda,j}\neq 0,
\]

and

\[
|(\widehat\Sigma \widehat u_\lambda-\xi)_j|\le \lambda
\quad\text{if }\widehat u_{\lambda,j}=0.
\]

---

## 2) Coordinate descent update

Fix all coordinates except the \(j\)-th. Write the current iterate as \(u^0\). Define

\[
a_j=\widehat\Sigma_{jj},
\]

and

\[
b_j=\xi_j-\sum_{k\neq j}\widehat\Sigma_{jk}u_k^0.
\]

As a function of \(v=u_j\), the objective becomes, up to constants independent of \(v\),

\[
q_j(v)=\frac12 a_jv^2-b_jv+\lambda |v|.
\]

Thus the coordinate update solves

\[
u_j^{\text{new}}
=
\arg\min_v\left\{\frac12 a_jv^2-b_jv+\lambda |v|\right\}.
\]

Using the soft-thresholding operator

\[
S(x,t)=\operatorname{sign}(x)(|x|-t)_+,
\]

the update is

\[
\boxed{
u_j^{\text{new}}
=
\frac{S(b_j,\lambda)}{a_j}
}
\]

or equivalently,

\[
\boxed{
u_j^{\text{new}}
=
S\left(
u_j^0-\frac{(\widehat\Sigma u^0-\xi)_j}{\widehat\Sigma_{jj}},
\frac{\lambda}{\widehat\Sigma_{jj}}
\right).
}
\]

A full coordinate descent iteration consists of cycling through \(j=1,\dots,p\).

---

## 3) Proximal gradient update

Split

\[
Q(u)=f(u)+\lambda \|u\|_1,
\]

where

\[
f(u)=\frac12 u^T\widehat\Sigma u-u^T\xi.
\]

Then

\[
\nabla f(u)=\widehat\Sigma u-\xi.
\]

Given current iterate \(u^0\) and step size \(\tau>0\), the proximal gradient update is

\[
u^{\text{new}}
=
\operatorname{prox}_{\tau\lambda\|\cdot\|_1}
\left(
u^0-\tau(\widehat\Sigma u^0-\xi)
\right).
\]

Because the proximal operator of the \(\ell_1\)-norm is soft-thresholding,

\[
\boxed{
u^{\text{new}}
=
S\left(
u^0-\tau(\widehat\Sigma u^0-\xi),
\tau\lambda
\right),
}
\]

componentwise,

\[
\boxed{
u_j^{\text{new}}
=
S\left(
u_j^0-\tau(\widehat\Sigma u^0-\xi)_j,
\tau\lambda
\right).
}
\]

For guaranteed monotone convergence, it is standard to take \(\tau\le 1/L\), where

\[
L=\lambda_{\max}(\widehat\Sigma).
\]

---

## 4) Coordinate descent implementation in R

The prompt as provided here refers to “the given R code” for generating the data and \(\xi^*\), but that code is not included in the message. Therefore the numerical iteration count and final vector cannot be uniquely reproduced here. The following code implements the required coordinate descent algorithm and will produce the requested numerical output when run with the supplied data-generating code.

The tuning parameter is

\[
\lambda=1.2\sqrt{\frac{\log p}{n}}
=
1.2\sqrt{\frac{\log 600}{600}}
\approx 0.123906.
\]

```r
soft <- function(x, t) {
  sign(x) * pmax(abs(x) - t, 0)
}

kkt_violation <- function(u, Shat, xi, lambda, zero.tol = 1e-8) {
  r <- as.vector(Shat %*% u - xi)

  nz <- abs(u) > zero.tol
  viol <- numeric(length(u))

  viol[nz] <- abs(r[nz] + lambda * sign(u[nz]))
  viol[!nz] <- pmax(abs(r[!nz]) - lambda, 0)

  list(
    max_violation = max(viol),
    active_size = sum(nz),
    worst_coordinate = which.max(viol),
    residual = r,
    component_violation = viol
  )
}

cd_lasso_precision <- function(Shat, xi, lambda,
                               tol = 1e-5,
                               maxit = 100000,
                               track = c(2, 4, 6, 8, 10)) {
  p <- length(xi)

  u <- numeric(p)
  grad <- -xi          # grad = Shat %*% u - xi, initially u = 0
  d <- diag(Shat)

  if (any(d <= 0)) stop("Some diagonal entries of Shat are nonpositive.")

  path <- matrix(NA_real_, nrow = maxit + 1, ncol = length(track))
  colnames(path) <- paste0("j=", track)
  path[1, ] <- u[track]

  l1.change <- Inf

  for (iter in seq_len(maxit)) {
    u.old.sweep <- u

    for (j in seq_len(p)) {
      old <- u[j]

      # b_j = xi_j - sum_{k != j} Shat[j,k] u_k
      # using grad_j = Shat[j,] u - xi_j
      z <- d[j] * old - grad[j]

      new <- soft(z, lambda) / d[j]

      if (new != old) {
        delta <- new - old
        u[j] <- new
        grad <- grad + delta * Shat[, j]
      }
    }

    l1.change <- sum(abs(u - u.old.sweep))
    path[iter + 1, ] <- u[track]

    if (l1.change < tol) break
  }

  path <- path[seq_len(iter + 1), , drop = FALSE]

  list(
    u = u,
    iter = iter,
    l1.change = l1.change,
    path = path,
    kkt = kkt_violation(u, Shat, xi, lambda)
  )
}
```

                               tol = 1e-5,
                               maxit = 1000000,
                               track = c(2, 4, 6, 8, 10)) {
