\]
and let \(\mathcal H\) denote the natural parameter space for \(\eta\). The joint density in canonical form is
\[
L(\eta;x_{1:n})
=\prod_{i=1}^n h(x_i)\exp\{\eta S_n-nA(\eta)\}.
\]

---

## (a) Sufficient statistic and MLE

By the Fisher–Neyman factorization theorem,
\[
L(\theta;x_{1:n})
=\prod_{i=1}^n h(x_i)\exp\{\eta(\theta)S_n-nB(\theta)\},
\]
so the statistic
\[
\boxed{S_n=\sum_{i=1}^n T(X_i)}
\]
is sufficient for \(\theta\).

The log-likelihood, up to an additive constant not depending on \(\theta\), is
\[
\ell(\theta)=\eta(\theta)S_n-nB(\theta).
\]

Equivalently, in the canonical parameterization,
\[
\ell(\eta)=\eta S_n-nA(\eta).
\]

An interior MLE \(\widehat \eta\) satisfies the likelihood equation
\[
0=\frac{\partial \ell}{\partial \eta}
=S_n-nA'(\eta),
\]
so
\[
\boxed{A'(\widehat\eta)=\bar T_n.}
\]

Thus, whenever \(\bar T_n\) lies in the range of \(A'\),
\[
\boxed{\widehat\eta=(A')^{-1}(\bar T_n).}
\]

Then the MLE for \(\theta\) is any \(\widehat\theta\) satisfying
\[
\eta(\widehat\theta)=\widehat\eta.
\]
If \(\eta(\theta)\) is one-to-one, then
\[
\boxed{\widehat\theta=\eta^{-1}\!\left((A')^{-1}(\bar T_n)\right).}
\]

Equivalently, differentiating with respect to \(\theta\),
\[
0=\ell'(\theta)=\eta'(\theta)S_n-nB'(\theta),
\]
so an interior MLE satisfies
\[
\boxed{\frac{B'(\widehat\theta)}{\eta'(\widehat\theta)}=\bar T_n}
\]
when \(\eta'(\widehat\theta)\neq 0\).

Boundary cases may occur if \(\bar T_n\) is outside the range of \(A'\).

---

## (b) Expression for \(A(\eta)\) in terms of \(\theta\)

The canonical log-partition function is
\[
A(\eta)=\log\int h(x)e^{\eta T(x)}\,d\mu(x).
\]

Since
\[
p(x\mid \theta)=h(x)\exp\{\eta(\theta)T(x)-B(\theta)\}
\]
is normalized, we must have
\[
B(\theta)=\log\int h(x)e^{\eta(\theta)T(x)}\,d\mu(x).
\]
Therefore
\[
\boxed{B(\theta)=A(\eta(\theta)).}
\]

If \(\eta(\theta)\) is one-to-one, then for \(\eta=\eta(\theta)\),
\[
\boxed{A(\eta)=B(\eta^{-1}(\eta)).}
\]

---

## (c) Uniqueness of the MLE

Assume \(T(x)\) is not constant on the support and \(\eta(\theta)\) is one-to-one.

For \(\eta\in \mathcal H\),
\[
A(\eta)=\log\int h(x)e^{\eta T(x)}\,d\mu(x).
\]

In a regular exponential family,
\[
A'(\eta)=\mathbb E_\eta[T(X)]
\]
and
\[
A''(\eta)=\operatorname{Var}_\eta(T(X)).
\]

Because \(T(X)\) is not almost surely constant under \(P_\eta\), we have
\[
\operatorname{Var}_\eta(T(X))>0.
\]
Therefore
\[
A''(\eta)>0,

so \(A\) is strictly convex.

\[
\ell(\eta)=\eta S_n-nA(\eta).
\]
Since \(A\) is strictly convex, \(-A\) is strictly concave, and hence \(\ell(\eta)\) is strictly concave in \(\eta\). Therefore \(\ell(\eta)\) has at most one maximizer over the natural parameter space.

\[
\boxed{\text{the MLE is unique.}}
\]

---

---

Let
\[
\eta_j=\eta(\theta_j),\qquad j=0,1.
\]
Since \(\eta(\theta)\) is strictly increasing and \(\theta_1>\theta_0\),
\[
\eta_1>\eta_0.
\]

The likelihood ratio is
\[
\frac{L(\theta_1)}{L(\theta_0)}
=
\exp\left\{(\eta_1-\eta_0)S_n-n[B(\theta_1)-B(\theta_0)]\right\}.
\]

Because \(\eta_1-\eta_0>0\), this likelihood ratio is an increasing function of \(S_n\). By the Neyman–Pearson lemma, the most powerful level-\(\alpha\) test rejects for large values of \(S_n\).

Choose \(c_\alpha\) such that
\[
P_{\theta_0}(S_n>c_\alpha)=\alpha.
\]
Because \(S_n\) is continuous, no randomization is needed.

Thus the MP level-\(\alpha\) test is
\[
\boxed{
\varphi_\alpha(X_1,\dots,X_n)
=
\mathbf 1\{S_n>c_\alpha\}.
}
\]

---

## (e) UMP test for \(H_0:\theta\le \theta_0\) vs. \(H_1:\theta>\theta_0\)

Consider the same test
\[
\boxed{
\varphi_\alpha=\mathbf 1\{S_n>c_\alpha\},
}
\]
where
\[
P_{\theta_0}(S_n>c_\alpha)=\alpha.
\]

\[
\beta_c(\eta)=P_\eta(S_n>c).
\]
Then
\[
\frac{d}{d\eta}\beta_c(\eta)
=
\operatorname{Cov}_\eta(\mathbf 1\{S_n>c\},S_n).
\]
Since \(\mathbf 1\{S_n>c\}\) is an increasing function of \(S_n\),
\[
\operatorname{Cov}_\eta(\mathbf 1\{S_n>c\},S_n)\ge 0.
\]
Therefore \(\beta_c(\eta)\) is nondecreasing in \(\eta\). Since \(\eta(\theta)\) is strictly increasing in \(\theta\), we also have
\[
P_\theta(S_n>c_\alpha)\le P_{\theta_0}(S_n>c_\alpha)=\alpha
\]
for every \(\theta\le \theta_0\). Hence \(\varphi_\alpha\) has size \(\alpha\).

Now fix any \(\theta_1>\theta_0\). By part (d), \(\varphi_\alpha\) is the most powerful level-\(\alpha\) test for
\[
H_0:\theta=\theta_0
\quad\text{vs.}\quad
H_1:\theta=\theta_1.
\]
If \(\psi\) is any test with
\[
\sup_{\theta\le \theta_0}E_\theta[\psi]\le \alpha,
\]
then in particular
\[
E_{\theta_0}[\psi]\le \alpha.
\]
Therefore, by the Neyman–Pearson lemma,
\[
E_{\theta_1}[\psi]\le E_{\theta_1}[\varphi_\alpha].
\]

Since \(\theta_1>\theta_0\) was arbitrary, \(\varphi_\alpha\) maximizes power simultaneously for every \(\theta>\theta_0\). Therefore

\[
\boxed{
\varphi_\alpha=\mathbf 1\{S_n>c_\alpha\}
\text{ is UMP level } \alpha.
}
\]

This is the Karlin–Rubin monotone likelihood ratio theorem in this one-parameter exponential family.

---

## (f) UMP test for \(H_0:\theta=\theta_0\) vs. \(H_1:\theta\neq \theta_0\)

Assume \(\theta_0\) is an interior point of the parameter space. Then there exist \(\theta_-<\theta_0<\theta_+\).

We show that, for \(0<\alpha<1\), a nontrivial UMP level-\(\alpha\) test does not exist.

For the right-sided simple alternative \(\theta_+>\theta_0\), by the Neyman–Pearson lemma, the unique MP level-\(\alpha\) test is
\[
\varphi_+=\mathbf 1\{S_n>c_+\},
\]
where
\[
P_{\theta_0}(S_n>c_+)=\alpha.
\]

For the left-sided simple alternative \(\theta_-<\theta_0\), the likelihood ratio
\[
\frac{L(\theta_-)}{L(\theta_0)}
=
\exp\left\{(\eta(\theta_-)-\eta(\theta_0))S_n-n[B(\theta_-)-B(\theta_0)]\right\}
\]
is decreasing in \(S_n\), because \(\eta(\theta_-)<\eta(\theta_0)\). Hence the unique MP level-\(\alpha\) test is
\[
\varphi_-=\mathbf 1\{S_n<c_-\},
\]
where
\[
P_{\theta_0}(S_n<c_-)=\alpha.
\]

If a UMP level-\(\alpha\) test \(\varphi\) for the two-sided alternative existed, then it would have to be MP against both \(\theta_+\) and \(\theta_-\). By uniqueness in the Neyman–Pearson lemma, we would need
\[
\varphi=\varphi_+\quad P_{\theta_0}\text{-a.s.}
\]
and
\[
\varphi=\varphi_-\quad P_{\theta_0}\text{-a.s.}
\]
Therefore \(\varphi_+=\varphi_-\) \(P_{\theta_0}\)-a.s.

But this is impossible. The rejection region of \(\varphi_+\) is an upper tail, while the rejection region of \(\varphi_-\) is a lower tail. Since \(S_n\) is continuous and \(0<\alpha<1\), these two regions cannot agree up to a null set.

Therefore,

\[
\boxed{
\text{there is no nontrivial UMP level-\(\alpha\) test for }
H_0:\theta=\theta_0
\text{ vs. }
H_1:\theta\neq\theta_0.
}
\]

A UMP unbiased two-sided test may exist in such exponential families, but a UMP test among all level-\(\alpha\) tests generally does not.

\[

\]

## (a) Sufficient statistic and MLE

\[
L(\theta;x_1,\dots,x_n)
=\prod_{i=1}^n h(x_i)\exp\left\{\eta(\theta)\sum_{i=1}^n T(x_i)-nB(\theta)\right\}.
\]

Thus

\[
L(\theta;x_1,\dots,x_n)
=\left(\prod_{i=1}^n h(x_i)\right)
\exp\{\eta(\theta)S_n-nB(\theta)\}.
\]

By the Neyman–Fisher factorization theorem,

\[
\boxed{S_n=\sum_{i=1}^n T(X_i)}
\]

is sufficient for \(\theta\).

The log-likelihood is

\[
\ell(\theta)
= C(x)+\eta(\theta)S_n-nB(\theta).
\]

Equivalently, in the canonical parameter \(\eta\),

\[
\ell(\eta)
= C(x)+\eta S_n-nA(\eta)
= C(x)+n\{\eta \bar T_n-A(\eta)\}.
\]

Hence the canonical MLE satisfies

\[
\widehat\eta
\in \arg\max_{\eta}\{\eta \bar T_n-A(\eta)\}.
\]

If the maximizer is interior, then the score equation is

\[
0=\frac{d}{d\eta}\ell(\eta)
= n\{\bar T_n-A'(\eta)\},
\]

so

\[
A'(\widehat\eta)=\bar T_n.
\]

Thus, when \(A'\) is invertible and the solution lies in the parameter space,

\[
\boxed{\widehat\eta=(A')^{-1}(\bar T_n)}
\]

and therefore

\[
\boxed{\widehat\theta=\eta^{-1}(\widehat\eta)}
\]

when \(\eta\) is one-to-one. More generally, the MLE set is

\[
\{\theta:\eta(\theta)=\widehat\eta\}.
\]

If \(\bar T_n\) lies outside the range of \(A'\), then the likelihood is maximized, if at all, at the boundary of the natural parameter space.

---

## (b) Relation between \(A(\eta)\) and \(B(\theta)\)

The canonical normalizing function is

\[
A(\eta)
=
\log \int h(x)\exp\{\eta T(x)\}\,dx.
\]

Since the original density is normalized,

\[
1=\int h(x)\exp\{\eta(\theta)T(x)-B(\theta)\}\,dx,
\]

so

\[
B(\theta)
=
\log\int h(x)\exp\{\eta(\theta)T(x)\}\,dx.
\]

Therefore

\[
\boxed{B(\theta)=A(\eta(\theta)).}
\]

If \(\eta\) is one-to-one, then for \(\eta=\eta(\theta)\),

\[
\boxed{A(\eta)=B(\eta^{-1}(\eta)).}
\]

More clearly, writing \(u\) for the canonical parameter,

\[
\boxed{A(u)=B(\theta(u)),\qquad \theta(u)=\eta^{-1}(u).}
\]

---

\[
\begin{aligned}
A(t\eta_1+(1-t)\eta_2)
&=
\log\int h(x)\exp\{(t\eta_1+(1-t)\eta_2)T(x)\}\,dx\\

\]

\[

\[

\mathbb P_{\theta_0}(S_n>c_\alpha)

\[

\[
H_0:\theta=\theta_0
\quad\text{vs.}\quad
H_1:\theta=\theta_+
\]

\[
\mathbb P_{\theta_0}(S_n>c_U)=\alpha,
\]

\[
\varphi_U=\mathbf 1\{S_n>c_U\}.
\]

If \(\varphi\) is UMP against all \(\theta\neq\theta_0\), it must in particular be MP against \(\theta_+\). Hence

\[
\varphi=\varphi_U
\quad
\mathbb P_{\theta_0}\text{-a.s.}
\]

Now take \(\theta_-<\theta_0\). Since \(\eta(\theta_-)-\eta(\theta_0)<0\), the likelihood ratio is decreasing in \(S_n\). Therefore the unique MP level-\(\alpha\) test for

\[
H_0:\theta=\theta_0
\quad\text{vs.}\quad
H_1:\theta=\theta_-
\]

rejects for small \(S_n\). Thus there exists \(c_L\) such that

\[
\mathbb P_{\theta_0}(S_n<c_L)=\alpha,
\]

\[
\varphi_L=\mathbf 1\{S_n<c_L\}.
\]

Again, if \(\varphi\) were UMP, it would have to satisfy

\[
\varphi=\varphi_L
\quad
\mathbb P_{\theta_0}\text{-a.s.}
\]

Therefore we would need

\[
\mathbf 1\{S_n>c_U\}
=
\mathbf 1\{S_n<c_L\}
\quad
\mathbb P_{\theta_0}\text{-a.s.}
\]

But this is impossible for \(0<\alpha<1\). Indeed, both rejection regions have probability \(\alpha\) under \(\theta_0\), but one is an upper tail and the other is a lower tail. Since \(S_n\) is continuous, the two sets cannot coincide almost surely.

\[
\boxed{
\text{For a genuine two-sided alternative and }0<\alpha<1,
\text{ there is no UMP level-}\alpha\text{ test.}
}
\]

Only trivial exceptions occur: if \(\alpha=0\) or \(\alpha=1\), or if \(\theta_0\) is a boundary point so that the alternative is effectively one-sided.

\[

\[

\mathbb P_{\theta_0}\text{-a.s.}

\[
\mathbf 1\{S_n>c_U\}
=
\mathbf 1\{S_n<c_L\}

\mathbb P_{\theta_0}\text{-a.s.}

\[

\[
\hat\theta_n \overset{p}{\to} \theta_0.
\]

Because \(\theta_0\) is interior and \(\hat\theta_n\to_p\theta_0\), with probability tending to one \(\hat\theta_n\) is an interior maximizer, so the first-order condition holds.

By Taylor expansion of the score around \(\theta_0\),

\[
0=U_n(\hat\theta_n)
=U_n(\theta_0)
+\left\{\int_0^1 H_n\big(\theta_0+t(\hat\theta_n-\theta_0)\big)\,dt\right\}
(\hat\theta_n-\theta_0).
\]

Define

\[
A_n
=
-\frac1n
\int_0^1
H_n\big(\theta_0+t(\hat\theta_n-\theta_0)\big)\,dt.
\]

Then

\[
0=U_n(\theta_0)-nA_n(\hat\theta_n-\theta_0),
\]

\[
\sqrt n(\hat\theta_n-\theta_0)
=
A_n^{-1}\frac{1}{\sqrt n}U_n(\theta_0).
\]

\[
\frac1{\sqrt n}U_n(\theta_0)
=
\frac1{\sqrt n}\sum_{i=1}^n s_{\theta_0}(X_i).
\]

\[
E_{\theta_0}[s_{\theta_0}(X)]=0,
\qquad
\operatorname{Var}_{\theta_0}(s_{\theta_0}(X))=I(\theta_0).
\]

\[
\frac1{\sqrt n}U_n(\theta_0)
\Rightarrow
N_d(0,I(\theta_0)).
\]

Also, by consistency of \(\hat\theta_n\), continuity of \(I(\theta)\), and a uniform law of large numbers for the Hessian,

\[
A_n \overset{p}{\to} I(\theta_0).
\]

\[
A_n^{-1}\overset{p}{\to} I(\theta_0)^{-1}.
\]

Therefore, by Slutsky’s theorem,

\[
\sqrt n(\hat\theta_n-\theta_0)
\Rightarrow
I(\theta_0)^{-1}Z,
\]

where \(Z\sim N_d(0,I(\theta_0))\). Hence

\[
I(\theta_0)^{-1}Z
\sim
N_d\left(0, I(\theta_0)^{-1}I(\theta_0)I(\theta_0)^{-1}\right)
=
N_d(0,I(\theta_0)^{-1}).
\]

Therefore,

\[
\boxed{
\sqrt n(\hat\theta_n-\theta_0)
\Rightarrow
N_d(0,I(\theta_0)^{-1})
}
\]

and equivalently,

\[
\boxed{
\hat\theta_n
=
\theta_0+
I(\theta_0)^{-1}\frac1n U_n(\theta_0)
+o_p(n^{-1/2}).
}
\]

Let \(\tilde\theta_n\) be a preliminary estimator satisfying

\[
\sqrt n(\tilde\theta_n-\theta_0)=O_p(1).
\]

Define the observed information matrix

\[
\widehat I_n(\theta)
=
-\frac1n H_n(\theta).
\]

The one-step estimator is the estimator obtained by applying one Newton-Raphson step to the likelihood score equation starting from \(\tilde\theta_n\):

\[
\boxed{
\theta_n^{(1)}
=
\tilde\theta_n
+
\widehat I_n(\tilde\theta_n)^{-1}
\frac1n U_n(\tilde\theta_n).
}
\]

Equivalently,

\[
\theta_n^{(1)}
=
\tilde\theta_n
-
H_n(\tilde\theta_n)^{-1}U_n(\tilde\theta_n).
\]

We prove that \(\theta_n^{(1)}\) is asymptotically equivalent to the MLE.

From Part 1,

\[
\sqrt n(\hat\theta_n-\theta_0)=O_p(1).
\]

Since also \(\sqrt n(\tilde\theta_n-\theta_0)=O_p(1)\), we have

\[
\hat\theta_n-\tilde\theta_n=O_p(n^{-1/2}).
\]

Now Taylor expand the score \(U_n\) around \(\tilde\theta_n\) in the direction of \(\hat\theta_n\). Since \(U_n(\hat\theta_n)=0\),

\[
0
=
U_n(\hat\theta_n)
=
U_n(\tilde\theta_n)
+
\left\{
\int_0^1
H_n\big(\tilde\theta_n+t(\hat\theta_n-\tilde\theta_n)\big)\,dt
\right\}
(\hat\theta_n-\tilde\theta_n).
\]

Define

\[
B_n
=
-\frac1n
\int_0^1
H_n\big(\tilde\theta_n+t(\hat\theta_n-\tilde\theta_n)\big)\,dt.
\]

Then

\[
\frac1n U_n(\tilde\theta_n)
=
B_n(\hat\theta_n-\tilde\theta_n).
\]

Therefore,

\[
\theta_n^{(1)}
=
\tilde\theta_n
+
\widehat I_n(\tilde\theta_n)^{-1}
B_n(\hat\theta_n-\tilde\theta_n).
\]

Subtracting \(\hat\theta_n\), we get

\[
\theta_n^{(1)}-\hat\theta_n
=
\left[
\widehat I_n(\tilde\theta_n)^{-1}B_n-I_d
\right]
(\hat\theta_n-\tilde\theta_n).
\]

Equivalently,

\[
\theta_n^{(1)}-\hat\theta_n
=
\widehat I_n(\tilde\theta_n)^{-1}
\left[
B_n-\widehat I_n(\tilde\theta_n)
\right]
(\hat\theta_n-\tilde\theta_n).
\]

By the uniform law of large numbers for the Hessian and consistency of both \(\tilde\theta_n\) and \(\hat\theta_n\),

\[
\widehat I_n(\tilde\theta_n)\overset{p}{\to} I(\theta_0),
\qquad
B_n\overset{p}{\to} I(\theta_0).
\]

Thus,

\[
\widehat I_n(\tilde\theta_n)^{-1}=O_p(1),
\qquad
B_n-\widehat I_n(\tilde\theta_n)=o_p(1).
\]

Since \(\hat\theta_n-\tilde\theta_n=O_p(n^{-1/2})\), it follows that

\[
\theta_n^{(1)}-\hat\theta_n
=
O_p(1)\,o_p(1)\,O_p(n^{-1/2})
=
o_p(n^{-1/2}).
\]

Hence

\[
\sqrt n(\theta_n^{(1)}-\hat\theta_n)\overset{p}{\to}0.
\]

Therefore,

\[
\sqrt n(\theta_n^{(1)}-\theta_0)
=
\sqrt n(\hat\theta_n-\theta_0)
+
\sqrt n(\theta_n^{(1)}-\hat\theta_n)
=
\sqrt n(\hat\theta_n-\theta_0)+o_p(1).
\]

\[

\Rightarrow

\]

\[

Let \(y=(y_1,\dots,y_n)^\top\), \(X\in\mathbb R^{n\times p}\), \(\widehat\Sigma=X^\top X/n\), and write \(X_j\) for the \(j\)th column of \(X\). I will state the asymptotic distribution under standard high-dimensional regularity assumptions: columns of \(X\) are normalized, suitable restricted eigenvalue/compatibility conditions hold, and the nodewise regression for \(X_j\) is sufficiently sparse. A typical sufficient condition is that \(X_i\) are i.i.d. sub-Gaussian with covariance \(\Sigma\) having eigenvalues bounded away from \(0,\infty\), the \(j\)th row of \(\Theta=\Sigma^{-1}\) is sparse, and

\[
k\frac{\log p}{\sqrt n}\to 0.
\]

---

## 1. Lasso estimator and inferential difficulty

The Lasso estimator is

\[
\widehat\beta^{\mathrm{L}}
\in \arg\min_{b\in\mathbb R^p}
\left\{
\frac{1}{2n}\|y-Xb\|_2^2+\lambda \|b\|_1
\right\},
\]

where typically

\[
\lambda \asymp \sigma \sqrt{\frac{\log p}{n}}.
\]

Under restricted eigenvalue assumptions and \(\|\beta\|_0\le k\), the Lasso satisfies the oracle-type bounds

\[
\|\widehat\beta^{\mathrm{L}}-\beta\|_1
=O_p\!\left(k\sigma \sqrt{\frac{\log p}{n}}\right),
\]

and

\[
\frac1n\|X(\widehat\beta^{\mathrm{L}}-\beta)\|_2^2
=O_p\!\left(\sigma^2 k\frac{\log p}{n}\right).
\]

However, the Lasso is not directly suitable for classical inference on a coordinate \(\beta_j\). The main reasons are:

1. **Regularization bias.** The \(\ell_1\)-penalty shrinks coefficients toward zero, producing bias of order \(\lambda\), which is typically much larger than \(n^{-1/2}\) when \(p\) is large.

2. **Nonnormality.** The Lasso is a nonsmooth, nonlinear estimator. Its coordinatewise distribution is generally not asymptotically normal.

3. **Model selection uncertainty.** The active set selected by the Lasso is random. Naively treating the selected model as fixed leads to invalid confidence intervals.

4. **High dimensionality.** If \(p>n\), the Gram matrix \(X^\top X/n\) is singular, so the usual OLS variance formula is unavailable.

To perform inference, one therefore removes the first-order Lasso bias. This leads to the debiased or desparsified Lasso.

---

## 2. Debiased Lasso estimator and limiting distribution

Fix \(j\in\{1,\dots,p\}\). To construct an approximate inverse of \(\widehat\Sigma\), regress \(X_j\) on the other columns \(X_{-j}\) using the nodewise Lasso:

\[
\widehat\gamma_j
\in
\arg\min_{\gamma\in\mathbb R^{p-1}}
\left\{
\frac{1}{2n}\|X_j-X_{-j}\gamma\|_2^2+\lambda_j\|\gamma\|_1
\right\},
\]

with

\[
\lambda_j\asymp \sqrt{\frac{\log p}{n}}.
\]

Define the residual

\[
z_j=X_j-X_{-j}\widehat\gamma_j.
\]

The debiased Lasso estimator of \(\beta_j\) is

\[
\widehat b_j
=
\widehat\beta_j^{\mathrm L}
+
\frac{z_j^\top (y-X\widehat\beta^{\mathrm L})}{z_j^\top X_j}.
\]

Equivalently, defining \(\widehat\theta_j\in\mathbb R^p\) by

\[
\widehat\theta_j
=
\frac{1}{\widehat\tau_j^2}
\begin{pmatrix}
-\widehat\gamma_{j,1}\\
\vdots\\
1\\
\vdots\\
-\widehat\gamma_{j,p-1}
\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
\widehat\tau_j^2=\frac{z_j^\top X_j}{n},
\]

we can write

\[
\widehat b_j
=
\widehat\beta_j^{\mathrm L}
+
\widehat\theta_j^\top
\frac{X^\top(y-X\widehat\beta^{\mathrm L})}{n}.
\]

The nodewise Lasso KKT conditions imply

\[
\|\widehat\Sigma \widehat\theta_j-e_j\|_\infty
=
O_p\!\left(\sqrt{\frac{\log p}{n}}\right).
\]

Now expand \(\widehat b_j-\beta_j\). Since \(y=X\beta+\varepsilon\),

\[
\widehat b_j-\beta_j
=
\frac{z_j^\top \varepsilon}{z_j^\top X_j}
+
\frac{z_j^\top X_{-j}(\beta_{-j}-\widehat\beta_{-j}^{\mathrm L})}{z_j^\top X_j}.
\]

The first term is the leading stochastic term. The second term is the bias remainder. By the nodewise Lasso KKT conditions,

\[
\max_{\ell\neq j}
\left|
\frac{z_j^\top X_\ell}{z_j^\top X_j}
\right|
=
O_p\!\left(\sqrt{\frac{\log p}{n}}\right).
\]

Therefore,

\[
\left|
\frac{z_j^\top X_{-j}(\beta_{-j}-\widehat\beta_{-j}^{\mathrm L})}{z_j^\top X_j}
\right|
\le
\max_{\ell\neq j}
\left|
\frac{z_j^\top X_\ell}{z_j^\top X_j}
\right|
\|\widehat\beta^{\mathrm L}-\beta\|_1.
\]

Using the Lasso oracle bound,

\[
\|\widehat\beta^{\mathrm L}-\beta\|_1
=
O_p\!\left(k\sigma\sqrt{\frac{\log p}{n}}\right),
\]

we get

\[
\left|
\frac{z_j^\top X_{-j}(\beta_{-j}-\widehat\beta_{-j}^{\mathrm L})}{z_j^\top X_j}
\right|
=
O_p\!\left(\sigma k\frac{\log p}{n}\right).
\]

If

\[
k\frac{\log p}{\sqrt n}\to 0,
\]

then this remainder is \(o_p(\sigma n^{-1/2})\), which is negligible relative to the \(n^{-1/2}\) stochastic term.

Conditional on \(X\), because \(\varepsilon\sim N(0,\sigma^2 I_n)\),

\[
\frac{z_j^\top \varepsilon}{z_j^\top X_j}
\mid X
\sim
N\left(
0,
\sigma^2\frac{\|z_j\|_2^2}{(z_j^\top X_j)^2}
\right).
\]

Define

\[
\widehat V_j
=
n\frac{\|z_j\|_2^2}{(z_j^\top X_j)^2}
=
\widehat\theta_j^\top \widehat\Sigma \widehat\theta_j.
\]

Then

\[
\frac{\sqrt n(\widehat b_j-\beta_j)}
{\sigma\sqrt{\widehat V_j}}
\overset{d}{\longrightarrow}
N(0,1).
\]

Equivalently,

\[
\widehat b_j
=
\beta_j
+
N\left(0,\frac{\sigma^2 \widehat V_j}{n}\right)
+
o_p(n^{-1/2}).
\]

Under random-design assumptions with sparse precision matrix row \(j\), one also has \(\widehat V_j\to_p \Theta_{jj}\), so

\[
\frac{\sqrt n(\widehat b_j-\beta_j)}
{\sigma\sqrt{\Theta_{jj}}}
\overset{d}{\longrightarrow}
N(0,1).
\]

---

## 3. Confidence interval with data-dependent estimation of \(\sigma^2\)

To avoid using the unknown \(\sigma\), one can estimate it by the square-root/scaled Lasso. Define \((\widehat\beta^{\mathrm{sc}},\widehat\sigma)\) as a solution of

\[
(\widehat\beta^{\mathrm{sc}},\widehat\sigma)
\in
\arg\min_{b\in\mathbb R^p,\ \tau>0}
\left\{
\frac{\|y-Xb\|_2^2}{2n\tau}
+\frac{\tau}{2}
+\lambda_{\mathrm{sc}}\|b\|_1
\right\},
\]

with

\[
\lambda_{\mathrm{sc}}\asymp \sqrt{\frac{\log p}{n}}.
\]

For fixed \(b\), the minimizing \(\tau\) is

\[
\tau=\frac{\|y-Xb\|_2}{\sqrt n},
\]

so at the solution,

\[
\widehat\sigma^2
=
\frac1n\|y-X\widehat\beta^{\mathrm{sc}}\|_2^2.
\]

Under the same sparsity and restricted eigenvalue assumptions, the square-root/scaled Lasso satisfies

\[
\|\widehat\beta^{\mathrm{sc}}-\beta\|_1
=
O_p\!\left(k\sigma\sqrt{\frac{\log p}{n}}\right),
\]

and

\[
\frac1n\|X(\widehat\beta^{\mathrm{sc}}-\beta)\|_2^2
=
O_p\!\left(\sigma^2 k\frac{\log p}{n}\right).
\]

Let \(\delta=\widehat\beta^{\mathrm{sc}}-\beta\). Then

\[
\widehat\sigma^2
=
\frac1n\|y-X\widehat\beta^{\mathrm{sc}}\|_2^2
=
\frac1n\|\varepsilon-X\delta\|_2^2.
\]

Expanding,

\[
\widehat\sigma^2
=
\frac1n\|\varepsilon\|_2^2
+
\frac1n\|X\delta\|_2^2
-
\frac{2}{n}\varepsilon^\top X\delta.
\]

Because \(\varepsilon_i\sim N(0,\sigma^2)\),

\[
\frac1n\|\varepsilon\|_2^2
=
\sigma^2+O_p\left(\frac{\sigma^2}{\sqrt n}\right).
\]

Also,

\[
\frac1n\|X\delta\|_2^2
=
O_p\!\left(\sigma^2 k\frac{\log p}{n}\right).
\]

Finally, using \(\|X^\top\varepsilon/n\|_\infty=O_p(\sigma\sqrt{\log p/n})\),

\[
\left|
\frac{2}{n}\varepsilon^\top X\delta
\right|
\le
2\left\|\frac{X^\top\varepsilon}{n}\right\|_\infty
\|\delta\|_1
=
O_p\!\left(\sigma^2 k\frac{\log p}{n}\right).
\]

Thus, if \(k\log p/n\to 0\),

\[
\frac{\widehat\sigma^2}{\sigma^2}\to_p 1.
\]

Use \(\widehat\beta^{\mathrm{sc}}\) as the initial estimator in the debiased Lasso construction and define

\[
\widehat b_j
=
\widehat\beta_j^{\mathrm{sc}}
+
\frac{z_j^\top (y-X\widehat\beta^{\mathrm{sc}})}{z_j^\top X_j}.
\]

Then

\[
\frac{\sqrt n(\widehat b_j-\beta_j)}
{\widehat\sigma\sqrt{\widehat V_j}}
\overset{d}{\longrightarrow}
N(0,1),
\]

where

\[
\widehat V_j
=
n\frac{\|z_j\|_2^2}{(z_j^\top X_j)^2}.
\]

Therefore, an asymptotic \(1-\alpha\) confidence interval for \(\beta_j\) is

\[
\boxed{
\left[
\widehat b_j
-
z_{1-\alpha/2}\,
\widehat\sigma
\sqrt{\frac{\widehat V_j}{n}},
\quad
\widehat b_j
+
z_{1-\alpha/2}\,
\widehat\sigma
\sqrt{\frac{\widehat V_j}{n}}
\right]
}
\]

or equivalently,

\[
\boxed{
\left[
\widehat b_j
-
z_{1-\alpha/2}\,
\widehat\sigma
\frac{\|z_j\|_2}{|z_j^\top X_j|},
\quad
\widehat b_j
+
z_{1-\alpha/2}\,
\widehat\sigma
\frac{\|z_j\|_2}{|z_j^\top X_j|}
\right].
}
\]

By Slutsky’s theorem, this interval has asymptotic coverage probability \(1-\alpha\).

## 1. Lasso and the inference difficulty

Let \(X\in\mathbb R^{n\times p}\) have rows \(X_{i\cdot}^\top\), and write

\[
y=X\beta+\varepsilon,\qquad \varepsilon\sim N(0,\sigma^2 I_n).
\]

Assume the columns of \(X\) are standardized, e.g. \(\|X_j\|_2^2/n=1\). The Lasso estimator is

\[
\widehat\beta
\in
\arg\min_{b\in\mathbb R^p}
\left\{
\frac{1}{2n}\|y-Xb\|_2^2+\lambda\|b\|_1
\right\},
\]

with tuning parameter typically \(\lambda\asymp \sigma\sqrt{\log p/n}\).

The main inference difficulty is that the Lasso is biased because of the \(\ell_1\)-penalty. Even in the orthogonal case \(X^\top X/n=I_p\), the Lasso is a coordinatewise soft-thresholding estimator,

\[
\widehat\beta_j
=
\operatorname{sgn}(z_j)(|z_j|-\lambda)_+,
\qquad 
z_j=\beta_j+\frac{X_j^\top\varepsilon}{n},
\]

so its distribution is non-Gaussian and has a point mass at \(0\). Thus naive Wald-type intervals centered at \(\widehat\beta_j\) are invalid. In high dimension \(p\gg n\), ordinary least squares is unavailable because \(X^\top X\) is singular, and post-selection inference after choosing a model by Lasso is also nonstandard because the selected model is random. The debiased Lasso corrects the first-order shrinkage bias.

---

## 2. Debiased Lasso and limiting distribution

Let

\[
\widehat\Sigma=\frac{1}{n}X^\top X.
\]

We want a vector \(\widehat\theta_j\in\mathbb R^p\) such that

\[
\widehat\Sigma \widehat\theta_j \approx e_j,
\]

where \(e_j\) is the \(j\)th standard basis vector. One common construction is the nodewise Lasso.

For fixed \(j\), regress \(X_j\) on \(X_{-j}\):

\[
\widehat\gamma_j
\in
\arg\min_{\gamma\in\mathbb R^{p-1}}
\left\{
\frac{1}{2n}\|X_j-X_{-j}\gamma\|_2^2+\lambda_j\|\gamma\|_1
\right\},
\qquad 
\lambda_j\asymp \sqrt{\frac{\log p}{n}}.
\]

Let

\[
\widehat r_j=X_j-X_{-j}\widehat\gamma_j,
\]

and define \(\widehat c_j\in\mathbb R^p\) by

\[
(\widehat c_j)_j=1,
\qquad
(\widehat c_j)_\ell=-(\widehat\gamma_j)_\ell,\quad \ell\neq j.
\]

Then \(X\widehat c_j=\widehat r_j\). Define

\[
\widehat\tau_j^2
=
\frac{1}{n}\|\widehat r_j\|_2^2+\lambda_j\|\widehat\gamma_j\|_1,
\qquad
\widehat\theta_j
=
\frac{\widehat c_j}{\widehat\tau_j^2}.
\]

By the KKT conditions for the nodewise Lasso,

\[
\|\widehat\Sigma\widehat\theta_j-e_j\|_\infty
\lesssim \lambda_j
\asymp \sqrt{\frac{\log p}{n}}.
\]

The debiased Lasso estimator of \(\beta_j\) is

\[
\widetilde\beta_j
=
\widehat\beta_j
+
\widehat\theta_j^\top \frac{1}{n}X^\top(y-X\widehat\beta).
\]

Using \(y=X\beta+\varepsilon\),

\[
\begin{aligned}
\widetilde\beta_j-\beta_j
&=
\widehat\beta_j-\beta_j
+
\widehat\theta_j^\top \frac{1}{n}X^\top X(\beta-\widehat\beta)
+
\widehat\theta_j^\top \frac{1}{n}X^\top\varepsilon \\
&=
\widehat\theta_j^\top \frac{1}{n}X^\top\varepsilon
+
(e_j-\widehat\Sigma \widehat\theta_j)^\top(\widehat\beta-\beta).
\end{aligned}
\]

Thus

\[
\widetilde\beta_j-\beta_j
=
\underbrace{\widehat\theta_j^\top \frac{1}{n}X^\top\varepsilon}_{\text{Gaussian leading term}}
+
\underbrace{(e_j-\widehat\Sigma \widehat\theta_j)^\top(\widehat\beta-\beta)}_{\text{remainder}}.
\]

Assume the usual high-dimensional conditions: a restricted eigenvalue or compatibility condition for \(X\), sparsity \(\|\beta\|_0\le k\), and

\[
k\frac{\log p}{\sqrt n}\to 0.
\]

Then by the standard Lasso oracle inequality,

\[
\|\widehat\beta-\beta\|_1
=
O_p\left(k\sigma\sqrt{\frac{\log p}{n}}\right).
\]

Therefore the remainder satisfies

\[
\left|
(e_j-\widehat\Sigma \widehat\theta_j)^\top(\widehat\beta-\beta)
\right|
\le
\|\widehat\Sigma\widehat\theta_j-e_j\|_\infty
\|\widehat\beta-\beta\|_1
=
O_p\left(\sigma k\frac{\log p}{n}\right),
\]

so

\[
\sqrt n\,
(e_j-\widehat\Sigma \widehat\theta_j)^\top(\widehat\beta-\beta)
=
o_p(\sigma).
\]

Let

\[
\widehat V_j
=
\widehat\theta_j^\top \widehat\Sigma \widehat\theta_j.
\]

Conditional on \(X\),

\[
\widehat\theta_j^\top \frac{1}{n}X^\top\varepsilon
\sim
N\left(0,\frac{\sigma^2}{n}\widehat V_j\right),
\]

because \(\varepsilon\sim N(0,\sigma^2 I_n)\). Hence

\[
\frac{\sqrt n(\widetilde\beta_j-\beta_j)}
{\sigma\sqrt{\widehat V_j}}
=
\frac{
\widehat\theta_j^\top X^\top\varepsilon
}{
\sigma\sqrt{n\widehat V_j}
}
+
o_p(1)
\;\;\xrightarrow{d}\;\;
N(0,1).
\]

Equivalently, if \(\widehat V_j\to_p V_j\), then

\[
\sqrt n(\widetilde\beta_j-\beta_j)
\;\xrightarrow{d}\;
N(0,\sigma^2 V_j).
\]

In the common random-design setting with \(\Sigma=\mathbb E[X_iX_i^\top]\) and precision matrix \(\Theta=\Sigma^{-1}\), one typically has \(V_j=\Theta_{jj}\), so

\[
\sqrt n(\widetilde\beta_j-\beta_j)
\;\xrightarrow{d}\;
N(0,\sigma^2\Theta_{jj}).
\]

---

## 3. Confidence interval with data-dependent variance estimation

We need estimate \(\sigma^2\). A convenient fully data-dependent method is the square-root/scaled Lasso:

\[
(\widehat\beta^{\,0},\widehat\sigma)
\in
\arg\min_{b\in\mathbb R^p,\ \tau>0}
\left\{
\frac{\|y-Xb\|_2^2}{2n\tau}

+\lambda_0\|b\|_1
\right\},
\qquad

\]

For fixed \(b\), the minimizing \(\tau\) is

\[
\tau=\frac{\|y-Xb\|_2}{\sqrt n},
\]

so \(\widehat\sigma\) is essentially the residual scale estimate. Under the same restricted eigenvalue and sparsity assumptions,

\[
\widehat\sigma/\sigma \xrightarrow{p} 1.
\]

Alternatively, one may take the residual variance estimator

\[
\widehat\sigma^2
=
\frac{1}{n}\|y-X\widehat\beta\|_2^2.
\]

Indeed, writing \(\Delta=\widehat\beta-\beta\),

\[
\widehat\sigma^2
=
\frac{1}{n}\|\varepsilon-X\Delta\|_2^2
=
\frac{1}{n}\|\varepsilon\|_2^2
+
\frac{1}{n}\|X\Delta\|_2^2
-
\frac{2}{n}\varepsilon^\top X\Delta.
\]

By the Lasso prediction bound,

\[
\frac{1}{n}\|X\Delta\|_2^2
=
O_p\left(\sigma^2 k\frac{\log p}{n}\right)
=
o_p(\sigma^2),
\]

and

\[
\left|
\frac{1}{n}\varepsilon^\top X\Delta
\right|
\le
\left\|\frac{1}{n}X^\top\varepsilon\right\|_\infty
\|\Delta\|_1
=
O_p\left(\sigma^2 k\frac{\log p}{n}\right)
=
o_p(\sigma^2).
\]

Also,

\[
\frac{1}{n}\|\varepsilon\|_2^2
\xrightarrow{p}
\sigma^2
\]

by the law of large numbers. Hence \(\widehat\sigma^2\to_p\sigma^2\).

Therefore an asymptotic \(1-\alpha\) confidence interval for \(\beta_j\) is

\[
\boxed{
\mathrm{CI}_{j,1-\alpha}
=
\left[
\widetilde\beta_j
-
z_{1-\alpha/2}\widehat\sigma
\sqrt{\frac{\widehat V_j}{n}},
\;
\widetilde\beta_j
+
z_{1-\alpha/2}\widehat\sigma
\sqrt{\frac{\widehat V_j}{n}}
\right],
}
\]

where

\[
\widehat V_j
=
\widehat\theta_j^\top \widehat\Sigma \widehat\theta_j.
\]

By Slutsky’s theorem,

\[
\frac{\sqrt n(\widetilde\beta_j-\beta_j)}
{\widehat\sigma\sqrt{\widehat V_j}}
\xrightarrow{d}
N(0,1),
\]

so

\[
\mathbb P\left(\beta_j\in \mathrm{CI}_{j,1-\alpha}\right)
\to
1-\alpha.
\]

Thus the debiased Lasso yields asymptotically valid coordinatewise inference despite \(p\) possibly being much larger than \(n\).

Let \(Y=(y_1,\dots,y_n)^\top\), \(X\in\mathbb R^{n\times p}\), \(\widehat\Sigma=X^\top X/n\). Assume throughout that the columns of \(X\) are standardized and that \(p\) may be much larger than \(n\).

## 1. Lasso and the inference difficulty

The Lasso estimator is

\[
\widehat\beta
\in \arg\min_{b\in\mathbb R^p}
\left\{
\frac{1}{2n}\|Y-Xb\|_2^2+\lambda \|b\|_1
\right\},
\]

with tuning parameter typically of order

\[
\lambda \asymp \sigma \sqrt{\frac{\log p}{n}}.
\]

The Lasso is useful for prediction and variable selection under sparsity, but it is not directly suitable for classical inference on a coordinate \(\beta_j\). The main reasons are:

1. **Shrinkage bias.** The \(\ell_1\)-penalty shrinks coefficients toward zero. The bias is of order \(\lambda\), and since  
   \[
   \sqrt n\,\lambda \asymp \sqrt{\log p},
   \]
   the bias is generally much larger than the \(n^{-1/2}\) scale needed for asymptotic normal inference.

2. **Nonstandard distribution.** The Lasso is a nonsmooth function of the data; its distribution has kinks and may have atoms at zero.

3. **Post-selection issues.** If one selects a model using the Lasso and then performs ordinary least squares inference as if the model were fixed, the resulting confidence intervals are generally invalid because they ignore selection uncertainty.

Thus, to construct valid confidence intervals for \(\beta_j\), one needs to remove the leading shrinkage bias. This motivates the debiased, or desparsified, Lasso.

---

## 2. Debiased Lasso estimator and limiting distribution

A standard form of the debiased Lasso is

\[
\widetilde\beta_j
=
\widehat\beta_j
+
\frac{1}{n}\widehat\theta_j^\top X^\top(Y-X\widehat\beta),
\]

where \(\widehat\theta_j\in\mathbb R^p\) is an approximate \(j\)-th column of the inverse Gram matrix \(\widehat\Sigma^{-1}\), chosen so that

\[
\widehat\Sigma \widehat\theta_j \approx e_j.
\]

A common way to construct \(\widehat\theta_j\) is by the nodewise Lasso.

For fixed \(j\), regress \(X_j\) on the remaining columns \(X_{-j}\):

\[
\widehat\gamma_j
\in
\arg\min_{\gamma\in\mathbb R^{p-1}}
\left\{
\frac{1}{2n}\|X_j-X_{-j}\gamma\|_2^2
+
\lambda_j\|\gamma\|_1
\right\}.
\]

Define the residual

\[
\widehat z_j=X_j-X_{-j}\widehat\gamma_j
\]

and

\[
\widehat\tau_j^2
=
\frac{1}{n}\widehat z_j^\top X_j.
\]

Then define \(\widehat\theta_j\in\mathbb R^p\) by inserting \(1\) in the \(j\)-th coordinate and \(-\widehat\gamma_j\) in the other coordinates, normalized by \(\widehat\tau_j^2\). Equivalently,

\[
X\widehat\theta_j=\frac{\widehat z_j}{\widehat\tau_j^2}.
\]

Then the debiased Lasso can be written as

\[
\widetilde\beta_j
=
\widehat\beta_j
+
\frac{\widehat z_j^\top(Y-X\widehat\beta)}
{\widehat z_j^\top X_j}.
\]

Now expand:

\[
Y=X\beta+\varepsilon.
\]

Therefore,

\[
\begin{aligned}
\widetilde\beta_j-\beta_j
&=
\widehat\beta_j-\beta_j
+
\frac{1}{n}\widehat\theta_j^\top X^\top X(\beta-\widehat\beta)
+
\frac{1}{n}\widehat\theta_j^\top X^\top\varepsilon \\
&=
\frac{1}{n}\widehat\theta_j^\top X^\top\varepsilon
+
\left(e_j^\top-\widehat\theta_j^\top\widehat\Sigma\right)
(\widehat\beta-\beta).
\end{aligned}
\]

The first term is the asymptotically normal stochastic term. The second term is the remainder/bias term.

Let

\[
\widehat V_j
=
\widehat\theta_j^\top\widehat\Sigma\widehat\theta_j
=
\frac{n\|\widehat z_j\|_2^2}{(\widehat z_j^\top X_j)^2}.
\]

Conditional on \(X\),

\[
\frac{1}{n}\widehat\theta_j^\top X^\top\varepsilon
\sim
N\left(0,\frac{\sigma^2}{n}\widehat V_j\right).
\]

Under standard high-dimensional regularity assumptions, namely:

- the rows \(X_i\) are sub-Gaussian with covariance \(\Sigma\),
- the eigenvalues of \(\Sigma\) are bounded away from \(0\) and \(\infty\),
- \(\beta\) is \(k\)-sparse with
  \[
  k\frac{\log p}{\sqrt n}\to 0,
  \]
- the \(j\)-th column of \(\Sigma^{-1}\) is sparse enough so that the nodewise Lasso consistently estimates it,

one has the usual Lasso rate

\[
\|\widehat\beta-\beta\|_1
=
O_p\left(k\sigma\sqrt{\frac{\log p}{n}}\right),
\]

and the nodewise Lasso satisfies

\[
\|\widehat\Sigma\widehat\theta_j-e_j\|_\infty
=
O_p\left(\sqrt{\frac{\log p}{n}}\right).
\]

Hence the remainder satisfies

\[
\begin{aligned}
\left|
\left(e_j^\top-\widehat\theta_j^\top\widehat\Sigma\right)
(\widehat\beta-\beta)
\right|
&\le
\|\widehat\Sigma\widehat\theta_j-e_j\|_\infty
\|\widehat\beta-\beta\|_1 \\
&=
O_p\left(
\sigma k\frac{\log p}{n}
\right).
\end{aligned}
\]

Therefore,

\[
\sqrt n\,
\left|
\left(e_j^\top-\widehat\theta_j^\top\widehat\Sigma\right)
(\widehat\beta-\beta)
\right|
=
O_p\left(
\sigma k\frac{\log p}{\sqrt n}
\right)
=
o_p(\sigma).
\]

Thus the remainder is negligible on the \(n^{-1/2}\) scale. Consequently,

\[
\frac{\sqrt n(\widetilde\beta_j-\beta_j)}
{\sigma\sqrt{\widehat V_j}}
\overset{d}{\longrightarrow}
N(0,1).
\]

Equivalently,

\[
\widetilde\beta_j
=
\beta_j
+
\frac{1}{n}\widehat\theta_j^\top X^\top\varepsilon
+
o_p(n^{-1/2}),
\]

and if \(\widehat V_j\to_p \Omega_{jj}\), where \(\Omega=\Sigma^{-1}\), then

\[
\sqrt n(\widetilde\beta_j-\beta_j)
\overset{d}{\longrightarrow}
N(0,\sigma^2\Omega_{jj}).
\]

---

## 3. Confidence interval with data-dependent estimation of \(\sigma^2\)

A consistent estimator of \(\sigma^2\) may be obtained from a scaled Lasso or square-root Lasso. For example, define \((\widehat\beta^{\,\mathrm{sc}},\widehat\sigma)\) by

\[
(\widehat\beta^{\,\mathrm{sc}},\widehat\sigma)
\in
\arg\min_{b\in\mathbb R^p,\ \tau>0}
\left\{
\frac{\|Y-Xb\|_2^2}{2n\tau}
+\frac{\tau}{2}
+\lambda_{\mathrm{sc}}\|b\|_1
\right\},
\]

with

\[
\lambda_{\mathrm{sc}}\asymp \sqrt{\frac{\log p}{n}}.
\]

Under the same sparsity and design assumptions,

\[
\widehat\sigma \overset{p}{\longrightarrow} \sigma.
\]

Alternatively, one may use a residual estimator such as

\[
\widehat\sigma^2
=
\frac{1}{n}\|Y-X\widehat\beta\|_2^2,
\]

or with a degrees-of-freedom correction,

\[
\widehat\sigma^2
=
\frac{\|Y-X\widehat\beta\|_2^2}{n-\|\widehat\beta\|_0},
\]

provided \(\|\widehat\beta\|_0=o_p(n)\). Under the usual Lasso prediction bounds, these are consistent when \(k\log p/n\to 0\).

Thus an asymptotic \(1-\alpha\) confidence interval for \(\beta_j\) is

\[
\boxed{
\left[
\widetilde\beta_j
-
z_{1-\alpha/2}\,
\widehat\sigma
\sqrt{\frac{\widehat V_j}{n}},
\quad
\widetilde\beta_j
+
z_{1-\alpha/2}\,
\widehat\sigma
\sqrt{\frac{\widehat V_j}{n}}
\right]
}
\]

where

\[
\widehat V_j
=
\widehat\theta_j^\top\widehat\Sigma\widehat\theta_j
=
\frac{n\|\widehat z_j\|_2^2}{(\widehat z_j^\top X_j)^2}.
\]

Equivalently, using the nodewise residual form,

\[
\sqrt{\frac{\widehat V_j}{n}}
=
\frac{\|\widehat z_j\|_2}{|\widehat z_j^\top X_j|},
\]

so the interval can be written as

\[
\boxed{
\left[
\widetilde\beta_j
-
z_{1-\alpha/2}\,
\widehat\sigma
\frac{\|\widehat z_j\|_2}{|\widehat z_j^\top X_j|},
\quad
\widetilde\beta_j
+
z_{1-\alpha/2}\,
\widehat\sigma
\frac{\|\widehat z_j\|_2}{|\widehat z_j^\top X_j|}
\right].
}
\]

By the limiting distribution above and Slutsky’s theorem,

\[
\mathbb P\left(\beta_j\in \mathrm{CI}_{j,1-\alpha}\right)
\to
1-\alpha.
\]

Assume \((Y_i,D_i,H_i,e_i)\), \(i=1,\dots,n\), are i.i.d. with finite second moments and mean zero. Write the structural model as

\[
Y_i = D_i\beta + H_i\psi + e_i,
\]

where \(H_i\) is unobserved. For simplicity I first treat \(D_i,H_i\) as scalar; the vector generalization is stated below.

---

## 1. When is OLS consistent for \(\beta\)?

If we regress \(Y_i\) on \(D_i\) alone, the OLS estimator is

\[
\widehat\beta_{\text{OLS}}
=
\frac{\sum_{i=1}^n D_iY_i}{\sum_{i=1}^n D_i^2}.
\]

Using the structural equation,

\[
\widehat\beta_{\text{OLS}}
=
\frac{\sum_i D_i(D_i\beta + H_i\psi + e_i)}{\sum_i D_i^2}
=
\beta
+
\psi \frac{\sum_i D_iH_i}{\sum_i D_i^2}
+
\frac{\sum_i D_ie_i}{\sum_i D_i^2}.
\]

By the law of large numbers,

\[
\widehat\beta_{\text{OLS}}
\overset{p}{\longrightarrow}
\beta
+
\psi \frac{\mathbb E[D_iH_i]}{\mathbb E[D_i^2]}
+
\frac{\mathbb E[D_ie_i]}{\mathbb E[D_i^2]}.
\]

Assuming \(e_i\) is independent of \(D_i\) and centered, \(\mathbb E[D_ie_i]=0\). Hence

\[
\operatorname{plim}\widehat\beta_{\text{OLS}}
=
\beta
+
\psi \frac{\operatorname{Cov}(D_i,H_i)}{\operatorname{Var}(D_i)}.
\]

Therefore OLS is consistent for \(\beta\) iff

\[
\psi\,\mathbb E[D_iH_i]=0.
\]

Equivalently, the composite error term

\[
u_i := H_i\psi + e_i
\]

must be uncorrelated with \(D_i\):

\[
\mathbb E[D_i u_i]=0.
\]

Thus OLS is consistent if there is no omitted-variable bias, for example if

\[
\operatorname{Cov}(D_i,H_i)=0,
\]

or if \(\psi=0\), meaning the hidden variable does not affect \(Y_i\). If \(H_i\) affects \(Y_i\) and is correlated with \(D_i\), then OLS is generally inconsistent.

For vector-valued \(D_i\) and \(H_i\), with

\[
Y_i = D_i^\top \beta + H_i^\top \psi + e_i,
\]

OLS satisfies

\[
\operatorname{plim}\widehat\beta_{\text{OLS}}
=
\beta
+
\left(\mathbb E[D_iD_i^\top]\right)^{-1}
\mathbb E[D_iH_i^\top]\psi,
\]

assuming \(\mathbb E[D_iD_i^\top]\) is nonsingular. Hence OLS is consistent iff

\[
\mathbb E[D_iH_i^\top]\psi=0.

\[
Y_i = D_i\beta + H_i\psi + e_i,

\[
\widehat\beta_{\mathrm{OLS}}
=
\frac{\sum_{i=1}^n D_iY_i}{\sum_{i=1}^n D_i^2}.
\]

Substituting the structural equation,

\[
\widehat\beta_{\mathrm{OLS}}
=
\frac{\sum_i D_i(D_i\beta + H_i\psi + e_i)}{\sum_i D_i^2}
=
\beta
+
\psi\frac{\sum_i D_iH_i}{\sum_i D_i^2}
+
\frac{\sum_i D_ie_i}{\sum_i D_i^2}.
\]

By the law of large numbers,

\[
\widehat\beta_{\mathrm{OLS}}
\overset{p}{\longrightarrow}
\beta
+
\psi\frac{E[D_iH_i]}{E[D_i^2]}
+
\frac{E[D_ie_i]}{E[D_i^2]}.
\]

If \(e_i\) is independent of \(D_i\) and centered, then \(E[D_ie_i]=0\). Therefore,

\[
\plim \widehat\beta_{\mathrm{OLS}}
=
\beta
+
\psi\frac{E[D_iH_i]}{E[D_i^2]}.
\]

Hence OLS is consistent for \(\beta\) if and only if

\[
\psi E[D_iH_i]=0.
\]

In particular, OLS is consistent if any of the following hold:

1. \(H_i\) has no direct effect on \(Y_i\), i.e. \(\psi=0\);
2. \(D_i\) is uncorrelated with the hidden confounder \(H_i\), i.e.

   \[
   E[D_iH_i]=\operatorname{Cov}(D_i,H_i)=0;
   \]

3. more generally, the omitted-variable term is mean-orthogonal to \(D_i\):

   \[
   E[D_i(H_i\psi+e_i)] = 0.
   \]

\[
\operatorname{Bias}_{\infty}(\widehat\beta_{\mathrm{OLS}})
=
\psi\frac{E[D_iH_i]}{E[D_i^2]}.
\]

For vector-valued \(D_i\), the corresponding condition is

\[
E[D_i(H_i\psi+e_i)] = 0,

and under \(E[e_i\mid D_i]=0\), this reduces to

\[
E[D_iH_i]\psi = 0.

An instrumental variable is an observed variable \(Z_i\) satisfying two key conditions.

\[
u_i = H_i\psi + e_i

denote the composite structural error when \(H_i\) is omitted. A valid instrument \(Z_i\) for \(D_i\) satisfies:

### Relevance

\[
E[Z_iD_i]\neq 0

\[

\[

\[

\[
E[Z_iH_i]=0,
\qquad
E[Z_ie_i]=0.

\[
\widehat\beta_{\mathrm{IV}}
=
\frac{\sum_{i=1}^n Z_iY_i}{\sum_{i=1}^n Z_iD_i}.
\]

\[
\widehat\beta_{\mathrm{IV}}
=
\frac{\sum_i Z_i(D_i\beta+u_i)}{\sum_i Z_iD_i}
=
\beta
+
\frac{\sum_i Z_iu_i}{\sum_i Z_iD_i}.
\]

By the law of large numbers,

\[
\widehat\beta_{\mathrm{IV}}
\overset{p}{\longrightarrow}
\beta
+
\frac{E[Z_iu_i]}{E[Z_iD_i]}.
\]

Under instrument exogeneity, \(E[Z_iu_i]=0\), and under relevance, \(E[Z_iD_i]\neq 0\). Therefore,

\[
\widehat\beta_{\mathrm{IV}}
\overset{p}{\longrightarrow}
\beta.
\]

Thus \(\widehat\beta_{\mathrm{IV}}\) is consistent for \(\beta\).

\[
P_Z = Z(Z'Z)^{-1}Z'.
\]

The 2SLS estimator is

\[
\widehat\beta_{\mathrm{2SLS}}
=
(D'P_ZD)^{-1}D'P_ZY.
\]

Equivalently, one may view it as:

1. First stage: regress \(D\) on \(Z\) and compute fitted values \(\widehat D=P_ZD\).
2. Second stage: regress \(Y\) on \(\widehat D\).

Under the relevance rank condition and the moment condition

\[
E[Z_i(Y_i-D_i'\beta)] = E[Z_iu_i]=0,
\]

the 2SLS estimator is consistent:

\[
\widehat\beta_{\mathrm{2SLS}}\overset{p}{\longrightarrow}\beta.
\]

So a valid IV removes the bias caused by the hidden confounder \(H_i\) by using only variation in \(D_i\) that is induced by \(Z_i\), which is assumed unrelated to \(H_i\) and \(e_i\).

\operatorname{Bias}_{\infty}
=
\psi\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(D_i,H_i)}{\operatorname{Var}(D_i)}.
\]

For vector \(D_i\in\mathbb R^p\) and \(H_i\in\mathbb R^q\), the corresponding probability limit is

\[
\operatorname{plim}\widehat\beta_{\mathrm{OLS}}
=
\beta
+
\left(\mathbb E[D_iD_i^\top]\right)^{-1}
\mathbb E[D_iH_i^\top]\psi,
\]

assuming \(\mathbb E[D_iD_i^\top]\) is nonsingular. Hence OLS is consistent iff

\[
\mathbb E[D_iH_i^\top]\psi=0.
\]

---

## 2. Instrumental variable and consistent IV estimator

An instrumental variable is a variable \(Z_i\) satisfying two main conditions.

### Instrument relevance

The instrument must be correlated with the treatment \(D_i\). In the scalar case,

\[
\mathbb E[Z_iD_i]\neq 0.
\]

For vector \(D_i\), the rank condition is

\[
\operatorname{rank}\left(\mathbb E[Z_iD_i^\top]\right)=p,
\]

where \(p=\dim(D_i)\).

### Instrument exogeneity / exclusion

The instrument must be uncorrelated with the structural error in the outcome equation. Here the structural error when regressing \(Y_i\) on \(D_i\) is

\[
u_i=H_i\psi+e_i.
\]

Thus we require

\[
\mathbb E[Z_i u_i]=0,
\]

or equivalently,

\[
\mathbb E[Z_iH_i]\psi+\mathbb E[Z_ie_i]=0.
\]

A sufficient condition is

\[
Z_i\perp (H_i,e_i),
\]

or at least

\[
\mathbb E[Z_iH_i]=0,
\qquad
\mathbb E[Z_ie_i]=0.
\]

The exclusion restriction means that \(Z_i\) affects \(Y_i\) only through \(D_i\), not directly and not through the hidden confounder \(H_i\).

---

### Scalar IV estimator

Assume \(Z_i,D_i,Y_i\) are centered and scalar. The moment condition is

\[
\mathbb E[Z_i(Y_i-D_i\beta)]=0.
\]

Since

\[
Y_i=D_i\beta+H_i\psi+e_i,
\]

we have

\[
\mathbb E[Z_iY_i]
=
\mathbb E[Z_iD_i]\beta
+
\mathbb E[Z_iH_i]\psi
+
\mathbb E[Z_ie_i].
\]

By instrument exogeneity,

\[
\mathbb E[Z_iH_i]\psi+\mathbb E[Z_ie_i]=0.
\]

Therefore,

\[
\mathbb E[Z_iY_i]=\mathbb E[Z_iD_i]\beta.
\]

If \(\mathbb E[Z_iD_i]\neq 0\), then

\[
\beta
=
\frac{\mathbb E[Z_iY_i]}{\mathbb E[Z_iD_i]}.
\]

The natural IV estimator is therefore

\[
\widehat\beta_{\mathrm{IV}}
=
\frac{\sum_{i=1}^n Z_iY_i}{\sum_{i=1}^n Z_iD_i}.
\]

By the law of large numbers and the continuous mapping theorem,

\[
\widehat\beta_{\mathrm{IV}}
\overset{p}{\longrightarrow}
\frac{\mathbb E[Z_iY_i]}{\mathbb E[Z_iD_i]}
=
\beta.
\]

Thus \(\widehat\beta_{\mathrm{IV}}\) is consistent.

If the variables are not centered, the centered sample covariance version is

\[
\widehat\beta_{\mathrm{IV}}
=
\frac{\sum_i (Z_i-\bar Z)(Y_i-\bar Y)}
{\sum_i (Z_i-\bar Z)(D_i-\bar D)}.
\]

---

### Vector form and 2SLS estimator

Let \(D_i\in\mathbb R^p\) and let \(Z_i\in\mathbb R^m\) be a vector of instruments with \(m\ge p\). The IV moment condition is

\[
\mathbb E\left[Z_i(Y_i-D_i^\top\beta)\right]=0.
\]

The relevance/rank condition is

\[
\operatorname{rank}\left(\mathbb E[Z_iD_i^\top]\right)=p.
\]

If \(m=p\), the exactly identified IV estimator is

\[
\widehat\beta_{\mathrm{IV}}
=
\left(\sum_{i=1}^n Z_iD_i^\top\right)^{-1}
\left(\sum_{i=1}^n Z_iY_i\right).
\]

If \(m>p\), a standard consistent estimator is the two-stage least squares estimator

\[
\widehat\beta_{\mathrm{2SLS}}
=
(D^\top P_ZD)^{-1}D^\top P_ZY,
\]

where \(D\) is the \(n\times p\) treatment matrix, \(Z\) is the \(n\times m\) instrument matrix, and

\[
P_Z=Z(Z^\top Z)^{-1}Z^\top
\]

is the projection matrix onto the column space of \(Z\).

Equivalently, two-stage least squares proceeds by:

1. First stage: regress \(D\) on \(Z\), obtaining fitted values \(\widehat D=P_ZD\).
2. Second stage: regress \(Y\) on \(\widehat D\).

Under the relevance condition and the exogeneity/exclusion condition,

\[
\mathbb E[Z_i(H_i^\top\psi+e_i)]=0,
\]

the IV/2SLS estimator is consistent for \(\beta\).

Let \(X\) denote the \(n\times p\) matrix whose \(i\)th row is \(X_i^T\), so that  
\[
\widehat \Sigma=\frac{X^T X}{n}.
\]
Also write \(S=S^*=\{j:u_j^*\neq 0\}\), \(s=|S|\), and for a vector \(b\), write
\[
\|b_S\|_1=\sum_{j\in S}|b_j|,\qquad \|b_{S^c}\|_1=\sum_{j\notin S}|b_j|.
\]

Since \(u^*=\Gamma \xi^*=\Sigma^{-1}\xi^*\), we have
\[
\Sigma u^*=\xi^*.
\]

---

## 1) Sub-Gaussianity of \(u^{*T}X_i\)

Because \(X_i\sim N(0,\Sigma)\), the scalar random variable
\[
u^{*T}X_i
\]
is Gaussian with mean \(0\) and variance
\[
\operatorname{Var}(u^{*T}X_i)=u^{*T}\Sigma u^*.
\]
Since the eigenvalues of \(\Sigma\) are bounded above by \(\sigma_1\),
\[
u^{*T}\Sigma u^*\le \sigma_1\|u^*\|_2^2.
\]
Thus
\[
u^{*T}X_i\sim N\bigl(0,u^{*T}\Sigma u^*\bigr)
\]
is sub-Gaussian with scale parameter at most
\[
\sqrt{u^{*T}\Sigma u^*}\le \sqrt{\sigma_1}\|u^*\|_2.
\]

Equivalently, for every \(t\in \mathbb R\),
\[
\mathbb E\exp\{t u^{*T}X_i\}
=\exp\left(\frac{t^2}{2}u^{*T}\Sigma u^*\right)
\le \exp\left(\frac{t^2}{2}\sigma_1\|u^*\|_2^2\right).
\]

---

## 2) Choice of \(\lambda_0\) for \(\Omega_0(\lambda_0)\)

We need to control
\[
\|\widehat\Sigma u^*-\xi^*\|_\infty.
\]
Since \(\xi^*=\Sigma u^*\),
\[
\widehat\Sigma u^*-\xi^*
=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n X_iX_i^T u^*-\Sigma u^*.
\]
For coordinate \(j\),
\[
\left(\widehat\Sigma u^*-\xi^*\right)_j
=
\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n X_{ij}(X_i^T u^*)-\mathbb E\left[X_{ij}(X_i^T u^*)\right].
\]

Now \(X_{ij}=e_j^T X_i\sim N(0,\Sigma_{jj})\), and since \(\Sigma_{jj}\le \lambda_{\max}(\Sigma)\le \sigma_1\),
\[
X_{ij}
\]
is sub-Gaussian with scale at most \(\sqrt{\sigma_1}\). By part 1, \(X_i^T u^*\) is sub-Gaussian with scale at most \(\sqrt{\sigma_1}\|u^*\|_2\). Therefore the product has sub-exponential scale of order
\[
\sigma_1\|u^*\|_2.
\]

Using the stated sub-Gaussian product concentration inequality, there is a universal constant \(C>0\) such that for every \(t>0\),
\[
\mathbb P\left(
\left|
\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n X_{ij}(X_i^T u^*)
-\mathbb E[X_{ij}(X_i^T u^*)]
\right|
>
C\sigma_1\|u^*\|_2
\left\{\sqrt{\frac tn}+\frac tn\right\}
\right)
\le 2e^{-t}.
\]

Take
\[
t=\log\frac p\varepsilon.
\]
Then for each fixed \(j\),
\[
\mathbb P\left(
\left|
(\widehat\Sigma u^*-\xi^*)_j
\right|
>
C\sigma_1\|u^*\|_2
\left\{
\sqrt{\frac{\log(p/\varepsilon)}{n}}
+
\frac{\log(p/\varepsilon)}{n}
\right\}
\right)
\le \frac{2\varepsilon}{p}.
\]
A union bound over \(j=1,\dots,p\) gives
\[
\mathbb P\left(
\|\widehat\Sigma u^*-\xi^*\|_\infty>\lambda_0
\right)
\le 2\varepsilon,
\]
where one may take
\[
\boxed{
\lambda_0
=
C\sigma_1\|u^*\|_2
\left\{
\sqrt{\frac{\log(p/\varepsilon)}{n}}
+
\frac{\log(p/\varepsilon)}{n}
\right\}.
}
\]
Thus
\[
\boxed{
\mathbb P(\Omega_0(\lambda_0))\ge 1-2\varepsilon.
}
\]

If the product concentration inequality is stated only in its small-deviation form, then under \(\log(p/\varepsilon)\lesssim n\) one can take the simpler choice
\[
\lambda_0
\asymp
\sigma_1\|u^*\|_2
\sqrt{\frac{\log(p/\varepsilon)}{n}}.
\]

Also, since \(\|u^*\|_2=\|\Sigma^{-1}\xi^*\|_2\le \sigma_0^{-1}\|\xi^*\|_2\), a fully deterministic upper bound is
\[
\lambda_0
\asymp
\frac{\sigma_1}{\sigma_0}\|\xi^*\|_2
\left\{
\sqrt{\frac{\log(p/\varepsilon)}{n}}
+
\frac{\log(p/\varepsilon)}{n}
\right\}.
\]

---

## 3) Basic inequality

Define the objective
\[
Q_\lambda(u)
=
\frac12 u^T\widehat\Sigma u-u^T\xi^*+\lambda\|u\|_1.
\]
By definition of \(\widehat u_\lambda\),
\[
Q_\lambda(\widehat u_\lambda)\le Q_\lambda(u)
\]
for every \(u\in\mathbb R^p\). Hence
\[
\frac12 \widehat u_\lambda^T\widehat\Sigma \widehat u_\lambda
-\widehat u_\lambda^T\xi^*
+\lambda\|\widehat u_\lambda\|_1
\le
\frac12 u^T\widehat\Sigma u
-u^T\xi^*
+\lambda\|u\|_1.
\]
Let \(\Delta=\widehat u_\lambda-u\). Then
\[
\widehat u_\lambda=u+\Delta.
\]
Expanding,
\[
\frac12 \widehat u_\lambda^T\widehat\Sigma \widehat u_\lambda
-\widehat u_\lambda^T\xi^*
=
\frac12 u^T\widehat\Sigma u-u^T\xi^*
+
(\widehat\Sigma u-\xi^*)^T\Delta
+
\frac12 \Delta^T\widehat\Sigma\Delta.
\]
Since
\[
\Delta^T\widehat\Sigma\Delta
=
\frac1n\|X\Delta\|_2^2,
\]
we obtain
\[
\frac1{2n}\|X(\widehat u_\lambda-u)\|_2^2
+
(\widehat\Sigma u-\xi^*)^T(\widehat u_\lambda-u)
+
\lambda\|\widehat u_\lambda\|_1
\le
\lambda\|u\|_1.
\]

Thus
\[
\boxed{
\frac{1}{2n}\|X(\widehat u_\lambda-u)\|_2^2
+
(\widehat\Sigma u-\xi^*)^T(\widehat u_\lambda-u)
+
\lambda\|\widehat u_\lambda\|_1
\le
\lambda\|u\|_1.
}
\]

---

## 4) Cone-type inequality on \(\Omega_0(\lambda_0)\)

Take \(u=u^*\) in the basic inequality and define
\[
\Delta=\widehat u_\lambda-u^*.
\]
Then
\[
\frac1{2n}\|X\Delta\|_2^2
+
(\widehat\Sigma u^*-\xi^*)^T\Delta
+
\lambda\|\widehat u_\lambda\|_1
\le
\lambda\|u^*\|_1.
\]
On \(\Omega_0(\lambda_0)\),
\[
\| \widehat\Sigma u^*-\xi^*\|_\infty\le \lambda_0,
\]
so by Hölder's inequality,
\[
(\widehat\Sigma u^*-\xi^*)^T\Delta
\ge
-\lambda_0\|\Delta\|_1.
\]
Thus
\[
\frac1{2n}\|X\Delta\|_2^2
-\lambda_0\|\Delta\|_1
+
\lambda\|\widehat u_\lambda\|_1
\le
\lambda\|u^*\|_1.
\]

Because \(u^*_{S^c}=0\),
\[
\|\widehat u_\lambda\|_1
=
\|u^*_S+\Delta_S\|_1+\|\Delta_{S^c}\|_1.
\]
By the reverse triangle inequality,
\[
\|u^*_S+\Delta_S\|_1
\ge
\|u^*_S\|_1-\|\Delta_S\|_1.
\]
Therefore
\[
\|\widehat u_\lambda\|_1
\ge
\|u^*\|_1-\|\Delta_S\|_1+\|\Delta_{S^c}\|_1.
\]
Plugging this into the previous inequality gives
\[
\frac1{2n}\|X\Delta\|_2^2
-\lambda_0\|\Delta\|_1
+
\lambda\left(
\|u^*\|_1-\|\Delta_S\|_1+\|\Delta_{S^c}\|_1
\right)
\le
\lambda\|u^*\|_1.
\]
Canceling \(\lambda\|u^*\|_1\),
\[
\frac1{2n}\|X\Delta\|_2^2
+
\lambda\|\Delta_{S^c}\|_1
\le
\lambda\|\Delta_S\|_1+\lambda_0\|\Delta\|_1.
\]
Equivalently,
\[
\frac1{2n}\|X\Delta\|_2^2
+
(\lambda-\lambda_0)\|\Delta_{S^c}\|_1
\le
(\lambda+\lambda_0)\|\Delta_S\|_1.
\]
Now add \((\lambda-\lambda_0)\|\Delta_S\|_1\) to both sides:
\[
\frac1{2n}\|X\Delta\|_2^2
+
(\lambda-\lambda_0)\|\Delta\|_1
\le
2\lambda\|\Delta_S\|_1.
\]
Taking \(\lambda=A_0\lambda_0\) with \(A_0>1\),
\[
\lambda-\lambda_0=(A_0-1)\lambda_0,
\qquad
2\lambda=2A_0\lambda_0.
\]
Hence
\[
\boxed{
\frac{1}{2n}\|X(\widehat u_\lambda-u^*)\|_2^2
+
(A_0-1)\lambda_0\|\widehat u_\lambda-u^*\|_1
\le
2A_0\lambda_0
\sum_{j\in S^*}|\widehat u_{\lambda,j}-u_j^*|.
}
\]

---

## 5) Prediction and \(\ell_1\)-error bounds under compatibility

Let
\[
\Delta=\widehat u_\lambda-u^*,
\qquad
L_S=\|\Delta_S\|_1,
\qquad
L=\|\Delta\|_1,
\qquad
Q=\Delta^T\widehat\Sigma\Delta
=

Let \(X\) denote the \(n\times p\) matrix whose \(i\)th row is \(X_i^T\), so that  
\[
\widehat \Sigma=\frac{X^T X}{n}.
\]
Also write \(S=S^*=\{j:u_j^*\neq 0\}\), \(s=|S|\), and for a vector \(b\), write
\[
\|b_S\|_1=\sum_{j\in S}|b_j|,\qquad \|b_{S^c}\|_1=\sum_{j\notin S}|b_j|.
\]

Since \(u^*=\Gamma \xi^*=\Sigma^{-1}\xi^*\), we have
\[
\Sigma u^*=\xi^*.
\]

---

## 1) Sub-Gaussianity of \(u^{*T}X_i\)

Because \(X_i\sim N(0,\Sigma)\), the scalar random variable
\[
u^{*T}X_i
\]
is Gaussian with mean \(0\) and variance
\[
\operatorname{Var}(u^{*T}X_i)=u^{*T}\Sigma u^*.
\]
Since the eigenvalues of \(\Sigma\) are bounded above by \(\sigma_1\),
\[
u^{*T}\Sigma u^*\le \sigma_1\|u^*\|_2^2.
\]
Thus
\[
u^{*T}X_i\sim N\bigl(0,u^{*T}\Sigma u^*\bigr)
\]
is sub-Gaussian with scale parameter at most
\[
\sqrt{u^{*T}\Sigma u^*}\le \sqrt{\sigma_1}\|u^*\|_2.
\]

Equivalently, for every \(t\in \mathbb R\),
\[
\mathbb E\exp\{t u^{*T}X_i\}
=\exp\left(\frac{t^2}{2}u^{*T}\Sigma u^*\right)
\le \exp\left(\frac{t^2}{2}\sigma_1\|u^*\|_2^2\right).
\]

---

## 2) Choice of \(\lambda_0\) for \(\Omega_0(\lambda_0)\)

We need to control
\[
\|\widehat\Sigma u^*-\xi^*\|_\infty.
\]
Since \(\xi^*=\Sigma u^*\),
\[
\widehat\Sigma u^*-\xi^*
=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n X_iX_i^T u^*-\Sigma u^*.
\]
For coordinate \(j\),
\[
\left(\widehat\Sigma u^*-\xi^*\right)_j
=
\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n X_{ij}(X_i^T u^*)-\mathbb E\left[X_{ij}(X_i^T u^*)\right].
\]

Now \(X_{ij}=e_j^T X_i\sim N(0,\Sigma_{jj})\), and since \(\Sigma_{jj}\le \lambda_{\max}(\Sigma)\le \sigma_1\),
\[
X_{ij}
\]
is sub-Gaussian with scale at most \(\sqrt{\sigma_1}\). By part 1, \(X_i^T u^*\) is sub-Gaussian with scale at most \(\sqrt{\sigma_1}\|u^*\|_2\). Therefore the product has sub-exponential scale of order
\[
\sigma_1\|u^*\|_2.
\]

Using the stated sub-Gaussian product concentration inequality, there is a universal constant \(C>0\) such that for every \(t>0\),
\[
\mathbb P\left(
\left|
\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n X_{ij}(X_i^T u^*)
-\mathbb E[X_{ij}(X_i^T u^*)]
\right|
>
C\sigma_1\|u^*\|_2
\left\{\sqrt{\frac tn}+\frac tn\right\}
\right)
\le 2e^{-t}.
\]

Take
\[
t=\log\frac p\varepsilon.
\]
Then for each fixed \(j\),
\[
\mathbb P\left(
\left|
(\widehat\Sigma u^*-\xi^*)_j
\right|
>
C\sigma_1\|u^*\|_2
\left\{
\sqrt{\frac{\log(p/\varepsilon)}{n}}
+
\frac{\log(p/\varepsilon)}{n}
\right\}
\right)
\le \frac{2\varepsilon}{p}.
\]
A union bound over \(j=1,\dots,p\) gives
\[
\mathbb P\left(
\|\widehat\Sigma u^*-\xi^*\|_\infty>\lambda_0
\right)
\le 2\varepsilon,
\]
where one may take
\[
\boxed{
\lambda_0
=
C\sigma_1\|u^*\|_2
\left\{
\sqrt{\frac{\log(p/\varepsilon)}{n}}
+
\frac{\log(p/\varepsilon)}{n}
\right\}.
}
\]
Thus
\[
\boxed{
\mathbb P(\Omega_0(\lambda_0))\ge 1-2\varepsilon.
}
\]

If the product concentration inequality is stated only in its small-deviation form, then under \(\log(p/\varepsilon)\lesssim n\) one can take the simpler choice
\[
\lambda_0
\asymp
\sigma_1\|u^*\|_2
\sqrt{\frac{\log(p/\varepsilon)}{n}}.
\]

Also, since \(\|u^*\|_2=\|\Sigma^{-1}\xi^*\|_2\le \sigma_0^{-1}\|\xi^*\|_2\), a fully deterministic upper bound is
\[
\lambda_0
\asymp
\frac{\sigma_1}{\sigma_0}\|\xi^*\|_2
\left\{
\sqrt{\frac{\log(p/\varepsilon)}{n}}
+
\frac{\log(p/\varepsilon)}{n}
\right\}.
\]

---

Define the objective
\[
Q_\lambda(u)
=
\frac12 u^T\widehat\Sigma u-u^T\xi^*+\lambda\|u\|_1.
\]
By definition of \(\widehat u_\lambda\),
\[
Q_\lambda(\widehat u_\lambda)\le Q_\lambda(u)

for every \(u\in\mathbb R^p\). Hence
\[
\frac12 \widehat u_\lambda^T\widehat\Sigma \widehat u_\lambda
-\widehat u_\lambda^T\xi^*
+\lambda\|\widehat u_\lambda\|_1
\le
\frac12 u^T\widehat\Sigma u
-u^T\xi^*
+\lambda\|u\|_1.
\]
Let \(\Delta=\widehat u_\lambda-u\). Then
\[
\widehat u_\lambda=u+\Delta.
\]

\[
\frac12 \widehat u_\lambda^T\widehat\Sigma \widehat u_\lambda
-\widehat u_\lambda^T\xi^*
=
\frac12 u^T\widehat\Sigma u-u^T\xi^*
+
(\widehat\Sigma u-\xi^*)^T\Delta
+
\frac12 \Delta^T\widehat\Sigma\Delta.
\]
Since
\[
\Delta^T\widehat\Sigma\Delta
=
\frac1n\|X\Delta\|_2^2,
\]
we obtain
\[
\frac1{2n}\|X(\widehat u_\lambda-u)\|_2^2
+
(\widehat\Sigma u-\xi^*)^T(\widehat u_\lambda-u)
+
\lambda\|\widehat u_\lambda\|_1
\le
\lambda\|u\|_1.
\]

Thus
\[
\boxed{
\frac{1}{2n}\|X(\widehat u_\lambda-u)\|_2^2
+
(\widehat\Sigma u-\xi^*)^T(\widehat u_\lambda-u)
+
\lambda\|\widehat u_\lambda\|_1
\le
\lambda\|u\|_1.
}
\]

---

\[

\[

\lambda\|u^*\|_1.

\[

\[

\]

Because \(u^*_{S^c}=0\),
\[

=

By the reverse triangle inequality,
\[

Therefore

\le

\le

Now add \((\lambda-\lambda_0)\|\Delta_S\|_1\) to both sides:
\[

+
(\lambda-\lambda_0)\|\Delta\|_1
\le
2\lambda\|\Delta_S\|_1.
\]
Taking \(\lambda=A_0\lambda_0\) with \(A_0>1\),
\[

\qquad
2\lambda=2A_0\lambda_0.
\]
Hence
\[

\frac{1}{2n}\|X(\widehat u_\lambda-u^*)\|_2^2
+
(A_0-1)\lambda_0\|\widehat u_\lambda-u^*\|_1
\le
2A_0\lambda_0
\sum_{j\in S^*}|\widehat u_{\lambda,j}-u_j^*|.

\]

=

=

=

\[
\sigma_1\|u^*\|_2.
\]

\[
\mathbb P\left(

>
C\sigma_1\|u^*\|_2

>

=

+

\[

## 3) Basic inequality

\[
Q_\lambda(u)
=
\frac12 u^T\hat\Sigma u-u^T\xi^*+\lambda\|u\|_1.
\]

\[
Q_\lambda(\hat u_\lambda)\le Q_\lambda(u)

for every \(u\in\mathbb R^p\).

\[

\[

=

+

\[

+

\le

\[

\[

\ge

+

\le
\lambda\|u^*\|_1+\lambda_0\|\Delta\|_1.

\[

=

\[

\ge

\ge
\|u^*\|_1-\|\Delta_{S^*}\|_1+\|\Delta_{(S^*)^c}\|_1.

\[
\frac{1}{2n}\|X\Delta\|_2^2
+
\lambda\|\Delta_{(S^*)^c}\|_1
\le
\lambda\|\Delta_{S^*}\|_1
+
\lambda_0\|\Delta\|_1.
\]
Equivalently,
\[
\frac{1}{2n}\|X\Delta\|_2^2
+

\le
(\lambda+\lambda_0)\|\Delta_{S^*}\|_1.

\[
\frac{1}{2n}\|X\Delta\|_2^2
+

\le
(A_0+1)\lambda_0\|\Delta_{S^*}\|_1.

Adding \((A_0-1)\lambda_0\|\Delta_{S^*}\|_1\) to both sides yields
\[
\frac{1}{2n}\|X\Delta\|_2^2
+
(A_0-1)\lambda_0\|\Delta\|_1
\le
2A_0\lambda_0\|\Delta_{S^*}\|_1.

\[

\frac{1}{2n}\|X(\hat u_\lambda-u^*)\|_2^2
+
(A_0-1)\lambda_0\|\hat u_\lambda-u^*\|_1
\le
2A_0\lambda_0

}
\]

---

## 5) Bounds under empirical compatibility

Let
\[
R=\frac1n\|X\Delta\|_2^2,
\qquad
L=\|\Delta\|_1,
\qquad
L_S=\|\Delta_{S^*}\|_1.
\]

From the sharper inequality in part 4,
\[
\frac12 R
+
(A_0-1)\lambda_0\|\Delta_{(S^*)^c}\|_1
\le
(A_0+1)\lambda_0\|\Delta_{S^*}\|_1.
\]
Dropping the nonnegative prediction term gives the cone condition
\[
\|\Delta_{(S^*)^c}\|_1
\le
\frac{A_0+1}{A_0-1}\|\Delta_{S^*}\|_1.
\]
Thus, if \(\eta_0>1\) and \(A_0\) is chosen so that
\[
\boxed{
\frac{A_0+1}{A_0-1}\le \eta_0,
}
\]
then \(\Delta\) lies in the compatibility cone. Equivalently, it suffices to take
\[
\boxed{
A_0\ge \frac{\eta_0+1}{\eta_0-1}.
}
\]

On \(\Omega_{\mathrm{Comp}}\), we therefore have
\[
\nu_0^2 L_S^2
\le
s\,\Delta^T\hat\Sigma\Delta
=
sR.
\]
Hence
\[
L_S\le \frac{\sqrt{sR}}{\nu_0}.
\]

From the inequality in part 4,
\[
\frac12 R\le 2A_0\lambda_0 L_S.
\]
Using the compatibility bound,
\[
\frac12 R
\le
2A_0\lambda_0\frac{\sqrt{sR}}{\nu_0}.
\]
If \(R>0\), divide by \(\sqrt R\) to get
\[
\sqrt R
\le
\frac{4A_0}{\nu_0}\lambda_0\sqrt{s}.
\]
Thus
\[
R
\le
\frac{16A_0^2}{\nu_0^2}s\lambda_0^2.
\]
Therefore
\[
\boxed{
\frac1n\|X(\hat u_\lambda-u^*)\|_2^2
\le
\frac{16A_0^2}{\nu_0^2}|S^*|\lambda_0^2.
}
\]

Next, from part 4 again,
\[
(A_0-1)\lambda_0 L
\le
2A_0\lambda_0 L_S.
\]
Thus
\[
L
\le
\frac{2A_0}{A_0-1}L_S.
\]
Using \(L_S\le \sqrt{sR}/\nu_0\) and the prediction bound just obtained,
\[
L_S
\le
\frac{\sqrt{s}}{\nu_0}\sqrt R
\le
\frac{\sqrt{s}}{\nu_0}
\cdot
\frac{4A_0}{\nu_0}\lambda_0\sqrt{s}
=
\frac{4A_0}{\nu_0^2}s\lambda_0.
\]
Hence
\[
L
\le
\frac{2A_0}{A_0-1}
\cdot
\frac{4A_0}{\nu_0^2}s\lambda_0
=
\frac{8A_0^2}{(A_0-1)\nu_0^2}s\lambda_0.
\]
Therefore
\[
\boxed{
\|\hat u_\lambda-u^*\|_1
\le
\frac{8A_0^2}{(A_0-1)\nu_0^2}|S^*|\lambda_0.
}
\]

Thus the desired statement holds with, for example,
\[
\boxed{
M_0
=
\max\left\{
\frac{16A_0^2}{\nu_0^2},
\frac{8A_0^2}{(A_0-1)\nu_0^2}
\right\}.
}
\]

---

## 6) Outline for proving \(P(\Omega_{\mathrm{Comp}})\ge 1-2\varepsilon\)

Let
\[
\mathcal C(S^*,\eta_0)
=
\left\{
b\in\mathbb R^p:
\|b_{(S^*)^c}\|_1\le \eta_0\|b_{S^*}\|_1
\right\}.
\]

The goal is to show that with high probability,
\[
b^T\hat\Sigma b
\gtrsim
\|b\|_2^2
\]
uniformly over \(b\in\mathcal C(S^*,\eta_0)\).

### Step 1: Population compatibility

For every \(b\),
\[
b^T\Sigma b\ge \sigma_0\|b\|_2^2.
\]
Also,
\[
\|b_{S^*}\|_1\le \sqrt{s}\|b_{S^*}\|_2\le \sqrt{s}\|b\|_2.
\]
Thus
\[
\|b\|_2^2\ge \frac{\|b_{S^*}\|_1^2}{s}.
\]
So at the population level,
\[
b^T\Sigma b
\ge
\frac{\sigma_0}{s}\|b_{S^*}\|_1^2.
\]

### Step 2: Uniform lower concentration over the cone

Write
\[
X=Z\Sigma^{1/2},
\]
where the rows of \(Z\) are i.i.d. \(N(0,I_p)\). Consider
\[
T=\mathcal C(S^*,\eta_0)\cap \mathbb S^{p-1}.
\]
For \(b\in T\),
\[
\|b\|_1
\le
(1+\eta_0)\|b_{S^*}\|_1
\le
(1+\eta_0)\sqrt{s}.
\]
Therefore \(T\) has Gaussian width bounded by
\[
w(T)\lesssim (1+\eta_0)\sqrt{s\log(ep/s)}.
\]

By the Gaussian matrix deviation inequality/Gordon’s theorem, with probability at least \(1-2e^{-t^2}\),
\[
\inf_{b\in T}\frac1{\sqrt n}\|Xb\|_2
\ge
\sqrt{\sigma_0}
-
C\sqrt{\sigma_1}\frac{w(T)+t}{\sqrt n}.
\]
Taking \(t=\sqrt{\log(1/\varepsilon)}\), this event has probability at least \(1-2\varepsilon\).

### Step 3: Sample size condition

If for some \(0<\nu_0<\sqrt{\sigma_0}\),
\[
C\sqrt{\sigma_1}
\frac{(1+\eta_0)\sqrt{s\log(ep/s)}+\sqrt{\log(1/\varepsilon)}}{\sqrt n}
\le
\sqrt{\sigma_0}-\nu_0,
\]
equivalently if
\[
\boxed{
n
\gtrsim
\frac{\sigma_1}{(\sqrt{\sigma_0}-\nu_0)^2}
\left[
(1+\eta_0)^2s\log(ep/s)+\log(1/\varepsilon)
\right],
}
\]
then
\[
\inf_{b\in T}\frac1{\sqrt n}\|Xb\|_2\ge \nu_0.
\]
By homogeneity, for all \(b\in \mathcal C(S^*,\eta_0)\),
\[
b^T\hat\Sigma b
=
\frac1n\|Xb\|_2^2
\ge
\nu_0^2\|b\|_2^2
\ge
\frac{\nu_0^2}{s}\|b_{S^*}\|_1^2.
\]
Thus
\[
\nu_0^2\|b_{S^*}\|_1^2
\le
s\, b^T\hat\Sigma b,
\]
which is exactly \(\Omega_{\mathrm{Comp}}\).

Hence, under the stated sample size condition,
\[
\boxed{
\mathbb P(\Omega_{\mathrm{Comp}})\ge 1-2\varepsilon.
}
\]

b^T\hat\Sigma b
\gtrsim

\[

b^T\Sigma b
\ge

\[

\le

\[

\[
C\sqrt{\sigma_1}
\frac{(1+\eta_0)\sqrt{s\log(ep/s)}+\sqrt{\log(1/\varepsilon)}}{\sqrt n}
\le

\]

\[
\boxed{

\gtrsim
\frac{\sigma_1}{(\sqrt{\sigma_0}-\nu_0)^2}
\left[

\[

\[
b^T\hat\Sigma b
=

\ge

\ge

\]

\[
\nu_0^2\|b_{S^*}\|_1^2
\le
s\, b^T\hat\Sigma b,
\]

\[
\boxed{
\mathbb P(\Omega_{\mathrm{Comp}})\ge 1-2\varepsilon.

\]

Let the rows of \(X\) be \(X_i^T\), so that \(\hat\Sigma=X^TX/n\) and \((Xu)_i=X_i^Tu\). Write

\[
S^*=\{j:u_j^*\neq 0\},\qquad s=|S^*|.
\]

Also note throughout that since \(u^*=\Sigma^{-1}\xi^*\),

\[
\Sigma u^*=\xi^*.
\]

---

## 1) Sub-Gaussianity of \(u^{*T}X_i\)

Since \(X_i\sim N(0,\Sigma)\),

\[
u^{*T}X_i\sim N\left(0,u^{*T}\Sigma u^*\right).
\]

Because the eigenvalues of \(\Sigma\) lie in \([\sigma_0,\sigma_1]\),

\[
u^{*T}\Sigma u^*\le \sigma_1\|u^*\|_2^2.
\]

Thus for every \(t\in\mathbb R\),

\[
\mathbb E e^{t u^{*T}X_i}
=\exp\left(\frac{t^2}{2}u^{*T}\Sigma u^*\right)
\le \exp\left(\frac{t^2}{2}\sigma_1\|u^*\|_2^2\right).
\]

Therefore \(u^{*T}X_i\) is sub-Gaussian with scale parameter

\[
\boxed{\sqrt{\sigma_1}\,\|u^*\|_2.}
\]

---

## 2) Choice of \(\lambda_0\) for \(\Omega_0(\lambda_0)\)

We want to control

\[
\|\hat\Sigma u^*-\xi^*\|_\infty.
\]

Since \(\xi^*=\Sigma u^*\), for each coordinate \(j\),

\[
(\hat\Sigma u^*-\xi^*)_j
=
\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n X_{ij}(X_i^Tu^*)-\mathbb E[X_{ij}(X_i^Tu^*)].
\]

Now \(X_{ij}\) is Gaussian with variance \(\Sigma_{jj}\le \sigma_1\), hence sub-Gaussian with scale at most \(\sqrt{\sigma_1}\). By part 1, \(X_i^Tu^*\) is sub-Gaussian with scale at most \(\sqrt{\sigma_1}\|u^*\|_2\). Therefore the product \(X_{ij}(X_i^Tu^*)\) is sub-exponential with scale of order

\[
\sigma_1\|u^*\|_2.
\]

Using the given sub-Gaussian product concentration bound, there is a universal constant \(C>0\) such that for each fixed \(j\),

\[
\mathbb P\left(
\left|
(\hat\Sigma u^*-\xi^*)_j
\right|
>
C\sigma_1\|u^*\|_2
\left[
\sqrt{\frac{t}{n}}+\frac{t}{n}
\right]
\right)
\le 2e^{-t}.
\]

Apply the union bound over \(j=1,\dots,p\). Taking

\[
t=\log\frac{p}{\varepsilon},
\]

we get

\[
\mathbb P\left(
\|\hat\Sigma u^*-\xi^*\|_\infty
>
C\sigma_1\|u^*\|_2
\left[
\sqrt{\frac{\log(p/\varepsilon)}{n}}
+
\frac{\log(p/\varepsilon)}{n}
\right]
\right)
\le 2p e^{-t}=2\varepsilon.
\]

Thus one valid choice is

\[
\boxed{
\lambda_0
=
C\sigma_1\|u^*\|_2
\left[
\sqrt{\frac{\log(p/\varepsilon)}{n}}
+
\frac{\log(p/\varepsilon)}{n}
\right].
}
\]

Then

\[
\boxed{
\mathbb P\bigl(\Omega_0(\lambda_0)\bigr)\ge 1-2\varepsilon.
}
\]

If \(\log(p/\varepsilon)\lesssim n\), this simplifies to

\[
\lambda_0
\asymp
\sigma_1\|u^*\|_2
\sqrt{\frac{\log(p/\varepsilon)}{n}}.
\]

Also, since \(\|u^*\|_2=\|\Sigma^{-1}\xi^*\|_2\le \sigma_0^{-1}\|\xi^*\|_2\), one may further upper bound \(\|u^*\|_2\) by \(\|\xi^*\|_2/\sigma_0\).

---

## 3) Basic inequality

By definition,

\[
\hat u_\lambda
=
\arg\min_u
\left\{
\frac12u^T\hat\Sigma u-u^T\xi^*+\lambda\|u\|_1
\right\}.
\]

Therefore for any \(u\in\mathbb R^p\),

\[
\frac12\hat u_\lambda^T\hat\Sigma \hat u_\lambda
-
\hat u_\lambda^T\xi^*
+
\lambda\|\hat u_\lambda\|_1
\le
\frac12u^T\hat\Sigma u
-
u^T\xi^*
+
\lambda\|u\|_1.
\]

Let

\[
\Delta=\hat u_\lambda-u.
\]

Then \(\hat u_\lambda=u+\Delta\). Expanding the quadratic term,

\[
\frac12\hat u_\lambda^T\hat\Sigma \hat u_\lambda
-
\frac12u^T\hat\Sigma u
=
u^T\hat\Sigma \Delta+\frac12\Delta^T\hat\Sigma \Delta.
\]

Also,

\[
\hat u_\lambda^T\xi^*-u^T\xi^*=\xi^{*T}\Delta.
\]

Hence

\[
\frac12\Delta^T\hat\Sigma \Delta
+
(\hat\Sigma u-\xi^*)^T\Delta
+
\lambda\|\hat u_\lambda\|_1
\le
\lambda\|u\|_1.
\]

Since \(\Delta^T\hat\Sigma \Delta=\|X\Delta\|_2^2/n\), we obtain

\[

\frac{1}{2n}\|X(\hat u_\lambda-u)\|_2^2
+

\lambda\|\hat u_\lambda\|_1
\le
\lambda\|u\|_1.
}
\]

---

Take \(u=u^*\) in the basic inequality and define

\[
\Delta=\hat u_\lambda-u^*.

\[

\[

\le
\lambda\|u^*\|_1+\lambda_0\|\Delta\|_1.
\]

Cancel \(\lambda\|u^*\|_1\). Since

\[

\[
\frac1{2n}\|X\Delta\|_2^2
+
(\lambda-\lambda_0)\|\Delta_{S^{*c}}\|_1
\le
(\lambda+\lambda_0)\|\Delta_{S^*}\|_1.
\]

Now take \(\lambda=A_0\lambda_0\), where \(A_0>1\). Then

\[
\frac1{2n}\|X\Delta\|_2^2
+
(A_0-1)\lambda_0\|\Delta_{S^{*c}}\|_1
\le
(A_0+1)\lambda_0\|\Delta_{S^*}\|_1.
\]

Adding \((A_0-1)\lambda_0\|\Delta_{S^*}\|_1\) to both sides gives

\[
\frac1{2n}\|X\Delta\|_2^2
+
(A_0-1)\lambda_0\|\Delta\|_1
\le
2A_0\lambda_0\|\Delta_{S^*}\|_1.
\]

Equivalently,

\[
\boxed{
\frac{1}{2n}\|X(\hat u_\lambda-u^*)\|_2^2
+
(A_0-1)\lambda_0\|\hat u_\lambda-u^*\|_1
\le
2A_0\lambda_0

---

\[
\Delta=\hat u_\lambda-u^*,
\qquad
q=\frac1n\|X\Delta\|_2^2

\[
\nu_0^2\|\Delta_{S^*}\|_1^2
\le
s\,\Delta^T\hat\Sigma\Delta
=
sq.
\]

\[
\|\Delta_{S^*}\|_1
\le

\[
\frac q2
\le
2A_0\lambda_0\|\Delta_{S^*}\|_1.

Using the compatibility bound,

\le

\le
\frac{4A_0}{\nu_0}\sqrt{s}\lambda_0,

\[
\boxed{
q
=

M_0
=
\max\left\{
\frac{16A_0^2}{\nu_0^2},

\right\}.

\[
\boxed{
\frac1n\|X(\hat u_\lambda-u^*)\|_2^2

M_0 s\lambda_0^2,
}

\[
\boxed{
\|\hat u_\lambda-u^*\|_1
\le
M_0 s\lambda_0.
}

\[
C(S^*,\eta_0)

(1+\eta_0)\sqrt{s\log(ep/s)}.

b^T\hat\Sigma b
\ge
\frac{\sigma_0}{2}\|b\|_2^2

\[
s\,b^T\hat\Sigma b
\ge
\frac{\sigma_0}{2}s\|b\|_2^2

\frac{\sigma_0}{2}\|b_{S^*}\|_1^2.

\[
\nu_0^2\le \frac{\sigma_0}{2}.
\]

\[
\boxed{
\mathbb P(\Omega_{\mathrm{Comp}})\ge 1-2\varepsilon.
}
\]

\]

---

## 2) Choice of \(\lambda_0\) for \(\Omega_0(\lambda_0)\)

We want to control

\[
\|\hat\Sigma u^*-\xi^*\|_\infty.
\]

Since \(\xi^*=\Sigma u^*\), for each coordinate \(j\),

\[
(\hat\Sigma u^*-\xi^*)_j
=
\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n X_{ij}(X_i^Tu^*)-\mathbb E[X_{ij}(X_i^Tu^*)].
\]

Now \(X_{ij}\) is Gaussian with variance \(\Sigma_{jj}\le \sigma_1\), hence sub-Gaussian with scale at most \(\sqrt{\sigma_1}\). By part 1, \(X_i^Tu^*\) is sub-Gaussian with scale at most \(\sqrt{\sigma_1}\|u^*\|_2\). Therefore the product \(X_{ij}(X_i^Tu^*)\) is sub-exponential with scale of order

\[
\sigma_1\|u^*\|_2.
\]

Using the given sub-Gaussian product concentration bound, there is a universal constant \(C>0\) such that for each fixed \(j\),

\[
\mathbb P\left(
\left|
(\hat\Sigma u^*-\xi^*)_j
\right|
>
C\sigma_1\|u^*\|_2
\left[
\sqrt{\frac{t}{n}}+\frac{t}{n}
\right]
\right)
\le 2e^{-t}.
\]

Apply the union bound over \(j=1,\dots,p\). Taking

\[
t=\log\frac{p}{\varepsilon},
\]

we get

\[
\mathbb P\left(
\|\hat\Sigma u^*-\xi^*\|_\infty
>
C\sigma_1\|u^*\|_2
\left[
\sqrt{\frac{\log(p/\varepsilon)}{n}}
+
\frac{\log(p/\varepsilon)}{n}
\right]
\right)
\le 2p e^{-t}=2\varepsilon.
\]

Thus one valid choice is

\[
\boxed{
\lambda_0
=
C\sigma_1\|u^*\|_2
\left[
\sqrt{\frac{\log(p/\varepsilon)}{n}}
+
\frac{\log(p/\varepsilon)}{n}
\right].
}
\]

Then

\[
\boxed{
\mathbb P\bigl(\Omega_0(\lambda_0)\bigr)\ge 1-2\varepsilon.
}
\]

If \(\log(p/\varepsilon)\lesssim n\), this simplifies to

\[
\lambda_0
\asymp
\sigma_1\|u^*\|_2
\sqrt{\frac{\log(p/\varepsilon)}{n}}.
\]

Also, since \(\|u^*\|_2=\|\Sigma^{-1}\xi^*\|_2\le \sigma_0^{-1}\|\xi^*\|_2\), one may further upper bound \(\|u^*\|_2\) by \(\|\xi^*\|_2/\sigma_0\).

---

## 3) Basic inequality

By definition,

\[
\hat u_\lambda
=
\arg\min_u
\left\{
\frac12u^T\hat\Sigma u-u^T\xi^*+\lambda\|u\|_1
\right\}.
\]

Therefore for any \(u\in\mathbb R^p\),

\[
\frac12\hat u_\lambda^T\hat\Sigma \hat u_\lambda
-
\hat u_\lambda^T\xi^*
+
\lambda\|\hat u_\lambda\|_1
\le
\frac12u^T\hat\Sigma u
-
u^T\xi^*
+
\lambda\|u\|_1.
\]

Let

\[
\Delta=\hat u_\lambda-u.
\]

Then \(\hat u_\lambda=u+\Delta\). Expanding the quadratic term,

\[
\frac12\hat u_\lambda^T\hat\Sigma \hat u_\lambda
-
\frac12u^T\hat\Sigma u
=
u^T\hat\Sigma \Delta+\frac12\Delta^T\hat\Sigma \Delta.
\]

Also,

\[
\hat u_\lambda^T\xi^*-u^T\xi^*=\xi^{*T}\Delta.
\]

Hence

\[
\frac12\Delta^T\hat\Sigma \Delta
+
(\hat\Sigma u-\xi^*)^T\Delta
+
\lambda\|\hat u_\lambda\|_1
\le
\lambda\|u\|_1.
\]

Since \(\Delta^T\hat\Sigma \Delta=\|X\Delta\|_2^2/n\), we obtain

\[
\boxed{
\frac{1}{2n}\|X(\hat u_\lambda-u)\|_2^2
+
(\hat\Sigma u-\xi^*)^T(\hat u_\lambda-u)
+
\lambda\|\hat u_\lambda\|_1
\le
\lambda\|u\|_1.
}
\]

---

## 4) Oracle inequality on \(\Omega_0(\lambda_0)\)

Take \(u=u^*\) in the basic inequality and define

\[
\Delta=\hat u_\lambda-u^*.
\]

Then

\[
\frac1{2n}\|X\Delta\|_2^2
+
(\hat\Sigma u^*-\xi^*)^T\Delta
+
\lambda\|\hat u_\lambda\|_1
\le
\lambda\|u^*\|_1.
\]

On \(\Omega_0(\lambda_0)\),

\[
\| \hat\Sigma u^*-\xi^*\|_\infty\le \lambda_0,
\]

so by Hölder’s inequality,

\[
\left|(\hat\Sigma u^*-\xi^*)^T\Delta\right|
\le
\lambda_0\|\Delta\|_1.
\]

Therefore

\[
\frac1{2n}\|X\Delta\|_2^2
+
\lambda\|\hat u_\lambda\|_1
\le
\lambda\|u^*\|_1+\lambda_0\|\Delta\|_1.
\]

Since \(u^*_{S^{*c}}=0\), we have

\[
\|\hat u_\lambda\|_1
=
\|u^*_{S^*}+\Delta_{S^*}\|_1+\|\Delta_{S^{*c}}\|_1.
\]

By the reverse triangle inequality,

\[
\|u^*_{S^*}+\Delta_{S^*}\|_1
\ge
\|u^*_{S^*}\|_1-\|\Delta_{S^*}\|_1.
\]

Thus

\[
\|\hat u_\lambda\|_1
\ge
\|u^*\|_1-\|\Delta_{S^*}\|_1+\|\Delta_{S^{*c}}\|_1.
\]

Substitute this into the previous inequality:

\[
\frac1{2n}\|X\Delta\|_2^2
+
\lambda\left(
\|u^*\|_1-\|\Delta_{S^*}\|_1+\|\Delta_{S^{*c}}\|_1
\right)
\le
\lambda\|u^*\|_1+\lambda_0\|\Delta\|_1.
\]

Cancel \(\lambda\|u^*\|_1\). Since

\[
\|\Delta\|_1=\|\Delta_{S^*}\|_1+\|\Delta_{S^{*c}}\|_1,
\]

we get

\[
\frac1{2n}\|X\Delta\|_2^2
+
(\lambda-\lambda_0)\|\Delta_{S^{*c}}\|_1
\le
(\lambda+\lambda_0)\|\Delta_{S^*}\|_1.
\]

Now take \(\lambda=A_0\lambda_0\), where \(A_0>1\). Then

\[
\frac1{2n}\|X\Delta\|_2^2
+
(A_0-1)\lambda_0\|\Delta_{S^{*c}}\|_1
\le
(A_0+1)\lambda_0\|\Delta_{S^*}\|_1.
\]

Adding \((A_0-1)\lambda_0\|\Delta_{S^*}\|_1\) to both sides gives

\[
\frac1{2n}\|X\Delta\|_2^2
+
(A_0-1)\lambda_0\|\Delta\|_1
\le
2A_0\lambda_0\|\Delta_{S^*}\|_1.
\]

Equivalently,

\[
\boxed{
\frac{1}{2n}\|X(\hat u_\lambda-u^*)\|_2^2
+
(A_0-1)\lambda_0\|\hat u_\lambda-u^*\|_1
\le
2A_0\lambda_0
\sum_{j\in S^*}
|\hat u_{\lambda,j}-u_j^*|.
}
\]

---

Let again

\[
\Delta=\hat u_\lambda-u^*,
\qquad
q=\frac1n\|X\Delta\|_2^2
=
\Delta^T\hat\Sigma\Delta.
\]

From the stronger inequality derived above,

\[
\frac q2
+
(A_0-1)\lambda_0\|\Delta_{S^{*c}}\|_1
\le
(A_0+1)\lambda_0\|\Delta_{S^*}\|_1.
\]

In particular,

\[
(A_0-1)\|\Delta_{S^{*c}}\|_1
\le
(A_0+1)\|\Delta_{S^*}\|_1.
\]

Hence

\[
\|\Delta_{S^{*c}}\|_1
\le
\frac{A_0+1}{A_0-1}\|\Delta_{S^*}\|_1.
\]

To use the compatibility condition, choose \(A_0\) large enough so that

\[
\frac{A_0+1}{A_0-1}\le \eta_0.
\]

This is possible provided \(\eta_0>1\), for example any

\[
\boxed{
A_0\ge \frac{\eta_0+1}{\eta_0-1}
}
\]

works. Thus \(\Delta\) lies in the compatibility cone.

On \(\Omega_{\mathrm{Comp}}\),

\[
\nu_0^2\|\Delta_{S^*}\|_1^2
\le
s\,\Delta^T\hat\Sigma\Delta
=
sq.
\]

Therefore

\[
\|\Delta_{S^*}\|_1
\le
\frac{\sqrt{s q}}{\nu_0}.
\]

From part 4,

\[
\frac q2
\le
2A_0\lambda_0\|\Delta_{S^*}\|_1.
\]

Using the compatibility bound,

\[
\frac q2
\le
\frac{2A_0\lambda_0}{\nu_0}\sqrt{s q}.
\]

If \(q=0\), the desired prediction bound is trivial. Otherwise divide by \(\sqrt q\):

\[
\frac{\sqrt q}{2}
\le
\frac{2A_0\lambda_0}{\nu_0}\sqrt{s}.
\]

Thus

\[
\sqrt q
\le
\frac{4A_0}{\nu_0}\sqrt{s}\lambda_0,
\]

and so

\[
\boxed{
q
=
\frac1n\|X(\hat u_\lambda-u^*)\|_2^2
\le
\frac{16A_0^2}{\nu_0^2}s\lambda_0^2.
}
\]

Now we bound \(\|\Delta\|_1\). From part 4,

\[
(A_0-1)\lambda_0\|\Delta\|_1
\le
2A_0\lambda_0\|\Delta_{S^*}\|_1.
\]

Thus

\[
\|\Delta\|_1
\le
\frac{2A_0}{A_0-1}\|\Delta_{S^*}\|_1
\le
\frac{2A_0}{(A_0-1)\nu_0}\sqrt{s q}.
\]

Using the prediction bound,

\[
\sqrt q
\le
\frac{4A_0}{\nu_0}\sqrt{s}\lambda_0,
\]

so

\[
\|\Delta\|_1
\le
\frac{2A_0}{(A_0-1)\nu_0}
\sqrt{s}
\cdot
\frac{4A_0}{\nu_0}\sqrt{s}\lambda_0.
\]

Therefore

\[
\boxed{
\|\hat u_\lambda-u^*\|_1
\le
\frac{8A_0^2}{(A_0-1)\nu_0^2}s\lambda_0.
}
\]

Hence the desired inequalities hold with, for example,

\[
\boxed{
M_0
=
\max\left\{
\frac{16A_0^2}{\nu_0^2},
\frac{8A_0^2}{(A_0-1)\nu_0^2}
\right\}.
}
\]

Thus, on \(\Omega_0(\lambda_0)\cap\Omega_{\mathrm{Comp}}\),

\[
\boxed{
\frac1n\|X(\hat u_\lambda-u^*)\|_2^2
\le
M_0 s\lambda_0^2,
}
\]

and

\[
\boxed{
\|\hat u_\lambda-u^*\|_1
\le
M_0 s\lambda_0.
}
\]

---

## 6) Outline for proving \(\mathbb P(\Omega_{\mathrm{Comp}})\ge 1-2\varepsilon\)

Let

\[
C(S^*,\eta_0)
=
\left\{
b\in\mathbb R^p:
\|b_{S^{*c}}\|_1
\le
\eta_0\|b_{S^*}\|_1
\right\}
\]

be the compatibility cone.

### Step 1: Population compatibility

Since \(\lambda_{\min}(\Sigma)\ge \sigma_0\),

\[
b^T\Sigma b\ge \sigma_0\|b\|_2^2.
\]

Also,

\[
\|b_{S^*}\|_1^2\le s\|b_{S^*}\|_2^2\le s\|b\|_2^2.
\]

Thus

\[
\sigma_0\|b_{S^*}\|_1^2
\le
s\,b^T\Sigma b.
\]

So the population compatibility constant is at least \(\sqrt{\sigma_0}\).

### Step 2: Uniform lower concentration of \(\hat\Sigma\) on the cone

Use a standard restricted eigenvalue/cone concentration theorem for sub-Gaussian designs.

Since \(X_i\sim N(0,\Sigma)\) and the eigenvalues of \(\Sigma\) lie in \([\sigma_0,\sigma_1]\), Gaussian design theory implies that, with high probability,

\[
b^T\hat\Sigma b
\ge
\frac{\sigma_0}{2}\|b\|_2^2
\qquad
\text{for all } b\in C(S^*,\eta_0),
\]

provided

\[
n
\gtrsim
\left(\frac{\sigma_1}{\sigma_0}\right)^2
(1+\eta_0)^2
s\log\frac{ep}{s}
+
\log\frac1\varepsilon.
\]

Equivalently, this follows by applying an \(\varepsilon\)-net or Gaussian width argument to the set

\[
\left\{
b\in C(S^*,\eta_0): \|b\|_2=1
\right\},
\]

whose Gaussian width is of order

\[
(1+\eta_0)\sqrt{s\log(ep/s)}.
\]

### Step 3: Deduce empirical compatibility

If

\[
b^T\hat\Sigma b
\ge
\frac{\sigma_0}{2}\|b\|_2^2
\]

for all \(b\in C(S^*,\eta_0)\), then

\[
s\,b^T\hat\Sigma b
\ge
\frac{\sigma_0}{2}s\|b\|_2^2
\ge
\frac{\sigma_0}{2}\|b_{S^*}\|_1^2.
\]

Therefore \(\Omega_{\mathrm{Comp}}\) holds with any

\[
\nu_0^2\le \frac{\sigma_0}{2}.
\]

Thus, under the sample size condition above,

\[
\boxed{
\mathbb P(\Omega_{\mathrm{Comp}})\ge 1-2\varepsilon.
}
\]

\[

\[

\[

=

For \(x>1\), the density is

\[
f(x)=c\frac{\log x}{x^2}.
\]

## (a) Normalizing constant \(c\)

We need

\[
1=\int_1^\infty c\frac{\log x}{x^2}\,dx.
\]

Use the substitution \(u=\log x\), so \(x=e^u\), \(dx=e^u\,du\), and \(x^2=e^{2u}\). Then

\[
\int_1^\infty \frac{\log x}{x^2}\,dx
=
\int_0^\infty u e^{-u}\,du
=
\Gamma(2)=1.
\]

Therefore

\[
\boxed{c=1}.
\]

So

\[
f(x)=\frac{\log x}{x^2}, \qquad x>1.
\]

---

## (b) Moments \(\mathbb E[X^k]\), \(k=1,2,\dots\)

For \(k\ge 1\),

\[
\mathbb E[X^k]
=
\int_1^\infty x^k \frac{\log x}{x^2}\,dx
=
\int_1^\infty x^{k-2}\log x\,dx.
\]

Again let \(u=\log x\). Then

\[
x=e^u,\qquad dx=e^u\,du,
\]

so

\[
x^{k-2}\,dx=e^{(k-2)u}e^u\,du=e^{(k-1)u}\,du.
\]

Thus

\[
\mathbb E[X^k]
=
\int_0^\infty u e^{(k-1)u}\,du.
\]

If \(k=1\), this is

\[
\int_0^\infty u\,du=\infty.
\]

If \(k>1\), then \(e^{(k-1)u}\) grows exponentially, so

\[
\int_0^\infty u e^{(k-1)u}\,du=\infty.
\]

Therefore, for every positive integer \(k\),

\[
\boxed{\mathbb E[X^k]=\infty.}
\]

So no positive integer moment is finite.

---

## (c) MGF of \(X\)

The moment generating function would be

\[
M_X(t)=\mathbb E[e^{tX}]
=
\int_1^\infty e^{tx}\frac{\log x}{x^2}\,dx.
\]

For any \(t>0\),

\[
e^{tx}\frac{\log x}{x^2}\to \infty
\qquad \text{as } x\to\infty,
\]

and in particular the integral diverges. Hence

\[
M_X(t)=\infty \qquad \text{for all } t>0.
\]

At \(t=0\), \(M_X(0)=1\). For \(t<0\), the integral is finite because the exponential factor decays.

However, an MGF must be finite on some open interval containing \(0\). Since \(M_X(t)=\infty\) for every \(t>0\), the MGF does not exist in the usual sense.

\[
\boxed{\text{The MGF of }X\text{ does not exist.}}
\]

---

## (d) Density of \(Y=X_1X_2\)

Let

\[
Z=\log X.
\]

Since \(X>1\), we have \(Z>0\). By the change-of-variables formula,

\[
f_Z(z)=f_X(e^z)e^z.
\]

Using \(f_X(x)=\frac{\log x}{x^2}\), we get

\[
f_Z(z)
=
\frac{z}{e^{2z}}e^z
=
z e^{-z}, \qquad z>0.
\]

Thus

\[
Z\sim \operatorname{Gamma}(2,1),
\]

with shape \(2\) and rate \(1\).

Now let

\[
Z_1=\log X_1,\qquad Z_2=\log X_2.
\]

Then \(Z_1,Z_2\) are independent \(\operatorname{Gamma}(2,1)\) random variables. Since gamma random variables with the same rate add, by the gamma convolution theorem,

\[
W:=\log Y=\log(X_1X_2)=Z_1+Z_2
\sim \operatorname{Gamma}(4,1).
\]

Therefore

\[
f_W(w)=\frac{w^{4-1}e^{-w}}{\Gamma(4)}
=
\frac{w^3e^{-w}}{6},
\qquad w>0.
\]

Since \(Y=e^W\), we use another change of variables:

\[
w=\log y,\qquad \frac{dw}{dy}=\frac1y.
\]

Thus for \(y>1\),

\[
f_Y(y)
=
f_W(\log y)\frac1y
=
\frac{(\log y)^3 e^{-\log y}}{6}\frac1y.
\]

Because \(e^{-\log y}=1/y\), this becomes

\[
f_Y(y)
=
\frac{(\log y)^3}{6y^2}, \qquad y>1.
\]

Hence

\[
\boxed{
f_Y(y)=
\begin{cases}
\dfrac{(\log y)^3}{6y^2}, & y>1,\\[1em]
0, & y\le 1.
\end{cases}
}
\]

[2024 summer phd probability — problem 3]

Part I, Problem 3. Suppose $X$ has density $f(x) = c\, \frac{\log x}{x^2}$ for $x > 1$.
(a) Find the normalizing constant $c$.
(b) Find $\mathbb{E}[X^k]$ for $k = 1, 2, \dots$ if it exists, or verify it does not.
(c) Find the MGF of $X$ if it exists, or verify it does not.
(d) If $X_1, X_2$ are independent copies of $X$, find the density of $Y = X_1 X_2$.

### (a) Normalizing constant

We need
\[
1=\int_1^\infty c\,\frac{\log x}{x^2}\,dx.
\]
Let \(u=\log x\), so \(x=e^u\), \(dx=e^u\,du\), and \(x^{-2}dx=e^{-u}du\). Then
\[
\int_1^\infty \frac{\log x}{x^2}\,dx
=\int_0^\infty u e^{-u}\,du
=\Gamma(2)=1.
\]
Therefore,
\[
\boxed{c=1.}
\]

So
\[
f(x)=\frac{\log x}{x^2}, \qquad x>1.
\]

---

### (b) Moments \(\mathbb E[X^k]\), \(k=1,2,\dots\)

For real \(k\),
\[
\mathbb E[X^k]
=\int_1^\infty x^k \frac{\log x}{x^2}\,dx
=\int_1^\infty x^{k-2}\log x\,dx.
\]
Again use \(u=\log x\), \(x=e^u\). Then
\[
x^{k-2}\,dx=e^{(k-2)u}e^u\,du=e^{(k-1)u}\,du,
\]
so
\[
\mathbb E[X^k]
=\int_0^\infty u e^{(k-1)u}\,du.
\]

This integral converges iff \(k-1<0\), i.e. iff \(k<1\). In that case,
\[
\int_0^\infty u e^{-(1-k)u}\,du=\frac{1}{(1-k)^2}.
\]

But for \(k=1,2,\dots\), we have \(k\ge 1\), so the integral diverges. Therefore,
\[
\boxed{\mathbb E[X^k]=\infty \quad \text{for every integer } k\ge 1.}
\]

In particular, even \(\mathbb E[X]\) does not exist finitely.

### (c) Moment generating function

The moment generating function would be
\[
M_X(t)=\mathbb E[e^{tX}]
=\int_1^\infty e^{tx}\frac{\log x}{x^2}\,dx.
\]

For \(t>0\), the integrand grows exponentially. More formally, for sufficiently large \(x\),
\[
\frac{e^{tx}}{x^2}\ge 1,
\]
so
\[
e^{tx}\frac{\log x}{x^2}\ge \log x,
\]
and
\[
\int^\infty \log x\,dx=\infty.
\]
Thus
\[
M_X(t)=\infty \qquad \text{for every } t>0.
\]

At \(t=0\),
\[
M_X(0)=1.
\]

\[

\]

\[

\[
f_U(u)=f_X(e^u)e^u
=\frac{\log(e^u)}{(e^u)^2}e^u
=u e^{-u}, \qquad u>0.
\]

\[
U_i\sim \operatorname{Gamma}(2,1),
\]
with density
\[
f_U(u)=u e^{-u}, \qquad u>0.
\]

Now
\[
Y=X_1X_2=e^{U_1+U_2}.
\]
Since \(U_1,U_2\) are independent Gamma\((2,1)\) random variables, by closure of gamma distributions with common rate,
\[

\]

\[

\]
then
\[

\]

\[

\]

\[
