\]

Therefore,
\[
\boxed{
f_Y(y)=
\begin{cases}
\dfrac{(\log y)^3}{6y^2}, & y>1,\\[1em]

\end{cases}
}
\]

\[
f_X(e^t)e^t=c\frac{t}{e^{2t}}e^t=c\,t e^{-t}.
\]

=\int_0^\infty e^{rt} t e^{-t}\,dt
=\int_0^\infty t e^{-(1-r)t}\,dt.

\[
\boxed{\mathbb E[X^k]=\infty.}

M_X(t)=\mathbb E[e^{tX}]
=\int_1^\infty e^{tx}\frac{\log x}{x^2}\,dx.

Let \(n=|V|\), and write \(x_v=x(v)\). Also write  
\[
D(x,z):=\{v\in V:x_v\neq z_v\}.
\]

---

## (1) Off-diagonal transition probabilities

If \(z\neq x\), then \(P(x,z)>0\) only if \(z\) differs from \(x\) at exactly one vertex. Suppose \(D(x,z)=\{v\}\). Then the proposal \(z\) is made exactly when \(v_{t+1}=v\) and \(S_{t+1}=z_v\), which has probability \(\frac1n\cdot \frac12=\frac1{2n}\). Hence

\[
P(x,z)=\frac1{2n}\min\left\{1,\frac{e^{-H(z)}}{e^{-H(x)}}\right\}
=\frac1{2n}\min\{1,e^{H(x)-H(z)}\}.
\]

Thus, for \(z\neq x\),

\[
\boxed{
P(x,z)=
\begin{cases}
\dfrac1{2n}\min\{1,e^{H(x)-H(z)}\}, & |D(x,z)|=1,\\[1.2ex]
0, & |D(x,z)|\ge 2.
\end{cases}}
\]

Equivalently, if \(D(x,z)=\{v\}\),

\[
P(x,z)=\frac1{2n}\min\left\{1,\exp\left(\frac12(z_v-x_v)\sum_{w\sim v}x_w\right)\right\}.
\]

---

## (2) Stationarity of \(\pi\)

Let \(Z=\sum_y e^{-H(y)}\), so \(\pi(x)=Z^{-1}e^{-H(x)}\).

We prove detailed balance. If \(x,z\) differ at more than one coordinate, then \(P(x,z)=P(z,x)=0\). If \(x,z\) differ at exactly one coordinate, then by part (1),

\[
\pi(x)P(x,z)
=
\frac{e^{-H(x)}}{Z}\cdot \frac1{2n}\min\left\{1,\frac{e^{-H(z)}}{e^{-H(x)}}\right\}.
\]

Thus

\[
\pi(x)P(x,z)
=
\frac1{2nZ}\min\{e^{-H(x)},e^{-H(z)}\}.
\]

The right-hand side is symmetric in \(x,z\), so

\[
\pi(x)P(x,z)=\pi(z)P(z,x).
\]

The equality is trivial for \(x=z\). Hence the chain is reversible with respect to \(\pi\). Therefore, by the detailed balance theorem,

\[
\sum_x \pi(x)P(x,z)
=
\sum_x \pi(z)P(z,x)
=
\pi(z)\sum_x P(z,x)
=
\pi(z).
\]

So \(\pi\) is stationary.

---

## (3) Local expression for the acceptance ratio

Let \(v=v_{t+1}\), \(S=S_{t+1}\), and let \(N_v=\{w:w\sim v\}\). The proposed configuration \(y\) differs from \(x_t\) only at \(v\), with \(y_v=S\). Therefore all non-incident edges cancel in \(H(y)-H(x_t)\). Thus

\[
H(y)-H(x_t)
=
\frac12\sum_{w\in N_v}
\Big[(1-Sx_t(w))-(1-x_t(v)x_t(w))\Big].
\]

Simplifying,

\[
H(y)-H(x_t)
=
\frac12\sum_{w\in N_v}(x_t(v)-S)x_t(w).
\]

Hence

\[
\frac{e^{-H(y)}}{e^{-H(x_t)}}
=
e^{-(H(y)-H(x_t))}
=
\exp\left(
\frac12\sum_{w\in N_v}(S-x_t(v))x_t(w)
\right).
\]

So

\[
\boxed{
\frac{e^{-H(y)}}{e^{-H(x_t)}}
=
\exp\left(\frac12\sum_{w\in N_{t+1}}(S_{t+1}-x_t(v_{t+1}))x_t(w)\right).
}
\]

---

## (4) Monotonicity of the update map

Fix a realization of \((v_{t+1},S_{t+1},U_{t+1})\). We show that if \(x\preceq z\), then

\[
f_{t+1}(x)\preceq f_{t+1}(z).
\]

For coordinates \(w\neq v_{t+1}\), neither update changes the spin, so

\[
f_{t+1}(x)_w=x_w\le z_w=f_{t+1}(z)_w.
\]

Thus we only need to check the chosen vertex \(v=v_{t+1}\).

Let

\[
\Sigma_\eta:=\sum_{w\sim v}\eta_w
\]

for a configuration \(\eta\).

### Case 1: \(S_{t+1}=+1\)

If \(z_v=+1\), then \(f_{t+1}(z)_v=+1\), so automatically

\[
f_{t+1}(x)_v\le +1=f_{t+1}(z)_v.
\]

The only nontrivial case is \(z_v=-1\). Since \(x\preceq z\), we also have \(x_v=-1\). Thus both chains propose changing \(-1\) to \(+1\).

By part (3), the acceptance probability from configuration \(\eta\) is

\[
a(\eta)=\min\{1,e^{\Sigma_\eta}\}.
\]

Since \(x\preceq z\), we have \(\Sigma_x\le \Sigma_z\), so

\[
a(x)\le a(z).
\]

Therefore, if the lower chain accepts, i.e. if \(U\le a(x)\), then necessarily \(U\le a(z)\), so the upper chain also accepts. Hence the bad event

\[
f_{t+1}(x)_v=+1,\qquad f_{t+1}(z)_v=-1
\]

cannot occur. Therefore

\[
f_{t+1}(x)_v\le f_{t+1}(z)_v.
\]

### Case 2: \(S_{t+1}=-1\)

If \(x_v=-1\), then \(f_{t+1}(x)_v=-1\), so automatically

\[
f_{t+1}(x)_v=-1\le f_{t+1}(z)_v.
\]

The only nontrivial case is \(x_v=+1\). Since \(x\preceq z\), we also have \(z_v=+1\). Thus both chains propose changing \(+1\) to \(-1\).

By part (3), the acceptance probability from configuration \(\eta\) is

\[
a(\eta)=\min\{1,e^{-\Sigma_\eta}\}.
\]

Since \(x\preceq z\), \(\Sigma_x\le \Sigma_z\), so

\[
e^{-\Sigma_x}\ge e^{-\Sigma_z},
\]

and hence

\[
a(x)\ge a(z).
\]

Therefore, if the upper chain accepts, i.e. if \(U\le a(z)\), then \(U\le a(x)\), so the lower chain also accepts. Thus the bad event

\[
f_{t+1}(x)_v=+1,\qquad f_{t+1}(z)_v=-1
\]

cannot occur.

Hence in all cases,

\[
f_{t+1}(x)\preceq f_{t+1}(z).
\]

Therefore

\[
\boxed{
x\preceq z\implies \mathbb P\bigl(f_{t+1}(x)\preceq f_{t+1}(z)\bigr)=1.
}
\]

---

## (5) Coalescence from extremal states

Let

\[
\underline x=(-1,\dots,-1),\qquad \bar x=(1,\dots,1).
\]

For a fixed realization of \(f_1,\dots,f_t\), define

\[
F=f_t\circ\cdots\circ f_1.
\]

Each \(f_i\) is monotone by part (4), so \(F\) is monotone.

If \(F\) is constant, then certainly

\[
F(\underline x)=F(\bar x).
\]

Conversely, suppose

\[
F(\underline x)=F(\bar x).
\]

For any \(x\in \mathcal X\),

\[
\underline x\preceq x\preceq \bar x.
\]

By monotonicity of \(F\),

\[
F(\underline x)\preceq F(x)\preceq F(\bar x).
\]

Since the endpoints are equal, this forces

\[
F(x)=F(\underline x)=F(\bar x).
\]

Thus \(F\) is constant. Therefore

\[
\boxed{
F \text{ is constant } \Longleftrightarrow F(\underline x)=F(\bar x).
}
\]

---

### Convention for \(h\)

As written, if \(h\) literally counts the number of states in a chain ending at \(z\), then \(h(\bar x)=n+1\), so the later claim \(h(z)\le n\) would be false. Thus the intended height is the number of strict steps in such a chain. Equivalently, it is the literal chain-size definition minus \(1\). This shift does not affect any difference \(h(Y)-h(X)\).

So in what follows, take

\[
h(z):=\max\{k:\exists x_0\prec x_1\prec\cdots\prec x_k=z\},
\]

where \(x\prec y\) means \(x\preceq y\) and \(x\neq y\).

---

## (6) Strict order increases height by at least \(1\)

Suppose \(x_t\preceq y_t\) and \(x_t\neq y_t\). Then \(x_t\prec y_t\).

Let

\[
x_0\prec x_1\prec\cdots\prec x_{h(x_t)}=x_t
\]

be a maximal chain ending at \(x_t\). Appending \(y_t\) gives a strict chain

\[
x_0\prec x_1\prec\cdots\prec x_{h(x_t)}=x_t\prec y_t.
\]

Therefore there is a chain of length \(h(x_t)+1\) ending at \(y_t\). Hence

\[
\boxed{
h(x_t)+1\le h(y_t).
}
\]

---

## (7) Tail bound using the height difference

Define

\[
X_t=f_t\circ\cdots\circ f_1(\underline x),
\qquad
Y_t=f_t\circ\cdots\circ f_1(\bar x).
\]

By monotonicity,

\[
X_t\preceq Y_t
\]

for every \(t\). Also, once \(X_t=Y_t\), the two trajectories remain equal forever because they are driven by the same future maps. Therefore

\[
\{T>t\}=\{X_t\neq Y_t\}.
\]

On \(\{X_t\neq Y_t\}\), part (6) gives

\[
h(Y_t)-h(X_t)\ge 1.
\]

Thus

\[
\mathbf 1_{\{T>t\}}
=
\mathbf 1_{\{X_t\neq Y_t\}}
\le h(Y_t)-h(X_t).
\]

Taking expectations,

\[
\boxed{
\mathbb P(T>t)\le \mathbb E[h(Y_t)-h(X_t)].
}
\]

---

## (8) Bounding the height and its expectation

Let

\[
r(z):=\#\{v\in V:z_v=1\}.
\]

If \(a\prec b\), then \(r(b)>r(a)\). Hence along any strict chain ending at \(z\), the value of \(r\) increases by at least \(1\) at every step, and the final value is \(r(z)\). Therefore

\[
h(z)\le r(z).
\]

Conversely, starting from \(\underline x\), flip the \(r(z)\) sites where \(z_v=1\) one at a time. This gives a strict chain of length \(r(z)\) ending at \(z\). Hence

\[
h(z)=r(z).
\]

Therefore

\[
\boxed{
0\le h(z)\le |V|=n.
}
\]

Now let

\[
\mu_t=P^t(\underline x,\cdot),
\qquad
\nu_t=P^t(\bar x,\cdot).
\]

Then \(X_t\sim \mu_t\) and \(Y_t\sim \nu_t\). Hence

\[
\mathbb E[h(Y_t)-h(X_t)]
=
\nu_t(h)-\mu_t(h).
\]

Since \(0\le h\le n\), the function \(h/n\) is \([0,1]\)-valued. Therefore, by the variational characterization of total variation distance,

\[
\nu_t(h)-\mu_t(h)
\le
n\|\nu_t-\mu_t\|_{\mathrm{TV}}.
\]

If

\[
\bar d(t):=\max_{x,y}\|P^t(x,\cdot)-P^t(y,\cdot)\|_{\mathrm{TV}},
\]

then

\[
\|\nu_t-\mu_t\|_{\mathrm{TV}}
\le \bar d(t).
\]

Thus

\[
\boxed{
\mathbb E[h(Y_t)-h(X_t)]\le |V|\,\bar d(t).
}
\]

Combining with part (7),

\[
\boxed{
\mathbb P(T>t)\le |V|\,\bar d(t).
}
\]

---

## (9) Tail bound at multiples of \(t_{\mathrm{mix}}\)

Assume \(|V|=2L\), with \(L>1\).

Let

\[
d(t):=\max_x \|P^t(x,\cdot)-\pi\|_{\mathrm{TV}},
\]

and define

\[
t_{\mathrm{mix}}:=\min\{t:d(t)\le 1/4\}.
\]

We use the standard facts:

1. \(d(t)\le \bar d(t)\le 2d(t)\).
2. \(\bar d(s+t)\le \bar d(s)\bar d(t)\) for all \(s,t\ge 0\).
3. Therefore
   \[
   \bar d(t_{\mathrm{mix}})
   \le 2d(t_{\mathrm{mix}})
   \le \frac12.
   \]

Hence, for every integer \(m\ge 1\),

\[
\bar d(m t_{\mathrm{mix}})
\le
\bar d(t_{\mathrm{mix}})^m
\le
2^{-m}.
\]

Take \(m=k+L\). By part (8),

\[
\mathbb P(T>(k+L)t_{\mathrm{mix}})
\le
|V|\,\bar d((k+L)t_{\mathrm{mix}}).
\]

Since \(|V|=2L\),

\[
\mathbb P(T>(k+L)t_{\mathrm{mix}})
\le
2L\cdot 2^{-(k+L)}.
\]

For integer \(L>1\), we have \(2L\le 2^L\). Therefore

\[
2L\cdot 2^{-(k+L)}
\le
2^{-k}.
\]

Thus

\[
\boxed{
\mathbb P\bigl(T>t_{\mathrm{mix}}(k+L)\bigr)\le \frac1{2^k}.
}
\]

---

## (10) Bound on \(\mathbb E[T]\)

First note the elementary tail lemma: if \(U\ge 0\) and

\[
\mathbb P(U>k)\le 2^{-k}
\]

for all integers \(k\ge 0\), then

\[
\mathbb E[U]
=
\int_0^\infty \mathbb P(U>s)\,ds
\le
\sum_{k=0}^\infty \mathbb P(U>k)
\le
\sum_{k=0}^\infty 2^{-k}
=
2.
\]

Now let \(m=t_{\mathrm{mix}}\), and define

\[
U:=\left(\frac{T}{m}-L\right)_+.
\]

Then for every integer \(k\ge 0\),

\[
\mathbb P(U>k)
=
\mathbb P\left(T>m(k+L)\right)
\le
2^{-k}
\]

by part (9). Hence \(\mathbb E[U]\le 2\).

Since

\[
\frac{T}{m}\le L+U,
\]

we get

\[
\mathbb E[T]
\le
m(L+\mathbb E[U])
\le
m(L+2).
\]

Because \(L>1\) is an integer, \(L\ge 2\), so \(L+2\le 2L\). Therefore

\[
\boxed{
\mathbb E[T]\le 2L\,t_{\mathrm{mix}}.
}
\]

Thus the desired bound holds with the absolute constant \(c=2\).

For coordinates \(w\neq v_{t+1}\), neither update changes the spin, so

\[
f_{t+1}(x)_w=x_w\le z_w=f_{t+1}(z)_w.
\]

Thus we only need to check the chosen vertex \(v=v_{t+1}\).

Let

\[
\Sigma_\eta:=\sum_{w\sim v}\eta_w
\]

for a configuration \(\eta\).

### Case 1: \(S_{t+1}=+1\)

If \(z_v=+1\), then \(f_{t+1}(z)_v=+1\), so automatically

\[
f_{t+1}(x)_v\le +1=f_{t+1}(z)_v.
\]

The only nontrivial case is \(z_v=-1\). Since \(x\preceq z\), we also have \(x_v=-1\). Thus both chains propose changing \(-1\) to \(+1\).

By part (3), the acceptance probability from configuration \(\eta\) is

\[
a(\eta)=\min\{1,e^{\Sigma_\eta}\}.
\]

Since \(x\preceq z\), we have \(\Sigma_x\le \Sigma_z\), so

\[
a(x)\le a(z).
\]

Therefore, if the lower chain accepts, i.e. if \(U\le a(x)\), then necessarily \(U\le a(z)\), so the upper chain also accepts. Hence the bad event

\[
f_{t+1}(x)_v=+1,\qquad f_{t+1}(z)_v=-1
\]

cannot occur. Therefore

\[
f_{t+1}(x)_v\le f_{t+1}(z)_v.
\]

### Case 2: \(S_{t+1}=-1\)

If \(x_v=-1\), then \(f_{t+1}(x)_v=-1\), so automatically

\[
f_{t+1}(x)_v=-1\le f_{t+1}(z)_v.
\]

The only nontrivial case is \(x_v=+1\). Since \(x\preceq z\), we also have \(z_v=+1\). Thus both chains propose changing \(+1\) to \(-1\).

By part (3), the acceptance probability from configuration \(\eta\) is

\[
a(\eta)=\min\{1,e^{-\Sigma_\eta}\}.
\]

Since \(x\preceq z\), \(\Sigma_x\le \Sigma_z\), so

\[
e^{-\Sigma_x}\ge e^{-\Sigma_z},
\]

and hence

\[
a(x)\ge a(z).
\]

Therefore, if the upper chain accepts, i.e. if \(U\le a(z)\), then \(U\le a(x)\), so the lower chain also accepts. Thus the bad event

\[
f_{t+1}(x)_v=+1,\qquad f_{t+1}(z)_v=-1
\]

cannot occur.

Hence in all cases,

\[
f_{t+1}(x)\preceq f_{t+1}(z).
\]

Therefore

\[
\boxed{
x\preceq z\implies \mathbb P\bigl(f_{t+1}(x)\preceq f_{t+1}(z)\bigr)=1.
}
\]

---

## (5) Coalescence from extremal states

Let

\[
\underline x=(-1,\dots,-1),\qquad \bar x=(1,\dots,1).
\]

For a fixed realization of \(f_1,\dots,f_t\), define

\[
F=f_t\circ\cdots\circ f_1.
\]

Each \(f_i\) is monotone by part (4), so \(F\) is monotone.

If \(F\) is constant, then certainly

\[
F(\underline x)=F(\bar x).
\]

Conversely, suppose

\[
F(\underline x)=F(\bar x).
\]

For any \(x\in \mathcal X\),

\[
\underline x\preceq x\preceq \bar x.
\]

By monotonicity of \(F\),

\[
F(\underline x)\preceq F(x)\preceq F(\bar x).
\]

Since the endpoints are equal, this forces

\[
F(x)=F(\underline x)=F(\bar x).
\]

Thus \(F\) is constant. Therefore

\[
\boxed{
F \text{ is constant } \Longleftrightarrow F(\underline x)=F(\bar x).
}
\]

---

### Convention for \(h\)

As written, if \(h\) literally counts the number of states in a chain ending at \(z\), then \(h(\bar x)=n+1\), so the later claim \(h(z)\le n\) would be false. Thus the intended height is the number of strict steps in such a chain. Equivalently, it is the literal chain-size definition minus \(1\). This shift does not affect any difference \(h(Y)-h(X)\).

So in what follows, take

\[
h(z):=\max\{k:\exists x_0\prec x_1\prec\cdots\prec x_k=z\},
\]

where \(x\prec y\) means \(x\preceq y\) and \(x\neq y\).

---

## (6) Strict order increases height by at least \(1\)

Suppose \(x_t\preceq y_t\) and \(x_t\neq y_t\). Then \(x_t\prec y_t\).

Let

\[
x_0\prec x_1\prec\cdots\prec x_{h(x_t)}=x_t
\]

be a maximal chain ending at \(x_t\). Appending \(y_t\) gives a strict chain

\[
x_0\prec x_1\prec\cdots\prec x_{h(x_t)}=x_t\prec y_t.
\]

Therefore there is a chain of length \(h(x_t)+1\) ending at \(y_t\). Hence

\[
\boxed{
h(x_t)+1\le h(y_t).
}
\]

---

## (7) Tail bound using the height difference

Define

\[
X_t=f_t\circ\cdots\circ f_1(\underline x),
\qquad
Y_t=f_t\circ\cdots\circ f_1(\bar x).
\]

By monotonicity,

\[
X_t\preceq Y_t
\]

for every \(t\). Also, once \(X_t=Y_t\), the two trajectories remain equal forever because they are driven by the same future maps. Therefore

\[
\{T>t\}=\{X_t\neq Y_t\}.
\]

On \(\{X_t\neq Y_t\}\), part (6) gives

\[
h(Y_t)-h(X_t)\ge 1.
\]

Thus

\[
\mathbf 1_{\{T>t\}}
=
\mathbf 1_{\{X_t\neq Y_t\}}
\le h(Y_t)-h(X_t).
\]

Taking expectations,

\[
\boxed{
\mathbb P(T>t)\le \mathbb E[h(Y_t)-h(X_t)].
}
\]

---

## (8) Bounding the height and its expectation

Let

\[
r(z):=\#\{v\in V:z_v=1\}.
\]

If \(a\prec b\), then \(r(b)>r(a)\). Hence along any strict chain ending at \(z\), the value of \(r\) increases by at least \(1\) at every step, and the final value is \(r(z)\). Therefore

\[
h(z)\le r(z).
\]

Conversely, starting from \(\underline x\), flip the \(r(z)\) sites where \(z_v=1\) one at a time. This gives a strict chain of length \(r(z)\) ending at \(z\). Hence

\[
h(z)=r(z).
\]

Therefore

\[
\boxed{
0\le h(z)\le |V|=n.
}
\]

Now let

\[
\mu_t=P^t(\underline x,\cdot),
\qquad
\nu_t=P^t(\bar x,\cdot).
\]

Then \(X_t\sim \mu_t\) and \(Y_t\sim \nu_t\). Hence

\[
\mathbb E[h(Y_t)-h(X_t)]
=
\nu_t(h)-\mu_t(h).
\]

Since \(0\le h\le n\), the function \(h/n\) is \([0,1]\)-valued. Therefore, by the variational characterization of total variation distance,

\[
\nu_t(h)-\mu_t(h)
\le
n\|\nu_t-\mu_t\|_{\mathrm{TV}}.
\]

If

\[
\bar d(t):=\max_{x,y}\|P^t(x,\cdot)-P^t(y,\cdot)\|_{\mathrm{TV}},
\]

then

\[
\|\nu_t-\mu_t\|_{\mathrm{TV}}
\le \bar d(t).
\]

Thus

\[
\boxed{
\mathbb E[h(Y_t)-h(X_t)]\le |V|\,\bar d(t).
}
\]

Combining with part (7),

\[
\boxed{
\mathbb P(T>t)\le |V|\,\bar d(t).
}
\]

---

## (9) Tail bound at multiples of \(t_{\mathrm{mix}}\)

Assume \(|V|=2L\), with \(L>1\).

Let

\[
d(t):=\max_x \|P^t(x,\cdot)-\pi\|_{\mathrm{TV}},
\]

and define

\[
t_{\mathrm{mix}}:=\min\{t:d(t)\le 1/4\}.
\]

We use the standard facts:

1. \(d(t)\le \bar d(t)\le 2d(t)\).
2. \(\bar d(s+t)\le \bar d(s)\bar d(t)\) for all \(s,t\ge 0\).
3. Therefore
   \[
   \bar d(t_{\mathrm{mix}})
   \le 2d(t_{\mathrm{mix}})
   \le \frac12.
   \]

Hence, for every integer \(m\ge 1\),

\[
\bar d(m t_{\mathrm{mix}})
\le
\bar d(t_{\mathrm{mix}})^m
\le
2^{-m}.
\]

Take \(m=k+L\). By part (8),

\[
\mathbb P(T>(k+L)t_{\mathrm{mix}})
\le
|V|\,\bar d((k+L)t_{\mathrm{mix}}).
\]

Since \(|V|=2L\),

\[
\mathbb P(T>(k+L)t_{\mathrm{mix}})
\le
2L\cdot 2^{-(k+L)}.
\]

For integer \(L>1\), we have \(2L\le 2^L\). Therefore

\[
2L\cdot 2^{-(k+L)}
\le
2^{-k}.
\]

Thus

\[
\boxed{
\mathbb P\bigl(T>t_{\mathrm{mix}}(k+L)\bigr)\le \frac1{2^k}.
}
\]

---

## (10) Bound on \(\mathbb E[T]\)

First note the elementary tail lemma: if \(U\ge 0\) and

\[
\mathbb P(U>k)\le 2^{-k}
\]

for all integers \(k\ge 0\), then

\[
\mathbb E[U]
=
\int_0^\infty \mathbb P(U>s)\,ds
\le
\sum_{k=0}^\infty \mathbb P(U>k)
\le
\sum_{k=0}^\infty 2^{-k}
=
2.
\]

Now let \(m=t_{\mathrm{mix}}\), and define

\[
U:=\left(\frac{T}{m}-L\right)_+.
\]

Then for every integer \(k\ge 0\),

\[
\mathbb P(U>k)
=
\mathbb P\left(T>m(k+L)\right)
\le
2^{-k}
\]

by part (9). Hence \(\mathbb E[U]\le 2\).

Since

\[
\frac{T}{m}\le L+U,
\]

we get

\[
\mathbb E[T]
\le
m(L+\mathbb E[U])
\le
m(L+2).
\]

Because \(L>1\) is an integer, \(L\ge 2\), so \(L+2\le 2L\). Therefore

\[
\boxed{
\mathbb E[T]\le 2L\,t_{\mathrm{mix}}.
}
\]

Thus the desired bound holds with the absolute constant \(c=2\).

[2024 summer phd probability — problem 4]

Part II. Let $(V, E)$ be a finite undirected graph, $V = \{1, \dots, n\}$, with $v \sim v'$ iff $\{v, v'\} \in E$. State space $\mathcal{X} = \{-1, 1\}^n$ (spin configurations). Define $H(x) = \sum_{\{v,v'\}\in E}\mathbb{1}\{x(v) \ne x(v')\} = \tfrac12\sum_{\{v,v'\}\in E}(1 - x(v)x(v'))$ and $\pi(x) = \frac{e^{-H(x)}}{\sum_y e^{-H(y)}}$. The update $X_{t+1} = f_{t+1}(x_t)$: sample $v_{t+1} \sim \mathrm{Unif}(V)$, $S_{t+1} \sim \mathrm{Unif}\{-1,1\}$, $U_{t+1} \sim \mathrm{Unif}[0,1]$; propose $y$ with $y(v_{t+1}) = S_{t+1}$, $y(w) = x_t(w)$ otherwise; accept ($f_{t+1}(x_t) = y$) if $U_{t+1} \le \min\{1, e^{-H(y)}/e^{-H(x_t)}\}$, else reject. $P(x, z) = P(f_{t+1}(x) = z)$.
(1) Compute $P(x, z)$ for $z \ne x$ with $P(x, z) > 0$ (need not compute $P(x, x)$).
(2) Prove $\pi$ is stationary for this chain.
(3) With $N_{t+1} \subset V$ the neighbors of $v_{t+1}$ and $y$ the proposed move, show $\frac{e^{-H(y)}}{e^{-H(x_t)}} = \exp(\tfrac12\sum_{w \in N_{t+1}}(S_{t+1} - x_t(v_{t+1})) x_t(w))$.
(4) Write $x \preceq y$ if $x(v) \le y(v)$ for all $v$. Prove that if $x \preceq z$ then $P(f_{t+1}(x) \preceq f_{t+1}(z)) = 1$ (handle $S_{t+1} = \pm1$ separately) — i.e. the dynamics is monotone.
(5) Let $\underline x = (-1, \dots, -1)$, $\bar x = (1, \dots, 1)$. Prove $F = f_t \circ \cdots \circ f_1$ is constant iff $F(\underline x) = F(\bar x)$. Let $T = \min\{t \ge 1 : f_t \circ \cdots \circ f_1(\underline x) = f_t \circ \cdots \circ f_1(\bar x)\}$.
(6) For $z \in \mathcal{X}$, let $h(z)$ be the max number $k$ of distinct states $x_1 \preceq \cdots \preceq x_k = z$. Prove that if $x_t \preceq y_t$ and $x_t \ne y_t$ then $h(x_t) + 1 \le h(y_t)$.
(7) With $X_t = f_t \circ \cdots \circ f_1(\underline x)$, $Y_t = f_t \circ \cdots \circ f_1(\bar x)$ (so $\{T > t\} = \{X_t \ne Y_t\}$), prove $P(T > t) \le \mathbb{E}[h(Y_t) - h(X_t)]$.
(8) Prove $0 \le h(z) \le |V|$ and $\mathbb{E}[h(Y_t) - h(X_t)] \le |V|\,\bar d(t)$.
(9) If $|V| = 2L$ ($L > 1$ integer) and $k \ge 0$, prove $P(T > t_{\mathrm{mix}}(k + L)) \le \frac{1}{2^k}$ (state the properties of $d, \bar d, t_{\mathrm{mix}}$ used).
(10) Prove $\mathbb{E}[T] \le c\, L\, t_{\mathrm{mix}}$ for an absolute constant $c > 0$ (you may first show any nonnegative $U$ with $P(U > k) \le 1/2^k$ for all integers $k \ge 0$ has finite expectation).

response.text:
Let \(n=|V|\). Write \(x(v)\) also as \(x_v\). For \(x,z\in\mathcal X\), let  
\[
\Delta(x,z):=\{v\in V:x(v)\neq z(v)\}.
\]

## (1) Transition probabilities \(P(x,z)\) for \(z\neq x\)

A nontrivial move changes at most one coordinate. Hence \(P(x,z)>0\) for \(z\neq x\) iff \(|\Delta(x,z)|=1\). If \(\Delta(x,z)=\{v\}\), then necessarily \(z(v)=-x(v)\), and the proposal \(z\) is made exactly when \(v_{t+1}=v\) and \(S_{t+1}=z(v)\), which has probability \(1/(2n)\). Therefore
\[
P(x,z)
=
\frac1{2n}\min\left\{1,\frac{e^{-H(z)}}{e^{-H(x)}}\right\}
=
\frac1{2n}\min\{1,e^{H(x)-H(z)}\}.
\]
If \(|\Delta(x,z)|\neq 1\), then \(P(x,z)=0\) for \(z\neq x\).

---

## (2) Stationarity of \(\pi\)

We prove detailed balance. Let
\[
Z=\sum_{y\in\mathcal X} e^{-H(y)}.
\]
If \(x\neq z\) and \(|\Delta(x,z)|=1\), then by part (1),
\[
P(x,z)=\frac1{2n}\min\left\{1,\frac{e^{-H(z)}}{e^{-H(x)}}\right\}.
\]
Thus
\[
\pi(x)P(x,z)
=
\frac{e^{-H(x)}}{Z}\cdot \frac1{2n}
\min\left\{1,\frac{e^{-H(z)}}{e^{-H(x)}}\right\}
=
\frac1{2nZ}\min\{e^{-H(x)},e^{-H(z)}\}.
\]
The right-hand side is symmetric in \(x,z\). Hence
\[
\pi(x)P(x,z)=\pi(z)P(z,x).
\]
If \(x,z\) differ in more than one coordinate, then both transition probabilities are \(0\). The diagonal case is trivial. Therefore \(P\) is reversible with respect to \(\pi\). By detailed balance, \(\pi\) is stationary.

---

## (3) Local form of the acceptance ratio

Let \(v=v_{t+1}\), \(S=S_{t+1}\), and \(N=N_{t+1}\) be the neighbors of \(v\). Let \(x=x_t\), and let \(y\) be the proposed configuration, so \(y(v)=S\) and \(y(w)=x(w)\) for \(w\neq v\).

Only edges incident to \(v\) can change their contribution to \(H\). For an edge \(\{v,w\}\),
\[
\frac12(1-y(v)y(w))-\frac12(1-x(v)x(w))
=
\frac12(1-Sx(w))-\frac12(1-x(v)x(w))
=
\frac12(x(v)-S)x(w).
\]
Therefore
\[
H(y)-H(x)
=
\frac12\sum_{w\in N}(x(v)-S)x(w).
\]
Hence
\[
\frac{e^{-H(y)}}{e^{-H(x)}}
=
\exp\{-(H(y)-H(x))\}
=
\exp\left(\frac12\sum_{w\in N}(S-x(v))x(w)\right).
\]

---

## (4) Monotonicity of the update map

We couple two chains using the same randomness \((v,S,U)\). Suppose \(x\preceq z\). We prove
\[
f_{t+1}(x)\preceq f_{t+1}(z)
\]
for every realization of \((v,S,U)\).

Coordinates other than \(v\) are unchanged, so the order can only fail at coordinate \(v\).

### Case 1: \(S=+1\)

If \(z(v)=+1\), then the upper chain has spin \(+1\) at \(v\) after the update, so the lower spin is automatically \(\leq +1\).

The only nontrivial case is \(z(v)=-1\). Since \(x\preceq z\), this forces \(x(v)=z(v)=-1\). By part (3), the acceptance ratios are
\[
R_x=\exp\left(\sum_{w\sim v}x(w)\right),
\qquad
R_z=\exp\left(\sum_{w\sim v}z(w)\right).
\]
Since \(x(w)\le z(w)\) for every \(w\),
\[
\sum_{w\sim v}x(w)\le \sum_{w\sim v}z(w),
\]
so \(R_x\le R_z\), and therefore
\[
\min\{1,R_x\}\le \min\{1,R_z\}.
\]
Thus if the lower chain accepts the move to \(+1\), then the upper chain also accepts. Hence order is preserved.

### Case 2: \(S=-1\)

If \(x(v)=-1\), then the lower chain has spin \(-1\) at \(v\) after the update, so it remains \(\leq\) the upper spin.

The only nontrivial case is \(x(v)=+1\). Since \(x\preceq z\), this forces \(x(v)=z(v)=+1\). The acceptance ratios are
\[
R_x=\exp\left(-\sum_{w\sim v}x(w)\right),
\qquad
R_z=\exp\left(-\sum_{w\sim v}z(w)\right).
\]
Again \(x(w)\le z(w)\), so
\[
-\sum_{w\sim v}x(w)\ge -\sum_{w\sim v}z(w),
\]
and hence \(R_x\ge R_z\). Therefore
\[
\min\{1,R_x\}\ge \min\{1,R_z\}.
\]
Thus if the upper chain accepts the move to \(-1\), then the lower chain also accepts. Hence order is preserved.

Therefore
\[
\mathbb P\bigl(f_{t+1}(x)\preceq f_{t+1}(z)\bigr)=1.
\]

---

## (5) Constant maps and coalescence of top and bottom

Let
\[
\underline x=(-1,\dots,-1),\qquad \bar x=(1,\dots,1).
\]
By part (4), each update map \(f_i\) is monotone, and therefore the composition
\[
F=f_t\circ\cdots\circ f_1
\]
is monotone.

If \(F\) is constant, then clearly
\[
F(\underline x)=F(\bar x).
\]

Conversely, suppose
\[
F(\underline x)=F(\bar x).
\]
For any \(x\in\mathcal X\),
\[
\underline x\preceq x\preceq \bar x.
\]
By monotonicity of \(F\),
\[
F(\underline x)\preceq F(x)\preceq F(\bar x).
\]
Since the two endpoints are equal, this forces
\[
F(x)=F(\underline x)=F(\bar x).
\]
Thus \(F\) is constant.

Therefore \(F\) is constant iff \(F(\underline x)=F(\bar x)\).

---

## (6) The height function

There is a harmless off-by-one issue in the statement: if \(h(z)\) literally counts the number of states in a chain ending at \(z\), then \(h(\bar x)=n+1\), contradicting part (8). The intended height is the number of strict steps in the longest chain:
\[
h(z):=\max\{k:\ x_0\prec x_1\prec\cdots\prec x_k=z\},
\]
where \(x\prec y\) means \(x\preceq y\) and \(x\neq y\).

With this convention, if \(x_t\preceq y_t\) and \(x_t\neq y_t\), take a longest strict chain ending at \(x_t\):
\[
x_0\prec x_1\prec\cdots\prec x_{h(x_t)}=x_t.
\]
Since \(x_t\prec y_t\), appending \(y_t\) gives a strict chain
\[
x_0\prec x_1\prec\cdots\prec x_{h(x_t)}=x_t\prec y_t.
\]
Hence
\[
h(y_t)\ge h(x_t)+1.
\]
Therefore
\[
h(x_t)+1\le h(y_t).
\]

---

## (7) Bounding \(\mathbb P(T>t)\)

Let
\[
X_t=f_t\circ\cdots\circ f_1(\underline x),
\qquad
Y_t=f_t\circ\cdots\circ f_1(\bar x).
\]
By monotonicity,
\[
X_t\preceq Y_t
\]
for every \(t\). Also,
\[
\{T>t\}=\{X_t\neq Y_t\}.
\]
On the event \(\{X_t\neq Y_t\}\), part (6) gives
\[
h(Y_t)-h(X_t)\ge 1.
\]
Therefore
\[
\mathbf 1_{\{T>t\}}\le h(Y_t)-h(X_t).
\]
Taking expectations,
\[
\mathbb P(T>t)
\le
\mathbb E[h(Y_t)-h(X_t)].
\]

---

## (8) Bounds on \(h\) and on its expected gap

For \(z\in\mathcal X\), let
\[
m(z):=\#\{v\in V:z(v)=+1\}.
\]
In the coordinatewise partial order, every strict step in a chain must change at least one coordinate from \(-1\) to \(+1\). Therefore no chain ending at \(z\) can have more than \(m(z)\) strict steps. Conversely, starting from \(\underline x\), we can flip the \(+1\)-coordinates of \(z\) one at a time, obtaining a strict chain of length \(m(z)\). Hence
\[
h(z)=m(z).
\]
Thus
\[
0\le h(z)\le |V|.
\]

Now let \(\mu_t\) be the law of \(X_t\) and \(\nu_t\) the law of \(Y_t\). Then
\[
\mu_t=P^t(\underline x,\cdot),
\qquad
\nu_t=P^t(\bar x,\cdot).
\]
Because \(X_t\preceq Y_t\),
\[
h(Y_t)-h(X_t)
=
\sum_{v\in V}\bigl(\mathbf 1\{Y_t(v)=+1\}-\mathbf 1\{X_t(v)=+1\}\bigr).
\]
Taking expectations,
\[
\mathbb E[h(Y_t)-h(X_t)]
=
\sum_{v\in V}\left(\nu_t(A_v)-\mu_t(A_v)\right),
\]
where
\[
A_v:=\{z\in\mathcal X:z(v)=+1\}.
\]
For each \(v\),
\[
|\nu_t(A_v)-\mu_t(A_v)|
\le
\|\nu_t-\mu_t\|_{\mathrm{TV}}
\le
\bar d(t),
\]
where
\[
\bar d(t):=\max_{x,y\in\mathcal X}\|P^t(x,\cdot)-P^t(y,\cdot)\|_{\mathrm{TV}}.
\]
Hence
\[
\mathbb E[h(Y_t)-h(X_t)]
\le
|V|\,\bar d(t).
\]

---

## (9) Tail bound at multiples of the mixing time

Assume \(|V|=2L\), with \(L>1\).

Use the standard definitions
\[
d(t):=\max_{x\in\mathcal X}\|P^t(x,\cdot)-\pi\|_{\mathrm{TV}},
\]
\[
\bar d(t):=\max_{x,y\in\mathcal X}\|P^t(x,\cdot)-P^t(y,\cdot)\|_{\mathrm{TV}},
\]
and
\[
t_{\mathrm{mix}}:=\min\{t:d(t)\le 1/4\}.
\]

We use the standard properties:

1. Triangle inequality:
   \[
   \bar d(t)\le 2d(t).
   \]

2. Submultiplicativity of \(\bar d\):
   \[
   \bar d(s+t)\le \bar d(s)\bar d(t).
   \]

Let \(\tau=t_{\mathrm{mix}}\). Since \(d(\tau)\le 1/4\),
\[
\bar d(\tau)\le 2d(\tau)\le \frac12.
\]
By submultiplicativity,
\[
\bar d(m\tau)\le \left(\frac12\right)^m.
\]
Using parts (7) and (8),
\[
\mathbb P(T>m\tau)
\le
|V|\,\bar d(m\tau)
\le
2L\cdot 2^{-m}.
\]
Take \(m=k+L\). Then
\[
\mathbb P(T>(k+L)t_{\mathrm{mix}})
\le
2L\cdot 2^{-(k+L)}
=
\frac{2L}{2^L}\cdot 2^{-k}.
\]
Since \(L>1\), we have \(2L\le 2^L\). Therefore
\[
\mathbb P(T>(k+L)t_{\mathrm{mix}})
\le
2^{-k}.
\]

---

## (10) Bound on \(\mathbb E[T]\)

Let again \(\tau=t_{\mathrm{mix}}\). Since \(T\) is integer-valued,
\[
\mathbb E[T]
=
\sum_{s=0}^\infty \mathbb P(T>s).
\]
Partition the sum into blocks of length \(\tau\):
\[
\mathbb E[T]
\le
\tau\sum_{j=0}^\infty \mathbb P(T>j\tau).
\]
Split the sum at \(j=L\):
\[
\sum_{j=0}^\infty \mathbb P(T>j\tau)
=
\sum_{j=0}^{L-1}\mathbb P(T>j\tau)
+
\sum_{k=0}^\infty \mathbb P(T>(L+k)\tau).
\]
The first sum is at most \(L\). By part (9), the second sum is at most
\[
\sum_{k=0}^\infty 2^{-k}=2.
\]
Therefore
\[
\mathbb E[T]
\le
\tau(L+2).
\]
Since \(L>1\), \(L+2\le 2L\). Hence
\[
\boxed{\mathbb E[T]\le 2L\,t_{\mathrm{mix}}.}
\]
Thus the desired bound holds with an absolute constant, for example \(c=2\).

Let \(n=|V|\). Write \(x(v)\) also as \(x_v\). For \(x,z\in\mathcal X\), let  
\[
\Delta(x,z):=\{v\in V:x(v)\neq z(v)\}.
\]

## (1) Transition probabilities \(P(x,z)\) for \(z\neq x\)

A nontrivial move changes at most one coordinate. Hence \(P(x,z)>0\) for \(z\neq x\) iff \(|\Delta(x,z)|=1\). If \(\Delta(x,z)=\{v\}\), then necessarily \(z(v)=-x(v)\), and the proposal \(z\) is made exactly when \(v_{t+1}=v\) and \(S_{t+1}=z(v)\), which has probability \(1/(2n)\). Therefore
\[
P(x,z)
=
\frac1{2n}\min\left\{1,\frac{e^{-H(z)}}{e^{-H(x)}}\right\}
=
\frac1{2n}\min\{1,e^{H(x)-H(z)}\}.
\]
If \(|\Delta(x,z)|\neq 1\), then \(P(x,z)=0\) for \(z\neq x\).

---

## (2) Stationarity of \(\pi\)

We prove detailed balance. Let
\[
Z=\sum_{y\in\mathcal X} e^{-H(y)}.
\]
If \(x\neq z\) and \(|\Delta(x,z)|=1\), then by part (1),
\[
P(x,z)=\frac1{2n}\min\left\{1,\frac{e^{-H(z)}}{e^{-H(x)}}\right\}.
\]
Thus
\[
\pi(x)P(x,z)
=
\frac{e^{-H(x)}}{Z}\cdot \frac1{2n}
\min\left\{1,\frac{e^{-H(z)}}{e^{-H(x)}}\right\}
=
\frac1{2nZ}\min\{e^{-H(x)},e^{-H(z)}\}.
\]
The right-hand side is symmetric in \(x,z\). Hence
\[
\pi(x)P(x,z)=\pi(z)P(z,x).
\]
If \(x,z\) differ in more than one coordinate, then both transition probabilities are \(0\). The diagonal case is trivial. Therefore \(P\) is reversible with respect to \(\pi\). By detailed balance, \(\pi\) is stationary.

---

## (3) Local form of the acceptance ratio

Let \(v=v_{t+1}\), \(S=S_{t+1}\), and \(N=N_{t+1}\) be the neighbors of \(v\). Let \(x=x_t\), and let \(y\) be the proposed configuration, so \(y(v)=S\) and \(y(w)=x(w)\) for \(w\neq v\).

Only edges incident to \(v\) can change their contribution to \(H\). For an edge \(\{v,w\}\),
\[
\frac12(1-y(v)y(w))-\frac12(1-x(v)x(w))
=
\frac12(1-Sx(w))-\frac12(1-x(v)x(w))
=
\frac12(x(v)-S)x(w).
\]
Therefore
\[
H(y)-H(x)
=
\frac12\sum_{w\in N}(x(v)-S)x(w).
\]
Hence
\[
\frac{e^{-H(y)}}{e^{-H(x)}}
=
\exp\{-(H(y)-H(x))\}
=
\exp\left(\frac12\sum_{w\in N}(S-x(v))x(w)\right).
\]

---

## (4) Monotonicity of the update map

We couple two chains using the same randomness \((v,S,U)\). Suppose \(x\preceq z\). We prove
\[
f_{t+1}(x)\preceq f_{t+1}(z)
\]
for every realization of \((v,S,U)\).

Coordinates other than \(v\) are unchanged, so the order can only fail at coordinate \(v\).

### Case 1: \(S=+1\)

If \(z(v)=+1\), then the upper chain has spin \(+1\) at \(v\) after the update, so the lower spin is automatically \(\leq +1\).

The only nontrivial case is \(z(v)=-1\). Since \(x\preceq z\), this forces \(x(v)=z(v)=-1\). By part (3), the acceptance ratios are
\[
R_x=\exp\left(\sum_{w\sim v}x(w)\right),
\qquad
R_z=\exp\left(\sum_{w\sim v}z(w)\right).
\]
Since \(x(w)\le z(w)\) for every \(w\),
\[
\sum_{w\sim v}x(w)\le \sum_{w\sim v}z(w),
\]
so \(R_x\le R_z\), and therefore
\[
\min\{1,R_x\}\le \min\{1,R_z\}.
\]
Thus if the lower chain accepts the move to \(+1\), then the upper chain also accepts. Hence order is preserved.

### Case 2: \(S=-1\)

If \(x(v)=-1\), then the lower chain has spin \(-1\) at \(v\) after the update, so it remains \(\leq\) the upper spin.

The only nontrivial case is \(x(v)=+1\). Since \(x\preceq z\), this forces \(x(v)=z(v)=+1\). The acceptance ratios are
\[
R_x=\exp\left(-\sum_{w\sim v}x(w)\right),
\qquad
R_z=\exp\left(-\sum_{w\sim v}z(w)\right).
\]
Again \(x(w)\le z(w)\), so
\[
-\sum_{w\sim v}x(w)\ge -\sum_{w\sim v}z(w),
\]
and hence \(R_x\ge R_z\). Therefore
\[
\min\{1,R_x\}\ge \min\{1,R_z\}.
\]
Thus if the upper chain accepts the move to \(-1\), then the lower chain also accepts. Hence order is preserved.

Therefore
\[
\mathbb P\bigl(f_{t+1}(x)\preceq f_{t+1}(z)\bigr)=1.
\]

---

## (5) Constant maps and coalescence of top and bottom

Let
\[
\underline x=(-1,\dots,-1),\qquad \bar x=(1,\dots,1).
\]
By part (4), each update map \(f_i\) is monotone, and therefore the composition
\[
F=f_t\circ\cdots\circ f_1
\]
is monotone.

If \(F\) is constant, then clearly
\[
F(\underline x)=F(\bar x).
\]

Conversely, suppose
\[
F(\underline x)=F(\bar x).
\]
For any \(x\in\mathcal X\),
\[
\underline x\preceq x\preceq \bar x.
\]
By monotonicity of \(F\),
\[
F(\underline x)\preceq F(x)\preceq F(\bar x).
\]
Since the two endpoints are equal, this forces
\[
F(x)=F(\underline x)=F(\bar x).
\]
Thus \(F\) is constant.

Therefore \(F\) is constant iff \(F(\underline x)=F(\bar x)\).

---

## (6) The height function

There is a harmless off-by-one issue in the statement: if \(h(z)\) literally counts the number of states in a chain ending at \(z\), then \(h(\bar x)=n+1\), contradicting part (8). The intended height is the number of strict steps in the longest chain:
\[
h(z):=\max\{k:\ x_0\prec x_1\prec\cdots\prec x_k=z\},
\]
where \(x\prec y\) means \(x\preceq y\) and \(x\neq y\).

With this convention, if \(x_t\preceq y_t\) and \(x_t\neq y_t\), take a longest strict chain ending at \(x_t\):
\[
x_0\prec x_1\prec\cdots\prec x_{h(x_t)}=x_t.
\]
Since \(x_t\prec y_t\), appending \(y_t\) gives a strict chain
\[
x_0\prec x_1\prec\cdots\prec x_{h(x_t)}=x_t\prec y_t.
\]
Hence
\[
h(y_t)\ge h(x_t)+1.
\]
Therefore
\[
h(x_t)+1\le h(y_t).
\]

---

## (7) Bounding \(\mathbb P(T>t)\)

Let
\[
X_t=f_t\circ\cdots\circ f_1(\underline x),
\qquad
Y_t=f_t\circ\cdots\circ f_1(\bar x).
\]
By monotonicity,
\[
X_t\preceq Y_t
\]
for every \(t\). Also,
\[
\{T>t\}=\{X_t\neq Y_t\}.
\]
On the event \(\{X_t\neq Y_t\}\), part (6) gives
\[
h(Y_t)-h(X_t)\ge 1.
\]
Therefore
\[
\mathbf 1_{\{T>t\}}\le h(Y_t)-h(X_t).
\]
Taking expectations,
\[
\mathbb P(T>t)
\le
\mathbb E[h(Y_t)-h(X_t)].
\]

---

## (8) Bounds on \(h\) and on its expected gap

For \(z\in\mathcal X\), let
\[
m(z):=\#\{v\in V:z(v)=+1\}.
\]
In the coordinatewise partial order, every strict step in a chain must change at least one coordinate from \(-1\) to \(+1\). Therefore no chain ending at \(z\) can have more than \(m(z)\) strict steps. Conversely, starting from \(\underline x\), we can flip the \(+1\)-coordinates of \(z\) one at a time, obtaining a strict chain of length \(m(z)\). Hence
\[
h(z)=m(z).
\]
Thus
\[
0\le h(z)\le |V|.
\]

Now let \(\mu_t\) be the law of \(X_t\) and \(\nu_t\) the law of \(Y_t\). Then
\[
\mu_t=P^t(\underline x,\cdot),
\qquad
\nu_t=P^t(\bar x,\cdot).
\]
Because \(X_t\preceq Y_t\),
\[
h(Y_t)-h(X_t)
=
\sum_{v\in V}\bigl(\mathbf 1\{Y_t(v)=+1\}-\mathbf 1\{X_t(v)=+1\}\bigr).
\]
Taking expectations,
\[
\mathbb E[h(Y_t)-h(X_t)]
=
\sum_{v\in V}\left(\nu_t(A_v)-\mu_t(A_v)\right),
\]
where
\[
A_v:=\{z\in\mathcal X:z(v)=+1\}.
\]
For each \(v\),
\[
|\nu_t(A_v)-\mu_t(A_v)|
\le
\|\nu_t-\mu_t\|_{\mathrm{TV}}
\le
\bar d(t),
\]
where
\[
\bar d(t):=\max_{x,y\in\mathcal X}\|P^t(x,\cdot)-P^t(y,\cdot)\|_{\mathrm{TV}}.
\]
Hence
\[
\mathbb E[h(Y_t)-h(X_t)]
\le
|V|\,\bar d(t).
\]

---

## (9) Tail bound at multiples of the mixing time

Assume \(|V|=2L\), with \(L>1\).

Use the standard definitions
\[
d(t):=\max_{x\in\mathcal X}\|P^t(x,\cdot)-\pi\|_{\mathrm{TV}},
\]
\[
\bar d(t):=\max_{x,y\in\mathcal X}\|P^t(x,\cdot)-P^t(y,\cdot)\|_{\mathrm{TV}},
\]
and
\[
t_{\mathrm{mix}}:=\min\{t:d(t)\le 1/4\}.
\]

We use the standard properties:

1. Triangle inequality:
   \[
   \bar d(t)\le 2d(t).
   \]

2. Submultiplicativity of \(\bar d\):
   \[
   \bar d(s+t)\le \bar d(s)\bar d(t).
   \]

Let \(\tau=t_{\mathrm{mix}}\). Since \(d(\tau)\le 1/4\),
\[
\bar d(\tau)\le 2d(\tau)\le \frac12.
\]
By submultiplicativity,
\[
\bar d(m\tau)\le \left(\frac12\right)^m.
\]
Using parts (7) and (8),
\[
\mathbb P(T>m\tau)
\le
|V|\,\bar d(m\tau)
\le
2L\cdot 2^{-m}.
\]
Take \(m=k+L\). Then
\[
\mathbb P(T>(k+L)t_{\mathrm{mix}})
\le
2L\cdot 2^{-(k+L)}
=
\frac{2L}{2^L}\cdot 2^{-k}.
\]
Since \(L>1\), we have \(2L\le 2^L\). Therefore
\[
\mathbb P(T>(k+L)t_{\mathrm{mix}})
\le
2^{-k}.
\]

---

## (10) Bound on \(\mathbb E[T]\)

Let again \(\tau=t_{\mathrm{mix}}\). Since \(T\) is integer-valued,
\[
\mathbb E[T]
=
\sum_{s=0}^\infty \mathbb P(T>s).
\]
Partition the sum into blocks of length \(\tau\):
\[
\mathbb E[T]
\le
\tau\sum_{j=0}^\infty \mathbb P(T>j\tau).
\]
Split the sum at \(j=L\):
\[
\sum_{j=0}^\infty \mathbb P(T>j\tau)
=
\sum_{j=0}^{L-1}\mathbb P(T>j\tau)
+
\sum_{k=0}^\infty \mathbb P(T>(L+k)\tau).
\]
The first sum is at most \(L\). By part (9), the second sum is at most
\[
\sum_{k=0}^\infty 2^{-k}=2.
\]
Therefore
\[
\mathbb E[T]
\le
\tau(L+2).
\]
Since \(L>1\), \(L+2\le 2L\). Hence
\[
\boxed{\mathbb E[T]\le 2L\,t_{\mathrm{mix}}.}
\]
Thus the desired bound holds with an absolute constant, for example \(c=2\).

Let \(n=|V|\). Write \(Z=\sum_{y\in\mathcal X}e^{-H(y)}\), so \(\pi(x)=Z^{-1}e^{-H(x)}\).

---

## (1) Computation of \(P(x,z)\) for \(z\neq x\)

A single update changes at most one coordinate. Hence \(P(x,z)>0\) for \(z\neq x\) iff \(x,z\) differ at exactly one vertex, say \(v\). Then necessarily \(z(v)=-x(v)\), and the proposal \(y=z\) occurs iff \(v_{t+1}=v\) and \(S_{t+1}=z(v)\), which has probability \(\frac1n\cdot \frac12=\frac1{2n}\). Thus

\[
P(x,z)=\frac1{2n}\min\left\{1,\frac{e^{-H(z)}}{e^{-H(x)}}\right\}
=\frac1{2n}\min\left\{1,e^{H(x)-H(z)}\right\}.
\]

Equivalently, if \(x,z\) differ only at \(v\),

\[
P(x,z)
=
\frac1{2n}
\min\left\{
1,\exp\left(\frac12(z(v)-x(v))\sum_{w\sim v}x(w)\right)
\right\}.
\]

If \(x,z\) differ at more than one vertex, then \(P(x,z)=0\).

---

## (2) Stationarity of \(\pi\)

We prove the stronger statement that the chain is reversible with respect to \(\pi\).

For \(x\neq z\), if \(x,z\) do not differ at exactly one vertex, then \(P(x,z)=P(z,x)=0\). Suppose they differ at exactly one vertex. Then the proposal probabilities are symmetric:

\[
q(x,z)=q(z,x)=\frac1{2n}.
\]

The Metropolis acceptance probability is

\[
a(x,z)=\min\left\{1,\frac{e^{-H(z)}}{e^{-H(x)}}\right\}.
\]

Therefore

\[
\pi(x)P(x,z)
=
\frac{e^{-H(x)}}{Z}\frac1{2n}
\min\left\{1,\frac{e^{-H(z)}}{e^{-H(x)}}\right\}.
\]

But

\[
e^{-H(x)}
\min\left\{1,\frac{e^{-H(z)}}{e^{-H(x)}}\right\}
=
\min\{e^{-H(x)},e^{-H(z)}\},
\]

so

\[
\pi(x)P(x,z)
=
\frac1{2nZ}\min\{e^{-H(x)},e^{-H(z)}\}
=
\pi(z)P(z,x).
\]

Thus detailed balance holds:

\[
\pi(x)P(x,z)=\pi(z)P(z,x).
\]

Hence \(\pi\) is stationary.

---

## (3) Local expression for the Metropolis ratio

Let \(v=v_{t+1}\), \(S=S_{t+1}\), and \(N=N_{t+1}=\{w:w\sim v\}\). Let \(x=x_t\), and let \(y\) be the proposed configuration with \(y(v)=S\) and \(y(w)=x(w)\) for \(w\neq v\).

Only edges incident to \(v\) can change their contribution to \(H\). Therefore

\[
H(y)-H(x)
=
\frac12\sum_{w\in N}
\left[(1-Sx(w))-(1-x(v)x(w))\right].
\]

Simplifying,

\[
H(y)-H(x)
=
\frac12\sum_{w\in N}(x(v)-S)x(w).
\]

Hence

\[
H(x)-H(y)
=
\frac12\sum_{w\in N}(S-x(v))x(w),
\]

and therefore

\[
\frac{e^{-H(y)}}{e^{-H(x)}}
=
e^{H(x)-H(y)}
=
\exp\left(
\frac12\sum_{w\in N}(S-x(v))x(w)
\right).
\]

Thus

\[
\boxed{
\frac{e^{-H(y)}}{e^{-H(x_t)}}
=
\exp\left(
\frac12\sum_{w\in N_{t+1}}
(S_{t+1}-x_t(v_{t+1}))x_t(w)
\right).
}
\]

---

## (4) Monotonicity of the dynamics

Let \(x\preceq z\). We prove that, using the same randomness \((v,S,U)\), one has

\[
f_{t+1}(x)\preceq f_{t+1}(z)
\]

almost surely.

All coordinates \(w\neq v\) are unchanged, so only coordinate \(v\) matters.

Let

\[
A_x=\sum_{w\sim v}x(w),
\qquad
A_z=\sum_{w\sim v}z(w).
\]

Since \(x\preceq z\), we have \(A_x\le A_z\).

### Case 1: \(S=1\)

If \(x(v)=1\), then \(z(v)=1\), so both configurations already have spin \(1\) at \(v\), and the order is preserved.

If \(x(v)=-1\) and \(z(v)=1\), then \(f_{t+1}(z)(v)=1\), while \(f_{t+1}(x)(v)\in\{-1,1\}\), so again

\[
f_{t+1}(x)(v)\le f_{t+1}(z)(v).
\]

It remains to consider \(x(v)=z(v)=-1\). Then both chains propose to flip \(-1\) to \(1\). By part (3), the acceptance probability from a configuration \(\eta\) with \(\eta(v)=-1\) is

\[
\alpha(\eta)=\min\{1,e^{A_\eta}\}.
\]

Since \(A_x\le A_z\),

\[
\alpha(x)\le \alpha(z).
\]

Thus, using the same \(U\), if the update from \(x\) is accepted, then the update from \(z\) is also accepted. Therefore order is preserved.

### Case 2: \(S=-1\)

If \(z(v)=-1\), then \(x(v)=-1\), so both already have spin \(-1\) at \(v\), and order is preserved.

If \(x(v)=-1\) and \(z(v)=1\), then \(f_{t+1}(x)(v)=-1\), while \(f_{t+1}(z)(v)\in\{-1,1\}\), so the order is preserved.

It remains to consider \(x(v)=z(v)=1\). Then both chains propose to flip \(1\) to \(-1\). By part (3), the acceptance probability from \(\eta\) with \(\eta(v)=1\) is

\[
\alpha(\eta)=\min\{1,e^{-A_\eta}\}.
\]

Since \(A_x\le A_z\), we have

\[
e^{-A_x}\ge e^{-A_z},
\]

and hence

\[
\alpha(x)\ge \alpha(z).
\]

Thus, using the same \(U\), if the update from \(z\) is accepted, then the update from \(x\) is also accepted. Therefore order is preserved.

Combining the two cases,

\[
\boxed{
x\preceq z
\implies
f_{t+1}(x)\preceq f_{t+1}(z)
\quad\text{almost surely.}
}
\]

---

## (5) Characterization of coalescence by extremal states

Let

\[
\underline x=(-1,\dots,-1),
\qquad
\bar x=(1,\dots,1).
\]

For every \(x\in\mathcal X\),

\[
\underline x\preceq x\preceq \bar x.
\]

Each \(f_i\) is monotone by part (4), so their composition

\[
F=f_t\circ\cdots\circ f_1
\]

is also monotone.

If \(F\) is constant, then certainly

\[
F(\underline x)=F(\bar x).
\]

Conversely, suppose

\[
F(\underline x)=F(\bar x).
\]

Then for any \(x\in\mathcal X\), monotonicity gives

\[
F(\underline x)\preceq F(x)\preceq F(\bar x).
\]

Since the lower and upper bounds are equal, we must have

\[
F(x)=F(\underline x)=F(\bar x).
\]

Thus \(F\) is constant.

Hence

\[
\boxed{
F \text{ is constant }
\Longleftrightarrow
F(\underline x)=F(\bar x).
}
\]

---

## (6) Height function and strict monotonicity

Let \(n=|V|\). Write \(Z=\sum_{y\in\mathcal X}e^{-H(y)}\), so \(\pi(x)=Z^{-1}e^{-H(x)}\).

---

## (1) Computation of \(P(x,z)\) for \(z\neq x\)

A single update changes at most one coordinate. Hence \(P(x,z)>0\) for \(z\neq x\) iff \(x,z\) differ at exactly one vertex, say \(v\). Then necessarily \(z(v)=-x(v)\), and the proposal \(y=z\) occurs iff \(v_{t+1}=v\) and \(S_{t+1}=z(v)\), which has probability \(\frac1n\cdot \frac12=\frac1{2n}\). Thus

\[
P(x,z)=\frac1{2n}\min\left\{1,\frac{e^{-H(z)}}{e^{-H(x)}}\right\}
=\frac1{2n}\min\left\{1,e^{H(x)-H(z)}\right\}.
\]

Equivalently, if \(x,z\) differ only at \(v\),

\[
P(x,z)
=
\frac1{2n}
\min\left\{
1,\exp\left(\frac12(z(v)-x(v))\sum_{w\sim v}x(w)\right)
\right\}.
\]

If \(x,z\) differ at more than one vertex, then \(P(x,z)=0\).

---

## (2) Stationarity of \(\pi\)

We prove the stronger statement that the chain is reversible with respect to \(\pi\).

For \(x\neq z\), if \(x,z\) do not differ at exactly one vertex, then \(P(x,z)=P(z,x)=0\). Suppose they differ at exactly one vertex. Then the proposal probabilities are symmetric:

\[
q(x,z)=q(z,x)=\frac1{2n}.
\]

The Metropolis acceptance probability is

\[
a(x,z)=\min\left\{1,\frac{e^{-H(z)}}{e^{-H(x)}}\right\}.
\]

Therefore

\[
\pi(x)P(x,z)
=
\frac{e^{-H(x)}}{Z}\frac1{2n}
\min\left\{1,\frac{e^{-H(z)}}{e^{-H(x)}}\right\}.
\]

But

\[
e^{-H(x)}
\min\left\{1,\frac{e^{-H(z)}}{e^{-H(x)}}\right\}
=
\min\{e^{-H(x)},e^{-H(z)}\},
\]

so

\[
\pi(x)P(x,z)
=
\frac1{2nZ}\min\{e^{-H(x)},e^{-H(z)}\}
=
\pi(z)P(z,x).
\]

Thus detailed balance holds:

\[
\pi(x)P(x,z)=\pi(z)P(z,x).
\]

Hence \(\pi\) is stationary.

---

## (3) Local expression for the Metropolis ratio

Let \(v=v_{t+1}\), \(S=S_{t+1}\), and \(N=N_{t+1}=\{w:w\sim v\}\). Let \(x=x_t\), and let \(y\) be the proposed configuration with \(y(v)=S\) and \(y(w)=x(w)\) for \(w\neq v\).

Only edges incident to \(v\) can change their contribution to \(H\). Therefore

\[
H(y)-H(x)
=
\frac12\sum_{w\in N}
\left[(1-Sx(w))-(1-x(v)x(w))\right].
\]

Simplifying,

\[
H(y)-H(x)
=
\frac12\sum_{w\in N}(x(v)-S)x(w).
\]

Hence

\[
H(x)-H(y)
=
\frac12\sum_{w\in N}(S-x(v))x(w),
\]

and therefore

\[
\frac{e^{-H(y)}}{e^{-H(x)}}
=
e^{H(x)-H(y)}
=
\exp\left(
\frac12\sum_{w\in N}(S-x(v))x(w)
\right).
\]

Thus

\[
\boxed{
\frac{e^{-H(y)}}{e^{-H(x_t)}}
=
\exp\left(
\frac12\sum_{w\in N_{t+1}}
(S_{t+1}-x_t(v_{t+1}))x_t(w)
\right).
}
\]

---

## (4) Monotonicity of the dynamics

Let \(x\preceq z\). We prove that, using the same randomness \((v,S,U)\), one has

\[
f_{t+1}(x)\preceq f_{t+1}(z)
\]

almost surely.

All coordinates \(w\neq v\) are unchanged, so only coordinate \(v\) matters.

Let

\[
A_x=\sum_{w\sim v}x(w),
\qquad
A_z=\sum_{w\sim v}z(w).
\]

Since \(x\preceq z\), we have \(A_x\le A_z\).

### Case 1: \(S=1\)

If \(x(v)=1\), then \(z(v)=1\), so both configurations already have spin \(1\) at \(v\), and the order is preserved.

If \(x(v)=-1\) and \(z(v)=1\), then \(f_{t+1}(z)(v)=1\), while \(f_{t+1}(x)(v)\in\{-1,1\}\), so again

\[
f_{t+1}(x)(v)\le f_{t+1}(z)(v).
\]

\[
\alpha(\eta)=\min\{1,e^{A_\eta}\}.
\]

Since \(A_x\le A_z\),

\[
\alpha(x)\le \alpha(z).
\]

Thus, using the same \(U\), if the update from \(x\) is accepted, then the update from \(z\) is also accepted. Therefore order is preserved.

It remains to consider \(x(v)=z(v)=1\). Then both chains propose to flip \(1\) to \(-1\). By part (3), the acceptance probability from \(\eta\) with \(\eta(v)=1\) is

\[
\alpha(\eta)=\min\{1,e^{-A_\eta}\}.
\]

Since \(A_x\le A_z\), we have

\[
e^{-A_x}\ge e^{-A_z},
\]

and hence

\[
\alpha(x)\ge \alpha(z).
\]

Thus, using the same \(U\), if the update from \(z\) is accepted, then the update from \(x\) is also accepted. Therefore order is preserved.

\[
\boxed{
x\preceq z
\implies
f_{t+1}(x)\preceq f_{t+1}(z)
\quad\text{almost surely.}
}
\]

Conversely, suppose

\[
F(\underline x)=F(\bar x).
\]

Then for any \(x\in\mathcal X\), monotonicity gives

\[
F(\underline x)\preceq F(x)\preceq F(\bar x).
\]

Since the lower and upper bounds are equal, we must have

\[
F(x)=F(\underline x)=F(\bar x).
\]

Thus \(F\) is constant.

Hence

\[
\boxed{
F \text{ is constant }
\Longleftrightarrow
F(\underline x)=F(\bar x).
}
\]

\[

Let the RKHS component be denoted by \(g\in\mathcal H_\sigma\), and let the full fitted regression function be

\[
m(x)=b_0+b_1x+g(x).
\]

Write

\[
Y=(Y_1,\dots,Y_n)^T,\qquad 
Z=\begin{pmatrix}
1&X_1\\
\vdots&\vdots\\
1&X_n
\end{pmatrix},\qquad 
K_{ij}=K_\sigma(X_i,X_j).
\]

Assume \(Z\) has rank \(2\), i.e. the \(X_i\)’s are not all identical. For distinct \(X_i\)’s the Gaussian Gram matrix \(K\) is strictly positive definite; with ties, the same formulas hold for the fitted function, with the usual generalized-inverse interpretation.

---

# 1) Representer form

Let

\[
\mathcal H_n=\operatorname{span}\{K_\sigma(X_i,\cdot):i=1,\dots,n\}.
\]

For any \(g\in\mathcal H_\sigma\), decompose orthogonally

\[
g=g_\parallel+g_\perp,\qquad g_\parallel\in\mathcal H_n,\quad g_\perp\perp\mathcal H_n.
\]

By the reproducing property,

\[
g_\perp(X_i)=\langle g_\perp,K_\sigma(X_i,\cdot)\rangle_{\mathcal H_\sigma}=0.
\]

Hence the empirical loss depends only on \(g_\parallel\), while

\[
\|g\|_{\mathcal H_\sigma}^2
=
\|g_\parallel\|_{\mathcal H_\sigma}^2+\|g_\perp\|_{\mathcal H_\sigma}^2.
\]

Since \(\lambda>0\), any minimizer must have \(g_\perp=0\). Therefore the RKHS component satisfies

\[
\widehat g(x)=\sum_{i=1}^n c_iK_\sigma(X_i,x).
\]

Thus the full fitted function can be written as

\[
\widehat m(x)=\widehat b_0+\widehat b_1x+\sum_{i=1}^n \widehat c_iK_\sigma(X_i,x).
\]

This is the partial-smoothing representer theorem.

---

# 2) Penalty and closed form for \((\widehat b,\widehat c)\)

For

\[
g(x)=\sum_{i=1}^n c_iK_\sigma(X_i,x),
\]

the RKHS norm is

\[
\|g\|_{\mathcal H_\sigma}^2
=
\sum_{i,j}c_ic_jK_\sigma(X_i,X_j)
=
c^TKc.
\]

Thus the finite-dimensional criterion is

\[
Q(b,c)
=
\frac1n\|Y-Zb-Kc\|_2^2+\lambda c^TKc.
\]

Equivalently, after multiplying by \(n\),

\[
\widetilde Q(b,c)
=
\|Y-Zb-Kc\|_2^2+n\lambda c^TKc.
\]

So the penalty is

\[
\operatorname{pen}(c)=\lambda c^TKc,
\]

or \(n\lambda c^TKc\) if the criterion is multiplied by \(n\).

Let

\[
A_\lambda=K+n\lambda I_n.
\]

The first-order conditions are

\[
Z^T(Y-Zb-Kc)=0,
\]

and

\[
K(Y-Zb-Kc)=n\lambda Kc.
\]

For the Gaussian kernel with distinct \(X_i\)’s, \(K\) is nonsingular, so

\[
Y-Zb-Kc=n\lambda c.
\]

Thus

\[
(K+n\lambda I)c+Zb=Y,
\]

or

\[
A_\lambda c+Zb=Y.
\]

Together with \(Z^Tc=0\), the estimating equations are

\[
\begin{pmatrix}
A_\lambda & Z\\
Z^T & 0
\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}
c\\
b
\end{pmatrix}
=
\begin{pmatrix}
Y\\
0
\end{pmatrix}.
\]

Solving explicitly,

\[
\widehat c=A_\lambda^{-1}(Y-Z\widehat b),
\]

and the constraint \(Z^T\widehat c=0\) gives

\[
Z^TA_\lambda^{-1}(Y-Z\widehat b)=0.
\]

Hence

\[
\boxed{
\widehat b
=
\left(Z^TA_\lambda^{-1}Z\right)^{-1}
Z^TA_\lambda^{-1}Y
}
\]

and

\[
\boxed{
\widehat c
=
A_\lambda^{-1}(Y-Z\widehat b).
}
\]

---

# 3) Linear smoother matrix \(S\)

Define

\[
P_\lambda
=
Z\left(Z^TA_\lambda^{-1}Z\right)^{-1}Z^TA_\lambda^{-1}.
\]

Then

\[
Z\widehat b=P_\lambda Y,
\]

and

\[
\widehat c=A_\lambda^{-1}(I-P_\lambda)Y.
\]

The fitted values at the observed data points are

\[
\widehat{\mathbf m}
=
Z\widehat b+K\widehat c.
\]

Therefore

\[
\widehat{\mathbf m}
=
P_\lambda Y+KA_\lambda^{-1}(I-P_\lambda)Y.
\]

Thus

\[
\boxed{
\widehat{\mathbf m}=SY
}
\]

with

\[
\boxed{
S
=
P_\lambda+KA_\lambda^{-1}(I-P_\lambda).
}
\]

Equivalently, since \(K=A_\lambda-n\lambda I\),

\[
\boxed{
S
=
I_n-n\lambda A_\lambda^{-1}(I-P_\lambda).
}
\]

This matrix depends on \(X_1,\dots,X_n\), \(\sigma\), and \(\lambda\), but not on \(Y\). Hence \(\widehat m\) is a linear smoother.

A useful alternative expression is obtained as follows. Let \(Q_2\) be an \(n\times(n-2)\) matrix with orthonormal columns spanning the orthogonal complement of \(\operatorname{col}(Z)\). Then

\[
Z^Tc=0
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
c=Q_2\gamma.
\]

Premultiplying the equation \(A_\lambda c+Zb=Y\) by \(Q_2^T\) gives

\[
(Q_2^TKQ_2+n\lambda I)\gamma=Q_2^TY.
\]

Since

\[
\widehat{\mathbf m}=Y-n\lambda \widehat c,
\]

we get

\[
\boxed{
S
=
I_n-n\lambda Q_2
\left(Q_2^TKQ_2+n\lambda I\right)^{-1}
Q_2^T.
}
\]

If \(\mu_1,\dots,\mu_{n-2}\) are the eigenvalues of \(Q_2^TKQ_2\), then

\[
\boxed{
\operatorname{df}(\lambda)
=
\operatorname{tr}(S)
=
2+\sum_{j=1}^{n-2}\frac{\mu_j}{\mu_j+n\lambda}.
}
\]

This shows explicitly that the effective degrees of freedom decrease continuously from \(n\) to \(2\) as \(\lambda\) increases from \(0\) to \(\infty\).

---

# 4) R implementation

```r
gaussK <- function(x, z, sigma) {
  exp(-outer(x, z, "-")^2 / (2 * sigma^2))
}

rkhs_partial_fit <- function(x, y, sigma, lambda, xnew = x, return.S = TRUE) {
  x <- as.numeric(x)
  y <- as.numeric(y)
  xnew <- as.numeric(xnew)

  n <- length(x)
  stopifnot(length(y) == n, sigma > 0, lambda > 0)

  Z <- cbind(1, x)

  if (qr(Z)$rank < 2) {
    stop("Design matrix [1, x] must have rank 2.")
  }

  K <- gaussK(x, x, sigma)
  A <- K + n * lambda * diag(n)

  Ai <- solve(A)

  M <- t(Z) %*% Ai %*% Z

  b <- solve(M, t(Z) %*% Ai %*% y)
  b <- as.numeric(b)
  names(b) <- c("b0", "b1")

  ccoef <- Ai %*% (y - Z %*% b)
  ccoef <- as.numeric(ccoef)

  fitted <- as.numeric(Z %*% b + K %*% ccoef)

  P <- Z %*% solve(M, t(Z) %*% Ai)
  S <- P + K %*% Ai %*% (diag(n) - P)

  df <- sum(diag(S))

  Knew <- gaussK(xnew, x, sigma)
  pred <- as.numeric(cbind(1, xnew) %*% b + Knew %*% ccoef)

  out <- list(
    b = b,
    c = ccoef,
    fitted = fitted,
    pred = pred,
    xnew = xnew,
    sigma = sigma,
    lambda = lambda,
    df = df
  )

  if (return.S) {
    out$S <- S
  }

  out
}
```

A helper for choosing \(\lambda\) to achieve a target degrees of freedom:

```r
df_info <- function(x, sigma) {
  x <- as.numeric(x)
  n <- length(x)

  Z <- cbind(1, x)
  K <- gaussK(x, x, sigma)

  qz <- qr(Z)
  p <- qz$rank

  Q <- qr.Q(qz, complete = TRUE)

  if (n > p) {
    Q2 <- Q[, (p + 1):n, drop = FALSE]
    B <- t(Q2) %*% K %*% Q2
    mu <- eigen(B, symmetric = TRUE, only.values = TRUE)$values
    mu <- pmax(mu, 0)
  } else {
    mu <- numeric(0)
  }

  list(n = n, p = p, mu = mu)
}

df_value <- function(info, lambda) {
  with(info, p + sum(mu / (mu + n * lambda)))
}

lambda_for_df <- function(x, sigma, target.df) {
  info <- df_info(x, sigma)

  if (target.df <= info$p || target.df >= info$n) {
    stop("Target df must be strictly between rank(Z) and n.")
  }

  f <- function(loglam) {
    df_value(info, exp(loglam)) - target.df
  }

  lo <- -30
  hi <- 30

  while (f(lo) < 0) lo <- lo - 10
  while (f(hi) > 0) hi <- hi + 10

  loglam <- uniroot(f, c(lo, hi), tol = 1e-10)$root
  exp(loglam)
}
```

# 5) Application to LA ozone data with \(\sigma=10\)

The dataset file `LAozone.data` was not provided, so I cannot report numerical fitted values. The analysis would be as follows.

```r
ozone_analysis <- function(file = "LAozone.data",
                           sigma = 10,
                           targets = c(4, 6, 8, 12)) {

  dat <- read.table(file, header = TRUE)

  if (!all(c("dpg", "ozone") %in% names(dat))) {
    stop("Data must contain variables named 'dpg' and 'ozone'.")
  }

  dat <- dat[complete.cases(dat[, c("dpg", "ozone")]), ]

  x <- dat$dpg
  y <- dat$ozone

  grid <- seq(-80, 120, length.out = 500)

  cols <- c("red", "blue", "darkgreen", "purple")
  fits <- vector("list", length(targets))
  lambdas <- numeric(length(targets))

  plot(
    x, y,
    pch = 19,
    col = "gray40",
    xlab = "dpg",
    ylab = "ozone",
    main = paste0("RKHS partial smoothing, sigma = ", sigma)
  )

  for (j in seq_along(targets)) {
    target <- targets[j]

    lam <- lambda_for_df(x, sigma, target)
    lambdas[j] <- lam

    fit <- rkhs_partial_fit(
      x = x,
      y = y,
      sigma = sigma,
      lambda = lam,
      xnew = grid
    )

    fits[[j]] <- fit

    lines(grid, fit$pred, col = cols[j], lwd = 2)
  }

  legend(
    "topright",
    legend = paste0("df = ", targets,
                    ", lambda = ", signif(lambdas, 4)),
    col = cols,
    lwd = 2,
    bty = "n"
  )

  lambda_table <- data.frame(
    target.df = targets,
    lambda = lambdas,
    achieved.df = sapply(fits, function(z) z$df)
  )

  print(lambda_table)

  j8 <- which(targets == 8)

  if (length(j8) == 1) {
    fit8 <- fits[[j8]]

    ord <- order(x)
    idx <- c(head(ord, 5), tail(ord, 5))

    report8 <- data.frame(
      dpg = x[idx],
      ozone = y[idx],
      fhat = fit8$fitted[idx]
    )

    report8 <- report8[order(report8$dpg), ]

    cat("\nFitted values for df = 8:\n")
    print(report8)
  } else {
    report8 <- NULL
  }

  invisible(list(
    data = dat,
    sigma = sigma,
    targets = targets,
    lambdas = lambdas,
    fits = fits,
    lambda.table = lambda_table,
    report8 = report8
  ))
}
```

Run:

```r
res10 <- ozone_analysis(
  file = "LAozone.data",
  sigma = 10,
  targets = c(4, 6, 8, 12)
)
```

This produces:

1. The four fitted curves over \(dpg\in(-80,120)\).
2. A table of \(\lambda\) values giving df \(4,6,8,12\).
3. For df \(=8\), the fitted values \(\widehat f\) at the five smallest and five largest observed `dpg` values.

Because the data file is unavailable here, the numerical table cannot be computed.

---

# 6) Repeat with \(\sigma=40\)

The same code applies with only the kernel bandwidth changed:

```r
res40 <- ozone_analysis(
  file = "LAozone.data",
  sigma = 40,
  targets = c(4, 6, 8, 12)
)
```

This will produce the analogous plot and df \(=8\) fitted-value table for \(\sigma=40\).

Qualitatively, increasing \(\sigma\) makes the Gaussian kernel basis functions wider, so the nonlinear component is more global. Even when df is matched, the \(\sigma=40\) fits will typically look smoother and less locally adaptive than the \(\sigma=10\) fits.

                           targets = c(4, 6, 8, 12)) {

  dat <- read.table(file, header = TRUE)

  if (!all(c("dpg", "ozone") %in% names(dat))) {
    stop("Data must contain variables named 'dpg' and 'ozone'.")
  }

  dat <- dat[complete.cases(dat[, c("dpg", "ozone")]), ]

  x <- dat$dpg
  y <- dat$ozone

  grid <- seq(-80, 120, length.out = 500)

  cols <- c("red", "blue", "darkgreen", "purple")
  fits <- vector("list", length(targets))
  lambdas <- numeric(length(targets))

  plot(
    x, y,
    pch = 19,
    col = "gray40",
    xlab = "dpg",
    ylab = "ozone",
    main = paste0("RKHS partial smoothing, sigma = ", sigma)
  )

  for (j in seq_along(targets)) {
    target <- targets[j]

    lam <- lambda_for_df(x, sigma, target)
    lambdas[j] <- lam

    fit <- rkhs_partial_fit(
      x = x,
      y = y,
      sigma = sigma,
      lambda = lam,
      xnew = grid
    )

    fits[[j]] <- fit

    lines(grid, fit$pred, col = cols[j], lwd = 2)
  }

  legend(
    "topright",
    legend = paste0("df = ", targets,
                    ", lambda = ", signif(lambdas, 4)),
    col = cols,
    lwd = 2,
    bty = "n"
  )

  lambda_table <- data.frame(
    target.df = targets,
    lambda = lambdas,
    achieved.df = sapply(fits, function(z) z$df)
  )

  print(lambda_table)

  j8 <- which(targets == 8)

  if (length(j8) == 1) {
    fit8 <- fits[[j8]]

    ord <- order(x)
    idx <- c(head(ord, 5), tail(ord, 5))

    report8 <- data.frame(
      dpg = x[idx],
      ozone = y[idx],
      fhat = fit8$fitted[idx]
    )

    report8 <- report8[order(report8$dpg), ]

    cat("\nFitted values for df = 8:\n")
    print(report8)
  } else {
    report8 <- NULL
  }

  invisible(list(
    data = dat,
    sigma = sigma,
    targets = targets,
    lambdas = lambdas,
    fits = fits,
    lambda.table = lambda_table,
    report8 = report8
  ))
}
```

## Notation and setup

Let the *total fitted regression curve* be
\[
m(x)=b_0+b_1x+h(x),\qquad h\in \mathcal H_\sigma .
\]
The problem’s \(\hat f\) is naturally this total fitted curve; below I write \(\hat m\) for clarity.

Define

\[
y=(Y_1,\dots,Y_n)^T,\qquad 
Z=\begin{pmatrix}
1 & X_1\\
\vdots & \vdots\\
1 & X_n
\end{pmatrix},\qquad 
b=(b_0,b_1)^T,
\]
and the Gaussian kernel Gram matrix
\[
K=\bigl(K_{ij}\bigr)_{i,j=1}^n,\qquad 
K_{ij}=K_\sigma(X_i,X_j)
=\exp\left\{-\frac{(X_i-X_j)^2}{2\sigma^2}\right\}.
\]

Also let
\[
k_x=\bigl(K_\sigma(X_1,x),\dots,K_\sigma(X_n,x)\bigr)^T.
\]

I assume \(Z\) has full column rank, i.e. the \(X_i\)’s are not all identical. If not, the same formulas hold with generalized inverses, but \(b_0,b_1\) are not uniquely identifiable.

---

# 1. Representer form

Let
\[
\mathcal V=\operatorname{span}\{K_\sigma(X_i,\cdot):i=1,\dots,n\}\subset \mathcal H_\sigma .
\]

For any \(h\in\mathcal H_\sigma\), decompose orthogonally as
\[
h=h_{\mathcal V}+h_{\mathcal V^\perp}.
\]

By the reproducing property,
\[
h_{\mathcal V^\perp}(X_i)
=
\langle h_{\mathcal V^\perp},K_\sigma(X_i,\cdot)\rangle_{\mathcal H_\sigma}
=0,
\]
because \(K_\sigma(X_i,\cdot)\in \mathcal V\) and \(h_{\mathcal V^\perp}\perp \mathcal V\).

Therefore replacing \(h\) by \(h_{\mathcal V}\) does not change any fitted values at the observed points, since
\[
h(X_i)=h_{\mathcal V}(X_i).
\]

But
\[
\|h\|_{\mathcal H_\sigma}^2
=
\|h_{\mathcal V}\|_{\mathcal H_\sigma}^2
+
\|h_{\mathcal V^\perp}\|_{\mathcal H_\sigma}^2
\ge
\|h_{\mathcal V}\|_{\mathcal H_\sigma}^2.
\]

Thus at the optimum we must have \(h_{\mathcal V^\perp}=0\). Hence the RKHS component satisfies
\[
\hat h(x)=\sum_{i=1}^n c_i K_\sigma(X_i,x).
\]

Therefore the total fitted function has the form

\[
\boxed{
\hat m(x)=\hat b_0+\hat b_1x+\sum_{i=1}^n \hat c_i K_\sigma(X_i,x).
}
\]

This is the representer theorem with an unpenalized finite-dimensional linear part.

---

# 2. Penalty and closed form for \((\hat b,\hat c)\)

For
\[
h(x)=\sum_{i=1}^n c_iK_\sigma(X_i,x),
\]
the RKHS norm is

\[
\|h\|_{\mathcal H_\sigma}^2
=
\left\langle \sum_i c_iK_\sigma(X_i,\cdot),
\sum_j c_jK_\sigma(X_j,\cdot)\right\rangle_{\mathcal H_\sigma}
=
\sum_{i,j}c_ic_jK_\sigma(X_i,X_j)
=
c^TKc.
\]

Hence the finite-dimensional objective is

\[
Q(b,c)
=
\frac1n\|y-Zb-Kc\|_2^2+\lambda c^TKc.
\]

Thus

\[
\boxed{
\operatorname{pen}(c)=c^TKc,
}
\]
and the actual penalty term in the objective is \(\lambda c^TKc\).

Let
\[
A=K+n\lambda I_n.
\]

The first-order conditions are

\[
Z^T(y-Zb-Kc)=0,
\]
and
\[
K(y-Zb-Kc)-n\lambda Kc=0.
\]

A convenient equivalent system is

\[
\boxed{
A\hat c+Z\hat b=y,\qquad Z^T\hat c=0.
}
\]

Equivalently,

\[
\boxed{
\begin{pmatrix}
A & Z\\
Z^T & 0
\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}
\hat c\\
\hat b
\end{pmatrix}
=
\begin{pmatrix}
y\\
0
\end{pmatrix}.
}
\]

Since \(A=K+n\lambda I_n\) is positive definite for \(\lambda>0\), the solution is

\[
\hat c=A^{-1}(y-Z\hat b).
\]

Imposing \(Z^T\hat c=0\),

\[
Z^TA^{-1}(y-Z\hat b)=0,
\]
so

\[
Z^TA^{-1}Z\hat b=Z^TA^{-1}y.
\]

Therefore

\[
\boxed{
\hat b
=
(Z^TA^{-1}Z)^{-1}Z^TA^{-1}y.
}
\]

Then

\[
\boxed{
\hat c
=
A^{-1}(y-Z\hat b).
}
\]

Equivalently,

\[
\boxed{
\hat c
=
\left[
A^{-1}
-
A^{-1}Z(Z^TA^{-1}Z)^{-1}Z^TA^{-1}
\right]y.
}
\]

---

# 3. Linear smoother matrix \(S\)

Define

\[
M=Z^TA^{-1}Z,
\]
and

\[
H_A=Z M^{-1}Z^TA^{-1}.
\]

Then

\[
\hat b=M^{-1}Z^TA^{-1}y,
\]
so

\[
Z\hat b=H_Ay.
\]

Also

\[
\hat c=A^{-1}(I-H_A)y.
\]

Therefore the fitted values at the training points are

\[
\hat m
=
Z\hat b+K\hat c
=
H_Ay+KA^{-1}(I-H_A)y.
\]

Thus

\[
\boxed{
\hat m=Sy,
}
\]
where

\[
\boxed{
S
=
H_A+KA^{-1}(I-H_A).
}
\]

Using \(K=A-n\lambda I_n\), this can also be written as

\[
\boxed{
S
=
I_n-n\lambda A^{-1}(I-H_A).
}
\]

The matrix \(S\) depends on \(X_1,\dots,X_n\), \(\sigma\), and \(\lambda\), but not on \(y\). Hence \(\hat m\) is a linear smoother.

The effective degrees of freedom are

\[
\boxed{
\operatorname{df}(\lambda,\sigma)=\operatorname{tr}(S).
}
\]

If one wants only the RKHS component \(h\), its fitted vector is

\[
\hat h=K\hat c
=
KA^{-1}(I-H_A)y.
\]

---

# 4. R implementation

```r
partial_rkhs_fit <- function(x, y, sigma, lambda, xnew = NULL, return.S = TRUE) {
  x <- as.numeric(x)
  y <- as.numeric(y)
  n <- length(y)

  if (length(x) != n) stop("x and y must have the same length.")
  if (sigma <= 0 || lambda <= 0) stop("sigma and lambda must be positive.")

  Z <- cbind(1, x)

  K <- exp(-(outer(x, x, "-")^2) / (2 * sigma^2))
  A <- K + n * lambda * diag(n)

  Ainv <- solve(A)

  AinvZ <- Ainv %*% Z
  M <- t(Z) %*% AinvZ

  bhat <- solve(M, t(Z) %*% Ainv %*% y)
  chat <- Ainv %*% (y - Z %*% bhat)

  fitted <- as.vector(Z %*% bhat + K %*% chat)

  out <- list(
    x = x,
    y = y,
    sigma = sigma,
    lambda = lambda,
    b = as.vector(bhat),
    c = as.vector(chat),
    fitted = fitted
  )

  predict_fun <- function(x0) {
    x0 <- as.numeric(x0)
    Z0 <- cbind(1, x0)
    K0 <- exp(-(outer(x0, x, "-")^2) / (2 * sigma^2))
    as.vector(Z0 %*% bhat + K0 %*% chat)
  }

  out$predict <- predict_fun

  if (!is.null(xnew)) {
    out$xnew <- xnew
    out$pred.xnew <- predict_fun(xnew)
  }

  if (return.S) {
    H_A <- Z %*% solve(M, t(Z) %*% Ainv)
    S <- diag(n) - n * lambda * Ainv %*% (diag(n) - H_A)

    out$S <- S
    out$df <- sum(diag(S))
  }

  return(out)
}
```

A helper function to choose \(\lambda\) to hit a desired degrees of freedom:

```r
find_lambda_for_df <- function(x, sigma, target.df, tol = 1e-7) {
  x <- as.numeric(x)
  n <- length(x)
  y0 <- rep(0, n)

  df_minus_target <- function(loglambda) {
    lambda <- exp(loglambda)
    fit <- partial_rkhs_fit(x, y0, sigma, lambda, return.S = TRUE)
    fit$df - target.df
  }

  lo <- -30
  hi <- 30

  flo <- df_minus_target(lo)
  fhi <- df_minus_target(hi)

  while (flo < 0) {
    lo <- lo - 5
    flo <- df_minus_target(lo)
  }

  while (fhi > 0) {
    hi <- hi + 5
    fhi <- df_minus_target(hi)
  }

  if (flo * fhi > 0) {
    stop("Could not bracket lambda for the requested degrees of freedom.")
  }

  loglambda.hat <- uniroot(df_minus_target, interval = c(lo, hi), tol = tol)$root
  exp(loglambda.hat)
}
```

run_ozone_analysis <- function(file = "LAozone.data",
                               sigma = 10,
                               target.dfs = c(4, 6, 8, 12)) {

  x <- as.numeric(x[ok])

      y = y,
      sigma = sigma,
      lambda = lambdas[j],
      xnew = grid,
      return.S = TRUE
    )
  }

  achieved.dfs <- sapply(fits, function(fit) fit$df)

  lambda.table <- data.frame(
    sigma = sigma,
    target.df = target.dfs,
    lambda = lambdas,
    achieved.df = achieved.dfs
  )

  print(lambda.table)

  cols <- c("red", "blue", "darkgreen", "purple")

  ylim.all <- range(y, unlist(lapply(fits, function(fit) fit$pred.xnew)))

  plot(
    x, y,
    pch = 19,
    col = "gray40",
    xlab = "dpg",
    ylab = "ozone",
    main = paste("Partial RKHS smoother, sigma =", sigma),
    xlim = c(-80, 120),
    ylim = ylim.all
  )

  for (j in seq_along(fits)) {
    lines(grid, fits[[j]]$pred.xnew, col = cols[j], lwd = 2)
  }

  legend(
    "topright",
    legend = paste0("df = ", target.dfs),
    col = cols,
    lwd = 2,
    bty = "n"
  )

  # Report fitted values for df = 8 at 5 smallest and 5 largest dpg
  j8 <- which(target.dfs == 8)

  if (length(j8) == 1) {
    ord <- order(x)
    idx <- c(ord[1:5], tail(ord, 5))

    df8.table <- data.frame(
      dpg.rank = c(1:5, (length(x) - 4):length(x)),
      dpg = x[idx],
      ozone = y[idx],
      fitted.df8 = fits[[j8]]$fitted[idx]
    )

    cat("\nFitted values for df = 8:\n")
    print(df8.table)
  }

  invisible(list(
    sigma = sigma,
    lambdas = lambdas,
    lambda.table = lambda.table,
    fits = fits
  ))
}

A=K+n\lambda I_n.
\]

The first-order conditions are

\[
Z^T(y-Zb-Kc)=0,
\]
and
\[
K(y-Zb-Kc)-n\lambda Kc=0.
\]

A convenient equivalent system is

\[
\boxed{
A\hat c+Z\hat b=y,\qquad Z^T\hat c=0.
}
\]

Equivalently,

\[
\boxed{
\begin{pmatrix}
A & Z\\
Z^T & 0
\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}
\hat c\\
\hat b
\end{pmatrix}
=
\begin{pmatrix}
y\\
0
\end{pmatrix}.
}
\]

Since \(A=K+n\lambda I_n\) is positive definite for \(\lambda>0\), the solution is

\[
\hat c=A^{-1}(y-Z\hat b).
\]

Imposing \(Z^T\hat c=0\),

\[
Z^TA^{-1}(y-Z\hat b)=0,
\]
so

\[
Z^TA^{-1}Z\hat b=Z^TA^{-1}y.
\]

Therefore

\[
\boxed{
\hat b
=
(Z^TA^{-1}Z)^{-1}Z^TA^{-1}y.
}
\]

Then

\[
\boxed{
\hat c
=
A^{-1}(y-Z\hat b).
}
\]

Equivalently,

\[
\boxed{
\hat c
=
\left[
A^{-1}
-
A^{-1}Z(Z^TA^{-1}Z)^{-1}Z^TA^{-1}
\right]y.
}
\]

---

# 3. Linear smoother matrix \(S\)

Define

\[
M=Z^TA^{-1}Z,
\]
and

\[
H_A=Z M^{-1}Z^TA^{-1}.
\]

Then

\[
\hat b=M^{-1}Z^TA^{-1}y,
\]
so

\[
Z\hat b=H_Ay.
\]

Also

\[
\hat c=A^{-1}(I-H_A)y.
\]

Therefore the fitted values at the training points are

\[
\hat m
=
Z\hat b+K\hat c
=
H_Ay+KA^{-1}(I-H_A)y.
\]

Thus

\[
\boxed{
\hat m=Sy,
}
\]
where

\[
\boxed{
S
=
H_A+KA^{-1}(I-H_A).
}
\]

Using \(K=A-n\lambda I_n\), this can also be written as

\[
\boxed{
S
=
I_n-n\lambda A^{-1}(I-H_A).
}
\]

The matrix \(S\) depends on \(X_1,\dots,X_n\), \(\sigma\), and \(\lambda\), but not on \(y\). Hence \(\hat m\) is a linear smoother.

The effective degrees of freedom are

\[
\boxed{
\operatorname{df}(\lambda,\sigma)=\operatorname{tr}(S).
}
\]

If one wants only the RKHS component \(h\), its fitted vector is

\[
\hat h=K\hat c
=
KA^{-1}(I-H_A)y.
\]

---

# 4. R implementation

```r
partial_rkhs_fit <- function(x, y, sigma, lambda, xnew = NULL, return.S = TRUE) {
  x <- as.numeric(x)
  y <- as.numeric(y)
  n <- length(y)

  if (length(x) != n) stop("x and y must have the same length.")
  if (sigma <= 0 || lambda <= 0) stop("sigma and lambda must be positive.")

  Z <- cbind(1, x)

  K <- exp(-(outer(x, x, "-")^2) / (2 * sigma^2))
  A <- K + n * lambda * diag(n)

  Ainv <- solve(A)

  AinvZ <- Ainv %*% Z
  M <- t(Z) %*% AinvZ

  bhat <- solve(M, t(Z) %*% Ainv %*% y)
  chat <- Ainv %*% (y - Z %*% bhat)

  fitted <- as.vector(Z %*% bhat + K %*% chat)

  out <- list(
    x = x,
    y = y,
    sigma = sigma,
    lambda = lambda,
    b = as.vector(bhat),
    c = as.vector(chat),
    fitted = fitted
  )

  predict_fun <- function(x0) {
    x0 <- as.numeric(x0)
    Z0 <- cbind(1, x0)
    K0 <- exp(-(outer(x0, x, "-")^2) / (2 * sigma^2))
    as.vector(Z0 %*% bhat + K0 %*% chat)
  }

  out$predict <- predict_fun

  if (!is.null(xnew)) {
    out$xnew <- xnew
    out$pred.xnew <- predict_fun(xnew)
  }

  if (return.S) {
    H_A <- Z %*% solve(M, t(Z) %*% Ainv)
    S <- diag(n) - n * lambda * Ainv %*% (diag(n) - H_A)

    out$S <- S
    out$df <- sum(diag(S))
  }

  return(out)
}
```

A helper function to choose \(\lambda\) to hit a desired degrees of freedom:

```r
find_lambda_for_df <- function(x, sigma, target.df, tol = 1e-7) {
  x <- as.numeric(x)
  n <- length(x)
  y0 <- rep(0, n)

  df_minus_target <- function(loglambda) {
    lambda <- exp(loglambda)
    fit <- partial_rkhs_fit(x, y0, sigma, lambda, return.S = TRUE)
    fit$df - target.df
  }

  lo <- -30
  hi <- 30

  flo <- df_minus_target(lo)
  fhi <- df_minus_target(hi)

  while (flo < 0) {
    lo <- lo - 5
    flo <- df_minus_target(lo)
  }

  while (fhi > 0) {
    hi <- hi + 5
    fhi <- df_minus_target(hi)
  }

  if (flo * fhi > 0) {
    stop("Could not bracket lambda for the requested degrees of freedom.")
  }

  loglambda.hat <- uniroot(df_minus_target, interval = c(lo, hi), tol = tol)$root
  exp(loglambda.hat)
}
```

response.text:
## Notation

Write the penalized RKHS component as \(g\in\mathcal H_\sigma\), and write the full fitted regression function as  
\[
m(x)=b_0+b_1x+g(x).
\]
The problem’s \(\hat f\) in later parts is therefore the full fitted function \(\hat m\).

Let

\[
Y=(Y_1,\dots,Y_n)^T,\qquad 
Z=\begin{pmatrix}
1&X_1\\
\vdots&\vdots\\
1&X_n
\end{pmatrix},
\qquad 
b=(b_0,b_1)^T,
\]
and let \(K\) be the Gaussian kernel Gram matrix
\[
K_{ij}=K_\sigma(X_i,X_j)=\exp\left\{-\frac{(X_i-X_j)^2}{2\sigma^2}\right\}.
\]
Also define
\[
\eta=n\lambda,\qquad A=K+\eta I_n.
\]

Assume \(Z\) has full column rank, i.e. the \(X_i\)’s are not all identical. If not, one should drop the redundant column or use a generalized inverse.

---

# 1) Representer form

For fixed \(b_0,b_1\), minimize over \(g\in\mathcal H_\sigma\)
\[
\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\{Y_i-b_0-b_1X_i-g(X_i)\}^2+\lambda\|g\|_{\mathcal H_\sigma}^2.
\]

Let
\[
\mathcal H_n=\operatorname{span}\{K_\sigma(X_i,\cdot):i=1,\dots,n\}.
\]
For any \(g\in\mathcal H_\sigma\), decompose orthogonally as
\[
g=g_\parallel+g_\perp,
\qquad 
g_\parallel\in\mathcal H_n,\quad g_\perp\perp\mathcal H_n.
\]
By the reproducing property,
\[
g_\perp(X_i)=\langle g_\perp,K_\sigma(X_i,\cdot)\rangle_{\mathcal H_\sigma}=0.
\]
Therefore the residual sum of squares depends only on \(g_\parallel\), while
\[
\|g\|_{\mathcal H_\sigma}^2
=
\|g_\parallel\|_{\mathcal H_\sigma}^2+\|g_\perp\|_{\mathcal H_\sigma}^2
\ge \|g_\parallel\|_{\mathcal H_\sigma}^2.
\]
Since \(\lambda>0\), any minimizer must have \(g_\perp=0\). Hence the penalized component has the representer form
\[
\hat g(x)=\sum_{i=1}^n c_i K_\sigma(X_i,x).
\]

Thus the full fitted function can be written as
\[
\boxed{
\hat m(x)=\hat b_0+\hat b_1x+\sum_{i=1}^n \hat c_i K_\sigma(X_i,x)
}
\]
with coefficients independent of the evaluation point \(x\).

This is the representer theorem applied with an unpenalized linear part.

---

# 2) Penalty and closed form for \((\hat b,\hat c)\)

If
\[
g(x)=\sum_{i=1}^n c_iK_\sigma(X_i,x),
\]
then by the reproducing property,
\[
\|g\|_{\mathcal H_\sigma}^2
=
\sum_{i,j=1}^n c_ic_jK_\sigma(X_i,X_j)
=
c^TKc.
\]
Therefore the finite-dimensional criterion is
\[
Q(b,c)
=
\frac1n\|Y-Zb-Kc\|_2^2+\lambda c^TKc.
\]
Equivalently, multiplying by \(n\),
\[
\|Y-Zb-Kc\|_2^2+\eta c^TKc,
\qquad \eta=n\lambda.
\]

Let
\[
r=Y-Zb-Kc.
\]
The first-order condition with respect to the RKHS component gives
\[
\hat g=\frac1{n\lambda}\sum_{i=1}^n r_iK_\sigma(X_i,\cdot).
\]
Thus we may take
\[
c=\frac{r}{n\lambda}=\frac r\eta,
\]
so that
\[
r=\eta c.
\]
Since
\[
r=Y-Zb-Kc,
\]
we get
\[
Y-Zb-Kc=\eta c,
\]
or
\[
(K+\eta I)c+Zb=Y.
\]
The first-order condition with respect to \(b\) gives
\[
Z^Tr=0.
\]
Since \(r=\eta c\), this is equivalent to
\[
Z^Tc=0.
\]

Therefore \((\hat c,\hat b)\) solves the block system
\[
\boxed{
\begin{pmatrix}
K+\eta I & Z\\
Z^T & 0
\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}
\hat c\\
\hat b
\end{pmatrix}
=
\begin{pmatrix}
Y\\
0
\end{pmatrix}.
}
\]

Let
\[
A=K+\eta I,\qquad G=Z^TA^{-1}Z.
\]
Since \(A\succ0\) and \(Z\) has full column rank, \(G\succ0\). From
\[
A\hat c+Z\hat b=Y,
\]
we have
\[
\hat c=A^{-1}(Y-Z\hat b).
\]
Using \(Z^T\hat c=0\),
\[
Z^TA^{-1}(Y-Z\hat b)=0.
\]
Hence
\[
G\hat b=Z^TA^{-1}Y.
\]
Thus
\[
\boxed{
\hat b=(Z^TA^{-1}Z)^{-1}Z^TA^{-1}Y.
}
\]
Then
\[
\boxed{
\hat c=A^{-1}(Y-Z\hat b).
}
\]

Equivalently, defining
\[
P_A=Z(Z^TA^{-1}Z)^{-1}Z^TA^{-1},
\]
we have
\[
\boxed{
\hat c=A^{-1}(I-P_A)Y.
}
\]

---

# 3) Linear smoother matrix \(S\)

The fitted values at the observed covariates are
\[
\hat{\mathbf f}
=
\begin{pmatrix}
\hat m(X_1)\\
\vdots\\
\hat m(X_n)
\end{pmatrix}
=
Z\hat b+K\hat c.
\]

Using the formulas above,
\[
Z\hat b=P_AY,
\]
and
\[
\hat c=A^{-1}(I-P_A)Y.
\]
Therefore
\[
\hat{\mathbf f}
=
P_AY+KA^{-1}(I-P_A)Y.
\]
Thus
\[
\boxed{
\hat{\mathbf f}=SY
}
\]
where
\[
\boxed{
S=P_A+KA^{-1}(I-P_A).
}
\]
Equivalently, since \(K=A-\eta I\),
\[
KA^{-1}=I-\eta A^{-1},
\]
so
\[
\boxed{
S=I-\eta A^{-1}(I-P_A).
}
\]

The matrix \(S\) depends on \(X_1,\dots,X_n\), \(\sigma\), and \(\lambda\), but not on \(Y\). Hence this is a linear smoother.

The effective degrees of freedom are
\[
\boxed{
\operatorname{df}=\operatorname{tr}(S).
}
\]

---

# 4) R implementation

```r
partial.rkhs <- function(x, y, sigma, lambda, xnew = NULL, return.S = TRUE) {
  stopifnot(sigma > 0, lambda > 0)
  
  x <- as.numeric(x)
  y <- as.numeric(y)
  keep <- is.finite(x) & is.finite(y)
  x <- x[keep]
  y <- y[keep]
  
  n <- length(y)
  Z <- cbind(1, x)
  colnames(Z) <- c("(Intercept)", "x")
  
  if (qr(Z)$rank < 2) {
    stop("Design matrix [1, x] is not full rank.")
  }
  
  # Kernel matrix
  D <- outer(x, x, "-")
  K <- exp(-(D^2) / (2 * sigma^2))
  
  eta <- n * lambda
  A <- K + eta * diag(n)
  
  # Inverses/solves
  Ainv <- solve(A, diag(n))
  AinvZ <- Ainv %*% Z
  Ainvy <- Ainv %*% y
  
  G <- crossprod(Z, AinvZ)  # Z^T A^{-1} Z
  
  b <- drop(solve(G, crossprod(Z, Ainvy)))
  names(b) <- c("b0", "b1")
  
  ccoef <- drop(Ainvy - AinvZ %*% b)
  
  fitted <- drop(Z %*% b + K %*% ccoef)
  
  # Smoother matrix
  # P_A = Z (Z^T A^{-1} Z)^{-1} Z^T A^{-1}
  P <- Z %*% solve(G, t(AinvZ))
  Sfull <- P + K %*% Ainv %*% (diag(n) - P)
  df <- sum(diag(Sfull))
  
  # Prediction at new x-values
  pred <- NULL
  if (!is.null(xnew)) {
    xnew <- as.numeric(xnew)
    Znew <- cbind(1, xnew)
    Dnew <- outer(xnew, x, "-")
    Knew <- exp(-(Dnew^2) / (2 * sigma^2))
    pred <- drop(Znew %*% b + Knew %*% ccoef)
  }
  
  list(
    b = b,
    c = ccoef,
    fitted = fitted,
    pred = pred,
    df = df,
    S = if (return.S) Sfull else NULL,
    x = x,
    y = y,
    sigma = sigma,
    lambda = lambda
  )
}
```

A helper to choose \(\lambda\) for a target degrees of freedom:

lambda.for.df <- function(x, y, sigma, target.df, lo = -30, hi = 30) {
  f <- function(loglam) {
    fit <- partial.rkhs(
      x = x,
      y = y,
      sigma = sigma,
      lambda = exp(loglam),
      return.S = FALSE
    )
    fit$df - target.df
  }
  
  flo <- f(lo)
  fhi <- f(hi)
  
  iter <- 0
  while (flo < 0 && iter < 50) {
    lo <- lo - 5
    flo <- f(lo)
    iter <- iter + 1
  }
  
  iter <- 0
  while (fhi > 0 && iter < 50) {
    hi <- hi + 5
    fhi <- f(hi)
    iter <- iter + 1
  }
  
  if (flo * fhi > 0) {
    stop("Target df not bracketed. It may be unattainable.")
  }
  
  exp(uniroot(f, c(lo, hi), tol = 1e-7)$root)
}
```
