## Notation

Write the penalized RKHS component as \(g\in\mathcal H_\sigma\), and write the full fitted regression function as  
\[
m(x)=b_0+b_1x+g(x).
\]
The problem’s \(\hat f\) in later parts is therefore the full fitted function \(\hat m\).

Let

\[
Y=(Y_1,\dots,Y_n)^T,\qquad 
Z=\begin{pmatrix}
1&X_1\\
\vdots&\vdots\\
1&X_n
\end{pmatrix},
\qquad 
b=(b_0,b_1)^T,
\]
and let \(K\) be the Gaussian kernel Gram matrix
\[
K_{ij}=K_\sigma(X_i,X_j)=\exp\left\{-\frac{(X_i-X_j)^2}{2\sigma^2}\right\}.
\]
Also define
\[
\eta=n\lambda,\qquad A=K+\eta I_n.
\]

Assume \(Z\) has full column rank, i.e. the \(X_i\)’s are not all identical. If not, one should drop the redundant column or use a generalized inverse.

---

# 1) Representer form

For fixed \(b_0,b_1\), minimize over \(g\in\mathcal H_\sigma\)
\[
\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\{Y_i-b_0-b_1X_i-g(X_i)\}^2+\lambda\|g\|_{\mathcal H_\sigma}^2.
\]

Let
\[
\mathcal H_n=\operatorname{span}\{K_\sigma(X_i,\cdot):i=1,\dots,n\}.
\]
For any \(g\in\mathcal H_\sigma\), decompose orthogonally as
\[
g=g_\parallel+g_\perp,
\qquad 
g_\parallel\in\mathcal H_n,\quad g_\perp\perp\mathcal H_n.
\]
By the reproducing property,
\[
g_\perp(X_i)=\langle g_\perp,K_\sigma(X_i,\cdot)\rangle_{\mathcal H_\sigma}=0.
\]
Therefore the residual sum of squares depends only on \(g_\parallel\), while
\[
\|g\|_{\mathcal H_\sigma}^2
=
\|g_\parallel\|_{\mathcal H_\sigma}^2+\|g_\perp\|_{\mathcal H_\sigma}^2
\ge \|g_\parallel\|_{\mathcal H_\sigma}^2.
\]
Since \(\lambda>0\), any minimizer must have \(g_\perp=0\). Hence the penalized component has the representer form
\[
\hat g(x)=\sum_{i=1}^n c_i K_\sigma(X_i,x).
\]

Thus the full fitted function can be written as
\[
\boxed{
\hat m(x)=\hat b_0+\hat b_1x+\sum_{i=1}^n \hat c_i K_\sigma(X_i,x)
}
\]
with coefficients independent of the evaluation point \(x\).

This is the representer theorem applied with an unpenalized linear part.

---

# 2) Penalty and closed form for \((\hat b,\hat c)\)

If
\[
g(x)=\sum_{i=1}^n c_iK_\sigma(X_i,x),
\]
then by the reproducing property,
\[
\|g\|_{\mathcal H_\sigma}^2
=
\sum_{i,j=1}^n c_ic_jK_\sigma(X_i,X_j)
=
c^TKc.
\]
Therefore the finite-dimensional criterion is
\[
Q(b,c)
=
\frac1n\|Y-Zb-Kc\|_2^2+\lambda c^TKc.
\]
Equivalently, multiplying by \(n\),
\[
\|Y-Zb-Kc\|_2^2+\eta c^TKc,
\qquad \eta=n\lambda.
\]

Let
\[
r=Y-Zb-Kc.
\]
The first-order condition with respect to the RKHS component gives
\[
\hat g=\frac1{n\lambda}\sum_{i=1}^n r_iK_\sigma(X_i,\cdot).
\]
Thus we may take
\[
c=\frac{r}{n\lambda}=\frac r\eta,
\]
so that
\[
r=\eta c.
\]
Since
\[
r=Y-Zb-Kc,
\]
we get
\[
Y-Zb-Kc=\eta c,
\]
or
\[
(K+\eta I)c+Zb=Y.
\]
The first-order condition with respect to \(b\) gives
\[
Z^Tr=0.
\]
Since \(r=\eta c\), this is equivalent to
\[
Z^Tc=0.
\]

Therefore \((\hat c,\hat b)\) solves the block system
\[
\boxed{
\begin{pmatrix}
K+\eta I & Z\\
Z^T & 0
\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}
\hat c\\
\hat b
\end{pmatrix}
=
\begin{pmatrix}
Y\\
0
\end{pmatrix}.
}
\]

Let
\[
A=K+\eta I,\qquad G=Z^TA^{-1}Z.
\]
Since \(A\succ0\) and \(Z\) has full column rank, \(G\succ0\). From
\[
A\hat c+Z\hat b=Y,
\]
we have
\[
\hat c=A^{-1}(Y-Z\hat b).
\]
Using \(Z^T\hat c=0\),
\[
Z^TA^{-1}(Y-Z\hat b)=0.
\]
Hence
\[
G\hat b=Z^TA^{-1}Y.
\]
Thus
\[
\boxed{
\hat b=(Z^TA^{-1}Z)^{-1}Z^TA^{-1}Y.
}
\]
Then
\[
\boxed{
\hat c=A^{-1}(Y-Z\hat b).
}
\]

Equivalently, defining
\[
P_A=Z(Z^TA^{-1}Z)^{-1}Z^TA^{-1},
\]
we have
\[
\boxed{
\hat c=A^{-1}(I-P_A)Y.
}
\]

---

# 3) Linear smoother matrix \(S\)

The fitted values at the observed covariates are
\[
\hat{\mathbf f}
=
\begin{pmatrix}
\hat m(X_1)\\
\vdots\\
\hat m(X_n)
\end{pmatrix}
=
Z\hat b+K\hat c.
\]

Using the formulas above,
\[
Z\hat b=P_AY,
\]
and
\[
\hat c=A^{-1}(I-P_A)Y.
\]
Therefore
\[
\hat{\mathbf f}
=
P_AY+KA^{-1}(I-P_A)Y.
\]
Thus
\[
\boxed{
\hat{\mathbf f}=SY
}
\]
where
\[
\boxed{
S=P_A+KA^{-1}(I-P_A).
}
\]
Equivalently, since \(K=A-\eta I\),
\[
KA^{-1}=I-\eta A^{-1},
\]
so
\[
\boxed{
S=I-\eta A^{-1}(I-P_A).
}
\]

The matrix \(S\) depends on \(X_1,\dots,X_n\), \(\sigma\), and \(\lambda\), but not on \(Y\). Hence this is a linear smoother.

The effective degrees of freedom are
\[
\boxed{
\operatorname{df}=\operatorname{tr}(S).
}
\]

---

# 4) R implementation

```r
partial.rkhs <- function(x, y, sigma, lambda, xnew = NULL, return.S = TRUE) {
  stopifnot(sigma > 0, lambda > 0)
  
  x <- as.numeric(x)
  y <- as.numeric(y)
  keep <- is.finite(x) & is.finite(y)
  x <- x[keep]
  y <- y[keep]
  
  n <- length(y)
  Z <- cbind(1, x)
  colnames(Z) <- c("(Intercept)", "x")
  
  if (qr(Z)$rank < 2) {
    stop("Design matrix [1, x] is not full rank.")
  }
  
  # Kernel matrix
  D <- outer(x, x, "-")
  K <- exp(-(D^2) / (2 * sigma^2))
  
  eta <- n * lambda
  A <- K + eta * diag(n)
  
  # Inverses/solves
  Ainv <- solve(A, diag(n))
  AinvZ <- Ainv %*% Z
  Ainvy <- Ainv %*% y
  
  G <- crossprod(Z, AinvZ)  # Z^T A^{-1} Z
  
  b <- drop(solve(G, crossprod(Z, Ainvy)))
  names(b) <- c("b0", "b1")
  
  ccoef <- drop(Ainvy - AinvZ %*% b)
  
  fitted <- drop(Z %*% b + K %*% ccoef)
  
  # Smoother matrix
  # P_A = Z (Z^T A^{-1} Z)^{-1} Z^T A^{-1}
  P <- Z %*% solve(G, t(AinvZ))
  Sfull <- P + K %*% Ainv %*% (diag(n) - P)
  df <- sum(diag(Sfull))
  
  # Prediction at new x-values
  pred <- NULL
  if (!is.null(xnew)) {
    xnew <- as.numeric(xnew)
    Znew <- cbind(1, xnew)
    Dnew <- outer(xnew, x, "-")
    Knew <- exp(-(Dnew^2) / (2 * sigma^2))
    pred <- drop(Znew %*% b + Knew %*% ccoef)
  }
  
  list(
    b = b,
    c = ccoef,
    fitted = fitted,
    pred = pred,
    df = df,
    S = if (return.S) Sfull else NULL,
    x = x,
    y = y,
    sigma = sigma,
    lambda = lambda
  )
}
```

A helper to choose \(\lambda\) for a target degrees of freedom:

```r
lambda.for.df <- function(x, y, sigma, target.df, lo = -30, hi = 30) {
  f <- function(loglam) {
    fit <- partial.rkhs(
      x = x,
      y = y,
      sigma = sigma,
      lambda = exp(loglam),
      return.S = FALSE
    )
    fit$df - target.df
  }
  
  flo <- f(lo)
  fhi <- f(hi)
  
  iter <- 0
  while (flo < 0 && iter < 50) {
    lo <- lo - 5
    flo <- f(lo)
    iter <- iter + 1
  }
  
  iter <- 0
  while (fhi > 0 && iter < 50) {
    hi <- hi + 5
    fhi <- f(hi)
    iter <- iter + 1
  }
  
  if (flo * fhi > 0) {
    stop("Target df not bracketed. It may be unattainable.")
  }
  
  exp(uniroot(f, c(lo, hi), tol = 1e-7)$root)
}
```

## (1) Simulation design: three true groups, \(p=10\), and varying \(K\)

A clean simulation should have a known true clustering, some informative variables, and some noise variables. I would use balanced Gaussian clusters with only the first two variables informative.

Let

\[
n=180,\qquad n_1=n_2=n_3=60,\qquad p=10.
\]

Generate true labels \(Z_i\in\{1,2,3\}\) with exactly 60 observations per group, and generate

\[
X_i\mid Z_i=k \sim N_p(\mu_k,I_p),
\]

where

\[
\mu_1=(2.5,0,0,\ldots,0),
\]

\[
\mu_2=\left(-1.25,\frac{2.5\sqrt 3}{2},0,\ldots,0\right),
\]

\[
\mu_3=\left(-1.25,-\frac{2.5\sqrt 3}{2},0,\ldots,0\right).
\]

Thus the three true centers form an equilateral triangle in the first two coordinates, and variables \(3,\ldots,10\) are pure noise.

Before applying any clustering method, standardize each variable to sample mean zero and sample variance one. This is essential because both \(k\)-means and the penalized methods are scale-sensitive.

For ordinary \(k\)-means, run the algorithm for

\[
K=1,2,3,4,5,6
\]

with many random starts, for example 50 starts, and record:

1. within-cluster sum of squares,
2. adjusted Rand index, ARI, comparing estimated clusters to true labels,
3. possibly the silhouette score or gap statistic.

A typical qualitative outcome is:

| Fitted \(K\) | Behavior | ARI behavior |
|---|---|---|
| \(K=1\) | all observations in one cluster | ARI \(=0\) |
| \(K=2\) | two true groups are merged | ARI around \(0.55\)–\(0.60\) |
| \(K=3\) | recovers the three true groups | ARI close to \(1\) |
| \(K=4\) | one true group is split | ARI decreases |
| \(K=5,6\) | more true groups are split | ARI decreases further |

For example, in the ideal perfectly separated case, if \(K=2\) merges two true groups, the ARI is approximately \(0.57\). If \(K=4\) splits one true group into two equal pieces, the ARI is approximately \(0.87\). Thus ARI is maximized at the true value \(K=3\), while the within-cluster sum of squares decreases monotonically with \(K\), so one looks for an elbow near \(K=3\).

A reproducible simulation skeleton is:

```r
set.seed(2025)

n.per <- 60
K.true <- 3
p <- 10
n <- K.true * n.per

mu <- matrix(0, nrow = 3, ncol = p)
mu[1,1:2] <- c(2.5, 0)
mu[2,1:2] <- c(-1.25,  2.5 * sqrt(3)/2)
mu[3,1:2] <- c(-1.25, -2.5 * sqrt(3)/2)

z <- rep(1:3, each = n.per)

X <- matrix(0, nrow = n, ncol = p)
for (i in 1:n) {
  X[i,] <- mu[z[i],] + rnorm(p)
}

X <- scale(X)

for (K in 1:6) {
  fit <- kmeans(X, centers = K, nstart = 50)
  # compute WSS, ARI, silhouette, etc.
}
```

---

## (2) Identity using the assignment matrix \(L\)

Let \(X\in \mathbb R^{n\times p}\) be the data matrix, with rows \(X_i^\top\). Let \(C\in \mathbb R^{K\times p}\) be the matrix of cluster centers, with rows \(C_k^\top\). Define the assignment matrix

\[
L_{ik}=\mathbf 1(X_i\in A_k).
\]

Thus each row of \(L\) contains exactly one 1.

For coordinate \(j\), let

\[
X^{(j)}=(X_{1j},\ldots,X_{nj})^\top\in\mathbb R^n,
\]

and

\[
C^{(j)}=(C_{1j},\ldots,C_{Kj})^\top\in\mathbb R^K.
\]

Then

\[
(LC^{(j)})_i
=
\sum_{k=1}^K L_{ik}C_{kj}.
\]

If \(X_i\in A_k\), then \(L_{ik}=1\), and hence

\[
(LC^{(j)})_i=C_{kj}.
\]

Therefore,

\[
X_{ij}-(LC^{(j)})_i
=
X_{ij}-C_{kj}
\qquad\text{whenever }X_i\in A_k.
\]

Now

\[
\sum_{k=1}^K\sum_{X_i\in A_k}\|X_i-C_k\|^2
=
\sum_{k=1}^K\sum_{X_i\in A_k}\sum_{j=1}^p (X_{ij}-C_{kj})^2.
\]

Interchanging the order of summation gives

\[
=
\sum_{j=1}^p
\sum_{k=1}^K\sum_{X_i\in A_k}
(X_{ij}-C_{kj})^2.
\]

But the inner sum is exactly

\[
\sum_{i=1}^n
\left(X_{ij}-(LC^{(j)})_i\right)^2
=
(X^{(j)}-LC^{(j)})^\top (X^{(j)}-LC^{(j)}).
\]

Hence

\[
\sum_{k=1}^K\sum_{X_i\in A_k}\|X_i-C_k\|^2
=
\sum_{j=1}^p
(X^{(j)}-LC^{(j)})^\top (X^{(j)}-LC^{(j)}).
\]

Therefore, with the \(1/n\) scaling included consistently,

\[
\frac1n\sum_{k=1}^K\sum_{X_i\in A_k}\|X_i-C_k\|^2
+
\lambda\sum_{j=1}^p \|C^{(j)}\|
\]

equals

\[
\sum_{j=1}^p
\left\{
\frac1n
(X^{(j)}-LC^{(j)})^\top (X^{(j)}-LC^{(j)})
+
\lambda \|C^{(j)}\|
\right\}.
\]

As written without the \(1/n\) on the left-hand squared-error term, the displayed identity would be off by a factor of \(n\). The correct identity is the one above.

---

## (3) Sparse \(k\)-means algorithm and analysis of the simulated data

The penalized objective is

\[
F(L,C)
=
\frac1n\sum_{k=1}^K\sum_{X_i\in A_k}\|X_i-C_k\|^2
+
\lambda\sum_{j=1}^p \|C^{(j)}\|_2.
\]

Using part (2),

\[
F(L,C)
=
\sum_{j=1}^p
\left\{
\frac1n\|X^{(j)}-LC^{(j)}\|_2^2
+
\lambda \|C^{(j)}\|_2
\right\}.
\]

Thus, for fixed assignments \(L\), the center update separates across variables \(j\). This is a group-lasso-type update, because the entire vector

\[
C^{(j)}=(C_{1j},\ldots,C_{Kj})^\top
\]

is either shrunk toward zero or set exactly to zero.

### Fixed \(L\): update for \(C^{(j)}\)

Fix \(L\), and define

\[
D=L^\top L=\operatorname{diag}(n_1,\ldots,n_K),
\]

where \(n_k\) is the number of observations assigned to cluster \(k\). Also define

\[
s_j=L^\top X^{(j)}\in\mathbb R^K.
\]

Then for coordinate \(j\), we minimize

\[
Q_j(c)
=
\frac1n \|X^{(j)}-Lc\|_2^2+\lambda\|c\|_2.
\]

Expanding,

\[
Q_j(c)
=
\frac1n
\left[
(X^{(j)})^\top X^{(j)}
-2s_j^\top c
+
c^\top D c
\right]
+
\lambda\|c\|_2.
\]

The constant term can be ignored. The KKT condition is

\[
0\in \frac{2}{n}(Dc-s_j)+\lambda \partial \|c\|_2.
\]

At \(c=0\), the subdifferential is

\[
\partial \|c\|_2\big|_{c=0}
=
\{u:\|u\|_2\le 1\}.
\]

Thus \(c=0\) is optimal if and only if

\[
\left\|\frac{2}{n}s_j\right\|_2\le \lambda.
\]

If

\[
\left\|\frac{2}{n}s_j\right\|_2>\lambda,
\]

then the solution is nonzero and satisfies

\[
\frac{2}{n}(Dc-s_j)+\lambda \frac{c}{\|c\|_2}=0.
\]

Equivalently,

\[
\left(D+\alpha I_K\right)c=s_j,
\]

where

\[
\alpha=\frac{n\lambda}{2\|c\|_2}.
\]

Therefore

\[
c=(D+\alpha I_K)^{-1}s_j,
\]

with \(\alpha>0\) chosen to satisfy

\[
\alpha
=
\frac{n\lambda}{2\|(D+\alpha I_K)^{-1}s_j\|_2}.
\]

This one-dimensional equation can be solved by bisection or Newton's method.

When the clusters are balanced so that \(n_1=\cdots=n_K=m\), this reduces to the ordinary group soft-thresholding formula

\[
C^{(j)}
=
\left(
1-\frac{n\lambda}{2\|s_j\|_2}
\right)_+
D^{-1}s_j.
\]

### Fixed \(C\): update for \(L\)

Given \(C\), the penalty term is fixed, so each observation is assigned to the nearest penalized center:

\[
\widehat z_i
=
\arg\min_{1\le k\le K}\|X_i-C_k\|_2^2.
\]

Thus

\[
L_{ik}=1(\widehat z_i=k).
\]

### Sparse \(k\)-means pseudocode

Use \(K=3\), since the true number of clusters is 3, and pre-specify

\[
\lambda=0.30.
\]

The value \(\lambda=0.30\) is chosen before seeing the data. For the present standardized simulation it is large enough to eliminate most noise variables but small enough to retain the first two variables.

```
Input: standardized data X, number of clusters K=3, penalty λ=0.30

For r = 1,...,R random starts:
    Initialize L using ordinary k-means with K=3.

    Repeat until convergence:
        1. Center update:
           For each variable j=1,...,p:
               Compute s_j = L^T X^(j).
               If ||(2/n) s_j||_2 <= λ:
                   Set C^(j) = 0.
               Else:
                   Find α > 0 solving
                       α = nλ / {2 ||(D+αI)^(-1)s_j||_2}
                   Set C^(j) = (D+αI)^(-1)s_j.

        2. Assignment update:
           For each observation i:
               assign i to the cluster k minimizing ||X_i - C_k||_2^2.

        3. Compute objective F(L,C).

    Store final solution.

Return the run with smallest objective.
```

Each block update decreases the objective. Because the objective is nonconvex in \((L,C)\) jointly, multiple random starts are important.

### Analysis of the simulated data

For the simulated data in part (1), using \(K=3\) and \(\lambda=0.30\), the sparse \(k\)-means algorithm typically selects exactly the first two variables:

\[
\widehat S
=
\{j:\|\widehat C^{(j)}\|_2>0\}
=
\{1,2\}.
\]

Variables \(3,\ldots,10\) have

\[
\widehat C^{(j)}=0,
\qquad j=3,\ldots,10.
\]

Thus they do not contribute to the distance calculation after shrinkage.

After matching labels to the true labels, the estimated centers in the first two coordinates are shrunk versions of the ordinary \(k\)-means centers. Approximately, after standardization, the true centers are proportional to

\[
(1.23,0),\qquad (-0.62,1.07),\qquad (-0.62,-1.07),
\]

and the sparse \(k\)-means centers are smaller in norm because of the group penalty. The assignments, however, are essentially unchanged because the irrelevant coordinates are removed.

A representative summary is:

| Method | \(K\) | Selected variables | ARI |
|---|---:|---|---:|
| ordinary \(k\)-means | 3 | all 10 used | close to \(1\) |
| sparse \(k\)-means, \(\lambda=0.30\) | 3 | \(\{1,2\}\) | close to \(1\) |

The main gain of sparse \(k\)-means here is interpretability and robustness to the eight irrelevant variables.

---

## (4) Penalized Gaussian mixture model and EM algorithm

Now consider the Gaussian mixture model

\[
f(x)
=
\sum_{k=1}^K \pi_k f_k(x;\theta_k),
\]

with

\[
\pi_k>0,\qquad \sum_{k=1}^K\pi_k=1.
\]

For comparability with the \(k\)-means methods, take

\[
f_k(x;\theta_k)
=
\phi_p(x;C_k,\Sigma),
\]

where \(C_k\in\mathbb R^p\) is the mean of component \(k\), and \(\Sigma\) is a common diagonal covariance matrix,

\[
\Sigma=\operatorname{diag}(\sigma_1^2,\ldots,\sigma_p^2).
\]

The penalty is

\[
n\lambda\sum_{j=1}^p
\frac{\|C^{(j)}\|_2}{\|\widetilde C^{(j)}\|_2},
\]

where \(\widetilde C^{(j)}\) is an initial unpenalized estimator, for example from an ordinary Gaussian mixture or ordinary \(k\)-means. Define adaptive weights

\[
w_j=\frac{1}{\|\widetilde C^{(j)}\|_2+\varepsilon},
\]

with a small \(\varepsilon>0\) to avoid division by zero.

The penalized observed log-likelihood is

\[
\ell_p(\Theta)
=
\sum_{i=1}^n
\log\left[
\sum_{k=1}^K
\pi_k
\phi_p(X_i;C_k,\Sigma)
\right]
-
n\lambda
\sum_{j=1}^p
w_j\|C^{(j)}\|_2.
\]

Here

\[
\Theta=(\pi_1,\ldots,\pi_K,C_1,\ldots,C_K,\Sigma).
\]

Let latent indicators

\[
L_{ik}=\mathbf 1(Z_i=k).
\]

The complete-data penalized log-likelihood, up to constants, is

\[
\ell_{c,p}(\Theta)
=
\sum_{i=1}^n\sum_{k=1}^K
L_{ik}
\left[
\log\pi_k
-\frac12\log|\Sigma|
-\frac12(X_i-C_k)^\top\Sigma^{-1}(X_i-C_k)
\right]
-
n\lambda\sum_{j=1}^p w_j\|C^{(j)}\|_2.
\]

---

### E-step

Given current parameter estimates \(\Theta^{(t)}\), compute the posterior responsibilities

\[
\tau_{ik}^{(t)}
=
\mathbb E[L_{ik}\mid X_i,\Theta^{(t)}].
\]

Thus

\[
\tau_{ik}^{(t)}
=
\frac{
\pi_k^{(t)}
\phi_p(X_i;C_k^{(t)},\Sigma^{(t)})
}{
\sum_{\ell=1}^K
\pi_\ell^{(t)}
\phi_p(X_i;C_\ell^{(t)},\Sigma^{(t)})
}.
\]

These are soft cluster assignments.

Define

\[
N_k^{(t)}
=
\sum_{i=1}^n \tau_{ik}^{(t)}.
\]

---

### M-step

The \(Q\)-function is

\[
Q_p(\Theta\mid \Theta^{(t)})
=
\sum_{i=1}^n\sum_{k=1}^K
\tau_{ik}^{(t)}
\left[
\log\pi_k
-\frac12\log|\Sigma|
-\frac12(X_i-C_k)^\top\Sigma^{-1}(X_i-C_k)
\right]
-
n\lambda\sum_{j=1}^p w_j\|C^{(j)}\|_2.
\]

#### Update for mixing proportions

Maximize

\[
\sum_{k=1}^K N_k^{(t)}\log\pi_k
\]

subject to \(\sum_k\pi_k=1\). Using Lagrange multipliers,

\[
\pi_k^{(t+1)}
=
\frac{N_k^{(t)}}{n}.
\]

#### Update for the means

For fixed \(\Sigma^{(t)}\), the mean update separates by variables because \(\Sigma\) is diagonal.

For coordinate \(j\), define

\[
s_j^{(t)}
=
\left(
\sum_{i=1}^n \tau_{i1}^{(t)}X_{ij},
\ldots,
\sum_{i=1}^n \tau_{iK}^{(t)}X_{ij}
\right)^\top
\in\mathbb R^K,
\]

and

\[
D^{(t)}
=
\operatorname{diag}(N_1^{(t)},\ldots,N_K^{(t)}).
\]

Also define the soft cluster means

\[
\bar X_{kj}^{(t)}
=
\frac{\sum_{i=1}^n\tau_{ik}^{(t)}X_{ij}}{N_k^{(t)}}.
\]

For coordinate \(j\), we minimize the negative penalized \(Q\)-function contribution

\[
\frac{1}{2\sigma_j^{2(t)}}
\sum_{k=1}^K
\sum_{i=1}^n
\tau_{ik}^{(t)}(X_{ij}-C_{kj})^2
+
n\lambda w_j\|C^{(j)}\|_2.
\]

Equivalently,

\[
\frac{1}{2\sigma_j^{2(t)}}
\sum_{k=1}^K
N_k^{(t)}
(C_{kj}-\bar X_{kj}^{(t)})^2
+
n\lambda w_j\|C^{(j)}\|_2.
\]

Let \(c=C^{(j)}\). The KKT condition is

\[
0
\in
\frac{1}{\sigma_j^{2(t)}}(D^{(t)}c-s_j^{(t)})
+
n\lambda w_j\,\partial\|c\|_2.
\]

Thus

\[
C^{(j),(t+1)}=0
\]

if and only if

\[
\left\|
\frac{s_j^{(t)}}{\sigma_j^{2(t)}}
\right\|_2
\le
n\lambda w_j.
\]

If this condition fails, then the solution is nonzero and satisfies

\[
\frac{1}{\sigma_j^{2(t)}}(D^{(t)}c-s_j^{(t)})
+
n\lambda w_j\frac{c}{\|c\|_2}
=0.
\]

Therefore

\[
\left(D^{(t)}+\alpha I_K\right)c=s_j^{(t)},
\]

where

\[
\alpha
=
\frac{n\lambda w_j\sigma_j^{2(t)}}{\|c\|_2}.
\]

Hence

\[
c=
\left(D^{(t)}+\alpha I_K\right)^{-1}s_j^{(t)},
\]

with \(\alpha>0\) satisfying

\[
\alpha
=
\frac{n\lambda w_j\sigma_j^{2(t)}}
{
\left\|
(D^{(t)}+\alpha I_K)^{-1}s_j^{(t)}
\right\|_2
}.
\]

Again, this is a one-dimensional root-finding problem.

#### Update for variances

After updating the means, update the common diagonal variances by

\[
\sigma_j^{2(t+1)}
=
\frac1n
\sum_{i=1}^n\sum_{k=1}^K
\tau_{ik}^{(t)}
\left(X_{ij}-C_{kj}^{(t+1)}\right)^2.
\]

This gives an EM or generalized EM algorithm. If the mean and variance updates are iterated inside the M-step until convergence, the M-step is exact. If they are performed once, this is an ECM algorithm, which still increases the penalized likelihood at each iteration under the usual regularity conditions.

---

### Penalized mixture EM pseudocode

Use \(K=3\). For the simulation, pre-specify for example

\[
\lambda_{\text{mix}}=0.05.
\]

Because the likelihood and least-squares objectives have different scales, \(\lambda_{\text{mix}}\) need not equal the sparse \(k\)-means penalty.

```
Input: standardized data X, K=3, penalty λ_mix=0.05

1. Initialize:
   - Run ordinary k-means or unpenalized Gaussian mixture.
   - Obtain initial means \tilde C.
   - Set adaptive weights w_j = 1/(||\tilde C^(j)||_2 + ε).

2. Initialize π_k, C_k, and σ_j^2.

Repeat until convergence:

   E-step:
       For each i,k compute
           τ_ik = π_k φ_p(X_i; C_k, Σ) /
                  sum_l π_l φ_p(X_i; C_l, Σ).

   M-step:
       Update
           N_k = sum_i τ_ik,
           π_k = N_k / n.

       For each variable j:
           Compute s_j = (sum_i τ_i1 X_ij, ..., sum_i τ_iK X_ij)^T.
           If ||s_j / σ_j^2||_2 <= n λ_mix w_j:
               Set C^(j) = 0.
           Else:
               Find α > 0 satisfying
                   α = n λ_mix w_j σ_j^2 /
                       ||(D+αI)^(-1)s_j||_2.
               Set
                   C^(j) = (D+αI)^(-1)s_j.

       Update each σ_j^2:
           σ_j^2 = (1/n) sum_i sum_k τ_ik (X_ij - C_kj)^2.

Return π, C, Σ, posterior probabilities τ_ik.
```

---

### Analysis of the simulated data

For the simulated data from part (1), the true model is a Gaussian mixture with three components and only the first two variables informative. Thus the penalized Gaussian mixture model should recover:

\[
\widehat S
=
\{j:\|\widehat C^{(j)}\|_2>0\}
=
\{1,2\}.
\]

The estimated mixing proportions should be close to balanced:

\[
\widehat \pi_1\approx \widehat \pi_2\approx \widehat \pi_3\approx \frac13.
\]

The estimated centers in variables 1 and 2 should be close to the true standardized means, up to label switching and small shrinkage. Variables \(3,\ldots,10\) should have estimated center vectors exactly zero.

A representative summary is:

| Method | Selected variables | ARI | Comments |
|---|---|---:|---|
| Penalized Gaussian mixture EM | \(\{1,2\}\) | close to \(1\) | soft assignments, estimates \(\pi_k\) and variances |

The posterior probabilities

\[
\widehat\tau_{ik}
\]

should be close to 0 or 1 for most observations because the clusters are well separated.

---

## (5) Comparison of ordinary \(k\)-means, sparse \(k\)-means, and penalized Gaussian mixtures

### Ordinary \(k\)-means

Advantages:

1. Simple and fast.
2. Works well when clusters are roughly spherical and similarly sized.
3. In this simulation, with the correct \(K=3\), it recovers the true clusters well.

Disadvantages:

1. Requires \(K\) to be chosen.
2. Uses all variables, including the eight noise variables.
3. Sensitive to scaling.
4. Gives hard assignments only.
5. Does not quantify uncertainty.

In this simulation, ordinary \(k\)-means performs well at \(K=3\), but performance deteriorates for \(K\neq 3\). When \(K=2\), it merges two true groups; when \(K>3\), it splits true groups.

---

### Sparse \(k\)-means

Advantages:

1. Performs clustering and variable selection simultaneously.
2. Correctly identifies variables 1 and 2 as relevant.
3. Removes the influence of noise variables \(3,\ldots,10\).
4. Improves interpretability.

Disadvantages:

1. Still requires \(K\) to be specified.
2. Requires choosing \(\lambda\).
3. The objective is nonconvex, so multiple starts are needed.
4. The centers are biased toward zero because of shrinkage.
5. Requires centering and scaling; otherwise the penalty is not meaningful.

In this simulation, sparse \(k\)-means gives essentially the same clustering accuracy as ordinary \(k\)-means with \(K=3\), but it has the important advantage of selecting the true relevant variables.

---

### Penalized Gaussian mixture model

Advantages:

1. Provides a probabilistic clustering model.
2. Gives soft assignments through posterior probabilities.
3. Estimates mixing proportions and variances.
4. Can be extended to unequal covariance structures.
5. The adaptive group penalty performs variable selection.

Disadvantages:

1. More computationally expensive.
2. More model-dependent than \(k\)-means.
3. The likelihood can have local maxima, so initialization matters.
4. If unrestricted covariance matrices are used, Gaussian mixture likelihoods may be unbounded without constraints.
5. Requires choosing \(\lambda\), and the likelihood-scale \(\lambda\) is not directly comparable to the least-squares \(\lambda\).

In this simulation, because the data truly come from Gaussian clusters, the penalized mixture model is well matched to the data-generating mechanism. It recovers the three groups, selects variables 1 and 2, and gives useful posterior uncertainty measures.

---

## Final conclusion

For the simulated data with three Gaussian groups and \(p=10\), ordinary \(k\)-means recovers the clusters well only when \(K=3\), but it uses all variables. Sparse \(k\)-means with \(K=3\) and pre-specified \(\lambda=0.30\) correctly eliminates the eight noise variables and keeps variables 1 and 2. The penalized Gaussian mixture EM algorithm also selects variables 1 and 2, provides soft assignments, and estimates mixing proportions and variances. In this setting, all three methods cluster well when \(K=3\), but the two penalized methods are preferable because they identify the sparse signal structure.

## (1) Simulation design: three true groups, \(p=10\), and varying \(K\)

A clean simulation should have a known true clustering, some informative variables, and some noise variables. I would use balanced Gaussian clusters with only the first two variables informative.

Let

\[
n=180,\qquad n_1=n_2=n_3=60,\qquad p=10.
\]

Generate true labels \(Z_i\in\{1,2,3\}\) with exactly 60 observations per group, and generate

\[
X_i\mid Z_i=k \sim N_p(\mu_k,I_p),
\]

where

\[
\mu_1=(2.5,0,0,\ldots,0),
\]

\[
\mu_2=\left(-1.25,\frac{2.5\sqrt 3}{2},0,\ldots,0\right),
\]

\[
\mu_3=\left(-1.25,-\frac{2.5\sqrt 3}{2},0,\ldots,0\right).
\]

Thus the three true centers form an equilateral triangle in the first two coordinates, and variables \(3,\ldots,10\) are pure noise.

Before applying any clustering method, standardize each variable to sample mean zero and sample variance one. This is essential because both \(k\)-means and the penalized methods are scale-sensitive.

For ordinary \(k\)-means, run the algorithm for

\[
K=1,2,3,4,5,6
\]

with many random starts, for example 50 starts, and record:

1. within-cluster sum of squares,
2. adjusted Rand index, ARI, comparing estimated clusters to true labels,
3. possibly the silhouette score or gap statistic.

A typical qualitative outcome is:

| Fitted \(K\) | Behavior | ARI behavior |
|---|---|---|
| \(K=1\) | all observations in one cluster | ARI \(=0\) |
| \(K=2\) | two true groups are merged | ARI around \(0.55\)–\(0.60\) |
| \(K=3\) | recovers the three true groups | ARI close to \(1\) |
| \(K=4\) | one true group is split | ARI decreases |
| \(K=5,6\) | more true groups are split | ARI decreases further |

For example, in the ideal perfectly separated case, if \(K=2\) merges two true groups, the ARI is approximately \(0.57\). If \(K=4\) splits one true group into two equal pieces, the ARI is approximately \(0.87\). Thus ARI is maximized at the true value \(K=3\), while the within-cluster sum of squares decreases monotonically with \(K\), so one looks for an elbow near \(K=3\).

A reproducible simulation skeleton is:

```r
set.seed(2025)

n.per <- 60
K.true <- 3
p <- 10
n <- K.true * n.per

mu <- matrix(0, nrow = 3, ncol = p)
mu[1,1:2] <- c(2.5, 0)
mu[2,1:2] <- c(-1.25,  2.5 * sqrt(3)/2)
mu[3,1:2] <- c(-1.25, -2.5 * sqrt(3)/2)

z <- rep(1:3, each = n.per)

X <- matrix(0, nrow = n, ncol = p)
for (i in 1:n) {
  X[i,] <- mu[z[i],] + rnorm(p)
}

X <- scale(X)

for (K in 1:6) {
  fit <- kmeans(X, centers = K, nstart = 50)
  # compute WSS, ARI, silhouette, etc.
}
```

---

## (2) Identity using the assignment matrix \(L\)

Let \(X\in \mathbb R^{n\times p}\) be the data matrix, with rows \(X_i^\top\). Let \(C\in \mathbb R^{K\times p}\) be the matrix of cluster centers, with rows \(C_k^\top\). Define the assignment matrix

\[
L_{ik}=\mathbf 1(X_i\in A_k).
\]

Thus each row of \(L\) contains exactly one 1.

For coordinate \(j\), let

\[
X^{(j)}=(X_{1j},\ldots,X_{nj})^\top\in\mathbb R^n,
\]

and

\[
C^{(j)}=(C_{1j},\ldots,C_{Kj})^\top\in\mathbb R^K.
\]

Then

\[
(LC^{(j)})_i
=
\sum_{k=1}^K L_{ik}C_{kj}.
\]

If \(X_i\in A_k\), then \(L_{ik}=1\), and hence

\[
(LC^{(j)})_i=C_{kj}.
\]

Therefore,

\[
X_{ij}-(LC^{(j)})_i
=
X_{ij}-C_{kj}
\qquad\text{whenever }X_i\in A_k.
\]

Now

\[
\sum_{k=1}^K\sum_{X_i\in A_k}\|X_i-C_k\|^2
=
\sum_{k=1}^K\sum_{X_i\in A_k}\sum_{j=1}^p (X_{ij}-C_{kj})^2.
\]

Interchanging the order of summation gives

\[
=
\sum_{j=1}^p
\sum_{k=1}^K\sum_{X_i\in A_k}
(X_{ij}-C_{kj})^2.
\]

But the inner sum is exactly

\[
\sum_{i=1}^n
\left(X_{ij}-(LC^{(j)})_i\right)^2
=
(X^{(j)}-LC^{(j)})^\top (X^{(j)}-LC^{(j)}).
\]

Hence

\[
\sum_{k=1}^K\sum_{X_i\in A_k}\|X_i-C_k\|^2
=
\sum_{j=1}^p
(X^{(j)}-LC^{(j)})^\top (X^{(j)}-LC^{(j)}).
\]

Therefore, with the \(1/n\) scaling included consistently,

\[
\frac1n\sum_{k=1}^K\sum_{X_i\in A_k}\|X_i-C_k\|^2
+
\lambda\sum_{j=1}^p \|C^{(j)}\|
\]

equals

\[
\sum_{j=1}^p
\left\{
\frac1n
(X^{(j)}-LC^{(j)})^\top (X^{(j)}-LC^{(j)})
+
\lambda \|C^{(j)}\|
\right\}.
\]

As written without the \(1/n\) on the left-hand squared-error term, the displayed identity would be off by a factor of \(n\). The correct identity is the one above.

---

## (3) Sparse \(k\)-means algorithm and analysis of the simulated data

The penalized objective is

\[
F(L,C)
=
\frac1n\sum_{k=1}^K\sum_{X_i\in A_k}\|X_i-C_k\|^2
+
\lambda\sum_{j=1}^p \|C^{(j)}\|_2.
\]

Using part (2),

\[
F(L,C)
=
\sum_{j=1}^p
\left\{
\frac1n\|X^{(j)}-LC^{(j)}\|_2^2
+
\lambda \|C^{(j)}\|_2
\right\}.
\]

Thus, for fixed assignments \(L\), the center update separates across variables \(j\). This is a group-lasso-type update, because the entire vector

\[
C^{(j)}=(C_{1j},\ldots,C_{Kj})^\top
\]

is either shrunk toward zero or set exactly to zero.

### Fixed \(L\): update for \(C^{(j)}\)

Fix \(L\), and define

\[
D=L^\top L=\operatorname{diag}(n_1,\ldots,n_K),
\]

where \(n_k\) is the number of observations assigned to cluster \(k\). Also define

\[
s_j=L^\top X^{(j)}\in\mathbb R^K.
\]

Then for coordinate \(j\), we minimize

\[
Q_j(c)
=
\frac1n \|X^{(j)}-Lc\|_2^2+\lambda\|c\|_2.
\]

Expanding,

\[
Q_j(c)
=
\frac1n
\left[
(X^{(j)})^\top X^{(j)}
-2s_j^\top c
+
c^\top D c
\right]
+
\lambda\|c\|_2.
\]

The constant term can be ignored. The KKT condition is

\[
0\in \frac{2}{n}(Dc-s_j)+\lambda \partial \|c\|_2.
\]

At \(c=0\), the subdifferential is

\[
\partial \|c\|_2\big|_{c=0}
=
\{u:\|u\|_2\le 1\}.
\]

Thus \(c=0\) is optimal if and only if

\[
\left\|\frac{2}{n}s_j\right\|_2\le \lambda.
\]

If

\[
\left\|\frac{2}{n}s_j\right\|_2>\lambda,
\]

then the solution is nonzero and satisfies

\[
\frac{2}{n}(Dc-s_j)+\lambda \frac{c}{\|c\|_2}=0.
\]

Equivalently,

\[
\left(D+\alpha I_K\right)c=s_j,
\]

where

\[
\alpha=\frac{n\lambda}{2\|c\|_2}.
\]

Therefore

\[
c=(D+\alpha I_K)^{-1}s_j,
\]

with \(\alpha>0\) chosen to satisfy

\[
\alpha
=
\frac{n\lambda}{2\|(D+\alpha I_K)^{-1}s_j\|_2}.
\]

This one-dimensional equation can be solved by bisection or Newton's method.

When the clusters are balanced so that \(n_1=\cdots=n_K=m\), this reduces to the ordinary group soft-thresholding formula

\[
C^{(j)}
=
\left(
1-\frac{n\lambda}{2\|s_j\|_2}
\right)_+
D^{-1}s_j.
\]

### Fixed \(C\): update for \(L\)

Given \(C\), the penalty term is fixed, so each observation is assigned to the nearest penalized center:

\[
\widehat z_i
=
\arg\min_{1\le k\le K}\|X_i-C_k\|_2^2.
\]

Thus

\[
L_{ik}=1(\widehat z_i=k).
\]

### Sparse \(k\)-means pseudocode

Use \(K=3\), since the true number of clusters is 3, and pre-specify

\[
\lambda=0.30.
\]

The value \(\lambda=0.30\) is chosen before seeing the data. For the present standardized simulation it is large enough to eliminate most noise variables but small enough to retain the first two variables.

```
Input: standardized data X, number of clusters K=3, penalty λ=0.30

For r = 1,...,R random starts:
    Initialize L using ordinary k-means with K=3.

    Repeat until convergence:
        1. Center update:
           For each variable j=1,...,p:
               Compute s_j = L^T X^(j).
               If ||(2/n) s_j||_2 <= λ:
                   Set C^(j) = 0.
               Else:
                   Find α > 0 solving
                       α = nλ / {2 ||(D+αI)^(-1)s_j||_2}
                   Set C^(j) = (D+αI)^(-1)s_j.

        2. Assignment update:
           For each observation i:
               assign i to the cluster k minimizing ||X_i - C_k||_2^2.

        3. Compute objective F(L,C).

    Store final solution.

Return the run with smallest objective.
```

Each block update decreases the objective. Because the objective is nonconvex in \((L,C)\) jointly, multiple random starts are important.

### Analysis of the simulated data

For the simulated data in part (1), using \(K=3\) and \(\lambda=0.30\), the sparse \(k\)-means algorithm typically selects exactly the first two variables:

\[
\widehat S
=
\{j:\|\widehat C^{(j)}\|_2>0\}
=
\{1,2\}.
\]

Variables \(3,\ldots,10\) have

\[
\widehat C^{(j)}=0,
\qquad j=3,\ldots,10.
\]

Thus they do not contribute to the distance calculation after shrinkage.

After matching labels to the true labels, the estimated centers in the first two coordinates are shrunk versions of the ordinary \(k\)-means centers. Approximately, after standardization, the true centers are proportional to

\[
(1.23,0),\qquad (-0.62,1.07),\qquad (-0.62,-1.07),
\]

and the sparse \(k\)-means centers are smaller in norm because of the group penalty. The assignments, however, are essentially unchanged because the irrelevant coordinates are removed.

A representative summary is:

| Method | \(K\) | Selected variables | ARI |
|---|---:|---|---:|
| ordinary \(k\)-means | 3 | all 10 used | close to \(1\) |
| sparse \(k\)-means, \(\lambda=0.30\) | 3 | \(\{1,2\}\) | close to \(1\) |

The main gain of sparse \(k\)-means here is interpretability and robustness to the eight irrelevant variables.

---

## (4) Penalized Gaussian mixture model and EM algorithm

Now consider the Gaussian mixture model

\[
f(x)
=
\sum_{k=1}^K \pi_k f_k(x;\theta_k),
\]

with

\[
\pi_k>0,\qquad \sum_{k=1}^K\pi_k=1.
\]

For comparability with the \(k\)-means methods, take

\[
f_k(x;\theta_k)
=
\phi_p(x;C_k,\Sigma),
\]

where \(C_k\in\mathbb R^p\) is the mean of component \(k\), and \(\Sigma\) is a common diagonal covariance matrix,

\[
\Sigma=\operatorname{diag}(\sigma_1^2,\ldots,\sigma_p^2).
\]

The penalty is

\[
n\lambda\sum_{j=1}^p
\frac{\|C^{(j)}\|_2}{\|\widetilde C^{(j)}\|_2},
\]

where \(\widetilde C^{(j)}\) is an initial unpenalized estimator, for example from an ordinary Gaussian mixture or ordinary \(k\)-means. Define adaptive weights

\[
w_j=\frac{1}{\|\widetilde C^{(j)}\|_2+\varepsilon},
\]

with a small \(\varepsilon>0\) to avoid division by zero.

The penalized observed log-likelihood is

\[
\ell_p(\Theta)
=
\sum_{i=1}^n
\log\left[
\sum_{k=1}^K
\pi_k
\phi_p(X_i;C_k,\Sigma)
\right]
-
n\lambda
\sum_{j=1}^p
w_j\|C^{(j)}\|_2.
\]

Here

\[
\Theta=(\pi_1,\ldots,\pi_K,C_1,\ldots,C_K,\Sigma).
\]

Let latent indicators

\[
L_{ik}=\mathbf 1(Z_i=k).
\]

The complete-data penalized log-likelihood, up to constants, is

\[
\ell_{c,p}(\Theta)
=
\sum_{i=1}^n\sum_{k=1}^K
L_{ik}
\left[
\log\pi_k
-\frac12\log|\Sigma|
-\frac12(X_i-C_k)^\top\Sigma^{-1}(X_i-C_k)
\right]
-
n\lambda\sum_{j=1}^p w_j\|C^{(j)}\|_2.
\]

---

### E-step

Given current parameter estimates \(\Theta^{(t)}\), compute the posterior responsibilities

\[
\tau_{ik}^{(t)}
=
\mathbb E[L_{ik}\mid X_i,\Theta^{(t)}].
\]

Thus

\[
\tau_{ik}^{(t)}
=
\frac{
\pi_k^{(t)}
\phi_p(X_i;C_k^{(t)},\Sigma^{(t)})
}{
\sum_{\ell=1}^K
\pi_\ell^{(t)}
\phi_p(X_i;C_\ell^{(t)},\Sigma^{(t)})
}.
\]

These are soft cluster assignments.

Define

\[
N_k^{(t)}
=
\sum_{i=1}^n \tau_{ik}^{(t)}.
\]

---

### M-step

The \(Q\)-function is

\[
Q_p(\Theta\mid \Theta^{(t)})
=
\sum_{i=1}^n\sum_{k=1}^K
\tau_{ik}^{(t)}
\left[
\log\pi_k
-\frac12\log|\Sigma|
-\frac12(X_i-C_k)^\top\Sigma^{-1}(X_i-C_k)
\right]
-
n\lambda\sum_{j=1}^p w_j\|C^{(j)}\|_2.
\]

#### Update for mixing proportions

Maximize

\[
\sum_{k=1}^K N_k^{(t)}\log\pi_k
\]

subject to \(\sum_k\pi_k=1\). Using Lagrange multipliers,

\[
\pi_k^{(t+1)}
=
\frac{N_k^{(t)}}{n}.
\]

#### Update for the means

For fixed \(\Sigma^{(t)}\), the mean update separates by variables because \(\Sigma\) is diagonal.

For coordinate \(j\), define

\[
s_j^{(t)}
=
\left(
\sum_{i=1}^n \tau_{i1}^{(t)}X_{ij},
\ldots,
\sum_{i=1}^n \tau_{iK}^{(t)}X_{ij}
\right)^\top
\in\mathbb R^K,
\]

and

\[
D^{(t)}
=
\operatorname{diag}(N_1^{(t)},\ldots,N_K^{(t)}).
\]

Also define the soft cluster means

\[
\bar X_{kj}^{(t)}
=
\frac{\sum_{i=1}^n\tau_{ik}^{(t)}X_{ij}}{N_k^{(t)}}.
\]

For coordinate \(j\), we minimize the negative penalized \(Q\)-function contribution

\[
\frac{1}{2\sigma_j^{2(t)}}
\sum_{k=1}^K
\sum_{i=1}^n
\tau_{ik}^{(t)}(X_{ij}-C_{kj})^2
+
n\lambda w_j\|C^{(j)}\|_2.
\]

Equivalently,

\[
\frac{1}{2\sigma_j^{2(t)}}
\sum_{k=1}^K
N_k^{(t)}
(C_{kj}-\bar X_{kj}^{(t)})^2
+
n\lambda w_j\|C^{(j)}\|_2.
\]

Let \(c=C^{(j)}\). The KKT condition is

\[
0
\in
\frac{1}{\sigma_j^{2(t)}}(D^{(t)}c-s_j^{(t)})
+
n\lambda w_j\,\partial\|c\|_2.
\]

Thus

\[
C^{(j),(t+1)}=0
\]

if and only if

\[
\left\|
\frac{s_j^{(t)}}{\sigma_j^{2(t)}}
\right\|_2
\le
n\lambda w_j.
\]

If this condition fails, then the solution is nonzero and satisfies

\[
\frac{1}{\sigma_j^{2(t)}}(D^{(t)}c-s_j^{(t)})
+
n\lambda w_j\frac{c}{\|c\|_2}
=0.
\]

Therefore

\[
\left(D^{(t)}+\alpha I_K\right)c=s_j^{(t)},
\]

where

\[
\alpha
=
\frac{n\lambda w_j\sigma_j^{2(t)}}{\|c\|_2}.
\]

Hence

\[
c=
\left(D^{(t)}+\alpha I_K\right)^{-1}s_j^{(t)},
\]

with \(\alpha>0\) satisfying

\[
\alpha
=
\frac{n\lambda w_j\sigma_j^{2(t)}}
{
\left\|
(D^{(t)}+\alpha I_K)^{-1}s_j^{(t)}
\right\|_2
}.
\]

Again, this is a one-dimensional root-finding problem.

#### Update for variances

After updating the means, update the common diagonal variances by

\[
\sigma_j^{2(t+1)}
=
\frac1n
\sum_{i=1}^n\sum_{k=1}^K
\tau_{ik}^{(t)}
\left(X_{ij}-C_{kj}^{(t+1)}\right)^2.
\]

This gives an EM or generalized EM algorithm. If the mean and variance updates are iterated inside the M-step until convergence, the M-step is exact. If they are performed once, this is an ECM algorithm, which still increases the penalized likelihood at each iteration under the usual regularity conditions.

---

### Penalized mixture EM pseudocode

Use \(K=3\). For the simulation, pre-specify for example

\[
\lambda_{\text{mix}}=0.05.
\]

Because the likelihood and least-squares objectives have different scales, \(\lambda_{\text{mix}}\) need not equal the sparse \(k\)-means penalty.

```
Input: standardized data X, K=3, penalty λ_mix=0.05

1. Initialize:
   - Run ordinary k-means or unpenalized Gaussian mixture.
   - Obtain initial means \tilde C.
   - Set adaptive weights w_j = 1/(||\tilde C^(j)||_2 + ε).

2. Initialize π_k, C_k, and σ_j^2.

Repeat until convergence:

   E-step:
       For each i,k compute
           τ_ik = π_k φ_p(X_i; C_k, Σ) /
                  sum_l π_l φ_p(X_i; C_l, Σ).

   M-step:
       Update
           N_k = sum_i τ_ik,
           π_k = N_k / n.

       For each variable j:
           Compute s_j = (sum_i τ_i1 X_ij, ..., sum_i τ_iK X_ij)^T.
           If ||s_j / σ_j^2||_2 <= n λ_mix w_j:
               Set C^(j) = 0.
           Else:
               Find α > 0 satisfying
                   α = n λ_mix w_j σ_j^2 /
                       ||(D+αI)^(-1)s_j||_2.
               Set
                   C^(j) = (D+αI)^(-1)s_j.

       Update each σ_j^2:
           σ_j^2 = (1/n) sum_i sum_k τ_ik (X_ij - C_kj)^2.

Return π, C, Σ, posterior probabilities τ_ik.
```

---

### Analysis of the simulated data

For the simulated data from part (1), the true model is a Gaussian mixture with three components and only the first two variables informative. Thus the penalized Gaussian mixture model should recover:

\[
\widehat S
=
\{j:\|\widehat C^{(j)}\|_2>0\}
=
\{1,2\}.
\]

The estimated mixing proportions should be close to balanced:

\[
\widehat \pi_1\approx \widehat \pi_2\approx \widehat \pi_3\approx \frac13.
\]

The estimated centers in variables 1 and 2 should be close to the true standardized means, up to label switching and small shrinkage. Variables \(3,\ldots,10\) should have estimated center vectors exactly zero.

A representative summary is:

| Method | Selected variables | ARI | Comments |
|---|---|---:|---|
| Penalized Gaussian mixture EM | \(\{1,2\}\) | close to \(1\) | soft assignments, estimates \(\pi_k\) and variances |

The posterior probabilities

\[
\widehat\tau_{ik}
\]

should be close to 0 or 1 for most observations because the clusters are well separated.

---

## (5) Comparison of ordinary \(k\)-means, sparse \(k\)-means, and penalized Gaussian mixtures

### Ordinary \(k\)-means

Advantages:

1. Simple and fast.
2. Works well when clusters are roughly spherical and similarly sized.
3. In this simulation, with the correct \(K=3\), it recovers the true clusters well.

Disadvantages:

1. Requires \(K\) to be chosen.
2. Uses all variables, including the eight noise variables.
3. Sensitive to scaling.
4. Gives hard assignments only.
5. Does not quantify uncertainty.

In this simulation, ordinary \(k\)-means performs well at \(K=3\), but performance deteriorates for \(K\neq 3\). When \(K=2\), it merges two true groups; when \(K>3\), it splits true groups.

---

### Sparse \(k\)-means

Advantages:

1. Performs clustering and variable selection simultaneously.
2. Correctly identifies variables 1 and 2 as relevant.
3. Removes the influence of noise variables \(3,\ldots,10\).
4. Improves interpretability.

Disadvantages:

1. Still requires \(K\) to be specified.
2. Requires choosing \(\lambda\).
3. The objective is nonconvex, so multiple starts are needed.
4. The centers are biased toward zero because of shrinkage.
5. Requires centering and scaling; otherwise the penalty is not meaningful.

In this simulation, sparse \(k\)-means gives essentially the same clustering accuracy as ordinary \(k\)-means with \(K=3\), but it has the important advantage of selecting the true relevant variables.

---

### Penalized Gaussian mixture model

Advantages:

1. Provides a probabilistic clustering model.
2. Gives soft assignments through posterior probabilities.
3. Estimates mixing proportions and variances.
4. Can be extended to unequal covariance structures.
5. The adaptive group penalty performs variable selection.

Disadvantages:

1. More computationally expensive.
2. More model-dependent than \(k\)-means.
3. The likelihood can have local maxima, so initialization matters.
4. If unrestricted covariance matrices are used, Gaussian mixture likelihoods may be unbounded without constraints.
5. Requires choosing \(\lambda\), and the likelihood-scale \(\lambda\) is not directly comparable to the least-squares \(\lambda\).

In this simulation, because the data truly come from Gaussian clusters, the penalized mixture model is well matched to the data-generating mechanism. It recovers the three groups, selects variables 1 and 2, and gives useful posterior uncertainty measures.

---

## Final conclusion

For the simulated data with three Gaussian groups and \(p=10\), ordinary \(k\)-means recovers the clusters well only when \(K=3\), but it uses all variables. Sparse \(k\)-means with \(K=3\) and pre-specified \(\lambda=0.30\) correctly eliminates the eight noise variables and keeps variables 1 and 2. The penalized Gaussian mixture EM algorithm also selects variables 1 and 2, provides soft assignments, and estimates mixing proportions and variances. In this setting, all three methods cluster well when \(K=3\), but the two penalized methods are preferable because they identify the sparse signal structure.

## (1) Simulation design for ordinary \(K\)-means

A convenient simulation should contain a small number of genuinely clustering variables and several pure noise variables. Let

\[
n=150,\qquad p=10,\qquad n_1=n_2=n_3=50,
\]

and generate independent observations from

\[
X_i\mid Z_i=k \sim N_p(\mu_k,I_p),\qquad k=1,2,3,
\]

with equal group sizes and

\[
\mu_1=(3,0,3,0,\ldots,0)^T,
\]

\[
\mu_2=\left(-\frac32,\frac{3\sqrt 3}{2},-\frac32,0,\ldots,0\right)^T,
\]

\[
\mu_3=\left(-\frac32,-\frac{3\sqrt 3}{2},-\frac32,0,\ldots,0\right)^T.
\]

Thus only variables \(1,2,3\) are informative; variables \(4,\ldots,10\) are pure noise. Also

\[
\mu_1+\mu_2+\mu_3=0,
\]

so the relevant variables are centered in the population. The pairwise squared distances between true centers are

\[
\|\mu_1-\mu_2\|^2=\|\mu_1-\mu_3\|^2=47.25,
\]

\[
\|\mu_2-\mu_3\|^2=27,
\]

so the clusters are well-separated.

For ordinary \(K\)-means, one can fit \(K=1,2,\ldots,6\), using many random starts, say 100 starts, and record

\[
W_K=\sum_{k=1}^K\sum_{i:X_i\in A_k}\|X_i-\widehat C_k\|^2,
\]

the adjusted Rand index relative to the true labels, and optionally silhouette width or the gap statistic.

A typical pattern is:

| fitted \(K\) | behavior | expected/typical within-cluster SSE per observation | ARI behavior |
|---|---|---:|---:|
| 1 | all groups merged | \(\approx 23.4\) | 0 |
| 2 | two nearby groups merged | \(\approx 14.4\) | \(\approx 0.57\) |
| 3 | true grouping recovered | \(\approx 9.8\) | close to 1 |
| 4,5,6 | true groups split | decreasing \(W_K\) | decreases from the \(K=3\) value |

The decrease of \(W_K\) is monotone in \(K\), so \(W_K\) alone cannot choose \(K\). The elbow in \(W_K\), the silhouette, or the gap statistic should identify \(K=3\) for this simulation.

---

## (2) Identity for the penalized objective

Let \(X\in\mathbb R^{n\times p}\) be the data matrix and let \(C\in\mathbb R^{K\times p}\) be the matrix of cluster centers, with row \(C_k^T\). Let

\[
C^{(j)}=(C_{1j},\ldots,C_{Kj})^T
\]

be the vector of cluster centers for variable \(j\), and let

\[
X^{(j)}=(X_{1j},\ldots,X_{nj})^T
\]

be the \(j\)-th column of the data matrix.

Let \(L\in\{0,1\}^{n\times K}\) be the cluster-assignment matrix,

\[
L_{ik}=\mathbf 1\{X_i\in A_k\}.
\]

Each row of \(L\) contains exactly one 1. Therefore, for observation \(i\) assigned to cluster \(k\),

\[
(LC^{(j)})_i=\sum_{\ell=1}^K L_{i\ell}C_{\ell j}=C_{kj}.
\]

Hence

\[
X_{ij}-(LC^{(j)})_i=X_{ij}-C_{kj}
\]

whenever \(X_i\in A_k\). Therefore,

\[
\sum_{k=1}^K\sum_{X_i\in A_k}\|X_i-C_k\|^2
=
\sum_{i=1}^n\sum_{j=1}^p\left(X_{ij}-(LC^{(j)})_i\right)^2.
\]

Rearranging the order of summation gives

\[
\sum_{k=1}^K\sum_{X_i\in A_k}\|X_i-C_k\|^2
=
\sum_{j=1}^p (X^{(j)}-LC^{(j)})^T(X^{(j)}-LC^{(j)}).
\]

Thus the penalized objective satisfies

\[
\frac1n\sum_{k=1}^K\sum_{X_i\in A_k}\|X_i-C_k\|^2
+
\lambda\sum_{j=1}^p\|C^{(j)}\|_2
\]

\[
=
\sum_{j=1}^p
\left\{
\frac1n (X^{(j)}-LC^{(j)})^T(X^{(j)}-LC^{(j)})
+
\lambda\|C^{(j)}\|_2
\right\}.
\]

This is the desired separability across variables.

Remark: if the unscaled SSE is used on the left, then the \(1/n\) must also be removed from the right.

---

## (3) Sparse penalized \(K\)-means algorithm and analysis of the simulated data

We minimize

\[
Q(L,C)
=
\frac1n\sum_{k=1}^K\sum_{X_i\in A_k}\|X_i-C_k\|^2
+
\lambda\sum_{j=1}^p\|C^{(j)}\|_2.
\]

For the simulation, I pre-specify

\[
K=3,\qquad \lambda=0.5.
\]

Because the variables have the same noise variance in the simulation, no scaling is necessary, although in real applications the variables should be standardized.

### Center update for fixed assignments

Fix \(L\). For variable \(j\), write \(x=X^{(j)}\) and \(c=C^{(j)}\). Define

\[
D=L^TL=\operatorname{diag}(n_1,\ldots,n_K),
\]

where \(n_k\) is the current cluster size, and

\[
z=L^Tx.
\]

The \(j\)-th subproblem is

\[
\min_{c\in\mathbb R^K}
\left\{
\frac1n(x-Lc)^T(x-Lc)+\lambda\|c\|_2
\right\}.
\]

Ignoring terms not involving \(c\), this is

\[
\min_c
\left\{
\frac1n c^TDc-\frac2n z^Tc+\lambda\|c\|_2
\right\}.
\]

The KKT condition is

\[
0\in \frac2n(Dc-z)+\lambda\,\partial\|c\|_2.
\]

Thus \(c=0\) is optimal if and only if

\[
\left\|\frac2n z\right\|_2\le \lambda,
\]

or equivalently

\[
\|z\|_2\le \frac{n\lambda}{2}.
\]

If \(c\neq 0\), then

\[
\frac2n(Dc-z)+\lambda \frac{c}{\|c\|_2}=0,
\]

so

\[
\left(D+\gamma I_K\right)c=z,
\qquad
\gamma=\frac{n\lambda}{2\|c\|_2}.
\]

Thus the nonzero solution can be found by solving the one-dimensional equation

\[
\gamma\left\|(D+\gamma I_K)^{-1}z\right\|_2=\frac{n\lambda}{2}.
\]

In the balanced case \(n_k=m\) for all \(k\), so \(D=mI_K\). Let

\[
\bar x_j=(\bar x_{1j},\ldots,\bar x_{Kj})^T
\]

be the vector of cluster sample means for variable \(j\). Then

\[
z=m\bar x_j,
\]

and the solution simplifies to the group soft-thresholding rule

\[
C^{(j)}
=
\left(
1-\frac{n\lambda}{2m\|\bar x_j\|_2}
\right)_+
\bar x_j.
\]

Thus either all cluster centers for variable \(j\) are retained, or all are set to zero.

### Pseudocode

**Input:** data \(X\), number of clusters \(K\), penalty \(\lambda\), number of random starts \(R\).

1. For each start \(r=1,\ldots,R\):

   1. Initialize labels using random initialization or ordinary \(K\)-means++.

   2. Repeat until labels no longer change:

      - Form the assignment matrix \(L\).

      - For each variable \(j=1,\ldots,p\):

        - Let \(x=X^{(j)}\), \(D=L^TL\), and \(z=L^Tx\).

        - If \(\|z\|_2\le n\lambda/2\), set

          \[
          C^{(j)}=0.
          \]

        - Otherwise solve

          \[
          \gamma\left\|(D+\gamma I_K)^{-1}z\right\|_2=\frac{n\lambda}{2}
          \]

          and set

          \[
          C^{(j)}=(D+\gamma I_K)^{-1}z.
          \]

      - Reassign each observation to its nearest penalized center:

        \[
        \widehat g_i=\arg\min_{1\le k\le K}\|X_i-C_k\|^2.
        \]

   3. Store the final objective value.

2. Return the solution with the smallest objective over the \(R\) starts.

This alternating procedure decreases the objective at each step and converges to a local minimum.

### Analysis for the simulation

For the simulation,

\[
n=150,\qquad n_k=50,\qquad K=3,\qquad \lambda=0.5.
\]

Thus, once the clusters are approximately balanced,

\[
\frac{n\lambda}{2n_k}
=
\frac{150(0.5)}{2(50)}
=
0.75.
\]

The true center-vector norm for each informative variable is

\[
\|(3,-3/2,-3/2)^T\|_2
=
\sqrt{13.5}
\approx 3.67,
\]

and the same norm holds for variables 2 and 3. Therefore variables \(1,2,3\) easily survive the threshold.

For a noise variable \(j\ge 4\), the empirical cluster means are approximately

\[
\bar x_j\sim N_3(0,50^{-1}I_3),
\]

so

\[
\|\bar x_j\|_2=O_p\left(\sqrt{\frac3{50}}\right)\approx 0.245,
\]

which is well below the threshold \(0.75\). Hence the sparse \(K\)-means algorithm selects variables

\[
\{1,2,3\}
\]

and sets the center vectors for variables \(4,\ldots,10\) equal to zero.

The retained center vectors are shrunk. The approximate shrinkage factor is

\[
1-\frac{0.75}{3.67}\approx 0.796.
\]

Thus the penalized estimated centers are approximately

\[
\widehat C_1\approx (2.39,0,2.39,0,\ldots,0),
\]

\[
\widehat C_2\approx (-1.19,2.07,-1.19,0,\ldots,0),
\]

\[
\widehat C_3\approx (-1.19,-2.07,-1.19,0,\ldots,0),
\]

up to sampling error and label switching.

Because the true clusters are well separated, the clustering ARI is typically close to 1. Compared with ordinary \(K\)-means, the main gain is interpretability and robustness: the sparse method identifies the truly relevant variables and removes the seven noise variables from the distance calculation.

---

## (4) Penalized Gaussian mixture model and EM algorithm

Now consider the Gaussian mixture model

\[
f(x)=\sum_{k=1}^K \pi_k f_k(x;\theta_k),
\]

where

\[
f_k(x;\theta_k)=\phi_p(x;C_k,\Sigma_k).
\]

The penalized observed log-likelihood is

\[
\ell_p(\theta)
=
\sum_{i=1}^n
\log\left\{
\sum_{k=1}^K \pi_k\phi_p(X_i;C_k,\Sigma_k)
\right\}
-
n\lambda\sum_{j=1}^p
\frac{\|C^{(j)}\|_2}{\|\widetilde C^{(j)}\|_2}.
\]

Here \(\widetilde C\) is an initial unpenalized estimator, such as the ordinary Gaussian mixture MLE or the ordinary \(K\)-means centers. In practice one uses

\[
w_j=\frac1{\|\widetilde C^{(j)}\|_2+\varepsilon}
\]

with a small \(\varepsilon>0\), so the penalty is

\[
n\lambda\sum_{j=1}^p w_j\|C^{(j)}\|_2.
\]

The weights make this an adaptive group-lasso penalty.

Let \(L_{ik}\) be the latent class indicator:

\[
L_{ik}=\mathbf 1\{Z_i=k\}.
\]

The complete-data penalized log-likelihood is

\[
\ell_{c,p}(\theta)
=
\sum_{i=1}^n\sum_{k=1}^K
L_{ik}
\left[
\log \pi_k
-
\frac p2\log(2\pi)
-
\frac12\log|\Sigma_k|
-
\frac12(X_i-C_k)^T\Sigma_k^{-1}(X_i-C_k)
\right]
-
n\lambda\sum_{j=1}^p w_j\|C^{(j)}\|_2.
\]

### E-step

Given current parameter estimates \(\theta^{(t)}\), compute the posterior probabilities

\[
\tau_{ik}^{(t)}
=
E[L_{ik}\mid X_i,\theta^{(t)}]
=
\frac{
\pi_k^{(t)}
\phi_p(X_i;C_k^{(t)},\Sigma_k^{(t)})
}{
\sum_{\ell=1}^K
\pi_\ell^{(t)}
\phi_p(X_i;C_\ell^{(t)},\Sigma_\ell^{(t)})
}.
\]

Define

\[
n_k^{(t)}=\sum_{i=1}^n\tau_{ik}^{(t)}
\]

and

\[
\bar X_k^{(t)}
=
\frac1{n_k^{(t)}}\sum_{i=1}^n \tau_{ik}^{(t)}X_i.
\]

### M-step: mixing proportions

Maximizing the expected complete-data log-likelihood with respect to \(\pi_k\), subject to \(\sum_k\pi_k=1\), gives

\[
\pi_k^{(t+1)}=\frac{n_k^{(t)}}{n}.
\]

### M-step: means with group penalty

For fixed covariance matrices, the mean update solves

\[
\min_{C}
\left\{
\frac12
\sum_{k=1}^K
n_k^{(t)}
(C_k-\bar X_k^{(t)})^T
\Omega_k^{(t)}
(C_k-\bar X_k^{(t)})
+
n\lambda\sum_{j=1}^p w_j\|C^{(j)}\|_2
\right\},
\]

where

\[
\Omega_k^{(t)}=(\Sigma_k^{(t)})^{-1}.
\]

For general covariance matrices this is a convex problem in \(C\) for fixed \(\Sigma_k\). It can be solved by block-coordinate descent over variables \(j\). Fix \(j\) and hold all other coordinates fixed. Define

\[
a_{kj}
=
\bar X_{kj}^{(t)}
-
\frac1{\omega_{k,jj}^{(t)}}
\sum_{\ell\ne j}
\omega_{k,j\ell}^{(t)}
\left(C_{k\ell}-\bar X_{k\ell}^{(t)}\right),
\]

where \(\omega_{k,j\ell}^{(t)}\) is the \((j,\ell)\)-entry of \(\Omega_k^{(t)}\). Also define

\[
d_{kj}=n_k^{(t)}\omega_{k,jj}^{(t)}
\]

and

\[
D_j=\operatorname{diag}(d_{1j},\ldots,d_{Kj}).
\]

The block update for \(c=C^{(j)}\) is

\[
\min_{c\in\mathbb R^K}
\left\{
\frac12\sum_{k=1}^K d_{kj}(c_k-a_{kj})^2
+
n\lambda w_j\|c\|_2
\right\}.
\]

Let

\[
r_j=D_j a_j.
\]

The KKT conditions give:

- If

  \[
  \|r_j\|_2\le n\lambda w_j,
  \]

  then

  \[
  C^{(j)}=0.
  \]

- Otherwise, \(C^{(j)}\neq 0\), and

  \[
  C^{(j)}
  =
  (D_j+\alpha I_K)^{-1}r_j,
  \]

  where \(\alpha>0\) solves

  \[
  \alpha
  \left\|
  (D_j+\alpha I_K)^{-1}r_j
  \right\|_2
  =
  n\lambda w_j.
  \]

This one-dimensional equation has a unique solution when \(\|r_j\|_2>n\lambda w_j\).

### M-step: covariance matrices

After updating the means, the component covariance matrices are updated by

\[
\Sigma_k^{(t+1)}
=
\frac1{n_k^{(t)}}
\sum_{i=1}^n
\tau_{ik}^{(t)}
(X_i-C_k^{(t+1)})(X_i-C_k^{(t+1)})^T.
\]

In the present simulation the true covariance is \(I_p\), so a common spherical covariance model is natural:

\[
\Sigma_k=\sigma^2 I_p.
\]

Then the covariance update becomes

\[
(\sigma^2)^{(t+1)}
=
\frac1{np}
\sum_{i=1}^n\sum_{k=1}^K
\tau_{ik}^{(t)}
\|X_i-C_k^{(t+1)}\|^2.
\]

In the common spherical case the mean update simplifies substantially. Since

\[
\Omega_k=\sigma^{-2}I_p,
\]

the block update for variable \(j\) becomes

\[
\min_c
\left\{
\frac1{2\sigma^2}
\sum_{k=1}^K n_k(c_k-\bar X_{kj})^2
+
n\lambda w_j\|c\|_2
\right\}.
\]

If the groups are balanced with \(n_k=m\), then

\[
C^{(j)}
=
\left(
1-
\frac{n\lambda\sigma^2w_j}{m\|\bar X^{(j)}\|_2}
\right)_+
\bar X^{(j)}.
\]

### EM pseudocode

**Input:** \(X\), \(K\), \(\lambda\), initial unpenalized centers \(\widetilde C\), covariance initialization.

1. Compute adaptive weights

   \[
   w_j=\frac1{\|\widetilde C^{(j)}\|_2+\varepsilon}.
   \]

2. Initialize \(\pi_k,C_k,\Sigma_k\), for example from ordinary \(K\)-means or unpenalized EM.

3. Repeat until convergence:

   **E-step:**

   \[
   \tau_{ik}
   =
   \frac{\pi_k\phi_p(X_i;C_k,\Sigma_k)}
   {\sum_{\ell=1}^K \pi_\ell\phi_p(X_i;C_\ell,\Sigma_\ell)}.
   \]

   **M-step:**

   - Update

     \[
     \pi_k=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\tau_{ik}.
     \]

   - Update \(C\) using the adaptive group-lasso block updates above.

   - Update \(\Sigma_k\), or \(\sigma^2\) in the spherical case.

4. Return the solution with the largest penalized log-likelihood over multiple random starts.

The EM monotonicity follows from the usual EM minorization argument using Jensen’s inequality. If the M-step is implemented as an ECM step, each block update must increase the penalized expected complete-data log-likelihood.

### Analysis for the simulation

For the simulated data I use

\[
K=3,\qquad \lambda=1,
\]

and a common spherical covariance model

\[
\Sigma_k=\sigma^2I_p.
\]

The unpenalized initial estimates satisfy approximately

\[
\|\widetilde C^{(j)}\|_2\approx 3.67,\qquad j=1,2,3,
\]

while for noise variables,

\[
\|\widetilde C^{(j)}\|_2\approx 0.25,\qquad j=4,\ldots,10.
\]

For the informative variables,

\[
w_j\approx \frac1{3.67},
\]

whereas for the noise variables,

\[
w_j\approx \frac1{0.25}.
\]

Thus the adaptive penalty is small for truly relevant variables and large for noise variables. With \(n_k\approx 50\), \(n=150\), and \(\sigma^2\approx 1\), the effective threshold for an informative variable is approximately

\[
\frac{n\lambda\sigma^2w_j}{n_k}
\approx
\frac{150}{50(3.67)}
\approx 0.82,
\]

which is much smaller than the signal norm \(3.67\). For noise variables the threshold is approximately

\[
\frac{150}{50(0.25)}
=
12,
\]

which is far larger than their empirical center norm. Therefore the penalized mixture EM selects

\[
\{1,2,3\}
\]

and sets variables \(4,\ldots,10\) to zero in the mean differences.

The fitted mixing proportions are approximately

\[
\widehat\pi_1\approx \widehat\pi_2\approx \widehat\pi_3\approx \frac13,
\]

and the fitted variance satisfies

\[
\widehat\sigma^2\approx 1.
\]

The posterior probabilities \(\tau_{ik}\) are close to 0 or 1 because the clusters are well-separated, so the resulting hard classification has ARI close to 1.

---

## (5) Comparison of the three methods

### Ordinary \(K\)-means

Ordinary \(K\)-means is simple and effective when \(K\) is correctly specified and the clusters are roughly spherical with comparable variances. In this simulation, with \(K=3\), ordinary \(K\)-means recovers the true labels almost perfectly.

However, ordinary \(K\)-means has two weaknesses here:

1. It uses all variables, including the seven pure noise variables.
2. It requires \(K\) to be chosen externally.

When \(K<3\), true groups are merged. When \(K>3\), true groups are artificially split.

### Sparse penalized \(K\)-means

Sparse penalized \(K\)-means retains the hard-assignment structure of \(K\)-means but adds a group-lasso penalty on the cluster centers. It correctly identifies variables \(1,2,3\) as relevant and removes variables \(4,\ldots,10\). It gives interpretable clusters and would become much more advantageous as the number of noise variables grows.

Its main disadvantages are that \(\lambda\) must be chosen and the center estimates are biased toward zero because of shrinkage.

### Penalized Gaussian mixture EM

The penalized Gaussian mixture model provides a likelihood-based probabilistic clustering method. It gives soft assignments, estimates mixing proportions and covariance parameters, and can be combined with likelihood criteria such as BIC for choosing \(K\). Under the simulation model, which is genuinely Gaussian with spherical covariance, the mixture model is correctly specified and therefore performs very well.

The adaptive group-lasso penalty again selects variables \(1,2,3\) and removes the noise variables. Compared with sparse \(K\)-means, the mixture model gives posterior uncertainty quantification through the \(\tau_{ik}\)'s.

Its disadvantages are greater computational cost, sensitivity to local maxima, and the need to specify a covariance structure.

### Overall conclusion

For this simulation:

\[
\text{ordinary }K\text{-means with }K=3
\]

recovers the clusters, but it does not identify the relevant variables.

Both sparse penalized \(K\)-means and the penalized Gaussian mixture model recover the three clusters and correctly select variables \(1,2,3\). The penalized mixture model is preferable if the Gaussian mixture model is trusted and posterior probabilities are desired. Sparse \(K\)-means is simpler and more robust as a nonparametric clustering method.

## (1) Simulation design for ordinary \(K\)-means

A convenient simulation should contain a small number of genuinely clustering variables and several pure noise variables. Let

\[
n=150,\qquad p=10,\qquad n_1=n_2=n_3=50,
\]

and generate independent observations from

\[
X_i\mid Z_i=k \sim N_p(\mu_k,I_p),\qquad k=1,2,3,
\]

with equal group sizes and

\[
\mu_1=(3,0,3,0,\ldots,0)^T,
\]

\[
\mu_2=\left(-\frac32,\frac{3\sqrt 3}{2},-\frac32,0,\ldots,0\right)^T,
\]

\[
\mu_3=\left(-\frac32,-\frac{3\sqrt 3}{2},-\frac32,0,\ldots,0\right)^T.
\]

Thus only variables \(1,2,3\) are informative; variables \(4,\ldots,10\) are pure noise. Also

\[
\mu_1+\mu_2+\mu_3=0,
\]

so the relevant variables are centered in the population. The pairwise squared distances between true centers are

\[
\|\mu_1-\mu_2\|^2=\|\mu_1-\mu_3\|^2=47.25,
\]

\[
\|\mu_2-\mu_3\|^2=27,
\]

so the clusters are well-separated.

For ordinary \(K\)-means, one can fit \(K=1,2,\ldots,6\), using many random starts, say 100 starts, and record

\[
W_K=\sum_{k=1}^K\sum_{i:X_i\in A_k}\|X_i-\widehat C_k\|^2,
\]

the adjusted Rand index relative to the true labels, and optionally silhouette width or the gap statistic.

A typical pattern is:

| fitted \(K\) | behavior | expected/typical within-cluster SSE per observation | ARI behavior |
|---|---|---:|---:|
| 1 | all groups merged | \(\approx 23.4\) | 0 |
| 2 | two nearby groups merged | \(\approx 14.4\) | \(\approx 0.57\) |
| 3 | true grouping recovered | \(\approx 9.8\) | close to 1 |
| 4,5,6 | true groups split | decreasing \(W_K\) | decreases from the \(K=3\) value |

The decrease of \(W_K\) is monotone in \(K\), so \(W_K\) alone cannot choose \(K\). The elbow in \(W_K\), the silhouette, or the gap statistic should identify \(K=3\) for this simulation.

---

## (2) Identity for the penalized objective

Let \(X\in\mathbb R^{n\times p}\) be the data matrix and let \(C\in\mathbb R^{K\times p}\) be the matrix of cluster centers, with row \(C_k^T\). Let

\[
C^{(j)}=(C_{1j},\ldots,C_{Kj})^T
\]

be the vector of cluster centers for variable \(j\), and let

\[
X^{(j)}=(X_{1j},\ldots,X_{nj})^T
\]

be the \(j\)-th column of the data matrix.

Let \(L\in\{0,1\}^{n\times K}\) be the cluster-assignment matrix,

\[
L_{ik}=\mathbf 1\{X_i\in A_k\}.
\]

Each row of \(L\) contains exactly one 1. Therefore, for observation \(i\) assigned to cluster \(k\),

\[
(LC^{(j)})_i=\sum_{\ell=1}^K L_{i\ell}C_{\ell j}=C_{kj}.
\]

Hence

\[
X_{ij}-(LC^{(j)})_i=X_{ij}-C_{kj}
\]

whenever \(X_i\in A_k\). Therefore,

\[
\sum_{k=1}^K\sum_{X_i\in A_k}\|X_i-C_k\|^2
=
\sum_{i=1}^n\sum_{j=1}^p\left(X_{ij}-(LC^{(j)})_i\right)^2.
\]

Rearranging the order of summation gives

\[
\sum_{k=1}^K\sum_{X_i\in A_k}\|X_i-C_k\|^2
=
\sum_{j=1}^p (X^{(j)}-LC^{(j)})^T(X^{(j)}-LC^{(j)}).
\]

Thus the penalized objective satisfies

\[
\frac1n\sum_{k=1}^K\sum_{X_i\in A_k}\|X_i-C_k\|^2
+
\lambda\sum_{j=1}^p\|C^{(j)}\|_2
\]

\[
=
\sum_{j=1}^p
\left\{
\frac1n (X^{(j)}-LC^{(j)})^T(X^{(j)}-LC^{(j)})
+
\lambda\|C^{(j)}\|_2
\right\}.
\]

This is the desired separability across variables.

Remark: if the unscaled SSE is used on the left, then the \(1/n\) must also be removed from the right.

---

## (3) Sparse penalized \(K\)-means algorithm and analysis of the simulated data

We minimize

\[
Q(L,C)
=
\frac1n\sum_{k=1}^K\sum_{X_i\in A_k}\|X_i-C_k\|^2
+
\lambda\sum_{j=1}^p\|C^{(j)}\|_2.
\]

For the simulation, I pre-specify

\[
K=3,\qquad \lambda=0.5.
\]

Because the variables have the same noise variance in the simulation, no scaling is necessary, although in real applications the variables should be standardized.

### Center update for fixed assignments

Fix \(L\). For variable \(j\), write \(x=X^{(j)}\) and \(c=C^{(j)}\). Define

\[
D=L^TL=\operatorname{diag}(n_1,\ldots,n_K),
\]

where \(n_k\) is the current cluster size, and

\[
z=L^Tx.
\]

The \(j\)-th subproblem is

\[
\min_{c\in\mathbb R^K}
\left\{
\frac1n(x-Lc)^T(x-Lc)+\lambda\|c\|_2
\right\}.
\]

Ignoring terms not involving \(c\), this is

\[
\min_c
\left\{
\frac1n c^TDc-\frac2n z^Tc+\lambda\|c\|_2
\right\}.
\]

The KKT condition is

\[
0\in \frac2n(Dc-z)+\lambda\,\partial\|c\|_2.
\]

Thus \(c=0\) is optimal if and only if

\[
\left\|\frac2n z\right\|_2\le \lambda,
\]

or equivalently

\[
\|z\|_2\le \frac{n\lambda}{2}.
\]

If \(c\neq 0\), then

\[
\frac2n(Dc-z)+\lambda \frac{c}{\|c\|_2}=0,
\]

so

\[
\left(D+\gamma I_K\right)c=z,
\qquad
\gamma=\frac{n\lambda}{2\|c\|_2}.
\]

Thus the nonzero solution can be found by solving the one-dimensional equation

\[
\gamma\left\|(D+\gamma I_K)^{-1}z\right\|_2=\frac{n\lambda}{2}.
\]

In the balanced case \(n_k=m\) for all \(k\), so \(D=mI_K\). Let

\[
\bar x_j=(\bar x_{1j},\ldots,\bar x_{Kj})^T
\]

be the vector of cluster sample means for variable \(j\). Then

\[
z=m\bar x_j,
\]

and the solution simplifies to the group soft-thresholding rule

\[
C^{(j)}
=
\left(
1-\frac{n\lambda}{2m\|\bar x_j\|_2}
\right)_+
\bar x_j.
\]

Thus either all cluster centers for variable \(j\) are retained, or all are set to zero.

### Pseudocode

**Input:** data \(X\), number of clusters \(K\), penalty \(\lambda\), number of random starts \(R\).

1. For each start \(r=1,\ldots,R\):

   1. Initialize labels using random initialization or ordinary \(K\)-means++.

   2. Repeat until labels no longer change:

      - Form the assignment matrix \(L\).

      - For each variable \(j=1,\ldots,p\):

        - Let \(x=X^{(j)}\), \(D=L^TL\), and \(z=L^Tx\).

        - If \(\|z\|_2\le n\lambda/2\), set

          \[
          C^{(j)}=0.
          \]

        - Otherwise solve

          \[
          \gamma\left\|(D+\gamma I_K)^{-1}z\right\|_2=\frac{n\lambda}{2}
          \]

          and set

          \[
          C^{(j)}=(D+\gamma I_K)^{-1}z.
          \]

      - Reassign each observation to its nearest penalized center:

        \[
        \widehat g_i=\arg\min_{1\le k\le K}\|X_i-C_k\|^2.
        \]

   3. Store the final objective value.

2. Return the solution with the smallest objective over the \(R\) starts.

This alternating procedure decreases the objective at each step and converges to a local minimum.

### Analysis for the simulation

For the simulation,

\[
n=150,\qquad n_k=50,\qquad K=3,\qquad \lambda=0.5.
\]

Thus, once the clusters are approximately balanced,

\[
\frac{n\lambda}{2n_k}
=
\frac{150(0.5)}{2(50)}
=
0.75.
\]

The true center-vector norm for each informative variable is

\[
\|(3,-3/2,-3/2)^T\|_2
=
\sqrt{13.5}
\approx 3.67,
\]

and the same norm holds for variables 2 and 3. Therefore variables \(1,2,3\) easily survive the threshold.

For a noise variable \(j\ge 4\), the empirical cluster means are approximately

\[
\bar x_j\sim N_3(0,50^{-1}I_3),
\]

so

\[
\|\bar x_j\|_2=O_p\left(\sqrt{\frac3{50}}\right)\approx 0.245,
\]

which is well below the threshold \(0.75\). Hence the sparse \(K\)-means algorithm selects variables

\[
\{1,2,3\}
\]

and sets the center vectors for variables \(4,\ldots,10\) equal to zero.

The retained center vectors are shrunk. The approximate shrinkage factor is

\[
1-\frac{0.75}{3.67}\approx 0.796.
\]

Thus the penalized estimated centers are approximately

\[
\widehat C_1\approx (2.39,0,2.39,0,\ldots,0),
\]

\[
\widehat C_2\approx (-1.19,2.07,-1.19,0,\ldots,0),
\]

\[
\widehat C_3\approx (-1.19,-2.07,-1.19,0,\ldots,0),
\]

up to sampling error and label switching.

Because the true clusters are well separated, the clustering ARI is typically close to 1. Compared with ordinary \(K\)-means, the main gain is interpretability and robustness: the sparse method identifies the truly relevant variables and removes the seven noise variables from the distance calculation.

---

## (4) Penalized Gaussian mixture model and EM algorithm

Now consider the Gaussian mixture model

\[
f(x)=\sum_{k=1}^K \pi_k f_k(x;\theta_k),
\]

where

\[
f_k(x;\theta_k)=\phi_p(x;C_k,\Sigma_k).
\]

The penalized observed log-likelihood is

\[
\ell_p(\theta)
=
\sum_{i=1}^n
\log\left\{
\sum_{k=1}^K \pi_k\phi_p(X_i;C_k,\Sigma_k)
\right\}
-
n\lambda\sum_{j=1}^p
\frac{\|C^{(j)}\|_2}{\|\widetilde C^{(j)}\|_2}.
\]

Here \(\widetilde C\) is an initial unpenalized estimator, such as the ordinary Gaussian mixture MLE or the ordinary \(K\)-means centers. In practice one uses

\[
w_j=\frac1{\|\widetilde C^{(j)}\|_2+\varepsilon}
\]

with a small \(\varepsilon>0\), so the penalty is

\[
n\lambda\sum_{j=1}^p w_j\|C^{(j)}\|_2.
\]

The weights make this an adaptive group-lasso penalty.

Let \(L_{ik}\) be the latent class indicator:

\[
L_{ik}=\mathbf 1\{Z_i=k\}.
\]

The complete-data penalized log-likelihood is

\[
\ell_{c,p}(\theta)
=
\sum_{i=1}^n\sum_{k=1}^K
L_{ik}
\left[
\log \pi_k
-
\frac p2\log(2\pi)
-
\frac12\log|\Sigma_k|
-
\frac12(X_i-C_k)^T\Sigma_k^{-1}(X_i-C_k)
\right]
-
n\lambda\sum_{j=1}^p w_j\|C^{(j)}\|_2.
\]

### E-step

Given current parameter estimates \(\theta^{(t)}\), compute the posterior probabilities

\[
\tau_{ik}^{(t)}
=
E[L_{ik}\mid X_i,\theta^{(t)}]
=
\frac{
\pi_k^{(t)}
\phi_p(X_i;C_k^{(t)},\Sigma_k^{(t)})
}{
\sum_{\ell=1}^K
\pi_\ell^{(t)}
\phi_p(X_i;C_\ell^{(t)},\Sigma_\ell^{(t)})
}.
\]

Define

\[
n_k^{(t)}=\sum_{i=1}^n\tau_{ik}^{(t)}
\]

and

\[
\bar X_k^{(t)}
=
\frac1{n_k^{(t)}}\sum_{i=1}^n \tau_{ik}^{(t)}X_i.
\]

### M-step: mixing proportions

Maximizing the expected complete-data log-likelihood with respect to \(\pi_k\), subject to \(\sum_k\pi_k=1\), gives

\[
\pi_k^{(t+1)}=\frac{n_k^{(t)}}{n}.
\]

### M-step: means with group penalty

For fixed covariance matrices, the mean update solves

\[
\min_{C}
\left\{
\frac12
\sum_{k=1}^K
n_k^{(t)}
(C_k-\bar X_k^{(t)})^T
\Omega_k^{(t)}
(C_k-\bar X_k^{(t)})
+
n\lambda\sum_{j=1}^p w_j\|C^{(j)}\|_2
\right\},
\]

where

\[
\Omega_k^{(t)}=(\Sigma_k^{(t)})^{-1}.
\]

For general covariance matrices this is a convex problem in \(C\) for fixed \(\Sigma_k\). It can be solved by block-coordinate descent over variables \(j\). Fix \(j\) and hold all other coordinates fixed. Define

\[
a_{kj}
=
\bar X_{kj}^{(t)}
-
\frac1{\omega_{k,jj}^{(t)}}
\sum_{\ell\ne j}
\omega_{k,j\ell}^{(t)}
\left(C_{k\ell}-\bar X_{k\ell}^{(t)}\right),
\]

where \(\omega_{k,j\ell}^{(t)}\) is the \((j,\ell)\)-entry of \(\Omega_k^{(t)}\). Also define

\[
d_{kj}=n_k^{(t)}\omega_{k,jj}^{(t)}
\]

and

\[
D_j=\operatorname{diag}(d_{1j},\ldots,d_{Kj}).
\]

The block update for \(c=C^{(j)}\) is

\[
\min_{c\in\mathbb R^K}
\left\{
\frac12\sum_{k=1}^K d_{kj}(c_k-a_{kj})^2
+
n\lambda w_j\|c\|_2
\right\}.
\]

Let

\[
r_j=D_j a_j.
\]

The KKT conditions give:

- If

  \[
  \|r_j\|_2\le n\lambda w_j,
  \]

  then

  \[
  C^{(j)}=0.
  \]

- Otherwise, \(C^{(j)}\neq 0\), and

  \[
  C^{(j)}
  =
  (D_j+\alpha I_K)^{-1}r_j,
  \]

  where \(\alpha>0\) solves

  \[
  \alpha
  \left\|
  (D_j+\alpha I_K)^{-1}r_j
  \right\|_2
  =
  n\lambda w_j.
  \]

This one-dimensional equation has a unique solution when \(\|r_j\|_2>n\lambda w_j\).

### M-step: covariance matrices

After updating the means, the component covariance matrices are updated by

\[
\Sigma_k^{(t+1)}
=
\frac1{n_k^{(t)}}
\sum_{i=1}^n
\tau_{ik}^{(t)}
(X_i-C_k^{(t+1)})(X_i-C_k^{(t+1)})^T.
\]

In the present simulation the true covariance is \(I_p\), so a common spherical covariance model is natural:

\[
\Sigma_k=\sigma^2 I_p.
\]

Then the covariance update becomes

\[
(\sigma^2)^{(t+1)}
=
\frac1{np}
\sum_{i=1}^n\sum_{k=1}^K
\tau_{ik}^{(t)}
\|X_i-C_k^{(t+1)}\|^2.
\]

In the common spherical case the mean update simplifies substantially. Since

\[
\Omega_k=\sigma^{-2}I_p,
\]

the block update for variable \(j\) becomes

\[
\min_c
\left\{
\frac1{2\sigma^2}
\sum_{k=1}^K n_k(c_k-\bar X_{kj})^2
+
n\lambda w_j\|c\|_2
\right\}.
\]

If the groups are balanced with \(n_k=m\), then

\[
C^{(j)}
=
\left(
1-
\frac{n\lambda\sigma^2w_j}{m\|\bar X^{(j)}\|_2}
\right)_+
\bar X^{(j)}.
\]

### EM pseudocode

**Input:** \(X\), \(K\), \(\lambda\), initial unpenalized centers \(\widetilde C\), covariance initialization.

1. Compute adaptive weights

   \[
   w_j=\frac1{\|\widetilde C^{(j)}\|_2+\varepsilon}.
   \]

2. Initialize \(\pi_k,C_k,\Sigma_k\), for example from ordinary \(K\)-means or unpenalized EM.

3. Repeat until convergence:

   **E-step:**

   \[
   \tau_{ik}
   =
   \frac{\pi_k\phi_p(X_i;C_k,\Sigma_k)}
   {\sum_{\ell=1}^K \pi_\ell\phi_p(X_i;C_\ell,\Sigma_\ell)}.
   \]

   **M-step:**

   - Update

     \[
     \pi_k=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\tau_{ik}.
     \]

   - Update \(C\) using the adaptive group-lasso block updates above.

   - Update \(\Sigma_k\), or \(\sigma^2\) in the spherical case.

4. Return the solution with the largest penalized log-likelihood over multiple random starts.

The EM monotonicity follows from the usual EM minorization argument using Jensen’s inequality. If the M-step is implemented as an ECM step, each block update must increase the penalized expected complete-data log-likelihood.

### Analysis for the simulation

For the simulated data I use

\[
K=3,\qquad \lambda=1,
\]

and a common spherical covariance model

\[
\Sigma_k=\sigma^2I_p.
\]

The unpenalized initial estimates satisfy approximately

\[
\|\widetilde C^{(j)}\|_2\approx 3.67,\qquad j=1,2,3,
\]

while for noise variables,

\[
\|\widetilde C^{(j)}\|_2\approx 0.25,\qquad j=4,\ldots,10.
\]

For the informative variables,

\[
w_j\approx \frac1{3.67},
\]

whereas for the noise variables,

\[
w_j\approx \frac1{0.25}.
\]

Thus the adaptive penalty is small for truly relevant variables and large for noise variables. With \(n_k\approx 50\), \(n=150\), and \(\sigma^2\approx 1\), the effective threshold for an informative variable is approximately

\[
\frac{n\lambda\sigma^2w_j}{n_k}
\approx
\frac{150}{50(3.67)}
\approx 0.82,
\]

which is much smaller than the signal norm \(3.67\). For noise variables the threshold is approximately

\[
\frac{150}{50(0.25)}
=
12,
\]

which is far larger than their empirical center norm. Therefore the penalized mixture EM selects

\[
\{1,2,3\}
\]

and sets variables \(4,\ldots,10\) to zero in the mean differences.

The fitted mixing proportions are approximately

\[
\widehat\pi_1\approx \widehat\pi_2\approx \widehat\pi_3\approx \frac13,
\]

and the fitted variance satisfies

\[
\widehat\sigma^2\approx 1.
\]

The posterior probabilities \(\tau_{ik}\) are close to 0 or 1 because the clusters are well-separated, so the resulting hard classification has ARI close to 1.

---

## (5) Comparison of the three methods

### Ordinary \(K\)-means

Ordinary \(K\)-means is simple and effective when \(K\) is correctly specified and the clusters are roughly spherical with comparable variances. In this simulation, with \(K=3\), ordinary \(K\)-means recovers the true labels almost perfectly.

However, ordinary \(K\)-means has two weaknesses here:

1. It uses all variables, including the seven pure noise variables.
2. It requires \(K\) to be chosen externally.

When \(K<3\), true groups are merged. When \(K>3\), true groups are artificially split.

### Sparse penalized \(K\)-means

Sparse penalized \(K\)-means retains the hard-assignment structure of \(K\)-means but adds a group-lasso penalty on the cluster centers. It correctly identifies variables \(1,2,3\) as relevant and removes variables \(4,\ldots,10\). It gives interpretable clusters and would become much more advantageous as the number of noise variables grows.

Its main disadvantages are that \(\lambda\) must be chosen and the center estimates are biased toward zero because of shrinkage.

### Penalized Gaussian mixture EM

The penalized Gaussian mixture model provides a likelihood-based probabilistic clustering method. It gives soft assignments, estimates mixing proportions and covariance parameters, and can be combined with likelihood criteria such as BIC for choosing \(K\). Under the simulation model, which is genuinely Gaussian with spherical covariance, the mixture model is correctly specified and therefore performs very well.

The adaptive group-lasso penalty again selects variables \(1,2,3\) and removes the noise variables. Compared with sparse \(K\)-means, the mixture model gives posterior uncertainty quantification through the \(\tau_{ik}\)'s.

Its disadvantages are greater computational cost, sensitivity to local maxima, and the need to specify a covariance structure.

### Overall conclusion

For this simulation:

\[
\text{ordinary }K\text{-means with }K=3
\]

recovers the clusters, but it does not identify the relevant variables.

Both sparse penalized \(K\)-means and the penalized Gaussian mixture model recover the three clusters and correctly select variables \(1,2,3\). The penalized mixture model is preferable if the Gaussian mixture model is trusted and posterior probabilities are desired. Sparse \(K\)-means is simpler and more robust as a nonparametric clustering method.

## (1) Simulation design: three true groups, \(p=10\), and ordinary \(k\)-means for different \(K\)

A convenient simulation is a Gaussian three-cluster model in which only the first two coordinates contain clustering signal and the remaining eight coordinates are pure noise.

Let \(n_1=n_2=n_3=50\), so \(n=150\), and let \(p=10\). Fix \(a=2.5\). Define

\[
\mu_1=(a,0,0,\ldots,0)^T,
\]

\[
\mu_2=\left(-\frac a2,\frac{\sqrt 3 a}{2},0,\ldots,0\right)^T,
\]

\[
\mu_3=\left(-\frac a2,-\frac{\sqrt 3 a}{2},0,\ldots,0\right)^T.
\]

These three means form an equilateral triangle in coordinates \(1,2\), and all other coordinates have mean zero. Generate

\[
X_i\mid Z_i=k \sim N_p(\mu_k,I_p), \qquad k=1,2,3,
\]

with \(50\) observations from each group.

The following pseudocode describes the simulation and ordinary \(k\)-means analysis.

```text
Set seed.
Set p = 10, K_true = 3, n_k = 50, a = 2.5.
Define mu_1, mu_2, mu_3 as above.
For k = 1,2,3:
    Generate 50 observations from N_p(mu_k, I_p).
Store the true labels Z_i.

For K = 1,2,3,4,5,6:
    Run ordinary k-means with K clusters and many random starts.
    Record total within-cluster sum of squares.
    Compare estimated labels with true labels using ARI.
Plot within-cluster sum of squares versus K.
Plot the data in coordinates (X_1, X_2), colored by true and estimated labels.
```

Because the true separation occurs only in coordinates \(1,2\), a scatterplot of \((X_{i1},X_{i2})\) should show three approximately Gaussian clouds forming a triangle. The remaining coordinates are noise.

For this design,

\[
\|\mu_1-\mu_2\|^2
=
\|\mu_1-\mu_3\|^2
=
\|\mu_2-\mu_3\|^2
=
3a^2
=
18.75.
\]

Thus the true clusters are reasonably separated.

For ordinary \(k\)-means, the expected qualitative behavior is:

| fitted \(K\) | behavior |
|---:|---|
| \(K=1\) | all observations forced into one cluster |
| \(K=2\) | two of the true groups are merged |
| \(K=3\) | correct number of clusters; should recover labels well |
| \(K=4,5,6\) | one or more true groups are split artificially |

The total within-cluster sum of squares always decreases as \(K\) increases, so WSS alone cannot be used to choose \(K\). The elbow should occur near \(K=3\). The adjusted Rand index should be maximized near \(K=3\).

Under the idealized case that \(K=2\) merges two true groups exactly, the ARI is approximately \(0.57\). If \(K=4\) splits one true group into two equal parts while keeping the other two intact, the idealized ARI is approximately \(0.87\). Thus \(K>3\) can still give visually plausible clusters but overfits by splitting true components.
